Dr. Mamdouh Mohamed AhmedMBBCh (Hons) · MSc Cardiovascular Medicine · MRCP (UK) · Founder, Onskore Academy · Author of The Essentials of MRCP

First Edition · 2026. Guideline currency: content reflects ESC and ACC/AHA practice guidelines available up to September 2026, including the 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease, 2025 ESC Myocarditis & Pericarditis, 2025 ESC Pregnancy, 2024 ESC AF, Hypertension, Chronic Coronary Syndromes and Peripheral & Aortic Diseases guidelines, and the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS and High Blood Pressure guidelines. Medicine is a changing science: check drug doses, indications and recommendation classes against the current official guideline text and local product information before clinical use.

How to Use This Book

Every chapter is built in the same order so that you always know where to look. The opener page gives you the chapter map, what the board expects, and the six numbers that win marks. Each topic then moves from mechanism to diagnosis to guideline-directed management, and closes with a Key Highlights panel — the revision layer you read the night before the exam. Each chapter ends with ten board-style questions with teaching explanations.

The guiding principle is the one I repeat in every lecture: a good mentor does not teach you what to think, but how to think. Mechanism boxes are there to make the rules logical, so you can rebuild them under pressure instead of memorising them.

The visual language

≥ 40 mmHg Every examinable number is printed in red bold — thresholds, doses, cut-offs, time windows.

marker highlight The single sentence in a section that matters most.

Term · Drug · Sign Defined terms in navy, drugs in teal, eponymous signs in violet.

I IIa IIb III Class of recommendation: recommended · should be considered · may be considered · not recommended. Letters A/B/C give the level of evidence.

NEW CHANGED Recommendation new or changed in the latest ESC guideline compared with its

predecessor.

ESC vs ACC/AHA tables Navy header for ESC, burgundy for ACC/AHA — the differences examiners like to ask about.

Chronic Heart Failure

From a raised natriuretic peptide to four foundational drugs — classifying, diagnosing and treating the failing heart in the 2026 era.

What the board expects you to know

  • The ESC 2026 two-phenotype classification (HFrEF < 50% / HFpEF ≥ 50%) and how it differs from ESC 2021 and ACC/AHA 2022.
  • Natriuretic peptide rule-out thresholds, their confounders, and the diagnostic pathway to echocardiography.
  • The four foundational drugs of HFrEF — mechanisms, start/target doses, rapid sequencing and safety monitoring.
  • Which add-on drugs, devices and interventions apply to which patient, and which drugs are harmful.
  • Evidence-based HFpEF therapy (SGLT2i, MRA, GLP-1 RA in obesity), iron deficiency criteria and HFimpEF management.

Numbers that win marks

< 50%LVEF — HFrEF (ESC 2026)
≥ 125 pg/mLNT-proBNP — chronic HF threshold (BNP ≥ 35)
36 hACEi washout before ARNI
< 100 µg/LFerritin (or 100–299 + TSAT < 20%) — iron deficiency
≥ 150 msLBBB QRS + LVEF ≤ 35% — Class I CRT
1–2 wkUp-titration interval for FMT

1.1 Definition, Classification & Epidemiology

DEFINITION

Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome of cardinal symptoms (breathlessness, fatigue, ankle swelling) with or without signs (raised JVP, crackles, oedema), caused by a structural and/or functional cardiac abnormality and corroborated by elevated natriuretic peptides and/or objective evidence of pulmonary or systemic congestion . It is not a diagnosis in itself — the underlying cause must always be sought.

The Universal Definition of HF (2021) and its Second Universal Definition (AHA/ACC/ESC/WHF with HFSA, HFA and JHFS, 2026) harmonise terminology across societies. The 2026 consensus reaffirms the stage continuum, emphasises Stage B (pre-HF) as the window for prevention, and describes three clinically actionable EF groups: reduced, preserved and improved EF, with trajectories of improvement, remission and recovery.

Classification by ejection fraction

The single most important examinable change of 2026: the ESC abolished HFmrEF . Patients with LVEF 41–49% share the pathophysiology (predominantly systolic dysfunction, often ischaemic) and the drug responsiveness of HFrEF, so they are now simply HFrEF.

LVEF > 40%

ESC 2026 HF guideline (Eur Heart J, ehag100); ESC 2021 HF (Eur Heart J 2021;42:3599); Heidenreich et al., Circulation 2022.

EXAM TRAP

Read the question's guideline frame. A patient with LVEF 45% is HFrEF under ESC 2026 but HFmrEF under ESC 2021 and ACC/AHA 2022. Therapy thresholds that are defined by trial entry criteria did not move: CRT and primary-prevention ICD still require LVEF ≤ 35%; digoxin (ESC 2026) is framed for LVEF ≤ 40%; vericiguat for LVEF < 45%.

Stages and functional class

ESC 2026 adopts the A–D staging long used by ACC/AHA, so that recommendations span prevention to advanced disease. Stages describe progression (a patient never moves backwards from C to B); NYHA class describes current symptoms and can fluctuate in both directions.

NYHA functional class
  • I — no limitation of ordinary activity.
  • II — slight limitation; ordinary activity causes symptoms.
  • III — marked limitation; less-than-ordinary activity causes
  • symptoms; comfortable at rest.
  • IV — symptoms at rest or with any activity.
Epidemiology (high yield)
  • Prevalence ≈ 1–2% of adults; ≥ 10% over age 70.
  • Lifetime risk ≈ 1 in 4–5 at age 55.
  • HFpEF is now ≈ half of all HF and rising (ageing, obesity,
  • hypertension).
  • After a first HF hospitalisation, mortality is high — each
  • readmission worsens prognosis.
WHAT CHANGED IN 2026 (ESC)
  • Two phenotypes only: HFrEF (< 50%) and HFpEF (≥ 50%); HFmrEF abolished.
  • Stages A–D adopted as the organising framework.
  • "Acute HF" renamed "decompensated HF" (DHF) — worsening may be gradual and some episodes are managed as outpatients.

New therapy nomenclature replaces "GDMT": Foundational Medical Therapy (FMT) — Class I for the general HF population with convincing morbidity/mortality benefit; Additional Medical Therapy (AMT) — Class IIa/IIb, or Class I in specific subsets; Guideline-Directed Interventional Therapy (GDIT) — devices and procedures.

New ESC evidence methodology: level B is split into B1 and B2.

Key highlightsDefinition & classification

  • HF = symptoms ± signs + cardiac abnormality, corroborated by raised NPs or objective congestion.
  • ESC 2026: HFrEF = LVEF < 50%; HFpEF = LVEF ≥ 50%; no HFmrEF.
  • ACC/AHA 2022 (and ESC 2021): HFrEF ≤ 40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥ 50%.
  • HFimpEF = rise of ≥ 10 points to above 40% — it is still HF, not cure.
  • Stages A→D only progress; NYHA I–IV fluctuates with symptoms.
  • ESC 2026 replaces "acute HF" with decompensated HF and "GDMT" with FMT / AMT / GDIT.
  • Device LVEF thresholds (≤ 35%) are unchanged by the new EF classification.

1.2 Aetiology & Pathophysiology

Causes

In high-income and most Arab/Egyptian cohorts, ischaemic heart disease is the most common cause of HFrEF, followed by dilated cardiomyopathy (genetic, toxic, post-myocarditis) and valvular disease. HFpEF is driven by ageing, hypertension, obesity, diabetes, AF and CKD — but specific, treatable phenotypes (amyloidosis, HCM, constriction) must be excluded.

Valvular AS, AR, primary MR Echo — always treat the valve first

Cardiomyopathies DCM, HCM, ARVC, LV non-compaction, restrictive CMR, genetics, family screening Infiltrative / storage ATTR / AL amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, Fabry Bone scintigraphy + free light chains; FDG-PET; T2*

  • trastuzumab, immune checkpoint inhibitors, radiation

  • oncology

  • thiamine deficiency

Why the failing heart keeps failing

An index injury reduces stroke volume. The body "reads" this as haemorrhage and activates the sympathetic nervous system, the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and vasopressin. These are life-saving in blood loss but, sustained over months, they cause vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention, myocyte hypertrophy, apoptosis and fibrosis — adverse remodelling: the LV dilates, becomes spherical, develops functional MR, and EF falls further.

MECHANISM — THE LOGIC OF FMT

Every foundational drug either blocks a harmful compensatory system or amplifies a protective one: Beta-blocker → blocks sympathetic toxicity (↓ HR, ↓ arrhythmia, reverse remodelling).

ACEi / ARB → blocks angiotensin II; ARNI adds neprilysin inhibition, raising endogenous natriuretic peptides (vasodilatation, natriuresis, antifibrotic).

MRA → blocks aldosterone "escape" (fibrosis, K⁺/Mg²⁺ loss).

SGLT2 inhibitor → osmotic natriuresis and glucosuria with neurohormonal-sparing decongestion, plus favourable myocardial and renal metabolic effects.

Diuretics treat congestion but do not reverse remodelling — they relieve symptoms, not prognosis.

Natriuretic peptide biology
  • Released from ventricular myocytes in response to wall
  • stress (BNP) — atria for ANP.
  • proBNP → BNP (active, t½ ≈ 20 min) + NT-proBNP
  • (inactive, t½ ≈ 1–2 h, renally cleared).
  • BNP is a neprilysin substrate → rises on sacubitril; NTproBNP is not → use NT-proBNP to monitor ARNI patients.
HFpEF — a systemic syndrome
  • Comorbidity-driven microvascular inflammation → titin
  • stiffening and fibrosis → ↑ LV stiffness.
  • Impaired relaxation, left atrial myopathy, chronotropic
  • incompetence, pulmonary hypertension.
  • Symptoms are exertional: filling pressures rise steeply on
  • exercise.

Key highlightsAetiology & pathophysiology

  • Ischaemic heart disease is the commonest cause of HFrEF.
  • HFpEF: ageing, hypertension, obesity, diabetes, AF, CKD — but exclude amyloid, HCM, constriction.
  • Reversible causes to always exclude: tachycardia, alcohol, thyroid, valve disease, ischaemia, RV pacing.
  • Neurohormonal activation (SNS, RAAS, AVP) drives remodelling — FMT blocks it.
  • BNP is degraded by neprilysin; NT-proBNP is used to monitor patients on sacubitril/valsartan.
  • Diuretics improve symptoms but not survival.

1.3 Clinical Assessment & Diagnosis

Symptoms and signs

Symptoms are sensitive but non-specific; signs are specific but insensitive (and often absent in treated patients or obesity). The most specific clinical findings for raised filling pressure are a raised JVP, a positive hepatojugular reflux and a third heart sound.

>80 S R · >240

AF

>220 S R · >660 AF—

ESC 2021 HF guideline and HFA consensus statements; ACC/AHA 2022 uses the same ambulatory (BNP ≥ 35 / NT-proBNP ≥ 125) and hospitalised (BNP ≥ 100 / NT-proBNP ≥ 300) values to define Stage B.

NPs higher than expected
  • Age, female sex
  • AF (≈ threefold higher cut-offs)
  • CKD (reduced clearance, esp. NT-proBNP)
  • ACS, PE, pulmonary hypertension, RV strain
  • Sepsis, critical illness, anaemia, hyperthyroidism
  • Sacubitril/valsartan — raises BNP only
NPs lower than expected
  • Obesity — values roughly halved (BMI > 30)
  • Flash pulmonary oedema (first hour)
  • "Upstream" causes: mitral stenosis, constrictive
  • pericarditis, tamponade
  • Treated, euvolaemic patients (diuretics, FMT)
  • Some HFpEF patients (especially obese)
EXAM TRAP

A normal NT-proBNP in a breathless obese patient does not exclude HFpEF, and a normal BNP does not exclude constrictive pericarditis. Conversely, in a patient on sacubitril/valsartan, a rising BNP may be a drug effect — the board answer is to follow NT-proBNP.

Core investigations

Prognostic markers

Poor prognosis in chronic HF is signalled by: persistently high NPs despite therapy, raised hs-troponin, hyponatraemia, low systolic BP, worsening renal function, QRS widening, recurrent hospitalisation, intolerance of FMT, peak VO₂ < 12–14 mL/kg/min, 6-minute walk < 300 m, cachexia and frailty. Validated scores (MAGGIC, Seattle HF Model) support — but never replace — clinical judgement.

Key highlightsClinical assessment & diagnosis

  • Most specific bedside signs: raised JVP, hepatojugular reflux, S3.
  • Chronic rule-out: NT-proBNP < 125 pg/mL / BNP < 35 pg/mL.
  • Acute rule-out: NT-proBNP < 300 / BNP < 100 pg/mL / MR-proANP < 120 pmol/L.
  • AF, age and CKD raise NPs; obesity lowers them; ARNI raises BNP but not NT-proBNP.
  • Every HF patient: ECG, echo, CXR, bloods including ferritin + TSAT.
  • CMR LGE pattern gives aetiology: subendocardial = ischaemic; mid-wall = DCM.
  • Suspected amyloid → bone scintigraphy plus free light chains/immunofixation (exclude AL).
  • Peak VO₂ < 12–14 mL/kg/min and 6MWD < 300 m mark poor prognosis.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • ACEi, ARNI or ARB as FMT in all patients I A
  • Beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol) as FMT I A
  • CHANGED MRA in symptomatic HF independent of LVEF I A
  • SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin) as FMT, independent of LVEF I A
  • Implementation
  • NEW Up-titrate FMT every 1–2 weeks towards target doses I C
  • NEW Continue FMT at the highest tolerated doses, even when asymptomatic or LVEF has improved I C Stage B (pre-HF)
  • NEW ACEi (ARB if intolerant) in asymptomatic LV dysfunction with LVEF ≤ 40% I A
  • NEW Beta-blocker in Stage B with LVEF < 50% I B1
  • NEW Eplerenone after MI with LVEF ≤ 40% and HF signs or diabetes I B1
  • ESC 2026 HF guideline (Eur Heart J, ehag100). Rows marked new/changed appear in the 2026 tables of new and revised recommendations.

1.4 Foundational Medical Therapy of HFrEF

Four drug classes — the "four pillars" — each reduce mortality and HF hospitalisation independently and additively. ESC 2026 names them Foundational Medical Therapy (FMT): a beta-blocker, an ACEi / ARNI / ARB, an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor. The modern priority is to get all four on board quickly at low dose, then uptitrate — not to perfect one drug before starting the next.

Sequencing — how fast, and in which order?

Neither ESC nor ACC/AHA mandates an order. The old "ACEi → beta-blocker → MRA" staircase took months and lost patients on the way. Both guidelines now favour starting all four within weeks, then up-titrating every 1–2 weeks. Choose the next drug by the patient's phenotype.

CLINICAL APPROACH — TAILOR THE ORDER TO THE PHENOTYPE
  • High HR, adequate BP: prioritise beta-blocker up-titration.
  • Low BP (SBP 90–100 mmHg): SGLT2i and MRA first (little BP effect); ARNI at 24/26 mg; stop non-HF antihypertensives.
  • High K⁺ / CKD: SGLT2i early (lowers hyperkalaemia risk); K⁺ binder to enable MRA/RAASi.
BOARD PEARL — STRONG-HF LOGIC

After a HF admission, rapid up-titration of RAASi, beta-blocker and MRA to full dose within 2 weeks of discharge, with close clinical/laboratory follow-up, reduced death or HF readmission at 180 days (STRONGHF). Speed is safe when monitoring is intense.

Safety monitoring

Beta-blocker practicalities
  • Start when clinically stable/euvolaemic; "start low, go
  • slow" (double every ≥ 2 weeks).
  • In mild decompensation: continue (halve if needed); stop
  • only in shock/low output.
  • Asthma is a relative contraindication; COPD is not — use a
  • β1-selective agent.
  • Target HR in sinus rhythm ≈ 60–70 bpm.
SGLT2i practicalities
  • Expect an initial eGFR dip (haemodynamic) — do not stop.
  • Mild diuretic effect: reduce loop dose if dry.
  • Risks: genital mycotic infection; euglycaemic ketoacidosis
  • (T1DM, fasting, surgery — hold ≥ 3 days pre-op).
  • Not for T1DM or dialysis.
MECHANISM — WHY ARNI ANGIOEDEMA AND THE 36-HOUR RULE

Neprilysin and ACE both degrade bradykinin. Inhibiting both at once (ACEi + sacubitril, or omapatrilat historically) causes bradykinin accumulation and high rates of angioedema. Hence the 36-hour ACEi washout before sacubitril/valsartan, and absolute contraindication with any history of angioedema.

Switching from an ARB needs no washout.

Key highlightsFoundational medical therapy

  • FMT = beta-blocker + ACEi/ARNI/ARB + MRA + SGLT2i — all Class I, level A (ESC 2026).
  • ESC 2026: MRA and SGLT2i are Class I independent of LVEF.
  • Start all four within weeks; up-titrate every 1–2 weeks; continue even if LVEF improves.
  • ACC/AHA 2022: ARNI is the preferred RAS inhibitor (1 A); ACEi only when ARNI not feasible.
  • ARNI: 36 h ACEi washout; contraindicated with prior angioedema; monitor NT-proBNP not BNP.
  • Evidence-based beta-blockers: bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, nebivolol (≥ 70 y) — not tartrate/ atenolol.
  • MRA: avoid if K⁺ > 5.0 or eGFR < 30; stop if K⁺ > 6.0.
  • Creatinine rise up to 50% on RAASi, and the early eGFR dip on SGLT2i, are expected — do not stop.
  • Drug Patient who qualifies ESC ACC/AHA 2022
  • K⁺ binders
  • (patiromer, SZC)
  • Hyperkalaemia limiting RAASi/MRA 2021: IIb C 2b B-R
  • ESC 2026 classes shown where confirmed; otherwise the ESC 2021 class is shown and labelled.

1.5 Additional Medical Therapy & Drugs to Avoid

ESC 2026 groups the remaining evidence-based drugs as Additional Medical Therapy (AMT): they help selected patients, or improve symptoms, but do not have the universal outcome benefit of FMT. The board tests who qualifies — the entry criteria of the trials.

Key trials
  • SHIFT — ivabradine ↓ CV death/HFH (driven by HFH), HR
  • ≥ 70 on beta-blocker.
  • VICTORIA — vericiguat (sGC stimulator) modest ↓ CV
  • death/HFH after worsening HF.
  • A-HeFT — H-ISDN ↓ mortality in African Americans.
  • DIG — digoxin neutral for mortality, ↓ HFH; DIGIT-HF —
  • digitoxin ↓ death or HFH in HFrEF on modern therapy →
  • 2026 upgrade.
  • GALACTIC-HF — omecamtiv mecarbil modest benefit; not
  • in guideline recommendations.
Digoxin safety
  • Aim for a low serum level: 0.5–0.9 ng/mL; levels
  • > 1.2 ng/mL are associated with harm.
  • Toxicity ↑ with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, renal
  • impairment, amiodarone, verapamil.
  • Digitoxin is hepatically cleared — attractive in CKD.
  • Toxicity ECG: bidirectional VT, atrial tachycardia with
  • block, regularised AF.

Diuretics

Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torasemide) relieve congestion. Use the lowest dose that maintains euvolaemia; self-adjustment by daily weight (e.g. extra dose if gain > 1.5–2 kg in 2–3 days) is taught to patients. Torasemide and bumetanide have better, more predictable oral bioavailability than furosemide (≈ 50%, highly variable) — but TRANSFORM-HF showed no mortality difference between torasemide and furosemide.

EXAM TRAP

A patient with HFrEF and AF with fast ventricular rate: the board answer for rate control is a beta-blocker ± digoxin — never diltiazem or verapamil. For rhythm control, amiodarone (or catheter ablation) — not flecainide.

1.6 Devices & Interventional Therapy — Overview

ESC 2026 calls these Guideline-Directed Interventional Therapy (GDIT). Device decisions are made after at least 3 months of optimised FMT (reassess LVEF — many patients improve above the threshold). Detailed ICD/CRT criteria, lead choice and programming are covered in Chapter 20; the essentials follow.

Key highlightsAdditional therapy & drugs to avoid

  • Ivabradine: sinus rhythm, HR ≥ 70, LVEF ≤ 35%, on max beta-blocker.
  • Vericiguat: recent worsening HF, LVEF < 45% — Class IIb.
  • Digoxin/digitoxin upgraded to IIa in ESC 2026 (DIGIT-HF) for LVEF ≤ 40%.
  • H-ISDN: ACC/AHA Class 1 in African Americans NYHA III–IV; ESC IIa.
  • Diuretics: symptom relief only; lowest effective dose; resistance → sequential nephron blockade.
  • Avoid in HFrEF: TZDs, diltiazem/verapamil, NSAIDs, saxagliptin, class IC drugs, triple RAAS block.
  • ASV is harmful in HFrEF with central sleep apnoea (SERVE-HF).
  • Recommendation (symptomatic, sinus rhythm, LVEF ≤ 35% on OMT) Class Level
  • LBBB, QRS ≥ 150 ms I A
  • LBBB, QRS 130–149 ms IIa B
  • Non-LBBB, QRS ≥ 150 ms IIa B
  • Non-LBBB, QRS 130–149 ms IIb B
  • QRS < 130 ms without a pacing indication III A
  • CHANGED HFrEF with an indication for ventricular pacing for high-degree AV block — CRT rather than RV pacing (2021: I A)
  • IIa B1
  • NEW Start FMT and plan CRT simultaneously when LBBB ≥ 150 ms and LVEF ≤ 35% (rather than waiting 3 months)
  • IIb C
  • NEW AV-node ablation + CRT in permanent AF with poor rate control and ≥ 1 HF hospitalisation IIa B1
BOARD PEARL — THE COAPT VS MITRA-FR PARADOX

TEER reduced death and HFH in COAPT but not in MITRA-FR. The difference is proportion: COAPT enrolled disproportionate MR (large regurgitant orifice relative to a not-so-dilated LV) on maximally titrated therapy; MITRA-FR enrolled proportionate MR in very dilated ventricles, where MR is a marker, not the driver, of disease. First optimise FMT and CRT; then treat MR that remains severe.

1.7 HF with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF)

HFpEF is a diagnosis of positive evidence, not of exclusion: LVEF ≥ 50% plus objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction or raised LV filling pressure, supported by raised NPs. The typical patient is an elderly woman with hypertension, obesity, diabetes and AF. Before labelling "HFpEF", actively exclude its mimics — amyloidosis, HCM, constriction, valve disease, pulmonary disease, obesity-related deconditioning.

Diagnosis

Key highlightsDevices & interventions

  • Reassess LVEF after ≥ 3 months of optimised FMT before primary-prevention ICD/CRT.
  • Primary ICD: LVEF ≤ 35%, NYHA II–III; ESC — ischaemic I A, non-ischaemic IIa A; never within 40 days of MI.
  • CRT Class I: sinus rhythm, LBBB, QRS ≥ 150 ms, LVEF ≤ 35%; QRS < 130 ms → no CRT (ESC).
  • ACC/AHA uses QRS ≥ 120 ms as CRT floor and gives non-ischaemic primary ICD Class 1.
  • ESC 2026 upgrades: mitral TEER (I), PA-pressure monitoring (IIa); CRT-for-AV-block downgraded to IIa.
  • TEER works in disproportionate secondary MR after FMT optimisation (COAPT criteria).
H₂FPEF score (0–9)
  • Heavy: BMI > 30 — 2
  • Hypertensive: ≥ 2 BP drugs — 1
  • Fibrillation (paroxysmal/persistent AF) — 3
  • Pulmonary hypertension: PASP > 35 mmHg — 1
  • Elder: age > 60 — 1
  • Filling pressure: E/e′ > 9 — 1
  • Score 0–1 low · 2–5 intermediate (test further) · 6–9 high
  • probability
HFA-PEFF score
  • Three domains — functional, morphological, biomarker;
  • each major criterion = 2 points, minor = 1 (max 2 per
  • domain).
  • Total ≥ 5 → HFpEF confirmed.
  • 2–4 → diastolic stress echo or invasive haemodynamics.
  • ≤ 1 → HFpEF unlikely.
  • Final step: search for specific aetiology (amyloid, HCM,
  • etc.).
DON'T CONFUSE — "HFPEF" THAT IS REALLY CARDIAC AMYLOIDOSIS

Red flags for ATTR amyloid: age > 65 with LVH but low/normal QRS voltage, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar canal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, low-flow AS, AV block, persistently raised troponin, intolerance of antihypertensives, and apical sparing on GLS. Work-up: bone scintigraphy + serum free light chains + serum/urine immunofixation. Grade 2–3 uptake with no monoclonal protein diagnoses ATTR without biopsy. ESC 2026: tafamidis (Class I, B) in variant ATTR with NYHA I–II; TTR silencer (vutrisiran) or stabiliser (tafamidis, acoramidis) in ATTR-CM NYHA I–III (Class I, A).

Treatment

Until 2021, no drug improved outcomes in HFpEF. The evidence changed with SGLT2 inhibitors (EMPERORPreserved, DELIVER), the non-steroidal MRA finerenone (FINEARTS-HF) and incretin-based weight loss (STEP-HFpEF, SUMMIT).

CLINICAL APPROACH — THE HFPEF CHECKLIST
  • Decongest: loop diuretic to euvolaemia.
  • FMT: SGLT2i + MRA (ESC 2026).
  • Phenotype: obese → GLP-1 RA; AF → rate/rhythm control, anticoagulate; hypertension → SBP < 130 mmHg; CAD → treat ischaemia.
  • Exclude specific causes: amyloid, HCM, constriction, valve disease.
  • Exercise training — improves capacity and QoL.

Key highlightsHFpEF

  • HFpEF = LVEF ≥ 50% + objective diastolic dysfunction/raised filling pressure + raised NPs.
  • Simplified criteria: LAVI > 34 mL/m², E/e′ > 9, PASP > 35 mmHg, LVMI ≥ 95 (F)/115 (M) g/m².
  • Invasive gold standard: PCWP ≥ 15 at rest or ≥ 25 mmHg on exercise.
  • H₂FPEF: AF scores 3, obesity 2; ≥ 6 = high probability.
  • ESC 2026 FMT for HFpEF: SGLT2i (I A) + MRA (I A).
  • Obese HFpEF (LVEF ≥ 45%, BMI ≥ 30): semaglutide or tirzepatide — IIa.
  • ACC/AHA 2022: SGLT2i 2a; MRA/ARNI/ARB 2b; nitrates/PDE-5i no benefit.
  • Always exclude ATTR amyloid: scintigraphy + light chains.
  • Comorbidity Board rules
  • Atrial fibrillation Anticoagulate by CHA₂DS₂-VA — DOAC preferred (not in mechanical valves / moderate–severe MS) Rate: beta-blocker ± digoxin; avoid non-DHP CCB in HFrEF
  • Rhythm: amiodarone; catheter ablation improves outcomes in selected HFrEF (CASTLE-AF)
  • Hypertension FMT drugs lower BP first; add amlodipine/felodipine if needed
  • Avoid moxonidine, α-blockers, non-DHP CCB (HFrEF)
  • Type 2 diabetes SGLT2i first; metformin safe unless eGFR < 30 / decompensated
  • GLP-1 RA neutral-to-beneficial; avoid TZDs and saxagliptin
  • Insulin can cause fluid retention — monitor
  • CKD &
  • hyperkalaemia
  • Do not withhold FMT for moderate CKD
  • K⁺ binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) enable RAASi/MRA continuation
  • COPD / asthma COPD: β1-selective blocker is safe
  • Asthma: relative caution; avoid non-selective agents
  • Sleep-disordered
  • breathing
  • Obstructive: CPAP for symptoms
  • Central (Cheyne–Stokes) in HFrEF: ASV contraindicated (SERVE-HF)
  • Obesity GLP-1 RA in HFpEF (IIa); bariatric surgery if BMI ≥ 35 after failed measures (IIb) "Obesity paradox" in observational data does not mean weight gain is protective
  • Depression, frailty,
  • cachexia
  • ESC 2026: assess anxiety, depression, frailty (IIa C)
  • SSRIs safe; avoid tricyclics
  • Thyroid Check TSH; amiodarone causes both hypo- and hyperthyroidism
  • Gout Avoid NSAIDs; use colchicine (short, renally adjusted) or steroids; allopurinol for prophylaxis

1.8 Iron Deficiency & Key Comorbidities

Iron deficiency

Iron deficiency (ID) affects up to half of HF patients, with or without anaemia, and independently worsens exercise capacity, QoL and outcomes. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, so HF-specific criteria are higher than laboratory "normal".

DEFINITION — IRON DEFICIENCY IN HF
  • Serum ferritin < 100 µg/L (ng/mL), or ferritin 100–299 µg/L with transferrin saturation (TSAT) < 20%.
  • Screen all HF patients (FBC, ferritin, TSAT).

IIa A

ACC/AHA 2022: IV iron in HFrEF with iron deficiency to improve functional status and QoL — 2a (B-R); ESAs to treat anaemia in HF — 3: No benefit. ESC 2026 carries a dedicated iron-deficiency recommendation table; its exact grading should be checked against the published text.

Evidence
  • FAIR-HF, CONFIRM-HF — FCM ↑ 6MWD, NYHA, QoL.
  • AFFIRM-AHF — FCM after AHF ↓ HF hospitalisations.
  • IRONMAN — ferric derisomaltose: ↓ HFH/CV death
  • (borderline).
  • HEART-FID — FCM: no significant benefit on hierarchical
  • endpoint.
  • IRONOUT-HF — oral iron does not replete stores or
  • improve VO₂.
Practical
  • Use IV iron — oral iron is poorly absorbed (hepcidin, gut
  • oedema).
  • Recheck ferritin/TSAT after ≈ 3 months and re-dose if still
  • deficient.
  • FCM can cause hypophosphataemia.
  • Do not use ESAs (darbepoetin — RED-HF neutral, ↑
  • thromboembolism).
  • Investigate for GI blood loss when appropriate.

Other comorbidities — the rules that are examined

BOARD PEARL

A patient in whom the MRA was stopped for K⁺ 5.8 mmol/L should not simply lose a mortality-reducing drug: the board answer is add a potassium binder and re-challenge (ESC 2021 IIb, ACC/AHA 2b). SGLT2 inhibitors also reduce hyperkalaemia risk.

Key highlightsIron deficiency & comorbidities

  • Iron deficiency: ferritin < 100, or 100–299 µg/L with TSAT < 20% — anaemia not required.
  • Treat with IV iron (FCM or ferric derisomaltose); oral iron is ineffective (IRONOUT-HF).
  • ESC 2023 FU: IV iron for symptoms/QoL Class I A; to reduce HFH Class IIa A.
  • ESAs are not recommended for anaemia in HF (RED-HF).
  • AF in HFrEF: beta-blocker ± digoxin for rate; never diltiazem/verapamil; consider ablation.
  • Diabetes in HF: SGLT2i first; avoid TZDs and saxagliptin.
  • Hyperkalaemia: binder and continue FMT rather than stop the MRA.

1.9 HFimpEF, Monitoring & Follow-up

HF with improved EF

Up to a quarter of patients with HFrEF improve LVEF on FMT. HFimpEF is remission, not cure: the ventricle often remains abnormal (strain, fibrosis, dilatation) and relapse is common when therapy is withdrawn.

Predictors of recovery
  • Non-ischaemic aetiology, female sex, shorter HF duration
  • Reversible trigger: tachycardia, alcohol, peripartum,
  • myocarditis, LBBB treated with CRT
  • Narrow QRS, smaller LV, less LGE on CMR
  • Early and full FMT
TRED-HF (withdrawal trial)
  • Recovered DCM, stepwise withdrawal of therapy.
  • ≈ 44% relapsed within 6 months (vs none on continued
  • therapy).
  • Consequence: continue FMT indefinitely.

ACC/AHA/HFSA 2022

In HFimpEF, continue GDMT to prevent relapse of HF and LV dysfunction, even if asymptomatic 1 B-R Non-pharmacological care

B 1/I B 2

Remote monitoring

Non-invasive telemonitoring (TIM-HF2) reduced days lost to unplanned CV hospitalisation or death (ESC 2021 IIb B). The implantable PA-pressure sensor (CardioMEMS) reduced HF hospitalisation in CHAMPION and MONITOR-HF (GUIDE-HF neutral overall) and is upgraded to IIa B1 in ESC 2026 for NYHA III patients with a prior HF hospitalisation. Device diagnostics (thoracic impedance, heart sounds, activity) are adjuncts. Routine NP-guided titration is not recommended (GUIDE-IT neutral).

Follow-up

CLINICAL APPROACH — STRUCTURED FOLLOW-UP
  • During titration: review every 1–2 weeks (clinic or nurse), with U&E after each change.
  • After discharge: first visit within 1–2 weeks (Chapter 2).
  • Stable patients: every 3–6 months — symptoms, volume, BP/HR, ECG (QRS, rhythm), renal function, K⁺, iron status.

Echo: after 3–6 months of optimised FMT (device decisions), and whenever clinical status changes. Ask every visit: are all four FMT drugs on board at target or maximally tolerated doses? If not, why not? Red flags for advanced HF referral: "I NEED HELP" (Chapter 2).

Key highlightsHFimpEF, monitoring & follow-up

  • HFimpEF: continue FMT indefinitely — ESC 2026 I C; ACC/AHA 1 B-R.
  • TRED-HF: ≈ 44% relapse within 6 months of withdrawal.
  • ESC 2026 allows gradual withdrawal only in highly selected patients (IIb C).
  • Exercise training: Class I — improves capacity, QoL and HFH.
  • CardioMEMS upgraded to IIa (ESC 2026) for NYHA III with prior HFH.
  • Routine NP-guided titration is not recommended (GUIDE-IT).
  • Most FMT drugs are contraindicated in pregnancy — counsel before conception.

1.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 61-year-old man with a previous anterior MI has exertional breathlessness. NT-proBNP is 860 pg/mL and echocardiography shows LVEF 45% with anterior hypokinesia. According to the ESC 2026 guideline, how is his HF classified and treated?

Answer B ESC 2026 abolished HFmrEF: LVEF < 50% is HFrEF and receives full FMT (beta-blocker, ACEi/ARNI/ARB, MRA, SGLT2i). Option A uses the abolished HFmrEF category, C ignores the reduced EF, E ignores symptoms; HFimpEF requires prior lower EF with ≥ 10-point improvement.

Q2 A 69-year-old woman (BMI 39 kg/m²) with paroxysmal AF and hypertension on three drugs has exertional dyspnoea. LVEF is 60%, E/e′ 12, PASP 38 mmHg. NT-proBNP is 105 pg/mL. What is the best interpretation?

Answer C H₂FPEF = obesity 2 + hypertension 1 + AF 3 + PH 1 + age 1 + E/e′ 1 = 9 — high probability. Obesity lowers NPs by roughly half, so a "normal" NT-proBNP does not exclude HFpEF. Constriction cannot be "confirmed" from these data.

Q3 A patient with HFrEF (LVEF 30%, NYHA II) takes ramipril 10 mg daily, bisoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. You decide to switch to sacubitril/valsartan. What is correct?

Answer B Combined ACE and neprilysin inhibition causes bradykinin accumulation and angioedema; a 36-hour ACEi washout is mandatory (ACC/AHA 3: Harm if not). No washout is needed from an ARB.

Q4 Three months after starting sacubitril/valsartan, a stable patient's BNP has risen from 310 to 420 pg/mL, while NT-proBNP fell from 1900 to 1100 pg/mL. He is euvolaemic. What is the best action?

Answer C BNP is a neprilysin substrate and rises on sacubitril; NT-proBNP is not, and its fall indicates benefit. Monitor ARNI patients with NT-proBNP. No reason to admit or stop the drug.

Q5 A 58-year-old with HFrEF (LVEF 28%, sinus rhythm, HR 76 bpm, BP 112/70, eGFR 48, K⁺ 4.6) takes bisoprolol 10 mg, sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg bd and eplerenone 50 mg. He remains NYHA II. What is the next best step?

Answer B He is missing the fourth pillar. An SGLT2i (Class I A, DAPA-HF/EMPEROR-Reduced) comes before any additional therapy. Ivabradine (HR ≥ 70) is an add-on only after FMT is complete; CRT needs a wide QRS.

Q6 A 66-year-old with HFrEF (NYHA III, on full FMT) has Hb 13.4 g/dL, ferritin 190 µg/L and TSAT 14%. What is the most appropriate management?

Answer C Iron deficiency in HF = ferritin 100–299 with TSAT < 20%, regardless of Hb. IV iron improves symptoms and QoL (ESC 2023 FU I A). Oral iron fails (IRONOUT-HF); ESAs are not recommended (RED-HF).

Q7 Four patients in sinus rhythm with LVEF 30%, NYHA II–III, after 3 months of optimised FMT. Which has a Class I ESC indication for CRT?

Answer C Class I CRT = LBBB with QRS ≥ 150 ms and LVEF ≤ 35%. LBBB 130–149 and non-LBBB ≥ 150 are IIa; non-LBBB 130– 149 IIb; QRS < 130 ms is Class III regardless of echo dyssynchrony (EchoCRT).

Q8 A 70-year-old with HFrEF (LVEF 32%) develops persistent AF at 128 bpm. BP 118/72; he is euvolaemic on bisoprolol 2.5 mg. Which drug should be avoided for rate control?

Answer C Non-dihydropyridine CCBs are negatively inotropic and worsen HFrEF. Rate control uses beta-blocker up-titration ± digoxin/digitoxin; amiodarone is acceptable for rhythm control.

Q9 A 44-year-old woman with idiopathic DCM (LVEF 25% at diagnosis) now has LVEF 56%, normal LV size and NTproBNP 90 pg/mL after 18 months of FMT. She asks to stop her medicines. Best advice?

Answer C HFimpEF is remission, not cure: TRED-HF showed ≈ 44% relapse within 6 months of withdrawal. ESC 2026 (I C) and ACC/AHA (1 B-R) recommend continuing therapy; withdrawal is only IIb in highly selected patients.

Q10 A 76-year-old woman with HFpEF (LVEF 58%, BMI 27 kg/m², sinus rhythm) remains NYHA II after decongestion. Which drug has a Class I recommendation in ESC 2026 to reduce HF events?

Answer C ESC 2026 FMT for HFpEF is an SGLT2i and an MRA (both I A). ARNI is IIb; GLP-1 RA is IIa and requires BMI ≥ 30; ivabradine and nitrates have no role in HFpEF.

2.1 Decompensated HF: Definitions & Phenotypes

DEFINITION

Decompensated HF (DHF) — called "acute HF" until ESC 2026 — is the rapid or gradual onset or worsening of HF symptoms and signs severe enough to need urgent evaluation and escalation of therapy, usually an unplanned hospitalisation. It may be de novo (first presentation) or, far more often (≈ 70–80%), acute-onchronic decompensation.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2026 (ESC)
  • "Acute HF" → "decompensated HF": worsening is often gradual, and some episodes are treated in day units or at home with IV diuretics.
  • In-hospital care is framed in three phases: initial management → stabilisation → pre-discharge and early post-discharge.
  • SGLT2i initiation in hospital once stabilised (I B1); urinary-sodium-guided diuretics (IIb B1); acetazolamide or thiazide add-on (IIa B1).
  • Cardiogenic shock: multidisciplinary shock team (I C); microaxial flow pump in selected STEMI-shock (IIa B1); tMCS and IABP not for unselected patients (III B1).
  • Durable LVAD upgraded to Class I; early referral to an advanced HF centre is Class I.

Clinical phenotypes

Haemodynamic profiles

Two bedside questions organise treatment: Is the patient congested ("wet" vs "dry")? Is the patient perfused ("warm" vs "cold")? Congestion is signalled by orthopnoea, raised JVP, oedema, hepatojugular reflux, crackles; hypoperfusion by cool clammy extremities, oliguria, confusion, narrow pulse pressure, rising lactate and creatinine.

Precipitants — the "CHAMPIT" screen

Identify and treat immediately the precipitants that need specific therapy (ESC). Beyond these, the commonest precipitants are non-adherence (drugs, salt, fluid), infection, AF, uncontrolled hypertension, NSAIDs/negative inotropes, renal dysfunction, anaemia, alcohol and thyroid disease.

Key highlightsDecompensated HF: definitions & phenotypes

  • ESC 2026 renamed acute HF decompensated HF; most episodes are acute-on-chronic.
  • Four phenotypes: ADHF (commonest), acute pulmonary oedema, isolated RV failure, cardiogenic shock.
  • Pulmonary oedema is fluid redistribution (afterload) → vasodilator; ADHF is fluid accumulation → diuretic.
  • Warm–wet is the commonest profile; cold–wet has the worst prognosis.
  • Forrester cut-offs: CI 2.2 L/min/m², PCWP 18 mmHg.
  • Screen immediately for CHAMPIT: ACS, hypertension, arrhythmia, mechanical cause, PE, infection, tamponade.

2.2 Initial Assessment & Investigations

The first hour has three goals: stabilise (airway, oxygenation, BP, rhythm), identify the phenotype and profile, and find the precipitant. Diagnosis and treatment run in parallel.

ICU/CCU admission criteria (any)
  • Need for intubation (or already intubated)
  • Signs of hypoperfusion; SBP < 90 mmHg
  • SpO₂ < 90% despite O₂; RR > 25/min with work of
  • breathing
  • HR < 40 or > 130 bpm
  • Lactate > 2 mmol/L
Markers of poor in-hospital outcome
  • Low SBP, high BUN/creatinine, hyponatraemia
  • Raised troponin and very high NPs
  • Cold–wet profile; need for inotropes
  • Persistent congestion at discharge — strongest predictor
  • of readmission

Key highlightsInitial assessment & investigations

  • Acute NP rule-out: BNP < 100, NT-proBNP < 300 pg/mL.
  • Echo immediately in shock or suspected mechanical cause; within 48 h in de novo HF.
  • Lung ultrasound B-lines beat CXR for interstitial oedema.
  • Lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L signals hypoperfusion.
  • PA catheter is not routine (ESCAPE); reserve for shock, refractory or unclear cases.
  • Residual congestion at discharge is the strongest predictor of early readmission.
  • Trial Design → result Take-home

  • decongestion at 3 days, shorter stay
  • Add acetazolamide early in volume
  • overload
  • CLOROTIC Hydrochlorothiazide + loop → greater weight loss; more
  • hypokalaemia and renal impairment
  • Thiazide works; monitor
  • electrolytes
  • EMPULSE Empagliflozin started in hospital → clinical benefit (win ratio) at
  • 90 days
  • SGLT2i in hospital (ESC 2026 I B1)
  • CARRESS-HF Ultrafiltration vs stepped pharmacological therapy in
  • cardiorenal syndrome → no benefit, more adverse events
  • UF only if pharmacological therapy
  • fails
  • STRONG-HF Rapid up-titration of GDMT before and within 2 weeks after
  • discharge → ↓ 180-day death or HF readmission

2.3 Decongestion — Diuretic Strategy

Congestion is the reason most patients are admitted, and residual congestion at discharge is the reason many come back . The modern approach is early, adequately dosed IV loop diuretic, with the response measured by natriuresis within hours rather than by weight after days.

MECHANISM — WHY LOOP S ALONE FAIL

Threshold drug: furosemide must reach a threshold concentration in the tubule; below it there is no natriuresis — so doubling a sub-threshold dose works better than giving it twice.

Post-diuretic Na⁺ retention: short half-life → rebound reabsorption between doses.

Braking / distal hypertrophy: chronic loop use increases Na⁺ reabsorption in the distal tubule (thiazide-sensitive) and proximal tubule (acetazolamide-sensitive) → rationale for sequential nephron blockade.

Absorption: oral furosemide bioavailability ≈ 50% and erratic with gut oedema → give IV.

IIa B1

NEW Short-term IV acetazolamide or oral hydrochlorothiazide added to loop diuretic in fluid overload IIa B1 NEW Urinary-sodium-guided diuretic therapy during the first days of treatment IIb B1

NEW Start an SGLT2 inhibitor in hospital once the patient is stabilised I B1

Intensive strategy of initiation and rapid up-titration of evidence-based therapy before discharge, with frequent follow-up in the first 6 weeks (2023 FU)

I B

Thromboprophylaxis (e.g. LMWH) if not already anticoagulated I A

ACC/AHA 2022: IV loop diuretic at a dose ≥ the equivalent oral dose (1, B-NR); add a thiazide when response is inadequate (2a, B-NR); continue and optimise GDMT in hospital (1, B-NR); thromboprophylaxis (1, B-R).

Worsening renal function (WRF) — interpret
  • correctly
  • A creatinine rise during effective decongestion
  • ("permissive" WRF) is not harmful — keep diuresing.
  • WRF with persistent congestion is the bad sign → intensify
  • decongestion.
  • Do not stop RAASi/ARNI reflexly; review only if creatinine
  • rises steeply, K⁺ > 5.5, or hypotension.
Hyponatraemia
  • Dilutional (congestion, AVP excess): fluid restriction, loop
  • diuretic; tolvaptan raises Na⁺ but did not improve
  • outcomes (EVEREST).
  • Depletional (over-diuresis, thiazides): stop thiazide,
  • cautious saline.
  • Hypertonic saline with high-dose loop diuretic is an option
  • in refractory cases.
CLINICAL APPROACH — DISCHARGE CRITERIA
  • Euvolaemic (no orthopnoea, JVP normal, minimal oedema); precipitant treated.
  • Stable on oral diuretic for ≥ 24–48 h; renal function stable.
  • FMT started (including SGLT2i), iron status checked, education given.
  • Follow-up visit within 1–2 weeks of discharge (ESC I C); intensive titration visits in the first 6 weeks.

Key highlightsDiuretic strategy

  • Start IV furosemide 20–40 mg (naive) or 1–2× the oral dose.
  • Inadequate response = urine Na⁺ < 50–70 mmol/L at 2 h or output < 100–150 mL/h in 6 h → double the dose.
  • DOSE: bolus = infusion; high dose (2.5×) decongests better.
  • Add acetazolamide (ADVOR) or a thiazide (CLOROTIC) — ESC 2026 IIa B1.
  • Start SGLT2i in hospital once stable — ESC 2026 I B1.
  • Creatinine rise during effective decongestion is acceptable — don't stop diuresis.
  • Ultrafiltration is a rescue therapy (CARRESS-HF negative).
  • STRONG-HF: rapid up-titration + close follow-up in first 6 weeks — I B.

2.4 Vasodilators, Inotropes & Supportive Care

Oxygen and ventilation

Give oxygen only when hypoxaemic — SpO₂ < 90% or PaO₂ < 60 mmHg (8 kPa); hyperoxia causes vasoconstriction. Non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP) reduces work of breathing, preload and LV afterload and avoids intubation in pulmonary oedema; it lowers BP, so use with caution in hypotension and RV failure.

Vasodilators

IV nitrates reduce preload (venodilatation) and, at higher doses, afterload — ideal for hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema. They are avoided when SBP is < 90 mmHg and used with caution in severe AS, HCM with obstruction, and RV infarction (preload-dependent). Tachyphylaxis develops within 24–48 h; PDE-5 inhibitor use within 24–48 h is a contraindication.

Inotropes and vasopressors

Inotropes are for hypoperfusion, not for congestion : they increase myocardial oxygen demand, provoke arrhythmias and, in observational data, increase mortality. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time, in patients with low output and end-organ hypoperfusion.

BOARD PEARL — THE PATIENT ON A BETA-BLOCKER

If a patient on high-dose beta-blocker needs inotropy, choose an agent that bypasses the β-receptor: milrinone (PDE-3) or levosimendan (calcium sensitiser). Dobutamine competes with the beta-blocker. Both inodilators lower BP — often combined with noradrenaline.

IIb C

ACC/AHA 2022: IV nitroglycerin or nitroprusside as adjuvant to diuretics for dyspnoea in the absence of hypotension (2b, B-NR).

EXAM TRAP

Do not stop the beta-blocker in every decompensated patient. Continue FMT unless there is shock, symptomatic hypotension or severe bradycardia; stopping beta-blockers during admission is associated with higher mortality. Withdraw (or halve) only in low-output states — and restart before discharge.

Other therapies
  • Morphine: not routine — associated with more ventilation,
  • ICU stay and death in registries.
  • Thromboprophylaxis: LMWH unless anticoagulated (I A).
  • Digoxin: AF with fast rate despite beta-blocker, or when
  • beta-blocker can't be up-titrated.
  • IV iron before/after discharge in iron deficiency (AFFIRMAHF: ↓ HF hospitalisations).
Failed agents (why they're examined)
  • Nesiritide (ASCEND-HF), serelaxin (RELAX-AHF-2),
  • ularitide (TRUE-AHF) — no mortality benefit.
  • Rolofylline (PROTECT) — no benefit, seizures.
  • Tolvaptan (EVEREST) — corrects Na⁺, no outcome
  • benefit.
  • Lesson: early outcome benefit in DHF comes from
  • decongestion and GDMT, not novel vasoactive drugs.

Key highlightsVasodilators, inotropes & supportive care

  • O₂ only if SpO₂ < 90%; NIV for respiratory distress (IIa B).
  • Vasodilators if SBP > 110 mmHg (IIb B) — best in hypertensive pulmonary oedema.
  • Inotropes only for hypotension with hypoperfusion (IIb C); never routinely (III C).
  • Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock; avoid dopamine (SOAP II).
  • On a beta-blocker? Choose milrinone or levosimendan over dobutamine.
  • Nitroprusside: cyanide toxicity in renal/hepatic failure; needs arterial line.
  • No routine opiates; continue beta-blocker unless shock/low output.

2.5 Acute Right Ventricular Failure

The RV is a thin-walled, compliant, afterload-sensitive chamber: a modest rise in PVR drops RV stroke volume sharply. As it dilates, the septum shifts left (ventricular interdependence), compressing the LV and reducing systemic output. RV coronary perfusion depends on the gradient between aortic pressure and RV pressure — so systemic hypotension begets RV ischaemia, which begets more hypotension .

Principles of management
  • Preload: fluid only if CVP low (< 8–10 mmHg); if CVP high,
  • diurese — overfilling worsens septal shift.
  • Afterload: correct hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inhaled
  • NO or prostacyclin; avoid excessive PEEP.
  • Perfusion pressure: noradrenaline to keep aortic > RV
  • pressure.
  • Contractility: dobutamine, milrinone or levosimendan.
  • Rhythm: restore sinus rhythm and AV synchrony (pace if
  • needed).
Haemodynamic markers of RV failure
  • RAP > 15 mmHg; RAP/PCWP ratio > 0.63
  • PAPi = (PASP − PADP) / RAP; < 0.9 in inferior MI predicts
  • RV failure
  • Echo: TAPSE < 17 mm, RV S′ < 9.5 cm/s, D-shaped LV

2.6 Cardiogenic Shock

DEFINITION

Cardiogenic shock (CS) is a primary cardiac disorder causing inadequate cardiac output and tissue hypoperfusion. Classical criteria: SBP < 90 mmHg for ≥ 30 min (or vasopressors needed to keep it ≥ 90) with adequate volume, plus hypoperfusion (cold extremities, oliguria < 30 mL/h, confusion, lactate > 2 mmol/L).

Haemodynamically: CI < 2.2 L/min/m² (< 1.8 without support) with PCWP > 15 mmHg. Normotensive shock — hypoperfusion without hypotension — exists and carries similar risk.

AMI accounts for most cases (predominantly LV failure; also mechanical complications and RV infarction). The rest are acute-on-chronic HF, myocarditis, Takotsubo, valve disease, arrhythmia, post-cardiotomy and drug toxicity. In-hospital mortality remains ≈ 30–50%.

SCAI SHOCK stages

Key highlightsAcute RV failure

  • The RV is afterload-sensitive and preload-dependent; hypotension causes RV ischaemia.
  • RV infarct: avoid nitrates and diuretics; cautious fluids; maintain AV synchrony; reperfuse.
  • Fluids only if CVP is low — overloading worsens septal shift.
  • Noradrenaline maintains coronary perfusion of the RV; add an inodilator for contractility.
  • PAPi < 0.9 and RAP/PCWP > 0.63 signal RV failure.
  • Stage Description Typical findings
  • E — Extremis Circulatory collapse Refractory arrest, ongoing CPR/ECPR,
  • multiple support devices
  • 2022 update: a three-axis model (shock severity × phenotype/aetiology × risk modifiers); the cardiac-arrest modifier is now "arrest with coma"; stages are dynamic — reassess repeatedly. Endorsed by ACC, AHA, ESC-ACVC, ISHLT, SCCM, STS.
Haemodynamic indices
  • Cardiac power output (CPO) = MAP × CO / 451 → < 0.6 W
  • = strongest haemodynamic predictor of death.
  • PAPi < 0.9 (AMI) → RV involvement.
  • Phenotypes: LV-dominant (↑ PCWP), RV-dominant (↑
  • RAP, RAP/PCWP > 0.63–0.8), biventricular.
  • Lactate clearance over 6–12 h tracks response.
Board sequence in AMI-CS
  • Immediate angiography; culprit-lesion-only PCI
  • (CULPRIT-SHOCK) — staged later.
  • Noradrenaline for hypotension, inotrope for low output.
  • Echo for mechanical complications (VSR, papillary
  • rupture, free wall).
  • Shock team decides on tMCS early — ideally before multiorgan failure.

Key highlightsCardiogenic shock

  • CS = SBP < 90 mmHg (or pressor-dependent) + hypoperfusion; CI < 2.2, PCWP > 15.
  • SCAI: A at risk · B beginning (no hypoperfusion) · C classic (lactate ≥ 2) · D deteriorating · E extremis.
  • CPO < 0.6 W is the strongest haemodynamic predictor of death.
  • AMI-CS: culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK); routine multivessel PCI is Class III.
  • Noradrenaline first; dopamine avoided; inotropes for low output.
  • Routine IABP (IABP-SHOCK II) and unselected tMCS/ECMO (ECLS-SHOCK) are Class III.
  • Microaxial pump (Impella CP) in selected STEMI-CS: IIa B1 (DanGer Shock).
  • Shock team: ESC 2026 Class I.
  • Intra-aortic balloon pump

2.7 Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support

Temporary MCS (tMCS) buys time. Always state the strategy before insertion: bridge to recovery (BTR), bridge to decision (BTD — neurological status unknown after arrest), bridge to bridge (BTB — to durable LVAD), bridge to candidacy (BTC) or bridge to transplant (BTT). A device without an exit strategy is a bridge to nowhere.

Physiology and timing
  • Tip 2–3 cm below the left subclavian artery (level of carina
  • on CXR).
  • Inflation at the dicrotic notch (aortic valve closure) → ↑
  • diastolic coronary perfusion.
  • Deflation just before systole (R wave) → ↓ afterload, ↓
  • MVO₂.
  • Early inflation / late deflation are harmful (↑ afterload, ARlike effect).
Contraindications
  • Moderate–severe aortic regurgitation
  • Aortic dissection, significant AAA
  • Severe peripheral arterial disease
  • Uncontrolled sepsis or bleeding, contraindication to
  • anticoagulation
  • Residual uses: bridge to surgery in mechanical complications (acute MR, VSR), refractory ischaemia, and as an LV vent on VA-ECMO.

Impella

A catheter-mounted microaxial pump drawing blood from the LV into the ascending aorta — true LV unloading. DanGer Shock (Impella CP in STEMI with LV-dominant CS, excluding comatose OHCA and RV failure) reduced 180-day all-cause death (≈ 46% vs 59%), at the cost of more severe bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal replacement therapy. Impella RP supports the RV (IVC → PA).

EXAM TRAP — IMPELLA CONTRAINDICATIONS

LV thrombus, mechanical aortic valve, severe AS or moderate–severe AR, severe PAD, and ventricular septal rupture (LV unloading can reverse the shunt and cause hypoxaemia). Haemolysis (↑ LDH, plasmafree Hb, dark urine) suggests malposition — reposition under echo.

VA-ECMO

Provides full cardiopulmonary support, typically femoral venous drainage and femoral arterial return. It is the only option in refractory arrest (ECPR) and biventricular failure with hypoxaemia. ECLS-SHOCK showed no 30-day mortality benefit of routine early ECMO in AMI-CS, with more bleeding and vascular complications — so selection is everything.

ECMO — contraindications
  • Non-recoverable heart and not a candidate for LVAD/
  • transplant
  • Severe irreversible neurological injury; prolonged no-flow
  • arrest
  • Unrepaired aortic dissection; severe AR
  • Contraindication to anticoagulation; terminal malignancy
Choosing the device
  • LV-dominant CS, oxygenating: Impella (± noradrenaline).
  • Biventricular failure, hypoxaemia or arrest: VA-ECMO ± LV
  • vent.
  • Isolated RV failure: Impella RP or RA–PA support.
  • Mechanical complication awaiting surgery: IABP or ECMO.

2.8 Advanced HF & Durable LVAD

Recognising advanced (Stage D) HF

Advanced HF is progression despite optimal therapy. The commonest error is late referral — after end-organ damage has made the patient ineligible for transplant or LVAD . ESC 2026 gives early consultation with an advanced HF centre a Class I recommendation.

3 Episodes of congestion needing high-dose IV diuretics, low output needing inotropes/vasoactive drugs, or malignant arrhythmias → > 1 unplanned visit or hospitalisation in the last 12 months

Key highlightsTemporary MCS

  • Define the exit strategy first: BTR, BTD, BTB, BTC, BTT.
  • IABP: inflate at dicrotic notch, deflate before systole; ≈ 0.5–1 L/min; contraindicated in AR, dissection.
  • Impella unloads the LV; VA-ECMO increases LV afterload.
  • DanGer Shock: Impella CP ↓ 180-day death in STEMI-CS, with more bleeding and limb ischaemia.
  • IABP-SHOCK II and ECLS-SHOCK: no mortality benefit from routine use.
  • Loss of pulsatility + pulmonary oedema on ECMO → LV venting (ECPELLA).
  • Harlequin syndrome: check the right radial saturation.
  • Impella contraindications: LV thrombus, mechanical AVR, severe AS/AR, VSR.
  • # Criterion
  • 4 Severe exercise limitation: unable to exercise, 6MWD < 300 m, or peak VO₂ < 12 mL/kg/min or < 50% predicted HFA/ESC definition (2018), used in ESC 2021; ESC 2026 also presents a "rule of three" and the I NEED HELP markers as referral tools.
"I NEED HELP" — refer now

  • E — Oedema / escalating diuretics

  • P — Prognostic medication: unable to up-titrate or need to
  • reduce FMT
INTERMACS profiles
  • 1 — Critical cardiogenic shock ("crash and burn")

  • inotropes")
  • 3 — Stable but inotrope-dependent
  • 4 — Resting symptoms on oral therapy ("frequent flyer")
  • 5 — Exertion intolerant (housebound)
  • 6 — Exertion limited ("walking wounded")
  • 7 — Advanced NYHA III
  • Profiles 1–2 ≈ SCAI C–E; LVAD outcomes are best in
  • profiles 2–4.

Durable LVAD

Current durable LVADs are continuous-flow centrifugal pumps; the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 dominates (the HVAD was withdrawn in 2021). MOMENTUM 3 showed HeartMate 3 is superior to the axial HeartMate II, mainly through far less pump thrombosis (≈ 1–2% vs ≈ 14%) and stroke. Survival with HM3 is ≈ 80% at 2 years and ≈ 58% at 5 years. REMATCH first proved destination therapy beats medical therapy (1-year survival ≈ 52% vs 25%).

Routine care
  • Warfarin INR 2.0–3.0; DOACs not used. ARIES-HM3:
  • omitting aspirin with HM3 reduced bleeding without more
  • thrombosis.
  • BP by Doppler (opening pressure ≈ MAP): target MAP
  • ≤ 80–85 mmHg — hypertension ↑ stroke and ↓ pump
  • output.
  • Continue HF drugs (beta-blocker, RAASi, MRA) for BP, RV,
  • arrhythmias.
  • Only adjustable parameter: pump speed; displayed flow is
  • estimated from power.
  • Pulse may be weak/absent — assess perfusion, not pulse.
Complications
  • Bleeding (commonest): GI angiodysplasia, acquired von
  • Willebrand deficiency (shear loss of large multimers) +
  • anticoagulation.
  • Driveline infection — commonest infection.
  • RV failure — early (LV unloading shifts septum, ↑ venous
  • return).
  • Stroke (ischaemic or haemorrhagic).
  • Pump thrombosis (rare with HM3).
  • De novo aortic regurgitation, ventricular arrhythmias,
  • suction events.
BOARD PEARL — ARREST IN AN LVAD PATIENT

An unresponsive LVAD patient without a palpable pulse may be perfused. Check the device (listen for the hum, alarms, power), Doppler MAP, capillary refill and end-tidal CO₂. If MAP is < 50 mmHg or unmeasurable and the patient is unresponsive, start chest compressions — dislodgement risk is outweighed by death from no flow. VT/VF is often haemodynamically tolerated with an LVAD (RV output limits flow) but should still be treated.

2.9 Heart Transplantation

Transplantation remains the gold-standard treatment for selected advanced HF, with 1-year survival ≈ 90% and median survival ≈ 12–13 years. Donor scarcity makes selection — and exclusion of those unlikely to benefit — central.

Age > 70 — relative, individualised

ISHLT listing criteria (2016; updated guidance for candidates 2024) and ESC 2021 contraindications table.

MECHANISM — WHY PVR MATTERS

A donor RV has never faced high pulmonary pressures. Implanted into a recipient with fixed pulmonary hypertension, it fails acutely — RV failure is a leading cause of early death after transplant. Hence the vasodilator challenge (nitroprusside, milrinone, iNO) and, if PVR stays high, LVAD unloading for months to remodel the pulmonary bed before listing (bridge to candidacy).

Key highlightsAdvanced HF & LVAD

  • Advanced HF: NYHA III–IV, LVEF ≤ 30%, > 1 admission/12 months, 6MWD < 300 m or VO₂ < 12.
  • I NEED HELP triggers referral; ESC 2026 early advanced-HF consultation = Class I (A).
  • ESC 2026 upgraded durable LVAD to Class I (was IIa); ACC/AHA: 1 A if inotrope/tMCS-dependent.
  • HeartMate 3 (centrifugal, maglev): pump thrombosis ≈ 1–2% (MOMENTUM 3).
  • LVAD: warfarin INR 2–3; aspirin can be omitted (ARIES-HM3); MAP ≤ 80–85 by Doppler.
  • Commonest complication = bleeding (acquired vWF deficiency, AVMs); commonest infection = driveline. ↑ Power + haemolysis = pump thrombosis; suction events = underfilled LV.
  • Severe RV failure is the key contraindication to isolated LVAD.
  • After transplantation

interactions

Mycophenolate mofetil Antiproliferative (IMPDH inhibitor) Leukopenia, GI upset; teratogenic Prednisolone Broad anti-inflammatory Diabetes, osteoporosis, infection — tapered

  • Everolimus / sirolimus mTOR inhibitor Poor wound healing, proteinuria,
  • dyslipidaemia; slow CAV and allow CNI
  • reduction (renal-sparing)
  • Induction (basiliximab,
  • ATG)
  • IL-2R blockade / T-cell depletion Used in high-risk or renal-sparing protocols

CYP3A4 inhibitors (azoles, clarithromycin, diltiazem, verapamil, grapefruit) raise tacrolimus levels; inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) lower them and provoke rejection.

Rejection
  • Acute cellular (T-cell): ISHLT 2004 grades 0R, 1R (mild),
  • 2R (moderate), 3R (severe). Treat ≥ 2R or any grade with
  • haemodynamic compromise — pulsed IV steroids ± ATG.
  • Antibody-mediated: donor-specific antibodies,
  • complement (C4d) on biopsy; pAMR 0–3. Plasmapheresis,
  • IVIG, rituximab.
  • Often asymptomatic → surveillance endomyocardial
  • biopsy; gene-expression profiling and donor-derived cellfree DNA reduce biopsy need.
Cardiac allograft vasculopathy
  • Diffuse, concentric intimal hyperplasia (immune + nonimmune) — epicardial and small vessels. Affects ≈ 30% at 5 years and ≈ 50% at 10 years.
  • Silent (denervation): presents as HF, arrhythmia or
  • sudden death.
  • Surveillance angiography ± IVUS; ISHLT grades CAV0–
  • CAV3.
  • Prevention: statins for all (pravastatin trial ↓ CAV and
  • rejection); mTOR inhibitors; PCI for focal disease;
  • retransplant for severe.

Finding Explanation / consequence

Exaggerated response to adenosine Denervation hypersensitivity → start at reduced dose (or avoid); prolonged AV block possible

  • Digoxin has little AV-nodal (rate) effect Its rate effect is vagally mediated
  • Two sets of P waves (biatrial technique);
  • RBBB common
  • Recipient atrial cuff remains; bicaval technique now preferred

Tricuspid regurgitation Biopsy-related chordal damage

DON'T CONFUSE — PTLD VS SKIN CANCER

The commonest malignancy after heart transplant is non-melanoma skin cancer (squamous cell carcinoma more than basal cell — the reverse of the general population). Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) is EBV-driven B-cell proliferation, highest risk in the first year and in EBV-negative recipients of EBV-positive donors; first step is reduction of immunosuppression.

Key highlightsHeart transplantation

  • Listing: peak VO₂ ≤ 12 mL/kg/min on beta-blocker (≤ 14 off); VE/VCO₂ > 35 if submaximal.
  • Fixed PVR (> 5 WU after vasodilator challenge) → donor RV failure → LVAD first, reassess.
  • BMI > 35, active malignancy, substance abuse, irreversible renal/hepatic failure are contraindications.
  • Early death: primary graft dysfunction; first year: infection and rejection; late: CAV and malignancy.
  • Cellular rejection: ISHLT 0R–3R; treat ≥ 2R with pulsed steroids.
  • CAV is silent; all recipients receive statins; mTOR inhibitors slow CAV.
  • Denervated heart: resting HR 90–110; atropine useless; adenosine exaggerated.
  • Commonest malignancy = skin SCC; PTLD is EBV-related.

2.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 72-year-old woman presents with sudden severe breathlessness. BP 196/104 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO₂ 84%, widespread crackles, warm peripheries. What is the most appropriate initial treatment combination?

Answer B Hypertensive acute pulmonary oedema = fluid redistribution with high afterload: NIV plus IV nitrate (SBP > 110 mmHg) with a loop diuretic. Inotropes are for hypoperfusion; routine morphine is not recommended; fluids/pressors are wrong.

Q2 A man with decompensated HFrEF receives IV furosemide 80 mg (twice his oral dose). At 2 h, spot urine sodium is 38 mmol/L; at 6 h urine output is 60 mL/h. What is the next step?

Answer B Urine Na⁺ < 50–70 mmol/L at 2 h and output < 100–150 mL/h at 6 h = inadequate natriuresis → double the loop dose. If still inadequate, add acetazolamide or thiazide; UF is rescue only.

Q3 A patient on bisoprolol 10 mg for HFrEF is admitted cold and wet: BP 86/60, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, oliguric. Noradrenaline has been started. Which inotrope is most logical?

Answer C Beta-blockade blunts dobutamine; milrinone (PDE-3) and levosimendan (calcium sensitiser) act beyond the βreceptor. Both vasodilate, hence combined with noradrenaline. Dopamine increases arrhythmias and mortality in shock (SOAP II).

Q4 A patient with anterior STEMI has SBP 82 mmHg on noradrenaline, cool extremities and lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Four hours later, despite adding dobutamine, lactate is 6.5 mmol/L and doses are rising. Which SCAI stage now applies?

Answer D Stage C (classic) requires intervention for hypoperfusion; failure to respond with rising lactate and escalating support = D (deteriorating). E = extremis (arrest, CPR/ECMO, multiple devices).

Q5 In a patient with STEMI complicated by cardiogenic shock and multivessel disease, which strategy is not recommended?

Answer C Routine IABP in AMI-CS is Class III (IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit). Culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK), immediate angiography, echo and noradrenaline are all appropriate.

Q6 On day 2 of peripheral VA-ECMO for fulminant myocarditis, the arterial line loses pulsatility, the aortic valve no longer opens on echo, and the CXR shows worsening pulmonary oedema. What is the best next step?

Answer C Retrograde ECMO flow raises LV afterload; a non-ejecting LV distends, causing pulmonary oedema and thrombus risk. Venting (Impella "ECPELLA", IABP, septostomy) unloads it. Increasing ECMO flow worsens afterload.

Q7 A patient on femoral VA-ECMO with severe ARDS shows SpO₂ 99% on the left foot probe but 78% on the right hand. The native heart is recovering. What is the diagnosis?

Answer B With femoral return, the recovering LV ejects deoxygenated blood (from injured lungs) to the aortic arch; the right arm and brain are hypoxaemic while the legs receive ECMO blood. Monitor the right radial; improve ventilation or convert to V-AV ECMO.

Q8 Eight months after HeartMate 3 implantation, a patient reports dark urine and breathlessness. LVAD power has risen and LDH is 3.4× the upper limit. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Answer C Rising power with haemolysis (LDH > 2.5–3× ULN, dark urine) and HF = pump thrombosis. Suction events and RV failure lower flow and power; driveline infection causes local signs and fever.

Q9 A 52-year-old with advanced HFrEF is referred for transplant. Right heart catheter: PASP 62 mmHg, PVR 6.2 WU, which remains 5.5 WU after a nitroprusside challenge. What is the best plan?

Answer C PVR > 5 WU despite vasodilator challenge risks donor RV failure. LVAD unloading often lowers PVR over months (bridge to candidacy), after which listing can be reconsidered. Isolated lung transplant does not address his HF.

Q10 A heart transplant recipient develops a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180 bpm. Which statement about acute treatment is correct?

Answer B The denervated heart is hypersensitive to adenosine (use a reduced dose). Vagal manoeuvres, digoxin and atropine work through vagal pathways and are ineffective; verapamil/diltiazem raise tacrolimus levels (CYP3A4).

What the board expects you to know

  • The five ESC 2023 phenotypes (DCM, NDLVC, HCM, ARVC, RCM) with their defining thresholds, and how CMR tissue characterisation points to the cause.
  • Who gets genetic testing, which genes are "high-risk" (LMNA, FLNC, DSP, PLN, RBM20, TMEM43), and how cascade screening is organised.
  • The 2010 Task Force criteria for ARVC, and every primary- and secondary-prevention ICD trigger in DCM, NDLVC, ARVC and sarcoid.
  • The non-invasive diagnosis of ATTR amyloid (exclude AL first; grade 2–3 bone-tracer uptake) and the diseasemodifying drugs.
  • How to separate restriction from constriction, and how to recognise and manage peripartum cardiomyopathy and Takotsubo syndrome.

Numbers that win marks

> 58 / > 52 mmLVEDD — LV dilatation, men / women
