2m, or 4m)

3.1 Classification, Work-up & Genetics

DEFINITION

A cardiomyopathy is a myocardial disorder in which the heart muscle is structurally and functionally abnormal in the absence of coronary artery disease, hypertension, valve disease or congenital heart disease sufficient to explain the abnormality. The phrase "sufficient to explain" matters: a patient can have mild hypertension and sarcomeric HCM.

The ESC 2023 guideline is the first single European guideline covering all cardiomyopathies. Its central idea is describe the phenotype first (morphology + function + tissue character), then search for the cause — genetic, acquired, or both. Genes and environment interact: a titin truncating variant may stay silent until alcohol, chemotherapy or pregnancy provide the "second hit".

The multiparametric work-up

Every patient: clinical history, a 3–4-generation pedigree, ECG, Holter, first-line bloods and multimodality imaging. Red flags on history, examination and ECG narrow the differential before any gene is sequenced.

CMR — the tissue-characterisation engine

Contrast CMR is recommended at initial evaluation of every cardiomyopathy (ESC 2023, I B). The LGE pattern is the most examined image finding in the chapter.

BOARD PEARL

Other imaging roles to remember: bone-tracer scintigraphy (DPD/PYP/HMDP) for suspected ATTR amyloid (I B); ¹⁸F-FDG-PET for suspected sarcoid (IIa C); CT coronary angiography to exclude CAD as the cause (IIa C); endomyocardial biopsy only when inflammation, infiltration or storage cannot be confirmed otherwise (IIa C).

Genetic testing and counselling

Cardiomyopathy genes show incomplete, age-related penetrance and variable expressivity. Most are autosomal dominant (50% transmission, male-to-male transmission possible). Suspect X-linked disease (Fabry, Danon, dystrophin) when males are worst affected and there is no male-to-male transmission; mitochondrial when only women transmit.

Index patient

Genetic testing in patients fulfilling diagnostic criteria when it enables diagnosis, prognosis, therapy, reproductive management, or cascade testing of relatives

I B

Genetic testing of a deceased individual with cardiomyopathy at post-mortem, if it helps surviving relatives

  • I C
  • Testing in a borderline phenotype only after specialist assessment IIb C

Relatives

Cascade testing of adult at-risk relatives once a P/LP variant is found in the family I B Cascade testing of paediatric relatives (considering disease, age of onset, family course) IIa B Relatives who do not carry the familial P/LP variant and have no phenotype → discharge (return if symptoms or new family data)

I C

No P/LP variant in proband (or not tested) → initial clinical screening of first-degree relatives (ECG + imaging)

I C

Diagnostic genetic testing of a phenotype-negative relative when the family has no confident (P/LP) genetic diagnosis

III C

Repeat long-term (IIa C); no predictive gene test on VUS

WHAT CHANGED IN 2023
  • One guideline for all cardiomyopathies, organised by phenotype, with a new NDLVC category. "LV non-compaction" dropped as a cardiomyopathy → hypertrabeculation trait.
  • Contrast CMR recommended in every patient at diagnosis (I B); genetic testing upgraded and extended to all phenotypes.
  • Family screening frequency: every 1–3 y before age 60, every 3–5 y after (penetrance reaches 70–90% by age 70).

Key highlightsClassification & work-up

  • ESC 2023 phenotypes: DCM, NDLVC, HCM, ARVC, RCM; LVNC is now a trait (hypertrabeculation).
  • LV dilatation = LVEDD > 58 mm (men) / > 52 mm (women); LVEDVi ≥ 75 / ≥ 62 mL/m².
  • NDLVC = non-ischaemic LV scar/fat on CMR (or isolated hypokinesia) without dilatation.
  • Contrast CMR at diagnosis in all (I B); bone scintigraphy for suspected ATTR (I B); FDG-PET for sarcoid (IIa C).
  • Ring-like LGE → DSP/FLNC; septal mid-wall → LMNA/DCM; diffuse subendocardial → amyloid; inferolateral + low T1 → Fabry.
  • Genetic testing of the proband: I B; cascade testing of adult relatives only once a P/LP variant is known (I B).
  • Never test a phenotype-negative relative when the family has no P/LP variant (III C).
  • Relatives who test negative for the familial P/LP variant are discharged (I C).

3.2 Dilated & Non-Dilated LV Cardiomyopathy

DCM affects roughly 1 in 250–400 adults and is the commonest indication for heart transplantation. Up to 40% of DCM carries a pathogenic variant — and 10–15% of alcohol-, chemotherapy- or pregnancy-associated DCM does too. An acquired trigger never excludes a genetic cause.

Aetiology

Genetic: TTN truncation (commonest, ≈ 15–25%), the arrhythmogenic "high-risk" genes (LMNA, FLNC, DSP, PLN, RBM20, TMEM43), DMD, BAG3, SCN5A, sarcomeric genes. Acquired: myocarditis, Chagas, HIV; alcohol, cocaine, anthracyclines, trastuzumab, immune checkpoint inhibitors; tachycardia/PVC-induced; peripartum; thyroid, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma; thiamine or selenium deficiency; iron overload.

PLN (R14del) Very low QRS voltage; posterolateral LGE High VA risk; PLN risk model

RBM20 Young, aggressive DCM, AF High-risk genotype

TMEM43 Arrhythmogenic CM, men very high risk (Newfoundland founder) High-risk genotype; avoid competitive sport

DMD X-linked; inferolateral subepicardial LGE; carriers may develop DCM Screen female carriers

MECHANISM — WHY LMNA KILLS EARLY

Lamin A/C sits in the nuclear envelope of conduction tissue and myocytes. Nuclear fragility produces conduction disease, atrial arrhythmia and ventricular arrhythmia years before systolic failure. Because the arrhythmic risk is dissociated from LVEF, an LVEF-only ICD rule misses these patients — hence the dedicated risk calculator (male sex, NSVT, LVEF, AV block, non-missense variant).

Specific acquired forms

Management of DCM/NDLVC

HF therapy as for HFrEF: ARNI/ACE-I, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; CRT by standard criteria. Recovered LVEF (HFimpEF) — do not withdraw GDMT : in TRED-HF, phased withdrawal led to relapse in ≈ 44% within 6 months.

  • Immunosuppression (prednisolone ± azathioprine) only for biopsy-proven, virus-negative
  • inflammatory DCM, giant-cell or eosinophilic myocarditis, and sarcoid.

Anticoagulation: in DCM/NDLVC + AF, use CHA₂DS₂-VASc (OAC I B at ≥ 2 men / ≥ 3 women) — unlike HCM and amyloid, where AF alone mandates OAC.

Exercise: avoid high-intensity/competitive sport if symptomatic, LVEF ≤ 40%, exercise-induced arrhythmia, or LMNA/TMEM43 variant (ESC 2022, III C).

SCD risk and ICD

SCD causes 25–35% of deaths in DCM. In non-ischaemic DCM, DANISH showed no all-cause mortality benefit from a primary-prevention ICD (despite fewer sudden deaths), which is why ESC grades the LVEF-based rule only IIa while ACC/AHA keep Class 1. Europe instead layers genotype and scar on top of LVEF.

IIa C

LMNA: estimated 5-y risk of life-threatening VA ≥ 10% plus NSVT, LVEF < 50% or AV conduction delay IIa C NEW High-risk genotype and LVEF > 35% with additional risk factors (ESC 2023) IIa C

Genetic testing (at least LMNA, PLN, RBM20, FLNC) if AV conduction delay at < 50 y or family history of DCM/SCD < 50 y

  • I B
  • CMR-LGE to assess aetiology and VA/SCD risk IIa B

ICD in incessant VA before the arrhythmia is controlled III C

EXAM TRAP

A 35-year-old with LMNA DCM, LVEF 45%, PR 260 ms and NSVT who now needs pacing for AV block should receive an ICD (with pacing capability), not a pacemaker. LVEF above 35% does not protect in laminopathy.

Key highlightsDCM & NDLVC

  • Up to 40% of DCM is genetic; TTN truncation is the commonest cause.
  • High-risk (arrhythmogenic) genes: LMNA, FLNC, DSP, PLN, RBM20, TMEM43.
  • LMNA = conduction disease + AF + VT before LV failure; ICD if 5-y risk ≥ 10% with NSVT, LVEF < 50% or AV delay (IIa C).
  • Primary ICD for LVEF ≤ 35% after 3 months OMT: ESC IIa A vs ACC/AHA Class 1.
  • ESC: LVEF < 50% + ≥ 2 risk factors (syncope, LGE, inducible SMVT, high-risk gene) → consider ICD.
  • Do not stop GDMT after LVEF recovery — TRED-HF relapse ≈ 44%.
  • PVC burden > 10–15% can cause reversible cardiomyopathy — ablate.
  • OAC in DCM + AF follows CHA₂DS₂-VASc (unlike HCM/amyloid).

3.3 Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy

ARVC is an inherited disease of the desmosome in which myocytes are progressively replaced by fibro-fatty tissue, starting in the epicardium and moving inwards. Prevalence ≈ 1 in 1000–5000; presentation typically between 10 and 50 years, men more severely affected. P/LP variants are found in up to 60% — PKP2 (plakophilin-2) is the commonest; others DSP, DSG2, DSC2, JUP. Inheritance is mostly autosomal dominant; Naxos (JUP) and Carvajal (DSP) are recessive cardiocutaneous forms.

MECHANISM — WHY EXERCISE MATTERS

Defective desmosomes cannot hold myocytes together under mechanical stress. Endurance exercise raises RV wall stress disproportionately (the thin RV faces a large rise in pulmonary pressure), accelerating myocyte detachment, fibro-fatty replacement and VT. This is why avoidance of high-intensity exercise is itself a therapy in ARVC (ESC 2023, I B).

The disease spectrum is now called arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy: classic right-dominant ARVC, biventricular, and left-dominant forms (DSP, FLNC, DES), which overlap with NDLVC. The "triangle of dysplasia" — RV inflow, outflow and apex — describes the classic RV sites (the apex is now recognised as less often involved than the subtricuspid and RVOT regions). 2010 Task Force criteria (TFC)

BEYOND 2010 — PADUA (2020)AND EUROPEAN TASK FORCE (2023/24)

2010 TFC ignore LV involvement and tissue characterisation; they remain the criteria cited by ESC 2023 for ARVC.

Padua criteria (2020) added CMR-LGE and separate LV criteria (LV LGE, low limb-lead QRS voltage, TWI V4–V6, RBBB-morphology PVCs), with left-dominant disease requiring a genetic variant. The European Task Force (2023) refinement defines ARVC, biventricular and arrhythmogenic LV cardiomyopathy phenotypes; ring-like LV LGE in ≥ 3 segments is a major LV criterion and the epsilon wave is only a minor criterion. Definite/borderline/possible thresholds are the same as 2010.

ECG and imaging clues

TWI V1–V3 in someone over 14 is the commonest ECG abnormality (seen in up to 85% of probands). Epsilon wave — low-amplitude signal after the QRS in V1–V3; specific but insensitive, and inter-observer agreement is poor.

Prolonged terminal activation duration (≥ 55 ms) and localised QRS widening in V1–V3 reflect delayed RV activation.

VT is LBBB-morphology; superior axis = RV inferior wall/apex origin (major); inferior axis = RVOT (minor — must exclude idiopathic RVOT VT).

DON'T CONFUSE — ARVC MIMICS

Idiopathic RVOT VT: normal sinus-rhythm ECG and RV, single inferior-axis morphology, no family history — benign, ablatable.

Athlete's heart: balanced RV + LV enlargement, no regional WMA, TWI regresses with detraining. Sarcoidosis: AV block, septal LGE, FDG uptake, age > 35. Also exclude RV volume overload (ASD, anomalous veins, Ebstein) and Brugada.

Management

Avoid high-intensity exercise in definite ARVC I B

Avoid high-intensity/competitive sport in genotype-positive, phenotype-negative relatives IIb C Annual ambulatory ECG monitoring I C

  • Primary prevention ICD (definite ARVC)
  • Arrhythmic syncope IIa B

Severe RV or LV systolic dysfunction IIa C

Symptomatic (presyncope/palpitations) + moderate RV or LV dysfunction + NSVT or inducible SMVT IIa C Use of the 2019 ARVC risk calculator for shared ICD decisions IIa B

  • Secondary prevention and arrhythmia control
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • ICD after cardiac arrest or haemodynamically unstable VA I B
  • ICD after haemodynamically tolerated SMVT IIa C
  • Beta-blocker in ARVC with PVCs, NSVT or VT I C
  • Amiodarone, or flecainide added to beta-blocker, when single-agent therapy fails IIa C

Catheter ablation (with epicardial access, 3D mapping) for recurrent SMVT/shocks despite betablocker IIa C

ICD programmed with ATP up to high rates IIa B

Severe dysfunction is commonly taken as RVFAC ≤ 17%, RVEF ≤ 35% or LVEF ≤ 35%; moderate as RVEF < 40% or LVEF < 45%.

BOARD PEARL

The 2019 ARVC risk calculator uses age, sex, recent (< 6 months) syncope, NSVT, PVC count/24 h, number of leads with TWI, and RVEF. Ablation in ARVC often needs an epicardial approach because the disease starts epicardially — and ablation reduces VT burden but does not replace an ICD.

3.4 Restrictive Cardiomyopathy vs Constriction

RCM is defined by restrictive physiology — a stiff ventricle whose pressure rises steeply with small increments of volume — with non-dilated ventricles and preserved (initially) LVEF. Big atria, small ventricles, normal EF, high filling pressures is the picture. It carries the worst prognosis of all phenotypes (adult genetic RCM ≈ 50% 5-y survival; over half of children die or are transplanted soon after diagnosis).

Key highlightsARVC

  • Desmosomal disease (PKP2 commonest); fibro-fatty replacement from epicardium inwards.
  • Definite ARVC = 2 major, 1 major + 2 minor, or 4 minor TFC criteria.
  • Major ECG criteria: TWI V1–V3 (> 14 y, no RBBB) and epsilon wave; VT LBBB superior axis.
  • CMR major: regional WMA + RVEDVi ≥ 110 (M) / ≥ 100 mL/m² (F) or RVEF ≤ 40%.
  • Echo major: regional WMA + PLAX RVOT ≥ 32 mm, PSAX ≥ 36 mm or FAC ≤ 33%.
  • Avoid high-intensity exercise in definite ARVC — I B.
  • Primary ICD (IIa): arrhythmic syncope; severe RV/LV dysfunction; moderate dysfunction + NSVT/inducible VT.
  • Naxos (JUP) and Carvajal (DSP) = recessive, woolly hair + keratoderma.
Endomyocardial fibrosis
  • Commonest RCM worldwide (tropical Africa,
  • India, South America); young people
  • Apical obliteration, atrioventricular valve
  • tethering (MR/TR), thrombus
  • Massive ascites out of proportion to oedema
  • Surgical endocardiectomy ± valve repair
  • improves survival
Hypereosinophilic (Löffler)
  • Eosinophils > 1.5 × 10⁹/L persistently
  • Necrotic → thrombotic → fibrotic stages
  • Steroids ± hydroxyurea; imatinib in FIP1L1–
  • PDGFRA disease
  • Anticoagulate for mural thrombus

Restriction versus constriction

Both give raised, equalised diastolic pressures and a dip-and-plateau (square-root) sign. The discriminating principle: in constriction the heart is enclosed in a rigid shell, so total cardiac volume is fixed — respiration shifts filling between the ventricles (ventricular interdependence) and intrathoracic pressure changes are not transmitted to the chambers. In restriction the muscle itself is stiff; the pericardium is normal, so interdependence is absent and myocardial relaxation (e′) is reduced.

EXAM TRAP

Respiratory variation in constriction can disappear with very high filling pressures and reappear after diuresis, and it may be absent in AF. If the echo is ambiguous, simultaneous LV/RV catheterisation with the systolic area index is the arbiter. Remember constriction = normal e′ with septal bounce; restriction = low e′ with high BNP .

ICD after cardiac arrest or unstable VA I C

EMB to exclude specific diagnoses (iron, storage, mitochondrial, amyloid, granulomatous; desmin myopathy)

  • IIa C
  • OAC in RCM with AF/flutter (unless contraindicated) IIa C

3.5 Cardiac Amyloidosis

Amyloidosis is extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins as β-pleated fibrils that show apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining. More than 30 precursor proteins exist, but > 95% of cardiac amyloid is AL or ATTR. Once thought rare, wild-type ATTR is found in ≈ 13% of patients with HFpEF and LV thickening and in ≈ 1 in 8 elderly patients undergoing TAVI.

Variable by variant

Treatment Haematological: daratumumabCyBorD; ASCT if eligibleTTR stabiliser or silencer Stabiliser/silencer; cascade genetic testing

Key highlightsRestriction vs constriction

  • RCM: big atria, small non-dilated ventricles, normal wall thickness, normal EF — worst prognosis phenotype.
  • Commonest RCM in adults in the West: amyloid; worldwide: endomyocardial fibrosis.
  • Constriction: septal bounce, mitral E variation > 25%, preserved e′, annulus reversus, expiratory hepatic reversal.
  • Restriction: low e′, inspiratory hepatic reversal, PASP often > 50 mmHg, very high BNP.
  • Cath: constriction = LVEDP–RVEDP ≤ 5 mmHg, RVEDP/RVSP > 1/3, discordant systolic pressures.
  • Children with RCM need catheter PVR every 6–12 months (transplant eligibility) — I B.
  • Iron overload: CMR T2* < 20 ms; treat with chelation or phlebotomy.
  • When to suspect it — red flags
  • ESC 2023 advises screening when LV wall thickness is ≥ 12 mm plus at least one red flag (or age > 65 with HF, unexplained LVH or severe AS).
Clinical & ECG
  • HF with "unexplained" hypotension; intolerance
  • of beta-blockers/ACE-I; hypertension that
  • "resolved"
  • Carpal tunnel (bilateral), spinal stenosis,
  • neuropathy, dysautonomia
  • Low or normal QRS voltage despite thick walls
  • (voltage–mass discordance; true low voltage in
  • only ≈ 30–50%)
  • Pseudo-infarct Q waves, AV block, AF
  • NT-proBNP disproportionately high; persistently
  • raised troponin
Imaging
  • Biventricular thickening, thick interatrial
  • septum and valves, small pericardial effusion
  • "Granular sparkling" myocardium (non-specific)
  • Reduced GLS with apical sparing ("cherry-ontop")
  • Restrictive filling, very low e′, low stroke volume
  • CMR: diffuse subendocardial/transmural LGE,
  • native T1 ↑, ECV > 0.40
EXAM TRAP

CMR can suggest amyloid but can neither prove it nor distinguish AL from ATTR. Similarly, a positive bone scan does not exclude AL — grade 1–3 uptake occurs in a minority of AL hearts. That is why the monoclonal-protein screen must accompany every bone scan .

Diagnostic algorithm

The monoclonal screen is three tests: serum free light chains (sFLC — κ/λ ratio, normal ≈ 0.26–1.65, wider in CKD), serum immunofixation and urine immunofixation. Electrophoresis without immunofixation is not sufficient.

BOARD PEARL

Perugini grading compares cardiac with rib uptake: grade 0 none, 1 less than bone, 2 equal, 3 greater (with reduced bone signal). Grade 2–3 + no monoclonal protein is > 98% specific for ATTR in a patient with a compatible echo/CMR. SPECT is mandatory — planar images mistake blood-pool activity for myocardial uptake. Technetium-DPD, PYP and HMDP are used; ordinary MDP bone scans are not.

Staging and prognosis

AL — Mayo 2012: dFLC ≥ 18 mg/dL, troponin T ≥ 0.025 ng/mL, NT-proBNP ≥ 1800 pg/mL (stages I–IV). ATTR — UK NAC: NT-proBNP > 3000 pg/mL and eGFR < 45 mL/min/1.73 m² (stages I–III; median survival ≈ 69 / 47 / 24 months); Mayo ATTRwt uses troponin T > 0.05 ng/mL and NT-proBNP > 3000 pg/mL.

Disease-modifying therapy for ATTR-CM

MECHANISM — STABILISE OR S I L ENCE

TTR circulates as a tetramer. Dissociation into monomers is the rate-limiting step for misfolding and fibril formation. Stabilisers (tafamidis, acoramidis) bind the thyroxine-binding sites and hold the tetramer together. Silencers (siRNA: patisiran, vutrisiran; antisense: inotersen, eplontersen) knock down hepatic TTR production by ≈ 80%. Neither removes established deposits — hence "treat early".

Tafamidis in genetically proven hereditary ATTR-CM with NYHA I–II I B

OAC in cardiac amyloidosis with AF or flutter, regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc (unless contraindicated) I B Contrast CMR for serial follow-up and assessment of therapy response IIa C

Supportive care — what differs from ordinary HF

Loop diuretics are the mainstay; the stiff, small ventricle is preload-dependent — over-diuresis causes hypotension and renal failure.

Beta-blockers and ACE-I/ARB/ARNI are poorly tolerated (fixed stroke volume → cardiac output depends on heart rate; autonomic neuropathy → hypotension). Stop them if they cause hypotension or fatigue. MRA and SGLT2 inhibitors are reasonable.

Avoid non-dihydropyridine CCBs (bind amyloid fibrils, profound hypotension/negative inotropy); use digoxin only with great caution at low dose.

AF: anticoagulate all; amiodarone is the usual rhythm drug; LA appendage thrombus is common even in sinus rhythm (atrial electromechanical dissociation).

Conduction disease: pacing as usual; in severe AS with ATTR, TAVI still improves outcome.

WHAT CHANGED SINCE 2023
  • Acoramidis (ATTRibute-CM) and vutrisiran (HELIOS-B) joined tafamidis as proven disease-modifying therapy (approvals 2024–2025).
  • ACC 2025 Concise Clinical Guidance on ATTR-CM: exclude AL first, start therapy at the earliest symptomatic stage, insufficient data for routine combination or switching.
  • CARDIO-TTRansform (eplontersen, ESC 2026) was neutral on its primary endpoint — silencer benefit on top of a stabiliser remains unproven.

Key highlightsCardiac amyloidosis

  • > 95% of cardiac amyloid is AL or ATTR; ATTRwt = elderly men with carpal tunnel years earlier.
  • Voltage–mass discordance (thick walls, normal/low QRS voltage) + apical-sparing strain = classic clues.
  • Exclude AL with sFLC + serum IFE + urine IFE — all three.
  • Grade 2–3 DPD/PYP/HMDP uptake (SPECT) + no M-protein = ATTR-CM without biopsy.
  • Any monoclonal protein → tissue diagnosis with typing; AL is a haematological emergency.
  • Tafamidis 61 mg daily: ESC I B for NYHA I–II; ACC/AHA 1 B-R for NYHA I–III.
  • Acoramidis (stabiliser) and vutrisiran (silencer, 25 mg SC every 3 months) also reduce events.
  • OAC in amyloid + AF regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc (ESC I B); avoid verapamil/diltiazem; digoxin with caution.
  • V142I (Val122Ile) = West African ancestry, cardiac-predominant ATTRv.

3.6 Sarcoidosis, Fabry & Storage Disease

Cardiac sarcoidosis

Non-caseating granulomas infiltrate the myocardium, then heal with scar. Cardiac involvement is found at autopsy in ≈ 20–30% of patients with systemic sarcoid but is clinically evident in only ≈ 5%; isolated cardiac sarcoid is increasingly recognised. Granulomas favour the basal septum (conduction system) and the lateral wall.

Three presentations
  • Conduction disease — Mobitz II or complete AV
  • block in a young adult
  • Ventricular arrhythmia — sustained
  • monomorphic VT (scar re-entry)
  • HF — dilated (thinned, aneurysmal basal
  • septum) or restrictive early
Diagnostic tools
  • CMR: patchy mid-wall/subepicardial LGE, basal
  • septum, RV insertion "hook"
  • ¹⁸F-FDG-PET (after carbohydrate-free, high-fat
  • preparation): focal uptake = active inflammation;
  • perfusion–FDG mismatch predicts events
  • EMB — specific but sensitivity only ≈ 20–30%
  • (patchy disease)

Unexplained Mobitz II or complete heart block in a patient under 60 should prompt a search for cardiac sarcoid (HRS 2014, IIa) — also consider giant-cell myocarditis, laminopathy and Lyme disease. Treatment: immunosuppression (prednisolone ≈ 30–40 mg/day tapering, often with methotrexate as steroid-sparer) for active inflammation on PET; it may improve LV function and sometimes AV block, but does not remove the arrhythmic substrate. VT: AAD (amiodarone/sotalol) → ablation.

EXAM TRAP

A patient with sarcoid and complete heart block needs a device that can defibrillate — the pacing indication itself raises SCD risk (IIa). Implanting a simple pacemaker is the wrong answer, even if LVEF is normal. The same logic applies to laminopathy.

Anderson–Fabry disease

X-linked lysosomal storage disease: GLA variants → deficient α-galactosidase A → accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in myocytes, endothelium, kidney and nerves. Men (hemizygous) are affected earlier and more severely; women (heterozygous) develop disease later through random X-inactivation (lyonisation). Found in ≈ 0.5–1% of adults labelled "HCM".

3.7 LV Hypertrabeculation (Non-compaction)

Prominent LV trabeculations with deep intertrabecular recesses and a thin compact epicardial layer, typically mid-lateral and apical. The old embryological theory ("arrested compaction") lacks proof in humans, and excessive trabeculation appears physiologically in athletes, in pregnancy, in sickle-cell disease and in people of African ancestry. ESC 2023 therefore treats it as a phenotypic trait, not a cardiomyopathy — preferring the term hypertrabeculation. Diagnostic ratios (non-compacted : compacted layer): Jenni (echo, end-systole) > 2.0; Petersen (CMR, enddiastole) > 2.3; Jacquier (CMR) trabeculated mass > 20% of LV mass. All are sensitive but poorly specific. What matters is the associated phenotype: hypertrabeculation with normal LV size and function in an asymptomatic person has an excellent prognosis; with LV dilatation/dysfunction it is managed as DCM (and genetic testing — MYH7, TTN, NKX2-5, PRDM16, LMNA; Barth syndrome (TAZ) in boys).

Complications follow LVEF: HF, arrhythmia, thromboembolism from the recesses.

Anticoagulate for AF, LV thrombus or prior embolism; many experts also anticoagulate when LVEF is severely reduced. Contrast echo separates trabeculae from thrombus.

Key highlightsSarcoid, Fabry & storage

  • Sarcoid: AV block + VT + basal septal LGE; FDG-PET shows activity; EMB sensitivity only ≈ 20–30%.
  • Unexplained high-grade AV block at age < 60 → look for cardiac sarcoid.
  • Sarcoid ICD: sustained VT/arrest or LVEF ≤ 35% (I B); pacing indication or significant LGE (IIa).
  • Steroids treat inflammation, not the scar — arrhythmic risk persists.
  • Fabry: X-linked α-Gal A deficiency; low native T1 + basal inferolateral LGE; women need genetic diagnosis.
  • Fabry therapy: ERT (agalsidase) or migalastat (amenable variants).
  • LVH + pre-excitation = Danon (X-linked, massive LVH), PRKAG2 or Pompe.
DON'T CONFUSE

Pregnancy and endurance training can produce criteria-meeting trabeculation that regresses. Diagnosing "LVNC" in a fit athlete with normal function and ECG is over-diagnosis — the board answer is reassurance (± follow-up), not sports disqualification or anticoagulation.

Key highlightsHypertrabeculation

  • ESC 2023: LVNC is a trait ("hypertrabeculation"), not a cardiomyopathy.
  • Jenni echo ratio > 2.0 in systole; Petersen CMR ratio > 2.3 in diastole.
  • Prognosis is dictated by LV size and function, not trabeculation.
  • Physiological in athletes, pregnancy and people of African ancestry.
  • OAC for AF, thrombus or embolism; Barth syndrome (X-linked TAZ) in boys with neutropenia.
  • Element Practical points
  • Arrhythmic protection Wearable cardioverter-defibrillator in the early months — LVEF often recovers, so defer the ICD decision (≈ 6 months)
  • Genetic testing Recommended in PPCM (ESC 2025 Pregnancy guideline)
  • Duration of HF therapy Continue for at least 12 months after full LV recovery, then taper slowly Prognosis: roughly 50% recover (LVEF ≥ 50%) within 6–12 months. Poor recovery predicted by LVEF < 30% at diagnosis, LVEDD > 60 mm, RV involvement, delayed diagnosis and African ancestry.

3.8 Peripartum Cardiomyopathy

DEFINITION (ESC/HFA)

HF secondary to LV systolic dysfunction with LVEF < 45%, occurring towards the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery (mostly in the first month postpartum), with no other identifiable cause. The LV may not be dilated.

Incidence varies from ≈ 1 in 100 (Nigeria, Haiti) to 1 in 1000–4000 (Europe, USA). Risk factors: pre-eclampsia/hypertension (in ≈ 1 in 4), African ancestry, multiparity, multiple gestation, older maternal age, prolonged tocolysis. About 15% carry cardiomyopathy gene variants — two-thirds TTN truncations — so PPCM overlaps with familial DCM.

Mechanism: oxidative stress activates cathepsin D, which cleaves prolactin into a cardiotoxic, anti-angiogenic 16-kDa fragment; placental sFlt-1 (high in pre-eclampsia) adds vascular injury — the rationale for the dopamine agonist bromocriptine.

Management — "BOARD" plus standard HF care

Relieve symptoms, betablockerLoop diuretics; β₁-selective beta-blocker (metoprolol, bisoprolol) safe in pregnancy; hydralazine + nitrate as antepartum vasodilator

Delivery Urgent delivery (usually caesarean) if haemodynamically unstable despite therapy; otherwise vaginal delivery with epidural is preferred

Cardiogenic shock Avoid dobutamine where possible (catecholamines may worsen PPCM); early MCS and transfer to a centre with ECMO/LVAD

BOARD PEARL — THE NEXT PREGNANCY

A subsequent pregnancy carries a risk of relapse of ≈ 20% even when LVEF has normalised, and of severe deterioration and death when it has not.

If LVEF has not recovered, a further pregnancy should be discouraged (mWHO class IV territory). Women with recovered function still need pre-conception counselling and close surveillance; HF drugs are switched to pregnancy-compatible agents before conception.

Key highlightsPeripartum cardiomyopathy

  • LVEF < 45% late in pregnancy or in the months postpartum, no other cause.
  • Risk: pre-eclampsia, African ancestry, multiparity, twins, older age; ≈ 15% genetic (TTN). 16-kDa prolactin + sFlt-1 → bromocriptine rationale; always combine with anticoagulation.
  • ACE-I/ARB/ARNI/MRA/SGLT2i contraindicated in pregnancy; start after delivery.
  • Wearable defibrillator early; defer ICD decision — many recover.
  • ≈ 50% recover; continue HF drugs ≥ 12 months after recovery.
  • Next pregnancy discouraged if LVEF not recovered; genetic testing recommended (ESC 2025).
  • Feature Findings
  • ECG Anterior ST elevation (often without reciprocal change, less in V1), then deep widespread T inversion with QTc prolongation over 24–48 h
  • Biomarkers Troponin rise modest relative to the extent of dysfunction; BNP/NT-proBNP markedly raised Coronary angiography Required to exclude ACS — obstructive CAD does not exclude TTS (coexists in ≈ 15%) CMR Oedema in the dysfunctional segments; no significant LGE (vs infarct or myocarditis) Recovery LV function recovers over days to weeks (usually within 3 months)
  • Complications and their treatment

3.9 Takotsubo Syndrome

Takotsubo syndrome (TTS; stress cardiomyopathy, "broken heart syndrome") is an acute, usually reversible LV dysfunction that mimics ACS. It accounts for ≈ 1–2% of suspected STEMI/ACS presentations. Around 90% of patients are post-menopausal women. It is not benign : in-hospital mortality in the InterTAK registry (≈ 4–5%) is comparable to ACS, and worse in men and after physical triggers.

MECHANISM

A catecholamine surge (emotional or physical stress, neurological injury, phaeochromocytoma, exogenous adrenaline/dobutamine) causes myocardial stunning. The apex has the highest density of β-adrenoceptors; at very high adrenaline levels β₂ receptors switch to Gi coupling (negative inotropy — "stimulus trafficking"), producing apical ballooning with a hypercontractile base. Microvascular spasm and inflammation contribute.

DON'T CONFUSE

Neurogenic stunning (subarachnoid haemorrhage) often spares the apex; sepsis cardiomyopathy is global and recovers in 7–10 days; phaeochromocytoma may cause "inverted" TTS (check metanephrines); myocarditis shows subepicardial LGE.

Key highlightsTakotsubo syndrome

  • ≈ 90% post-menopausal women; ≈ 1–2% of suspected ACS.
  • Wall-motion abnormality extends beyond one coronary territory; troponin modest, BNP high.
  • ST elevation → deep T inversion + QTc prolongation over 24–48 h.
  • CMR: oedema without LGE.
  • Always do coronary angiography; coexisting CAD does not exclude TTS.
  • Shock: look for LVOT obstruction — then fluids, β-blocker, phenylephrine; no inotropes.
  • In-hospital mortality ≈ 4–5% (like ACS); recurrence ≈ 2%/year.

3.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 76-year-old man with HFpEF, bilateral carpal tunnel release 8 years ago and a septal thickness of 16 mm has QRS voltages at the lower limit of normal. Serum free light-chain ratio is normal and serum and urine immunofixation are negative. DPD scintigraphy with SPECT shows grade 3 myocardial uptake. What is the next best step?

Answer C Grade 2–3 bone-tracer uptake with a negative monoclonal screen (all three tests) diagnoses ATTR-CM without biopsy. The next step is TTR genotyping (wild-type vs hereditary — cascade testing) and starting a stabiliser/silencer. Biopsy (A, B) is only for a positive M-protein or discordant results; CMR (E) cannot type amyloid.

Q2 A 38-year-old man has DCM with LVEF 42%, PR interval 240 ms, NSVT on Holter and a pathogenic LMNA variant. His estimated 5-year risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia is 14%. The best management is: Continue GDMT and repeat Holter in 1 year

Answer C LMNA carriers have arrhythmic risk out of proportion to LVEF. ESC recommends an ICD when the LMNA 5-year risk is ≥ 10% with NSVT, LVEF < 50% or AV conduction delay (IIa). A pacemaker alone (B) leaves him unprotected; waiting for LVEF ≤ 35% (A, D) is the classic error.

Q3 A 24-year-old footballer has T-wave inversion in V1–V3 (no RBBB), a run of non-sustained VT of LBBB morphology with superior axis on Holter, and CMR showing RV free-wall dyskinesia with RVEDVi 118 mL/m². How many 2010 Task Force major criteria are present, and what is the diagnosis?

Answer C Three major criteria: repolarisation (TWI V1–V3 over age 14, no RBBB), arrhythmia (NSVT/VT of LBBB morphology with superior axis) and CMR (regional dyskinesia + RVEDVi ≥ 110 mL/m² in a man). Two major criteria alone already define definite ARVC. Beware: an inferior-axis (RVOT) VT or > 500 PVCs/24 h is only minor; athletic RV dilatation lacks regional dyskinesia (E).

Q4 Echo in a 60-year-old with ascites and raised JVP shows a septal bounce, mitral E-wave inspiratory fall of 35%, medial e′ 12 cm/s higher than lateral e′, and expiratory hepatic-vein diastolic reversal. NT-proBNP is 180 pg/mL. The most likely diagnosis is:

Answer B Septal bounce, > 25% respiratory E variation, preserved e′ with annulus reversus, expiratory hepatic reversal and a near-normal BNP are the constriction pattern. Restrictive diseases (A, C, D) have low e′, inspiratory hepatic reversal and high BNP.

Q5 A 44-year-old woman presents with complete heart block. LVEF is 55%. CMR shows patchy basal septal and inferolateral mid-wall LGE; FDG-PET shows focal septal uptake and hilar nodes. Which device is most appropriate?

Answer C Cardiac sarcoid with a pacing indication → an ICD should be considered regardless of LVEF (ESC 2022, IIa). Steroids may improve conduction but do not remove the arrhythmic substrate (D). A simple pacemaker (A, B) is the trap.

Q6 A 71-year-old woman develops chest pain after her husband's funeral. ECG: anterior ST elevation. Angiography: 60% mid-RCA stenosis only; LV gram shows apical ballooning with hyperkinetic base. Two hours later she is hypotensive (BP 78/50) with a new harsh systolic murmur. What should be done first?

Answer C A new murmur with hypotension in apical Takotsubo suggests dynamic LVOT obstruction from the hypercontractile base (± SAM MR). Inotropes (A) and IABP (B) worsen obstruction; diuretics (E) reduce preload. Non-culprit RCA disease (D) does not explain the picture.

Q7 A 29-year-old woman is diagnosed with peripartum cardiomyopathy 2 weeks after delivery (LVEF 25%, no thrombus). She wishes to stop breastfeeding. Bromocriptine is started. Which additional therapy is mandatory with it?

Answer B Bromocriptine carries a thrombotic risk; ESC advises it always be accompanied by at least prophylactic anticoagulation. SGLT2i and ivabradine (A, D) are not first-line here; an ICD (E) is deferred because LVEF often recovers — a wearable defibrillator is preferred early.

Q8 A 35-year-old man is referred as "HCM" (septum 14 mm, concentric). He has neuropathic pain in the hands, angiokeratomas and microalbuminuria. CMR shows basal inferolateral LGE. Which additional CMR finding is most characteristic?

Answer B Fabry disease: sphingolipid storage lowers native T1 (a unique finding), with basal inferolateral LGE. High T1/ECV (A) is amyloid; short T2* (C) is iron; ring-like LGE (D) is DSP/FLNC; apical obliteration (E) is EMF.

Q9 The sister of a man with DCM carries the same VUS in TTN that was found in her brother; no pathogenic variant has been identified in the family. Her ECG and echo are normal. What is correct?

Answer D A VUS is not actionable: it can be used for segregation studies, but not for predictive testing or discharge. Without a P/LP variant, first-degree relatives need periodic clinical screening (ECG + imaging). A and C both wrongly treat the VUS as diagnostic.

Q10 An 80-year-old man with ATTRwt cardiomyopathy develops persistent AF. CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 2 and HAS-BLED 1. Heart rate is 95 bpm, BP 98/60. Which is the best plan?

Answer C AF in cardiac amyloid mandates anticoagulation irrespective of CHA₂DS₂-VASc (ESC I B). Non-DHP CCBs (A, B) bind amyloid and cause hypotension; digoxin loading (D) risks toxicity. Low-dose beta-blocker if tolerated, amiodarone for rhythm control.

What the board expects you to know

  • The diagnostic thresholds (15 mm, 13 mm in relatives, z-scores in children) and the gradients that define obstruction (30 and 50 mmHg).
  • The mechanism of SAM, the bedside manoeuvres and the invasive signs (spike-and-dome, Brockenbrough) that separate HCM from AS.
  • The stepwise drug ladder — beta-blocker, verapamil/diltiazem, disopyramide, cardiac myosin inhibitors — and the drugs to avoid.
  • Eligibility for myectomy versus alcohol septal ablation.
  • SCD risk stratification: HCM Risk-SCD thresholds (ESC) versus major risk markers (ACC/AHA), and where the two guidelines disagree.

Numbers that win marks

≥ 15 mmLV wall — HCM in adults (≥ 13 mm in relatives)
≥ 30 mmHgLVOT gradient — obstructive HCM
≥ 50 mmHgLVOT gradient — threshold for SRT
≥ 6%HCM Risk-SCD 5-y risk → ICD (ESC IIa)
≥ 30 mmMassive LVH — major SCD marker
< 50%LVEF — systolic dysfunction in HCM

4.1 Definition, Genetics & Morphology

DEFINITION (ESC 2023/AHA/ACC 2024)

Increased LV wall thickness (or mass), with or without RV hypertrophy, not solely explained by abnormal loading conditions. In adults: maximal end-diastolic wall thickness ≥ 15 mm in any segment by echo or CMR. In first-degree relatives or carriers of a P/LP variant: ≥ 13 mm. In children: z-score > 2.5 (asymptomatic, no family history) or > 2 (family history or positive genotype).

HCM is the commonest inherited cardiac disease: unexplained LVH occurs in ≈ 1 in 500 adults (and the genetic trait in up to 1 in 200), although clinically recognised disease is far rarer. It affects both sexes, all ethnic groups, and presents from infancy to old age; women tend to present later and more symptomatic.

Genetics

Autosomal dominant (50% risk to offspring) with incomplete, age-related penetrance and variable expressivity.

P/LP sarcomere variants in ≈ 30–40% of probands overall, up to ≈ 60% in familial disease and young patients.

MYBPC3 (myosin-binding protein C) and MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain) account for ≈ 70% of positive tests; others: TNNT2, TNNI3, TPM1, MYL2, MYL3, ACTC1.

Genotype-positive patients present younger and have more AF, HF and SCD than genotype-negative ("non-familial") HCM; ≥ 2 variants (≈ 5%) mean more severe disease.

About half of probands have no identifiable variant — likely polygenic plus hypertension/obesity; their relatives' risk is lower.

MECHANISM — HYPERCONTRACTILITY AT THE SARCOMERE

Most pathogenic variants increase the number of myosin heads available to bind actin (they destabilise the energy-saving super-relaxed state). The result is hyperdynamic contraction, impaired relaxation and excessive ATP consumption → energy starvation, myocyte hypertrophy, myocyte disarray and interstitial fibrosis. This is exactly the target of the cardiac myosin inhibitors, which push myosin back into the "off" state.

Morphology

Natural history. Most patients have a near-normal life expectancy; annual cardiovascular mortality in contemporary cohorts is ≈ 1% or less, and SCD ≈ 0.5%/year in adults. Morbidity comes from AF (≈ 20–25%, rising with age), HF (obstruction or diastolic dysfunction), stroke, and less often progression to systolic dysfunction.

Key highlightsDefinition & genetics

  • HCM = LVWT ≥ 15 mm (adults), ≥ 13 mm in relatives/variant carriers, not explained by loading.
  • Children: z-score > 2.5, or > 2 with family history/genotype.
  • Prevalence of unexplained LVH ≈ 1 in 500; autosomal dominant.
  • MYBPC3 and MYH7 ≈ 70% of positive genotypes; overall yield ≈ 30–40%.
  • Pathobiology = excess myosin cross-bridges → hypercontractility, poor relaxation, energy deficit, disarray.
  • Apical HCM: giant T-wave inversion; mid-ventricular HCM: apical aneurysm.
  • Adult SCD ≈ 0.5%/year; AF is the commonest sustained arrhythmia.
  • The mitral valve in HCM
  • SAM-related MR: posteriorly directed, mid-late systolic, severity tracks the gradient — expected to resolve after successful septal reduction.
  • Primary mitral abnormalities (in ≈ 10–20%): elongated anterior leaflet (> 30 mm), anomalous papillary muscle inserting directly into the anterior leaflet, accessory chordae, prolapse or chordal rupture. A central or anterior MR jet suggests an intrinsic valve problem that myectomy alone will not fix → surgical repair/replacement or papillary-muscle realignment.
  • Beyond obstruction — other symptom generators
  • Diastolic dysfunction: impaired relaxation +
  • stiff, fibrotic LV → high filling pressures, LA
  • dilatation, HFpEF
  • Microvascular ischaemia: small-vessel intimal
  • thickening, high wall stress, low capillary
  • density → angina with normal coronaries
  • Myocardial bridging of the LAD (common)
  • AF: loss of atrial kick in a stiff ventricle → abrupt
  • decompensation
  • Autonomic dysfunction: abnormal BP response
  • to exercise (≈ 25%)

4.2 Pathophysiology: LVOTO, SAM & the Mitral Valve

About one third of patients have obstruction at rest, one third only on provocation, and one third are nonobstructive — so ≈ 70% have obstructive physiology once provocation is performed . LVOTO is defined as a peak instantaneous gradient ≥ 30 mmHg (rest or provoked); ≥ 50 mmHg is the level at which obstruction is haemodynamically important and invasive therapy is considered.

MECHANISM — SAM IS DRAG,NOT ONLY VENTURI

The hypertrophied basal septum narrows and displaces the outflow tract. Anteriorly displaced papillary muscles and an elongated anterior leaflet put the leaflet into the ejection stream, which drags (pushes) it towards the septum — the systolic anterior motion (SAM). Venturi suction contributes later in systole.

Mitral-septal contact creates obstruction that is late-peaking and a posteriorly directed MR jet in mid-tolate systole. Anything that shrinks the LV cavity (↓ preload, ↓ afterload) or increases contractility worsens the gradient.

digoxin, tachycardia, post-extrasystolic beat, AF with rapid rate

↓ Gradient (murmur softer) Squatting, passive leg raise, isometric handgrip, phenylephrine, volume, beta-blocker, verapamil/diltiazem, disopyramide, myosin inhibitors, bradycardia (within limits)

Key highlightsPathophysiology

  • LVOTO = gradient ≥ 30 mmHg; ≥ 50 mmHg = haemodynamically significant.
  • ≈ 1/3 resting obstruction, ≈ 1/3 provocable, ≈ 1/3 non-obstructive.
  • SAM is driven mainly by flow drag on an anteriorly positioned, elongated leaflet.
  • SAM-MR is posterior and mid-late systolic; a central/anterior jet = intrinsic mitral disease.
  • Small cavity (↓ preload/afterload) or ↑ contractility → ↑ gradient.
  • Symptoms also arise from diastolic dysfunction, microvascular ischaemia and AF.

  • Carotid pulse Brisk upstroke, bifid Slow-rising, low volume (parvus et
  • tardus)
  • Valsalva / standing Louder Softer
  • Squat / passive leg raise Softer Louder
  • Handgrip Softer Softer or unchanged
  • Ejection click / A2 No click; A2 normal (may be paradoxically
  • split)
  • Click if bicuspid; soft A2
  • Beat after a PVC Gradient ↑ but aortic pulse pressure falls Gradient ↑ and aortic pulse pressure rises
  • ECG and ambulatory monitoring
  • The ECG is abnormal in ≈ 90% and may precede hypertrophy in carriers: LVH voltage with strain, deep narrow "dagger" Q waves in inferolateral leads (septal hypertrophy), giant T-wave inversion (apical HCM), LA enlargement, AF. Pre-excitation or AV block suggests a phenocopy (PRKAG2, Danon, Fabry, amyloid). 24–48-h ambulatory ECG at diagnosis and every 1–2 years screens for NSVT and AF (ESC I B; AHA/ACC 1).
  • Echocardiography
  • Measure maximal wall thickness in every segment on short-axis views, base to apex (I C).
  • SAM with mitral-septal contact; mid-systolic closure/notching of the aortic valve on M-mode.
  • CW Doppler through the LVOT: late-peaking, "dagger-shaped" envelope — distinguish from the MR jet (starts earlier, velocity usually > 6 m/s). Pulsed-wave mapping localises the level (LVOT vs mid-cavity).
  • Provocation if resting gradient < 50 mmHg: Valsalva sitting/semi-supine then standing. If still < 50 mmHg in a symptomatic patient → exercise echo (ESC I B; AHA/ACC 1). Dobutamine is not recommended — it creates non-physiological intracavitary gradients.
  • Diastolic assessment (E/e′, LA volume, TR velocity); GLS is reduced despite normal LVEF; LVEF in HCM is "supranormal" — an LVEF below 50% already means systolic dysfunction .
  • Contrast echo for apical hypertrophy, aneurysm or thrombus.
  • Cardiac MRI
  • CMR defines wall thickness where echo misses it (anterolateral wall, apex), detects apical aneurysm, guides SRT, and quantifies LGE — patchy mid-wall fibrosis in hypertrophied segments and at the RV insertion points, present in ≈ 65%. ≥ 15% of LV mass is "extensive" LGE (an SCD marker). CMR also points to phenocopies (amyloid, Fabry).

4.3 Clinical Features & Diagnosis

  • Symptoms
  • Many are asymptomatic and found by family screening, a murmur or an abnormal ECG.

Exertional dyspnoea (commonest), angina, fatigue, palpitations; symptoms are typically worse after meals, alcohol or dehydration.

Syncope: exertional or unexplained syncope is ominous (VT, LVOTO); post-exertional or clearly vasovagal syncope is not an SCD marker.

SCD may be the first manifestation, particularly in adolescents and young adults.

Examination

Harsh ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, not radiating to the carotids; increases with Valsalva and standing, decreases with squatting and handgrip.

Apical pansystolic murmur of SAM-MR; bifid (bisferiens) pulse; double or triple apical impulse; S4. Non-obstructive HCM may have no murmur at all.

Invasive haemodynamics

Used when non-invasive data are discordant. An end-hole catheter pulled back from LV apex to aorta shows a sub-aortic pressure drop.

Figure 4.1 · Schematic LV (red) and aortic (blue) pressures in obstructive HCM. The aortic trace shows an early spike (ejection before obstruction) and a late dome. After a PVC, post-extrasystolic potentiation increases contractility and obstruction: the LV–aortic gradient rises while the aortic pulse pressure falls — the Brockenbrough–Braunwald–Morrow sign. In fixed AS, aortic pulse pressure rises after a PVC.

EXAM TRAP

A "gradient" on dobutamine stress echo in a hypovolaemic, hyperdynamic ICU patient is not HCM. Equally, a patient with severe AS may develop sub-aortic dynamic obstruction immediately after AVR/TAVI (small hypertrophied cavity suddenly unloaded) — treat with fluids, beta-blocker and phenylephrine, and stop inotropes.

  • Sinus beat Beat after a PVC
  • PVC
  • LV (late peak)
  • Ao
  • spike dome
  • LV ↑ → gradient ↑
  • Ao pulse pressure ↓

Key highlightsDiagnosis

  • HCM murmur: left sternal edge, ↑ Valsalva/standing, ↓ squat/handgrip; bifid carotid pulse.
  • ECG abnormal in ≈ 90%; dagger Q waves, giant T inversion (apical).
  • Provoke with Valsalva and standing; exercise echo if symptomatic and gradient < 50 mmHg (I B).
  • Dobutamine provocation is not recommended.
  • CW Doppler LVOT: late-peaking dagger; MR jet is earlier and faster.
  • LVEF < 50% = systolic dysfunction in HCM.
  • CMR at diagnosis (I B); extensive LGE = ≥ 15% LV mass.
  • Spike-and-dome aortic trace; Brockenbrough: post-PVC gradient ↑, aortic pulse pressure ↓.
  • Coronary assessment (CT or invasive) before SRT in those at risk of CAD; EP study has no role in SCD stratification.

4.4 Differential: Athlete's Heart & Phenocopies

Wall thickness of 13–16 mm is the "grey zone" where HCM overlaps with athletic remodelling and hypertensive heart disease. The approach is to add evidence — cavity size, diastolic function, ECG, CMR, family history, genetics and the response to deconditioning or BP control.

DON'T CONFUSE — HYPERTENSION

Hypertensive LVH is usually concentric and mild (< 15 mm) and regresses with 6–12 months of tight BP control. Favour HCM with: family history, wall thickness ≥ 15 mm with bizarre asymmetry, RV hypertrophy, marked ECG repolarisation changes or Q waves, LGE at the RV insertion points, severe diastolic dysfunction, or a sarcomere variant. Elderly hypertensives with a sigmoid septum can develop genuine SAM and LVOTO — managed like obstructive HCM.

BOARD PEARL
  • LVH + ventricular pre-excitation = think storage disease (PRKAG2, Danon, Pompe), not sarcomeric HCM.
  • The HCM Risk-SCD calculator is not valid in phenocopies, elite athletes, or after septal reduction — and Danon disease needs early ICD and transplant referral.

4.5 Medical Therapy of Obstructive HCM

Drugs treat symptoms; none has been shown to reduce SCD. Titrate to symptoms, not to the number on the Doppler. General measures for every patient with LVOTO: avoid dehydration, large meals and excess alcohol; stop or avoid vasodilators (nitrates, PDE-5 inhibitors, dihydropyridines, ACE-I/ARB where possible) and digoxin ; lose weight; treat hypertension with beta-blockers or non-DHP calcium blockers rather than vasodilators.

Class 1 options

Key highlightsDifferential diagnosis

  • Grey zone = 13–16 mm; integrate cavity size, diastolic function, ECG, CMR, genetics.
  • Athlete: LVEDD > 55 mm, normal e′, no LGE, regression after ≈ 3 months detraining.
  • HCM: small cavity (< 45 mm), LA enlargement, abnormal ECG repolarisation, patchy LGE.
  • Hypertensive LVH regresses with 6–12 months of BP control.
  • Phenocopies: amyloid, Fabry, Danon, PRKAG2, Pompe, Noonan, mitochondrial, Friedreich.
  • Pre-excitation + LVH → storage disease.

Safety rule Start only if LVEF ≥ 55%; interrupt if LVEF < 50%; mandatory echo surveillance (REMS in USA); teratogenic — contraception required; mavacamten can reduce efficacy of hormonal

contraceptives

WHAT CHANGED 2023–2026
  • ESC 2023 and AHA/ACC 2024 both introduced cardiac myosin inhibitors for symptomatic obstructive HCM.
  • Second CMI aficamten approved (FDA, Dec 2025); MAPLE-HCM showed aficamten monotherapy beat metoprolol — raising the question of CMI as first line (not yet guideline-endorsed).
  • Non-obstructive HCM: mavacamten failed (ODYSSEY-HCM, 2025) but aficamten met both primary endpoints in ACACIA-HCM (2026) — the first positive trial in nHCM.
MECHANISM — WHY THE DRUGS WORK

Beta-blockers: ↓ contractility and heart rate → longer diastole, larger end-systolic cavity, less SAM (especially the exercise gradient).

Verapamil/diltiazem: negative inotropy + improved relaxation; their vasodilator effect can worsen severe resting obstruction.

Disopyramide: class Ia with strong negative inotropy; anticholinergic side-effects (dry mouth, urinary retention — caution in older men); monitor QTc (reduce if > 500 ms); may speed AV conduction in AF → give with a beta-blocker.

CMIs: fewer actin–myosin cross-bridges → ↓ hypercontractility and gradient, improved filling; excess dose → systolic dysfunction.

EXAM TRAP — ACUTE PULMONARY OEDEMA OR SHOCK IN HOCM

The instinctive treatment (IV furosemide, nitrates, inotropes) worsens obstruction. The correct management is IV fluids (if hypotensive), beta-blocker to slow the heart and a pure vasoconstrictor (phenylephrine) to expand the cavity. Dobutamine, milrinone, adrenaline and IABP are harmful.

Key highlightsMedical therapy

  • First line: non-vasodilating beta-blocker (I B); verapamil/diltiazem if BB fails or not tolerated (I B).
  • Avoid dehydration, nitrates, PDE-5 inhibitors, dihydropyridines and digoxin in LVOTO.
  • Add-on: disopyramide (I B) or mavacamten (ESC IIa A; AHA/ACC Class 1).
  • CMI: start if LVEF ≥ 55%, hold if LVEF < 50%; teratogenic; echo surveillance.
  • Disopyramide: anticholinergic effects, QTc (> 500 ms → reduce), give with AV-nodal blocker.
  • Verapamil harmful with rest gradient > 100 mmHg and hypotension.
  • Hypotension/pulmonary oedema: fluids + beta-blocker + phenylephrine — never inotropes.
  • Aficamten (FDA 2025) is the second CMI; ACACIA-HCM (2026) is the first positive trial in non-obstructive HCM.

4.6 Septal Reduction Therapy

SRT removes the anatomical substrate of obstruction. Candidates must meet three conditions: clinical (NYHA III–IV, or recurrent exertional syncope, despite maximum tolerated therapy), haemodynamic (rest or provoked LVOT gradient ≥ 50 mmHg due to septal hypertrophy and SAM) and anatomical (septal thickness adequate for a safe procedure — thin septa, ≤ 16 mm at the contact point, carry a VSD risk). Performed only by experienced teams: myectomy mortality < 1% in expert centres.

BOARD PEARL

Before ASA, confirm that the chosen septal perforator supplies the SAM–septal contact point with intracoronary myocardial contrast echo (I B) — this avoids infarcting the papillary muscle or RV. After ASA, monitor for complete heart block (usually within 48–72 h); pre-existing LBBB is a set-up for complete block after ASA (which causes RBBB). Neither procedure is performed to reduce SCD risk.

Key highlightsSeptal reduction therapy

  • SRT: gradient ≥ 50 mmHg + NYHA III–IV despite maximal therapy (I B) — at expert centres.
  • Recurrent exertional syncope due to LVOTO: IIa; selected NYHA II with MR/AF/LA dilatation: IIb.
  • Myectomy for children, very thick septa, intrinsic mitral disease, concomitant surgery.
  • Myectomy → LBBB; ASA → RBBB and pacemaker ≈ 10–20%.
  • ASA gradient falls over ≈ 3 months; guided by myocardial contrast echo.
  • Thin septum (≤ 16 mm at contact) → VSD risk.
  • SRT is for symptoms, not SCD prevention.

4.7 Non-obstructive HCM, Advanced HF & AF

Non-obstructive HCM with preserved LVEF

Symptoms arise from diastolic dysfunction and microvascular ischaemia. Beta-blockers or verapamil/ diltiazem (slower rate, longer filling) are first line; cautious diuretics for congestion. Angina without obstructive CAD: beta-blocker/CCB; nitrates or ranolazine may be tried only if no LVOTO.

Always exclude latent obstruction with exercise echo before labelling a symptomatic patient nonobstructive. AHA/ACC 2024 added a 2b option of valsartan in young, early-stage sarcomere-variant carriers to slow phenotype progression (VANISH).

ODYSSEY-HCM (mavacamten) was negative; ACACIA-HCM (aficamten, 2026) improved KCCQ and peak VO₂ — regulatory and guideline status awaited.

HCM with systolic dysfunction and advanced HF

DEFINITION

Because the normal HCM ventricle is hyperdynamic, LVEF < 50% defines systolic dysfunction ("end-stage" or hypokinetic HCM). It develops in ≈ 5%, usually with extensive LGE, and carries high mortality from HF and SCD.

  • Start full HFrEF therapy at LVEF < 50% (AHA/ACC 1) and look for another cause (CAD).
  • Stop negative inotropes — verapamil, diltiazem, disopyramide and CMIs.

ICD is reasonable at LVEF < 50% (AHA/ACC 2a; ESC counts it as a risk modifier); CRT for LVEF < 50% with LBBB and NYHA II–IV (AHA/ACC 2a).

NYHA III–IV despite therapy or refractory VA → transplant assessment with CPET; LVAD as bridge is limited by the small cavity. HCM patients may qualify for transplant even with preserved LVEF when restrictive physiology is severe.

Atrial fibrillation

AF affects ≈ 20–25% (more with age and LA size > 45 mm) and is poorly tolerated: the stiff LV depends on atrial systole and a long diastole. Thromboembolic risk in HCM is high irrespective of CHA₂DS₂-VASc , which should not be used.

EXAM TRAP

A 45-year-old with HCM and a single episode of paroxysmal AF has CHA₂DS₂-VASc 0. The answer is still anticoagulation (DOAC). Digoxin is avoided in obstructive HCM; flecainide/propafenone are avoided because of structural heart disease; amiodarone is the most widely used AAD.

4.8 Sudden Cardiac Death & the ICD

SCD is usually VF, often in adolescents and young adults, and may occur at rest or with exertion. Drugs and SRT do not prevent it; the ICD is the only proven protection. The two guidelines share the same risk markers but use them differently: ESC calculates a 5-year risk; AHA/ACC counts major risk markers .

Major; in Risk-SCD

  • LVEF < 50% = systolic dysfunction → HFrEF therapy, stop negative inotropes and CMIs.
  • End-stage HCM ≈ 5%; ICD and CRT reasonable; transplant for refractory NYHA III–IV.
  • AF in HCM → OAC regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc (ESC I B; AHA/ACC 1); DOAC first.
  • Device AF > 24 h → OAC (AHA/ACC 1).

BOARD PEARL — HCM RISK-SCD

The ESC calculator (validated age ≥ 16 y) uses 7 variables: age, maximal wall thickness, LA diameter, maximal LVOT gradient, family history of SCD, NSVT and unexplained syncope. HCM Risk-Kids is used under 16. Neither is valid in elite athletes, phenocopies (Fabry, amyloid, Noonan) or after myectomy/ASA. Reassess every 1–2 years (ESC: 1–3) or when status changes.

ICD not indicated

Device type Subcutaneous ICD acceptable when pacing is not needed; dual-chamber if pacing needed for LVOTO/bradycardia

EXAM TRAP

Abnormal BP response to exercise (failure to rise ≥ 20 mmHg or a fall of ≥ 20 mmHg) and LVOTO are no longer stand-alone ICD triggers. Myectomy or ASA "to reduce SCD risk" is never the correct answer, nor is amiodarone as an ICD substitute.

4.9 Sport, Pregnancy & Family Screening

Exercise and competitive sport

Old advice restricted all athletes with HCM. Newer registry data (LIVE-HCM, 2023) showed no excess arrhythmic events in people who exercise vigorously, and both guidelines now reject universal sports restriction . Low-to-moderate recreational exercise is recommended for everyone able to do it; decisions about vigorous or competitive sport are individualised by an expert team with shared decision-making.

Key highlightsSCD & ICD

  • Secondary prevention (arrest/sustained VT): ICD — I B (ESC), 1 (AHA/ACC).
  • HCM Risk-SCD (≥ 16 y): 7 variables; ≥ 6% → IIa; 4–6% → IIb; < 4% with LGE ≥ 15% or LVEF < 50% → IIb.
  • AHA/ACC major markers: FH SCD ≤ 50 y, LVWT ≥ 30 mm, unexplained syncope, apical aneurysm, LVEF < 50%.
  • ≥ 1 major marker → ICD reasonable (2a); none + NSVT/extensive LGE → 2b.
  • Extensive LGE = ≥ 15% of LV mass.
  • Children: HCM Risk-Kids; NSVT counts as a major marker.
  • No ICD in genotype-positive, phenotype-negative individuals.
  • Drugs and SRT do not reduce SCD.
  • Group ESC 2023 AHA/ACC 2024

  • VA (III)
  • Universal restriction not indicated; ICD
  • must not be implanted solely to permit
  • sport
  • Genotype +/
  • phenotype −
  • Competitive sport should be considered (IIa) Competitive sport of any intensity
  • reasonable
  • Pregnancy
  • Most women tolerate pregnancy well (maternal mortality very low); risk is concentrated in those with severe LVOTO, symptoms before pregnancy, LVEF < 50% or high arrhythmic risk — managed by the pregnancy heart team (mWHO II to III).
  • Continue beta-blockers (metoprolol or bisoprolol preferred; monitor fetal growth); verapamil is second line.
  • Mavacamten and aficamten are teratogenic — stop before conception (mavacamten washout ≈ 4 months) and ensure effective contraception.
  • Avoid hypovolaemia and vasodilation at delivery (blood loss, rapid epidural). Vaginal delivery is usual; caesarean for obstetric indications or severe obstruction/HF.
  • AF: cardioversion and LMWH as required. Offer pre-conception genetic counselling (50% transmission; preimplantation genetic testing available when a P/LP variant is known).
  • Family screening
  • First-degree relatives are screened with ECG + echo (± CMR). If the proband has a P/LP variant, cascade testing sorts relatives into carriers (lifelong surveillance) and non-carriers (discharged). If no variant is known, all first-degree relatives need periodic clinical screening.
CLINICAL APPROACH — GENOTYPE-POSITIVE,PHENOTYPE-NEGATIVE

These "G+/P−" individuals may show early ECG changes, crypts, elongated mitral leaflets or reduced e′ before hypertrophy. They need periodic ECG + echo, no drug therapy, no ICD, and may participate in competitive sport. The variant classification (P/LP vs VUS) should be re-reviewed periodically, because reclassification changes who can be discharged.

Key highlightsSport, pregnancy & family

  • No universal sports ban; moderate recreational exercise for all.
  • Vigorous/competitive sport: ESC IIb only if low risk, no LVOTO; AHA/ACC 2a after shared decision-making.
  • G+/P− individuals: sport allowed, no ICD, regular screening.
  • Pregnancy usually tolerated; continue beta-blockers; CMIs are teratogenic.
  • Adults relatives: ECG + echo every 3–5 y; children every 1–2 y (high-risk families) or 2–3 y.
  • Non-carriers of a familial P/LP variant are discharged.

4.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 32-year-old man with HCM (septum 22 mm) has exertional dyspnoea. Resting LVOT gradient is 18 mmHg and rises to 32 mmHg with Valsalva. What is the next investigation?

Answer B Symptomatic with a resting/provoked peak gradient < 50 mmHg → exercise echo to unmask LVOTO (ESC I B; AHA/ ACC 1). Dobutamine (A) and isoprenaline (E) produce non-physiological gradients; EP study (D) has no role.

Q2 A 58-year-old woman with obstructive HCM (gradient 90 mmHg) is admitted with pulmonary oedema after a diarrhoeal illness. BP 85/50, HR 118 sinus. Which treatment is most appropriate?

Answer C Hypovolaemia shrank the cavity and increased obstruction. Restore preload, slow the heart and raise afterload (phenylephrine). Diuretics/nitrates (A), inotropes (B, E) and IABP (D, which lowers afterload) all worsen the gradient.

Q3 A 46-year-old man with obstructive HCM remains NYHA III on bisoprolol 10 mg. LVEF 68%, provoked gradient 85 mmHg, no mitral abnormality. According to ESC 2023, which step comes before septal reduction?

Answer C ESC 2023 places a CMI (IIa A) or disopyramide (I B) as add-on before SRT when symptoms persist on a betablocker. Vasodilators (A, B) and digoxin (E) worsen obstruction; pacing (D) is IIb for those unsuitable for SRT.

Q4 A patient on mavacamten for 8 weeks has improved symptoms; routine echo shows LVEF 46%. What should be done?

Answer C An LVEF < 50% on a CMI mandates interruption (systolic dysfunction from excessive myosin inhibition), with reassessment before any rechallenge at a lower dose. Continuing (A, D) or escalating (B, E) is unsafe.

Q5 A 28-year-old woman with HCM has a maximal wall thickness of 31 mm, no syncope, no NSVT, no family history of SCD, LVEF 70%. Under AHA/ACC 2024, what is the recommendation regarding a primary-prevention ICD?

Answer B Massive LVH (≥ 30 mm) is a major risk marker; ≥ 1 major marker makes a primary ICD reasonable (2a), informed by a 5-year risk estimate. LGE is used as an arbitrator only when no major marker is present (C).

Q6 A 52-year-old man with HCM has a HCM Risk-SCD 5-year risk of 3.1%. CMR shows LGE involving 19% of LV mass; LVEF 60%. What does ESC 2023 recommend?

Answer B ESC 2023: low 5-year risk (< 4%) but extensive LGE (≥ 15%) or LVEF < 50% → ICD may be considered (IIb B). Risk ≥ 6% would be IIa (A). Amiodarone does not prevent SCD (E).

Q7 A 67-year-old man undergoes alcohol septal ablation. His baseline ECG showed LBBB. Which complication is he at particular risk of?

Answer B ASA typically causes RBBB; with pre-existing LBBB, the combination produces complete heart block (pacemaker rates ≈ 10–20% overall after ASA). Aortic regurgitation (C) is a myectomy risk; VSD (A) is more likely with a thin septum.

Q8 A 19-year-old male cyclist has a septum of 14 mm, LVEDD 58 mm, normal e′, peak VO₂ 62 mL/kg/min, no LGE, and ECG showing voltage criteria only. The most appropriate step is:

Answer D Mild symmetric thickening with a large cavity, normal diastolic function, very high VO₂ and no LGE favour physiological remodelling. Deconditioning with re-imaging resolves doubt. Disqualification, drugs or procedures (A, B, E) are inappropriate.

Q9 A 44-year-old woman with non-obstructive HCM develops paroxysmal AF. CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 1 (female sex). What is correct?

Answer C HCM carries high thromboembolic risk independent of CHA₂DS₂-VASc; OAC (DOAC first line) is recommended for clinical AF (ESC I B; AHA/ACC 1). Class IC drugs (E) are avoided in structural heart disease.

Q10 A 23-year-old man with "HCM" (concentric LVH 28 mm) has a short PR with delta waves, proximal muscle weakness, raised CK and mild learning difficulty. The most likely diagnosis is:

Answer B Young male + massive LVH + pre-excitation + skeletal myopathy + learning difficulty = Danon disease (X-linked LAMP2) — aggressive course, early ICD and transplant referral. Fabry (C) gives short PR but not massive LVH with myopathy at this age; Noonan (E) presents in infancy with PS.

Chapter 5

Myocarditis & Cardio-Oncology

Two faces of an injured myocardium — inflammation that must be recognised early, and cancer therapy that must be delivered safely.
