5.1 Myocarditis — Definitions, Causes & Presentation

DEFINITIONS — ESC 2025

Myocarditis: inflammatory disease of the myocardium, diagnosed on established histological, immunological and immunohistochemical criteria (EMB) or, non-invasively, by a compatible clinical picture plus confirmatory CMR.

Inflammatory myopericardial syndrome (IMPS): new umbrella term in the 2025 guideline, reflecting the continuum and frequent overlap between myocarditis and pericarditis (myopericarditis ↔

perimyocarditis).

Inflammatory cardiomyopathy: chronic myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction and remodelling (hypokinetic, dilated phenotype).

Time course: acute ≤ 4 weeks from onset; subacute weeks–months; chronic persistent low-grade inflammation.

Complicated myocarditis: LVEF < 50%, acute HF, sustained ventricular arrhythmia or advanced AV block — the group that needs a tertiary (hub) centre.

Epidemiology

True incidence is uncertain (many cases subclinical); estimated roughly 10–20 per 100 000 per year. Peak in young adults; men affected about twice as often as women.

Found in about 2–12% of sudden cardiac deaths in young people and athletes.

Up to 8–22% of patients with acute myocarditis carry a pathogenic variant in a DCM/ARVC gene (especially desmosomal genes such as DSP) — the variant raises the risk of recurrent "hot phases".

Aetiology

Rash + eosinophilia; stop the drug

Drug — immune/toxic Immune checkpoint inhibitors, anthracyclines, highdose cyclophosphamide, 5-FU, CAR-T, cocaine, amphetamines

  • ICI myocarditis: early, fulminant,
  • overlaps with myositis/myasthenia
  • Vaccine-related mRNA COVID-19 vaccines; historically smallpox
  • vaccine
  • Young male, 2–4 days after 2nd
  • dose, benign course
  • Hypereosinophilic Hypereosinophilic syndrome, EGPA, parasites,
  • malignancy
  • Endomyocardial fibrosis, apical
  • thrombus
MECHANISM — THREE PHASES OF VIRAL MYOCARDITIS

Viral entry and replication (days): coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR) mediates entry; viral protease 2A cleaves dystrophin → direct myocyte injury.

Immune phase (weeks): innate then T-cell–mediated injury; cross-reacting autoantibodies (molecular mimicry). Most damage occurs here — the rationale for immunosuppression only once virus is excluded.

Recovery or remodelling (months): viral clearance and healing, or persistent inflammation → inflammatory cardiomyopathy / DCM.

  • Clinical presentation
  • Presentation is heterogeneous; the board typically offers one of four scenarios.
RED FLAGS — SUSPECT A SPECIFIC (TREATABLE)CAUSE
  • High-grade AV block or sustained VT in a non-dilated ventricle → giant-cell myocarditis, cardiac sarcoidosis, Lyme.
  • Failure to improve within 1–2 weeks despite optimal HF therapy → EMB.
  • Peripheral eosinophilia, rash, new drug → eosinophilic (hypersensitivity) myocarditis.
  • Known autoimmune disease, thymoma, recent ICI therapy, ptosis/myalgia (myositis–myasthenia overlap).
  • Recurrent episodes or family history of cardiomyopathy/SCD → genetic testing (desmosomal variants).

Key highlightsMyocarditis — definitions & presentation

  • ESC 2025 unifies myocarditis and pericarditis under IMPS; chronic myocarditis with dysfunction = inflammatory cardiomyopathy.
  • Acute myocarditis = onset ≤ 4 weeks; complicated = LVEF < 50%, AHF, sustained VA or advanced AV block.
  • Viruses are the commonest cause in the West (parvovirus B19, HHV-6, enteroviruses); Chagas disease is the commonest cause of non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy in Latin America.
  • Fulminant myocarditis: shock within ~2 weeks, non-dilated, thickened LV.
  • AV block or VT in a non-dilated LV → think giant-cell myocarditis, sarcoid, Lyme.
  • Desmosomal gene variants are found in a minority and predict recurrence — test recurrent IMPS.

5.2 Diagnosis — ECG, Biomarkers, CMR & Biopsy

First-line work-up

Every suspected case needs ECG, hs-troponin, natriuretic peptide, CRP, chest X-ray and transthoracic echo. Coronary disease must be excluded (invasive or CT coronary angiography) whenever the presentation is infarct-like and the pre-test probability of CAD is not negligible.

Cardiac magnetic resonance — the non-invasive reference standard

CMR is recommended in suspected myocarditis to show oedema, necrosis and fibrosis and to exclude ischaemic injury. Best yield when performed early, ideally within 2 weeks of symptom onset.

Ferreira VM et al. JACC 2018; adopted by ESC 2025.

BOARD PEARL — LGE PATTERN TELLS THE STORY
  • Subepicardial / mid-wall, basal–mid inferolateral wall = viral myocarditis.
  • Subendocardial or transmural in a coronary territory = infarction (MINOCA pathway).
  • Patchy, multifocal, septal and RV insertion, with FDG-avid foci = sarcoidosis.
  • Diffuse subendocardial with thrombus = eosinophilic (Löffler) endomyocarditis.
  • Persistent LGE plus persistent oedema at 6 months carries a poor prognosis; LGE in the septum or involving ≥ 2 segments marks higher arrhythmic risk.

Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB)

EMB remains the definitive test and the only way to establish the histotype (lymphocytic, eosinophilic, giant-cell, granulomatous) and to exclude viral genome before immunosuppression. With experienced operators, major complications are < 1 in 1000 in adults (but up to 30% in infants).

Viral PCR on tissue is mandatory to exclude active infection

DON'T CONFUSE — THE DALLAS CRITERIA VS IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY

The Dallas criteria (inflammatory infiltrate with adjacent myocyte necrosis) are specific but insensitive because of sampling error. Modern diagnosis adds immunohistochemistry: ≥ 14 leucocytes/mm² including up to 4 monocytes/mm², with CD3+ T cells ≥ 7/mm². Take ≥ 3 (ideally 4–6) samples, from the LV when CMR shows LV-dominant disease.

5.3 Specific Forms — Fulminant, Giant-Cell, Eosinophilic, ICI & Vaccine

EXAM TRAP — GCM VS SARCOIDOSIS

Both have giant cells and both cause AV block and VT. In GCM giant cells lie at the edge of widespread necrosis with no granuloma and eosinophils are common; course is fulminant with median transplant-free survival of months without treatment. In sarcoidosis giant cells sit inside non-caseating granulomas with more fibrosis and a slower course. The GCM board answer is EMB, then combined immunosuppression including a calcineurin inhibitor .

Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis

ICIs (anti-PD-1: nivolumab, pembrolizumab; anti-PD-L1: atezolizumab, durvalumab; anti-CTLA-4: ipilimumab; anti-LAG-3: relatlimab) release T-cell brakes; T cells may cross-react with shared cardiac/ tumour antigens (e.g. α-myosin).

Incidence about 1% (range 0.5–1.5%), higher with combination ICI (e.g. ipilimumab + nivolumab); mortality historically 25–50%.

Timing: most within the first 12 weeks (median ~30 days, often after 1–2 doses); late cases occur.

Key highlightsDiagnosis of myocarditis

  • Baseline set: ECG, hs-troponin, NP, CRP, CXR, echo; exclude CAD if infarct-like.
  • Updated Lake Louise = ≥ 1 T2-based (oedema) + ≥ 1 T1-based (T1, ECV or non-ischaemic LGE) criterion.
  • Viral myocarditis LGE: subepicardial/mid-wall inferolateral; infarct LGE is subendocardial.
  • CMR for diagnosis is Class I; repeat CMR within 6 months is Class I (ESC 2025).
  • EMB: fulminant/shock, malignant VA or AV block, no response in 1–2 weeks, suspected GCM/ICI — and always before immunosuppression (viral PCR).
  • Viral serology is not useful; tissue PCR is.
  • Immunohistochemistry: ≥ 14 leucocytes/mm² with CD3+ ≥ 7/mm².
  • Overlap syndrome: myositis (raised CK, ptosis, dysphagia) and myasthenia gravis in up to ~1/3 — respiratory failure is a major cause of death.
  • ECG: new conduction disease (AV block, RBBB/fascicular block) — complete heart block predicts mortality. LVEF is normal in about half; do not be reassured by a normal echo.
  • Troponin: cTnI preferred for diagnosis because cTnT also rises from skeletal myositis.

Stop ICI in confirmed myocarditis. I C

Early (≤ 24 h) high-dose steroids — IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg/day (typically 3–5 days). I C Continue high-dose steroids until resolution of symptoms, LV dysfunction, conduction disease and cTn fall > 50% from peak; then switch to oral prednisolone and taper.

I C

Second-line immunosuppression in steroid-refractory disease (e.g. mycophenolate, abatacept, alemtuzumab, ATG, tocilizumab).

  • IIa C
  • Fulminant: ICU (level 3), IV methylprednisolone, full CV support including MCS. I C

Multidisciplinary discussion before re-challenge after uncomplicated ICI myocarditis. I C

BOARD PEARL — ICI "TRIAD"

Melanoma or lung cancer patient on combination ICI, 3–6 weeks in, with ptosis, proximal weakness, high CK and troponin, and a new AV block: myocarditis–myositis–myasthenia overlap. Stop ICI and give IV methylprednisolone within 24 hours — do not wait for CMR or biopsy if unstable.

Vaccine-related myocarditis (mRNA COVID-19)

Highest risk: males aged 12–29/39, after the second dose, symptoms within 2–4 days (almost all within a week). Higher with mRNA-1273 (Moderna) than BNT162b2.

Presents as chest pain with troponin rise and ST changes; LVEF usually preserved; CMR shows subepicardial LGE.

Course is typically mild and self-limiting — lower mortality than viral myocarditis; LGE may persist in some. The risk of myocarditis from SARS-CoV-2 infection itself is higher than from vaccination. Management as for uncomplicated myocarditis; subsequent mRNA doses usually deferred.

5.4 Management, Arrhythmias & Return to Sport

Where to manage

Uncomplicated (preserved LVEF, no arrhythmia, stable): short admission with ECG monitoring while troponin is rising; then outpatient follow-up.

Complicated (LVEF < 50%, AHF, sustained VA, advanced AV block) or fulminant: refer early to a hub centre with EMB, MCS and transplant capability — the ESC 2025 hub-and-spoke model.

Treatment principles

Key highlightsSpecific forms of myocarditis

  • Fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis: shock but excellent long-term survival if bridged (MCS) through the acute phase.
  • GCM: giant cells without granulomas, VT + AV block, relentless HF → combined immunosuppression with ciclosporin; may recur after transplant.
  • Eosinophilic: drug hypersensitivity, HES, EGPA → stop drug, steroids; watch for LV thrombus.
  • ICI myocarditis: ~1%, early (≤ 12 weeks), combination ICI, overlap with myositis/myasthenia; CHB = poor prognosis.
  • ICI myocarditis: stop ICI, IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg within 24 h, continue until cTn falls > 50%. mRNA vaccine myocarditis: young male, 2nd dose, 2–4 days, benign course.
  • Scenario Treatment
  • All myocarditis (ESC 2025) β-blocker for at least 6 months regardless of LVEF, for symptoms and arrhythmia risk (IIa C — based on observational data)
  • Cardiogenic shock Inotropes; early MCS — IABP as first bridge; VA-ECMO/Impella or biventricular support for SCAI D–E; bridge to recovery, durable LVAD or transplant
  • Proven autoimmune
  • histotype, virus-negative
  • Immunosuppression (steroids ± azathioprine/ciclosporin) for 6–12 months guided by repeat EMB/CMR
  • Uncomplicated viral No routine steroids, immunosuppressants, IVIG or antivirals
EXAM TRAP — NSAIDS IN MYOCARDITIS

Older teaching said "avoid NSAIDs in myocarditis" (animal data). ESC 2025 accepts NSAIDs/aspirin or paracetamol for chest pain in uncomplicated IMPS, especially when pericarditis dominates, but NSAIDs remain undesirable in HF with reduced EF. Steroids are not first-line in uncomplicated viral myocarditis.

Arrhythmias and sudden death

Acute phase: arrhythmias reflect active inflammation and may resolve — defer permanent devices where possible. A wearable cardioverter-defibrillator is reasonable in selected high-risk patients during the 3–6 month recovery window.

Chronic (healed) phase: scar-related monomorphic VT behaves like any cardiomyopathy — ICD by standard criteria; ablation best reserved for the post-inflammatory phase.

GCM and cardiac sarcoidosis are the exceptions: higher early arrhythmic risk, so ICD may be justified earlier.

Exercise restriction and return to sport

Exercise during active inflammation increases viral replication, myocyte necrosis and arrhythmic risk. All three authorities agree that no competitive or high-intensity exercise is allowed while inflammation is active ; they differ in the minimum period.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2025

First joint myocarditis–pericarditis guideline; IMPS and inflammatory cardiomyopathy introduced. Updated Lake Louise criteria formally adopted; CMR at diagnosis and within 6 months both Class I. Expanded EMB indications (malignant VA, LVEF < 40%, extensive LGE, suspected GCM/sarcoid, nonresponse). β-blockers for ≥ 6 months; neurohormonal withdrawal allowed after recovery; conservative, EMBguided immunosuppression. Exercise restriction shortened to at least 1 month, then individualised (was 3–6 months in 2020).

Prognosis and follow-up

Infarct-like presentation with preserved LVEF: excellent outcome; recurrence about 10–15%. Adverse predictors: LVEF impairment, RV dysfunction, fulminant or GCM histotype, QRS prolongation, septal/extensive LGE, persistent oedema at follow-up.

Follow-up with ECG, biomarkers, Holter, echo and CMR in the first 6 months; uncomplicated cases reassessed at 6, 12 and 24 months; complicated cases long term.

Key highlightsManagement & return to sport

  • Complicated/fulminant myocarditis → hub centre, early MCS, urgent EMB.
  • Steroids/immunosuppression only for virus-negative autoimmune histotypes (GCM, eosinophilic, sarcoid) or fulminant non-infectious disease — not for uncomplicated viral cases.
  • ESC 2025: β-blocker ≥ 6 months (IIa C); HF drugs may be withdrawn after 6 months of recovery.
  • Acute-phase arrhythmias: wearable defibrillator for 3–6 months; ICD by chronic-phase criteria (earlier for GCM/ sarcoid).
  • ICD Class I for non-tolerated SMVT in the chronic phase (ESC 2022).
  • Return to sport: ESC 2020 3–6 months; ESC 2025 ≥ 1 month then individualised; AHA/ACC 2025 ~4–6 weeks.
  • Return requires normal biomarkers, LV function, no CMR oedema and no complex VA on Holter/exercise test.

5.5 Cardio-Oncology — Definitions & Baseline Risk

Cancer survival has improved dramatically, and cardiovascular disease is now a leading cause of death in many survivors (e.g. early breast cancer). The aim of cardio-oncology is to deliver the best cancer therapy with the least cardiovascular harm — stopping cancer treatment is the last, not the first, resort.

DEFINITION — CANCER THERAPY–RELATED CARDIOVASCULAR TOXICITY (CTR-CVT)

ESC 2022 (with IC-OS consensus) replaced the vague word "cardiotoxicity" with CTR-CVT, an umbrella for cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD), myocarditis, vascular toxicity (ischaemia, vasospasm, thrombosis), hypertension, arrhythmias and QTc prolongation.

BOARD PEARL — GLS IS THE EARLY WARNING

A relative fall in global longitudinal strain of > 15% from baseline predicts a later LVEF drop and defines mild CTRCD even when LVEF is ≥ 50%. Use the same modality, same vendor and same laboratory throughout; 3D echo is preferred for LVEF (I B), CMR if echo is inadequate.

Baseline risk: the HFA-ICOS assessment

Before potentially cardiotoxic therapy, stratify the patient as low, moderate, high or very high risk using the Heart Failure Association–International Cardio-Oncology Society proformas (drug-class specific). This decides baseline tests, surveillance intensity, primary prevention and referral.

Weight Risk factors

Overall: low = no factor or one medium-1 factor · moderate = medium factors totalling 2–4 points · high = ≥ 5 medium points or any high factor · very high = any very-high factor

Adapted from Lyon AR et al. Eur J Heart Fail 2020 and ESC 2022; proformas differ by drug class.

CMR when echo is unavailable or non-diagnostic. IIa C

Cardiology referral before therapy in high and very high-risk patients (unless oncological emergency). I C

5.6 Cardiotoxicity by Cancer Therapy

Key highlightsCTRCD definitions & baseline risk

  • CTR-CVT is the umbrella; CTRCD = symptomatic (HF, 4 grades) or asymptomatic (3 grades).
  • Asymptomatic severe CTRCD = LVEF < 40%; moderate = fall ≥ 10 points to 40–49%.
  • Mild CTRCD = LVEF ≥ 50% with relative GLS fall > 15% and/or new cTn/NP rise.
  • Baseline ECG in all (I C); TTE in high/very high risk (I C); 3D-LVEF preferred (I B).
  • HFA-ICOS: prior HF/cardiomyopathy = very high; LVEF < 50%, age ≥ 80, prior anthracycline or chest RT = high.
  • Same imaging modality throughout treatment to avoid inter-technique variability.

MECHANISM — WHY ANTHRACYCLINE DAMAGE IS PERMANENT AND TRASTUZUMAB'S IS NOT

Anthracyclines bind topoisomerase IIβ in cardiomyocytes → DNA double-strand breaks, mitochondrial dysfunction and iron-dependent reactive oxygen species → myocyte death (cumulative, dose-dependent).

Dexrazoxane prevents it by altering TOP2β and chelating iron. Trastuzumab blocks HER2/neuregulin survival signalling needed for myocyte stress repair → myocyte dysfunction without death, hence recovery after interruption. The old "type I / type II" labels encode exactly this — but overlap exists, especially when trastuzumab follows anthracycline.

Anthracycline CTRCD — management

QTc prolongation

Many cancer drugs prolong QT (arsenic trioxide, vandetanib, nilotinib, ribociclib, vemurafenib, HDAC inhibitors), often compounded by vomiting, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and antiemetics (ondansetron, domperidone). Use Fridericia correction (QTcF = QT/∛RR). Upper normal: 450 ms men, 460 ms women.

Hypertension
  • Commonest CTR-CVT (VEGFi, TKIs, carfilzomib,
  • abiraterone).
  • First line: ACEi/ARB (I B); add dihydropyridine
  • CCB for rapid control (I C).
  • Avoid diltiazem/verapamil (CYP3A4 interactions
  • with TKIs).
  • Temporarily hold VEGFi if SBP ≥ 180 or DBP ≥
  • 110 mmHg.
AF and thrombosis
  • AF: ibrutinib, thoracic surgery, anthracyclines;
  • use CHA₂DS₂-VASc but recognise cancer adds risk

  • interactions.

  • 6 months; continue while cancer active.

5.7 Surveillance, Prevention, Radiation & Survivorship

Surveillance during therapy

Key highlightsCardiotoxicity by therapy

  • Anthracyclines: dose-dependent, largely irreversible; HF ~5% at 400 and ~26% at 550 mg/m² doxorubicin.
  • Trastuzumab: not dose-dependent, usually reversible; TTE every 3 months; interrupt only if LVEF < 40% or symptomatic (moderate — MDT).
  • VEGFi: hypertension is the commonest toxicity — ACEi/ARB first, then DHP-CCB.
  • Ponatinib → arterial occlusion; nilotinib → PAD/QT; dasatinib → PAH; ibrutinib → AF.
  • 5-FU/capecitabine → coronary vasospasm.
  • QTcF ≥ 500 ms → interrupt drug; 480–500 ms → weekly ECG; arsenic trioxide is the classic culprit.
BOARD PEARL — OTHER ANTHRACYCLINE-SPARING T ACT ICS

Limit cumulative dose, use continuous infusion rather than bolus, liposomal formulations and dexrazoxane; in HER2+ breast cancer, non-anthracycline regimens (e.g. TCH) are an option in high-risk patients.

Statin data (STOP-CA) show a reduction in LVEF decline with atorvastatin in lymphoma.

Radiation-induced heart disease (RIHD)

Radiotherapy to the chest (Hodgkin lymphoma, breast, lung, oesophagus) injures the microvasculature and endothelium of every cardiac structure. Risk depends on the mean heart dose (MHD), young age at exposure, concurrent anthracycline and conventional risk factors. For every 1 Gy MHD, major coronary events rise by about 7% (Darby, breast cancer). Clinical disease typically appears 10–20 years later.

EXAM TRAP — SURGERY AFTER MEDIASTINAL RADIATION

Cardiac surgery in RIHD is hazardous: porcelain aorta, mediastinal fibrosis, poor wound healing and damaged internal mammary arteries. Heart Team decisions therefore favour TAVI and PCI where feasible , and constrictive pericarditis after radiation carries a worse post-pericardiectomy survival than idiopathic constriction.

Survivorship — long-term follow-up

HSCT; RT 15–25 Gy MHD; RT 5–15 Gy + doxorubicin ≥ 100 mg/m²

Moderate Moderate baseline risk; doxorubicin 100–249 mg/m²; RT 5–15 Gy MHD; RT < 5 Gy + doxorubicin ≥ 100 mg/m²

Low Low baseline risk with normal end-of-therapy assessment; mild CTRCD that recovered; RT < 5 Gy MHD; doxorubicin < 100 mg/m²

Re-stratification of CV toxicity risk 5 years after therapy. I C

Echo at years 1, 3 and 5, then every 5 years, in very high- and early high-risk survivors. IIa C Non-invasive CAD screening every 5–10 years from 5 years after RT with MHD > 15 Gy. IIa C Carotid ultrasound every 5 years from 5 years after head/neck RT. IIa C

Long-term continuation of cardiac medication after severe CTRCD. I C

CV assessment (including TTE) before pregnancy or in the first trimester in female childhood/ adolescent survivors.

I C

DON'T CONFUSE — ACS IN A PATIENT WITH CANCER

An invasive strategy is still recommended for STEMI or high-risk NSTE-ACS if life expectancy is ≥ 6 months (I B); a conservative strategy is reasonable with poor prognosis (< 6 months) or very high bleeding risk (IIa C). Temporarily interrupt the causal cancer therapy (I C) and consider a short DAPT course when bleeding risk is very high (IIa C).

Key highlightsSurveillance, prevention, radiation & survivorship

  • Trastuzumab: TTE every 3 months; anthracyclines: TTE at 12 months after therapy for all, more frequent in high risk.
  • Primary prevention in high/very high risk: ACEi/ARB + β-blocker, statin, dexrazoxane, liposomal doxorubicin — all IIa B.
  • RIHD appears 10–20 years later; each 1 Gy MHD raises coronary events ~7%.
  • Radiation CAD is ostial/proximal; valves show regurgitation first, then stenosis; aorto-mitral curtain calcification.
  • Very high-risk survivor: doxorubicin ≥ 400 mg/m² or MHD > 25 Gy.
  • MHD > 15 Gy → CAD screening every 5–10 years starting 5 years after RT.
  • Annual CV risk review (ECG + NP) for all survivors of cardiotoxic therapy (I B); re-stratify at 5 years.

5.8 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 24-year-old man has chest pain 5 days after a flu-like illness. hs-TnT is 820 ng/L, ECG shows inferolateral ST elevation, and CT coronary angiography is normal. CMR shows increased T2 signal in the inferolateral wall but no LGE, with normal native T1 and ECV. What is the correct interpretation?

Answer C Updated Lake Louise requires one T2-based and one T1-based criterion. Oedema alone (T2) is supportive but not diagnostic. LGE absence does not exclude myocarditis (T1/ECV would also count). Normal coronaries plus troponin rise is a MINOCA working diagnosis — CMR clarifies the cause, not vasospasm by default.

Q2 A 45-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis presents with progressive HF over 3 weeks, recurrent sustained VT and new complete heart block. LVEF is 25% with a non-dilated LV. Coronary angiography is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

Answer B Rapidly progressive HF with VT and heart block in a non-dilated LV, with autoimmune disease (IBD), is giant-cell myocarditis until proven otherwise. EMB is essential — the histotype mandates combined immunosuppression (steroids + ciclosporin). Waiting on HF drugs alone loses the treatment window; steroids alone are inadequate for GCM.

Q3 A 68-year-old man with metastatic melanoma received his second dose of ipilimumab plus nivolumab 3 weeks ago. He has ptosis, proximal weakness, CK 4200 U/L, raised hs-TnI and a new RBBB with first-degree AV block. BP is stable, LVEF 55%. Which is the best immediate management?

Answer C ICI myocarditis–myositis–myasthenia overlap. ESC 2022: interrupt ICI (I C) and give early (≤ 24 h) IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg/day (I C) with continuous ECG monitoring for AV block (I C). Oral prednisolone is too weak; resuming ICI is contraindicated at this stage.

Q4 A 19-year-old professional footballer recovered from acute myocarditis 5 weeks ago. He is asymptomatic; troponin and CRP are normal; LVEF is 60%; repeat CMR shows no oedema and a small subepicardial LGE focus; Holter and exercise test show no arrhythmia. According to ESC 2025 and the AHA/ACC 2025 statement, which is most appropriate?

Answer C ESC 2025 restricts exercise for at least 1 month then individualises; AHA/ACC 2025 permits return from ~4–6 weeks when fully recovered. With normal biomarkers, LVEF, no oedema and no arrhythmia, shared decision-making supports graded return. The fixed 3–6 month rule came from ESC 2020.

Q5 A 52-year-old woman receiving adjuvant trastuzumab after doxorubicin has a routine TTE: LVEF fell from 62% to 46%; she is asymptomatic. How is this classified and managed?

Answer B A fall ≥ 10 points to 40–49% = asymptomatic moderate CTRCD. Start ACEi/ARB and β-blocker (I C); for HER2 therapy, continuation with closer monitoring is usually possible after MDT review. Interruption is mandatory only for LVEF < 40% or symptomatic HF.

Q6 A 60-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukaemia develops rest pain and an ankle–brachial index of 0.6. He also has impaired glucose tolerance and QTc 478 ms. Which TKI is he most likely taking?

Answer C Nilotinib causes progressive peripheral arterial disease, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia and QT prolongation. Dasatinib → pulmonary hypertension and pleural effusion; ponatinib → arterial occlusive events; imatinib is the least cardiotoxic; ibrutinib (BTK inhibitor) → AF.

Q7 A patient with acute promyelocytic leukaemia on arsenic trioxide is asymptomatic, but QTcF has increased to 512 ms. K⁺ is 3.3 mmol/L. What is the recommended action?

Answer B Asymptomatic QTcF ≥ 500 ms → temporary interruption with ECG every 24 h until resolution and correction of K⁺/ Mg²⁺ (I C). Permanent discontinuation is for TdP/sustained VA; re-challenge at reduced dose may be considered after MDT (IIb C).

Q8 A 44-year-old woman treated with mantle-field radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma aged 18 presents with exertional angina and a soft ejection systolic murmur. Which pattern of coronary disease is most likely?

Answer B Radiation-induced CAD typically involves the ostia and proximal segments within the field (left main, proximal LAD, RCA ostium), 10–20 years after exposure. The murmur hints at co-existing radiation valve disease (aorto-mitral calcification).

Q9 A 58-year-old woman with previous MI and PCI is scheduled to start doxorubicin for breast cancer. Baseline LVEF is 56%. Under the HFA-ICOS approach she is high risk. Which measure has a Class IIa B recommendation for primary prevention?

Answer B ESC 2022: ACEi/ARB and β-blocker (IIa B), statin (IIa B), dexrazoxane (IIa B) and liposomal doxorubicin (IIa B) for high/very high-risk patients. The other options have no role in CTRCD prevention.

Q10 A 17-year-old boy develops chest pain 3 days after his second mRNA COVID-19 vaccine. Troponin is raised, LVEF is 58%, and CMR shows subepicardial LGE and oedema. Which statement is correct?

Answer C mRNA vaccine myocarditis affects young males, mainly after the second dose within 2–4 days; LVEF is usually preserved and the course mild. Steroids and EMB are not routine for uncomplicated cases; progression to DCM is rare.

6.1 Definition, Spectrum & Coronary Physiology

DEFINITION

Chronic coronary syndromes (CCS) are the clinical presentations of coronary artery disease (CAD) during its stable phases — as opposed to acute coronary syndromes. The umbrella covers epicardial atherosclerosis and functional disease of the epicardial vessels and microcirculation. The US equivalent term is chronic coronary disease (CCD).

The ESC 2024 guideline deliberately widened the concept: CCS are defined by structural and/or functional alterations of the epicardial arteries and/or the microcirculation that produce a transient, usually reversible, mismatch between myocardial demand and blood supply. The typical presentations are: Suspected CAD with stable angina and/or

  • dyspnoea.
  • New-onset heart failure or LV dysfunction with
  • suspected CAD.
  • Stable patients < 1 year and > 1 year after ACS or
  • revascularisation.
  • Angina with vasospasm or microvascular disease
  • (ANOCA/INOCA).
  • Asymptomatic CAD detected at screening.
  • Long-standing established CAD under
  • surveillance.

Determinants of myocardial oxygen supply and demand

The heart extracts 70–80% of arterial oxygen at rest (coronary sinus saturation only ~30%), so extraction cannot rise much. Any increase in myocardial O₂ demand must be met almost entirely by an increase in coronary flow. Normal resting coronary flow is ~5% of cardiac output and can rise 3–5-fold with maximal vasodilation — this is the coronary flow reserve (CFR).

MECHANISM — WHY THE SUBENDOCARDIUM SUF F ERS FIRST

LV coronary flow occurs mainly in diastole (> 80% of left coronary flow): systolic compression throttles intramural vessels, most in the subendocardium.

LV perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic pressure − LVEDP. Tachycardia (shorter diastole), hypotension and high filling pressures all reduce subendocardial flow even with normal arteries.

The RV is thin and low-pressure, so its perfusion continues in systole — explaining why RV ischaemia needs proximal RCA disease or severe RV pressure overload.

Autoregulation keeps resting flow constant across a wide pressure range; below a distal pressure of roughly ~50 mmHg (higher with tachycardia or raised LVEDP) flow becomes pressure-dependent and ischaemia follows.

Haemodynamics of a stenosis

Resting flow is preserved by arteriolar dilation until the stenosis reaches ~85–90% diameter; maximal (hyperaemic) flow begins to fall at ~50% diameter stenosis. Hence a 70% lesion typically causes exertional angina, a > 90% lesion may cause rest ischaemia.

Resistance follows Poiseuille: proportional to length and inversely to radius⁴; turbulent (separation) losses rise with the square of flow — so a lesion that is trivial at rest becomes limiting at high flow. Functional significance also depends on the territory supplied (a 50% left main or proximal LAD lesion matters more than a 50% distal diagonal), viable myocardium and collaterals.

Conventional anatomical thresholds: ≥ 50% left main, ≥ 70% other epicardial vessels; 40–90% lesions are "intermediate" and need physiology (see Chapter 9).

The ischaemic cascade

Once supply falls short, events follow a reproducible sequence — which is why imaging detects ischaemia earlier and more sensitively than ECG, and why angina is the last and least reliable marker:

THE ISCHAEMIC CASCADE (EARLIEST→LATEST)

Perfusion heterogeneity (PET/SPECT/CMR) → metabolic shift (lactate, H⁺, K⁺) → diastolic dysfunction → systolic wall-motion abnormality (stress echo/CMR) → ECG changes (ST depression subendocardial; ST elevation transmural) → angina, which may never occur (silent ischaemia in diabetes and the elderly). Stunning is post-ischaemic dysfunction with restored, normal resting perfusion that recovers spontaneously; hibernation is chronic down-regulation of contraction with reduced perfusion but preserved metabolism (perfusion–FDG "mismatch" on PET) that recovers after revascularisation; scar shows matched defects and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) — segments with LGE < 25% transmurality usually recover, > 50% rarely. In STICH, however, viability did not identify who benefited from CABG.

6.2 Clinical Evaluation & Clinical Likelihood

ESC 2024 replaced the six-step 2019 pathway with four steps: (1) general clinical evaluation, (2) further cardiac examination and estimation of clinical likelihood, (3) diagnostic testing to confirm CCS and stratify event risk, (4) lifestyle, drugs and revascularisation where indicated. ACS must be excluded at every step — rest angina > 20 min, new-onset or crescendo angina, or a rising troponin are ACS until proven otherwise.

Key highlightsDefinition & physiology

  • CCS = structural and/or functional disease of epicardial arteries or microcirculation — ANOCA/INOCA is now inside the definition.
  • O₂ extraction is already 70–80% at rest → demand is met by ↑ flow; CFR normally 3–5.
  • Heart rate is the chief determinant of MVO₂ and also shortens diastolic perfusion time — the rationale for rate control in angina.
  • LV perfusion pressure = DBP − LVEDP; > 80% of left coronary flow is diastolic.
  • Maximal flow falls from ~50% stenosis; resting flow only beyond ~85–90%.
  • Ischaemic cascade: perfusion → metabolism → diastolic → systolic wall motion → ECG → angina.
  • Hibernation = reduced perfusion with preserved metabolism (PET mismatch); stunning = normal perfusion, transient dysfunction.
  • Characterising the symptom
  • Three features define angina: (1) constricting discomfort in the chest, neck, jaw, shoulder or arm; (2) provoked by exertion or emotion; (3) relieved by rest or nitrate within 5 min. Typical = 3 features, atypical = 2, non-anginal = 0–1.
  • ESC 2024 emphasises that the label "atypical" is unhelpful — women, the elderly and diabetics often describe dyspnoea, fatigue or epigastric discomfort. Exertional dyspnoea alone is an anginal equivalent and is incorporated into the likelihood model.

III Marked limitation — 1–2 blocks on the level or 1 flight of stairs at normal pace

IV Inability to carry out any physical activity without discomfort; angina may occur at rest Step 1–2: baseline tests

NEW In very low (≤ 5%) likelihood, defer further diagnostic testing. IIa B

Also examinable: Lp(a) at least once in life; hs-CRP/fibrinogen may add risk information. Ambulatory ECG only for suspected arrhythmia or vasospasm, not routine.

The Risk Factor–weighted Clinical Likelihood model

The old Diamond–Forrester-based tables (age, sex, symptom type) overestimated disease: in contemporary cohorts only ~10–15% of tested patients have obstructive CAD. The RF-CL model adds the number of risk factors to age, sex and symptoms, and the CACS-CL model further refines it using the calcium score.

Inputs
  • Age and sex
  • Symptoms: typical, atypical, non-anginal chest
  • pain, or dyspnoea
  • Number of risk factors (0–1, 2–3, 4–5): family
  • history of premature CAD, smoking,
  • dyslipidaemia, hypertension, diabetes
Modifiers that ↑ likelihood
  • Q waves, ST-T changes or LBBB on ECG
  • LV dysfunction / regional wall-motion
  • abnormality
  • Abnormal exercise ECG
  • Coronary calcification on any CT

Peripheral arterial disease

WHAT CHANGED IN 2024 (VS ESC 2019)

Six steps → four steps; classic pre-test probability → RF-CL and CACS-CL models.

Explicit "very low ≤ 5%" band where testing can be deferred; the 2019 "15% threshold" is gone. CCTA recommended for low–moderate likelihood with Class I A; ANOCA/INOCA invasive testing upgraded to Class I B.

New drug recommendations: colchicine (IIa A), semaglutide in obesity without diabetes (IIa B); ivabradine becomes Class III for angina without HF.

Key highlightsClinical evaluation

  • Typical angina = 3/3 features (constricting pain, exertional, relieved by rest/nitrate in 5 min); dyspnoea counts as an anginal equivalent.
  • CCS grade III = angina walking 1–2 blocks or 1 flight; grade IV = any activity/rest.
  • ECG, bloods (FBC, eGFR, lipids, HbA1c) and resting echo are Class I for all.
  • ESC 2024: likelihood by the RF-CL model (I B) — age, sex, symptoms, number of 5 risk factors.
  • Bands: ≤ 5% defer; > 5–15% low; > 15–50% moderate; > 50–85% high; > 85% very high.
  • CACS reclassifies low-likelihood patients (IIa B) — it does not diagnose obstruction, and CACS 0 does not exclude non-calcified plaque.

6.3 Choosing the Diagnostic Test

Two philosophies compete: anatomical testing (CCTA) is best at ruling out disease and detects non-obstructive plaque that still warrants prevention; functional testing (stress echo, SPECT, PET, CMR) is best at ruling in flow-limiting disease and quantifying the ischaemic burden that drives revascularisation. The lower the likelihood, the more you gain from CCTA's negative predictive value; the higher the likelihood, the more you need to know how much myocardium is ischaemic.

Invasive angiography

ICA (with a view to revascularisation) as the first test in de-novo symptoms highly suggestive of obstructive CAD occurring at a low level of exercise.

I C

When ICA is performed, pressure-wire assessment must be available and used for intermediate nonleft-main stenoses before revascularisation. I A

Radial artery as the preferred access site for ICA. I A

Stenosis grades: CAD-RADS 0 = no plaque; 1 = 1–24%; 2 = 25–49% (both non-obstructive → preventive therapy); 3 = 50–69% (functional test or FFR-CT); 4A = 70–99%; 4B = left main ≥ 50% or three-vessel ≥ 70% (→ ICA); 5 = total occlusion.

Modifiers: P (plaque burden P1–P4), HRP (high-risk plaque: positive remodelling, low attenuation < 30 HU, spotty calcification, napkin-ring sign), N (non-diagnostic), S (stent), G (graft), E (exceptions). An FFR-CT ≤ 0.80 in a 50–90% lesion supports functional significance.

Defining high event risk

CLINICAL APPROACH — PICKING THE TEST IN PRACTICE
  • Young, low–moderate likelihood, sinus rhythm, little calcium → CCTA.
  • Known CAD, prior stents/grafts, heavy calcium, AF → functional imaging (stents and calcium degrade CCTA).
  • Cannot exercise → pharmacological stress: dobutamine (echo/CMR) or vasodilator (adenosine, regadenoson, dipyridamole for SPECT/PET/CMR).
  • LBBB or paced rhythm → vasodilator perfusion imaging (exercise and dobutamine cause false septal defects).
  • Suspected balanced 3-vessel disease or CMD → PET with quantitative myocardial blood flow. Very high likelihood or angina at low workload → straight to ICA with physiology.
EXAM TRAP

Vasodilator stress (adenosine, regadenoson, dipyridamole) is contraindicated in bronchospasm, highgrade AV block and hypotension, and is reversed with aminophylline; dobutamine is avoided in severe hypertension, tachyarrhythmia and LVOT obstruction. Before a vasodilator SPECT the key instruction is no caffeine (coffee, tea, chocolate, cola) and methylxanthines, which competitively block adenosine receptors and cause false-negative tests. Dipyridamole is the opposite — it potentiates adenosine and must be stopped before adenosine stress (or used as the stressor).

6.4 Exercise ECG & the Duke Treadmill Score

The exercise ECG has lost its first-line diagnostic role (sensitivity and specificity only ~60%), but it remains a heavily examined test because it provides what imaging does not: functional capacity, chronotropic and BP response, arrhythmia provocation and a validated prognostic score. ESC 2024 keeps it for assessment of exercise tolerance, symptoms, BP response and event risk in selected patients, and for diagnosis only where imaging is unavailable.

Absolute contraindications
  • Acute MI within 2 days; high-risk unstable
  • angina
  • Uncontrolled symptomatic arrhythmia
  • Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis
  • Decompensated heart failure
  • Acute PE, myocarditis, pericarditis, aortic
  • dissection
Non-diagnostic resting ECG (use imaging)
  • LBBB, ventricular pacing, WPW pre-excitation
  • Resting ST depression ≥ 1 mm
  • LVH with strain; digoxin therapy
  • (RBBB impairs only V1–V3 interpretation)
  • Up-sloping ST depression Less specific; ≥ 1.5–2 mm at 80 ms considered abnormal by some
  • ST elevation in leads without Q
  • waves (not aVR/V1)
  • Transmural ischaemia — localises the culprit; stop test
  • ST depression Does not localise the ischaemic territory
  • Exertional hypotension SBP falls ≥ 10 mmHg (or below baseline) — suggests LM/3VD

Chronotropic incompetence Failure to reach 85% APMHR / chronotropic index < 0.8 (< 0.62 on β-blocker) Abnormal HR recovery Fall ≤ 12 bpm at 1 min (upright cool-down) — independent mortality predictor

Key highlightsChoosing the test

  • CCTA for likelihood > 5–50% (ESC I A); functional imaging for > 15–85% (I B); ICA first if very high likelihood or angina at low workload (I C).
  • CCTA has the highest sensitivity/NPV (~97%); stress CMR the highest specificity (~94%).
  • PET quantifies absolute flow — unmasks balanced ischaemia and microvascular disease.
  • High risk = ischaemia ≥ 10% LV (SPECT/PET), ≥ 3/16 segments (stress echo), ≥ 2/16 perfusion segments (CMR), DTS < −10.
  • High-risk anatomy: LM ≥ 50%, 3VD ≥ 70%, 2VD with proximal LAD.
  • CAD-RADS 4B = LM ≥ 50% or 3VD ≥ 70%; FFR-CT ≤ 0.80 = significant.
  • LBBB/paced → vasodilator perfusion; caffeine must be withheld 12–24 h before adenosine/regadenoson.
  • Category Finding
  • ST response ST depression ≥ 2 mm
  • Onset at low workload (< 5 METs / stage I) or low HR
  • Involving ≥ 5 leads
  • Persisting ≥ 5 min into recovery
  • ST elevation in non-Q leads
  • Haemodynamic Exertional hypotension; failure to raise SBP
  • Capacity / symptoms Exercise-limiting angina; poor capacity (< 5 METs)
  • Arrhythmia Sustained VT or VF during exercise or recovery
  • The Duke Treadmill Score (Bruce protocol)
FORMULA
  • DTS = exercise time (min) − (5 × maximal ST deviation in mm) − (4 × angina index)
  • Angina index: 0 = none · 1 = non-limiting angina · 2 = exercise-limiting angina.

Key highlightsExercise ECG

  • Positive = horizontal/down-sloping ST depression ≥ 1 mm at 60–80 ms after J point; test adequate at ≥ 85% APMHR.
  • ST depression does not localise; ST elevation in non-Q leads does.
  • Uninterpretable with LBBB, paced rhythm, WPW, digoxin, resting ST depression ≥ 1 mm.
  • DTS = time − 5 × ST(mm) − 4 × angina index; low ≥ +5, high < −10 (> 3%/yr).
  • Exertional hypotension (SBP ↓ ≥ 10 mmHg) and ST changes at < 5 METs suggest LM/3VD.
  • HR recovery ≤ 12 bpm at 1 min and chronotropic incompetence independently predict mortality.

6.5 ANOCA/INOCA, Vasospasm & Microvascular Angina

DEFINITIONS

ANOCA — angina with no obstructive coronary arteries (no stenosis ≥ 50%, or FFR > 0.80).

INOCA — the same, plus objective evidence of ischaemia.

MINOCA — myocardial infarction with non-obstructive arteries: an acute syndrome, covered with ACS.

Up to half of patients undergoing angiography for stable angina have no obstructive disease, more often women. This is not a benign "normal angiogram": persistent symptoms carry higher MACE rates, repeated admissions and poor quality of life. The ESC 2024 message is to identify the endotype, because therapy is endotype-specific.

Mixed CMD + spasm Overlapping features — common

Others to exclude Myocardial bridging, diffuse disease undercalled by angiography, non-cardiac painBridging: systolic "milking" of the LAD, worse with nitrates/tachycardia

Invasive coronary function testing

The comprehensive test (performed at the diagnostic angiogram) runs in sequence: (1) FFR/iFR to exclude flow-limiting epicardial disease; (2) adenosine hyperaemia to measure CFR and IMR (thermodilution) or HMR (Doppler); (3) incremental intracoronary acetylcholine to test endothelial function and provoke spasm.

Endothelial dysfunction: ACE inhibitor for symptom control. IIa B

AHA/ACC 2023: stratified medical therapy guided by invasive physiological testing in symptomatic non-obstructive CAD — Class 2a (B-R), based on CorMicA.

Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina

Diagnostic criteria (COVADIS)
  • Nitrate-responsive angina: at rest (night–early
  • morning), marked diurnal variation, provoked
  • by hyperventilation, suppressed by CCB but not
  • β-blocker.
  • Transient ischaemic ECG changes in ≥ 2
  • contiguous leads: ST elevation ≥ 0.1 mV, ST
  • depression ≥ 0.05 mV, or new negative U waves.
  • Documented spasm: transient total/subtotal
  • occlusion (> 90%) with angina and ECG change.
  • Definite VSA: criterion 1 + either 2 or 3.
Triggers and associations
  • Smoking — the strongest modifiable risk factor
  • Cocaine, amphetamines, cannabis
  • Triptans, ergots, 5-fluorouracil/capecitabine
  • Non-selective β-blockers (unopposed α)
  • Cold, hyperventilation, emotional stress,
  • magnesium deficiency
  • East-Asian ancestry; younger age; fewer classic
  • risk factors
MECHANISM — WHY Β-BLOCKERS CAN WORSEN SPASM

Coronary smooth muscle carries vasoconstricting α-receptors and vasodilating β2-receptors. Blocking β2 leaves α-mediated constriction unopposed. The same logic applies to cocaine chest pain.

In VSA, use a CCB (± long-acting nitrate) and avoid β-blockers, especially non-selective ones. Refractory VSA: high-dose CCB at bedtime, DHP + non-DHP combination, add long-acting nitrate or nicorandil, stop smoking and triggers, correct magnesium. Survivors of spasm-induced cardiac arrest are considered for an ICD. Stenting a spasm-prone segment does not treat VSA.

Microvascular angina

Treat risk factors aggressively (statin, ACE-I/ARB, BP, smoking, weight); consider aspirin/statin only if atherosclerosis is present.

Structural CMD (↓ CFR / ↑ IMR) → β-blocker first; alternatives CCB, ranolazine; nitrates are often ineffective.

  • Microvascular spasm/endothelial dysfunction → CCB; ACE-I improves endothelial function.
  • Cardiac rehabilitation and exercise training improve symptoms.
DON'T CONFUSE — SPASM VS MYOCARDIAL BRIDGE
  • Vasospasm Myocardial bridge
  • Timing of narrowing Whole cardiac cycle, transient episodes Systolic only ("milking")
  • Nitrates Relieve Worsen (reveal the bridge)
  • Treatment CCB, nitrates; avoid β-blockers β-blocker (or non-DHP CCB)

Key highlightsANOCA/INOCA

  • ANOCA = angina without stenosis ≥ 50%/FFR ≤ 0.80; INOCA adds proven ischaemia. Common in women; not benign.
  • Invasive coronary function testing in persistently symptomatic patients: ESC 2024 I B.
  • CMD = CFR < 2.0 and/or IMR ≥ 25 (HMR ≥ 1.9; PET MBF reserve < 2.0).
  • Epicardial spasm on ACh = symptoms + ECG change + ≥ 90% constriction; microvascular spasm = symptoms + ECG change without it.
  • VSA: CCB is Class I A, nitrates IIa B; avoid β-blockers; smoking is the key trigger.
  • Microvascular angina with ↓ CFR: β-blocker (IIa B); endothelial dysfunction: ACE-I (IIa B).
  • Myocardial bridge: systolic-only narrowing, worsened by nitrates, treated with β-blockers.

6.6 Anti-anginal Therapy

ESC 2024 abandoned the rigid "first-line / second-line" hierarchy: drugs are chosen by the patient's heart rate, blood pressure, LV function and comorbidities, starting with a β-blocker and/or CCB in most. Every symptomatic patient also needs short-acting nitrate for immediate relief and a timely review (2–4 weeks) of response. Remember the aim: anti-anginals relieve symptoms — only β-blockers after MI with reduced LVEF have prognostic benefit.

EXAM TRAP

Ivabradine is excellent for HFrEF (SHIFT) but harmful as an anti-anginal in patients without HF: in SIGNIFY, patients with activity-limiting angina had more CV death/non-fatal MI on ivabradine. Never combine it with verapamil or diltiazem (both CYP3A4 inhibitors and rate-slowing).

BOARD PEARL — CHOOSING BY HAEMODYNAMIC PROFILE
  • High HR, normal/high BP → β-blocker (or non-DHP CCB if LVEF normal).
  • Low HR / conduction disease → DHP CCB, ranolazine, trimetazidine, nitrates.
  • Low BP → ranolazine or trimetazidine (haemodynamically neutral).
  • HFrEF → β-blocker; add ivabradine if HR ≥ 70 in sinus rhythm; amlodipine is the safe CCB.
  • Asthma/COPD → CCB; cardioselective β-blocker is acceptable in COPD.

Key highlightsAnti-anginal therapy

  • Short-acting nitrate for all (I B); β-blocker and/or CCB first, tailored to HR and BP.
  • β-blocker target resting HR 55–60 bpm; prognostic benefit only post-MI with reduced LVEF/HFrEF.
  • Non-DHP CCBs are contraindicated in LVEF ≤ 40%; amlodipine/felodipine are safe in HFrEF.
  • Nitrate tolerance → nitrate-free interval 10–14 h; no nitrate within 24 h of sildenafil or 48 h of tadalafil.
  • Ranolazine: QT prolongation, CYP3A4 interactions; ESC IIa B vs ACC Class 1 add-on.
  • Ivabradine for angina without HF (LVEF > 40%) is ESC Class III (SIGNIFY).
  • Trimetazidine is contraindicated in Parkinson's disease; nicorandil causes mucosal ulceration.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • High bleeding risk without high ischaemic risk: stop DAPT at 1–3 months, continue single antiplatelet therapy.
  • I A
  • Long-term OAC indication (e.g. AF): OAC alone lifelong (DOAC preferred over VKA) once any post-PCI combination period is complete.
  • I B
  • Lipids

  • NEW Statin-intolerant, not at goal on ezetimibe: add bempedoic acid. I B
  • Anti-inflammatory
  • NEW Low-dose colchicine 0.5 mg daily in atherosclerotic CAD to reduce MI, stroke and need for revascularisation.

  • NEW Semaglutide in CCS without diabetes but with overweight/obesity (BMI > 27 kg/m²) to reduce CV death, MI or stroke.
  • IIa B
  • Also: PPI when on any antithrombotic combination or with high GI-bleeding risk; ACE-I (or ARB) when hypertension, LVEF ≤ 40%, diabetes or CKD coexist; β-blocker when LVEF ≤ 40%.
  • Intensifying antithrombotic therapy
  • In patients at high ischaemic risk (diffuse multivessel CAD plus diabetes, recurrent MI, PAD or CKD) and without high bleeding risk, a second antithrombotic added long-term to aspirin reduces events at the cost of bleeding:
  • Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd + aspirin (COMPASS, stable CAD/PAD): MACE ↓ 24% including CV death; major bleeding ↑.
  • Ticagrelor 60 mg bd 1–3 years after MI (PEGASUS-TIMI 54): MACE ↓ ~15%; bleeding ↑.
  • Extended thienopyridine DAPT beyond 12 months after DES (DAPT trial): stent thrombosis and MI ↓, bleeding ↑.
  • Anti-inflammatory therapy
  • LoDoCo2 (chronic CAD, colchicine 0.5 mg daily): composite of CV death, MI, ischaemic stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularisation ↓ ~31%. COLCOT showed benefit after recent MI.
  • CLEAR SYNERGY (colchicine started early after MI) was neutral — the evidence base is strongest in stable CAD.
  • Avoid in severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30) and with strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (clarithromycin, ciclosporin); GI upset is common initially.

6.7 Event Prevention

Disease-modifying therapy is what changes prognosis in CCS; revascularisation mostly changes symptoms. The pillars are lifestyle, antithrombotic therapy, intensive lipid lowering, anti-inflammatory therapy, and cardiometabolic drugs (SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA), plus BP control and vaccination.

  • Lifestyle — the non-negotiables
  • Smoking cessation: halves excess MI risk within
  • ~1 year; nicotine replacement, varenicline and
  • bupropion are acceptable.
  • Exercise: 150–300 min/week moderate or
  • 75–150 min/week vigorous aerobic activity, plus
  • resistance training.
  • Cardiac rehabilitation (exercise-based,
  • multidisciplinary): Class I A.
  • Diet: Mediterranean pattern, salt < 5 g/day,
  • saturated fat < 10% of energy, alcohol <
  • 100 g/week.
  • Weight: target BMI 20–25; screen for sleep
  • apnoea.
  • Psychosocial: screen and treat depression;
  • annual influenza vaccination.
WHAT CHANGED — LIPIDS 2025–2026

ESC/EAS 2025 focused update keeps the < 1.4 mmol/L / ≥ 50% target for very-high-risk patients (all CCS) and expands non-statin combinations (ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, bempedoic acid).

ACC/AHA 2026 dyslipidemia guideline returns to explicit LDL-C goals: < 55 mg/dL for very-high-risk ASCVD (non-HDL-C < 85 mg/dL), < 70 mg/dL for other ASCVD; Lp(a) measured at least once. ESC and ACC now effectively converge.

EXAM TRAP

"Stable CAD, no prior MI, LVEF 60%, on bisoprolol for 5 years — is it essential for prognosis?" No. Outside MI with reduced EF or HFrEF, β-blockers treat angina; they do not prolong life (AHA/ACC: Class 3 No benefit for MACE reduction without prior MI or LVEF ≤ 50%). Continue it only if it is needed for symptoms, rate control or hypertension.

Key highlightsEvent prevention

  • Aspirin 75–100 mg lifelong; clopidogrel is an equal alternative (ESC 2024 I A); aspirin now I B even without prior MI/revascularisation if obstructive CAD.
  • Post-PCI DAPT default 6 months; 1–3 months with high bleeding risk.
  • High ischaemic/low bleeding risk: add rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd (COMPASS) or ticagrelor 60 mg bd post-MI (PEGASUS).
  • LDL-C < 1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) and ≥ 50% reduction; ACC 2026 now also uses < 55 mg/dL for very-high-risk.
  • Colchicine 0.5 mg: ESC IIa A vs ACC 2b B-R.
  • SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA in T2DM: I A; semaglutide in BMI > 27 without diabetes: IIa B.
  • β-blockers are prognostic only with reduced LVEF/HF; NSAIDs and HRT are harmful.

6.8 Revascularisation — Prognosis versus Symptoms

Every revascularisation question must be answered twice: will it relieve symptoms? and will it prolong life or prevent MI? In CCS the first is usually yes (when angina persists on medical therapy); the second is yes only for specific anatomy and LV function. Revascularisation is added to — never substituted for — guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT).

What the landmark trials showed

ORBITA-2

Single-vessel stable angina; shamcontrolledORBITA: no significant ↑ exercise time on anti-anginals. ORBITA-2 (off anti-anginals): PCI reduced angina vs placebo →

PCI is a genuine anti-anginal therapy

To improve survival / reduce events

LVEF > 35% with functionally significant three-vessel disease: revascularisation in addition to GDMT to improve long-term survival and reduce CV death and spontaneous MI.

I A

Significant left main stenosis, low surgical risk: CABG over medical therapy alone to improve survival. I A LVEF ≤ 35%, multivessel CAD, suitable for surgery: CABG over medical therapy alone to improve longterm survival. I B

LVEF ≤ 35%: choose between revascularisation and medical therapy after Heart Team evaluation of anatomy, CAD–LV dysfunction correlation, comorbidity and life expectancy.

  • I C
  • LVEF ≤ 35%, high surgical risk: PCI as an alternative to CABG. IIb B
  • Process
  • Heart Team discussion for complex cases; patient-centred shared decision-making. I C
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Pressure wire (FFR/iFR) or QFR to select vessels in multivessel disease. I A

Choice of CABG vs PCI (left main, diabetes, SYNTAX thresholds) is detailed in Chapter 9. Proximal LAD disease in 1–2-vessel CAD is treated as high-risk anatomy in ESC 2024, but its prognostic benefit from revascularisation is less certain than for LM/3VD.

MECHANISM — WHY CABG S AV E S LIVES BUT PCI RARELY DOES IN CCS

A stent treats the lesion; a graft to the mid-vessel protects the whole territory from future plaque rupture anywhere proximal to the anastomosis ("surgical collateralisation"). Most MIs arise from plaques that were not severely stenotic beforehand, so treating the tightest lesion (PCI) relieves ischaemia but barely changes the MI risk, while bypassing proximal segments does. Hence the survival benefit of CABG in extensive disease (LM, 3VD, diabetes, LV dysfunction) and the symptom-only benefit of PCI in limited disease.

6.9 Special Situations

Ischaemic cardiomyopathy and new heart failure

CAD is the commonest cause of HFrEF, so every new HFrEF needs coronary assessment (CCTA if likelihood is low–moderate, ICA if high). Full HF therapy comes first; for angina use β-blocker, amlodipine, nitrates or ivabradine (HR ≥ 70, sinus rhythm) and avoid non-DHP CCBs. CABG, not PCI, adds long-term survival (STICHES vs REVIVED).

Refractory angina

Defined as angina lasting ≥ 3 months due to established reversible ischaemia in obstructive CAD, not controlled by optimal medical therapy and not amenable to (further) revascularisation, including CTO PCI. Coronary sinus reducer — hourglass stent raises coronary venous pressure and redistributes flow to ischaemic subendocardium; sham-controlled trials reduce angina.

EECP (diastolic lower-limb cuff inflation, 35 one-hour sessions) and spinal cord stimulation — may be considered.

Transmyocardial laser revascularisation — not recommended.

Women, elderly, CKD and diabetes

Women: more ANOCA/INOCA and microvascular angina; lower exercise-ECG specificity; think SCAD in young/peripartum women; systemic HRT does not protect and ↑ VTE.

Elderly: atypical symptoms (dyspnoea, fatigue); higher bleeding risk → shorter DAPT; weigh frailty and life expectancy before revascularisation.

Advanced CKD: ISCHEMIA-CKD found no benefit of a routine invasive strategy; minimise contrast; prefer functional imaging.

Diabetes: silent ischaemia is common; SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA with proven benefit; CABG preferred for multivessel disease (FREEDOM — Chapter 9).

Asymptomatic individuals and follow-up

No routine stress testing or CCTA in low-risk asymptomatic adults (CACS may refine prevention in intermediate risk). In established CCS, routine periodic stress testing or CCTA without a change in status is not recommended — reassess when symptoms worsen, LVEF falls or arrhythmia appears.

Key highlightsRevascularisation in CCS

  • Symptoms refractory to GDMT → revascularise significant lesions (I A); ORBITA-2 confirms PCI relieves angina.
  • Prognostic indications: LM ≥ 50%, functionally significant 3VD with LVEF > 35% (ESC I A), MVD with LVEF ≤ 35% (CABG I B).
  • ISCHEMIA: no reduction in death/MI with routine invasive strategy in moderate–severe ischaemia (LM and LVEF < 35% excluded).
  • STICHES: CABG ↓ all-cause death at 10 y in LVEF ≤ 35%; REVIVED: PCI did not.
  • COURAGE: PCI + OMT = OMT for death/MI; FAME 2: FFR-guided PCI ↓ urgent revascularisation.
  • ESC is more pro-revascularisation for 3VD (I A) than ACC 2021 (2b); ACC 2023 moved to 2a for MVD.
  • Valve disease: coronary assessment (ICA, or CCTA if likelihood is lower) precedes valve surgery; in TAVI candidates, NOTION-3 showed fewer MACE with PCI of proximal lesions with FFR ≤ 0.80 or ≥ 90% stenosis. Sexual activity ≈ 3–5 METs; PDE-5 inhibitors are safe in stable CAD but never with nitrates or nicorandil.

Key highlightsSpecial situations

  • New HFrEF → exclude CAD; CABG (not PCI) adds survival in LVEF ≤ 35% with MVD.
  • Refractory angina (≥ 3 months): coronary sinus reducer, EECP, spinal cord stimulation; TMLR not recommended.
  • Women: more INOCA; think SCAD; HRT is harmful for CV prevention.
  • ISCHEMIA-CKD: no benefit of routine invasive strategy in advanced CKD.
  • Routine repeat stress testing/CCTA in stable patients is not recommended.
  • No nitrates within 24 h of sildenafil/vardenafil or 48 h of tadalafil.

6.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 38-year-old woman has non-anginal chest pain; she has no risk factors, a normal ECG and a normal echocardiogram. Her estimated pre-test likelihood of obstructive CAD by the RF-CL model is 3%. According to ESC 2024, what is the most appropriate next step?

Answer C Very low likelihood (≤ 5%): ESC 2024 recommends deferring further diagnostic tests (IIa B). CCTA is for > 5–50%; exercise ECG and imaging generate false positives in very-low-prevalence groups; ICA is never the answer here.

Q2 A 58-year-old man with exertional chest tightness, hypertension and dyslipidaemia has a clinical likelihood of 25%. He is in sinus rhythm at 62 bpm, BMI 26, eGFR 85. Which first-line test carries a Class I, Level A recommendation in ESC 2024?

Answer B CCTA is Class I A for low–moderate (> 5–50%) likelihood, and his characteristics predict good image quality. Functional imaging is I B for > 15–85%. Exercise ECG is no longer a first-line diagnostic test; CACS only reclassifies; ICA is for very high likelihood.

Q3 On a Bruce protocol a patient exercises for 5 min, develops 2 mm horizontal ST depression and stops because of chest pain. What is his Duke treadmill score and risk category?

Answer D DTS = 5 − (5 × 2) − (4 × 2) = −13 → high risk (< −10, annual mortality > 3%) → invasive angiography. The angina index is 2 because angina limited the test.

Q4 A 52-year-old woman has recurrent exertional and rest angina for a year despite amlodipine. Angiography shows smooth coronaries; FFR 0.92, CFR 1.6, IMR 38. Intracoronary acetylcholine produces no epicardial constriction and no ECG change. Which treatment is best supported by ESC 2024?

Answer B Structural microvascular dysfunction (CFR < 2.0, IMR ≥ 25) without spasm: β-blockers are IIa B for microvascular angina with reduced flow reserve. Nitrates are often ineffective in CMD; ivabradine is Class III in angina without HF; no epicardial lesion to stent.

Q5 A 44-year-old smoker has recurrent chest pain at 5 a.m. with transient ST elevation in II, III and aVF that resolves with sublingual GTN. Angiography shows non-obstructive plaque. He was started on metoprolol after an ED visit and his episodes have become more frequent. What is the best management?

Answer C Classic vasospastic angina (early-morning rest pain, transient ST elevation, nitrate-responsive). CCBs are Class I A; β-blockers — especially non-selective ones such as propranolol — leave α-constriction unopposed and worsen spasm. Stenting does not treat VSA.

Q6 A 64-year-old man with CCS and angina (CCS class II) has LVEF 60%, sinus rhythm at 78 bpm on bisoprolol 10 mg and amlodipine 10 mg. Which add-on drug is explicitly not recommended (Class III) by ESC 2024?

Answer C SIGNIFY showed more CV death/MI with ivabradine in activity-limiting angina without HF; ESC 2024 makes add-on ivabradine Class III in CCS with LVEF > 40% and no HF. The other drugs are legitimate add-ons.

Q7 A 66-year-old man had PCI with a drug-eluting stent 2 years ago for stable angina. He is intolerant of aspirin (dyspepsia despite PPI). He has no bleeding history and is in sinus rhythm. What is the recommended long-term antithrombotic therapy?

Answer B Clopidogrel 75 mg is an equally effective and safe alternative to aspirin for long-term single antiplatelet therapy after MI/PCI (ESC 2024 I A). OAC has no role in sinus rhythm; ticagrelor 90 mg bd is an ACS dose; high-dose aspirin only increases GI toxicity.

Q8 Which statement about low-dose colchicine in chronic coronary syndromes is correct?

Answer B ESC 2024: colchicine 0.5 mg daily IIa A (LoDoCo2); AHA/ACC 2023: 2b B-R. It is anti-inflammatory, not lipidlowering; strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors such as clarithromycin cause toxicity.

Q9 A 61-year-old man with stable CCS class II angina, well controlled on two anti-anginals, has 14% reversible LV ischaemia on SPECT. CCTA shows a 75% mid-RCA and a 70% mid-LCx stenosis; the left main is normal; LVEF 55%. According to the ISCHEMIA trial, a routine invasive strategy compared with medical therapy would be expected to: Reduce all-cause mortality

Answer C ISCHEMIA (moderate–severe ischaemia, LM excluded, LVEF ≥ 35%) showed no reduction in the primary composite or all-cause death with a routine invasive strategy; symptom/QoL benefit was seen in patients with angina. His angina is controlled → optimise medical therapy.

Q10 A 67-year-old man has HFrEF (LVEF 28%) with three-vessel CAD and good distal targets. He has mild angina, is on full GDMT and is a reasonable surgical candidate. Which statement is best supported by evidence?

Answer B STICH extended follow-up (STICHES) showed lower all-cause mortality with CABG + medical therapy at 10 years in LVEF ≤ 35% (ESC 2024 I B). REVIVED-BCIS2 found no benefit from PCI. Viability testing did not predict CABG benefit in STICH. Ivabradine is indicated in HFrEF with HR ≥ 70.

7.1 Myocardial Injury & the Universal Definition of MI

The Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (UDMI) is a joint ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF consensus that separates two concepts examiners love to blur: myocardial injury (a biochemical finding) and myocardial infarction (injury caused by ischaemia). The 4th UDMI (2018) is still the language of most guidelines, question banks and trials; the 5th UDMI (2026), released at ESC Congress 2026, replaces the numbered types with three clinical categories. You must be fluent in both.

Troponin: the analytical ground rules

The decision limit is the 99th percentile upper reference limit (URL) of a healthy reference population, assay-specific.

A high-sensitivity (hs) assay must measure troponin in ≥ 50% of healthy individuals and have a coefficient of variation ≤ 10% at the 99th percentile.

Sex-specific 99th percentile thresholds are recommended (women have lower values — e.g. hs-cTnT roughly 9 ng/L in women versus ≈ 17 ng/L in men against a pooled 14 ng/L); the 5th UDMI endorses them explicitly to reduce under-diagnosis in women.

cTnT and cTnI are equally cardiac-specific for clinical purposes; CK-MB is now only a fallback when troponin is unavailable.

Skeletal-muscle disease and CKD can raise cTnT (re-expression in regenerating muscle); cTnI is less affected.

DEFINITION — UNSTABLE ANGINA IN THE HS-TROPONIN ERA

Ischaemic symptoms at rest or minimal exertion without acute cardiomyocyte injury (troponin not above the URL, or no dynamic change). With hs assays, UA is shrinking: many former "UA" patients are re-classified as NSTEMI, and UA carries a substantially lower short-term risk (see Chapter 8).

The five types of MI — 4th UDMI (2018)

BOARD PEARL
  • The procedural numbers are a favourite:
  • PCI > 5×, CABG > 10×, both within 48 h, and both need something more than troponin . A troponin rise alone after PCI is procedural myocardial injury, not type 4a MI.

Other definitions that appear in MCQs

Reinfarction vs recurrent MI
  • Reinfarction: new MI within 28 days of an incident MI.
  • Recurrent MI: new MI after 28 days.
  • If cTn is already elevated but stable or falling, a > 20% rise
  • in the second sample (3–6 h) supports reinfarction.
  • ST re-elevation ≥ 1 mm or new Q waves strengthens the
  • diagnosis.
Prior (silent) MI — ECG criteria
  • Any Q wave in V2–V3 > 0.02 s or a QS complex.
  • Q ≥ 0.03 s and ≥ 1 mm deep in I, II, aVL, aVF or V4–V6 in
  • any two contiguous leads.
  • R ≥ 0.04 s in V1–V2 with R/S ≥ 1 and a concordant upright
  • T — posterior MI (absent conduction defect).
  • Or imaging: regional loss of viable myocardium that is
  • thinned and not contracting.

Non-type-1 causes of troponin rise to keep in mind: tachy-/bradyarrhythmia, shock, anaemia, hypoxia, severe AS, myocarditis, contusion, cardiotoxic chemotherapy, infiltrative disease, HF, acute PE, pulmonary hypertension, Takotsubo, stroke/SAH, sepsis, CKD, extreme exertion and rhabdomyolysis (cTnT).

The 5th Universal Definition of MI (2026)

Published in August 2026 (EHJ / Circulation / JACC), the 5th UDMI keeps the injury-versus-infarction concept but replaces the numbered types with three pathophysiology-based categories aligned with ICD-11 coding.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2026 — 5 TH UDMI
  • Numbered types (1–5, 4a–c) replaced by primary, secondary and procedure-related MI.
  • Diagnosis graded as likely on clinical grounds and confirmed by coronary and/or cardiac imaging (acute coronary lesion, new RWMA, or new loss of viable myocardium).
  • Sex-specific 99th percentile troponin thresholds explicitly endorsed.
  • Delta criteria are not fixed: an absolute change is favoured at low troponin concentrations and a relative change at high concentrations, sampled 1–2 h apart.
  • MINOCA re-expanded as "myocardial injury with non-obstructive coronary arteries" — still a working (intermediate) diagnosis.
  • Procedure-related MI window widened to 30 days; emphasis moves from troponin multiples to evidence of a procedural coronary complication (± new RWMA).
  • OMI-type ECG patterns (de Winter, Wellens, posterior MI, Aslanger, Sgarbossa) are acknowledged; STEMI/NSTEMI terminology is retained.
EXAM TRAP
  • Most current question banks and the ESC 2023 / ACC/AHA 2025 ACS guidelines still use 4th UDMI language.
  • If a stem says "type 2 MI" or "type 4a", answer within that framework. If it says "secondary MI" or "procedure-related MI", it is testing the 2026 definition.

Key highlightsUniversal definition of MI

  • Myocardial injury = cTn > 99th percentile URL; acute if there is a rise/fall; MI = acute injury + evidence of ischaemia.
  • hs-assay criteria: detectable in ≥ 50% of healthy people, CV ≤ 10% at the 99th percentile; use sex-specific thresholds.
  • Type 4a: > 5× URL within 48 h of PCI; type 5: > 10× URL within 48 h of CABG — each plus ECG, angiographic or imaging evidence.
  • Type 4b = stent thrombosis; type 4c = restenosis; type 3 = sudden cardiac death before biomarkers.
  • Reinfarction ≤ 28 days; recurrent MI > 28 days; a > 20% rise on a raised baseline supports reinfarction. 5th UDMI (2026): primary, secondary and procedure-related MI (≤ 30 days); type 3 abolished; imaging confirms MI.
  • SCAD, spasm, embolism and late stent thrombosis are primary MI under the 5th UDMI.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • In a working diagnosis of MINOCA, follow a diagnostic algorithm to determine the underlying cause. I B CMR is recommended in patients with MINOCA without an obvious underlying cause. I B
  • Manage MINOCA according to the final established underlying diagnosis, consistent with the relevant disease guideline.
  • I B

7.2 MINOCA, SCAD & Secondary (Type 2) MI

MINOCA — a working diagnosis

MINOCA accounts for roughly 5–10% of acute MI; patients are younger and more often women than those with obstructive MI. The label is a working diagnosis that obliges you to look for the cause — it is not a final diagnosis. Non-ischaemic mimics that also show "troponin-positive non-obstructive coronaries" (myocarditis, Takotsubo, cardiomyopathy) are excluded from MINOCA once identified.

DEFINITION — MINOCA (4 TH UDMI/ESC 2023)
  • Acute MI fulfilling UDMI criteria;
  • Non-obstructive coronary arteries at angiography — no stenosis ≥ 50% in any major epicardial vessel; No overt alternative explanation for the presentation.
BOARD PEARL

CMR is the pivotal test: a subendocardial/transmural LGE in a coronary territory = true MI; subepicardial/ mid-wall LGE = myocarditis; oedema without LGE in an apical-ballooning pattern = Takotsubo. Perform it early (ideally within the first 2 weeks) — oedema and myocarditis LGE fade.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD)

SCAD is a non-atherosclerotic separation of the coronary wall by an intramural haematoma (with or without an intimal tear) that compresses the true lumen. It causes up to about a third of MI in women younger than 50 and is the leading cause of pregnancy-associated MI (most often postpartum).

Associations
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia — the commonest association;
  • screen renal, iliac and cerebrovascular beds (CTA/MRA).
  • Pregnancy/postpartum, multiparity, hormonal therapy.
  • Extreme emotional or physical stress (isometric exercise,
  • Valsalva).
  • Connective tissue disease (Marfan, vascular Ehlers–
  • Danlos, Loeys–Dietz).
Angiographic types (Saw classification)
  • Type 1 — contrast staining, double lumen
  • (pathognomonic).
  • Type 2 — long, smooth, diffuse narrowing (most
  • common); 2a normal distal vessel, 2b to the apex.
  • Type 3 — focal/tubular, mimics atherosclerosis; IVUS/
  • OCT needed.
  • Type 4 — abrupt total occlusion, usually distal.
EXAM TRAP

A 38-year-old woman two weeks postpartum with anterior STEMI and a long smooth LAD narrowing — the answer is not stent-the-LAD if she is stable with TIMI 3 flow. Conservative management, beta-blocker, and FMD screening. Statins are not indicated for SCAD itself in the absence of another indication.

Secondary (type 2) MI

Type 2 MI is common in older, comorbid inpatients (sepsis, GI bleeding, rapid AF, hypoxia, postoperative hypotension) and carries a higher long-term mortality than type 1 MI, largely from the precipitating illness and underlying CAD.

Management principle: treat the trigger (transfuse, rate-control, restore BP/oxygenation). Routine DAPT, anticoagulation and invasive angiography are not automatic — they may harm (bleeding). Look for underlying obstructive CAD once the patient is stable (non-invasive or invasive testing as appropriate); treat risk factors.

5th UDMI requires objective support for secondary MI — obstructive CAD without an acute lesion and/or a new RWMA / loss of viable myocardium; otherwise the label is acute myocardial injury.

DON'T CONFUSE

Acute non-ischaemic myocardial injury (e.g. sepsis without ischaemic features, PE, myocarditis) versus type 2 MI (the same triggers plus ischaemic symptoms, ECG or imaging evidence). A troponin rise in sepsis without ischaemic criteria is injury, not infarction.

7.3 The STEMI ECG & STEMI Equivalents

The ECG is the triage tool of reperfusion: it must be recorded and interpreted within 10 min of first medical contact (FMC). The underlying question is not "is there ST elevation?" but "is there an acutely occluded coronary artery that needs immediate reperfusion? " — hence the growing language of occlusion MI (OMI).

Key highlightsMINOCA, SCAD & type 2 MI

  • MINOCA = MI + no stenosis ≥ 50% + no alternative diagnosis; a working diagnosis requiring a cause.
  • CMR is recommended in MINOCA without an obvious cause (Class I, B) — it separates MI, myocarditis and Takotsubo.
  • IVUS/OCT reveals plaque disruption; acetylcholine testing reveals epicardial or microvascular spasm.
  • SCAD: young women, peripartum, FMD; type 2 angiographic pattern is the most common.
  • SCAD is managed conservatively unless there is ongoing ischaemia/instability; avoid fibrinolysis; give a betablocker; screen for FMD.
  • Type 2 MI: treat the precipitant; routine antithrombotics and early angiography are not automatic.
  • Type 2 MI has worse long-term survival than type 1 MI.
  • Finding Threshold (new, at the J point, in ≥ 2 contiguous leads)
  • Pathological Q wave Duration ≥ 40 ms (≥ 30 ms in most leads for prior-MI criteria; see 7.1)

STEMI equivalents — treat as STEMI

Some patterns signal an acute occlusion and warrant an immediate reperfusion strategy despite the absence of classic ST elevation (posterior MI, de Winter, bundle-branch block or paced rhythm with ongoing ischaemia, hyperacute T waves — ESC 2023). Others (Wellens, the aVR pattern) identify very-high-risk anatomy that needs urgent angiography.

SGARBOSSA CRITERIA (LBBB/PACED RHYTHM)
DIFFERENTIAL OF ST ELEVATION
  • Acute pericarditis — diffuse concave STE, PR
  • depression (PR elevation in aVR), no reciprocal change
  • except aVR/V1.
  • Early repolarisation — J-point notching, young, fastresolving with exercise.
  • LV aneurysm — persistent STE with Q waves weeks
  • after MI.
  • Takotsubo — anterior STE, often without reciprocal
  • change.
  • LVH / LBBB / paced — secondary (discordant)
  • repolarisation.
  • Brugada type 1 — coved STE ≥ 2 mm V1–V2.
  • Hyperkalaemia — peaked T, broad QRS, pseudo-STE
  • V1–V2.
  • Coronary spasm — transient STE resolving with
  • nitrates.
EXAM TRAP

Circumflex occlusion is the classic "ECG-silent" STEMI — the lateral/posterior wall is poorly represented on the 12-lead. Ongoing ischaemic pain with a non-diagnostic 12-lead demands V7–V9 (and V3R–V4R in inferior MI), serial ECGs and bedside echo for an RWMA. Persistent pain refractory to medical therapy is itself an indication for immediate angiography.

Key highlightsSTEMI ECG & equivalents

  • STE ≥ 1 mm in two contiguous leads; in V2–V3 ≥ 2 mm men ≥ 40, ≥ 2.5 mm men < 40, ≥ 1.5 mm women.
  • Posterior leads V7–V9 ≥ 0.5 mm; right-sided V3R–V4R ≥ 0.5 mm (≥ 1 mm men < 30).
  • STD V1–V3 with tall R and upright T = posterior MI until proven otherwise.
  • de Winter = up-sloping STD with tall T waves in V1–V6 → proximal LAD occlusion → primary PCI.
  • Wellens (biphasic or deep T inversion V2–V3, pain-free) → critical LAD stenosis → angiography, never stress testing.
  • STE aVR and/or V1 with STD in ≥ 8 leads → left main / multivessel ischaemia.
  • LBBB or paced rhythm with ongoing ischaemia → STEMI pathway; Sgarbossa score ≥ 3 is specific.
  • Inferior STEMI: STE III > II suggests RCA; always record V4R.

7.4 Initial Management, Reperfusion Strategy & Time Targets

The time chain

Myocardial salvage is time-dependent — the "wavefront" of necrosis spreads from subendocardium to epicardium over roughly 3–6 h. The system is organised around first medical contact (FMC) and the moment of STEMI diagnosis (ECG interpretation), which ESC uses as "time zero".

FMC → device ≤ 90 min

Transfer from non-PCI centre Diagnosis → wire ≤ 120 min FMC → device ≤ 120 min; doorin–door-out ≤ 30 min Fibrinolysis (when PCI not timely) Diagnosis → bolus ≤ 10 min Door-to-needle ≤ 30 min

  • Assess lysis success (ST resolution) 60–90 min after bolus 60–90 min
  • Routine angiography after successful
  • lysis
  • 2–24 h 2–24 h

Recommendation Class Level

If timely primary PCI cannot be performed, fibrinolysis within 12 h of symptom onset in patients without contraindications.

I A

Primary PCI beyond 12 h when symptoms persist, or with haemodynamic instability or life-threatening arrhythmias.

  • I C
  • Routine primary PCI in late presenters (12–48 h) after symptom onset. IIa B

Routine PCI of an occluded IRA in asymptomatic patients presenting > 48 h after onset. III A After fibrinolysis

Transfer to a PCI-capable centre immediately after fibrinolysis. I A

Rescue PCI for failed fibrinolysis (ST resolution < 50% within 60–90 min), haemodynamic or electrical instability, or worsening ischaemia.

I A

Emergency angiography and PCI if recurrent ischaemia or evidence of re-occlusion after initially successful lysis.

  • I B
  • Angiography and PCI of the IRA, if indicated, 2–24 h after successful fibrinolysis. I A

Initial supportive care

IIa A

Continuous ECG monitoring and defibrillator capacity as soon as possible in suspected STEMI. I B Analgesia: titrated IV opioids may be used for severe pain, and a mild anxiolytic for the very anxious patient — both are low-evidence, individualised measures. Sublingual/IV nitrates relieve ischaemic pain but are avoided with hypotension, RV infarction or recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.

MECHANISM — WHY MORPHINE AND OXYGEN FELL FROM FAVOUR

Morphine delays gastric emptying and absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors, postponing platelet inhibition by hours (a pharmacodynamic interaction shown for clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor). Supplemental oxygen in normoxic patients causes coronary vasoconstriction and did not reduce mortality or infarct size (DETO2X-AMI, AVOID) — hence the SpO₂ < 90% trigger.

  • Resuscitated cardiac arrest
  • Persistent STE after ROSC → primary PCI (ESC Class I, B).

Haemodynamically stable, resuscitated OHCA without persistent STE → routine immediate angiography is not recommended (Class III, A — COACT, TOMAHAWK); delayed/selective angiography instead. Temperature control after OHCA in patients who remain unresponsive: continuous core-temperature monitoring and active prevention of fever (> 37.7 °C) (Class I, B).

Pre-hospital cooling with rapid infusion of large volumes of cold IV fluid is not recommended (Class III, A).

BOARD PEARL

For the 120-minute rule, the clock starts at STEMI diagnosis, not at symptom onset (ESC). Symptom-onset time decides eligibility for reperfusion (≤ 12 h); diagnosis-to-wire time decides which reperfusion. Very early presenters (< 2–3 h) with a large anterior infarct and low bleeding risk gain most from immediate lysis when PCI will be delayed.

Key highlightsReperfusion strategy & time targets

  • ECG within 10 min of FMC; reperfusion for all STEMI ≤ 12 h from symptom onset (Class I, A).
  • Primary PCI if diagnosis-to-wire ≤ 120 min; otherwise fibrinolysis within 10 min of diagnosis (ESC) / door-toneedle ≤ 30 min (ACC/AHA).
  • ACC/AHA: FMC-to-device ≤ 90 min, ≤ 120 min if transferred; door-in–door-out ≤ 30 min.
  • Late presenters 12–48 h: primary PCI reasonable (IIa); asymptomatic occluded IRA > 48 h: no PCI (III, A — OAT).
  • Oxygen only if SpO₂ < 90%; routine oxygen is Class III.
  • IV beta-blocker at primary PCI if no HF and SBP > 120 mmHg (IIa).
  • Resuscitated OHCA with persistent STE → primary PCI; without STE and stable → no routine immediate angiography.
