7.5 Fibrinolysis & the Pharmaco-Invasive Strategy

Fibrinolysis remains the reperfusion strategy wherever primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 min of diagnosis. Its benefit is greatest within the first 2–3 h of symptoms, when the thrombus is fresh and fibrinpoor; it falls steeply thereafter. Fibrin-specific agents are preferred, and the strategy is now always pharmaco-invasive: lysis is followed by transfer and angiography.

MECHANISM

Fibrinolytics convert plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin. Fibrin-specific agents (tenecteplase > reteplase ≈ alteplase) act preferentially on clot-bound plasminogen and cause less systemic fibrinogen depletion. Streptokinase is non-fibrin-specific and antigenic — never re-use it after 5 days (antibodies). Lysis also exposes thrombin and activates platelets: this is why an antiplatelet and an anticoagulant must accompany every lytic.

EXAM TRAP
  • The windows differ: ESC treats ischaemic stroke within 6 months as absolute, ACC/AHA within 3 months.
  • Menstruation is not a contraindication. A prior haemorrhagic stroke at any time is absolute in both. An elderly patient with prior stroke of unknown type → treat as haemorrhagic → no lysis.

Adjunctive therapy with fibrinolysis

Recommendation Class Level

Anticoagulation until revascularisation (if performed) or for the hospital stay, up to 8 days. I A Enoxaparin IV followed by SC should be considered in preference to UFH. IIa A

Judging success — and what to do next

Markers of reperfusion (60–90 min)
  • ST-segment resolution ≥ 50% in the lead with the greatest
  • initial elevation — the key marker.
  • Relief of chest pain.
  • Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR, 60–120 bpm) —
  • benign "reperfusion arrhythmia"; do not suppress.
  • Early troponin/CK peak ("washout").
Complications
  • Intracranial haemorrhage ~0.9–1%; risk ↑ with age,
  • female sex, low weight, prior stroke, hypertension on
  • admission.
  • Major extracranial bleeding 4–13%.
  • Streptokinase: hypotension, allergy.
  • Free wall rupture — late lysis increases risk.
BOARD PEARL

Never "lyse and leave". After successful lysis → angiography at 2–24 h (not earlier than 2 h, to avoid the pro-thrombotic post-lytic window unless rescue is needed). After failed lysis → immediate rescue PCI; repeat fibrinolysis is not recommended. STREAM: early pre-hospital TNK (within 3 h of symptoms) followed by timely angiography gave outcomes similar to primary PCI; ICH excess in patients ≥ 75 y led to half-dose TNK.

Key highlightsFibrinolysis

  • Lyse when diagnosis-to-wire would exceed 120 min; bolus within 10 min of diagnosis (ESC); fibrin-specific agent (I, B).
  • Tenecteplase: single weight-based bolus 30–50 mg; half dose at age ≥ 75.
  • Absolute contraindications: prior ICH (ever), ischaemic stroke < 6 months (ESC) / < 3 months (ACC/AHA), aortic dissection, active bleeding, recent head trauma/surgery.
  • Co-therapy: aspirin + clopidogrel (75 mg LD if > 75 y) + enoxaparin (preferred) up to 8 days.
  • Success = ST resolution ≥ 50% at 60–90 min; failure → rescue PCI, not re-lysis.
  • Successful lysis → routine angiography 2–24 h (I, A); recurrent ischaemia → emergency PCI.
  • AIVR after lysis is a marker of reperfusion — no antiarrhythmic.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Routine thrombus aspiration. III A
  • Routine deferred stenting. III B
  • ACC/AHA 2025 upgraded intravascular imaging (IVUS/OCT) for left-main and complex lesions to Class 1, and gives routine aspiration thrombectomy Class 3.
  • Antithrombotic therapy for primary PCI

7.6 Primary PCI, Adjunctive Antithrombotics & Complete Revascularisation

Procedural choices in primary PCI

EXAM TRAP

Fondaparinux is contraindicated as the sole anticoagulant for primary PCI — catheter thrombosis (OASIS-6). Prasugrel is contraindicated after any prior stroke/TIA. Pre-treatment with a P2Y12 inhibitor is optional in STEMI (IIb) but not recommended routinely in NSTE-ACS when early angiography is planned (Chapter 8).

Multivessel disease — complete revascularisation

About half of STEMI patients have significant non-culprit disease. Trials (CvLPRIT, DANAMI-3-PRIMULTI, COMPLETE, FIRE in the elderly) consistently show that complete revascularisation reduces cardiovascular death/MI and repeat revascularisation compared with culprit-only PCI — except in cardiogenic shock, where CULPRIT-SHOCK showed that immediate multivessel PCI increases death or renal replacement therapy.

Recommendation Class Level

NEW Invasive epicardial functional assessment of non-culprit segments of the IRA during the index procedure.

III C

NSTE-ACS

NEW Complete revascularisation should be considered in NSTE-ACS with multivessel disease. IIa C Cardiogenic shock

Culprit-lesion-only PCI during the index procedure. I B

Staged PCI of non-IRA should be considered. IIa C

BOARD PEARL

Two different "no" answers in STEMI with multivessel disease: no routine multivessel PCI in cardiogenic shock (CULPRIT-SHOCK), and no late PCI of an occluded IRA in an asymptomatic stable patient > 48 h (OAT). Everywhere else, complete revascularisation wins.

Key highlightsPrimary PCI & revascularisation

  • Radial access (I, A), DES (I, A); routine thrombus aspiration (III, A) and deferred stenting (III, B) are not recommended.
  • Default DAPT: aspirin + prasugrel or ticagrelor for 12 months; clopidogrel only if potent agents unavailable/ contraindicated.
  • UFH is the default anticoagulant (I, C); enoxaparin (IIa, B) or bivalirudin with full-dose infusion (IIa, A) are alternatives; fondaparinux III in primary PCI.
  • GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors only for bail-out (IIa, C); cangrelor in P2Y12-naïve patients (IIb, A).
  • STEMI + MVD, stable: complete revascularisation at index or within 45 days (I, A), guided by angiographic severity.
  • Cardiogenic shock: culprit-only PCI (I, B); immediate non-culprit PCI is harmful.
  • ACC/AHA 2025 gives complete revascularisation Class 1 in both STEMI and NSTE-ACS; ESC gives IIa in NSTEACS.

7.7 Cardiogenic Shock & Mechanical Complications

Cardiogenic shock

Cardiogenic shock complicates about 5–10% of STEMI and remains the leading cause of in-hospital death (mortality ~40–50%). Most cases are due to extensive LV infarction; always exclude a mechanical complication, RV infarction and tamponade with immediate echocardiography.

DEFINITION — CARDIOGENIC SHOCK

SBP < 90 mmHg for > 30 min (or vasopressors needed to maintain ≥ 90) plus hypoperfusion — cold extremities, oliguria (< 30 mL/h), altered mentation, lactate > 2 mmol/L — with adequate filling (PCWP > 15–18 mmHg) and cardiac index < 2.2 L/min/m². The SCAI stages A (at risk) → B (beginning) → C (classic) → D (deteriorating) → E (extremis) grade severity.

IIa C

Short-term mechanical circulatory support may be considered in ACS with severe/refractory shock. IIb C Routine use of an intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) in cardiogenic shock without mechanical complications.

III B

Transfer to a shock-capable centre — Class 1

DanGer Shock (2024): microaxial pump in STEMI shock (comatose OHCA excluded) reduced 180-day death (45.8% vs 58.5%) at the cost of more complications.

Mechanical complications

Mechanical complications are now rare (< 1% each) with primary PCI, but mortality remains very high. They cluster in first/large infarcts, late presenters, the elderly, women and patients receiving late or no reperfusion. Timing is bimodal — within 24 h and at 3–5 days (range 1–14 days).

MECHANISM — WHY THE POSTEROMEDIAL PAPILLARY MUSCLE RUPTURES

The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply (PDA — usually from the RCA), whereas the anterolateral muscle has a dual supply (LAD diagonals and LCx marginals). Hence PMR follows inferior/ posterior MI and involves the posteromedial muscle several times more often.

True LV aneurysm
  • Wide neck; wall contains (scarred) myocardium;
  • dyskinetic.
  • Usually anterior/apical after LAD occlusion.
  • ECG: persistent STE with Q waves weeks after MI.
  • Complications: HF, VT, thrombus/embolism; rupture rare.
  • Surgery for refractory HF/VT.
Pseudoaneurysm (contained rupture)
  • Narrow neck (neck diameter < 50% of fundus); wall =
  • pericardium + thrombus.
  • Often inferior/posterolateral.
  • High risk of rupture → surgical repair regardless of
  • symptoms.
  • Diagnosed with echo contrast, CMR or CT.
CLINICAL APPROACH — MECHANICAL COMPLICATIONS (ESC 2023)
  • Any new murmur, sudden haemodynamic deterioration or PEA after MI → immediate
  • echocardiography.

Treatment is decided by the Heart Team; surgery is the definitive therapy for VSR, PMR and FWR; percutaneous VSR closure or transcatheter edge-to-edge repair are options in selected, high-risk patients.

IABP or short-term MCS may stabilise the patient as a bridge to surgery (ACC/AHA 2025: MCS as bridge — Class 2a).

In stabilised VSR, delayed surgery (after some days of support) allows the necrotic septum to fibrose and reduces operative mortality; deteriorating patients go immediately.

LV thrombus

Occurs mainly after large anterior/apical infarcts with akinesia or aneurysm; incidence ~5–15% in the PCI era (higher on CMR); most form within the first 2 weeks.

CMR (LGE with long inversion time) is the most sensitive test; contrast echo is better than non-contrast echo.

Treatment: OAC (VKA or DOAC — DOACs are increasingly used) for 3–6 months (ESC 2023: IIa, C), stopped when thrombus resolves on re-imaging; combine with antiplatelets for the shortest period (minimise triple therapy).

Routine prophylactic anticoagulation after anterior MI without thrombus is not established.

Right ventricular infarction

Accompanies up to 30–50% of inferior STEMIs (proximal RCA occlusion); haemodynamically important in a minority. Suspect it whenever an inferior MI becomes hypotensive — especially after nitrates.

EXAM TRAP

Day 4 after late-presenting inferior MI, sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension with a soft murmur → papillary muscle rupture (not VSR, whose murmur is loud with a thrill). Sudden PEA on day 3 of a first anterior MI in an elderly hypertensive woman → free wall rupture/tamponade.

7.8 Post-MI Therapy, Risk Stratification & ICD Timing

In-hospital risk assessment

Before discharge
  • Echocardiography during the admission for LV/RV
  • function, mechanical complications and LV thrombus
  • (ESC: I, B).
  • CMR if echo is inconclusive or diagnosis uncertain
  • (MINOCA).
  • GRACE score for prognosis (see Chapter 8).
  • Early discharge (48–72 h) is appropriate for low-risk
  • patients after successful primary PCI.
  • Re-assess LVEF at 6–12 weeks when it is reduced —
  • stunned myocardium recovers.

Long-term pharmacotherapy

NEW Treatment-naïve patients: start high-intensity statin + ezetimibe in hospital when the goal is unlikely to be reached with statin alone (ESC/EAS 2025).

  • IIa B
  • Neurohormonal therapy

Key highlightsShock & complications

  • Shock: SBP < 90 mmHg > 30 min + hypoperfusion; CI < 2.2 L/min/m²; emergency culprit PCI (I, B).
  • Routine IABP is Class III; microaxial pump is ACC/AHA 2a after DanGer Shock; routine VA-ECMO not recommended.
  • Mechanical complications peak within 24 h and at 3–5 days; echo is the first test.
  • VSR: loud murmur + thrill, O₂ step-up in RV. PMR: posteromedial (single PDA supply), soft murmur, flash oedema. FWR: PEA/tamponade.
  • Pseudoaneurysm (narrow neck) → surgery; true aneurysm → persistent STE, HF, VT, thrombus.
  • LV thrombus → OAC 3–6 months (IIa, C), guided by repeat imaging.
  • RV infarct: hypotension + clear lungs + ↑ JVP; V4R; fluids, AV synchrony, avoid nitrates/diuretics.
  • VF in the first 48 h is not an ICD indication; sustained VT/VF after 48 h is.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Beta-blocker in patients with LVEF ≤ 40%. I A
  • CHANGED Routine beta-blocker for all ACS patients regardless of LVEF. IIb B
  • ACE inhibitor (ARB if intolerant) in HF, LVEF ≤ 40%, diabetes, hypertension and/or CKD. I A ACE inhibitor should be considered in all ACS patients. IIa A
  • MRA in patients with LVEF ≤ 40% and HF or diabetes. I A
  • Other
  • Low-dose colchicine (0.5 mg once daily), particularly if other risk factors are insufficiently controlled. IIb A Participation in a comprehensive, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme. I A
  • Annual influenza vaccination. I A
  • Antithrombotic duration and de-escalation are covered in Chapter 8.
WHAT CHANGED — EVIDENCE AFTER ESC 2023

Beta-blockers with preserved LVEF: REDUCE-AMI (2024) and REBOOT (2025) found no reduction in death/MI with LVEF ≥ 50%; BETAMI-DANBLOCKER (2025) suggested benefit, concentrated in mildly reduced LVEF (40–49%). The board answer: beta-blocker is mandatory for LVEF ≤ 40%, reasonable for 41–49%, and optional/individualised for preserved LVEF.

SGLT2 inhibitors started early after MI (EMPACT-MI, DAPA-MI) did not reduce the primary end-point — no routine indication without HF, diabetes or CKD.

Colchicine: COLCOT positive, but CLEAR (2024) was neutral — keep IIb.

Cardiac rehabilitation: the first dedicated ESC guideline (2026) reinforces referral of every post-MI patient.

Primary-prevention ICD after MI — when?

Sudden death risk is highest in the first month after MI, yet early ICD implantation (DINAMIT, IRIS) did not improve survival — arrhythmic deaths fell, non-arrhythmic deaths rose. LV function also recovers substantially after reperfusion. Hence the waiting periods.

LVEF ≤ 30%, NYHA I ICD — IIa, B ICD — Class 1

LVEF ≤ 40% + NSVT ICD if sustained monomorphic VT inducible at EPS (IIa) ICD if inducible sustained VT/VF at EPS — Class 1

  • Early (≤ 40 days) period ICD or wearable defibrillator may be considered in selected
  • patients (incomplete revascularisation, pre-existing LV
  • dysfunction, arrhythmias > 48 h after onset) — IIb, C
  • Wearable defibrillator may
  • be reasonable (2b)
  • Sustained VT/VF > 48 h
  • after MI

Secondary-prevention ICD Secondary-prevention ICD

BOARD PEARL

A patient with LVEF 30% on day 3 after primary PCI does not get an ICD now. Up-titrate GDMT, consider a wearable defibrillator if high risk, and re-measure LVEF at 6–12 weeks . The exception is sustained VT/VF occurring beyond 48 h (or unrelated to ischaemia) — that is secondary prevention and needs no waiting period.

Key highlightsPost-MI therapy & ICD

  • High-intensity statin for all (I, A); LDL-C < 55 mg/dL and ≥ 50% reduction (ESC); add ezetimibe then PCSK9i.
  • ESC/EAS 2025: intensify LLT during the ACS admission (I, C); consider in-hospital statin + ezetimibe (IIa, B).
  • ACC/AHA 2025: add non-statin if LDL-C ≥ 70 mg/dL (1), reasonable at 55–69 (2a).
  • Beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor and MRA are Class I when LVEF ≤ 40%; routine beta-blocker with preserved EF is IIb.
  • Colchicine 0.5 mg daily IIb; cardiac rehabilitation and influenza vaccination Class I.
  • Killip IV = cardiogenic shock; mortality rises steeply from class I to IV.
  • ICD: wait ≥ 40 days post-MI (≥ 90 days post-revascularisation, ACC/AHA); LVEF ≤ 35% NYHA II–III or ≤ 30% NYHA I.

7.9 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 64-year-old man undergoes elective PCI of the LAD for stable angina. Baseline hs-cTnI is normal. At 12 h, hscTnI is 4 × the 99th percentile URL; he is asymptomatic, the ECG is unchanged and the final angiogram showed no complication. How is this best classified under the 4th UDMI?

Answer C Type 4a MI needs cTn > 5× URL within 48 h plus ischaemic ECG change, new Q waves, imaging loss of viable myocardium or an angiographic complication. A 4× rise without any of these is procedural myocardial injury. Type 4c is restenosis; type 2 is supply–demand imbalance.

Q2 A 58-year-old woman has 90 min of crushing chest pain. The ECG shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in V1– V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves; no ST elevation. Troponin is pending. What is the most appropriate next step?

Answer B ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R and upright T is a posterior (usually LCx) occlusion — a STEMI equivalent. Confirm with V7–V9 (≥ 0.5 mm) but do not delay reperfusion. Troponin algorithms and delayed angiography are NSTE-ACS pathways; fondaparinux is Class III in primary PCI.

Q3 A 52-year-old man presents to a non-PCI hospital 2 h after onset of anterior STEMI. The nearest PCI centre can achieve wire crossing about 150 min after diagnosis. He has no contraindication to lysis. What is the best strategy?

Answer B Diagnosis-to-wire time exceeds 120 min, so fibrinolysis within 10 min is indicated, followed by immediate transfer for a pharmaco-invasive strategy (rescue PCI if failed, angiography at 2–24 h if successful). Half-dose TNK is for age ≥ 75; GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors are not added to lysis.

Q4 Ninety minutes after tenecteplase for inferior STEMI, a patient still has chest pain and ST elevation has fallen by only 30%. BP is 110/70 mmHg. What is the next step?

Answer C ST resolution < 50% at 60–90 min with ongoing pain = failed lysis → rescue PCI (I, A). Repeat lysis is ineffective and increases bleeding; streptokinase adds nothing. The 2–24 h window applies only after successful lysis.

Q5 According to the ESC 2023 guideline, which of the following is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis in STEMI?

Answer C ESC lists ischaemic stroke within 6 months as absolute (ACC/AHA uses 3 months). TIA within 6 months, oral anticoagulation and refractory hypertension (> 180/110) are relative; menstruation is not a contraindication.

Q6 A 71-year-old man presented 20 h after onset of an inferior STEMI and received no reperfusion. On day 4 he develops sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension. A soft, short apical systolic murmur is heard. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Answer C Late-presenting inferior MI, day 3–5, flash pulmonary oedema with a soft or absent murmur = papillary muscle rupture, almost always posteromedial because of its single PDA blood supply. VSR gives a loud murmur with a thrill; free wall rupture gives tamponade/PEA.

Q7 A 66-year-old man with inferior STEMI becomes hypotensive (78/50 mmHg) after sublingual nitrate. The lungs are clear and the JVP is raised to the angle of the jaw, rising on inspiration. V4R shows 1.5 mm ST elevation. What is the most appropriate immediate management while the cath lab is prepared?

Answer C Hypotension, clear lungs and raised JVP with Kussmaul's sign and STE in V4R = RV infarction, a preload-dependent state. Give cautious fluids and reperfuse urgently. Diuretics, nitrates, morphine and beta-blockers all reduce preload or contractility and worsen shock.

Q8 A 69-year-old woman with anterior STEMI is in cardiogenic shock. Angiography shows an occluded proximal LAD and a 90% RCA and 80% LCx stenosis. What is the recommended revascularisation strategy?

Answer B CULPRIT-SHOCK: culprit-only PCI at the index procedure reduced death or renal replacement therapy compared with immediate multivessel PCI (ESC I, B; ACC/AHA routine non-culprit PCI Class 3). Staged non-culprit PCI may follow. Routine IABP is Class III.

Q9 A 36-year-old woman, 3 weeks postpartum, presents with chest pain and anterior T-wave inversion; hs-troponin is rising. Angiography shows a long, smooth, tapering narrowing of the mid-to-distal LAD with TIMI 3 flow. She is painfree and stable. What is the best management?

Answer C Type 2 (diffuse, smooth) SCAD in a peripartum woman. Stable patients with preserved flow are managed conservatively — most dissections heal. Stenting risks propagating the haematoma, lysis may extend it, and provocation testing is dangerous in a dissected artery.

Q10 A 60-year-old man has undergone successful primary PCI for anterior STEMI. On day 3, echo shows LVEF 30%. He is NYHA class II with no arrhythmias beyond the first hour. What is the most appropriate plan regarding suddendeath prevention?

Answer C Early ICD after MI did not improve survival (DINAMIT, IRIS) and LVEF often recovers after reperfusion. Re-assess at 6–12 weeks (ESC) / after 40 days (ACC/AHA; 90 days after revascularisation). A wearable defibrillator may be considered in selected high-risk patients. Prophylactic amiodarone has no survival benefit.

What the board expects you to know

  • How the hs-troponin 0/1-h and 0/2-h algorithms rule out, rule in and "observe" — and why cut-offs are assayspecific.
  • The very-high-risk and high-risk criteria that set immediate (< 2 h) versus early (< 24 h) angiography.
  • The pharmacology of aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors, cangrelor and parenteral anticoagulants — doses, contraindications and switching.

8.1 NSTE-ACS: Definitions, Pathophysiology & Presentation

ESC 2023 merged STEMI and NSTE-ACS into one ACS guideline, framing the diagnosis as a working diagnosis that evolves: every patient enters as "suspected ACS", the ECG sorts STEMI from NSTE-ACS, and troponin sorts NSTEMI from unstable angina (UA). NSTE-ACS is now more common than STEMI; patients are older and have more comorbidity, and although in-hospital mortality is lower than in STEMI, mortality at 6–12 months is similar or higher .

Clinical presentations of UA
  • Rest angina — prolonged (> 20 min).
  • New-onset angina (within 2 months) of at least CCS class
  • II–III.
  • Crescendo angina — more frequent, longer, lower
  • threshold.
  • Post-MI angina — within 2 weeks of MI.
Atypical presentations — think ACS
  • Elderly (> 75 y), women, diabetes, CKD, dementia.
  • Dyspnoea, epigastric pain, fatigue, syncope.
  • A normal ECG does not exclude NSTE-ACS (normal in up
  • to ~30%).
  • Pain reproduced by palpation or relieved by nitrates is not
  • diagnostic either way.
MECHANISM — WHY ISCHAEMIA WITHOUT ST ELEVATION

In NSTE-ACS the culprit is usually a non-occlusive platelet-rich thrombus (or an occlusion with good collaterals). Ischaemia is predominantly subendocardial, which projects as ST depression rather than elevation. Intermittent occlusion and distal micro-embolisation of platelet aggregates explain the waxing-waning symptoms and troponin release — and why antiplatelet therapy is the cornerstone.

EXAM TRAP

About 25% of patients labelled NSTEMI have a totally occluded culprit artery at angiography — most often the circumflex. They have larger infarcts and higher mortality. Refractory pain, haemodynamic instability or new RWMA on echo despite a "non-diagnostic" ECG are indications for immediate angiography.

Initial evaluation

12-lead ECG within 10 min of FMC; repeat with recurrent symptoms and if non-diagnostic; add V7–V9 and V3R–V4R when relevant.

hs-cTn at presentation with results within 60 min of blood sampling (ESC: I, B).

Echocardiography for RWMA, LV function and alternative diagnoses (aortic dissection, PE, pericardial effusion, AS, HCM).

CCTA is useful in low-to-intermediate probability patients with normal or inconclusive hs-cTn/ECG to exclude ACS (ESC 2023: IIa, A).

Life-threatening differentials: aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, oesophageal rupture.

Key highlightsNSTE-ACS definitions

  • NSTEMI = ischaemic symptoms + no persistent STE + dynamic hs-cTn above the 99th URL; UA = no troponin rise.
  • UA presentations: rest (> 20 min), new-onset (< 2 months), crescendo, post-MI (< 2 weeks).
  • Plaque rupture (~2/3) — thin-cap fibroatheroma, red thrombus; erosion — intact cap, white platelet thrombus, younger smokers/women.
  • Short-term mortality is lower than STEMI but 6–12-month mortality is similar or higher.
  • ~25% of NSTEMIs have an occluded artery (often LCx).
  • ECG ≤ 10 min; hs-cTn result ≤ 60 min; CCTA to exclude ACS in low-intermediate risk (IIa, A).
  • Assay / algorithm Very low (0 h) Low (0 h) + no Δ High (0 h) Δ rule-in
  • hs-cTnT Elecsys — 0/1 h < 5 < 12 and Δ < 3 ≥ 52 Δ1h ≥ 5
  • hs-cTnI Architect — 0/1 h < 4 < 5 and Δ < 2 ≥ 64 Δ1h ≥ 6
  • hs-cTnI Centaur — 0/1 h < 3 < 6 and Δ < 3 ≥ 120 Δ1h ≥ 12
  • hs-cTnT Elecsys — 0/2 h < 5 < 14 and Δ < 4 ≥ 52 Δ2h ≥ 10
  • Values apply only to the named assay and only within the validated algorithm; always use the local laboratory's version.

8.2 High-Sensitivity Troponin & the 0/1-h and 0/2-h Algorithms

High-sensitivity assays detect troponin in most healthy people and measure small changes precisely. Two consequences follow: (1) MI is detected earlier, so very low values or a flat curve over 1–2 h safely rule out MI; (2) more patients have measurable troponin from non-ACS causes, so interpretation depends on the absolute value, the delta and the clinical context.

MECHANISM — WHY THE CUT-OFFS ARE ASSAY-SPECIFIC

Troponin assays are not standardised: different antibodies recognise different epitopes of cTnI (and cTnT is a different protein altogether), so the same blood gives different numbers on different platforms. Each algorithm's thresholds were derived and validated for one assay and cannot be transposed. The logic is constant: very low baseline (below or near the limit of detection) or low baseline + tiny delta → rule out; high baseline or large delta → rule in; everything else → observe.

Use the ESC 0 h/2 h algorithm as the best alternative. I B

Additional testing at 3 h if the first two hs-cTn measurements are inconclusive and no alternative diagnosis explains the condition.

I B

Routine measurement of additional biomarkers (h-FABP, copeptin) on top of hs-cTn for diagnosis. III B

EXAM TRAP

The "very low single sample" rule-out is invalid in early presenters (chest pain < 3 h) — troponin may not yet have risen. It is also unreliable in late presenters with falling troponin, in whom the delta may be small because the peak has passed. A rule-out does not mean "no coronary disease": it means no MI; UA and stable CAD remain possible.

DON'T CONFUSE — "RULE-IN" IS NOT "TYPE 1 MI"

About a quarter of rule-in patients have another diagnosis — type 2 MI, myocarditis, Takotsubo, PE, HF, tachyarrhythmia or sepsis. Rule-in plus a high clinical probability of type 1 MI leads to angiography; otherwise, look for the alternative cause.

8.3 Risk Stratification: Ischaemic & Bleeding Scores

Risk assessment in NSTE-ACS answers two questions: how soon to angiography (ischaemic risk) and how aggressive the antithrombotic regimen can be (bleeding risk). Clinical features and hs-cTn level carry most of the prognostic information; scores make it reproducible.

Bleeding risk

Major bleeding after ACS carries a mortality impact comparable to recurrent MI. The contemporary standard is the Academic Research Consortium for High Bleeding Risk (ARC-HBR) definition: HBR = BARC 3 or 5 bleeding risk ≥ 4% at 1 year, or intracranial haemorrhage risk ≥ 1%.

Key highlightshs-troponin algorithms

  • ESC 0 h/1 h algorithm is first choice (I, B); 0 h/2 h the alternative (I, B); third sample at 3 h if still inconclusive (I, B).
  • Rule-out: very low 0 h value (pain > 3 h) or low 0 h + small Δ; NPV > 99.5%.
  • Rule-in: high 0 h value or large Δ; PPV ~70–75%.
  • Example — hs-cTnT Elecsys 0/1 h: rule-out < 5 or < 12 with Δ < 3; rule-in ≥ 52 or Δ ≥ 5 ng/L.
  • Cut-offs are assay-specific and never interchangeable.
  • Copeptin/h-FABP on top of hs-cTn: not recommended routinely (III).
  • Major criteria Minor criteria
  • Anticipated long-term oral anticoagulation
  • Severe/end-stage CKD (eGFR < 30 mL/min)
  • Hb < 11 g/dL
  • Spontaneous bleeding needing admission/transfusion in
  • past 6 months, or recurrent
  • Moderate/severe thrombocytopenia (< 100 × 10⁹/L)
  • Chronic bleeding diathesis
  • Liver cirrhosis with portal hypertension
  • Active malignancy (excluding non-melanoma skin) within
  • 12 months
  • Previous spontaneous ICH (any time); traumatic ICH
  • within 12 months; brain AVM
  • Moderate/severe ischaemic stroke within 6 months
  • Non-deferrable major surgery on DAPT; major surgery/
  • trauma within 30 days before PCI
  • Age ≥ 75 y
  • Moderate CKD (eGFR 30–59 mL/min)
  • Hb 11–12.9 g/dL (men) / 11–11.9 g/dL (women)
  • Spontaneous bleeding within 12 months not meeting the
  • major criterion
  • Long-term oral NSAID or steroid use
  • Any ischaemic stroke not meeting the major criterion
BOARD PEARL

Oral anticoagulation alone makes a patient HBR (major criterion) — as does eGFR < 30, Hb < 11 or platelets < 100. Age ≥ 75 is only a minor criterion: an otherwise well 78-year-old is not HBR unless a second minor criterion (e.g. eGFR 45) is present.

Key highlightsRisk stratification

  • GRACE > 140 = high risk → angiography within 24 h.
  • TIMI UA/NSTEMI score: 7 one-point variables, including aspirin use in the past 7 days and ≥ 2 anginal episodes in 24 h.
  • HEART 0–3 = low risk suitable for early discharge.
  • ARC-HBR: ≥ 1 major or ≥ 2 minor criteria; OAC, eGFR < 30, Hb < 11, platelets < 100, recent cancer, prior ICH are major.
  • PRECISE-DAPT ≥ 25 favours short DAPT; DAPT score ≥ 2 favours prolonged DAPT.
  • BARC 3–5 = major bleeding; BARC 3c = intracranial; BARC 5 = fatal.

8.4 Invasive Strategy: Timing & Revascularisation

An invasive strategy (angiography with intent to revascularise) is the default for most NSTE-ACS patients; the question is when. Trials of early versus delayed angiography (TIMACS, VERDICT, meta-analyses) show no overall mortality benefit from very early angiography, but benefit in higher-risk subgroups (GRACE > 140) and shorter hospital stay. In contrast, unstable patients cannot wait.

PCI or CABG in NSTE-ACS

Revascularisation mode follows chronic-coronary principles: left main and multivessel disease → Heart Team with SYNTAX score, diabetes and LV function. Diabetes + multivessel disease favours CABG (FREEDOM).

In stabilised patients needing CABG, surgery can be timed around P2Y12 washout (ticagrelor 3 days, clopidogrel 5 days, prasugrel 7 days), bridging with cangrelor or a GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor only if very high thrombotic risk.

Culprit-first PCI with staged completion is the usual strategy when PCI is chosen.

CLINICAL APPROACH — SPECIAL POPULATIONS

Older/frail patients: apply the same diagnostic and invasive strategies, individualised to frailty, comorbidity and wishes; adjust doses (renal function, weight). The benefit of an invasive strategy persists in the elderly but bleeding rises.

CKD: same invasive strategy; minimise contrast (iso-osmolar/low-osmolar agents, hydration); doseadjust enoxaparin, fondaparinux and GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors. Diabetes: higher risk; invasive strategy favoured; check glucose; avoid hypoglycaemia; favour SGLT2i/ GLP-1 RA per diabetes guidelines.

Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest without STE: no routine immediate angiography in stable patients (COACT, TOMAHAWK).

Key highlightsInvasive strategy

  • Very high risk (shock, refractory pain, VT/VF, mechanical complication, ischaemic AHF, intermittent STE) → angiography < 2 h (I, C).
  • High risk (confirmed NSTEMI, dynamic ST/T, transient STE, GRACE > 140) → < 24 h (IIa, A).
  • Inpatient invasive strategy for high-risk NSTE-ACS is Class I, A; low risk → selective invasive after testing (I, A).
  • Very early angiography does not reduce mortality overall — benefit concentrates in high-risk patients.
  • Complete revascularisation in NSTE-ACS: ESC IIa, C versus ACC/AHA Class 1.
  • P2Y12 washout before CABG: ticagrelor 3, clopidogrel 5, prasugrel 7 days.

8.5 Antiplatelet Pharmacology

MECHANISM — THREE PATHWAYS OF PLATELET ACTIVATION

Platelets adhere to exposed collagen/vWF, then amplify their own activation through thromboxane A₂ (COX-1 pathway — blocked by aspirin), ADP acting on the P2Y12 receptor (blocked by thienopyridines and ticagrelor/cangrelor) and thrombin acting on PAR-1 (vorapaxar). All pathways converge on the GP IIb/IIIa receptor, which cross-links platelets via fibrinogen — the final common pathway blocked by GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors.

III A

Pre-treatment may be considered in NSTE-ACS not expected to undergo early (< 24 h) angiography, and in STEMI undergoing primary PCI.

  • IIb C / B
  • GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors for bail-out (no-reflow, thrombotic complication). IIa C
  • Pre-treatment with GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors when anatomy is unknown. III A

Cangrelor in P2Y12-naïve patients undergoing PCI. IIb A

EXAM TRAP

Stroke history decides the drug: prior stroke/TIA → no prasugrel; prior ICH → no ticagrelor (and no prasugrel). Ticagrelor dyspnoea is benign and non-bronchospastic — reassure or switch; it is not a sign of heart failure. When switching down from ticagrelor, a loading dose of clopidogrel 600 mg is given because ticagrelor's reversible binding offsets quickly.

Key highlightsAntiplatelet pharmacology

  • Aspirin LD 150–300 mg, MD 75–100 mg lifelong (I, A).
  • Clopidogrel: 2-step CYP2C19 prodrug; prasugrel: 1-step prodrug; ticagrelor and cangrelor: direct and reversible.
  • Prasugrel 60/10 mg (5 mg if ≥ 75 y or < 60 kg); contraindicated after stroke/TIA.
  • Ticagrelor 180/90 mg bd; 60 mg bd for extended therapy; dyspnoea, pauses, gout.
  • ESC: prasugrel preferred over ticagrelor in PCI-treated ACS (IIa, B — ISAR-REACT 5).
  • No routine P2Y12 pre-treatment in NSTE-ACS if angiography < 24 h (III, A); GP IIb/IIIa only for bail-out.
  • Cangrelor: onset ~2 min, offset < 1 h; load thienopyridines after the infusion ends.
  • De-escalation from ticagrelor to clopidogrel: 600 mg LD 24 h after last ticagrelor dose.

8.6 Parenteral Anticoagulants

Parenteral anticoagulation is recommended for all ACS patients at diagnosis (ESC: I, A) to limit thrombin generation until revascularisation; it is normally stopped immediately after uncomplicated PCI. The choice depends on timing of angiography, renal function and bleeding risk.

MECHANISM — WHY FONDAPARINUX NEEDS A UFH BOLUS IN THE CATH LAB

Fondaparinux inhibits only factor Xa. Catheters and guidewires activate the contact pathway and generate thrombin directly on foreign surfaces; without some anti-IIa activity, thrombus forms on the catheter (OASIS-5/-6). A standard UFH bolus at the time of PCI solves this — the reason fondaparinux is not used as the sole anticoagulant for primary PCI.

BOARD PEARL

OASIS-5 : fondaparinux vs enoxaparin in NSTE-ACS — similar ischaemic efficacy at 9 days, major bleeding almost halved, and lower 30-day and 6-month mortality. The benefit was driven by less bleeding — the proof that bleeding kills.

Key highlightsParenteral anticoagulants

  • Parenteral anticoagulation for all ACS at diagnosis (I, A); stop after uncomplicated PCI.
  • UFH at PCI 70–100 IU/kg (50–70 with GPI), ACT 250–350 s.
  • Fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily when angiography is not expected within 24 h (I, B); UFH bolus at PCI.
  • Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg bd; once daily if CrCl < 30; no UFH–LMWH crossover (III, B).
  • Bivalirudin: full-dose infusion up to 4 h after primary PCI; drug of choice in HIT.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • In HBR patients, aspirin or P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy after 1 month of DAPT may be considered. IIb B De-escalation of P2Y12 inhibitor (to clopidogrel) as an alternative DAPT strategy to reduce bleeding. IIb A De-escalation of antiplatelet therapy in the first 30 days after ACS. III B
  • Prolongation
  • Adding a second antithrombotic agent to aspirin for extended long-term secondary prevention in patients at high ischaemic risk without HBR.
  • IIa A
  • The same in patients at moderate ischaemic risk without HBR. IIb A
  • Gastroprotection
  • Proton pump inhibitor with combination antithrombotic therapy in patients at increased GI bleeding risk. I A

8.7 DAPT Duration, De-escalation & High Bleeding Risk

The default after ACS is 12 months of DAPT with a potent P2Y12 inhibitor. Contemporary DES have made stent thrombosis rare, so the modern debate is how to reduce bleeding without losing ischaemic protection — by shortening DAPT, dropping aspirin early, or de-escalating the P2Y12 inhibitor.

CLINICAL APPROACH — WHO IS "HIGH ISCHAEMIC RISK" ?

ESC 2023 risk enhancers favouring prolonged therapy: complex/diffuse multivessel CAD plus ≥ 1 of — diabetes requiring medication, recurrent MI, polyvascular disease (CAD + PAD), CKD (eGFR 15–59); also premature (< 45 y) or accelerated CAD, systemic inflammatory disease, and complex PCI (≥ 3 stents, ≥ 3 lesions, total stent length > 60 mm, bifurcation with 2 stents, left main, CTO, history of stent thrombosis on antiplatelets).

EXAM TRAP

Long-term clopidogrel monotherapy is at least as good as aspirin monotherapy (HOST-EXAM; ESC 2024 CCS: I, A as an alternative). A "P2Y12-inhibitor monotherapy" answer after short DAPT refers mostly to ticagrelor: early clopidogrel monotherapy after only 1 month in ACS failed non-inferiority (STOPDAPT-2 ACS).

8.8 Oral Anticoagulation plus Antiplatelets (AF + PCI) & Chronic Therapy

About 6–8% of patients undergoing PCI also need long-term oral anticoagulation — mostly for AF, less often for mechanical valves, LV thrombus or VTE. Triple therapy (OAC + aspirin + P2Y12) roughly doubles-totriples bleeding. The trials (WOEST, PIONEER AF-PCI, RE-DUAL PCI, AUGUSTUS, ENTRUST-AF PCI) converge on one rule: drop aspirin early and use a DOAC plus clopidogrel .

BOARD PEARL — AUGUSTUS IN ONE LINE

2 × 2 design: apixaban vs VKA → less bleeding with apixaban; aspirin vs placebo (on top of OAC + P2Y12) → aspirin increased bleeding with no significant reduction in ischaemic events (a small excess of stent thrombosis in the first 30 days without aspirin). Hence "triple therapy up to 1 week, longer only if thrombotic risk is high".

Key highlightsDAPT & HBR

  • Default DAPT after ACS: 12 months (I, A).
  • Event-free at 3–6 months, not high ischaemic risk: SAPT, preferably P2Y12 (IIa, A).
  • HBR: monotherapy after 1 month DAPT (ESC IIb, B); ACC/AHA: ticagrelor monotherapy after ≥ 1 month is Class De-escalation to clopidogrel: IIb, A — but never in the first 30 days (III, B).
  • High ischaemic risk, no HBR, beyond 12 months: ticagrelor 60 mg bd or rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd + aspirin (IIa, A).
  • PPI with combination antithrombotics if GI bleeding risk (I, A); prefer pantoprazole with clopidogrel.

Elective PCI, HBR DAPT shortened to 1–3 months, then single antiplatelet

High ischaemic risk, no HBR Add rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd (COMPASS) or ticagrelor 60 mg bd (post-MI, PEGASUS) to aspirin (IIa, A)

DON'T CONFUSE — DUAL ANTIPLATELET VS DUAL PATHWAY

DAPT = aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (two platelet pathways). Dual pathway inhibition (DPI) = aspirin + rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd ("vascular dose", COMPASS) — targets platelets and thrombin generation; benefit greatest in polyvascular disease, diabetes, CKD. The vascular dose is not an AF stroke-prevention dose.

CLINICAL APPROACH — NON-CARDIAC SURGERY ON ANTIPLATELET THERAPY

Defer elective surgery until DAPT is complete: ideally 6 months after elective PCI and 12 months after ACS; time-sensitive surgery may be considered after at least 1 month (elective PCI) / 3 months (ACS). Continue aspirin peri-operatively when bleeding risk allows; interrupt P2Y12 inhibitors (ticagrelor 3–5, clopidogrel 5, prasugrel 7 days) and resume within 24–48 h.

Very high thrombotic risk: bridging with cangrelor or a short-acting GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor in a PCIcapable centre.

8.9 Secondary Prevention after ACS

The drugs that change prognosis after MI — statin-based lipid lowering, beta-blocker when LVEF is reduced, RAAS inhibition, MRA — are detailed in Chapter 7 (7.8). The board also tests the targets and the lifestyle and system measures, which together halve recurrent events.

Key highlightsOAC + antiplatelets & chronic therapy

  • AF + PCI: DOAC preferred over VKA (I, A); aspirin stopped within ≤ 1 week; OAC + clopidogrel to 12 months (ACS) or 6 months (CCS).
  • High stent-thrombosis risk: triple therapy up to 1 month (IIa, C); HBR: stop antiplatelet at 6 months (IIa, B).
  • Never prasugrel or ticagrelor in triple therapy (III, C).
  • ACC/AHA 2025: stop aspirin at 1–4 weeks, continue OAC + clopidogrel (Class 1).
  • Beyond 12 months: OAC monotherapy (AFIRE, EPIC-CAD).
  • CCS: elective PCI → DAPT 6 months; clopidogrel is an alternative to aspirin for lifelong SAPT (I, A).
  • Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd + aspirin (COMPASS) = dual pathway inhibition for high ischaemic risk without HBR.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2025–2026

ESC/EAS 2025 dyslipidaemia update: intensify lipid lowering during the ACS admission if already on therapy (I, C); in-hospital statin + ezetimibe for treatment-naïve patients unlikely to reach goal on statin alone (IIa, B); bempedoic acid recommended for statin-intolerant patients not at goal. ACC/AHA 2025 ACS: add non-statin therapy if LDL-C ≥ 70 mg/dL (Class 1) and consider it at 55–69 mg/dL (2a); lipid panel at 4–8 weeks; cardiac rehabilitation before discharge (Class 1) with homebased option (2a). ESC 2026: first dedicated guideline on cardiac rehabilitation — every post-ACS patient should be referred.

EXAM TRAP

NSAIDs (other than low-dose aspirin) should be avoided after ACS — they increase bleeding with antithrombotics and increase recurrent MI and HF. Hormone replacement therapy is not used for secondary prevention. Vitamin supplements and omega-3 fatty acid mixtures do not reduce events (icosapent ethyl is the exception in selected hypertriglyceridaemic patients).

Key highlightsSecondary prevention

  • LDL-C < 55 mg/dL and ≥ 50% reduction (ESC); < 40 mg/dL after recurrent event within 2 years.
  • Office SBP 120–129 mmHg if tolerated (ESC 2024).
  • HbA1c < 7%; SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA with proven CV benefit in diabetes.
  • Exercise 150–300 min/week moderate intensity; comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation (I, A).
  • Annual influenza vaccination (I, A); smoking cessation drugs are safe after ACS.
  • Lp(a) > 50 mg/dL is a risk enhancer; avoid NSAIDs.

8.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 49-year-old man presents 6 h after 30 min of chest tightness, now resolved. The ECG is normal. hs-cTnT (Elecsys) at presentation is 3 ng/L. What is the most appropriate next step according to the ESC 0 h/1 h algorithm?

Answer B A single very low hs-cTnT (< 5 ng/L) with chest pain onset > 3 h earlier rules out MI (NPV > 99.5%). A 1-h sample is needed only if the pain began < 3 h ago or the 0-h value is not very low. Rule-out does not exclude CAD — outpatient assessment follows.

Q2 A 66-year-old woman with suspected NSTE-ACS has hs-cTnT of 20 ng/L at 0 h and 22 ng/L at 1 h. The ECG shows non-specific T-wave flattening. What is the recommended next step?

Answer C 0 h of 20 ng/L is above the rule-out threshold (< 12) but below rule-in (≥ 52), and Δ1h of 2 is below the rule-in delta (≥ 5): the observe zone. ESC recommends a third sample at 3 h (I, B) with echo; copeptin adds nothing routinely (III).

Q3 A 71-year-old man with NSTEMI has recurrent chest pain despite IV nitrates and beta-blocker, with dynamic 2 mm ST depression in V3–V6. BP 125/75 mmHg. What is the recommended timing of angiography?

Answer A Recurrent/refractory chest pain despite medical treatment is a very-high-risk criterion → immediate invasive strategy < 2 h (I, C), regardless of normal BP. < 24 h is for high-risk (e.g. GRACE > 140) stable patients.

Q4 A 63-year-old man with a lacunar ischaemic stroke 2 years ago undergoes PCI for NSTEMI. Which P2Y12 inhibitor is most appropriate?

Answer C Any prior stroke/TIA contraindicates prasugrel at any dose (TRITON net harm). Ticagrelor is permitted after ischaemic stroke (not after ICH). Clopidogrel would be used only if potent agents are contraindicated.

Q5 A 58-year-old man is admitted overnight with NSTEMI (GRACE 128); angiography is scheduled for the next morning. He has received aspirin. What should be done about P2Y12 inhibition?

Answer D When angiography is planned within 24 h in NSTE-ACS, routine P2Y12 pre-treatment is Class III, A (ACCOAST, ISARREACT 5, DUBIUS): no ischaemic benefit, more bleeding, and it complicates urgent CABG. Load at the time of PCI. GP IIb/IIIa pre-treatment is also Class III.

Q6 A patient with NSTE-ACS has been on fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily for 36 h and now goes to the cath lab for PCI. What is required?

Answer C Fondaparinux inhibits only Xa; catheter thrombosis occurred without additional anti-IIa cover (OASIS-5/6). A standard UFH bolus at PCI is mandatory. Switching to enoxaparin (crossover) adds bleeding; GPIs are for bail-out only.

Q7 A 74-year-old woman with permanent AF (CHA₂DS₂-VA 4) undergoes uncomplicated PCI for NSTEMI. Bleeding risk is moderate; stent-thrombosis risk is not high. Which regimen is recommended after discharge?

Answer C Default after ACS-PCI in AF: DOAC (preferred over VKA) + clopidogrel with aspirin stopped within ≤ 1 week, continued up to 12 months, then OAC alone. Ticagrelor/prasugrel in triple therapy is Class III; OAC alone from discharge leaves the new stent unprotected.

Q8 Which patient meets the ARC-HBR definition of high bleeding risk?

Answer B Hb < 11 g/dL is a major ARC-HBR criterion (one major suffices). Age ≥ 75, chronic NSAID use and eGFR 30–59 are minor criteria and need two; eGFR 65–70 is not a criterion; a remote TIA is not a criterion.

Q9 A 57-year-old man completed 12 months of aspirin + ticagrelor after anterior STEMI without bleeding. He has diabetes on insulin, PAD and eGFR 52 mL/min. What is the most appropriate long-term antithrombotic strategy?

Answer B Diffuse CAD with insulin-treated diabetes, PAD (polyvascular) and CKD = high ischaemic risk without HBR → add a second antithrombotic to aspirin long term (IIa, A): ticagrelor 60 mg bd (PEGASUS) or rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd (COMPASS). Rivaroxaban 20 mg is an AF dose; prasugrel is not used for extended therapy.

Q10 Three weeks after PCI for NSTEMI, a patient on aspirin + ticagrelor wants to reduce bleeding risk; he has had troublesome epistaxis. He is not HBR by ARC criteria. According to the ACC/AHA 2025 guideline, which step is supported by a Class 1 recommendation once he reaches 1 month?

Answer B ACC/AHA 2025 gives a Class 1 recommendation to transition to ticagrelor monotherapy ≥ 1 month after PCI in patients who tolerate DAPT, to reduce bleeding (TWILIGHT, TICO, ULTIMATE-DAPT). ESC 2023 is more conservative (SAPT after 3–6 months, IIa; after 1 month only in HBR, IIb). Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg is never given without aspirin.

9.1 Invasive Coronary Angiography

Invasive coronary angiography (ICA) remains the reference standard for coronary anatomy, but in chronic coronary syndromes it is no longer a diagnostic first step for most patients — it is performed when the result is likely to lead to revascularisation. In CCS, ICA should be accompanied by the ability to measure physiology; a stenosis on an angiogram is a picture, not a verdict.

  • symptoms refractory to GDMT
  • ICA as first test (Class I C) with a view to revascularisation
  • High event risk on non-invasive testing Ischaemia ≥ 10%, LM/3VD on CCTA, DTS < −10
  • Inconclusive or discordant non-invasive
  • tests
  • ICA with invasive functional assessment
  • New LV dysfunction/HF with suspected
  • CAD; survived cardiac arrest/VT
  • Define ischaemic aetiology
  • Before valve or other cardiac surgery CCTA acceptable when likelihood is lower
  • Persistent angina with non-obstructive
  • CAD
  • ICA + invasive coronary function testing (Chapter 6)
Relative contraindications (none absolute)
  • Acute kidney injury; decompensated HF
  • Uncontrolled hypertension, fever/active
  • infection
  • Active bleeding, severe coagulopathy (INR > 1.8
  • for femoral)
  • Severe hypokalaemia, digoxin toxicity

  • premedication
  • Patient unwilling to consider revascularisation
Complications of diagnostic ICA
  • Death ~0.1% (higher with LM disease, severe AS,
  • LVEF < 30%)
  • MI ~0.05%; stroke ~0.07%
  • Arrhythmia ~0.4% — VF from deep RCA/conus
  • injection
  • Vascular ~0.4%; contrast reaction ~0.4%
  • Major complications overall < 2%

Access: radial first

Transradial access reduces access-site bleeding and vascular complications; in ACS it also reduces mortality (RIVAL in STEMI subgroup, RIFLE-STEACS, MATRIX). It is Class I A in ESC 2024 (preferred access for ICA) and ACC/AHA/SCAI 2021 (both ACS and stable disease).

EXAM TRAP — RETROPERITONEAL HAEMORRHAGE

Hypotension and bradycardia/tachycardia with flank or back pain after femoral access, no visible groin haematoma, falling haemoglobin: suspect a high puncture (above the inguinal ligament) with retroperitoneal bleeding. Next step: fluids/blood, reverse anticoagulation as appropriate, non-contrast CT (if stable) and endovascular balloon tamponade or covered stent if ongoing bleeding.

Reading the angiogram

Dominance: right-dominant (PDA from RCA) in ~80–85%; left-dominant ~7–10%; codominant the rest. Visual estimation over-calls moderate and under-calls diffuse disease; it correlates poorly with physiology in 40–70% lesions — hence FFR/iFR.

TIMI flow grade: 0 no antegrade flow beyond occlusion · 1 penetration without distal filling · 2 slow but complete filling · 3 normal. TIMI frame count and myocardial blush grade quantify microvascular perfusion.

SYNTAX score integrates lesion number, location, dominance and complexity (occlusion, bifurcation, calcium, length, thrombus) — see 9.4.

9.2 Coronary Physiology — FFR, iFR, QFR

DEFINITIONS

Fractional flow reserve (FFR) = Pd / Pa during maximal hyperaemia (IV adenosine 140 µg/kg/min or IC bolus). Because microvascular resistance is minimal and constant at hyperaemia, the pressure ratio equals the ratio of maximal flow with the stenosis to the maximal flow if the artery were normal.

Normal = 1.0.

Non-hyperaemic pressure ratios (NHPR) — iFR (wave-free period of diastole), RFR, dPR, resting Pd/Pa — need no adenosine.

QFR / angiography-derived FFR — computed from two angiographic projections, no wire.

CFR = hyperaemic / resting flow — reflects epicardial and microvascular function; IMR isolates the microcirculation (Chapter 6).

Key highlightsInvasive angiography

  • In CCS, ICA is for very high likelihood (> 85%), refractory or low-threshold angina, high-risk non-invasive results, or inconclusive testing.
  • Diagnostic ICA: mortality ~0.1%; major complications < 2%.
  • Radial access is Class I A (ESC 2024, ACC 2021); reduces bleeding, and mortality in ACS.
  • Radial occlusion is prevented with heparin (~5000 U) and patent haemostasis.
  • Retroperitoneal bleed: shock without groin haematoma after high femoral puncture.
  • Right dominance in ~80–85%; visual stenosis correlates poorly with physiology.
  • Index
  • Significant
  • if Evidence / notes
  • FFR ≤ 0.80 DEFER, FAME, FAME 2; 0.75–0.80 is a grey zone (below 0.75 nearly always ischaemic) iFR ≤ 0.89 Non-inferior to FFR for guiding PCI (DEFINE-FLAIR, iFR-SWEDEHEART); fewer symptoms, shorter procedures
  • RFR / dPR ≤ 0.89 Equivalent diastolic resting ratios
  • Resting Pd/
  • Pa
  • ≤ 0.91 Whole-cycle resting ratio
  • QFR ≤ 0.80 FAVOR III China: QFR-guided PCI better than angiography-guided
  • FFR-CT ≤ 0.80 Non-invasive, from CCTA (Chapter 6)
  • CFR < 2.0 Epicardial stenosis and/or microvascular dysfunction

NEW …or with QFR (≤ 0.80). I B

Pressure measurement (FFR/iFR) or computation (QFR) to guide lesion selection in multivessel disease. I A CFR (or related flow indices) as a complementary investigation. IIa B

  • Resting Pd/Pa, dPR, RFR or angiography-derived vessel FFR as alternatives. IIb C
  • NEW Systematic, routine wire-based pressure assessment of all coronary vessels. III A

ACC/AHA/SCAI 2021: FFR or iFR to guide PCI of intermediate stenoses without documented ischaemia — Class 1 (A); PCI should not be performed when FFR > 0.80 or iFR > 0.89 in SIHD — Class 3: No benefit (B-R).

MECHANISM — WHY PHYSIOLOGY BEATS THE EYE

The haemodynamic effect of a stenosis depends on its length, entry/exit angles, the mass of myocardium it supplies, and collaterals — none visible as "percent diameter". A 60% proximal LAD lesion supplying a large territory can be ischaemic (FFR 0.70) while a 70% lesion in a small branch, or in a territory already infarcted, may not be (FFR 0.85). FFR measures the flow lost; the angiogram measures the shadow.

BOARD PEARL

FFR is independent of heart rate, BP and contractility (it is a ratio at maximal hyperaemia) and has a theoretical normal of 1.0 in every artery and every patient — that is why a single cut-off works. Adenosine side-effects (flushing, dyspnoea, chest tightness, transient AV block) are expected; iFR avoids them.

Key highlightsCoronary physiology

  • FFR = Pd/Pa at maximal hyperaemia; significant ≤ 0.80 (grey zone 0.75–0.80).
  • iFR, RFR, dPR significant at ≤ 0.89; resting Pd/Pa ≤ 0.91; QFR ≤ 0.80.
  • ESC 2024: pressure wire for intermediate non-LM lesions (I A); QFR (I B); routine wiring of all vessels (III A).
  • ACC 2021: do not stent SIHD lesions with FFR > 0.80 / iFR > 0.89 (3: No benefit).
  • FFR falsely high: microvascular dysfunction, prior infarct in territory, downstream disease behind a LM lesion.
  • Serial/diffuse disease: use pull-back; a gradual pressure loss predicts poor PCI results.
  • FAME: FFR guidance ↓ events; FAME 2: PCI of FFR-positive lesions ↓ urgent revascularisation.

9.3 Intravascular Imaging — IVUS & OCT

Intravascular imaging (IVI) answers three questions the angiogram cannot: how big is the vessel (for sizing), what is the plaque (calcium, lipid, thrombus — for lesion preparation) and how good is the result (expansion, apposition, edge dissection — for optimisation). Meta-analyses and trials (IVUS-XPL, ULTIMATE, RENOVATE-COMPLEX-PCI, OCTOBER) show fewer target-vessel failures, stent thromboses and cardiac deaths with IVI-guided PCI, especially in complex lesions.

Recommendation Class Level

IVUS for procedural guidance, particularly LM or complex lesions, to reduce ischaemic events. IIa B OCT as a reasonable alternative to IVUS for procedural guidance — except in ostial left main. IIa B IVUS to define severity of intermediate left main stenosis. IIa B

WHAT CHANGED IN 2024

IVI guidance for complex PCI moved from Class IIa (ESC 2018: IVUS/OCT "should be considered" to optimise stenting in selected patients) to Class I A in ESC 2024, driven by RENOVATE-COMPLEX-PCI, OCTOBER and network meta-analyses showing lower cardiac death and stent thrombosis.

DON'T CONFUSE — STENT FAILURE MECHANISMS ON IMAGING

Under-expansion (MSA too small for the vessel) — commonest mechanical cause of both restenosis and early thrombosis; fixed with high-pressure non-compliant balloon (± calcium modification). Malapposition (struts not touching the wall; stent may be well expanded) — acute (under-sizing) or late acquired (positive remodelling, thrombus resolution).

Neointimal hyperplasia — homogeneous tissue inside a well-expanded stent (restenosis).

Neoatherosclerosis — lipid-laden, calcified or ruptured tissue within the stent, usually > 1 year; OCT is best to detect it.

Key highlightsIntravascular imaging

  • OCT: ~10× resolution, 1–2 mm penetration, needs contrast; IVUS: 5–6 mm penetration, no contrast, best for ostial LM and CKD.
  • LM IVUS MLA < 6 mm² = significant (Western); non-LM MLA is a poor decision tool — use physiology.
  • Optimal stent: MSA > 5.5 mm² IVUS / > 4.5 mm² OCT and > 80–90% of reference.
  • LM targets "5-6-7-8 mm²" (LCx, LAD, POC, proximal LM).
  • Treat edge dissection ≥ 60°/≥ 3 mm/medial; malapposition matters if > 0.4 mm and > 1 mm long.
  • ESC 2024: IVI guidance for LM, true bifurcation and long lesions — Class I A; ACC 2021: 2a.
  • Calcium "rule of 5" (> 180°, > 0.5 mm, > 5 mm) → plaque modification before stenting.
  • Tertiles: low ≤ 22 · intermediate 23–32 · high ≥ 33. It predicts outcome after PCI far more than after CABG — the essence of "complex disease → surgery".
  • SYNTAX Score II / 2020 add clinical variables (age, creatinine clearance, LVEF, LM, PAD, COPD, diabetes…) to predict individual long-term mortality with each strategy.

9.4 PCI versus CABG — the Heart Team Decision

Once revascularisation is indicated (Chapter 6), the mode is chosen by the Heart Team — interventional cardiologist, cardiac surgeon and non-invasive cardiologist — with the patient. The decision integrates anatomical complexity (SYNTAX score), diabetes, LV function, surgical risk (STS score, EuroSCORE II), the likelihood of complete revascularisation, and patient preference.

The SYNTAX score

Angiographic score summing every lesion ≥ 50% in vessels ≥ 1.5 mm, weighted by the myocardium supplied (dominance-dependent) and adverse features: total occlusion (> 3 months = CTO), bifurcation/ trifurcation, aorto-ostial, severe tortuosity, length > 20 mm, heavy calcification, thrombus, diffuse/ small-vessel disease.

MECHANISM — COMPLETENESS MATTERS

Complete revascularisation = treatment of all functionally significant stenoses in vessels ≥ 1.5 mm supplying viable myocardium. Residual SYNTAX score > 8 after PCI predicts higher mortality. CABG more often achieves it in diffuse disease and CTOs; hybrid revascularisation (LIMA–LAD, often minimally invasive, plus PCI of non-LAD vessels) combines the survival benefit of the arterial graft with the avoidance of vein grafts.

Key highlightsPCI vs CABG

  • SYNTAX tertiles: ≤ 22 low, 23–32 intermediate, ≥ 33 high; it predicts PCI (not CABG) outcomes.
  • LM: CABG preferred (ESC I A); PCI alternative if SYNTAX ≤ 22 (I A), considered if 23–32 (IIa A).
  • Diabetes + MVD: CABG (FREEDOM) — ESC I A, ACC 1 A.
  • LVEF ≤ 35%: CABG (STICHES) — ESC I B, ACC 1 B-R.
  • EXCEL/NOBLE: LM PCI matches CABG early but has more repeat revascularisation and MI later.
  • FAME 3: FFR-guided PCI not non-inferior to CABG in 3VD.
  • Complete revascularisation (vessels ≥ 1.5 mm) is the goal; hybrid = LIMA–LAD + PCI elsewhere.

9.5 CABG — Conduits & Surgical Principles

The survival benefit of CABG is largely the benefit of the left internal mammary (thoracic) artery to the LAD. The IMA is an elastic artery with an intact internal elastic lamina and endothelium that produces abundant nitric oxide, so it almost never develops atherosclerosis.

Pre-operative β-blocker to reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation. IIa B

ACC levels: IMA–LAD B-NR; radial artery B-R; BIMA B-NR; β-blocker B-R. The 2018 ESC/EACTS document remains the current ESC reference for surgical technique; revascularisation indications were updated in ESC 2024.

CLINICAL APPROACH — ANGINA AFTER CABG

Measure BP in both arms: a gradient suggests subclavian stenosis stealing flow from the LIMA (coronary–subclavian steal) → subclavian stenting.

Early (< 30 days) ischaemia → graft failure until proven otherwise → urgent angiography. Late: native-vessel PCI is preferred over PCI of a degenerated SVG; redo CABG favoured when there is no patent IMA to the LAD. If considered safe, PCI is the first choice over redo CABG (ESC 2018 IIa C).

BOARD PEARL

Off-pump CABG does not reduce death or stroke overall and may reduce graft patency; its clearest indication is a calcified/porcelain ascending aorta, where a no-touch technique avoids aortic cross-clamping.

Postoperative AF occurs in ~20–40% of patients.

Key highlightsCABG

  • LIMA–LAD patency > 90% at 10 y; SVG ~50–60%.
  • Radial artery over SVG for the second target with a high-grade stenosis — ESC I B, ACC 1 B-R.
  • Competitive flow (non-severe native stenosis) causes arterial graft atrophy ("string sign").
  • Skeletonised IMA in high sternal-infection risk (obese diabetics) — ESC I B.
  • Porcelain aorta → off-pump, no-touch technique (I B).
  • Angina after CABG: check both-arm BPs (subclavian steal); prefer native-vessel PCI over SVG PCI.

9.6 Stent Thrombosis & Restenosis

Stent thrombosis (ST)

Stent thrombosis is sudden thrombotic occlusion of a stented segment. It usually presents as STEMI or sudden death and carries high early mortality (typically quoted at 10–25%). With current-generation DES and appropriate DAPT, definite/probable ST is ~0.5–1% at one year — lower than with bare-metal or first-generation drug-eluting stents.

ARC certainty
  • Definite — angiographic or pathological
  • confirmation
  • Probable — unexplained death ≤ 30 days, or MI
  • in the stented territory without angiographic
  • confirmation
  • Possible — unexplained death > 30 days
Timing
  • Acute: < 24 h
  • Subacute: 24 h–30 days
  • Late: 30 days–1 year

Very late: > 1 year

CLINICAL APPROACH — SUSPECTED STENT THROMBOSIS

Treat as STEMI: immediate primary PCI (thrombus aspiration selectively, high-pressure balloon). Use intravascular imaging to identify the mechanism (under-expansion, malapposition, edge dissection, neoatherosclerosis) and correct it.

Check adherence; switch clopidogrel to ticagrelor or prasugrel; consider GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor for heavy thrombus.

In-stent restenosis (ISR)

Restenosis is gradual lumen re-narrowing (angiographic ≥ 50%), usually presenting as recurrent stable angina between 3–12 months; roughly ~10% present as ACS (usually NSTEMI).

9.7 Procedural Complications & Contrast-Associated AKI

Contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI)

DEFINITION

Rise in serum creatinine ≥ 0.5 mg/dL (44 µmol/L) or ≥ 25% from baseline within 48–72 h of intravascular contrast, without another cause. (KDIGO AKI: ↑ ≥ 0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or ≥ 1.5× baseline within 7 days.) Creatinine peaks at 2–5 days and usually returns to baseline in 1–3 weeks; a minority need dialysis.

Risk factors (Mehran score)
  • Pre-existing CKD — eGFR < 60, especially < 30
  • (the key factor)
  • Diabetes with CKD
  • Hypotension, IABP/shock, HF (LVEF < 40%),
  • anaemia
  • Age > 75
  • High contrast volume; repeated exposure within
  • 72 h
Ineffective strategies
  • N-acetylcysteine — no benefit (PRESERVE)
  • Sodium bicarbonate over saline — no benefit
  • (PRESERVE)
  • Prophylactic haemodialysis — not recommended
  • Routine withholding of ACE-I/diuretics —
  • unproven

Key highlightsStent failure

  • ST timing: acute < 24 h, subacute to 30 d, late to 1 y, very late > 1 y.
  • Premature DAPT cessation is the strongest early predictor; under-expansion the key mechanical one.
  • ST presents as STEMI with high mortality — primary PCI plus imaging to fix the cause.
  • Clinical restenosis: balloon 20–30%, BMS 10–20%, DES 3–5%.
  • Balloon restenosis = negative remodelling; stent restenosis = neointimal hyperplasia.
  • ISR: image first; treat with DES or drug-coated balloon; neoatherosclerosis explains very late failures.
  • Measure Detail
  • Contrast Low- or iso-osmolar agents; minimise volume — contrast volume/eGFR ratio < 3.7 (or total < 2–3 × eGFR); biplane, IVUS-guided "zero-contrast" PCI in advanced CKD
  • Drugs High-intensity statin pre-treatment in statin-naïve patients; withhold metformin at the time of contrast if eGFR < 30 (or AKI) and restart after 48 h if renal function is stable
  • Monitoring Creatinine at 48–72 h in high-risk patients
  • ACC/AHA/SCAI 2021: in patients undergoing cardiac catheterisation with contrast, measures should be taken to minimise the risk of contrast-induced AKI — Class 1 (C-LD).
DON'T CONFUSE — CA-AKI VS CHOLESTEROL ATHEROEMBOLISM
  • CA-AKI Atheroembolic renal disease
  • Onset 24–72 h Days to weeks, often stepwise
  • Course Usually recovers in
  • 1–3 weeks
  • Often progressive, may be irreversible
  • Clues None beyond
  • creatinine
  • Livedo reticularis, blue toes, eosinophilia, eosinophiluria, low
  • complement, retinal Hollenhorst plaques

Coronary complications of PCI

9.8 Antithrombotic Therapy Around Revascularisation

Detailed DAPT algorithms, bleeding-risk scores and ACS regimens are covered in Chapter 8. For elective PCI and CABG in chronic coronary disease the examinable essentials are:

(thrombus, no-reflow)

After PCI — default Aspirin + clopidogrel 6 months → single antiplatelet lifelong (aspirin or clopidogrel) High bleeding risk DAPT 1–3 months → single antiplatelet (P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy acceptable) High thrombotic risk

  • (complex LM, bifurcation,
  • CTO, prior ST)
  • Prasugrel or ticagrelor may be used initially; prolonged DAPT if bleeding risk low

AF with PCI Triple therapy (OAC + aspirin + clopidogrel) usually ≤ 1 week → OAC + clopidogrel (up to 6 months in CCS) → OAC alone; DOAC preferred; ticagrelor/prasugrel not in triple therapy

Key highlightsComplications & CA-AKI

  • CA-AKI: creatinine ↑ ≥ 0.5 mg/dL or ≥ 25% at 48–72 h; the main risk factor is pre-existing CKD.
  • Prevention: isotonic saline hydration, low/iso-osmolar contrast, minimal volume (contrast/eGFR < 3.7), statin; NAC and bicarbonate do not work.
  • Atheroembolism: delayed renal failure with livedo, blue toes and eosinophilia.
  • Ellis III perforation: balloon tamponade + covered stent + pericardiocentesis.
  • No-reflow: IC adenosine, verapamil or nitroprusside; embolic protection for SVG.
  • Pseudoaneurysm = systolic bruit, thrombin injection; AV fistula = continuous bruit, often self-closes.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Continue aspirin up to the time of CABG to reduce ischaemic events. I B
  • Urgent CABG: discontinue clopidogrel and ticagrelor for at least 24 h to reduce major bleeding. I B ACC levels: aspirin B-R; P2Y12 discontinuation B-NR. For elective CABG the conventional stopping intervals are ticagrelor 3 days, clopidogrel 5 days, prasugrel 7 days (ESC).
EXAM TRAP

A patient 3 weeks after DES asks to stop clopidogrel for dental extraction. The answer is no — premature DAPT interruption is the strongest risk factor for early stent thrombosis. Dental work proceeds on DAPT with local haemostasis; elective non-cardiac surgery requiring P2Y12 cessation is ideally postponed until at least 6 months after elective PCI (12 months after ACS).

Key highlightsAntithrombotic therapy

  • Elective PCI: clopidogrel 600 mg load; UFH 70–100 U/kg.
  • DAPT 6 months after elective PCI; 1–3 months if high bleeding risk (details: Chapter 8).
  • AF + PCI: triple therapy ≤ 1 week, then OAC + clopidogrel, then OAC alone.
  • Before CABG: continue aspirin; stop ticagrelor 3 d, clopidogrel 5 d, prasugrel 7 d; ≥ 24 h if urgent.
  • Never interrupt DAPT early for minor procedures.
  • ACC/AHA/SCAI 2021: benefit of CTO PCI for symptoms after treatment of non-CTO lesions is uncertain (2b B-R).
  • Calcified lesions

9.9 Complex & High-Risk PCI

The board does not examine technique, but it does expect you to recognise complex lesion subsets, the principle behind each strategy and the evidence for when to intervene.

Bifurcation lesions

Medina classification — three digits for proximal main branch, distal main branch and side branch (1 = ≥ 50% stenosis). True bifurcation = significant disease in both main branch and side branch: 1,1,1 · 1,0,1 · 0,1,1.

Provisional stenting (stent the main branch, treat the side branch only if compromised) is the default strategy.

A planned two-stent technique is reasonable for a large side branch with long ostial disease — e.g. double-kissing (DK) crush in complex true LM bifurcations (DKCRUSH-V).

Proximal optimisation (POT) and imaging guidance (OCTOBER: OCT-guided bifurcation PCI ↓ MACE) improve results.

Chronic total occlusions (CTO)

Definition: TIMI 0 flow for ≥ 3 months; present in ~15–25% of diagnostic angiograms in CAD. Collaterals preserve viability but usually provide only the flow of a severe stenosis — ischaemia on exertion is the rule.

Success in expert hands ~85–90% (antegrade wiring, dissection–re-entry, retrograde via collaterals); higher perforation/tamponade risk than conventional PCI.

Evidence: EuroCTO improved angina/QoL; DECISION-CTO showed no reduction in hard events. CTO PCI is for symptoms (or a large ischaemic territory) refractory to medical therapy — not for prognosis.

EXAM TRAP

Never implant a stent across a lesion where the balloon has not fully expanded — an under-expanded stent in calcium cannot be rescued reliably and predisposes to restenosis and stent thrombosis. Prepare the lesion first.

Saphenous vein graft PCI

Friable degenerated plaque → distal embolisation and no-reflow; use distal embolic protection (filter) where feasible.

Prefer PCI of the native vessel (including CTO) over a degenerated SVG; DES in SVG does not clearly outperform BMS long-term.

High-risk PCI and mechanical circulatory support

CHIP (complex, higher-risk and indicated patients) combines complex anatomy (unprotected LM, last remaining vessel, heavy calcium, CTO), poor LV function and comorbidity. Options include IABP (BCIS-1: no reduction in early MACCE) and microaxial flow pumps (PROTECT II: no significant reduction in the primary endpoint). ACC/AHA/SCAI 2021: elective MCS insertion as an adjunct to high-risk PCI may be reasonable in selected patients (2b B-R). REVIVED-BCIS2 reminds us that PCI in severe LV dysfunction does not improve survival — the indication must be symptoms or a clear Heart Team decision.

BOARD PEARL

Drug-coated balloons (DCB) deliver antiproliferative drug without leaving metal: established for in-stent restenosis and effective in small vessels (< 3 mm; BASKET-SMALL 2) with only ~1 month of DAPT in that trial — attractive when bleeding risk is high.

Key highlightsComplex PCI

  • Medina: proximal MB, distal MB, SB; true bifurcation = 1,1,1 / 1,0,1 / 0,1,1.
  • Provisional stenting is default; DK-crush for complex true LM bifurcation.
  • CTO = TIMI 0 for ≥ 3 months; CTO PCI is for symptoms (EuroCTO), not hard outcomes (DECISION-CTO).
  • Heavy calcium: prepare with atherectomy or IVL; never stent an undilatable lesion.
  • SVG PCI: embolic protection; native-vessel PCI preferred.
  • Elective MCS for high-risk PCI: ACC 2b B-R.

9.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 60-year-old man with stable angina has a 60% mid-LAD stenosis. iFR is 0.91 and FFR 0.84. He is on two antianginals with occasional angina. What is the most appropriate management of this lesion?

Answer B Both indices are above the ischaemic thresholds (iFR > 0.89, FFR > 0.80): stenting is not beneficial (ACC 2021 Class 3: No benefit; DEFER/FAME). Non-LM IVUS area is a poor decision tool; symptoms are controlled.

Q2 A left main stenosis appears intermediate on angiography; there is also a severe proximal LAD stenosis. The LM FFR measured with the wire in the LCx is 0.84. Which statement is correct?

Answer B Severe downstream disease limits hyperaemic flow through the LM, so LM FFR is falsely high (serial-lesion concept). IVUS MLA assesses LM severity independently (ACC 2a). The guide must be disengaged during measurement.

Q3 Intravascular ultrasound of an isolated ostial–mid left main shows a minimal lumen area of 5.1 mm² in a 65-yearold European patient with exertional angina. The best interpretation is: Non-significant — defer

Answer B In Western patients LM MLA < 6 mm² correlates with FFR ≤ 0.80 and indicates significant disease (deferral is safe at ≥ 6 mm²). The 4 mm² cut-off applies to non-LM vessels; OCT is poor for the ostial LM.

Q4 After IVUS-guided stenting of a proximal LAD lesion, the minimal stent area is 4.6 mm²; the mean reference lumen area is 8.0 mm²; there is no edge dissection. The next step is:

Answer B Relative expansion is only ~58% (4.6/8.0) — well below the > 80–90% target — and the IVUS absolute target is > 5.5 mm² (4.5 mm² is the OCT threshold). Under-expansion is fixed with a high-pressure non-compliant balloon, not another stent.

Q5 A 62-year-old woman with insulin-treated diabetes, LVEF 50% and three-vessel disease involving the proximal LAD (SYNTAX 26) has angina despite therapy. EuroSCORE II is 1.8%. What is the recommended revascularisation strategy?

Answer B Diabetes with multivessel disease involving the LAD and acceptable surgical risk: CABG with LIMA–LAD (ESC 2024 I A; ACC 2021 1 A; FREEDOM). PCI is reserved for very high surgical risk.

Q6 A 71-year-old non-diabetic man has isolated distal left main bifurcation disease with SYNTAX 18, LVEF 55% and moderate COPD. According to ESC 2024, which option is correct?

Answer C Low-complexity LM (SYNTAX ≤ 22): PCI is a Class I A alternative to CABG when completeness equals surgery (ESC 2024); CABG remains the overall preferred mode. ISCHEMIA excluded LM disease.

Q7 Twelve days after elective DES implantation a patient stopped clopidogrel on his own. He presents with anterior STEMI. Angiography confirms thrombotic occlusion within the stent. This event is best classified as: Acute stent thrombosis

Answer B Subacute = 24 h–30 days; angiographic confirmation makes it "definite" (ARC). Premature DAPT discontinuation is the strongest early risk factor.

Q8 A 74-year-old diabetic with eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m² needs coronary angiography. Which measure has proven benefit in preventing contrast-associated AKI?

Answer C Hydration with isotonic saline and minimal volumes of low/iso-osmolar contrast are the evidence-based measures. PRESERVE showed no benefit of NAC or bicarbonate; prophylactic dialysis is not recommended; statins, if anything, are protective.

Q9 Eight years after CABG (LIMA–LAD, SVG–OM, SVG–RCA) a patient has recurrent anterior ischaemia. Left-arm BP is 30 mmHg lower than the right. What is the most likely mechanism?

Answer B The in-situ LIMA arises from the subclavian artery; proximal subclavian stenosis (arm BP difference) reverses or reduces LIMA flow — coronary–subclavian steal — treated by subclavian stenting. LIMA atherosclerosis is rare.

Q10 A patient on aspirin and ticagrelor after NSTE-ACS 4 months ago now needs non-urgent CABG for complex multivessel disease. What is the correct antiplatelet management?

Answer B Continue aspirin through CABG (ACC 1 B-R); stop ticagrelor 3 days (clopidogrel 5, prasugrel 7) before elective surgery to limit bleeding, resuming P2Y12 therapy after surgery to complete 12 months post-ACS.

What the board expects you to know

  • Grade AS by Vmax, mean gradient and AVA, recognise the measurement errors that create a discordant grade, and resolve it with dobutamine echo or CT calcium scoring.
  • List every trigger for aortic valve replacement — symptomatic and asymptomatic — including the 2025 upgrade of early intervention for asymptomatic high-gradient AS.
  • Choose between TAVI and SAVR using age, surgical risk and anatomy, and state where ESC 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 disagree.
  • Anticipate and manage TAVI complications — conduction block, paravalvular leak, stroke, coronary obstruction — and prescribe the correct antithrombotic regimen.

≥ 4 m/sVmax — severe AS (MG ≥ 40 mmHg)
