10.1 Aetiology, Pathophysiology & Natural History

Aortic stenosis (AS) is the most common primary valve lesion leading to intervention in Europe and North America. Its prevalence climbs steeply with age — roughly 12% of people over 75 years have some degree of AS — so the burden rises with every ageing population. Valvular AS must be distinguished from obstruction below the valve (fixed subaortic membrane, dynamic LVOT obstruction in HCM) and above it (supravalvular AS).

Causes of valvular AS

MECHANISM · CALCIFIC AS IS NOT "WEAR AND TEAR"

The initiation phase resembles atherosclerosis: endothelial injury, lipid (LDL, lipoprotein(a)) infiltration and inflammation. The propagation phase is an active osteogenic programme — valvular interstitial cells differentiate into osteoblast-like cells and calcium begets calcium. This explains why statins failed to slow established AS (SALTIRE, SEAS, ASTRONOMER): once propagation is established, lipid lowering no longer steers the disease. Lp(a) lowering is under investigation.

Left ventricular response

Pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy normalises wall stress (Laplace: stress ∝ P × r / 2h). The price: diastolic dysfunction, reduced coronary flow reserve and subendocardial ischaemia even with normal coronaries.

Replacement fibrosis (late gadolinium enhancement on CMR) marks the transition from adaptive hypertrophy to decompensation and is not fully reversible after valve replacement.

Atrial kick contributes up to a third of LV filling in a stiff ventricle — new AF can precipitate sudden decompensation.

LVEF usually remains preserved until late; a falling EF in AS is most often afterload mismatch and recovers after AVR, unlike EF decline in regurgitant lesions.

The damage extends beyond the LV: LA enlargement and AF → pulmonary hypertension → TR → RV dysfunction (the basis of cardiac damage staging, §10.5).

Symptoms and their mechanism

Asymptomatic severe AS
  • Sudden death is rare: < 1% per year.
  • Most become symptomatic within 5 years; eventfree survival at 2 years is only ~ 50% in several series.
  • Faster progression: heavy calcification, Vmax ≥
  • 5 m/s, older age, CKD/dialysis, Lp(a).
Symptomatic severe AS
  • Mortality rises abruptly once symptoms appear
  • — about 50% at 1–2 years.
  • PARTNER 1B (inoperable): 1-year mortality ~
  • 50% with medical therapy vs ~ 31% with TAVI.
  • Every symptomatic patient needs an AVR
  • decision — not a follow-up appointment.
  • Average haemodynamic progression once AS is at least moderate: Vmax ↑ ~ 0.3 m/s/year, mean gradient ↑ ~ 7 mmHg/year, AVA ↓ ~ 0.1 cm²/year — with wide individual variation.
EXAM TRAP

"Aortic sclerosis" (thickened/calcified leaflets, Vmax ≤ 2.5 m/s) is not benign: it is a marker of increased cardiovascular risk and a minority progress to AS. It needs risk-factor management, not AVR.

Key highlightsAetiology & natural history

  • Calcific trileaflet AS is the commonest cause overall; BAV is the commonest cause below 70 years; rheumatic AS almost always coexists with mitral disease.
  • Calcific AS is an active, atherosclerosis-like then osteogenic process — statins do not slow established AS.
  • LV adapts by concentric hypertrophy; replacement fibrosis (LGE) marks irreversible decompensation.
  • Classic survival after symptom onset: angina 5 y, syncope 3 y, heart failure 2 y.
  • Asymptomatic severe AS: sudden death < 1%/year; most develop symptoms within 5 years.
  • Typical progression: Vmax +0.3 m/s, MG +7 mmHg, AVA −0.1 cm² per year.
  • A falling EF in AS is usually afterload mismatch and recovers after AVR.

10.2 Clinical Assessment

Examination — signs that grade severity

DON'T CONFUSE · EJECTION MURMUR AT THE BASE
  • HCM (LVOTO): murmur ↑ with Valsalva and standing, ↓ with squatting/handgrip; brisk (jerky) carotid; A2 preserved.
  • Valvular AS: murmur ↓ with Valsalva; slow-rising carotid; soft A2.
  • Aortic sclerosis: ejection murmur but normal carotid upstroke and normal A2.
  • Supravalvular AS: BP and pulse greater in the right arm (Coandă effect), no click.

Initial investigations

Baseline RBBB = strongest predictor of pacemaker after TAVI

Chest X-ray Often normal heart size; post-stenotic ascending aortic dilatation; valve calcium on lateral film TTE Key test: aetiology, severity, LV size/function, other valves, aorta (§10.3)

TOE Planimetry when TTE inadequate; BAV morphology; endocarditis; peri-procedural guidance Cardiac CT Calcium score when severity is uncertain (§10.4)

  • TAVI planning: annulus size, coronary heights, sinuses, access vessels
  • Coronary CTA to exclude CAD in lower-risk patients
  • CMR LV volumes/mass, fibrosis (LGE, ECV), aorta, alternative diagnoses (amyloid, HCM)
  • Catheterisation Coronary angiography before AVR when CAD is possible
  • Invasive haemodynamics only when non-invasive tests are inconclusive or discordant
  • Test Typical findings / role
  • Natriuretic
  • peptides

BNP/NT-proBNP for risk stratification and to arbitrate symptoms

BOARD PEARL · THINK AMYLOID

Transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis coexists in roughly 1 in 8 elderly patients referred for TAVI. Clues: lowflow low-gradient physiology, low QRS voltage for the wall thickness, carpal tunnel syndrome, apical-sparing strain. Screen with bone scintigraphy (DPD/PYP) plus serum/urine light chains. Dual pathology does not contraindicate TAVI.

EXAM TRAP · CATHETER CROSSING
  • Retrograde crossing of a severely stenotic valve to measure gradients carries a risk of cerebral embolism.
  • Invasive assessment is reserved for discordant or non-diagnostic non-invasive studies — it is not routine.

Key highlightsClinical assessment

  • Signs of severe AS: slow-rising small pulse, late-peaking murmur, soft/absent A2, reversed S2 split, sustained apex, S4, thrill.
  • Murmur loudness does not grade AS — it falls as flow falls.
  • Ejection click implies a mobile (usually bicuspid) valve; it disappears with calcification.
  • HCM murmur increases with Valsalva; AS murmur decreases.
  • ECG: LVH with strain; baseline RBBB predicts pacemaker after TAVI.
  • CT has two roles: calcium scoring (severity) and TAVI planning (annulus, coronary heights, access).
  • Screen for ATTR amyloid in elderly low-flow AS — present in about 1 in 8 TAVI candidates.

10.3 Echocardiographic Grading & Pitfalls

Severity is judged from three core measurements — peak velocity (Vmax), mean gradient (MG) and aortic valve area (AVA) by the continuity equation — supported by the velocity ratio (dimensionless index), valve calcification and LV response. The mean gradient is the most robust parameter; the AVA carries the error of squaring the LVOT diameter.

DEFINITION · THE CONTINUITY EQUATION

Flow in the LVOT = flow through the valve: AVA = (π × (LVOT d/2)² × VTILVOT) / VTIAV. A 1 mm error in a 20 mm LVOT diameter changes the AVA by about 10%. The velocity ratio (VTILVOT/VTIAV or VLVOT/VAV) removes the diameter from the equation — a ratio < 0.25 corresponds to an AVA < 25% of the LVOT area.

ACC/AHA staging of AS

BOARD PEARL · WHEN NUMBERS DISAGREE

Echocardiography underestimates AS far more often than it overestimates it. A mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg with a calculated AVA of 1.1 cm² is severe AS until proven otherwise — the LVOT was probably under-measured. Conversely, an AVA ≤ 1.0 cm² with MG < 40 mmHg is the entry point to the low-flow algorithm (§10.4).

MECHANISM · ECHO VS CATHETER GRADIENTS

Doppler peak instantaneous gradient (4V²) is always higher than the catheter peak-to-peak gradient, which is non-physiological (LV and aortic peaks occur at different times).

The mean gradient agrees best between the two methods.

The catheter Gorlin formula becomes unreliable at low output — the same problem as low-flow echo.

10.4 Low-Flow, Low-Gradient AS

About a third of patients with an AVA ≤ 1.0 cm² have a mean gradient < 40 mmHg — a discordant grade. Before labelling it, exclude measurement error (LVOT diameter, Doppler alignment, BP). Then classify by flow (stroke volume index, SVi) and ejection fraction. Low flow is defined as SVi ≤ 35 mL/m² — and it can coexist with a normal EF.

Key highlightsEcho grading

  • Severe AS: Vmax ≥ 4 m/s, MG ≥ 40 mmHg, AVA ≤ 1.0 cm² (≤ 0.6 cm²/m²), velocity ratio < 0.25.
  • Very severe: Vmax ≥ 5 m/s or MG ≥ 60 mmHg.
  • Mean gradient is the most robust parameter; AVA error comes from squaring the LVOT diameter.
  • Always use a multi-window search including the right parasternal view.
  • ACC/AHA stages: C1/C2 asymptomatic severe (EF ≥ / < 50%); D1 high-gradient, D2 LF-LG reduced EF, D3 paradoxical LF-LG.
  • Grade D3 only when normotensive (SBP < 140 mmHg).
  • High-flow states inflate gradients; low-flow states hide severe AS.
  • Category Definition Typical patient Next step
  • Normal-flow LG AVA ≤ 1.0, MG < 40, LVEF ≥
  • 50%, SVi > 35 mL/m²
  • Usually moderate AS or
  • measurement error (small body
  • size, LVOT under-measured)
  • Re-measure; follow as
  • moderate
  • Classical LF-LG AS — dobutamine stress echocardiography
  • Low-dose dobutamine (start 5 µg/kg/min, increase in steps to a maximum of 20 µg/kg/min) increases stroke volume and distinguishes a truly severe valve from a moderately stenotic valve that a weak ventricle cannot open fully (pseudo-severe AS).
EXAM TRAP · LACK OF FLOW RESERVE≠INOPERABLE

Absent contractile reserve predicts high operative risk with SAVR, but survival is still far better after AVR than with medical therapy. The board answer is confirm severity (CT calcium) and proceed — TAVI is often preferred — not "refer for palliation".

Paradoxical LF-LG AS — CT calcium scoring

Dobutamine is unhelpful here: the problem is preload and afterload (small cavity, hypertension, AF, MR), not contractility. Instead, quantify the Agatston aortic valve calcium score on non-contrast CT. Thresholds are sex-specific because women develop severe AS with less calcium and more fibrosis.

Unlikely < 1600 < 800

ESC/EACTS integrated imaging algorithm; ACC/AHA 2020 uses the same "likely" thresholds (≥ 2000 men, ≥ 1200 women).

CLINICAL APPROACH · CRITERIA THAT INCREASE THE LIKELIHOOD OF TRUE SEVERE PARADOXICAL LF-

  • Typical symptoms without another explanation
  • Age > 70 years
  • LVH (beyond what hypertension explains) or
  • reduced longitudinal strain
  • MG 30–40 mmHg; AVA ≤ 0.8 cm²
  • Low flow confirmed by another method (3D
  • LVOT, CMR, invasive)
  • High CT calcium score (Table 10.10)

Key highlightsLow-flow, low-gradient AS

  • Low flow = SVi ≤ 35 mL/m²; it can occur with normal EF (paradoxical LF-LG).
  • Classical LF-LG (EF < 50%) → dobutamine stress echo; paradoxical LF-LG → CT calcium score.
  • DSE dose: 5 up to 20 µg/kg/min; flow reserve = SV ↑ ≥ 20%.
  • True severe: MG ≥ 40 mmHg with AVA ≤ 1.0 cm² on DSE; pseudo-severe: AVA rises > 1.0 cm².
  • Absent flow reserve = worse prognosis, yet AVR still improves survival.
  • Calcium score: severe likely ≥ 2000 AU (men) / ≥ 1200 AU (women); highly likely ≥ 3000/1600; unlikely < 1600/800.
  • Normal-flow low-gradient AS is usually moderate AS or a measurement error.

  • Limiting symptoms (dyspnoea, angina, dizziness/syncope) at a low workload Patient is symptomatic → AVR (Class I) Fall in systolic BP below baseline (ESC: sustained fall > 20 mmHg; ACC/AHA:
  • fall ≥ 10 mmHg from baseline to peak)
  • High risk — AVR reasonable
  • Reduced exercise capacity for age/sex ACC/AHA: AVR reasonable (IIa)
  • Complex ventricular arrhythmia; ST depression ≥ 2 mm Adverse markers; ST depression alone is non-specific (LVH)
  • Exercise echocardiography adds prognosis: an exercise-induced rise in mean gradient > 20 mmHg, absent contractile reserve, or exercise PASP > 60 mmHg predicts early events.
  • Biomarkers and imaging markers

10.5 Risk Stratification of Asymptomatic AS

"Asymptomatic" must be proven: many elderly patients have silently reduced their activity. Three tools refine risk — exercise testing, biomarkers and imaging markers of myocardial damage.

Exercise testing

Contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS (risk of syncope, VT, death) — the board's favourite "never". Safe and recommended in physically active, apparently asymptomatic patients with severe AS to unmask symptoms and stratify risk; performed under medical supervision.

Cardiac damage staging

Staging extra-valvular damage (Généreux) predicts mortality after AVR better than valve haemodynamics alone — each step roughly adds risk.

BOARD PEARL · EVOLVED

EVOLVED randomised asymptomatic severe AS with CMR mid-wall fibrosis to early AVR vs surveillance: no significant reduction in the primary end point (death or unplanned AS hospitalisation) — the trial was underpowered and early AVR was delayed a median of ~5 months. Fibrosis remains a risk marker, not a stand-alone indication.

10.6 Indications for Intervention

The single most important decision in AS is when to replace the valve. The rule has always been "symptoms or LV dysfunction". The 2025 ESC/EACTS guideline shifts the default further upstream: in asymptomatic high-gradient severe AS with preserved EF and low procedural risk, early intervention is now an evidence-based (Class IIa, level A) alternative to watchful waiting.

The evidence behind early intervention

Key highlightsAsymptomatic risk stratification

  • Exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS and recommended to confirm asymptomatic status in active patients.
  • Abnormal test: symptoms, BP fall (ESC > 20 mmHg sustained; ACC ≥ 10 mmHg), complex arrhythmia.
  • Exercise echo: MG rise > 20 mmHg or exercise PASP > 60 mmHg = high risk.
  • High-risk markers: Vmax ≥ 5 m/s, progression ≥ 0.3 m/s/y, BNP > 3× normal, LVEF < 50–55%.
  • Cardiac damage stages 0–4: LV → LA/MV → pulmonary/TV → RV.
  • CMR fibrosis predicts events; EVOLVED did not prove fibrosis-guided early AVR.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Intervention in asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF < 50% without another cause. I B
  • Intervention in asymptomatic severe AS with symptoms demonstrated on exercise testing. I C CHANGED Intervention should be considered in asymptomatic severe high-gradient AS with LVEF ≥ 50% (normal exercise test if feasible) and low procedural risk, as an alternative to close active surveillance.
  • IIa A
  • Concomitant surgery
  • SAVR in severe AS undergoing CABG or surgery of the ascending aorta or another valve. I C SAVR should be considered in moderate AS undergoing CABG or surgery of the ascending aorta or another valve, after Heart Team discussion.
  • IIa C
  • CHANGED = upgraded or revised versus ESC/EACTS 2021.
WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 (VS ESC 2021)

Asymptomatic high-gradient AS with LVEF ≥ 50%: early intervention upgraded to IIa, level A. In 2021 this required a normal exercise test plus an additional risk marker (Vmax > 5 m/s, BNP > 3× normal, or calcification with progression ≥ 0.3 m/s/year) at IIa B.

Those 2021 risk markers (very severe AS, BNP, rapid progression, LVEF < 55%, BP fall on exercise) remain useful to prioritise timing but no longer gate eligibility.

Symptomatic LF-LG AS: emphasis moved from "flow reserve" to "careful confirmation of severity" by any means (DSE, CT calcium score).

Close active surveillance (clinical + echo review about every 6 months) is the stated alternative for patients who decline or are unsuitable.

Symptomatic LF-LG severe AS with reduced EF (D2). I B-NR

Symptomatic LF-LG severe AS with normal EF (D3) if AS is the most likely cause of symptoms. I B-NR Class IIa / IIb — asymptomatic, low surgical risk

  • Very severe AS: Vmax ≥ 5 m/s. IIa B-NR
  • Reduced exercise tolerance or fall in SBP ≥ 10 mmHg on exercise testing. IIa B-NR
  • BNP > 3× normal. IIa B-NR
  • Rapid progression: Vmax increase ≥ 0.3 m/s/year. IIa B-NR
  • Progressive LVEF decline to < 60% on ≥ 3 serial studies. IIb B-NR

Moderate AS (stage B) undergoing other cardiac surgery. IIb C-EO

Moderate AS

Moderate AS is not benign: event rates approach those of severe AS when the LV is already damaged (reduced EF, cardiac damage stage ≥ 2).

Outside concomitant cardiac surgery, routine AVR for moderate AS is not recommended; manage the ventricle (GDMT for HFrEF) and follow closely.

TAVR UNLOAD (TAVI in moderate AS with HFrEF) did not meet its primary end point; larger trials (e.g. EXPAND TAVR II, PROGRESS) are ongoing.

Follow up moderate calcific AS at least annually; re-assess promptly after any new symptom.

EXAM TRAP · THE "ASYMPTOMATIC" 85-YEAR-OLD

A sedentary 85-year-old who "has no symptoms" but walks only to the bathroom is not reliably asymptomatic. A supervised exercise test (or 6-minute walk) often reveals symptoms and converts the indication to Class I.

Key highlightsIndications for intervention

  • Symptomatic severe AS (high-gradient or confirmed LF-LG with reduced EF) → intervention, Class I.
  • Paradoxical LF-LG (normal EF): ESC IIa; ACC/AHA I (stage D3).
  • Asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF < 50% or exercise-induced symptoms → Class I.
  • ESC 2025: asymptomatic high-gradient AS, LVEF ≥ 50%, low risk → early intervention IIa, level A (RECOVERY, AVATAR, EARLY TAVR).
  • ACC/AHA 2020 still requires a risk marker: Vmax ≥ 5 m/s, BNP > 3×, progression ≥ 0.3 m/s/y, or abnormal exercise test (IIa).
  • Severe AS at CABG/other cardiac surgery → concomitant SAVR (Class I); moderate AS → ESC IIa, ACC IIb.
  • Futility: no intervention if benefit in survival or QoL beyond 1 year is unlikely (III).
  • Moderate AS: no routine AVR outside concomitant surgery; TAVR UNLOAD neutral.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • CHANGED TAVI is recommended in patients aged ≥ 70 years with tricuspid AS, if anatomy is suitable (transfemoral).
  • I A
  • CHANGED SAVR is recommended in patients aged < 70 years if surgical risk is low. I B
  • SAVR or TAVI for the remaining patients according to individual clinical, anatomical and procedural characteristics.
  • I B
  • CHANGED Non-transfemoral TAVI should be considered in patients unsuitable for both surgery and transfemoral access.
  • IIa B
  • NEW TAVI may be considered for severe bicuspid AS in patients at increased surgical risk, if anatomy is suitable.
  • IIb B
  • Balloon aortic valvuloplasty may be considered as a bridge to SAVR/TAVI in haemodynamically unstable patients or before urgent high-risk non-cardiac surgery.
  • IIb C

10.7 TAVI versus SAVR

Once intervention is indicated, the Heart Team (interventional cardiologist, cardiac surgeon, imaging specialist, anaesthetist, geriatrician as needed) chooses the mode in a Heart Valve Centre, and the recommendation is discussed with the patient. Three axes decide: age / life expectancy, procedural risk and anatomy (valve morphology, annulus, coronary heights, access).

The trial foundation — one line each

  • PARTNER 1A, CoreValve
  • HR — high risk
  • TAVI non-inferior (self-expanding superior) to SAVR → TAVI for high risk

WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 (VS ESC 2021)

TAVI age threshold lowered from ≥ 75 to ≥ 70 years (tricuspid valve, suitable anatomy).

SAVR preferred below 70 (was < 75) when surgical risk is low; the 2021 numeric risk cut-offs (STSPROM/EuroSCORE II < 4% low, > 8% high) now sit within a broader Heart Team assessment. Non-transfemoral TAVI upgraded from IIb C to IIa B.

First explicit recommendation for TAVI in bicuspid AS (IIb B, increased surgical risk only).

Beyond age: factors that tip the balance

Bicuspid AS
  • Challenges: elliptical, asymmetric annulus,
  • calcified raphe, associated aortopathy → higher
  • PVL, pacemaker, annular rupture and stroke

Lifetime management and prosthesis choice

A patient treated at 65–70 may outlive the first bioprosthesis. Plan the second procedure at the first: TAV-in-SAV is generally straightforward; TAV-in-TAV risks coronary access loss and sinus sequestration. Choosing SAVR first allows a larger valve (± annular enlargement) and later valve-in-valve TAVI. Mechanical vs biological (ACC/AHA 2020): mechanical reasonable < 50 y; shared decision 50–65 y; bioprosthesis reasonable > 65 y. ESC places the mechanical threshold at < 60 y and bioprosthesis at > 65 y for the aortic position.

The Ross procedure (pulmonary autograft to aortic position, homograft to pulmonary) is an option for young adults in expert centres — no anticoagulation, excellent haemodynamics, but a two-valve operation with risk of autograft dilatation.

BOARD PEARL · FUTILITY IS A CLASS III

A patient with severe AS but metastatic cancer, advanced dementia or severe frailty expected to live < 1 year should not undergo TAVI or SAVR. The board answer is palliative/medical therapy — and, if symptoms need temporary relief, balloon valvuloplasty (IIb).

10.8 Complications of TAVI

Major complications have fallen sharply with smaller sheaths, CT planning and operator experience; transfemoral access is now used in > 95% of cases. Conduction disturbance remains the most frequent complication ; paravalvular leak and stroke carry the most prognostic weight.

Key highlightsTAVI vs SAVR

  • Decision by the Heart Team in a Heart Valve Centre (I C), shared with the patient.
  • ESC 2025: TAVI ≥ 70 y with tricuspid AS and suitable anatomy (I A); SAVR < 70 y at low surgical risk (I B).
  • ACC/AHA 2020: SAVR < 65 y; shared decision 65–80 y; TF-TAVI > 80 y or life expectancy < 10 y.
  • Non-TF TAVI upgraded to IIa B (2025) when surgery and TF access are unsuitable.
  • Bicuspid AS: TAVI only at increased surgical risk (IIb B); otherwise SAVR.
  • Favour SAVR: endocarditis, surgical CAD/MV/TV/aortic disease, low coronary heights, unsuitable annulus.
  • Balloon valvuloplasty is only a bridge (IIb).
  • Plan lifetime management — the first valve decides the options for the second.
  • Complication Frequency Risk factors Prevention / management
  • Leaflet thrombosis

  • Subclinical in
  • ~10–15% on CT
  • No anticoagulation; valve type Clinical valve thrombosis

  • Conduction disturbances and pacing
  • The AV node and left bundle lie just beneath the membranous septum, millimetres below the aortic annulus — compressed by the stent frame. New LBBB occurs in a large minority, especially with self-expanding valves; high-grade AV block may appear late (after discharge), so monitoring is structured.

IIa B

Ambulatory ECG monitoring or EP study should be considered for new LBBB with QRS > 150 ms or PR > 240 ms without further prolongation over > 48 h.

IIa C

Ambulatory monitoring or EP study may be considered in pre-existing conduction disease with QRS or PR prolongation > 20 ms.

  • IIb C
  • Prophylactic pacing before TAVI in RBBB without another pacing indication. III C

An EP study with HV interval ≥ 70 ms is commonly used to justify pacing in patients with new LBBB.

MECHANISM · WHY PVL MATTERS

Surgical valves are sewn in; transcatheter valves are held by radial force against an irregular calcified annulus. Gaps between frame and annulus leak in diastole. Even moderate PVL imposes a volume load on a small, stiff, hypertrophied LV that tolerates it poorly — hence the association of moderate or greater PVL with increased late mortality.

EXAM TRAP · HYPOTENSION STRAIGHT AFTER VALVE DEPLOYMENT

Sudden hypotension with new regional wall motion abnormality and ST change after TAVI deployment = coronary obstruction (usually left main) until proven otherwise → aortic root angiography and bail-out PCI. Hypotension with pericardial effusion = annular rupture or wire perforation of the LV. Remember suicide LV: abrupt afterload removal in a hypertrophied LV causes dynamic LVOT obstruction — treat with fluids and β-blocker, avoid inotropes.

10.9 Antithrombotic Therapy after AVR

After TAVI the default has shifted to less: single antiplatelet therapy in patients without another indication, and anticoagulant alone in those with one. Three trials drive this — POPular TAVI (aspirin alone caused less bleeding than aspirin + clopidogrel, with no excess thrombotic events; and OAC alone beat OAC + clopidogrel), GALILEO (rivaroxaban-based strategy in patients without OAC indication: more death/thromboembolism and more bleeding) and ATLANTIS (apixaban not superior to standard care).

IIb B-NR

VKA (INR 2.5) for at least 3 months may be reasonable in patients at low bleeding risk. IIb B-NR Low-dose rivaroxaban (10 mg) + aspirin in patients without another OAC indication — harmful. III B-R

Key highlightsTAVI complications

  • Commonest complication: conduction disturbance — LBBB and AV block; PPM higher with self-expanding valves.
  • Strongest predictor of pacemaker: pre-existing RBBB; also deep implantation and oversizing.
  • Pace for AV block persisting 24–48 h (I B) or new alternating BBB (I C); monitor new LBBB with QRS > 150 ms or PR > 240 ms (IIa C).
  • No prophylactic pacing before TAVI for RBBB alone (III).
  • Moderate or greater PVL increases mortality — prevented by CT-based sizing.
  • Stroke ~2–3%; cerebral embolic protection not proven.
  • Coronary obstruction < 1% but lethal; highest risk with low coronary height and valve-in-valve → BASILICA / chimney stenting.
  • Subclinical leaflet thrombosis (HALT) is common on CT — treat only clinical valve thrombosis with OAC.
CLINICAL APPROACH · AFTER SURGICAL BIOPROSTHETIC AVR
  • No other indication: low-dose aspirin, or VKA for the first 3 months in patients at low bleeding risk (both guideline-supported options); then aspirin.
  • AF after bioprosthetic AVR: DOACs are acceptable beyond the first 3 months (and many use them from the start).
  • Mechanical AVR: lifelong VKA — DOACs are contraindicated (RE-ALIGN, PROACT Xa).

Key highlightsAntithrombotic therapy

  • No OAC indication after TAVI: aspirin 75–100 mg alone — ESC 2025 I A for 12 months, then long-term aspirin IIa C.
  • OAC indication: OAC alone (I B) — adding clopidogrel only increases bleeding (POPular TAVI cohort B).
  • Routine DAPT after TAVI is not recommended (POPular TAVI cohort A).
  • Routine OAC without an indication is not recommended (GALILEO harm, ATLANTIS neutral).
  • ACC/AHA 2020 is more permissive: DAPT 3–6 months or VKA 3 months are IIb options.
  • Mechanical valves: VKA only — never a DOAC.
  • Heyde syndrome

10.10 Medical Therapy, Heyde Syndrome & Follow-up

Medical therapy — what it can and cannot do

No drug alters the natural history of AS. Statins (SALTIRE, SEAS, ASTRONOMER) did not slow progression; prescribe them only for their usual atherosclerotic indications.

Hypertension (about a third of patients) adds a second afterload — treat it, starting low and titrating slowly (ACE inhibitor/ARB reasonable); avoid hypotension and volume depletion.

Heart failure awaiting intervention: cautious diuretics; GDMT if EF reduced. In decompensated severe AS with low EF, nitroprusside under invasive monitoring can be a bridge — but vasodilators may cause profound hypotension because output cannot rise across a fixed obstruction.

AF: poorly tolerated (loss of atrial kick); restore/maintain rhythm where possible. Native AS is not "valvular AF" — DOACs are appropriate.

Endocarditis prophylaxis: only after prosthetic valve implantation (including TAVI) or previous IE; good dental hygiene for all.

DEFINITION · HEYDE SYNDROME

The triad of severe AS, GI bleeding from angiodysplasia and acquired von Willebrand syndrome type 2A.

High shear stress across the stenotic valve unfolds large von Willebrand factor multimers, which are then cleaved by ADAMTS13; loss of high-molecular-weight multimers impairs platelet adhesion in the highshear microcirculation of angiodysplastic lesions.

Presents as iron-deficiency anaemia or recurrent occult/overt GI (often small-bowel) bleeding in an elderly patient.

Lab clue: loss of HMW multimers on multimer analysis; prolonged PFA-100 closure time; reduced vWF activity/antigen ratio.

Definitive treatment is aortic valve replacement (TAVI or SAVR) — multimers normalise within hours to days and bleeding recurrence falls. Persistent or recurrent syndrome after AVR suggests significant PVL or patient–prosthesis mismatch.

The same mechanism operates in HCM with LVOT obstruction and with LVADs.

Special situations

Check aortic dimensions in BAV

Concomitant MR Often secondary; improves after AVR in many; severe primary MR → combined surgery Dialysis / CKD Rapid progression; higher procedural risk; bioprostheses degenerate faster Follow-up intervals

yearly from ~5 years; TAVI: annually)

BOARD PEARL · PATIENT EDUCATION IS PART OF FOLLOW-UP

The asymptomatic patient under surveillance must be told to report any exertional symptom immediately — not wait for the next appointment. Symptom onset converts a stable condition into one with high shortterm mortality.

10.11 Subvalvular & Supravalvular AS

Fixed obstruction below or above a normal aortic valve accounts for a minority of congenital LVOT obstruction (bicuspid valve remains the commonest). Both present in children and young adults, show a high-velocity jet with a structurally normal valve and, unlike valvular AS, have a preserved A2 and no ejection click.

Key highlightsMedical therapy, Heyde & follow-up

  • No medical therapy changes the course of AS; statins do not slow progression.
  • Treat hypertension cautiously; vasodilators risk hypotension with a fixed obstruction.
  • AF in native AS: DOACs are appropriate (not "valvular AF").
  • Heyde syndrome = AS + angiodysplasia bleeding + acquired vWD type 2A (loss of HMW multimers) → cured by AVR.
  • Asymptomatic severe AS: review at least every 6 months (ESC); ACC/AHA 6–12 months.
  • Moderate AS: yearly (ESC) / every 1–2 y (ACC); mild AS: every 2–3 y (ESC) / 3–5 y (ACC).
  • Symptomatic AS before high-risk non-cardiac surgery or pregnancy → treat the valve first.
DON'T CONFUSE · THREE CAUSES OF AN LVOT GRADIENT
  • Valvular AS: fixed, calcified/doming valve, soft A2, click if bicuspid.
  • Fixed subaortic membrane: fixed gradient, normal valve, AR, young patient.
  • HCM with SAM: dynamic late-peaking "dagger-shaped" jet, ↑ with Valsalva; Brockenbrough–
  • Braunwald–Morrow sign invasively.

Key highlightsSub- and supravalvular AS

  • Both have a normal aortic valve, loud A2 and no ejection click.
  • Subaortic membrane: associated with VSD/coarctation/Shone; causes progressive AR; treated surgically and may recur.
  • Supravalvular AS: Williams syndrome (elastin, 7q11.23), hypercalcaemia, elfin facies.
  • Supravalvular AS clue: right-arm BP higher than left (Coand8 effect); coronary ostial stenosis risk.
  • Intervention usually for symptoms or mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg (plus AR/LV dysfunction for subaortic).

10.12 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 78-year-old hypertensive woman has exertional dyspnoea. BP is 128/76 mmHg. TTE: calcified trileaflet valve, AVA 0.75 cm² (indexed 0.45 cm²/m²), mean gradient 31 mmHg, LVEF 65%, SVi 29 mL/m², small hypertrophied LV. Which test best establishes AS severity?

Answer B Paradoxical low-flow, low-gradient AS (EF ≥ 50%, SVi ≤ 35 mL/m²). The problem is preload/afterload, not contractility, so DSE (A) is uninformative. CT calcium score arbitrates: ≥ 1200 AU in a woman makes severe AS likely. Exercise testing (C) is unsafe in a symptomatic patient.

Q2 A 70-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) has AVA 0.8 cm² and MG 22 mmHg. On dobutamine up to 20 µg/kg/min, stroke volume rises by 35%, MG rises to 27 mmHg and AVA to 1.3 cm². What is the best management?

Answer C Flow reserve is present (SV ↑ ≥ 20%) and AVA rises above 1.0 cm² with flow while the gradient stays low — pseudo-severe AS. The valve is moderately stenotic; treat the cardiomyopathy. CT (D) is used when flow reserve is absent. AVR (A, B) is not indicated for pseudo-severe AS.

Q3 A 66-year-old active man has no symptoms. TTE: Vmax 4.4 m/s, MG 48 mmHg, tricuspid valve, LVEF 62%. A treadmill test to 10 METs is normal with an appropriate BP rise. EuroSCORE II 1.2%. According to ESC/EACTS 2025, which is the most appropriate recommendation?

Answer B ESC 2025: in asymptomatic severe high-gradient AS with LVEF ≥ 50% and low procedural risk, intervention should be considered (IIa A) as an alternative to close surveillance. At < 70 years with low surgical risk, the mode is SAVR (I B), not TAVI (C). Statins (E) do not slow AS.

Q4 An 81-year-old woman with severe high-gradient AS reports two episodes of presyncope while climbing stairs. Which of the following is contraindicated?

Answer D Exertional presyncope in severe AS is a symptom — the patient is symptomatic and exercise testing is contraindicated. All other options are part of the TAVI/SAVR work-up.

Q5 A 72-year-old man has symptomatic severe AS (tricuspid valve), STS-PROM 2%, suitable iliofemoral anatomy and no concomitant disease requiring surgery. According to ESC/EACTS 2025, which approach carries a Class I recommendation?

Answer B ESC 2025 recommends TAVI in patients ≥ 70 years with tricuspid AS and suitable anatomy (I A), even at low surgical risk. SAVR (A) is Class I for < 70 years at low risk. Under ACC/AHA 2020 this 72-year-old would fall into the shared-decision band (65–80 y).

Q6 Two days after self-expanding TAVI, a patient has new LBBB with QRS 162 ms and PR 210 ms, both stable over 48 hours. There is no AV block. What is the most appropriate step?

Answer C New LBBB with QRS > 150 ms or PR > 240 ms, stable for > 48 h: ambulatory ECG monitoring or EP study (IIa C) to detect delayed high-grade AV block. Immediate pacing (A) is for persistent high-grade AV block or new alternating BBB.

Q7 A 79-year-old woman with permanent AF (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5) undergoes uncomplicated transfemoral TAVI. She has no recent coronary stent. What antithrombotic regimen is recommended?

Answer C With a separate OAC indication, OAC alone is recommended (ESC I B). POPular TAVI cohort B: adding clopidogrel increased bleeding without benefit (A). Rivaroxaban + aspirin (E) was harmful in GALILEO — and that trial excluded patients with an OAC indication.

Q8 An 84-year-old man with severe AS has recurrent iron-deficiency anaemia; capsule endoscopy shows smallbowel angiodysplasia. Platelet count and INR are normal. Which laboratory finding is expected, and what is the definitive treatment?

Answer B Heyde syndrome: shear-induced unfolding and ADAMTS13 cleavage of vWF produces acquired vWD type 2A with loss of HMW multimers. AVR (TAVI or SAVR) corrects the defect and reduces rebleeding. D describes TTP.

Q9 A 19-year-old with learning difficulties, a friendly outgoing personality and a history of infantile hypercalcaemia has an ejection systolic murmur. BP is 20 mmHg higher in the right arm. Echo shows a normal trileaflet aortic valve with high velocity at the sinotubular junction. Which gene region is implicated?

Answer B Williams syndrome — elastin deletion at 7q11.23 — causes supravalvular AS (hourglass STJ narrowing), peripheral pulmonary stenoses and hypercalcaemia. The Coand8 effect directs the jet into the innominate artery, raising right-arm BP. FBN1 = Marfan; TBX5 = Holt–Oram; NOTCH1 = familial BAV.

Q10 During valve-in-valve TAVI inside a degenerated stented surgical bioprosthesis with externally mounted leaflets, the patient becomes profoundly hypotensive immediately after deployment, with anterior ST elevation. Pre-procedure CT showed a virtual valve-to-coronary distance of 3 mm. What is the most likely cause?

Answer C Valve-in-valve inside a surgical valve with externally mounted leaflets and a VTC < 4 mm is the highest-risk setting for coronary obstruction — the displaced leaflet seals the left main ostium. Prevention: BASILICA or chimney stenting. Suicide LV (B) causes hypotension without ST elevation and responds to fluids and β-blockade.

What the board expects you to know

11.1 Aetiology & Pathophysiology

Aortic regurgitation (AR) results from disease of the leaflets, of the aortic root that suspends them, or both. In developed countries root/ascending aortic dilatation and the bicuspid valve are the leading causes of chronic AR ; rheumatic disease still dominates where rheumatic fever is endemic. Identifying the mechanism matters because it decides whether the valve can be repaired or must be replaced, and whether the aorta must be replaced too.

DEFINITION · FUNCTIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF AR (E L KHOURY)

Type I — normal cusp motion with dilatation of the functional aortic annulus (Ia STJ/ascending, Ib root, Ic annulus) or cusp perforation (Id) → central jet.

Type II — cusp prolapse (excess tissue or commissural disruption) → eccentric jet, directed away from the prolapsing cusp.

Type III — cusp restriction (rheumatic, calcific, thickened) → often large central or eccentric jet; least repairable.

Chronic AR — a double load

Volume overload (regurgitant volume) and pressure overload (a large stroke volume ejected into the aorta raises systolic pressure) → eccentric plus concentric hypertrophy. AR produces the largest enddiastolic volumes of any valve lesion (cor bovinum). The large compliant LV accommodates the regurgitant volume at near-normal LVEDP; total stroke volume is high, so pulse pressure is wide.

Exercise is well tolerated for years: tachycardia shortens diastole (less time to regurgitate) and peripheral vasodilatation reduces the regurgitant fraction.

Decompensation: wall stress rises (Laplace), EF falls by afterload mismatch, then by irreversible myocardial fibrosis. LVESD/LVESV track this transition better than EF — hence their central role in timing surgery.

Coronary perfusion is reduced by low aortic diastolic pressure and high LVEDP; angina may be nocturnal (bradycardia lengthens diastole and lowers diastolic pressure).

Key highlightsAetiology & pathophysiology

  • Leading causes of chronic AR: root/ascending dilatation and bicuspid valve; acute AR: endocarditis and type A dissection.
  • Aortitis (syphilis, Takayasu, GCA, spondyloarthropathies) causes AR via the root.
  • El Khoury: Type I dilatation/perforation, Type II prolapse, Type III restriction.
  • Chronic AR = volume + pressure overload → eccentric + concentric LVH, very large EDV, wide pulse pressure.
  • Early EF decline is afterload mismatch; end-systolic size identifies the transition to irreversibility.
  • Acute AR: normal-sized stiff LV, high LVEDP, premature mitral closure, narrow pulse pressure, short murmur.

11.2 Clinical Features & Eponymous Signs

Symptoms and natural history

Long asymptomatic phase; symptoms (exertional dyspnoea, then orthopnoea/PND, angina, palpitations from a forceful heartbeat, especially lying on the left side) appear late, often after the LV has dilated. Asymptomatic severe AR with normal LV: progression to symptoms or LV dysfunction ~4–6% per year; sudden death < 0.2% per year.

Asymptomatic LV dysfunction develops at < 3.5% per year — but once LVESD > 50 mm, the risk of death, symptoms or LV dysfunction rises to ~10–20% per year.

Once symptomatic, mortality exceeds ~10% per year with angina and ~20% per year with heart failure.

The murmur

High-pitched, blowing, early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge, best heard sitting forward in held expiration with the diaphragm.

Loudest at the right sternal edge → suspect root disease (dilatation, dissection) rather than leaflet disease.

In chronic AR, duration (not loudness) correlates with severity; in acute or decompensated AR the murmur shortens as LV and aortic pressures equalise.

Accompanying systolic flow murmur (high stroke volume) without AS; Austin Flint murmur — mid/ late-diastolic apical rumble from the AR jet impinging on the anterior mitral leaflet.

DON'T CONFUSE · AUSTIN FLINT VS MITRAL STENOSIS

Austin Flint: no opening snap, S1 normal or soft, no presystolic accentuation in AF, decreases with vasodilators (amyl nitrite), echo shows a normal mitral valve with jet fluttering the anterior leaflet. Rheumatic MS: loud S1, opening snap, commissural fusion on echo; murmur persists with

vasodilators.

Graham Steell murmur (PR in pulmonary hypertension) is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge that increases with inspiration.

BOARD PEARL · WIDE PULSE PRESSURE IS SENSITIVE,NOT SPECIFIC

A wide pulse pressure and collapsing pulse also occur in high-output states (thyrotoxicosis, anaemia, pregnancy, fever, AV fistula, Paget disease), PDA, and a stiff aorta in the elderly. Peripheral signs are absent in acute AR — their absence never excludes severe acute AR.

ECG and chest X-ray

ECG: LVH with tall R waves and deep narrow Q waves in lateral leads (volume overload), later strain pattern; PR prolongation in an abscess of endocarditis (new AV block = aortic root abscess). CXR: cardiomegaly with a "boot-shaped" LV; dilated ascending aorta; pulmonary oedema without cardiomegaly in acute AR.

Key highlightsClinical features

  • Early diastolic decrescendo murmur, sitting forward in expiration; right sternal edge = root disease.
  • Severity in chronic AR correlates with murmur duration, not intensity.
  • Austin Flint = apical diastolic rumble without opening snap in severe AR.
  • Hill sign > 60 mmHg suggests severe AR; Mayne = diastolic fall > 15 mmHg with arm elevation.
  • Asymptomatic severe AR, normal LV: SCD < 0.2%/y; LVESD > 50 mm → events ~10–20%/y.
  • New PR prolongation in aortic valve endocarditis = root abscess until proven otherwise.
  • Peripheral signs are absent in acute AR.
  • Beyond TTE

11.3 Grading AR Severity

TTE defines mechanism, severity, LV response and aortic dimensions. No single parameter suffices — integrate qualitative, semi-quantitative and quantitative measures with LV size . Chronic severe AR with a normal-sized LV should prompt re-evaluation of the grade (or of chronicity).

CW signal density Faint Dense Dense

Descending aorta flow reversal Brief, early diastolic Intermediate Holodiastolic, EDV > 20 cm/s Semi-quantitative

  • Vena contracta (mm) < 3 3–6 > 6
  • Jet width / LVOT width (central jets) < 25% 25–64% ≥ 65%
  • Pressure half-time (ms) > 500 200–500 < 200
  • Quantitative
  • EROA (mm²) < 10 10–29 ≥ 30
  • Regurgitant volume (mL/beat) < 30 30–59 ≥ 60
  • Regurgitant fraction < 30% 30–49% ≥ 50%
  • LV response (chronic)
  • LV size Normal Normal or dilated Dilated (unless acute)

ESC/EACTS and ASE/EACVI integrative criteria. Holodiastolic reversal in the abdominal aorta is highly specific for severe AR.

EXAM TRAP · PRESSURE HALF-TIME IS LOAD-DEPENDENT

PHT shortens not only with severe AR but also with a stiff LV and high LVEDP (e.g. LV dysfunction, acute AR) and lengthens with vasoconstriction. In chronic compensated severe AR, PHT may exceed 250 ms. Use it only as a supporting sign. Similarly, colour jet area is misleading — jets spread widely into a large LV.

Key highlightsGrading AR

  • Severe AR: VC > 6 mm, PHT < 200 ms, EROA ≥ 30 mm², RVol ≥ 60 mL, RF ≥ 50%, jet/LVOT ≥ 65%.
  • Holodiastolic reversal in the descending aorta (EDV > 20 cm/s) — and especially in the abdominal aorta — supports severe AR.
  • Chronic severe AR should have a dilated LV; if not, question the grade or suspect acute AR.
  • PHT and colour jet area are load- and technique-dependent — supportive only.
  • CMR when echo is equivocal; ECG-gated CT for aortic dimensions before surgery.
  • ACC/AHA C2 = LVEF ≤ 55%, LVESD > 50 mm or LVESDi > 25 mm/m².

11.4 Acute Aortic Regurgitation

Acute severe AR presents as sudden pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock in a patient whose nondilated ventricle cannot accommodate the regurgitant volume. It is a surgical emergency — medical therapy is only a bridge.

Recognise it
  • Tachycardia, hypotension, pulmonary oedema
  • Short, soft early diastolic murmur (may be
  • inaudible)
  • Soft S1 (premature mitral closure); S3
  • Pulse pressure not wide; no peripheral signs
  • Clues to cause: fever/embolic phenomena (IE);
  • tearing chest/back pain, pulse deficit
  • (dissection); trauma
Echo clues
  • Non-dilated, hyperdynamic LV
  • Very short PHT; steep CW deceleration
  • Premature mitral valve closure on M-mode;
  • diastolic MR
  • Flail/perforated cusp, vegetation, abscess,
  • dissection flap

TOE or CT aortography urgently to define cause

EXAM TRAP · BRADYCARDIA IS DANGEROUS IN AR

Anything that lengthens diastole (β-blockers, AV block from a root abscess, high vagal tone) increases regurgitant volume. The board answer to hypotension in acute AR is not IABP and not β-blockade — it is inotrope ± vasodilator as a bridge to urgent surgery.

11.5 Chronic AR: Timing of Surgery

The goal is to operate before irreversible LV dysfunction — after which survival after AVR is impaired — but not so early that the patient carries prosthesis risks for decades unnecessarily. Two sets of triggers apply: symptoms, and LV size/function thresholds in the asymptomatic patient. A third trigger is the aorta itself (§11.8), irrespective of AR severity.

Key highlightsAcute AR

  • Causes: infective endocarditis, type A dissection, trauma, prosthetic failure, iatrogenic.
  • Signs: shock, pulmonary oedema, soft S1, short soft murmur, no wide pulse pressure.
  • Echo: premature mitral closure, very short PHT, non-dilated LV.
  • Treatment = urgent surgery; nitroprusside ± dobutamine as a bridge.
  • IABP is contraindicated; avoid β-blockers (except careful use in dissection).
  • Medical therapy
  • Treat hypertension (ACE inhibitor/ARB or dihydropyridine CCB preferred) — it increases regurgitant volume.
  • Vasodilators do not delay surgery in asymptomatic normotensive patients with normal LV function and are not recommended for that purpose.
  • Symptomatic patients unsuitable for surgery, or with LV dysfunction: GDMT including ACE-i/ARB/ARNI; avoid bradycardia.
  • Marfan syndrome: β-blocker and/or ARB (losartan) to slow root growth, before and after surgery.

Type of intervention

CHANGED Aortic valve repair should be considered in selected patients at experienced centres when durable results are expected.

IIa B

Valve-sparing aortic root replacement in young patients with aortic root dilatation, at experienced centres with durable results expected.

I B

NEW TAVI may be considered for severe AR in symptomatic patients ineligible for surgery, if anatomy is suitable, in experienced centres (dedicated devices).

  • IIb B
  • CHANGED/NEW = revised or introduced versus ESC/EACTS 2021.
WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 (VS ESC 2021)

Early-surgery thresholds for low-risk asymptomatic patients now use indexed measures: LVESDi > 22 mm/m² (was > 20 mm/m²) and a new volumetric criterion, LVESVi > 45 mL/m²; LVEF ≤ 55% retained; level of evidence C → B.

Aortic valve repair upgraded from IIb C to IIa B.

First recommendation for TAVI in AR (IIb B) — inoperable symptomatic patients, dedicated devices. First guideline recommendation for the Ross procedure in selected young adults at expert centres.

Recommendation Class Level

Asymptomatic severe AR, LVEF > 55%, low surgical risk, with progressive LVEF decline to 55–60% on ≥ 3 studies or progressive dilatation to LVEDD > 65 mm.

IIb B-NR

MECHANISM · WHY END-SYSTOLIC,AND WHY INDEXED?

End-diastolic size reflects the volume load (it enlarges in every severe AR); end-systolic size reflects contractile performance against afterload, and is the best predictor of post-operative LV dysfunction and death. Women and small patients reach adverse outcomes at smaller absolute dimensions, so indexing to BSA avoids operating too late in small patients — the logic behind LVESDi and LVESVi.

BOARD PEARL · NO EF IS TOO LOW

Even with severe LV dysfunction, AVR improves survival in AR because much of the dysfunction is afterload mismatch. Operative risk is higher and recovery incomplete when EF < 25% or LVESD is very large, but poor LV function is not a contraindication to surgery in severe AR.

11.6 Surgical & Transcatheter Options

TAVI for aortic regurgitation

Pure AR is a hostile TAVI substrate: no calcium to anchor the valve, large and dilated annulus/root, and a high-volume regurgitant jet during deployment → embolisation, malposition and residual AR with conventional (off-label) valves.

Dedicated devices (e.g. JenaValve Trilogy, J-Valve) use locators/clips that grasp the native leaflets. In the ALIGN-AR study of high-risk patients, procedural success was high and mortality low, but new pacemakers were needed in about 1 in 4.

Reserved for symptomatic patients ineligible for surgery with suitable CT anatomy, in experienced centres (ESC 2025 IIb B).

Key highlightsTiming of surgery in chronic AR

  • Symptomatic severe AR → surgery regardless of EF (Class I, both guidelines).
  • ESC Class I (asymptomatic): LVEF ≤ 50%, LVESD > 50 mm or LVESDi > 25 mm/m².
  • ESC 2025 IIb (low risk): LVESDi > 22 mm/m², LVESVi > 45 mL/m² or LVEF ≤ 55%.
  • ACC/AHA: LVEF ≤ 55% is Class I; LVESD > 50 / LVESDi > 25 is IIa; LVEDD > 65 mm progressive is IIb.
  • Severe AR at other cardiac surgery → treat the valve (I).
  • Vasodilators treat hypertension but do not delay surgery in asymptomatic AR.
  • Low EF is not a contraindication to AVR in AR.
CLINICAL APPROACH · MATCHING OPERATION TO PHENOTYPE
  • Young, root aneurysm, pliable cusps → valve-sparing root replacement (David).
  • Isolated AR, cusp prolapse (BAV or tricuspid), normal root → cusp repair + annuloplasty in a repair centre.
  • Calcified/rheumatic cusps → AVR (± ascending replacement if ≥ 45 mm).
  • Elderly, inoperable, symptomatic → TAVI with a dedicated device.

Key highlightsSurgical & transcatheter options

  • Valve-sparing root replacement is Class I in young patients with root dilatation at experienced centres.
  • Aortic valve repair: ESC 2025 IIa B (upgraded) for selected patients in expert centres.
  • Bentall = composite valve–graft root replacement; David = valve reimplantation inside a graft.
  • Ross: pulmonary autograft to aortic position — young adults, no anticoagulation; first ESC recommendation in TAVI for AR: IIb B, inoperable symptomatic patients, dedicated devices (JenaValve); pacemaker ~1 in 4.
  • Genetics and associations

11.7 The Bicuspid Aortic Valve

The bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most common congenital heart defect, present in about 0.5–2% of the population (≈ 1%) with a male predominance of about 3:1. It is best viewed as a valvulo-aortopathy: a valve that tends to stenose or leak, attached to an aorta that tends to dilate — and both need lifelong surveillance.

Morphology and classification

  • — uncommon
  • Partial-fusion (forme fruste) BAV: small commissural fusion; three sinuses — easily
  • mistaken for tricuspid
  • Sievers (surgical) Type 0 — no raphe (true bicuspid)
  • Type 1 — one raphe (most common; L–R)
  • Type 2 — two raphes (functionally unicuspid)
BOARD PEARL · ECHO RECOGNITION

In the parasternal short-axis view in systole, the BAV opens as an elliptical "fish-mouth" orifice with two commissures; in diastole a raphe may mimic a third commissure — so diagnose BAV in systole . Long-axis clues: systolic doming and an eccentric closure line on M-mode.

Genetics
  • Heritable, with incomplete penetrance; ~9–10%
  • of first-degree relatives have BAV
  • Implicated genes include NOTCH1 (with early
  • calcification), GATA4/5, SMAD6
  • BAV + aortopathy + extra-aortic features →
  • genetics referral (Loeys–Dietz)
Associated lesions
  • Coarctation — BAV in ~50–75% of coarctation
  • patients
  • Turner syndrome — BAV in ~30%
  • Shone complex, VSD, PDA, subaortic membrane
  • Coronary variants: left dominance, short left
  • main
  • Intracranial aneurysm (especially with
  • coarctation)

Clinical course

Key highlightsBicuspid aortic valve

  • BAV ≈ 1% of the population, male : female ≈ 3:1; the commonest congenital heart defect.
  • Fused BAV with right–left fusion is the commonest phenotype (~70–80%); right–non fusion next.
  • Sievers: type 0 (no raphe), 1 (one raphe), 2 (two raphes).
  • Diagnose in systole (fish-mouth opening); a raphe mimics a commissure in diastole.
  • Associations: coarctation (BAV in 50–75%), Turner (~30%), Shone, NOTCH1.
  • AS is the commonest complication; AR affects younger men; IE risk is increased.

11.8 Bicuspid Aortopathy & Aortic Thresholds

MECHANISM · GENETICS AND HAEMODYNAMICS

Two forces dilate the BAV aorta: an intrinsic medial abnormality (fragmented elastin, smooth-muscle apoptosis) shared with other heritable aortopathies, and flow-mediated wall stress from an eccentric systolic jet striking the convexity of the ascending aorta. The intrinsic component dominates the root phenotype; the haemodynamic component dominates the ascending phenotype.

DEFINITION · MEASURING THE AORTA

Four levels: annulus (mid-systole), sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction and tubular ascending aorta (end-diastole).

Echo: leading-edge-to-leading-edge; CT/CMR: inner-to-inner, perpendicular to the flow axis (doubleoblique) — sinus-to-sinus maximum. Confirm any diameter used for surgical decisions with ECG-gated CT (or CMR); compare serial studies at the same level and modality.

Body size matters: indexed measures — aortic size index (diameter/BSA), aortic height index, and ACC/ AHA's cross-sectional area/height ratio ≥ 10 cm²/m.

IIa B-NR

BAV with diameter 5.0–5.4 cm plus a risk factor for dissection (family history of dissection, growth ≥ 0.3 cm/year, coarctation, root phenotype).

IIa B-NR

BAV undergoing surgical AV repair/replacement with root or ascending ≥ 4.5 cm: concomitant aortic replacement.

  • IIa B-NR
  • BAV with diameter 5.0–5.4 cm, no risk factor, low surgical risk. IIb B-NR
  • Sporadic (tricuspid-valve) root/ascending aneurysm — for comparison

Diameter ≥ 5.5 cm, or symptoms attributable to the aneurysm. I B-NR

Growth ≥ 0.3 cm/year in 2 consecutive years, or ≥ 0.5 cm in 1 year (confirmed by tomographic imaging).

  • I C-LD
  • Diameter ≥ 5.0 cm in an experienced multidisciplinary aortic team. IIa B-NR
  • Tricuspid AV surgery with ascending ≥ 4.5 cm: concomitant replacement. IIa B-NR

Recommendation Class Level

Tricuspid valve, tubular ascending aorta > 52 mm with low surgical risk: surgery should be considered. IIa B Surgery for tricuspid aortic valve disease with root/ascending ≥ 45 mm and low surgical risk: concomitant aortic replacement should be considered.

IIa B

Bicuspid valve undergoing surgery with ascending aorta ≥ 45 mm: concomitant replacement should be considered.

IIa C

ESC 2024 also lowers thresholds for additional risk features: uncontrolled hypertension, rapid growth, family history of dissection, aortic length, indexed diameter, root phenotype.

  • BAV — root phenotype ≥ 50 mm (I) Root phenotype is a risk factor → 50–54 mm (IIa)
  • At aortic valve surgery ≥ 45 mm (IIa) ≥ 45 mm (IIa)
  • Marfan syndrome ≥ 50 mm; ≥ 45 mm with risk
  • factors
  • ≥ 50 mm; ≥ 45 mm with risk factors
  • Loeys–Dietz (TGFBR1/2) ≥ 45 mm (lower with high-risk
  • features)
  • ≥ 45 mm; ≥ 40 mm with risk factors
  • Turner syndrome Indexed: ASI ≥ 2.5 cm/m² ASI ≥ 2.5 cm/m² + risk factors (IIa)

Rapid growth ≥ 3 mm/year lowers the threshold ≥ 0.3 cm/y × 2 years or ≥ 0.5 cm in 1 year → surgery (I)

EXAM TRAP · THE AORTA IS ITS OWN INDICATION

A patient with a BAV, mild AR and a root of 52 mm (root phenotype) needs surgery for the aorta (ESC 2024 Class I at ≥ 50 mm) — even though the valve alone would not justify it. Conversely, when the valve needs surgery, replace an aorta ≥ 45 mm at the same operation.

Family screening and surveillance

Any BAV: TTE screening of first-degree relatives is reasonable. IIa B-NR

BAV with aorta ≥ 4.0 cm (including after AVR): lifelong surveillance imaging, interval by diameter and growth rate.

I B-NR

BAV with HTAD or Loeys–Dietz features: medical genetics evaluation. I C-LD

CLINICAL APPROACH · PRACTICAL AORTIC SURVEILLANCE IN BAV

At diagnosis: TTE + one-time CT or CMR of the entire thoracic aorta (and exclusion of coarctation). Normal aorta: re-image every few years; dilated aorta: yearly once ≥ ~45 mm, or sooner if growth ≥ 3 mm/year.

Continue surveillance after isolated AVR — the root phenotype keeps growing.

Blood pressure control; avoid fluoroquinolones in established aneurysm (collagen toxicity signal) — individual judgement.

Key highlightsBicuspid aortopathy

  • Ascending phenotype is commonest (older, AS); root phenotype (young men, AR) grows faster and dissects more.
  • Universal threshold ≥ 55 mm (Class I) for tricuspid and bicuspid valves.
  • ESC 2024: BAV root phenotype ≥ 50 mm → surgery (I B).
  • ACC/AHA 2022: BAV 50–54 mm + risk factor (family history, growth ≥ 0.3 cm/y, coarctation, root phenotype) → IIa; area/height ≥ 10 cm²/m → IIa.
  • At aortic valve surgery, replace an aorta ≥ 45 mm (IIa, both).
  • Marfan ≥ 50 mm (≥ 45 with risk factors); Loeys–Dietz ≥ 45 mm; Turner ASI ≥ 2.5 cm/m².
  • Screen first-degree relatives by TTE — Class I when the proband's aorta is dilated.
  • Confirm surgical diameters with ECG-gated CT; keep imaging after AVR.
  • Exercise and sport
  • Asymptomatic mild–moderate AR with normal LV: most sports permitted with periodic review.
  • Significant aortic dilatation: avoid high-intensity isometric/static exercise and contact sport; tailor by diameter, phenotype and genetics.

11.9 Follow-up & Special Situations

Pregnancy

Chronic AR (even severe) with normal LV is usually well tolerated — the fall in SVR and rise in heart rate reduce regurgitation.

The risk lies in the aorta: pregnancy is advised against (mWHO IV) with a BAV aorta > 50 mm, Marfan aorta > 45 mm, or Turner ASI > 2.5 cm/m²; consider prophylactic surgery before conception. Marfan/BAV with dilated aorta: β-blocker throughout pregnancy; serial echo; delivery planning (caesarean when aorta significantly dilated).

ACE inhibitors/ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.

BOARD PEARL · ENDOCARDITIS PROPHYLAXIS

Native AR or a BAV alone does not require antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures under ESC guidance — prophylaxis is for prosthetic valves (including TAVI and repair with prosthetic material), previous IE and certain congenital lesions. Good dental hygiene is recommended for all.

Key highlightsFollow-up & special situations

  • Severe asymptomatic AR: review at least yearly; every 3–6 months near thresholds.
  • Borderline LV measurements → confirm with CMR before deciding on surgery.
  • Pregnancy is generally tolerated in AR; the aorta sets the risk (BAV > 50 mm, Marfan > 45 mm, Turner ASI > 2.5 cm/m²).
  • ACE-i/ARB are contraindicated in pregnancy — use β-blockers for aortopathy.
  • Native AR/BAV alone is not an indication for dental antibiotic prophylaxis.

11.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 45-year-old injecting drug user with Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia develops acute breathlessness. BP 85/50 mmHg, HR 125/min, bilateral crackles. TOE: perforated non-coronary cusp with severe AR, normal LV size, premature mitral valve closure. Which is the most appropriate management?

Answer C Acute severe AR from endocarditis with shock and pulmonary oedema → emergency surgery, bridged by inotrope ± vasodilator. IABP (A) increases regurgitation; β-blockade (B) removes the compensatory tachycardia; delaying surgery for antibiotics (D) is wrong in haemodynamic failure; TAVI (E) is contraindicated in active endocarditis.

Q2 A 38-year-old woman (BSA 1.55 m²) with a bicuspid valve and severe AR is asymptomatic and runs regularly. LVEF 60%, LVESD 41 mm, LVEDD 63 mm, aorta 39 mm. According to ESC/EACTS 2025, what is recommended?

Answer B LVESDi = 41/1.55 ≈ 26.5 mm/m² > 25 mm/m² → Class I surgery despite LVESD < 50 mm. Indexing protects small patients from late surgery. Vasodilators (C) do not delay surgery; LVEDD (D) is not an ESC criterion.

Q3 A 60-year-old man with asymptomatic severe AR has LVEF 53% (confirmed by CMR), LVESD 46 mm. His surgical risk is low. Which statement is correct?

Answer B ACC/AHA 2020 makes LVEF ≤ 55% a Class I trigger (stage C2). ESC 2025 uses LVEF ≤ 50% for Class I; LVEF ≤ 55% in a low-risk patient is IIb B.

Q4 A 55-year-old man with severe chronic AR has a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex. There is no opening snap and the mitral leaflets are thin and mobile on echo. The rumble softens after amyl nitrite. What is it?

Answer C Austin Flint: the AR jet restricts anterior mitral leaflet opening, producing an apical diastolic rumble without an opening snap; it softens with afterload reduction. Carey Coombs is acute rheumatic valvulitis; Graham Steell is pulmonary regurgitation.

Q5 Which echocardiographic finding is most specific for severe aortic regurgitation?

Answer C Holodiastolic reversal in the abdominal aorta is highly specific for severe AR. Colour jet length (A) is unreliable; PHT 380 ms (B) and VC 4 mm (D) suggest moderate AR.

Q6 A 29-year-old man with a bicuspid valve and mild AR has a sinus of Valsalva diameter of 51 mm (tubular ascending 40 mm) on gated CT, stable over a year. Family history is negative. What does ESC 2024 recommend?

Answer B BAV root phenotype (sinus > tubular, young man) behaves like a heritable aortopathy: ESC 2024 recommends surgery at ≥ 50 mm (I B). Waiting to 55 mm (A, C) applies to the ascending phenotype. TAVI (E) does not treat the aorta.

Q7 A 63-year-old man with a bicuspid valve is scheduled for SAVR for severe symptomatic AS. Gated CT shows a tubular ascending aorta of 47 mm. What is the best approach?

Answer C When aortic valve surgery is indicated, concomitant replacement of an aorta ≥ 45 mm is reasonable (ACC/AHA 2022 IIa; ESC IIa). A second sternotomy for the aorta later carries higher risk. TAVI (B) would leave the aneurysm.

Q8 A 34-year-old woman has a bicuspid valve with an ascending aorta of 46 mm. She has two children and a brother. What is the recommended family evaluation (ACC/AHA 2022)?

Answer C BAV is heritable (~9–10% of first-degree relatives affected); with a dilated aorta in the proband, TTE screening of all first-degree relatives is Class I (C-LD). FBN1 testing (B) is for suspected Marfan.

Q9 A 24-year-old woman with Turner syndrome (height 1.45 m, BSA 1.3 m²) has a bicuspid valve and an ascending aorta of 34 mm. She is considering pregnancy. What is the key issue?

Answer B In Turner syndrome absolute diameters mislead; ASI = 3.4/1.3 ≈ 2.6 cm/m². An ASI > 2.5 cm/m² carries high dissection risk — pregnancy is advised against (mWHO IV). ACE inhibitors (D) are teratogenic.

Q10 An 86-year-old frail man with severe symptomatic AR (NYHA III), non-calcified tricuspid valve, porcelain aorta and STS-PROM 12% is declined for surgery. CT shows a suitable annulus and root. What is the most appropriate option under ESC 2025?

Answer B ESC 2025 introduced TAVI for severe AR (IIb B) in symptomatic inoperable patients with suitable anatomy, using dedicated devices that grasp the leaflets. Conventional valves (A) risk embolisation in a non-calcified annulus; valvuloplasty (C) worsens AR; IABP (E) is contraindicated.
