12.1 Acute Rheumatic Fever & the Jones Criteria

Epidemiology and pathogenesis

Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is a delayed, non-suppurative autoimmune sequel of group A β-haemolytic streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis (not skin infection in classic teaching, although impetigo is now recognised as a contributor in some endemic settings). It follows the sore throat after a latent period of 2–3 weeks (chorea: 6–8 weeks or longer). Peak age is 5–15 years. Only about 0.3–3% of untreated GAS pharyngitis leads to ARF, so host susceptibility matters.

Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) — the chronic valvular damage that follows single severe or repeated attacks — remains the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children and young adults in low- and middle-income countries (South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East including parts of Egypt, and indigenous populations of Oceania). In high-income countries it is now a disease of immigrants and the elderly.

MECHANISM — MOLECULAR MIMICRY

Streptococcal M protein and N-acetyl-glucosamine share epitopes with cardiac myosin, laminin, valvular endothelium and basal-ganglia neurons. Cross-reactive antibodies and T cells produce a pancarditis (valvulitis dominant), arthritis (immune-complex, non-erosive), chorea (anti-neuronal antibodies) and skin lesions. The pathognomonic lesion is the Aschoff body (granuloma with Anitschkow "caterpillar" cells). As the aphorism has it, ARF "licks the joints but bites the heart".

The 2015 AHA Revised Jones Criteria

The 2015 revision made three changes that are examined repeatedly: (1) subclinical carditis detected by echocardiography now counts as a major criterion in all populations ; (2) criteria are stratified by the background risk of the population; (3) in moderate/high-risk populations monoarthritis and polyarthralgia can be major criteria, and the fever and ESR thresholds are lower.

DEFINITION — LOW-RISK POPULATION

ARF incidence ≤ 2 per 100,000 school-aged children (5–14 years) per year or all-age RHD prevalence ≤ 1 per 1000 population per year. Anyone not clearly from a low-risk setting is treated as moderate/high risk.

  • Major — carditis Clinical and/or subclinical (echo) Clinical and/or subclinical (echo)
  • Major — arthritis Polyarthritis only Monoarthritis or polyarthritis
  • Polyarthralgia (after excluding other causes)
  • Major — others Chorea · Erythema marginatum ·
  • Subcutaneous nodules
  • Chorea · Erythema marginatum ·
  • Subcutaneous nodules
  • Minor — joints Polyarthralgia Monoarthralgia
  • Minor — fever ≥ 38.5 °C ≥ 38.0 °C
  • Minor — inflammation Peak ESR ≥ 60 mm/h and/or CRP
  • ≥ 3.0 mg/dL
  • Peak ESR ≥ 30 mm/h and/or CRP ≥ 3.0 mg/dL
  • Component Low-risk population Moderate/high-risk population
  • Minor — ECG Prolonged PR for age (not if carditis is a
  • major)
  • Prolonged PR for age (not if carditis is a
  • major)
  • Initial ARF 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor

Recurrent ARF 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, or 3 minor

Adapted from Gewitz MH et al., AHA Scientific Statement, Circulation 2015. CRP must exceed the laboratory upper limit of normal; use the peak ESR.

EXAM TRAP — DOUBLE COUNTING

A joint manifestation counts once: if arthritis is used as a major criterion, arthralgia cannot be added as a minor.

A prolonged PR interval cannot be a minor criterion when carditis is already counted as a major. Exceptions to the GAS prerequisite: Sydenham chorea alone, or indolent carditis presenting months after the infection, may be sufficient for diagnosis — antibody titres have often normalised.

The five major manifestations

Accentuated by heat; associated with carditis

DON'T CONFUSE — POST-STREPTOCOCCAL REACTIVE ARTHRITIS (PSRA)

PSRA follows a shorter latency (< 10 days), is non-migratory, cumulative, involves small joints and axial skeleton, lasts longer and responds poorly to aspirin. Carditis is uncommon, but because the distinction is imperfect many authorities give secondary prophylaxis for about a year and re-image.

Investigations in suspected ARF

For every case
  • ESR and CRP (peak values)
  • Throat swab before antibiotics
  • ASO + anti-DNase B; repeat at 10–14 days if nondiagnostic
  • ECG — PR prolongation, sinus tachycardia,
  • occasionally higher-degree block
  • Chest X-ray, blood cultures if febrile
  • Echocardiography in all confirmed or
  • suspected cases
To exclude mimics
  • Septic arthritis — joint aspirate
  • Infective endocarditis — repeated blood cultures
  • SLE, JIA, reactive/viral arthritis — ANA, serology
  • Chorea mimics — Wilson (copper,
  • caeruloplasmin), drugs, SLE
  • Sickle-cell crisis, leukaemia — blood film

12.2 Treatment of ARF & Secondary Prophylaxis

Treatment has four aims: eradicate residual streptococci, suppress inflammation and relieve symptoms, manage heart failure, and — the only intervention proven to change the natural history — start secondary prophylaxis to prevent recurrences . Anti-inflammatory drugs relieve symptoms but have not been shown to prevent valve damage.

Key highlightsAcute rheumatic fever & Jones criteria

  • ARF follows GAS pharyngitis after 2–3 weeks; chorea after 6–8 weeks or more.
  • Diagnosis = evidence of GAS infection + 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor; recurrence may also be 3 minor. 2015 Jones: echo-detected (subclinical) carditis counts as a major criterion in all populations.
  • Low-risk population: ARF incidence ≤ 2/100,000 children/year or RHD prevalence ≤ 1/1000.
  • Moderate/high risk: monoarthritis and polyarthralgia become major; fever ≥ 38 °C and ESR ≥ 30 are minor.
  • Carditis = valvulitis; MR is the commonest acute lesion; MS appears years later.
  • Chorea alone or indolent carditis can establish ARF without GAS evidence.
  • Never double-count joints, or PR prolongation when carditis is major.
  • Target Treatment Notes
  • Chorea Supportive; carbamazepine or valproate (or haloperidol) if
  • disabling
  • Self-limiting in 8–15 weeks (up to
  • 2 years).
  • Activity Rest while febrile/arthritic; avoid strenuous exertion with
  • carditis
  • Strict bed rest has no proven
  • benefit.
  • Primary vs secondary prevention
  • Primary prevention = adequate treatment of GAS pharyngitis (single IM benzathine penicillin or 10 days of oral penicillin, started within 9 days of symptom onset), which reduces ARF attacks by up to 70–80%. Its weakness: up to one-third of patients with ARF do not recall a sore throat.
  • Secondary prevention = continuous antibiotic prophylaxis in anyone with prior ARF or established RHD.
  • Intramuscular benzathine penicillin is superior to oral penicillin; 2-weekly injections reduce recurrences more than 4-weekly, and 3-weekly dosing is used in high-risk patients or where recurrence occurs despite adherence.
BOARD PEARL

"Whichever is longer" is the key phrase. A 17-year-old with ARF and mild carditis needs prophylaxis until 27 (10 years) — not until 25. Prophylaxis continues after PMC or valve replacement: the new valve does not protect the other valves from recurrent carditis.

EXAM TRAP — PROPHYLAXIS≠ENDOCARDITIS PROPHYLAXIS

Rheumatic-fever prophylaxis does not double as endocarditis prophylaxis. Oral streptococci in patients on long-term penicillin are often relatively penicillin-resistant, so when IE prophylaxis is indicated (e.g. prosthetic valve, previous IE) AHA advice is to choose an agent from a different class (e.g. a macrolide or, where still used locally, clindamycin) rather than simply giving more penicillin.

12.3 Echocardiographic Diagnosis of RHD (WHF 2023)

Auscultation misses most early RHD. Screening studies in endemic regions find 3–10× more disease by echo than by stethoscope. The World Heart Federation (WHF) criteria, first published in 2012 and simplified in 2023, separate pathological regurgitation from the physiological trace MR/AR that is common in healthy children, and stage the disease to guide prophylaxis.

Timing Pansystolic in ≥ 1 envelope Pandiastolic in ≥ 1 envelope

Rwebembera J et al., 2023 WHF guidelines for the echocardiographic diagnosis of RHD. Nat Rev Cardiol 2024. Jet length is measured from the vena contracta to the last pixel of colour on non-zoomed images.

Key highlightsTreatment & secondary prophylaxis

  • Give benzathine penicillin at diagnosis even if the throat swab is negative.
  • Aspirin/naproxen for arthritis; response within 48 h supports the diagnosis.
  • Steroids (prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day) for severe carditis — symptomatic benefit, no proven valve protection.
  • Secondary prophylaxis: benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU IM every 3–4 weeks; IM beats oral.
  • No carditis: 5 years or to age 18–21; mild carditis: 10 years or to age 21–25; significant RHD: to age 40 or lifelong.
  • ESC 2025: 1.2 MIU every 3–4 weeks for 10 years in established RHD; lifelong if high risk.
  • Only secondary prophylaxis alters the natural history of RHD.
WHAT CHANGED IN WHF 2023 (VS 2012)

The 2012 "borderline" and "definite" RHD categories were replaced by a risk-based staging (A–D). Weight-adjusted MR jet length (1.5 cm in children < 30 kg) and age-adjusted leaflet-thickness cut-offs. Explicit guidance for handheld/simplified screening by non-experts, with confirmatory full echo. Echo criteria for carditis during ARF now require pathological MR and/or AR — consistent with the Jones requirement that carditis means valvulitis.

12.4 Rheumatic MS: Pathology, Physiology & Bedside

Aetiology and pathology

Rheumatic disease causes the vast majority of MS worldwide; about two-thirds of patients are women. The latent interval from ARF to symptomatic MS is ≈ 20 years in high-income countries but can be under 10 years in endemic regions, where juvenile MS in teenagers is still seen. In Western series degenerative MS due to mitral annular calcification (MAC) now accounts for a large share of severe MS (see 12.9). The hallmark of rheumatic MS is commissural fusion , beginning at the leaflet tips. Leaflet thickening, chordal fusion and shortening (a "subvalvular mat") and calcification follow. The orifice becomes a funnel with a fish-mouth shape in short axis; the still-pliable anterior leaflet body bows into the LV in diastole — the hockey-stick (diastolic doming) appearance.

Rheumatic MS
  • Commissural fusion — obligatory
  • Disease starts at tips and commissures
  • Subvalvular involvement common
  • Annulus spared
  • Amenable to PMC
Degenerative (MAC) MS
  • No commissural fusion
  • Calcium starts at the annulus / leaflet base
  • Tips and chordae spared
  • Elderly, CKD, hypertension

PMC useless

Rarer causes: radiation (aorto-mitral curtain calcification), congenital (parachute mitral valve — single papillary muscle; Shone complex), carcinoid (left-sided only with PFO or lung metastases), SLE/antiphospholipid, drugs (ergot, fenfluramine), mucopolysaccharidoses, and prosthetic/iatrogenic MS (small annuloplasty ring, TEER with multiple clips). Mimics of MS physiology: LA myxoma and cor triatriatum.

Key highlightsEcho diagnosis of RHD

  • Pathological MR: 2 views, jet ≥ 2 cm, velocity ≥ 3 m/s, pansystolic — all four needed.
  • Pathological AR: jet ≥ 1 cm, velocity ≥ 3 m/s, pandiastolic, 2 views.
  • Rheumatic anterior mitral leaflet: thickness ≥ 3 mm in those ≤ 20 years.
  • Stage A (isolated pathological regurgitation, young): prophylaxis optional; Stage B onwards: prophylaxis recommended.
  • Any MS (mean gradient ≥ 4 mmHg) = Stage C.
  • Excessive anterior leaflet tip motion suggests acute valvulitis.
  • Pathophysiology
  • The normal MVA is 4–6 cm². A diastolic gradient appears once the area falls below ≈ 2 cm²; symptoms on exertion become common at ≤ 1.5 cm² and at rest at ≤ 1.0 cm². The LA pressure rises to keep LV filling — the LV itself is usually protected (normal or small, normal function).
MECHANISM — WHY TACHYCARDIA IS THE E N E M Y

By the Gorlin relation, gradient ∝ (flow / area)². Flow across the mitral valve occurs only in diastole, so diastolic flow rate = stroke volume ÷ diastolic filling time. Tachycardia shortens diastole far more than systole, so the flow rate — and therefore the gradient (as its square) — rises steeply. Doubling the heart rate can more than double the gradient. This explains decompensation with AF, exercise, fever, anaemia, thyrotoxicosis and pregnancy (↑ CO and ↑ HR), and why β-blockers and rate control relieve symptoms.

Consequences cascade backward: LA dilatation → AF (in up to 40–60% of older patients) and LA/LAA thrombus → systemic embolism; pulmonary venous hypertension → passive (post-capillary) PH, which in some patients becomes combined pre- and post-capillary ("second stenosis") → RV pressure overload, functional TR, right HF. The LV may show low stroke volume from underfilling. Symptoms and complications

Exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND — often unmasked by AF, pregnancy or infection.

Haemoptysis: frothy (pulmonary oedema), pink; frank bleeding from ruptured dilated bronchial veins (pulmonary apoplexy); infarction; winter bronchitis.

Systemic embolism — may be the first presentation (stroke, limb, mesenteric).

Pressure effects of the giant LA: Ortner syndrome (hoarseness — left recurrent laryngeal nerve), dysphagia.

Fatigue, cold peripheries and ascites in advanced PH/low output; mitral facies (malar flush).

Examination

Pulmonary hypertension Advanced disease — intervene

DIFFERENTIAL — DIASTOLIC APICAL RUMBLE WITHOUT RHEUMATIC MS
  • Austin Flint murmur (severe AR): no loud S1, no OS.
  • Carey Coombs murmur: acute rheumatic valvulitis.
  • High-flow rumble: severe MR, large VSD/PDA — accompanied by S3 (an S3 argues against significant MS).
  • LA myxoma: tumour plop, positional symptoms, constitutional features.

ECG and chest X-ray

ECG: P mitrale (broad, notched P > 120 ms in II; deep negative terminal P in V1), AF, right-axis deviation and RVH when PH develops. LVH is not expected — if present, look for coexisting AR, MR or AS. CXR: straightened left heart border (enlarged LAA), double right heart border, splayed carina (> 90°), upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, prominent PA; occasionally mitral calcification or pulmonary haemosiderosis/ossification.

12.5 Grading Severity: Echo, Stress & Catheter

TTE is the key investigation: it confirms the rheumatic mechanism, grades severity, assesses consequences (LA size, SPAP, RV, TR), detects associated lesions and — critically — judges suitability for PMC. Planimetry of the MVA is the reference method because it measures the anatomical orifice and is independent of flow and heart rate.

SPAP (mmHg) < 30–50 > 50 often > 60

ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 define severe (clinically significant) MS as MVA ≤ 1.5 cm². *"Very severe" (≤ 1.0 cm²) was an ACC/AHA 2014 category and remains useful descriptively. Gradients are heart-rate and flow dependent and are not used to define severity.

Key highlightsRheumatic MS — pathology & bedside

  • Commissural fusion defines rheumatic MS and is what PMC splits.
  • Normal MVA 4–6 cm²; symptoms at ≤ 1.5 cm²; rest symptoms at ≤ 1.0 cm².
  • Gradient rises with the square of flow — tachycardia, AF and pregnancy precipitate failure.
  • Loud S1 + OS = pliable valve; the shorter the A2–OS interval, the tighter the stenosis.
  • Murmur length, not intensity, tracks severity; presystolic accentuation disappears in AF.
  • LV is protected in pure MS — LVH or LV dilatation implies another lesion.
  • Ortner syndrome = hoarseness from LA/PA compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
  • Four ways to measure MVA — and how each fails

Gain too high → underestimates

Pressure half-time MVA = 220 / PHT (Hatle) Invalid immediately after PMC (first 24–72 h) — abrupt change in LA/LV compliance

  • Significant AR (LV fills from two sides → PHT shortened
  • → MVA overestimated)
  • Stiff LV (elderly, LVH, HFpEF) shortens PHT;
  • tachycardia/AF with short diastoles; MAC-related MS;
  • ASD

Continuity equation MVA = LVOT area × VTILVOT / VTIMV Invalid with significant MR or AR; AF (average several beats)

  • PISA Flow convergence on atrial side,
  • corrected for funnel angle

Technically demanding; angle correction

EXAM TRAP — THE PHT THAT LIES

A patient with MS and moderate–severe AR has PHT 120 ms: the calculated MVA (1.8 cm²) is falsely large, because the regurgitant jet raises LV diastolic pressure and shortens the half-time. Use planimetry. Likewise, do not judge the result of PMC by PHT in the first 1–3 days.

Stress testing and discordance

Exercise (preferably) or dobutamine stress echo is indicated when symptoms and severity disagree — an asymptomatic patient with severe MS, or a symptomatic patient with only moderate MS.

Haemodynamically significant response: mean gradient > 15 mmHg on exercise (> 18 mmHg with dobutamine) and/or SPAP > 60 mmHg, or invasive PCWP > 25 mmHg with exercise.

If the gradient rises but the LV diastolic pressure does not, the MS is limiting; if both LVEDP and PCWP rise with an unchanged gradient, the symptoms are from LV diastolic dysfunction.

TOE, CT and catheterisation

TOE: mandatory before PMC to exclude LA/LAA thrombus and grade MR; after an embolic event; when TTE is inadequate. TOE is not better than TTE for the subvalvular apparatus.

Catheterisation: only when non-invasive data are inconclusive or discordant. Use a trans-septal LA pressure — PCWP overestimates the gradient (phase delay, damping, especially with coexisting MR). Severe MS: no LA–LV diastasis even at slow heart rates; giant LA a wave; slow y descent. Gorlin formula: MVA = CO / (DFP × HR × 37.7 × √mean gradient) — underestimates at low output.

BOARD PEARL — "SEVERE GRADIENT,MODERATE AREA"

MVA 1.7 cm² but mean gradient 14 mmHg at HR 115: first slow the heart rate and correct the high-output state (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, fever, pregnancy). A gradient must always be reported with its heart rate.

Conversely, a "low" gradient at HR 55 in low-output AF does not exclude severe MS.

12.6 Valve Anatomy, Wilkins Score & PMC Suitability

Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy (PMC) — also called balloon mitral valvotomy (BMV/PMBC) — uses a trans-septal Inoue balloon to split the fused commissures. It works only when there is commissural fusion to split and when the leaflets are pliable enough not to tear. Anatomical scoring therefore predicts both immediate success and complications.

EXAM TRAP — WHAT THE WILKINS SCORE MISSES

Commissural calcification (especially bicommissural) predicts failure and severe MR even with a low score.

  • Pre-existing MR is not included.
  • Uneven leaflet thickening and asymmetric commissural fusion predict leaflet tears.

The Cormier score (group 1–3; group 3 = any calcification on fluoroscopy) and newer 3D/commissural scores address these gaps.

Key highlightsGrading MS severity

  • Severe MS = MVA ≤ 1.5 cm² (ESC 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020); planimetry is the reference.
  • MVA = 220/PHT; PHT ≥ 150 ms ≈ severe, ≥ 220 ms ≈ MVA ≤ 1.0 cm².
  • PHT is unreliable early after PMC, with significant AR, stiff LV, ASD and MAC.
  • Gradient depends on HR and flow — always quote the heart rate; supportive, not defining.
  • Exercise mean gradient > 15 mmHg or SPAP > 60 mmHg = haemodynamically significant.
  • TOE before PMC to exclude LA thrombus; trans-septal (not PCWP) pressures for invasive grading.

Severe TR

ESC/EACTS VHD guidelines; unfavourable features are cumulative — a single one does not exclude PMC.

CLINICAL APPROACH — LA THROMBUS FOUND ON TOE

Anticoagulate with a VKA for 1–3 months and repeat TOE. If the thrombus has resolved, PMC can proceed; if it persists, surgery is preferred. A small thrombus confined to the LAA tip may be tolerated by very experienced operators, but the board answer is anticoagulate and re-image.

Results and complications of PMC

Success = final MVA ≥ 1.5 cm² (or doubling of the area) with no more than moderate (2+) MR. In favourable anatomy success exceeds 90%; the MVA typically doubles and SPAP falls promptly.

Complications
  • Procedural mortality ≈ 0.5–2%
  • Severe MR 2–10% — the most important; may
  • need urgent surgery
  • Tamponade (trans-septal or LV perforation) ≈ 1%
  • Embolism/stroke 0.5–1%
  • Residual iatrogenic ASD — usually small,
  • haemodynamically trivial
Long-term
  • Event-free survival ≈ 70–90% at 10 years in
  • favourable anatomy
  • Restenosis — repeat PMC possible if restenosis is
  • due to commissural refusion
  • Outcomes equal or superior to surgical closed or
  • open commissurotomy in RCTs
  • Continue rheumatic prophylaxis and
  • surveillance

Key highlightsWilkins score & PMC suitability

  • Wilkins score: mobility, thickening, calcification, subvalvular apparatus — each 1–4, total 4–16.
  • Score ≤ 8 favourable; ≥ 12 surgery; commissural calcium predicts failure regardless of score.
  • Absolute contraindications: LA thrombus, > mild MR, bicommissural/severe calcification, no commissural fusion, need for other cardiac surgery.
  • LA thrombus → VKA 1–3 months → repeat TOE.
  • PMC success = MVA ≥ 1.5 cm² with ≤ moderate MR; commonest serious complication is severe MR.
  • Repeat PMC is feasible for restenosis caused by commissural refusion.

12.7 Indications for Intervention: PMC vs Surgery

Severe symptomatic MS is a mechanical problem: medical therapy relieves congestion and slows the heart rate but does not alter prognosis. Untreated, 10-year survival once symptoms appear is roughly 50–60%, and patients in NYHA class IV rarely survive a few years. The decision tree has three questions: Is MS severe (MVA ≤ 1.5 cm²)? Are there symptoms or high-risk features? Is the anatomy (and clinical profile) favourable for PMC?

Asymptomatic patients

PMC should be considered in asymptomatic patients without unfavourable clinical/anatomical features who have high thromboembolic risk (prior embolism, dense LA spontaneous contrast, new-onset or paroxysmal AF) and/or high risk of haemodynamic decompensation (resting SPAP > 50 mmHg, need for major non-cardiac surgery, desire for pregnancy).

IIa C

Class/level as published in ESC/EACTS 2021; the 2025 guideline retains PMC as first-line therapy for clinically severe rheumatic MS (MVA ≤ 1.5 cm²) with favourable morphology and no contraindication.

Surgery

Closed commissurotomy (off-pump) — historic, still used in some low-resource settings; now largely replaced by PMC.

Open commissurotomy / repair — on bypass; allows thrombus removal, chordal release; durable in selected valves.

Mitral valve replacement — for heavily calcified, fibrotic valves or combined significant MR; mechanical valves are commonly chosen in young patients but raise the pregnancy/anticoagulation problem. Preserve the subvalvular apparatus where possible.

At surgery for MS with AF: concomitant surgical AF ablation and LAA occlusion/exclusion should be considered.

Moderate or severe TR (or tricuspid annular dilatation) → concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty.

Medical therapy and follow-up

Diuretics for congestion; β-blockers or rate-limiting CCBs (or ivabradine in sinus rhythm) lengthen diastole and lower the gradient. Digoxin helps rate control in AF.

β-blockade is one of the few situations in which acute pulmonary oedema benefits from a negatively chronotropic drug (others: HOCM with LVOTO).

Follow-up: asymptomatic severe MS yearly (clinical + echo); moderate MS every 2–3 years; after successful PMC as for asymptomatic patients, more often if restenosis.

Continue secondary rheumatic prophylaxis throughout.

BOARD PEARL — "MODERATE MS BUT BREATHLESS"

MVA 1.6–2.0 cm² with exertional dyspnoea: do an exercise echo. A mean gradient > 15 mmHg or SPAP > 60 mmHg with an unchanged LV filling pressure means the MS is responsible; also remember that MVA should be interpreted relative to body size — 1.6 cm² in a large patient may behave as severe.

12.8 AF, Anticoagulation & Pregnancy

Atrial fibrillation in MS

AF is common (rare in young patients in endemic regions, but in over half of older Western patients) and is a turning point: loss of atrial transport plus a fast ventricular rate can precipitate pulmonary oedema, and the combination of MS and AF carries a stroke risk far higher than either alone — historically quoted at up to 10–15% per year untreated. CHA₂DS₂-VA is not used: anticoagulation is indicated irrespective of score. Rate control: β-blockers first line; non-dihydropyridine CCB; digoxin as add-on.

Rhythm control: reasonable for new-onset AF with a small LA and short duration; amiodarone is the most effective drug. Cardioversion is best performed after PMC in severe MS because sinus rhythm is rarely durable while the stenosis persists.

Catheter ablation is less effective than in non-valvular AF; surgical ablation is preferred when the patient is going to theatre anyway.

VKA versus DOAC — the INVICTUS verdict

LANDMARK TRIAL — INVICTUS (NEJM 2022)

About 4500 patients with rheumatic heart disease and AF (most with MS) were randomised to rivaroxaban or dose-adjusted VKA. Rivaroxaban led to more of the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, MI or vascular/unknown death, and higher all-cause mortality (excess sudden and HF deaths), without less major bleeding. → VKA remains the anticoagulant of choice in AF with rheumatic MS.

Key highlightsIndications for intervention in MS

  • Intervene for symptomatic severe MS (MVA ≤ 1.5 cm²): PMC if anatomy favourable (ESC I B; ACC/AHA 1 A).
  • Surgery if unsuitable for PMC (ESC I C); PMC if surgery contraindicated or high risk (I C).
  • Suboptimal anatomy but favourable clinical profile → PMC first (ESC IIa C).
  • Asymptomatic: PMC for SPAP > 50 mmHg, high embolic risk (prior embolism, dense SEC, new/paroxysmal AF), planned pregnancy or major NCS.
  • ACC/AHA: asymptomatic + SPAP > 50 = 2a; new AF = 2b; exercise PCWP > 25 / gradient > 15 with MVA > 1.5 = 2b.
  • ESC excludes PMC with more than mild MR; ACC/AHA with ≥ moderate.
  • β-blockers/rate control and diuretics are bridges, not definitive treatment.
  • Situation Recommendation
  • AF + mild MS (MVA > 2.0 cm²), MR, AS, AR or
  • bioprosthesis > 3 months
  • DOAC preferred over VKA
  • Mechanical valve (any position) VKA only — DOACs contraindicated
WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 (ESC/EACTS)

The DOAC exclusion is now defined anatomically: MS with valve area ≤ 2.0 cm² (previously "moderateto-severe MS"), reflecting the INVICTUS population. Severe rheumatic MS is referred to as clinically severe MS (MVA ≤ 1.5 cm²).

A transcatheter option (TMVI) is introduced for selected inoperable patients with MAC-related MS (see 12.9).

EXAM TRAP — "NON-VALVULAR AF"

The old label "valvular AF" meant only two things: moderate–severe (rheumatic) MS and mechanical heart valves. A patient with AF and severe MR, AS or a bioprosthesis is a DOAC candidate. The ESC 2024 AF guideline dropped the term, but the exclusions remain.

Pregnancy — a pointer

MS is the valve lesion most likely to decompensate in pregnancy: the 30–50% rise in cardiac output and the higher heart rate raise the gradient steeply, typically in the second trimester (peak output, 24–30 weeks) and around delivery/first 72 h postpartum (autotransfusion). MS is often first diagnosed in pregnancy in endemic countries. Pre-conception: intervention (preferably PMC) is advised for MVA < 1.5 cm² before pregnancy; severe MS is a high-risk (mWHO III–IV) lesion.

During pregnancy: restrict activity, β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol, bisoprolol) and cautious diuretics.

PMC in pregnancy for NYHA III–IV or SPAP > 50 mmHg despite medical therapy, ideally after 20 weeks in an experienced centre with abdominal shielding. Surgery on bypass carries high fetal loss. Delivery: vaginal delivery with epidural for most; caesarean reserved for obstetric reasons or refractory severe MS/PH.

Anticoagulation for AF/thrombus follows the pregnancy guideline (LMWH versus VKA by trimester and dose). Full detail: see the chapter on heart disease in pregnancy.

Key highlightsAF, anticoagulation & pregnancy

  • AF + rheumatic MS → VKA irrespective of CHA₂DS₂-VA; target INR 2.0–3.0.
  • INVICTUS: rivaroxaban inferior to VKA in rheumatic AF, with higher mortality.
  • ESC 2025: DOACs not for AF with MS and MVA ≤ 2.0 cm², or mechanical valves.
  • Sinus rhythm + prior embolism or LA thrombus → VKA; dense SEC or large LA → consider VKA.
  • Cardioversion in severe MS is best done after PMC; amiodarone is the most effective antiarrhythmic.
  • Pregnancy: decompensation in the second trimester and peripartum; treat MVA < 1.5 cm² before conception.
  • PMC in pregnancy after 20 weeks for refractory symptoms or SPAP > 50 mmHg.

12.9 Degenerative (MAC) & Other Non-rheumatic MS

Mitral annular calcification (MAC) is a chronic degenerative process of the fibrous annulus, starting posteriorly. It is common in the elderly and associated with hypertension, diabetes, CKD/dialysis (calcium–phosphate), female sex, AS and atherosclerosis. Only a small minority (≈ 1–2%) develop degenerative mitral stenosis (DMS), when calcium extends into the base of the leaflets and narrows the inflow; MAC can equally cause MR by immobilising the leaflets and abolishing annular contraction.

Usually no OS; soft signs

Severity assessment Planimetry reliable Planimetry and PHT unreliable (non-planar orifice, stiff LV); continuity equation, mean gradient at controlled HR, CT

  • Progression MVA ↓ ≈ 0.1 cm²/year Slower (≈ 0.05 cm²/year)
  • PMC Treatment of choice Ineffective — nothing to split
  • Prognosis Excellent after PMC Poor — driven by age and comorbidity

Management of MAC-related MS

Confirm that MS — rather than LV diastolic dysfunction, AF or HFpEF — drives the symptoms (exercise echo, invasive haemodynamics).

Medical first: diuretics, heart-rate slowing (β-blocker, ivabradine), blood pressure and rhythm control. Surgery is high risk: extensive annular debridement risks atrioventricular groove disruption and circumflex injury; decisions are individualised by the Heart Team.

Transcatheter mitral valve implantation (TMVI) — valve-in-MAC using balloon-expandable TAVI valves or dedicated devices, or transcatheter surgery hybrids. Early registries show high procedural risk, LVOT obstruction (predicted by CT neo-LVOT area) and valve embolisation, with high 1-year mortality. ESC 2025 introduces TMVI as an option in highly selected inoperable patients with suitable anatomy (weak recommendation).

CT is essential to map calcium (distribution, circumferential extent) and to predict neo-LVOT obstruction.

Other non-rheumatic causes

Radiation-induced: calcification of the aorto-mitral curtain and anterior leaflet base, 10–20 years after mediastinal radiotherapy; often with AS, CAD, constriction. No commissural fusion → PMC not useful; redo sternotomy risk high.

Iatrogenic: after MV repair with a small annuloplasty ring (functional MS), after TEER (mean gradient > 5 mmHg predicts worse outcome), and prosthetic dysfunction (thrombus, pannus, degeneration, patient–prosthesis mismatch). Degenerated bioprostheses/rings can be treated by transcatheter valvein-valve / valve-in-ring. Congenital: parachute MV, supravalvular ring, Shone complex; Lutembacher syndrome = ASD + MS (the ASD decompresses the LA — the murmur may be soft and pulmonary oedema delayed; PHT

overestimates MVA).

Key highlightsDegenerative and other MS

  • MAC-related MS: elderly, CKD, calcium at the annulus/leaflet base, no commissural fusion — PMC is useless.
  • Planimetry and PHT are unreliable in MAC; use continuity, controlled-HR gradients and CT.
  • Treat medically first; surgery and TMVI are high risk — LVOT obstruction is the key TMVI hazard.
  • ESC 2025: TMVI may be considered (IIb) in highly selected inoperable MAC patients.
  • Radiation MS targets the aorto-mitral curtain; Lutembacher = ASD + MS.
  • After TEER, a mean gradient > 5 mmHg signals iatrogenic MS.

12.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 12-year-old boy in rural Upper Egypt (a high-risk population) presents with a swollen, painful right knee for 5 days, temperature 38.2 °C and ESR 45 mm/h. ASO titre is raised. Echocardiography shows no pathological regurgitation. Which statement is correct?

Answer B In moderate/high-risk populations monoarthritis is a major criterion and fever ≥ 38 °C and ESR ≥ 30 are minor — so 1 major + 2 minor with GAS evidence = ARF. The 38.5 °C and ESR 60 thresholds (C, D) apply to low-risk populations. PSRA has a shorter latency and poor NSAID response.

Q2 A 16-year-old girl had ARF with mild mitral regurgitation that resolved. In her country the WHO/WHF duration rules are followed. For how long should secondary prophylaxis continue?

Answer C Carditis with mild/resolved valve disease: 10 years after the last attack or until age 25, whichever is longer — 16 + 10 = 26. Five years/age 18 applies to ARF without carditis; lifelong/age 40 to significant RHD.

Q3 A 34-year-old woman has rheumatic MS with 2D planimetry MVA 1.1 cm², mean gradient 9 mmHg at HR 72, and moderate aortic regurgitation. The pressure half-time is 140 ms. What best explains the discrepancy?

Answer B Significant AR raises LV diastolic pressure and shortens the PHT, so 220/PHT gives a falsely large MVA (1.6 cm²). Planimetry is the reference. A basal plane (A) would overestimate planimetry, not PHT.

Q4 A 29-year-old woman with NYHA class II dyspnoea has MVA 1.0 cm², Wilkins score 7, trivial MR, no commissural calcium. TOE shows a 1.2 cm thrombus in the LA appendage. What is the next best step?

Answer C LA thrombus is a contraindication to PMC. Anticoagulate with a VKA for 1–3 months and repeat TOE; proceed if resolved, otherwise surgery. DOACs are not used in rheumatic MS.

Q5 A 45-year-old man with rheumatic MS (MVA 1.3 cm²) develops persistent AF. CHA₂DS₂-VA score is 0. Which anticoagulant strategy is recommended?

Answer D AF with rheumatic MS mandates a VKA irrespective of score. INVICTUS showed rivaroxaban was inferior with higher mortality; DOACs are not recommended with MVA ≤ 2.0 cm² (ESC 2025).

Q6 An asymptomatic 38-year-old woman has MVA 1.2 cm², Wilkins score 7, mild MR, no LA thrombus and resting SPAP 58 mmHg. What is the most appropriate management?

Answer B Asymptomatic severe MS with resting SPAP > 50 mmHg and favourable anatomy → PMC (ESC IIa; ACC/AHA 2a). Waiting risks irreversible PH. Pulmonary vasodilators are not indicated for post-capillary PH.

Q7 A 78-year-old woman on haemodialysis has exertional dyspnoea. Echo shows extensive posterior and anterior annular calcium extending into the leaflet bases, no commissural fusion, mean gradient 8 mmHg at HR 70. Which statement is correct?

Answer C MAC-related MS has no commissural fusion (PMC useless), PHT is unreliable (stiff LV, non-planar orifice), and there is rarely an OS. CT maps calcium and predicts neo-LVOT obstruction. Rheumatic prophylaxis is irrelevant.

Q8 Which auscultatory finding best indicates increasing severity of mitral stenosis?

Answer C Higher LA pressure opens the valve earlier, shortening A2–OS. Murmur length, not loudness, correlates with severity; an S3 argues against significant MS; S1 softens as the valve calcifies.

Q9 A 26-year-old woman with MVA 1.6 cm² reports dyspnoea on climbing stairs. Resting mean gradient is 6 mmHg at HR 68. What is the next best test?

Answer B Symptoms with only moderate MS: exercise echo. A mean gradient > 15 mmHg or SPAP > 60 mmHg on exercise indicates haemodynamically significant MS and may justify PMC.

Q10 A 24-year-old woman with known severe MS (MVA 0.9 cm²) is 26 weeks pregnant and in NYHA class III despite bisoprolol and furosemide. Anatomy is favourable. What is the best management?

Answer C Severe symptomatic MS in pregnancy despite medical therapy → PMC after 20 weeks in an experienced centre. Surgery on bypass carries high fetal loss; delivery or termination does not treat the valve.

13.1 Mitral Apparatus & Mechanisms of MR

The mitral valve is not two leaflets but an apparatus: a saddle-shaped annulus, anterior and posterior leaflets, chordae, two papillary muscles and the LV wall they arise from, plus the left atrium that carries the annulus. Competence requires all of them. Carpentier's surgical nomenclature divides each leaflet into three segments — posterior P1 (lateral), P2 (middle), P3 (medial) facing A1–A3 — with the anterolateral and posteromedial commissures between them.

DEFINITION — PRIMARY VS SECONDARY MR

Primary (degenerative/organic) MR: intrinsic disease of the leaflets or chordae — the valve is the disease .

Secondary (functional) MR: structurally normal leaflets that fail to coapt because the ventricle (ventricular SMR) or the atrium/annulus (atrial SMR) is remodelled — the valve is the victim . Primary MR is cured by fixing the valve; secondary MR is treated first by treating the ventricle or the atrium.

MECHANISM — JET DIRECTION POINTS TO THE LESION

Prolapse/flail: the jet goes away from the diseased leaflet — posterior leaflet flail → anteriorly directed jet hugging the aortic root side of the LA.

Restriction/tethering: the jet goes towards the restricted leaflet — inferior MI tethers P2/P3 → posteriorly directed jet. Ischaemic MR is central or posterior, never anterior.

Eccentric, wall-hugging (Coandă) jets look smaller on colour than they are — a classic cause of underestimation.

Causes worth knowing

Primary MR
  • Degenerative (MVP) — commonest in highincome countries
  • Rheumatic — commonest in endemic regions;
  • isolated MR in the young
  • Endocarditis (perforation, chordal rupture)
  • Congenital cleft (AVSD)
  • Connective tissue disease: Marfan, Ehlers–
  • Danlos
  • Drugs, radiation, MAC
Secondary MR
  • Ventricular: ischaemic cardiomyopathy, DCM,
  • LBBB/RV-pacing dyssynchrony (papillary muscle
  • dyssynchrony)
  • Atrial: long-standing AF, HFpEF, atrial myopathy
  • — annular dilatation and flattening with normal
  • LV
  • Dynamic/transient: ischaemia, takotsubo,
  • myocarditis, HOCM with SAM

13.2 Acute Mitral Regurgitation

In acute severe MR a normal-sized, non-compliant LA and LV receive a sudden volume load. LA pressure soars (giant v waves) → flash pulmonary oedema; forward stroke volume falls → cardiogenic shock, while LVEF is normal or hyperdynamic because the LV empties into the low-pressure LA.

Causes

Papillary muscle rupture after MI — classically the posteromedial muscle (single blood supply from the PDA, i.e. RCA or dominant circumflex), 2–7 days after an often small inferior/inferoposterior infarct.

Key highlightsAnatomy & mechanisms

  • Primary MR: diseased leaflets/chordae; secondary MR: normal leaflets, abnormal LV or LA.
  • Carpentier I = normal motion (annular dilatation, perforation); II = excessive (prolapse/flail); IIIa = restricted in systole and diastole (rheumatic); IIIb = systolic tethering (ischaemic/DCM).
  • P2 is the commonest prolapsing/flail segment.
  • Prolapse → jet away from the lesion; tethering → jet towards the restricted leaflet.
  • Inferior MI gives a posteriorly directed ischaemic MR jet; anterior jets are not ischaemic.
  • Atrial SMR = Carpentier type I with preserved LV size and function.
  • Spontaneous chordal rupture in degenerative disease (myxomatous or fibroelastic deficiency).
  • Infective endocarditis — perforation, chordal rupture.
  • Acute ischaemic tethering, takotsubo, myocarditis; trauma; prosthetic dysfunction.
  • Management
  • Afterload reduction: IV nitroprusside or nitrates if BP allows — increases forward flow and reduces regurgitant fraction.
  • Mechanical support: IABP (reduces afterload and augments coronary perfusion) or other MCS as a bridge.
  • Emergency surgery for papillary muscle rupture (with CABG as needed); replacement is often chosen for speed. Surgical mortality is high but medical mortality is prohibitive. Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is increasingly used in selected post-MI patients who are not surgical candidates.
  • Acute ischaemic tethering without rupture: revascularisation and unloading; MR often improves as the territory recovers.
EXAM TRAP — "THE MURMUR IS SOFT,SO THE MR IS MILD"

Day 4 after inferior STEMI: sudden pulmonary oedema, hypotension, a soft early systolic murmur, hyperdynamic LV on TTE with "only moderate" central MR. The board answer is urgent TOE for papillary muscle rupture and surgical referral. Differentiate from VSD (thrill, left-to-right step-up in O₂ saturation at RV level) — both give new murmurs and shock after MI.

13.3 Clinical Assessment & Echo Quantification

Symptoms and signs of chronic MR

Chronic severe MR is often asymptomatic for years because the dilated, compliant LA and eccentrically hypertrophied LV absorb the volume load. Fatigue and exertional dyspnoea, AF and palpitations follow. By the time symptoms appear, irreversible LV dysfunction may already be present — hence the emphasis on intervention before symptoms.

Displaced, hyperdynamic apex; soft S1 (primary MR); wide splitting of S2 (early A2); S3 (reflects rapid filling, not necessarily failure); mid-diastolic flow rumble in severe MR.

Holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla. Anterior leaflet prolapse → jet posterior → murmur to axilla/back; posterior leaflet prolapse → anterior jet → murmur to the base (may mimic AS). Secondary MR murmur is often soft or absent despite severe MR.

Key highlightsAcute MR

  • Acute severe MR: normal-sized LA/LV, giant v waves, flash pulmonary oedema, hyperdynamic LV.
  • The murmur is soft and early — may be inaudible; colour Doppler underestimates.
  • Posteromedial papillary muscle ruptures (single PDA supply), 2–7 days post-MI.
  • Treatment: nitroprusside/nitrates, IABP/MCS, emergency surgery.
  • Hyperdynamic LV + pulmonary oedema + questionable MR → TOE.
  • Echocardiographic grading
  • Grading is integrative : no single parameter is sufficient. Quantitative measures (EROA, regurgitant volume, regurgitant fraction) are preferred whenever feasible, and consequences (LV and LA dilatation, SPAP) complete the picture.

LV/LA dilated

ESC/EACTS 2025, EACVI and ASE recommendations. Mild MR: VC < 3 mm, EROA < 20 mm², RVol < 30 mL, RF < 30%. ACC/AHA 2020 and ASE apply the same thresholds (40 mm², 60 mL, 50%) to primary and secondary MR.

MECHANISM — WHY THE ESC ACCEPTS LOWER CUT-OFFS IN SECONDARY MR

The orifice in SMR is crescent/elliptical: 2D PISA assumes a hemisphere and underestimates the true EROA.

In a failing LV with low stroke volume, a regurgitant volume of 45 mL can represent a regurgitant fraction ≥ 50%.

Outcome data (e.g. post-MI cohorts) show excess mortality from EROA ≈ 20 mm² upwards — ischaemic MR is prognostically "severe" at smaller orifices.

PISA in one line

Flow = 2πr² × aliasing velocity; EROA = flow ÷ peak MR velocity; RVol = EROA × VTIMR. With aliasing velocity ≈ 40 cm/s and an MR velocity of ≈ 5 m/s, EROA ≈ r²/2 (r in cm). PISA overestimates in late-systolic MVP jets (not holosystolic) and underestimates in eccentric and crescentic orifices.

Beyond TTE

TOE (2D/3D): when TTE is non-diagnostic; to define the mechanism, segment and repairability; mandatory for TEER planning; intra-operative assessment of every repair.

CMR: when echo parameters are discordant — regurgitant volume = LV stroke volume (volumetric) − aortic forward flow (phase contrast); reference standard for LV volumes and EF; LGE in arrhythmic MVP.

Exercise echo: symptoms discordant with resting severity; exercise SPAP > 60 mmHg, dynamic MR increase (secondary MR, EROA rise ≥ 13 mm²), and lack of contractile reserve are adverse. BNP/NT-proBNP: rising values in asymptomatic severe MR identify patients at higher risk. Right heart catheterisation: confirm PH when SPAP is the sole surgical trigger; a giant v wave (> 2× mean PCWP) supports severe MR but is neither sensitive nor specific.

Proportionate versus disproportionate secondary MR

In ventricular SMR the regurgitant orifice grows with the ventricle. MR is proportionate when the EROA is what one would expect for the LV end-diastolic volume — it will respond to therapy that shrinks the LV (GDMT, CRT). MR is disproportionate when the EROA is large relative to a modestly dilated LV (EROA/LVEDV ratio above ≈ 0.14 mm²/mL) — the valve lesion itself adds load and valve-targeted therapy should help.

Key highlightsClinical assessment & quantification

  • Severe primary MR: EROA ≥ 40 mm², RVol ≥ 60 mL, RF ≥ 50%, VC ≥ 7 mm.
  • ESC severe ventricular SMR: EROA ≥ 30 mm² or RVol ≥ 45 mL; ACC/AHA uses the primary MR thresholds.
  • Pulmonary vein systolic flow reversal is highly specific for severe MR.
  • Eccentric jets and late-systolic MVP jets mislead colour and PISA — integrate and use TOE/CMR.
  • CMR resolves discordant echo grading and is the reference for LV volumes.
  • Disproportionate SMR (large EROA for LV size) responds to valve therapy — COAPT; proportionate SMR did not — MITRA-FR.

13.4 Chronic Primary MR: When to Operate

Natural history

Severe primary MR is not benign even without symptoms: most patients develop symptoms, LV dysfunction or AF within 6–10 years, and patients with a flail leaflet have an excess mortality of roughly 6% per year. Once symptoms appear, survival without surgery falls sharply. After surgery, survival is restored to near-normal only if the operation precedes LV dysfunction, AF and PH.

MECHANISM — WHY "NORMAL" LVEF IS NOT NORMAL IN MR

The LV ejects part of its stroke volume backwards into the low-impedance LA, so ejection indices are inflated. An LVEF of 60% in severe MR already reflects contractile impairment. After repair the "pop-off" into the LA is removed (afterload mismatch) and LVEF typically falls by about 10 percentage points. Hence the surgical triggers LVEF ≤ 60% and LVESD ≥ 40 mm — LVESD is less load-dependent than EF.

I B*

NEW Surgical repair is recommended in low-risk asymptomatic patients with preserved LV function when a durable repair is likely and ≥ 3 of: AF; resting SPAP > 50 mmHg; significant LA dilatation (LAVI ≥ 60 mL/m² or diameter ≥ 55 mm); concomitant secondary TR ≥ moderate.

I —

CHANGED Surgical repair should be considered in low-risk asymptomatic patients with preserved LV function when durable repair is likely and fewer than 3 of these features are present.

  • IIa B*
  • NEW Minimally invasive mitral surgery may be considered in experienced centres. IIb B

Transcatheter

CHANGED TEER should be considered in symptomatic patients who are inoperable or at high surgical risk, with suitable anatomy, when the procedure is not futile.

IIa B

Praz F et al., ESC/EACTS 2025. NEW / CHANGED = relative to ESC/EACTS 2021. *Level as in the 2021 guideline; — = level not confirmed at press. In 2021 TEER in primary MR was IIb B, and AF, SPAP > 50 mmHg or LA dilatation each gave a IIa B indication.

Medical therapy and follow-up

No drug alters the natural history of primary MR. Vasodilators are not indicated in normotensive patients with normal LV function; treat hypertension normally.

If LV dysfunction develops and surgery is not possible → standard HF therapy (including CRT when indicated).

Follow-up of asymptomatic severe MR with LVEF > 60%: clinical and echo every 6 months; moderate MR: yearly clinical review, echo every 1–2 years.

BOARD PEARL

An asymptomatic 54-year-old with a flail P2, LVEF 62% and LVESD 38 mm but new-onset AF and SPAP 55 mmHg: two ESC risk markers → repair should be considered (IIa); if the LA volume index were also ≥ 60 mL/m² (three markers) repair becomes recommended (Class I). Do not wait for symptoms — and do not rely on SPAP alone unless confirmed invasively.

13.5 Repair versus Replacement

For degenerative MR, repair is superior to replacement: lower operative mortality (< 1% in reference centres), better long-term survival, preserved LV geometry and function (the chordal–papillary continuity is kept), no need for lifelong anticoagulation and lower endocarditis risk.

Key highlightsTiming of surgery in primary MR

  • Class I surgery: symptoms, or asymptomatic LVEF ≤ 60% / LVESD ≥ 40 mm — ESC 2025 adds LVESDi ≥ 20 mm/m².
  • ESC 2025 new Class I: asymptomatic, preserved LV, low risk, durable repair likely and ≥ 3 of AF, SPAP > 50 mmHg, LA dilatation, ≥ moderate TR.
  • LA dilatation = LAVI ≥ 60 mL/m² or diameter ≥ 55 mm.
  • ACC/AHA early repair (2a) hinges on > 95% repair durability and < 1% mortality.
  • LVEF falls ≈ 10 points after repair — "normal" preoperative EF overestimates LV function.
  • No vasodilators for normotensive primary MR with normal LV.
  • Asymptomatic severe MR with normal LV: echo every 6 months.
Principles of repair
  • Restore leaflet motion (resect or neochord)
  • Create a large coaptation surface (≥ 5–8 mm)
  • Remodel and stabilise the annulus — ring
  • annuloplasty
  • Intra-operative TOE to confirm ≤ mild residual
  • MR
If replacement is needed
  • Preserve the subvalvular apparatus (chordal
  • sparing) to maintain LV geometry and function
  • Prosthesis choice per age, anticoagulation and
  • patient preference
  • Concomitant surgical AF ablation and LAA
  • occlusion when indicated
  • Tricuspid annuloplasty for severe TR, and
  • consider for moderate TR or annular dilatation
  • (≥ 40 mm or ≥ 21 mm/m²)
EXAM TRAP — NEW LVOT OBSTRUCTION AFTER REPAIR

Post-pump hypotension with a new systolic murmur after MV repair for a long, redundant anterior leaflet: systolic anterior motion (SAM) with LVOT obstruction and SAM-related MR (≈ 5–10%). It is not a failed repair. Treat with volume, β-blockade, stopping inotropes and raising afterload (phenylephrine); revise only if refractory. Risk factors: small hyperdynamic LV, long posterior leaflet, narrow aorto-mitral angle, small ring.

13.6 TEER & Transcatheter Replacement in Primary MR

Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) — MitraClip or PASCAL — is the catheter version of the surgical Alfieri stitch: via a trans-septal approach, a clip grasps the free edges of A2 and P2 and creates a double-orifice valve. It does not include an annuloplasty.

EVIDENCE IN ONE LINE EACH
  • EVEREST II: TEER was safer but less effective than surgery in operable patients — more residual MR and more surgery for MV dysfunction. Surgery remains standard for operable patients.
  • High/prohibitive-risk registries: durable MR reduction, symptom and quality-of-life improvement → TEER IIa in ESC 2025.
  • CLASP IID: PASCAL non-inferior to MitraClip in prohibitive-risk primary MR.
  • REPAIR-MR and PRIMARY trials are testing TEER against surgery in moderate-risk and older operable patients.

Key highlightsRepair vs replacement

  • Repair is preferred for degenerative MR — lower mortality, better LV function, no anticoagulation.
  • Posterior leaflet prolapse is repairable in > 95%; anterior/bileaflet disease needs an expert centre.
  • Rheumatic and calcified valves are least repairable.
  • If replacing, preserve the chordae to protect LV geometry.
  • SAM after repair → fluids, β-blocker, stop inotropes, vasoconstrictor.

13.7 Secondary MR: Ventricular & Atrial

Secondary MR is a marker and an amplifier of disease: even moderate SMR doubles mortality after MI or in HFrEF, but correcting the valve does not cure the myocardium. ESC 2025 formally separates two phenotypes that need different treatment.

Key highlightsTEER in primary MR

  • TEER = catheter Alfieri: A2–P2 clip, double-orifice valve, no annuloplasty.
  • Surgery remains first-line in operable primary MR (EVEREST II: TEER less effective).
  • ESC 2025: TEER IIa B (was IIb) for symptomatic inoperable/high-risk patients with suitable anatomy; ACC/AHA 2a B-NR.
  • Ideal anatomy: central lesion, MVA > 4 cm², no calcium, flail gap < 10 mm, width < 15 mm.
  • Aim for post-TEER mean gradient ≤ 5 mmHg; rheumatic valves are unsuitable.
  • Feature Ventricular SMR Atrial SMR
  • Jet Central or posterior; tenting height ↑ Central, broad; planar coaptation
  • First treatment HF GDMT + CRT + revascularisation Rhythm control, HFpEF therapy
  • (diuretics, SGLT2i)
  • Intervention TEER (Class I in selected patients) Surgery (annuloplasty + AF ablation
  • + LAAO) preferred; TEER if
  • inoperable
  • Step 1 — optimise the ventricle first
  • Before any valve intervention, SMR must be re-assessed after optimised GDMT (ARNI/ACE-I/ARB, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) and CRT when indicated , in a euvolaemic, normotensive state. Roughly 40% of patients with ventricular SMR improve meaningfully within 1–3 months of optimisation; CRT reduces MR by resynchronising the papillary muscles. Revascularise when ischaemia and viability justify it.
EXAM TRAP — "SEVERE" MR ON ADMISSION

A patient admitted with decompensated HFrEF, BP 170/95, has EROA 35 mm². The next step is not TEER: decongest, control BP, uptitrate GDMT (and CRT if QRS ≥ 150 ms LBBB) and re-grade the MR — ventricular SMR is dynamic and load-dependent. Similarly, intra-operative TOE under anaesthesia underestimates ischaemic MR.

Step 2 — TEER for persistent symptomatic ventricular SMR

Three RCTs frame the evidence (Table 13.4 plus the trials below). The unifying lesson: TEER helps when the MR is severe relative to the LV, the LV is not end-stage, GDMT is maximised and the procedure achieves a good MR reduction.

CLINICAL APPROACH — COAPT-LIKE ELIGIBILITY FOR TEER

  • SPAP ≤ 70 mmHg

  • Outside these criteria — advanced HF, very dilated LV — evaluate for LVAD or transplantation first; TEER is only a palliative IIb option.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 (ESC/EACTS) — SECONDARY MR

TEER for ventricular SMR upgraded from IIa B to I A (COAPT 5-year, RESHAPE-HF2, meta-analysis). Atrial and ventricular SMR defined as separate phenotypes with dedicated diagnostic criteria. New IIa B recommendation for surgery with AF ablation and LAAO in symptomatic atrial SMR. Moderate SMR at CABG: surgery may be considered (IIb).

Surgery for ischaemic MR — what the CTSN trials taught

Moderate ischaemic MR at CABG: adding repair reduced residual MR but did not improve LV

remodelling or survival, and increased neurological events/arrhythmias.

Severe ischaemic MR: restrictive annuloplasty vs chordal-sparing replacement — similar LV reverse remodelling and survival, but recurrent MR was far commoner after repair (≈ 59% at 2 years). Predictors of repair failure: large tenting, posterior leaflet angle, basal aneurysm, very dilated LV.

Key highlightsSecondary MR

  • Optimise GDMT, CRT and revascularisation first; re-grade SMR in a euvolaemic, normotensive state.
  • ESC severe ventricular SMR: EROA ≥ 30 mm² or RVol ≥ 45 mL; ACC/AHA uses 40/60.
  • COAPT (positive) vs MITRA-FR (neutral): disproportionate MR, smaller LV, stable maximal GDMT.
  • ESC 2025: TEER I A for symptomatic ventricular SMR meeting COAPT-like criteria (LVEF 20–50%, LVESD ≤ 70 mm, SPAP ≤ 70 mmHg, no severe RV dysfunction/TR).
  • RESHAPE-HF2: benefit extends to moderate-to-severe SMR; MATTERHORN: TEER non-inferior to surgery, safer.
  • Severe SMR + CABG → mitral surgery (ESC I; ACC/AHA 2a).
  • Atrial SMR: LVEF ≥ 50%, annular dilatation; surgery + AF ablation + LAAO (ESC IIa B); TEER IIb.

13.8 Mitral Valve Prolapse & the Arrhythmic MVP

Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is systolic displacement of one or both leaflets > 2 mm above the annular plane in a long-axis (parasternal or apical 3-chamber) view — the saddle-shaped annulus makes the apical 4- chamber view over-diagnose it. Prevalence is 2–3%. "Classic" MVP has leaflet thickness ≥ 5 mm.

Auscultation and dynamic manoeuvres

Mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur. Anything that reduces LV volume (standing, Valsalva strain, amyl nitrite) makes prolapse occur earlier — the click moves toward S1 and the murmur lengthens. Anything that increases LV volume (squatting, leg raise) delays the click and shortens the murmur; isometric handgrip (↑ afterload) delays the click but makes the murmur louder.

DON'T CONFUSE — MVP VERSUS HCM WITH LVOTO

Both murmurs increase with Valsalva and standing. In HCM the murmur is ejection-type at the left sternal edge, decreases with handgrip, and there is no click. MVP: click, apical late-systolic murmur that increases with handgrip. Complications

Progressive MR and chordal rupture (flail) — the commonest reason for surgery.

Infective endocarditis (higher with MR and thickened leaflets) — routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated for MVP alone.

AF; cerebral embolic events (weak association).

Ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death — annual SCD risk ≈ 0.2–0.4%, low in absolute terms but higher than the general population.

Arrhythmic MVP and mitral annular disjunction

Arrhythmic MVP (EHRA 2022 consensus) = MVP (with or without MAD) plus frequent or complex ventricular arrhythmias (frequent PVCs, NSVT, sustained VT/VF) without another arrhythmic substrate. Mitral annular disjunction (MAD) is a separation between the posterior leaflet hinge point and the top of the LV myocardium, so the annulus sits on the atrial wall during systole — visible as a systolic "curling" of the basal inferolateral wall.

MECHANISM — MECHANICAL STRETCH TO SCAR TO VT

Prolapse and MAD exert repetitive systolic traction on the papillary muscles and basal inferolateral wall.

This causes fibrosis (LGE on CMR) and triggers PVCs from the papillary muscles and fascicles, which can initiate VF. Arrhythmic risk is independent of MR severity — a patient with bileaflet prolapse and only mild MR can die suddenly.

CLINICAL APPROACH
  • All MVP patients with symptoms or red flags: Holter/extended monitoring and CMR.
  • β-blockers for symptomatic PVCs; catheter ablation of triggering PVCs (papillary muscle origin) in selected patients.
  • ICD for survivors of cardiac arrest or sustained VT (secondary prevention); primary-prevention ICD is individualised (LGE, NSVT, unexplained syncope).
  • MV surgery is for MR — its effect on arrhythmic risk is uncertain (listed by ESC 2025 as an evidence gap).

Key highlightsMVP & arrhythmic MVP

  • MVP = leaflet displacement > 2 mm above the annulus in a long-axis view; prevalence 2–3%.
  • Barlow: thick, bileaflet, young, MAD; FED: thin, single P2 flail, older.
  • Standing/Valsalva → earlier click, longer murmur; squatting → later click, shorter murmur.
  • MVP alone does not need endocarditis prophylaxis.
  • Arrhythmic MVP: young women, bileaflet prolapse, MAD, inferior T inversion, papillary-muscle PVCs, LGE on CMR.
  • Pickelhaube sign: lateral annular systolic velocity ≥ 16 cm/s.
  • Arrhythmic risk is independent of MR severity; ICD for secondary prevention.

13.9 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 58-year-old man is asymptomatic with a flail P2 segment and severe MR (EROA 55 mm²). LVEF 63%, LVESD 37 mm, height 162 cm, BSA 1.70 m² (LVESDi 21.8 mm/m²). Sinus rhythm, SPAP 35 mmHg. Per ESC 2025, what is the best management?

Answer C LVESD is < 40 mm, but indexed LVESD ≥ 20 mm/m² is a new ESC 2025 marker of LV dysfunction that triggers Class I surgery — important in smaller patients. Repair of a P2 flail is highly durable. TEER is for high-risk symptomatic patients; ACE-I has no role.

Q2 A 64-year-old woman develops sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension 5 days after an inferior STEMI treated late. A soft early systolic murmur is heard. TTE shows a hyperdynamic LV and an eccentric MR jet of uncertain severity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Answer C The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply (PDA) and ruptures 2–7 days after inferior MI. Acute severe MR gives a soft, early murmur and a hyperdynamic LV; confirm with TOE and send for emergency surgery.

Q3 A 70-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 32%, LVESD 55 mm) has severe secondary MR (EROA 38 mm²) and NYHA III symptoms. He has been on sacubitril/valsartan, bisoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin at maximally tolerated doses for 4 months; QRS 100 ms. SPAP 48 mmHg, normal RV function, no severe TR, no revascularisation target. Suitable TOE anatomy. Next step?

Answer C He meets COAPT-like criteria (LVEF 20–50%, LVESD ≤ 70 mm, SPAP ≤ 70, preserved RV, stable maximal GDMT). TEER is Class I A in ESC 2025. CRT is not indicated with QRS 100 ms; isolated surgery is only IIb.

Q4 Which feature best explains why MITRA-FR was neutral whereas COAPT was positive?

Answer B MITRA-FR patients had bigger ventricles (LVEDVi ≈ 135 mL/m²) and smaller EROA (≈ 31 mm²) — proportionate MR; COAPT enrolled disproportionate MR on stable maximal GDMT. Both used MitraClip in secondary MR.

Q5 According to ESC 2025, which quantitative finding defines severe ventricular secondary MR?

Answer B ESC accepts EROA ≥ 30 mm² and/or RVol ≥ 45 mL in ventricular SMR (crescent orifice, low flow). ACC/AHA and ASE retain 40 mm²/60 mL. VC ≥ 7 mm and RF ≥ 50% indicate severe MR.

Q6 A 76-year-old woman with long-standing permanent AF and HFpEF has severe MR. LVEF 62%, LVEDD 50 mm, no wall-motion abnormality, LAVI 78 mL/m², annulus 41 mm, normal leaflets with central jet. She remains NYHA III despite diuretics, rate control and an SGLT2 inhibitor; surgical risk is acceptable. Best option?

Answer B Atrial SMR (normal LV, dilated LA/annulus, AF/HFpEF). ESC 2025 new IIa B: surgery with annuloplasty plus surgical AF ablation and LAAO in symptomatic operable patients; TEER (IIb) is for those not eligible for surgery.

Q7 A 23-year-old woman with bileaflet MVP, mild MR and palpitations has inferior T-wave inversion and 14% polymorphic PVCs of papillary-muscle origin on Holter. Which investigation is most useful for risk stratification?

Answer B Red flags of arrhythmic MVP. CMR detects LGE in papillary muscles/inferolateral wall and MAD, the key markers of arrhythmic substrate. Arrhythmic risk is independent of MR severity.

Q8 Immediately after mitral repair for Barlow disease, the patient becomes hypotensive on inotropes with a new LVOT gradient and anteriorly directed MR. What is the first step?

Answer C SAM with LVOT obstruction after repair: fill the LV, stop inotropes, β-block and raise afterload. Inotropes, vasodilators and IABP worsen dynamic obstruction; revision only if refractory.

Q9 A frail 84-year-old with symptomatic (NYHA III) severe degenerative MR from an isolated P2 flail (gap 6 mm, width 11 mm, MVA 4.8 cm², no calcification) is judged high surgical risk by the Heart Team. What does ESC 2025 recommend?

Answer B ESC 2025 upgraded TEER in primary MR to IIa B for symptomatic high-risk/inoperable patients with suitable anatomy (ideal: central lesion, MVA > 4 cm², gap < 10 mm, width < 15 mm). It was IIb in 2021.

Q10 In chronic severe primary MR, why is an LVEF of 58% considered a trigger for surgery?

Answer B Part of the stroke volume goes backwards into the LA, so EF overstates contractility; after repair EF typically falls ~10 points. MR reduces rather than increases afterload.

What the board expects you to know

  • Classify TR (primary, atrial-secondary, ventricular-secondary, CIED-related), grade it up to "torrential", and state every threshold for concomitant and isolated tricuspid intervention.
  • Place transcatheter tricuspid therapy correctly: who benefits (TRILUMINATE, TRISCEND II), what it improves (quality of life) and what it has not yet shown (mortality).
  • Recognise carcinoid and drug-induced valve disease and the rules for managing multivalvular lesions.
  • Choose mechanical vs biological prosthesis by age and position; quote target INR by valve and patient risk; know why DOACs are contraindicated.
