14.1 Tricuspid Regurgitation

Trivial TR is a normal finding in most adults. Moderate-or-greater TR affects about 4% of people over 75 years and is independently associated with mortality — the old teaching that TR "disappears once the left heart is fixed" is wrong often enough to have changed the guidelines. The tricuspid valve is a low-pressure, highly dynamic, saddle-shaped structure with three unequal leaflets (anterior, posterior, septal) and a thin annulus that dilates mainly along its free (antero-posterior) wall; the septal portion is anchored to the fibrous skeleton and hardly moves.

Classification — mechanism decides treatment

MECHANISM

Why does the annulus dilate so easily? The tricuspid annulus has little fibrous tissue on its free wall.

Dilatation of the RA (atrial TR) or of the RV base (ventricular TR) pulls it into a flat, round orifice. Once coaptation is lost, TR causes more RV/RA dilatation — "TR begets TR". This is why a dilated annulus (≥ 40 mm or > 21 mm/m²) predicts progression even when TR is only mild at the time of left-sided surgery.

Clinical features

Symptoms
  • Fatigue and low-output symptoms, then oedema,
  • ascites, painful hepatomegaly, early satiety.
  • Pulmonary congestion may improve as TR
  • worsens (the RV "unloads" the lungs).
  • Late: cardiac cirrhosis, cachexia, renal
  • dysfunction (cardio-renal).
Signs
  • JVP: large cv (s) wave with rapid y descent; loss
  • of x descent.
  • Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal
  • border that increases on inspiration — Carvallo
  • sign.
  • Pulsatile liver, RV heave, RV S3 (louder on
  • inspiration).
  • Ascites and oedema out of proportion to lung
  • findings.
EXAM TRAP

Severe TR is frequently silent. With torrential TR the RA and RV equalise ("ventricularised" RA pressure), the jet is laminar and low-velocity, and the murmur may vanish. A low TR velocity in severe TR therefore underestimates PA pressure — invasive haemodynamics are needed before any intervention.

Echocardiographic grading

TTE is first-line; assess leaflet anatomy (3D en face), mechanism, annulus (apical 4-chamber, end-diastole), RV size and function (TAPSE, S′, FAC, RV free-wall strain), RA size, IVC, and estimated PA pressure. The traditional scale stops at "severe"; because transcatheter trials enrolled patients far beyond this, an extended five-grade scale is now routinely used.

Beyond echo — what the Heart Team needs

Right heart catheterisation when PA pressure is uncertain: PASP > 55 mmHg or PVR > 3 WU points to PH-driven (ventricular) TR; severe precapillary PH is a contraindication to isolated tricuspid intervention.

CMR: gold standard for RV volumes and EF; regurgitant fraction.

Cardiac CT: annulus sizing, RCA course and lead relationship for transcatheter planning. Risk scoring: TRI-SCORE (age ≥ 70, NYHA III–IV, right-HF signs, high daily loop-diuretic dose, low eGFR, raised bilirubin, LVEF < 60%, moderate/severe RV dysfunction) estimates in-hospital mortality after isolated tricuspid surgery — the score climbs steeply with late referral.

CLINICAL APPROACH

The window for tricuspid intervention closes silently. Once there is severe RV dysfunction, fixed PH, advanced liver/renal injury or diuretic-refractory ascites, correcting TR may not reverse the damage. Refer early — before the RV fails ; the 2025 ESC guideline explicitly asks for a Heart Team evaluation of disease stage (TR severity, RV/LV function, PA pressure), operative risk and likelihood of recovery before any decision.

Medical therapy

Loop diuretics for congestion; add an MRA (secondary hyperaldosteronism from hepatic congestion). Treat the cause: GDMT for HFrEF, PH-specific therapy where indicated, rhythm control in AF (reverses atrial remodelling in atrial TR).

Medical therapy should not delay referral in the absence of advanced RV dysfunction or severe PH.

Intervention — ESC/EACTS 2025

Concomitant with left-sided valve surgery

Tricuspid surgery in severe TR (primary or secondary) at the time of left-sided valve surgery. I B Tricuspid surgery in moderate TR at the time of left-sided valve surgery. IIa B

  • Recommendation Class Level
  • CHANGED Tricuspid annuloplasty in mild secondary TR with a dilated annulus (≥ 40 mm or
  • > 21 mm/m²) at the time of left-sided surgery.
  • IIb B

Isolated TR

Surgery in symptomatic operable patients with severe primary TR (without severe RV dysfunction). I C Surgery in severe secondary TR (symptomatic or with RV dilatation), without severe RV/LV dysfunction or severe pulmonary vascular disease.

IIa B

CHANGED Transcatheter tricuspid valve intervention (repair or replacement) in symptomatic severe TR despite optimal medical therapy, in patients at high surgical risk and anatomically suitable, without severe RV dysfunction or precapillary PH — to improve quality of life and RV remodelling. IIa A

Wording condensed; confirm exact phrasing against the published recommendation table.

Right-HF with severe primary TR (stage D) → isolated surgery. 2a B-NR

Right-HF with severe isolated secondary TR from annular dilatation (no PH or left-sided disease), poorly responsive to medical therapy.

2a B-NR

Asymptomatic severe primary TR (stage C) with progressive RV dilatation or dysfunction. 2b C-LD Right-HF with severe TR after previous left-sided surgery → isolated reoperation, if no severe PH or severe RV dysfunction.

2b B-NR

WHAT CHANGED IN 2025
  • Transcatheter tricuspid intervention upgraded from IIb C (2021, "inoperable patients") to IIa A — driven by TRILUMINATE, Tri.fr and TRISCEND II.
  • Concomitant annuloplasty for mild TR with a dilated annulus downgraded to IIb — the CTSN trial showed less TR progression but a higher permanent pacemaker rate.
  • Isolated surgery for symptomatic severe primary TR kept at Class I; explicit Heart Team staging of RV function and PH before intervention.

Surgical options

Ring annuloplasty (preferred for durability) or suture (De Vega) annuloplasty of the free wall; repair is preferred to replacement.

Replacement with a large bioprosthesis when leaflets are destroyed or tethering is severe — mechanical tricuspid valves thrombose readily (low closing pressure).

Isolated tricuspid surgery carries high in-hospital mortality, largely because patients arrive late with RV failure and organ damage.

BOARD PEARL

The CTSN trial (NEJM 2022) randomised patients having mitral surgery for degenerative MR with moderate TR or less-than-moderate TR plus annular dilatation. Adding annuloplasty reduced the composite of reoperation, TR progression or death at 2 years (3.9% vs 10.2%) but increased permanent pacemaker implantation (14.1% vs 2.5%). Less TR, more pacemakers, no proven survival benefit — hence the ESC downgrade.

Transcatheter tricuspid therapy

  • Costs: more severe bleeding and new pacemaker implantation;
  • needs anticoagulation.
  • Heterotopic caval
  • valves

TricValve (SVC/IVC) Palliate venous congestion without treating the valve; for torrential TR unsuitable for orthotopic therapy.

Annuloplasty Cardioband Direct annular reduction; limited use.

EXAM TRAP

"Transcatheter TR repair improves survival" — false (no trial has yet shown it). The board answer: it reduces TR and improves symptoms and quality of life. Also note that patients with severe RV dysfunction or precapillary PH are excluded — removing the "pop-off" can precipitate RV failure.

Key highlightsTricuspid regurgitation

  • Secondary TR (~90%) is ventricular (RV dilatation, tethering, PH) or atrial (AF/HFpEF, annular dilatation, preserved RV).
  • CIED-related TR: lead-induced (lead damages leaflet) vs lead-associated (bystander) — worsens in 20–30% after RV lead.
  • Severe TR: VC ≥ 7 mm, EROA ≥ 40 mm², RVol ≥ 45 mL, hepatic systolic flow reversal, dagger-shaped CW.
  • Beyond severe: massive (VC 14–20 mm) and torrential (VC ≥ 21 mm, EROA ≥ 80 mm²).
  • Dilated annulus = ≥ 40 mm or > 21 mm/m².
  • Severe TR at left-sided surgery → repair it (Class I); moderate → IIa; mild + dilated annulus → IIb (ESC 2025).
  • Isolated symptomatic severe primary TR → surgery Class I (ESC) vs 2a (ACC/AHA).
  • Transcatheter TR therapy: ESC 2025 IIa A for high-risk symptomatic patients; benefit = QoL, not proven survival.
  • Severe RV dysfunction or precapillary PH (PVR > 3 WU, PASP > 55 mmHg suggests PH-driven TR) → poor candidates.
  • Tricuspid replacement → bioprosthesis; mechanical valves thrombose on the right.

14.2 Tricuspid Stenosis

TS is rare and almost always rheumatic, virtually never isolated: it accompanies mitral (and often aortic) disease, usually with some TR. Pathologically it mirrors MS — commissural fusion, leaflet thickening and a fixed central orifice, usually without heavy calcification.

Causes
  • Rheumatic (overwhelmingly most common)
  • Carcinoid and drug-induced valve disease (mixed
  • TS + TR)
  • Prosthetic tricuspid valve thrombosis/
  • degeneration
  • RA myxoma or other mass, large vegetation, lead
  • entrapment
  • Congenital (tricuspid atresia), endomyocardial
  • fibrosis, Whipple disease
Clues
  • Giant a waves and slow y descent in the JVP
  • (sinus rhythm)
  • Mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal
  • border, louder on inspiration
  • Marked oedema/ascites with clear lungs in a
  • patient with "MS"
  • ECG: tall P waves (> 0.25 mV in II) without RVH
  • CXR: large RA without an enlarged pulmonary
  • artery
BOARD PEARL

A patient with obvious MS but no orthopnoea or pulmonary congestion and massive systemic venous congestion — think of coexisting TS "protecting" the lungs by limiting flow into the pulmonary circulation.

Supportive Diastolic doming, RA and IVC dilatation

The gradient is flow- and heart-rate-dependent: it rises with inspiration, exercise and tachycardia and is underestimated in low-output states or when AF is fast. Always average over several beats (≥ 5 in AF).

Management

Salt restriction and diuretics for congestion; rate control in AF; pre-operative diuresis improves hepatic function.

Surgery is recommended in symptomatic severe TS, and in severe TS at the time of left-sided valve intervention (ESC Class I).

Commissurotomy converting the valve to a functional bicuspid, ± annuloplasty; replacement with a bioprosthesis if repair fails.

Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty can be attempted if TS is isolated, or alongside PMC for MS — but it often converts TS into TR, so only in patients without significant TR.

Key highlightsTricuspid stenosis

  • TS is almost always rheumatic and associated with mitral disease; isolated TS is rare.
  • Significant TS = mean gradient ≥ 5 mmHg, PHT ≥ 190 ms, valve area ≤ 1.0 cm², VTI > 60 cm.
  • Signs: giant a wave, slow y descent, inspiratory diastolic rumble at LLSB, clear lungs despite anasarca.
  • Surgery for symptomatic severe TS or at left-sided surgery (Class I); bioprosthesis if replacement needed.
  • Balloon valvuloplasty only if TR is not significant — it tends to create TR.
  • Pulmonary regurgitation
  • Trivial PR is physiological. Pathological PR is usually secondary to pulmonary hypertension (annular dilatation) or the residuum of congenital repair — above all transannular-patch repair of tetralogy of Fallot, the commonest cause of severe PR in adults.

14.3 Pulmonary Valve Disease

Pulmonary stenosis

PS is overwhelmingly congenital — typically a thin, mobile, domed valve with fused commissures. A dysplastic (thickened, immobile, non-domed) valve is characteristic of Noonan syndrome and responds poorly to balloon dilatation. Supravalvular/peripheral PS suggests Williams or Alagille syndrome or congenital rubella. Acquired PS is rare (carcinoid, rheumatic, extrinsic compression).

Examination
  • Ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal
  • border.
  • Ejection click that softens on inspiration — the
  • only right-sided sound to do so.
  • As severity increases: click moves closer to S1
  • (then disappears), murmur peaks later, P2
  • softens and splitting widens.
  • Prominent a wave; RV heave.
Investigations
  • ECG: RVH, right axis deviation.
  • CXR: post-stenotic dilatation of the main/left PA.
  • Echo: CW Doppler peak velocity/gradient; RV
  • hypertrophy (not dilatation).
  • CMR/CT for sub- or supravalvular levels.

IIa C

The 2025 ACC/AHA ACHD guideline similarly favours balloon valvuloplasty for symptomatic moderate–severe valvular PS; verify class wording against that document.

P2 Loud Soft or absent

Doppler Sustained high diastolic velocity Dense signal with steep deceleration, reaching baseline before end-diastole (PHT < 100 ms)

Treatment Treat PH/left-heart cause Pulmonary valve replacement by RV volume criteria

DON'T CONFUSE

An early-diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge in a patient with rheumatic MS and PH is more often AR than a Graham Steell murmur, even without peripheral signs of AR.

IIa C

Transcatheter pulmonary valve implantation (TPVI; Melody, SAPIEN) is established for dysfunctional RV– PA conduits and increasingly for native/patched outflow tracts. It carries a notably higher long-term IE risk than surgical valves (see Chapter 15).

Key highlightsPulmonary valve disease

  • PS is congenital; dysplastic valve → Noonan; supravalvular → Williams.
  • The PS ejection click is the only right-sided event that softens with inspiration; the closer to S1, the more severe.
  • Severe PS = peak velocity > 4 m/s / peak gradient > 64 mmHg → balloon valvotomy even if asymptomatic.
  • Graham Steell = PR from PH (high-pitched, loud P2); post-TOF PR is low-pitched and may be silent.
  • Asymptomatic PVR after TOF: RVEDVi ≥ 160 mL/m², RVESVi ≥ 80 mL/m², falling exercise capacity, RV dysfunction, progressive TR.
  • TPVI is preferred when there is no native outflow tract; watch for IE.

14.4 Carcinoid & Drug-Induced Valve Disease

Carcinoid heart disease

Carcinoid heart disease (CaHD) develops in up to 20–50% of patients with carcinoid syndrome — flushing, diarrhoea and bronchospasm from a (usually small-bowel) neuroendocrine tumour with hepatic metastases, which let vasoactive amines bypass hepatic inactivation.

MECHANISM

Serotonin acts on 5-HT2B receptors on valve interstitial cells → fibroblast proliferation and plaque-like deposits of myofibroblasts and collagen on the downstream surfaces of right-sided leaflets and subvalvular apparatus. Leaflets become thickened, retracted and immobile ("fixed open") → TR with TS, and PR with PS. The lung (monoamine oxidase) inactivates serotonin, so left-sided valves are spared unless there is a right-to-left shunt (PFO), a bronchial carcinoid, or very high circulating levels .

Consider PFO closure at the same operation

Anticoagulation VKA for at least 3–6 months after tricuspid bioprosthesis (early prosthetic thrombosis described)

Drug-induced valve disease

The same 5-HT2B mechanism explains valvulopathy from several drugs — but these affect left and right valves (the drugs reach the left heart unmetabolised).

DEFINITION

Restrictive drug-induced valvulopathy: diffuse leaflet and chordal thickening with restricted motion and incomplete coaptation, without calcification or commissural fusion — "rheumatic-looking but without commissural fusion". Stopping the drug may halt progression; established severe lesions are managed as for other regurgitant disease. Radiation heart disease (years after mediastinal radiotherapy) also produces multivalve thickening and calcification.

14.5 Multiple & Mixed Valve Disease

Multiple VHD = lesions on ≥ 2 valves; mixed VHD = stenosis and regurgitation on the same valve. Both are common (rheumatic disease in the young; degenerative calcific disease with mitral annular calcification in the elderly; radiation; carcinoid; connective tissue disease; IE on two valves). The 2025 ESC/EACTS guideline gives multiple and mixed VHD a dedicated section with specific recommendations for the first time.

MECHANISM

Two rules explain most exam questions: (1) The proximal (upstream) lesion masks the distal one — MS reduces flow to a stenotic aortic valve, so AS gradients (and murmur) fall and AS is underestimated. (2) Every Doppler method that assumes normal flow is corrupted — gradients depend on flow; PHT is invalid with significant AR; the continuity equation fails with significant MR or AR through the "reference" orifice.

Key highlightsCarcinoid & drug-induced disease

  • Carcinoid heart disease needs hepatic metastases (or a bronchial primary) to cause syndrome and valve damage.
  • Right-sided: TR + TS, PR + PS; left side spared unless PFO, bronchial carcinoid or very high serotonin.
  • Mechanism = 5-HT2B activation → plaque on leaflets and chords.
  • Screen with NT-proBNP ± 5-HIAA, confirm with echo; look for a PFO.
  • Surgery = valve replacement with octreotide cover; VKA ≥ 3–6 months after TV bioprosthesis.
  • Ergot dopamine agonists (pergolide, cabergoline), fenfluramine/benfluorex, methysergide and MDMA cause restrictive, often left-sided, valvulopathy.
  • Combination What happens Assessment / management points
  • AR + MR Double volume load; LV dilates early Lower threshold for surgery; LV dimensions used cautiously
  • Mixed AS + AR High flow inflates gradient Vmax / mean gradient reflect combined severity; treat as severe if Vmax ≥ 4 m/s and symptomatic
  • Left-sided + TR PH-driven or annular TR Apply tricuspid thresholds (14.1) at the time of leftsided surgery Principles of intervention
  • Decide by the dominant lesion, integrating symptoms, LV/RV response and combined haemodynamic burden — two "moderate" lesions can behave like one severe lesion.
  • When surgery is indicated for one valve, significant disease of another valve is generally corrected at the same operation — a second operation carries higher risk.
  • In rheumatic disease with MS as the dominant lesion, PMC first (if favourable anatomy) can postpone double-valve surgery — but only if there is no significant AR or AS.
  • For transcatheter candidates, a staged approach (e.g. TAVI first, then reassess MR/TR) is common; secondary MR and TR often improve after TAVI.
  • Multimodality imaging (TOE, CT, CMR, stress echo, invasive haemodynamics) is frequently needed to resolve discordance.
EXAM TRAP

Before PMC, always look for AR and AS: removing mitral obstruction suddenly exposes a previously "protected" LV to the full aortic lesion and can cause acute pulmonary oedema.

14.6 Prosthetic Valves: Types & Choice

Every prosthesis trades one disease for another. The choice is a trade between durability (mechanical — but lifelong VKA with bleeding and thrombosis risk) and freedom from anticoagulation (biological — but structural valve deterioration and reintervention). The modern twist is lifetime management: planning today's valve so that tomorrow's valve-in-valve is possible.

Key highlightsMultiple & mixed VHD

  • The upstream lesion masks the downstream one (MS masks AS/AR).
  • Flow-dependent indices fail: PHT invalid with AR; continuity equation invalid with regurgitation at the reference site — use planimetry, CT, CMR.
  • Mixed AS/AR: Vmax and mean gradient integrate both lesions — Vmax ≥ 4 m/s means severe combined disease.
  • Two moderate lesions may justify intervention; correct all significant lesions at one operation.
  • PMC first in dominant rheumatic MS only when AR/AS are not significant.
  • Type Examples Key properties
  • Tilting disc Medtronic Hall, Björk–Shiley Single disc; medium–high thrombogenicity (older models) Caged ball Starr–Edwards Historical; highest thrombogenicity; high gradients
  • Stented
  • bioprosthesis
  • Porcine or bovine pericardial Commonest tissue valve; sewing ring and struts reduce
  • EOA
  • Stentless / sutureless Freestyle; Perceval Larger EOA (less PPM); technically demanding
  • Transcatheter (TAVI) Balloon- or self-expanding Larger EOA than surgical in small annuli; more PVL and pacemakers

  • position + pulmonary homograft)

  • near-normal haemodynamics and no OAC in young adults

  • Choosing the prosthesis

Aortic 60–65; mitral 65–70 Aortic 50–65

Overriding principle Shared decision with the informed patient (Class I in both); life expectancy, bleeding risk, adherence, pregnancy wishes, anatomy for future ViV

According to the desire of the informed patient. I C

When good-quality anticoagulation is unlikely (adherence, access), contraindicated (high bleeding risk) or declined.

  • I C
  • For reoperation after mechanical valve thrombosis despite good anticoagulation. I C
  • In women contemplating pregnancy. IIa C
  • When life expectancy is lower than the presumed durability of the bioprosthesis. IIa C
BOARD PEARL

Bioprostheses degenerate faster in the young, in the mitral position (higher closing pressure) and in highturnover states (renal failure, hyperparathyroidism, pregnancy). They last longest on the right side — which, together with the thrombosis risk of right-sided mechanical valves, is why tricuspid and pulmonary replacements are biological.

DON'T CONFUSE

Pregnancy: a bioprosthesis avoids warfarin embryopathy but risks reoperation; a mechanical valve carries the highest maternal risk of any valve lesion (valve thrombosis). The decision belongs to the patient after counselling — the ESC leans towards a bioprosthesis (IIa) in women planning pregnancy.

14.7 Antithrombotic Therapy with Prosthetic Valves

Mechanical valves — lifelong VKA

Thrombotic risk depends on three things: the prosthesis (design thrombogenicity), the position (tricuspid > mitral > aortic — low closing pressure and slow flow favour thrombus) and the patient (AF, LA stasis, LV dysfunction, prior embolism, hypercoagulability). Unanticoagulated, the risk of embolism with a mechanical valve is ~8% per year; VKA reduces it to ~1–2% per year. ESC sets a target INR (not just a range) to avoid drifting to the low end.

Key highlightsProsthesis types & choice

  • Thrombogenicity: caged ball > tilting disc > bileaflet.
  • ESC: mechanical aortic < 60 y, mitral < 65 y; bioprosthesis aortic > 65 y, mitral > 70 y.
  • ACC/AHA: mechanical AVR < 50 y; bioprosthesis > 65 y; 50–65 shared decision.
  • Mechanical if accelerated SVD risk (young, dialysis, hyperparathyroidism) or already on VKA for another mechanical valve.
  • Bioprosthesis if anticoagulation not feasible, after thrombosis of a well-anticoagulated mechanical valve, or pregnancy planned.
  • Right-sided replacements are biological; homograft preferred for extensive aortic root abscess.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Bileaflet or current tilting-disc AVR, no risk factors → INR 2.5 (2.0–3.0). 1 B-NR
  • Mechanical AVR with risk factors (AF, previous TE, LV dysfunction, hypercoagulable state) or oldergeneration valve → INR 3.0 (2.5–3.5). 1 B-NR
  • Mechanical MVR → INR 3.0 (2.5–3.5). 1 B-NR
  • Add aspirin 75–100 mg to VKA if there is an indication for antiplatelet therapy and bleeding risk is low. 2b B-R On-X AVR, no TE risk factors → INR 1.5–2.0 from 3 months after surgery, with aspirin. 2b B-R Dabigatran in any mechanical valve. 3:
  • Harm
  • B-R
  • Anti-Xa DOACs in mechanical valves (not assessed; not recommended). 3:
  • Harm
  • C-EO
WHY DOACS FAIL ON MECHANICAL VALVES

The artificial surface triggers contact (intrinsic) activation, and the surgical bed exposes tissue factor, generating a massive thrombin burst. Warfarin suppresses several factors (II, VII, IX, X); a single-target agent is overwhelmed. RE-ALIGN (dabigatran) was stopped for excess valve thrombosis, stroke and bleeding; PROACT Xa (apixaban vs warfarin in On-X AVR) was stopped early for excess thromboembolism. DOACs are contraindicated with any mechanical valve — and also with rheumatic moderate–severe MS with AF (INVICTUS: rivaroxaban inferior to VKA).

Recommendation Class Level

Lifelong OAC in TAVI patients with another indication — without added antiplatelet therapy unless recent PCI.

I B

Routine OAC after TAVI without an indication (GALILEO, ATLANTIS). III B

CHANGED Routine DAPT after TAVI to prevent valve thrombosis is not recommended (ESC 2025). Not recommended

EXAM TRAP

Rivaroxaban 10 mg + aspirin after TAVI without another OAC indication (GALILEO) increased death, thromboembolism and bleeding — ACC/AHA Class 3: Harm. Subclinical leaflet thrombosis (HALT) on CT is not by itself an indication for anticoagulation.

Peri-procedural management

INR 4.5–10, no bleeding Withhold dose(s); low-dose oral vitamin K optional

Fondaparinux Not for bridging mechanical valves

EMBOLISM DESPITE THERAPEUTIC INR

First check adherence, INR time-in-range and for valve thrombosis/IE (echo, blood cultures). Then: mechanical AVR → raise target INR from 2.5 to 3.0 or add aspirin 75–100 mg; mechanical MVR → raise target from 3.0 to 4.0 or add aspirin (ACC/AHA 2a). ESC: add low-dose aspirin after thromboembolism despite adequate INR (IIa C).

BOARD PEARL — PREGNANCY WITH A MECHANICAL VALVE

Warfarin dose ≤ 5 mg/day: continuing VKA throughout pregnancy is reasonable (lowest valve-thrombosis risk; embryopathy risk is dose-dependent). Dose > 5 mg: switch to dose-adjusted LMWH (twice daily, antiXa monitoring) or UFH in weeks 6–12. Switch to UFH/LMWH before planned delivery (~36 weeks). DOACs are never an option.

Key highlightsAntithrombotic therapy

  • ACC/AHA: mech AVR INR 2.5; mech AVR + risk factor or old valve 3.0; mech MVR 3.0.
  • ESC matrix: low-thrombogenic valve 2.5/3.0; medium 3.0/3.5; high 3.5/4.0 (without/with patient risk factor).
  • ESC patient risk factors: mitral/tricuspid position, prior TE, AF, any MS, LVEF < 35%.
  • On-X AVR: INR 1.5–2.0 + aspirin after 3 months (ACC/AHA 2b).
  • DOACs contraindicated in mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN, PROACT Xa) and rheumatic MS with AF (INVICTUS).
  • After TAVI without OAC indication: lifelong SAPT (I A); no routine OAC (III); no rivaroxaban + aspirin (Harm).
  • Surgical bioprosthesis: VKA 3 months mitral/tricuspid; aspirin or VKA for aortic; DOAC acceptable for AF after 3 months.
  • Minor procedures: do not stop VKA; major surgery: bridge high-risk mechanical valves only.
  • Patient–prosthesis mismatch (PPM)

14.8 Prosthetic Valve Dysfunction

Obtain a baseline TTE ~6 weeks–3 months after implantation: it is the patient's personal "normal" for that valve model and size. Thereafter: mechanical valves need echo only for new symptoms or signs; surgical bioprostheses annually after 5 years (earlier in the young); TAVI at discharge, 30 days and yearly. A rise in gradient must be interpreted against baseline — not against native-valve thresholds.

Is the gradient abnormal? — high gradient differential

Pressure half-time (ms) < 130 130–200 > 200

ASE/EACVI prosthetic valve recommendations; always compare with the valve-specific normal values and the patient's baseline.

MECHANISM — THREE CAUSES OF A HIGH GRADIENT

1. High flow (anaemia, sepsis, AR/MR through the prosthesis): gradient ↑ but DVI and EOA normal. 2. Patient–prosthesis mismatch: valve works normally but is too small for the patient — gradient high from day one, EOA equals the model's normal reference, leaflets move normally. 3. Intrinsic obstruction (thrombus, pannus, SVD, vegetation): gradient rising from baseline, DVI < 0.25, restricted leaflet motion on fluoroscopy/TOE/CT.

Mitral > 1.2 cm²/m² 0.91–1.2 ≤ 0.9

Consequences: persistent symptoms, less LV mass regression, higher HF and mortality — worst with LV dysfunction and in younger patients; mitral PPM causes persistent PH.

Prevention is the only cure: calculate the projected iEOA at operation; options are aortic root/annulus enlargement, stentless or sutureless valves, or TAVI (supra-annular designs have larger EOAs in small annuli).

Important for later: a small, mismatched surgical valve makes a future valve-in-valve gradient high (bioprosthetic valve fracture can help).

Mechanical valve obstruction: thrombus vs pannus

CLINICAL APPROACH — SUSPECTED MECHANICAL VALVE THROMBOSIS

New dyspnoea or embolism + muffled/absent click + new murmur ± low INR. Urgent TTE + TOE and cinefluoroscopy or CT to show restricted leaflet motion and thrombus size. Classify as obstructive vs non-obstructive and judge thrombus burden and the patient's condition.

Bioprosthetic valve thrombosis and HALT

Clinical bioprosthetic thrombosis (rising gradient ≥ 50% within 5 years, thickened immobile cusps, ± embolism): VKA (± UFH initially) before considering reintervention (ESC I C; ACC/AHA 2a) — gradients often normalise within 3 months.

HALT (hypo-attenuated leaflet thickening) with or without reduced leaflet motion on CT is frequent after TAVI and SAVR, often transient; no routine treatment if subclinical.

Structural valve deterioration and valve-in-valve

SVD (calcification, tears) is the main failure mode of bioprostheses: roughly one-third fail within 10–15 years, faster in the young and in the mitral position. VARC-3 grades haemodynamic deterioration as moderate (mean gradient rise ≥ 10 mmHg to ≥ 20 mmHg, or new ≥ moderate regurgitation) or severe (rise ≥ 20 mmHg to ≥ 30 mmHg, or new severe regurgitation), with a corresponding fall in EOA/DVI.

Recommendation Class Level

Redo surgery in symptomatic patients with a significant rise in gradient (thrombosis excluded) or severe regurgitation.

I C

Transfemoral aortic valve-in-valve should be considered by the Heart Team, depending on anatomy, prosthesis features and operative risk.

IIa B

Transcatheter mitral/tricuspid ViV may be considered in selected high-risk patients. IIb B Reoperation for paravalvular leak related to IE, or causing haemolysis needing repeated transfusion, or severe HF.

I C

Transcatheter closure of clinically significant PVL in high surgical-risk patients. IIa B ACC/AHA 2020

Symptomatic severe prosthetic stenosis → repeat surgery unless high/prohibitive risk. 1 B-NR Severely symptomatic bioprosthetic aortic stenosis at high/prohibitive risk → ViV at a Comprehensive Valve Center.

2a B-NR

Intractable haemolysis or HF from trans- or paravalvular leak → surgery unless high risk. 1 B-NR PVL with intractable haemolysis or NYHA III–IV, high surgical risk, suitable anatomy → percutaneous repair.

2a B-NR

EXAM TRAP — VALVE-IN-VALVE PITFALLS

Coronary obstruction: the failed leaflets are pushed up against the coronary ostia (short sinus-toostium distance, externally mounted leaflets) → CT planning; leaflet laceration (BASILICA) if needed.

High residual gradient in small surgical valves (true ID ≤ 19–21 mm) → supra-annular device ± bioprosthetic valve fracture.

Always exclude thrombosis (trial of VKA) and IE before labelling a failing bioprosthesis as SVD.

Paravalvular leak and haemolysis

PVL results from suture dehiscence, calcified or friable annulus, or IE (late new PVL = IE until proven otherwise). Small, high-velocity jets fragment red cells — haemolysis may be severe with a small leak and a soft or absent murmur .

Key highlightsProsthetic valve dysfunction

  • Baseline echo after implantation is the reference; judge every later gradient against it.
  • High gradient with normal DVI/EOA and normal leaflets = high flow or PPM; DVI < 0.25, AT > 100 ms = obstruction.
  • Severe aortic PPM iEOA ≤ 0.65 cm²/m² (≤ 0.55 if BMI ≥ 30); moderate ≤ 0.85; mitral severe ≤ 0.9.
  • Thrombus: early/any time, low INR, soft mobile mass, responds to lysis; pannus: late, dense fixed ring, surgery only.
  • Obstructive left-sided mechanical thrombosis: surgery if critically ill (ESC I); lysis if surgery not available/high risk or right-sided (IIa).
  • ACC/AHA favours slow-infusion low-dose lysis when thrombus < 0.8 cm², onset < 14 days, NYHA I–II.
  • Bioprosthetic thrombosis → VKA first; HALT without symptoms → no routine treatment.
  • Failed aortic bioprosthesis at high risk → ViV (watch coronary obstruction, small valve gradients).
  • Haemolysis + PVL needing transfusion or causing HF → reoperation (I) or transcatheter closure if high risk.

14.9 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 58-year-old man is scheduled for mitral repair for a flail posterior leaflet. TTE shows mild TR with a tricuspid annulus of 43 mm in end-diastole; RV function is normal. According to ESC/EACTS 2025, concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty is:

Answer C ESC 2025 downgraded annuloplasty for mild secondary TR with a dilated annulus (≥ 40 mm or > 21 mm/m²) to IIb — the CTSN trial showed less TR progression but more pacemakers. Severe TR is Class I, moderate TR IIa; ACC/AHA still gives 2a for stage B TR with annulus > 4.0 cm.

Q2 An 82-year-old woman with permanent AF and HFpEF has NYHA III symptoms, ascites and torrential TR (vena contracta 22 mm). RV size is increased but TAPSE is 18 mm; RHC shows PASP 38 mmHg and PVR 2 WU. TRI-SCORE predicts high surgical risk. Which statement is correct?

Answer B Atrial TR with preserved RV function and no precapillary PH at high surgical risk is the ideal transcatheter candidate (ESC 2025 IIa A). Torrential TR is treatable (TTVR especially). Trials (TRILUMINATE, TRISCEND II) improved QoL, not mortality. Isolated surgery for secondary TR is IIa, not I.

Q3 A 45-year-old woman with known rheumatic MS (MVA 1.1 cm²) has gross ascites and leg oedema but no

Answer C Giant a waves and a slow y descent indicate obstruction to RA emptying; TS "protects" the lungs, explaining venous congestion without pulmonary congestion. Secondary TR gives cv waves with a rapid y descent; constriction gives a rapid y descent.

Q4 A 60-year-old with flushing, diarrhoea and hepatic metastases from an ileal neuroendocrine tumour has thickened, retracted tricuspid and pulmonary leaflets. Echo also shows thickening of the mitral leaflets. The next best step is:

Answer B Serotonin is inactivated in the lung, so left-sided carcinoid involvement implies a right-to-left shunt (usually PFO), a bronchial primary or very high levels. A bubble study guides planning (PFO closure at valve surgery). Warfarin is only indicated after TV bioprosthesis.

Q5 A 26-year-old man had transannular-patch repair of tetralogy of Fallot in infancy. He is asymptomatic, but CMR shows free PR with RVEDVi 172 mL/m² and RVESVi 86 mL/m²; exercise capacity has fallen on serial CPET. The best management is:

Answer B Asymptomatic severe PR after TOF repair with RVEDVi ≥ 160 and/or RVESVi ≥ 80 mL/m² and falling objective exercise capacity meets ESC IIa criteria for PVR. Waiting for symptoms risks irreversible RV dysfunction. Balloon valvuloplasty treats stenosis, not regurgitation.

Q6 A 55-year-old man needs aortic valve replacement for bicuspid AS. He is on haemodialysis and adherent to medications. Which prosthesis does the ESC favour?

Answer C Risk of accelerated SVD (young age, haemodialysis, hyperparathyroidism) is a Class I indication for a mechanical valve when anticoagulation is feasible — bioprostheses calcify rapidly in dialysis patients.

Q7 A 67-year-old with a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve and AF asks to switch to apixaban. What is the correct advice and the ACC/AHA target INR?

Answer C DOACs are contraindicated with any mechanical valve (RE-ALIGN, PROACT Xa). ACC/AHA target INR is 3.0 for mechanical MVR (2.5 is for bileaflet AVR without risk factors). DOACs are acceptable with bioprostheses.

Q8 Three weeks after a lapse in warfarin, a 50-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve presents in pulmonary oedema and hypotension. Fluoroscopy shows an immobile leaflet; TOE shows a 1.2 cm² mobile thrombus. The hospital has cardiac surgery on site, and there are no major comorbidities. The best treatment is:

Answer B Obstructive left-sided mechanical valve thrombosis in a critically ill patient with a large thrombus (≥ 0.8 cm²) and available surgery → urgent/emergency surgery (ESC I B). Lysis is reserved for when surgery is unavailable/very high risk, right-sided valves, or small recent thrombi in NYHA I–II.

Q9 A 76-year-old had SAVR with a 19 mm stented bioprosthesis. Since surgery (baseline echo at 6 weeks) the mean gradient has been stable at 32 mmHg, EOA 1.0 cm² (normal for that model), DVI 0.33, leaflets thin and mobile. BSA is 2.0 m², BMI 27. The diagnosis is:

Answer C iEOA = 1.0/2.0 = 0.50 cm²/m² (≤ 0.65 → severe PPM). Gradient high from baseline, normal DVI and leaflet motion, EOA normal for the model — the valve works but is too small. Thrombosis/SVD/pannus produce a rising gradient and falling DVI.

Q10 Eighteen months after mechanical MVR, a patient has Hb 8.9 g/dL, LDH markedly raised, undetectable

Answer B Clinically significant Coombs-negative haemolysis with schistocytes after MVR suggests a paravalvular leak; small high-velocity jets may be inaudible. TOE (3D) localises it; transfusion-dependent haemolysis is a Class I indication for reoperation (or transcatheter closure if high risk).

Infective Endocarditis

Suspect early, image widely, treat with a team — and operate before the valve or the brain is lost.

What the board expects you to know

  • Apply the ESC 2023 modified Duke criteria (with CT, PET/CT and WBC-SPECT as major imaging criteria) and contrast them with the Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria.
  • Choose empirical and organism-specific antibiotic regimens with durations, and select patients for partial oral therapy (POET).
  • State every indication and the timing (emergency / urgent / non-urgent) of surgery — HF, uncontrolled infection, embolism with vegetation thresholds — including after stroke or intracranial haemorrhage.
  • Manage PVE, CIED infection and right-sided IE in people who inject drugs.
  • Know who needs prophylaxis, for which procedures, and with which drugs (no clindamycin).

Numbers that win marks

3 setsBlood cultures — 30 min apart, before antibiotics
< 24 h / 3–5 dEmergency / urgent surgery
≥ 10 mmVegetation — embolic-risk threshold
> 20 mmTricuspid vegetation + recurrent PE → surgery
≥ 10 daysIV before oral switch (POET)
2 gAmoxicillin — 30–60 min before dental procedure

15.1 Epidemiology, Pathogenesis & Microbiology

IE affects about 3–10 per 100,000 people per year, and its age-standardised incidence has risen in recent decades. In high-income countries it has become a disease of the elderly, the comorbid and the instrumented — prosthetic valves (up to 30% of cases), cardiac devices (~10%), haemodialysis and central lines — and is increasingly healthcare-associated and staphylococcal. In low- and middle-income countries rheumatic heart disease and oral streptococci still dominate, in younger patients. In-hospital mortality is 15–30% and 1-year mortality about 20–30%.

MECHANISM

Healthy endothelium resists bacterial adhesion. IE needs (1) endothelial damage — turbulent jets (regurgitant lesions, VSD, prosthetic material), catheters, or the direct injury of injected particulate matter; (2) a sterile platelet–fibrin nidus (non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis); and (3) bacteraemia with organisms that stick — staphylococci and streptococci carry adhesins (MSCRAMMs) that bind fibrinogen and fibronectin. S. aureus can also invade intact endothelium, which is why it causes IE on normal valves. Bacteria buried in the vegetation become metabolically dormant and antibiotic-tolerant — hence long, bactericidal, high-dose therapy.

Ventricular assist devices

Intermediate Rheumatic heart disease; non-rheumatic degenerative valve disease; congenital valve anomalies incl. bicuspid aortic valve; CIEDs; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Non-cardiac Injection drug use, haemodialysis, central venous catheters, diabetes, malignancy (esp. colorectal), immunosuppression, poor dental hygiene, recent hospitalisation

Organism Share Typical setting / exam associations

Fungi (Candida, Aspergillus) 1–2% PVE, PWID, immunosuppressed, long-term lines; large vegetations; mortality > 50%; surgery + lifelong azole suppression

  • Coxiella, Bartonella and other
  • fastidious organisms
  • — Culture-negative IE (15.3)
BOARD PEARL

Two organisms send you to another specialist: S. gallolyticus → colonoscopy (colonic neoplasia); Cutibacterium, CoNS or M. chimaera months after cardiac surgery → think prosthetic infection (M. chimaera from contaminated heater–cooler units presents very late).

15.2 Clinical Features & Imaging

IE is a great mimic. Consider it in anyone with fever plus a risk factor, fever with an embolic event or new regurgitant murmur, S. aureus bacteraemia, or unexplained stroke, spondylodiscitis or glomerulonephritis in a febrile patient. Fever occurs in up to 90%; a murmur in ~85%; embolic complications are present at diagnosis in up to 25%.

Blood cultures — the cornerstone

At least 3 sets (aerobic + anaerobic), ≥ 10 mL each, from a peripheral vein, 30 minutes apart, before antibiotics. In the septic patient, take them rapidly and start empirical therapy without delay. Bacteraemia in IE is continuous — timing relative to fever does not matter.

Key highlightsEpidemiology & microbiology

  • Incidence 3–10/100,000/year and rising; in-hospital mortality 15–30%.
  • S. aureus is now the commonest cause and the most aggressive (emboli, stroke, abscess, death).
  • Staphylococci + streptococci + enterococci ≈ 80% of cases.
  • High-risk groups: prior IE, prosthetic valves/repair material, cyanotic or prosthetic-repaired CHD, VADs.
  • S. gallolyticus → colonoscopy; HACEK → slow-growing, large vegetations, ceftriaxone.
  • Fungal IE: PVE/PWID/immunosuppressed; surgery plus long-term azole.
  • Rapid identification (MALDI-TOF) speeds targeted therapy; MIC testing guides dosing.
  • Repeat cultures every 24–48 h until negative — persistence beyond ~7 days signals uncontrolled infection.
  • Echocardiography

Pseudoaneurysm Pulsatile echo-free perivalvular space with colour flow

Perforation / fistula Interruption of tissue with colour flow across; fistula connects two cavities Prosthetic dehiscence New paravalvular regurgitation ± rocking motion

TOE when a prosthetic valve or intracardiac device is present. I B

TOE even when TTE is positive (to detect complications) — except isolated right-sided native-valve IE with a good-quality, unequivocal TTE.

I C

Repeat TTE/TOE within 5–7 days if the first study is negative/inconclusive but suspicion remains high. I C NEW Echocardiography should be considered in S. aureus, E. faecalis and some Streptococcus spp. bacteraemia.

IIa B

Repeat TTE/TOE as soon as a new complication is suspected (new murmur, embolism, persistent fever, HF, abscess, AV block).

  • I B
  • NEW TOE before switching from IV to oral antibiotics. I B
  • Intra-operative echocardiography in all IE surgery. I B

TTE/TOE at completion of antibiotic therapy in patients not operated. I C

EXAM TRAP

A normal TTE does not exclude IE: sensitivity is ~70% for native valves and ≤ 50% for prosthetic valves, versus > 90% for TOE. Even TOE can miss very small (< 3 mm) or very early vegetations and lesions on heavily calcified or prosthetic valves — repeat in 5–7 days and add CT or PET/CT.

Beyond echo — CT, nuclear imaging and MRI

Cardiac CT
  • More accurate than TOE for abscess,
  • pseudoaneurysm and fistula.
  • Pre-operative coronary assessment when aortic
  • vegetations make catheterisation risky.
  • Whole-body CT detects splenic/renal emboli and
  • the portal of entry.
[18F]FDG-PET/CT
  • Shows metabolic activity around prostheses,
  • devices and distant foci.
  • Most useful in PVE, where echo is limited.
  • Poor for brain (physiological uptake) — use MRI
  • for cerebral emboli and aneurysms.
  • Early post-operative uptake may reflect healing,
  • not infection — interpret with the time since
  • implantation.
BRAIN MRI

Cerebral lesions are found in up to 60–80% of patients with left-sided IE — mostly small, silent ischaemic lesions and microbleeds. Detecting an asymptomatic embolus can add a minor criterion and upgrade "possible" to "definite" IE. Suspected infective intracranial aneurysm → CTA/MRA; if negative but suspicion persists → catheter angiography (gold standard).

Key highlightsClinical features & imaging

  • ≥ 3 blood-culture sets, 30 min apart, ≥ 10 mL each, before antibiotics.
  • TTE first; TOE in essentially all suspected left-sided IE, all prosthetic valves and devices (Class I).
  • Repeat TOE in 5–7 days if negative with persisting suspicion.
  • ESC 2023: echo should be considered in S. aureus, E. faecalis and some streptococcal bacteraemia (IIa).
  • Cardiac CTA (NVE) and FDG-PET/CT + CTA (PVE) are Class I in possible IE.
  • CT beats TOE for abscess/pseudoaneurysm; MRI beats PET for brain.
  • New AV block in aortic IE = perivalvular abscess until proven otherwise.
  • TOE is required before switching to oral therapy (I B).

15.3 Diagnostic Criteria & Culture-Negative IE

The modified Duke criteria were built around blood cultures and echocardiography, so they perform poorly in PVE and CIED infection, where echo is normal or inconclusive in up to 30%. Two 2023 updates address this: the ESC 2023 modified Duke criteria and the independent Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria (International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases). Both upgrade advanced imaging to a major criterion.

Persistently positive cultures with organisms consistent with IE: ≥ 2 positive samples drawn > 12 h apart, or all of 3 / most of ≥ 4 with first and last ≥ 1 h apart

Single positive culture for Coxiella burnetii or phase I IgG titre > 1:800

Imaging Valvular, perivalvular/periprosthetic and foreign-material anatomical or metabolic lesions characteristic of IE by: echocardiography (TTE/TOE), cardiac CT, [18F]FDG-PET/CT or WBC-SPECT/ CT

  • Minor criteria
  • Predisposition High- or intermediate-risk heart condition, or injection drug use
  • Fever Temperature > 38 °C
  • Embolic vascular
  • dissemination

Including asymptomatic lesions detected by imaging only: major systemic/pulmonary emboli, infarcts, abscesses; haematogenous osteoarticular infection (spondylodiscitis); mycotic aneurysm; intracranial ischaemic/haemorrhagic lesions; conjunctival haemorrhage; Janeway lesions

Immunological Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor

Microbiological Positive blood culture not meeting a major criterion, or serological evidence of active infection with an organism consistent with IE

  • Classification
  • Definite 2 major; or 1 major + 3 minor; or 5 minor

Possible 1 major + 1–2 minor; or 3–4 minor

Rejected Criteria for definite/possible not met, with or without an alternative diagnosis

WHAT CHANGED IN 2023

E. faecalis became a "typical" organism (ESC); Duke-ISCVID widened the list further.

Cardiac CT, FDG-PET/CT and WBC-SPECT/CT joined echocardiography as major imaging criteria. Embolic lesions detected only by imaging count as a minor criterion.

Duke-ISCVID added a surgical major criterion and removed blood-culture timing rules.

Blood culture–negative IE (BCNIE)

BCNIE (~5–10% or more in some regions) has two main causes: antibiotics given before cultures (commonest) and fastidious or intracellular organisms. Always consider non-infective endocarditis if everything is negative.

DON'T CONFUSE — NON-BACTERIAL THROMBOTIC ENDOCARDITIS

Sterile vegetations in advanced malignancy (marantic, esp. mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma) and antiphospholipid syndrome / SLE (Libman–Sacks). Test ANA and antiphospholipid antibodies when cultures and serology are negative. Stroke is the commonest presentation; treat with anticoagulation (heparin/ VKA — not DOACs) and the underlying disease.

Key highlightsDiagnostic criteria

  • Definite IE: 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.
  • ESC 2023 typical organisms: oral streptococci, S. gallolyticus, HACEK, S. aureus, E. faecalis.
  • Imaging major criterion: echo, cardiac CT, FDG-PET/CT, WBC-SPECT/CT.
  • Coxiella: single positive culture or phase I IgG > 1:800 = major criterion.
  • Duke-ISCVID 2023: broader organism list (plus prosthetic-material organisms), surgical major criterion, no culture timing rules, PET/CT major only > 3 months post-implant.
  • Commonest cause of BCNIE = prior antibiotics; then Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, T. whipplei, fungi.
  • All negative → test for malignancy, APS/SLE (NBTE).
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Same setting, penicillin-allergic: cefazolin or vancomycin + gentamicin. IIb C
  • Early PVE (< 12 months) or healthcare-associated IE: vancomycin or daptomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin.
  • IIb C
  • Targeted therapy

15.4 Antimicrobial Therapy

PRINCIPLES

Bactericidal, high-dose, IV, prolonged — to sterilise dormant bacteria inside vegetations. Duration counts from the first day of effective therapy (first negative culture), not from surgery; restart a full course only if valve cultures are positive.

NVE generally 2–6 weeks; PVE ≥ 6 weeks. NVE treated with a new prosthesis during therapy continues the NVE regimen.

Aminoglycosides: no longer recommended in staphylococcal NVE (nephrotoxicity, no benefit); when used, once daily for ≤ 2 weeks.

Rifampicin only for foreign-material infection (PVE), started after 3–5 days once bacteraemia has cleared (prevents resistance; acts on biofilm).

Empirical therapy

EXAM TRAPS
  • Adding gentamicin to MSSA native-valve IE — not recommended (renal toxicity, no benefit).
  • Starting rifampicin on day 1 — wrong: wait 3–5 days until bacteraemia clears, and use it only with prosthetic material.

E. faecalis is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins — ceftriaxone works only in combination with ampicillin (synergistic PBP saturation).

Daptomycin must never be used as monotherapy for left-sided IE and is inactivated by surfactant (no role in pneumonia).

Outpatient and partial oral therapy

Treatment has two phases: a critical phase (first ~2 weeks — IV therapy in hospital, surgery, drainage of abscesses, removal of infected devices) and a continuation phase, in which stable patients can complete therapy as outpatients, IV (OPAT) or orally.

POET TRIAL (NEJM 2019)

400 stable patients with left-sided IE (streptococci, E. faecalis, S. aureus, CoNS) were randomised after ≥ 10 days of IV therapy to continue IV or switch to two oral drugs from different classes (e.g. amoxicillin + rifampicin, linezolid + rifampicin, dicloxacillin + fusidic acid, moxifloxacin + linezolid). Partial oral therapy was non-inferior for the composite of death, unplanned surgery, embolism and relapse (9.0% vs 12.1%), with benefit maintained at long-term follow-up. → ESC 2023 IIa A.

Key highlightsAntimicrobial therapy

  • Empirical community NVE/late PVE (≥ 12 months): ampicillin + ceftriaxone, or ampicillin + flucloxacillin + gentamicin (IIa).
  • Early PVE (< 12 months)/healthcare-associated: vancomycin (or daptomycin) + gentamicin + rifampicin (IIb).
  • Streptococci: penicillin/amoxicillin/ceftriaxone 4 weeks NVE, 6 weeks PVE; 2 weeks with gentamicin if uncomplicated NVE.
  • MSSA NVE: flucloxacillin or cefazolin 4–6 weeks, no gentamicin; PVE adds rifampicin (≥ 6 wk) + gentamicin (2 wk).
  • MRSA NVE: vancomycin; daptomycin 10 mg/kg only in combination.
  • E. faecalis: ampicillin + ceftriaxone 6 weeks (drug of choice if HLAR).
  • Rifampicin only for prosthetic material, after 3–5 days.
  • Partial oral therapy (POET) after ≥ 10 days IV in stable left-sided IE — IIa A; TOE first (I B).

15.5 Surgery & Complications

About 50% of patients with left-sided IE need surgery during the active phase. Surgery has three aims — treat heart failure, control uncontrolled infection and prevent embolism — and its benefit depends on timing. Operative risk (in-hospital mortality ~10–20%) should be weighed by the Endocarditis Team with IE-specific scores; it should not be vetoed by a single factor such as age.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2023 (VS ESC 2015)

The old size-only rows (vegetation > 30 mm IIa; > 15 mm IIb) were replaced by a single ≥ 10 mm threshold combined with embolism, another surgical indication, or (IIb) low surgical risk — reflecting the EASE trial.

Persistent bacteraemia > 1 week and S. aureus/non-HACEK Gram-negative PVE listed explicitly as uncontrolled-infection indications.

Surgery after ischaemic stroke upgraded to "without delay" (Class I) when HF, uncontrolled infection, abscess or high embolic risk is present.

WHY VEGETATION SIZE AND TIMING MATTER

Embolic risk (20–50% of patients) is highest before and during the first days of therapy and falls sharply after 2 weeks. The strongest predictors are vegetation size (≥ 10 mm) and mobility, mitral (especially anterior leaflet) location, change in size on therapy, S. aureus / S. gallolyticus / Candida, prior embolism and multivalvular involvement. Surgery prevents emboli only if it is done early — hence "urgent (3–5 days)", not "after completing antibiotics".

EASE TRIAL (NEJM 2012)

76 patients with left-sided IE, severe valve disease and vegetations > 10 mm: surgery within 48 h vs conventional care. Early surgery reduced the composite of in-hospital death or embolism at 6 weeks (3% vs 23%), driven by fewer emboli.

Neurological complications

Symptomatic stroke complicates 15–30% of left-sided IE (silent lesions far more), mostly within the first 2 weeks; S. aureus carries the highest risk. The dilemma: cardiopulmonary bypass with heparinisation may convert an ischaemic infarct to haemorrhage (post-operative haemorrhagic conversion ~2–7%), yet delay exposes the patient to further emboli and HF.

Recommendation Class Level

ICH with unstable status (HF, uncontrolled infection, persistent high embolic risk) → urgent/emergency surgery, weighing the chance of meaningful neurological recovery.

IIa C

Brain CT or MR angiography in suspected infective intracranial aneurysm; invasive angiography if noninvasive tests are negative but suspicion persists (IIa B). I B

Neurosurgery or endovascular therapy for large, growing or ruptured infective intracranial aneurysms. I C Mechanical thrombectomy in embolic stroke, if expertise is available in time. IIb C

Thrombolysis in embolic stroke due to IE. III C

Other complications

AV block New conduction delay = abscess near the AV node → urgent surgery; epicardial pacing at surgery should be considered with complete AV block plus pre-op conduction disease, S.

aureus, aortic root abscess, tricuspid involvement or prior valve surgery (IIa C)

Splenic infarct/abscess Persistent fever/abdominal pain; CT/US; large abscess may need splenectomy (timing vs valve surgery)

Infective aneurysm Cerebral > visceral; may rupture — especially if anticoagulated; DSA is the gold standard Acute kidney injury Immune-complex GN, renal infarcts, haemodynamic, drug toxicity (aminoglycosides, vancomycin), contrast — not a reason to delay surgery

Spondylodiscitis IE rate ~10× higher in pyogenic spondylodiscitis with bacteraemia → echo (I C); MRI or PET/CT for diagnosis (I C); > 6 weeks therapy for S. aureus/Candida or complicated lesions (IIa C)

Recommendation Class Level

No stroke, but surgery likely (e.g. S. aureus IE): replace oral anticoagulation with UFH under close monitoring.

IIa C

Thrombolytic therapy in patients with IE. III C

EXAM TRAP

IE itself is not an indication to start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy — neither prevents emboli. A patient already on OAC for AF or a mechanical valve generally continues (switching to heparin if surgery or bleeding is likely). Aspirin to "prevent emboli" is a wrong answer.

SURGICAL PRINCIPLES
  • Radical debridement of infected tissue is more important than the choice of prosthesis; mitral repair is preferred when feasible.
  • Extensive aortic root abscess → root replacement (homograft or composite graft).
  • Favour a biological substitute with recent stroke, intracranial bleeding, women of child-bearing age, frailty, poor adherence or expected prolonged post-operative course.

Pre-operative coronaries: CT coronary angiography when aortic vegetations are present in stable patients (I B); invasive angiography otherwise in patients at risk (I C); emergency surgery may proceed without coronary assessment (IIa C).

Key highlightsSurgery & complications

  • Emergency (< 24 h): refractory pulmonary oedema or shock from valve dysfunction/fistula (I B).
  • Urgent (3–5 days): HF, abscess/pseudoaneurysm/fistula/new AV block, enlarging vegetation (I B).
  • Persistent positive cultures > 1 week (IIa); S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative PVE (IIa); fungi/MDR (I).
  • Vegetation ≥ 10 mm + ≥ 1 embolus → urgent surgery (I B); + other indication (I C); isolated, low risk (IIb B).
  • TIA or ischaemic stroke without coma/haemorrhage → do not delay indicated surgery (I B).
  • ICH → delay > 1 month if stable (IIa C).
  • No thrombolysis for IE stroke (III); thrombectomy may be considered (IIb).
  • IE is not an indication for antithrombotics; stop them with major bleeding.
  • Feature Early PVE (< 12 months) Late PVE (≥ 12 months)
  • Empirical
  • therapy
  • Vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin As NVE (ampicillin + ceftriaxone, etc.)
  • Prognosis Worse; surgery usually needed Uncomplicated non-staphylococcal cases may be
  • treated medically
  • TOE is mandatory; a new paravalvular leak is a major criterion; add FDG-PET/CT and cardiac CTA in possible PVE (I B).
  • Surgery is recommended for early PVE (within 6 months of valve surgery) with new valve replacement and complete debridement (ESC I C), and in PVE with HF, severe prosthetic dysfunction, abscess, persistent fever, or S. aureus / non-HACEK Gram-negative infection.
  • Mechanical valves are more often infected by S. aureus; bioprostheses by streptococci, enterococci and CoNS.

15.6 Special Forms: PVE, CIED Infection, Right-Sided IE

Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE)

PVE occurs in 1–6% of prosthetic valve recipients and accounts for 20–30% of all IE. It is the most severe form: infection spreads to the sewing ring and annulus (abscess, dehiscence, fistula) rather than the leaflets, and echo is often inconclusive.

TRANSCATHETER VALVE ENDOCARDITIS

Post-TAVI IE: 0.3–1.9 per 100 patient-years (similar to SAVR), highest in the first year, especially the first 3 months; risk factors younger age, male sex, residual AR, renal dysfunction. Enterococci and S. aureus dominate. Vegetations may sit on the stent frame or on the mitral valve; TOE is often negative — use PET/ CT. In-hospital/30-day mortality 16–36%; surgery is the best option for complicated cases but is rarely done.

Post-TPVI IE (Melody/SAPIEN in the RVOT): 1.6–4.0 per 100 patient-years — higher than surgical pulmonary valves; S. aureus and oral streptococci; intracardiac echo or PET/CT may help.

CIED infection and CIED-related IE

CIED infection ranges from pocket infection to lead/valve IE with bacteraemia. S. aureus and CoNS dominate (CoNS commonest in chronic pocket infection). Risk factors: generator replacement or upgrade, pocket haematoma, renal failure, diabetes, temporary pacing before implant, multiple leads.

IIa C

Possible CIED-IE with occult Gram-positive bacteraemia or fungaemia persisting after a course of therapy → complete removal.

IIa C

Removal after a single positive blood culture with no other evidence of infection. III C Extend antibiotics to 4–6 weeks after extraction when septic emboli or prosthetic valves are present. IIa C Non-S. aureus CIED-IE without valve involvement or lead vegetations, negative follow-up cultures and no emboli → 2 weeks after extraction may be considered.

IIb C

Recommendation Class Level

Reimplant at a distant site, as late as possible, once infection has settled and cultures are negative ≥ 72 h (no vegetations) or ≥ 2 weeks (if vegetations were seen).

  • I C
  • Antibiotic envelope at reimplantation in selected high-risk patients. IIb B
BOARD PEARL

S. aureus bacteraemia in a patient with a CIED = CIED infection until proven otherwise; antibiotics alone fail because biofilm persists on the leads. The answer is complete percutaneous extraction of generator and all leads — even if only the pocket looks inflamed. Surgical extraction is reserved for very large vegetations (percutaneous aspiration is an alternative) or concomitant valve surgery. Bridge pacemaker-dependent patients with an externalised active-fixation lead; a wearable defibrillator for ICD patients.

  • Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures is not needed for CIEDs.
  • Right-sided IE and people who inject drugs (PWID)

Right-sided IE (5–10% of IE) mainly affects the tricuspid valve in PWID, patients with lines or devices, and CHD. S. aureus dominates (polymicrobial and fungal infection occur in PWID). It presents with fever, bacteraemia and septic pulmonary emboli (cough, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, cavitating nodules) rather than a murmur. Prognosis is better than left-sided IE — ~90% can be treated medically — but recurrence and reinfection are common.

Recommendation Class Level

Percutaneous aspiration (debulking) of right-sided septic masses in high-surgical-risk patients. IIb C

EXAM TRAP

An isolated large tricuspid vegetation is not by itself an indication for surgery — it needs recurrent septic emboli (and size > 20 mm) or another indication. If replacement is unavoidable, a bioprosthesis is preferred (avoid lifelong anticoagulation in PWID); valvectomy without replacement is a historical last resort.

15.7 Prevention & the Endocarditis Team

Everyday bacteraemia (tooth brushing, chewing) dwarfs procedure-related bacteraemia, so oral hygiene matters more than antibiotics. Since NICE 2008 withdrew routine prophylaxis, the incidence of oral-streptococcal IE rose in the UK, and a population-level case-crossover study linked invasive dental procedures to subsequent IE in high-risk patients — supporting the "high-risk patients + high-risk dental procedures" model used by the ESC and AHA.

NEW Transcatheter aortic and pulmonary valve prostheses. I C

Untreated cyanotic CHD; CHD treated with palliative shunts, conduits or other prostheses (after complete repair without residual defect: first 6 months only).

  • I C
  • NEW Ventricular assist devices. I C
  • NEW Transcatheter mitral and tricuspid valve repair. IIa C
  • NEW Heart transplant recipients. IIb C
  • Other patients at low risk. III C

Which procedures

Dental extractions, oral surgery (periodontal, implant, oral biopsy) and procedures manipulating the gingival or periapical region (incl. scaling and root canal).

I B

Key highlightsPVE, CIED, right-sided IE

  • PVE = 20–30% of IE; early (< 12 months) is nosocomial (S. aureus, CoNS), late behaves like NVE.
  • Early PVE (< 6 months) → surgery with complete debridement (I C).
  • Post-TAVI IE peaks in the first year; enterococci and S. aureus; TOE often negative → PET/CT.
  • CIED-IE: complete extraction without delay (I B); not after a single positive culture (III).
  • Reimplant at a distant site after ≥ 72 h negative cultures (no vegetation) or ≥ 2 weeks (vegetation).
  • Right-sided MSSA IE in PWID: 2 weeks of (flu)cloxacillin if uncomplicated and vegetation ≤ 20 mm.
  • Right-sided surgery: refractory RV failure from TR, ventilatory failure after emboli, vegetation > 20 mm with recurrent PE, left-sided involvement (I); persistent bacteraemia > 1 week (IIa).

  • IIa C

EXAM TRAP

Mitral valve prolapse, bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic heart disease, HCM and pacemakers are not indications for dental prophylaxis (intermediate risk). Routine dental prophylaxis is not recommended for GI endoscopy, TOE, bronchoscopy, vaginal delivery or cystoscopy. A TAVI patient, however, does need prophylaxis (Class I).

The Endocarditis Team

IE management is inherently multidisciplinary. The ESC recommends that complicated IE be managed early at a Heart Valve Centre with immediate surgical facilities and an Endocarditis Team; uncomplicated IE may be treated in a referring centre in regular communication with the reference centre.

Core members
  • Cardiologist and imaging specialist
  • Cardiac surgeon
  • Infectious diseases specialist / microbiologist
  • Neurologist / neurosurgeon, neuroradiologist
  • Nuclear medicine and radiology
  • Access to CIED extraction, addiction and social
  • services
Tasks
  • Diagnosis and imaging strategy
  • Antibiotic choice, duration, OPAT/oral switch
  • Indication and timing of surgery
  • Weekly review of every case
  • Follow-up: echo and inflammatory markers at
  • end of therapy; blood cultures if relapse
  • suspected; review at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months
RELAPSE VS REINFECTION

Relapse: same organism, usually within 6 months — treatment failure (inadequate course, persistent focus, PVE, difficult organism) → a further 4–6 weeks and consider surgery. Reinfection: different organism, usually later — reflects host risk (PWID, prior IE, dialysis) and carries a worse prognosis. Overall recurrence 2–9%.

Key highlightsPrevention & team

  • Prophylaxis only for high-risk patients undergoing gingival/periapical manipulation, extraction or oral surgery.
  • High-risk: prior IE; surgical or transcatheter prosthetic valves; prosthetic repair material; cyanotic/prostheticrepaired CHD; VAD (ESC).
  • Amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 min before; allergy → cephalexin 2 g, azithro/clarithromycin 500 mg or doxycycline 100 mg.
  • Clindamycin is no longer recommended.
  • MVP, BAV, RHD, HCM, CIED = intermediate risk — no routine prophylaxis.
  • S. aureus nasal screening and decolonisation before elective cardiac surgery/TAVI (I A).
  • Complicated IE → early referral to a Heart Valve Centre with an Endocarditis Team.

15.8 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 71-year-old man with a surgical aortic bioprosthesis (implanted 3 years ago) has fever for 3 weeks. Two bloodculture sets grow E. faecalis. TTE and TOE show no vegetation or abscess; FDG-PET/CT shows intense periprosthetic uptake. According to the ESC 2023 criteria, the diagnosis is:

Answer C E. faecalis is now a typical organism (2 cultures = major criterion), and FDG-PET/CT periprosthetic uptake is a major imaging criterion in ESC 2023. Two majors = definite IE even with a negative TOE. Under the old Duke criteria this would only be "possible".

Q2 A 54-year-old man with MSSA native aortic-valve IE is haemodynamically stable. Which regimen is recommended?

Answer B MSSA NVE: flucloxacillin (cloxacillin) or cefazolin for 4–6 weeks (I B). Gentamicin adds nephrotoxicity without benefit in staphylococcal NVE; rifampicin is reserved for prosthetic material; 2-week courses apply to uncomplicated rightsided MSSA IE in PWID; daptomycin must be combined.

Q3 A 68-year-old with E. faecalis native mitral IE; the isolate shows high-level aminoglycoside resistance. The best regimen is:

Answer C Ampicillin + ceftriaxone for 6 weeks is the regimen for HLAR E. faecalis (I B) — synergy by complementary PBP saturation, no aminoglycoside. Gentamicin is useless with HLAR; ceftriaxone alone is ineffective (intrinsic resistance).

Q4 A 45-year-old with streptococcal native mitral IE has a 14 mm mobile vegetation and moderate MR. On day 3 of appropriate antibiotics he develops a splenic infarct. There is no HF. The best management is:

Answer B Persistent vegetation ≥ 10 mm after ≥ 1 embolic episode despite appropriate antibiotics → urgent surgery within 3–5 days (ESC I B). Waiting loses the window when embolic risk is highest; antithrombotics do not prevent IE emboli.

Q5 A 38-year-old with S. aureus aortic IE and severe AR develops NYHA II–III dyspnoea. Brain MRI done for a transient arm weakness shows a small cortical infarct without haemorrhage; he is fully conscious. The most appropriate timing of surgery is:

Answer C After TIA or ischaemic stroke, with haemorrhage excluded and no coma, indicated surgery should not be delayed (ESC 2023 I B). Delay > 1 month applies to intracranial haemorrhage (IIa C).

Q6 A 60-year-old with a dual-chamber pacemaker has S. aureus bacteraemia. TOE shows a 9 mm vegetation on the RA lead; the valves are normal. The most appropriate management is:

Answer B Definite CIED-related IE → complete system extraction without delay plus antibiotics (I B); biofilm on retained hardware causes relapse. Reimplant at a distant site after ≥ 2 weeks of negative cultures because a vegetation was seen.

Q7 A 29-year-old who injects drugs has MSSA tricuspid IE with a 15 mm vegetation. He defervesced within 72 h, cultures cleared, and there are no metastatic foci, empyema or left-sided involvement. Which antibiotic course is acceptable?

Answer A Uncomplicated right-sided MSSA IE with rapid response (< 96 h), vegetation ≤ 20 mm, no emboli/empyema, no leftsided or prosthetic involvement → 2 weeks of (flu)cloxacillin without gentamicin. Glycopeptides are inferior for short courses; POET excluded PWID.

Q8 A 65-year-old with streptococcal native aortic IE has received 12 days of IV ceftriaxone. He has been afebrile for 5 days, CRP has fallen from 180 to 30 mg/L, WBC is normal. Before switching to oral amoxicillin plus rifampicin, which step is required?

Answer B TOE is recommended (I B) before switching to oral therapy to exclude abscess or other complications requiring surgery. He meets POET criteria: ≥ 10 days IV, afebrile > 2 days, CRP < 25% of peak.

Q9 Which patient should receive antibiotic prophylaxis before a dental extraction?

Answer C Transcatheter aortic prostheses are high-risk (ESC 2023 I C; AHA 2021). MVP, BAV, HCM and CIEDs are intermediate risk — no routine prophylaxis.

Q10 A shepherd with a mechanical aortic valve has fever and weight loss; three blood-culture sets are negative after 5 days (no prior antibiotics). TOE shows a small vegetation. The most useful next test is:

Answer B Culture-negative prosthetic-valve IE in a patient exposed to livestock suggests Q fever; phase I IgG > 1:800 is a major criterion. Treatment: doxycycline + hydroxychloroquine ≥ 18 months. Prolonged culture incubation adds little with modern systems.

What the board expects you to know

  • Which ion current underlies each action-potential phase — and which drug, gene or electrolyte disturbance targets it.
  • How to separate re-entry, automaticity and triggered activity, and predict their response to pacing, adenosine and drugs.
  • A reproducible approach to narrow- and wide-complex tachycardia, including the Brugada and Vereckei algorithms.
  • The contraindications, monitoring rules and interactions of every commonly used antiarrhythmic — especially amiodarone, flecainide/propafenone, sotalol, dofetilide, dronedarone and digoxin.
  • How to recognise and treat drug-induced QT prolongation, torsades de pointes and digoxin toxicity.

16.1 Action Potential & Ion Currents

Every antiarrhythmic drug, channelopathy and electrolyte ECG sign is explained by the cardiac action potential (AP). There are two basic AP types: the fast-response AP of atrial and ventricular myocytes and His– Purkinje fibres (Na⁺-driven upstroke, stable resting potential near −85 to −90 mV) and the slow-response AP of the sinus and AV nodes (Ca²⁺-driven upstroke, no true resting potential, spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation).

Fast-response (working myocardium, Purkinje) action potential

Slow-response (nodal) action potential and automaticity

Phase 4 — spontaneous diastolic depolarisation from the funny current If (HCN4; activated by hyperpolarisation, enhanced by cAMP) plus T-type Ca²⁺ current and the Ca²⁺ clock (SR Ca²⁺ release driving Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange).

Phase 0 — slow upstroke through L-type Ca²⁺ channels → slow conduction → the physiological AV-nodal delay. This is why verapamil, diltiazem and adenosine act on the node but not on atrial/ventricular muscle or most accessory pathways.

opens) hyperpolarises and flattens it. Adenosine works through the same IK,ACh/IK,Ado channel via A₁ receptors.

Refractoriness in muscle is voltage-dependent (ends with repolarisation); in the AV node it is timedependent and outlasts repolarisation (post-repolarisation refractoriness) — the basis of decremental conduction.

MECHANISM — CONDUCTION VS REFRACTORINESS

Two properties decide whether re-entry can occur. Conduction velocity depends on phase 0 (Na⁺ current and gap-junction coupling); refractory period depends on AP duration (phases 2–3). Their product — the wavelength — must be shorter than the circuit for re-entry to persist. Class I drugs mainly slow conduction (QRS ↑); class III drugs mainly prolong refractoriness (QT ↑). Both can terminate re-entry, but a drug that slows conduction more than it prolongs refractoriness can shorten the wavelength and promote reentry — the essence of class Ic proarrhythmia.

Key highlightsAction potential & ion currents

  • Phase 0 = INa (QRS); phase 2 = ICa,L vs IKr/IKs (ST); phase 3 = IKr, IKs, IK1 (T wave); phase 4 = IK1.
  • Nodal cells: phase 4 by If (HCN4) — blocked by ivabradine; phase 0 by ICa,L — blocked by verapamil/diltiazem.
  • IKr (hERG, KCNH2) is the target of almost every QT-prolonging drug and the gene for LQT2.
  • LQT1 = IKs loss (exercise/swimming); LQT3 = late INa gain (sleep/rest) — treated with mexiletine plus β-blocker.
  • SCN5A loss of function → Brugada syndrome and progressive conduction disease.
  • IKur is atrial-specific — the rationale for atrial-selective vernakalant.
  • AV-nodal refractoriness is time-dependent (outlasts the AP) → decremental conduction.
  • ARRHYTHMIA FUNDAMENTALS: MECHANISMS, ECG APPROACH & ANTIARRHYTHMIC
  • DRUGS

16.2 Mechanisms of Arrhythmia

Tachyarrhythmias arise from abnormal impulse formation (automaticity or triggered activity) or abnormal impulse conduction (re-entry). Re-entry is by far the most common mechanism of clinical sustained tachycardias (AVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter, scar-related VT).

Automaticity

Enhanced normal automaticity — faster firing of normal pacemaker cells: sinus tachycardia, inappropriate sinus tachycardia, some junctional rhythms.

Abnormal automaticity — partially depolarised myocytes (resting potential ~−60 mV) fire

spontaneously: accelerated idioventricular rhythm after reperfusion, automatic focal AT, junctional ectopic tachycardia (JET).

Clinical signature: warm-up at onset and cool-down at offset; cannot be initiated or terminated by programmed stimulation; overdrive suppression is transient; cardioversion does not terminate it (the focus simply restarts).

Triggered activity

Re-entry

Classic requirements: (1) two functionally distinct pathways joined at both ends; (2) unidirectional block in one limb; (3) slow enough conduction in the other so that tissue ahead has recovered — i.e. an excitable gap. A premature beat usually initiates it.

Anatomical re-entry
  • Fixed obstacle, fixed circuit, large excitable gap
  • AVRT (AV node + accessory pathway), typical flutter
  • (tricuspid annulus/CTI), bundle-branch re-entry, scarrelated VT (isthmus in MI scar)
  • Curable by ablating the critical isthmus
Functional re-entry
  • No anatomical obstacle — circuits determined by
  • refractoriness (leading circle, spiral waves/rotors,
  • anisotropy)
  • AF, polymorphic VT, VF
  • Small or absent excitable gap; ablation harder
  • ARRHYTHMIA FUNDAMENTALS: MECHANISMS, ECG APPROACH & ANTIARRHYTHMIC

DRUGS

MECHANISM — WHY AVNRT HAS A "SLOW" AND A "FAST" PATHWAY

The fast pathway conducts rapidly but has a long refractory period; the slow pathway conducts slowly but recovers quickly. A premature atrial beat finds the fast pathway still refractory, travels down the slow pathway (long PR), and returns up the now-recovered fast pathway → typical slow–fast AVNRT. The same logic (fast limb with long refractoriness + slow limb with short refractoriness) underlies every re-entrant circuit.

BOARD PEARL

Entrainment — pacing slightly faster than the tachycardia captures the circuit, and the tachycardia resumes at its own cycle length when pacing stops — proves re-entry with an excitable gap . A post-pacing interval within 30 ms of the tachycardia cycle length means the pacing site is in the circuit (used to find the ablation isthmus).

EXAM TRAP

An arrhythmia that cannot be cardioverted or that recurs immediately after DC shock is probably automatic (e.g. automatic AT, JET, AIVR). Repeated shocks are futile — treat the driver (ischaemia, catecholamines, electrolytes, fever) and use rate-slowing drugs.

Key highlightsMechanisms of arrhythmia

  • Re-entry is the commonest mechanism; needs two pathways, unidirectional block and slow conduction (excitable gap).
  • Wavelength = conduction velocity × refractory period; shorter wavelength favours re-entry.
  • Automatic rhythms warm up and cool down, are not induced/terminated by pacing, and do not respond to cardioversion.
  • EADs are pause/bradycardia-dependent (TdP, long QT); DADs are tachycardia/Ca²⁺-overload dependent (digoxin toxicity, CPVT, RVOT VT).
  • Adenosine-sensitive VT (RVOT) = cAMP-mediated triggered activity.
  • Entrainment is the hallmark of re-entry; post-pacing interval − TCL ≤ 30 ms = in the circuit.
  • Anatomical re-entry (AVRT, flutter, scar VT) is highly curable by isthmus ablation.
  • ARRHYTHMIA FUNDAMENTALS: MECHANISMS, ECG APPROACH & ANTIARRHYTHMIC
  • DRUGS

16.3 Systematic ECG Approach to Tachycardia

Every tachycardia is sorted by three questions, in this order: (1) Is the QRS narrow (< 120 ms) or wide (≥ 120 ms)? (2) Is the rhythm regular or irregular? (3) Where are the P waves, and how do they relate to the QRS? Always obtain a 12-lead ECG during tachycardia if the patient is stable — it is the single most valuable diagnostic test and guides ablation later.

Narrow-complex tachycardia — reading the P wave

Look for P waves in II, III, aVF and V1; compare with the sinus-rhythm ECG — a new "r′" in V1 or "s" in the inferior leads is a hidden P wave.

More P than QRS (AV block with tachycardia continuing) → atrial tachycardia or flutter; this excludes AVRT and makes AVNRT unlikely.

RP interval (onset of QRS to onset of the following P): short RP (RP < PR) vs long RP (RP > PR). A very short RP < 90 ms on the surface ECG (VA < 70 ms intracardiac) = typical AVNRT; RP > 90 ms but < PR favours orthodromic AVRT.

Long RP differential: sinus tachycardia, focal AT, atypical AVNRT, PJRT (slowly conducting posteroseptal pathway).

Full discriminators (pseudo r′, QRS alternans, response to BBB) are developed in Chapter 17.

DRUGS

Acute management when the diagnosis is not yet established

Principle: instability of any tachycardia → synchronised DC cardioversion . In a stable patient, record the 12-lead ECG, then escalate from manoeuvres to drugs to cardioversion.

EXAM TRAP

Verapamil given to a patient in VT (misdiagnosed as SVT with aberrancy) causes profound hypotension and haemodynamic collapse. A stable blood pressure does not suggest SVT — many patients tolerate VT for hours. When in doubt, treat as VT.

Key highlightsSystematic ECG approach

  • Three questions: QRS width (cut-off 120 ms), regularity, P–QRS relationship.
  • Regular narrow tachycardia at ~150 bpm = atrial flutter with 2:1 block until proved otherwise.
  • AV block during tachycardia excludes AVRT (both chambers are obligatory parts of the circuit).
  • RP < 90 ms (surface) → typical AVNRT; RP > 90 ms but < PR → AVRT; long RP → AT, atypical AVNRT, PJRT.
  • Adenosine: termination = AV-node-dependent; persistent atrial activity with block = flutter/AT.
  • Unstable → synchronised cardioversion (I B); verapamil in undiagnosed WCT is Class III.
  • ESC 2022: DC cardioversion is first-line (I B) even for tolerated SMVT if sedation risk is low; procainamide IIa, amiodarone IIb.
