16.4 Wide-Complex Tachycardia: VT vs SVT with Aberrancy

A regular wide-complex tachycardia (WCT) is VT in ~80% of unselected cases and in > 90% of patients with prior MI or structural heart disease. SVT with aberrancy accounts for ~15–20% and pre-excited tachycardia for ~1–5%. History beats ECG criteria: WCT in a patient with prior MI is VT. Clinical clues

Favour VT
  • Age > 35, prior MI, cardiomyopathy, HF, ICD
  • Cannon a waves (irregular) in the JVP
  • Variable S1 intensity and variable systolic BP (AV
  • dissociation)
Favour SVT
  • Young, structurally normal heart, long history of identical
  • episodes
  • Known BBB or pre-excitation with identical QRS in sinus
  • rhythm
  • Termination by vagal manoeuvres

ECG criteria that point to VT

MECHANISM — WHY VT "STARTS SLOWLY"

Aberrant SVT still enters the ventricles through the His–Purkinje system, so the initial part of the QRS is fast (sharp) and only the terminal part is delayed. VT starts in muscle and spreads cell-to-cell, so the initial forces are slow and broad. Almost every morphological criterion (RS > 100 ms, initial r in aVR, R-peak time in II, vi/vt ratio) is a measurement of this slow onset.

SVT with aberrancy

DRUGS

BOARD PEARL — THE LOGIC OF AVR

Normal ventricular activation (and aberrant SVT) moves away from aVR, so aVR starts negative. An initial R in aVR means activation starts at the apex/inferior wall and travels up toward the right shoulder — only VT does that. The aVR algorithm is quick and needs no morphology memory, but its specificity is lower than AV dissociation.

Pre-excited tachycardia — the third diagnosis

Pre-excited AF: irregular, very fast (often > 200–250 bpm) WCT with beat-to-beat variation in QRS width (varying fusion between pathway and AV node). Shortest pre-excited R–R ≤ 250 ms marks a dangerous pathway.

Antidromic AVRT: regular, maximally pre-excited; resembles VT (origin at the ventricular insertion of the pathway). Morphology identical to maximal pre-excitation in sinus rhythm; LBBB-like with late transition suggests an atriofascicular (Mahaim) pathway.

Criteria that discriminate VT from aberrancy do not discriminate VT from pre-excitation — history and the sinus-rhythm ECG are key.

DON'T CONFUSE — IRREGULAR WCT

AF with BBB Constant QRS morphology; rate usually < 200; Ashman beats after long–short cycles Pre-excited AF Varying width, very fast, bizarre; give procainamide/ibutilide or shock — never AV-nodal blockers

Polymorphic VT /

TdP

Continuously changing axis; TdP twists around baseline after a long–short sequence with

long QT

EXAM TRAP

No single algorithm is perfect — reported accuracy in validation cohorts is typically only ~75–85%, lower than in the derivation papers. Misclassifying VT as SVT is the dangerous error. If criteria are indeterminate and the patient has structural heart disease, it is VT.

Key highlightsVT vs SVT with aberrancy

  • WCT is VT in ~80%; > 90% with prior MI — history of MI is the single best predictor.
  • AV dissociation, capture and fusion beats are ~100% specific for VT but seen in a minority.
  • Brugada: no RS in V1–V6 → RS > 100 ms → AV dissociation → morphology in V1–2 and V6.
  • Vereckei: initial R in aVR → initial r/q > 40 ms → notched descent → vi/vt ≤ 1 = VT.
  • R-wave peak time in lead II ≥ 50 ms → VT; northwest axis → VT.
  • RBBB-like: taller left rabbit ear in V1 and R/S < 1 in V6 → VT. LBBB-like: any Q in V6, broad r > 30 ms in V1 → VT.
  • Negative precordial concordance = VT; positive concordance = VT or left posterior pathway.
  • Irregular, very fast WCT with varying width = pre-excited AF; AV-nodal blockers and IV amiodarone are harmful.
  • Hemodynamic stability never excludes VT.

16.5 Classifying Antiarrhythmic Drugs

The Vaughan-Williams classification (1970s) groups drugs by their dominant action: I = Na⁺-channel block, II = β-blockade, III = K⁺-channel block (AP prolongation), IV = Ca²⁺-channel block. It remains the language of exams, but it is imperfect: many drugs have several actions (amiodarone has all four), and important agents (adenosine, digoxin, ivabradine) do not fit. The modernised classification (Lei et al., Circulation 2018), adopted in the EHRA 2025 practical compendium, keeps the four classes and adds sub-classes and new classes.

Substrate modification

MECHANISM — USE-DEPENDENCE VS REVERSE USE-DEPENDENCE

Use-dependence (class Ic): drug binds during depolarisation and unbinds slowly in diastole, so block accumulates at fast rates → QRS widens during exercise or tachycardia → incessant slow VT and wide-complex proarrhythmia at high rates.

Reverse use-dependence (sotalol, dofetilide, quinidine): IKr block prolongs the AP most at slow rates → QT maximal after pauses and bradycardia → TdP typically "pause-dependent". Amiodarone lacks reverse usedependence, which is one reason its TdP risk is low despite marked QT prolongation.

  • DRUGS

Choosing an antiarrhythmic: the structural-heart-disease rule

The single most examined principle is that the heart's substrate — not the arrhythmia — decides which drug is safe.

EXAM TRAP — CAST

In CAST (post-MI patients with asymptomatic PVCs), flecainide and encainide suppressed the PVCs yet increased mortality (arrhythmic death) roughly two- to three-fold. Lesson: suppressing ectopy is not a surrogate for survival , and class Ic drugs are contraindicated after MI and in structural heart disease.

Key highlightsClassification

  • Vaughan-Williams I–IV: Na⁺, β, K⁺, Ca²⁺. Modernised scheme adds class 0 (ivabradine), Id (ranolazine), IIb–IIe (isoprenaline, atropine, digoxin, adenosine), V–VII.
  • Ia widens QRS and QT; Ib little ECG effect; Ic widens QRS (and PR) with little QT change.
  • Class Ic = marked use-dependence (worse at fast rates); IKr blockers = reverse use-dependence (worse at slow rates).
  • Amiodarone has class I, II, III and IV actions and no reverse use-dependence → low TdP (< 1–2%).
  • Structural heart disease/CAD → no class Ic (CAST). HFrEF → amiodarone (or dofetilide); no dronedarone.
  • EHRA 2025 compendium frames AAD use as Appropriate, Backup or Complementary to ablation/devices.

16.6 Sodium-Channel Blockers (Class I)

Flecainide and propafenone — the rules

Structural heart disease is the contraindication: prior MI/CAD, reduced LVEF or HF, severe LVH, significant valve disease.

Always co-prescribe an AV-nodal blocker (β-blocker or non-DHP CCB) when using class Ic for AF: slowing of the atrial rate can convert AF to "slow" flutter (~200 bpm) that conducts 1:1, often with raterelated QRS widening mimicking VT. Monitor the ECG after initiation/up-titration: reduce or stop if QRS widens by > 25% from baseline (or new BBB). An exercise test can unmask use-dependent QRS widening.

Pill-in-the-pocket (single oral dose at onset of AF): only after safety has been demonstrated in a monitored setting, in patients without structural disease, with a β-blocker/CCB taken beforehand. • •

  • • •
  • ARRHYTHMIA FUNDAMENTALS: MECHANISMS, ECG APPROACH & ANTIARRHYTHMIC

DRUGS

Class Ic agents can unmask a type 1 Brugada pattern (this is exploited in the drug-challenge test) and raise pacing thresholds.

Interaction: amiodarone raises flecainide levels — halve the flecainide dose if combined.

BOARD PEARL — PROCAINAMIDE IN PRE-EXCITED AF

Procainamide (and ibutilide) slow conduction and prolong refractoriness in the accessory pathway, reducing the pre-excited ventricular rate and often converting AF. That is why they, not AV-nodal blockers, are the drugs for stable pre-excited AF.

16.7 Potassium-Channel Blockers (Class III)

Amiodarone

The most effective and the most toxic antiarrhythmic. It blocks IKr, IKs, INa (inactivated channels), ICa,L and β-receptors (non-competitively). It is iodine-rich (~37% iodine by weight), highly lipophilic (volume of distribution ~60 L/kg) and has an elimination half-life of about 50 days (range 26–107). Onset after oral dosing takes days to weeks without a loading dose.

Dosing essentials
  • IV: 150 mg over 10 min, then 1 mg/min for 6 h, then
  • 0.5 mg/min for 18 h; extra 150 mg boluses for
  • breakthrough VT
  • Cardiac arrest (shock-refractory VF/pVT): 300 mg IV after
  • the 3rd shock, then 150 mg
  • Oral loading: total ~6–10 g over 1–3 weeks, then
  • maintenance 100–200 mg daily (lowest effective dose)
  • No renal dose adjustment; not dialysable
Indications
  • AF rhythm control in HFrEF/structural disease; rate control
  • in acute HF
  • Recurrent VT / ICD shocks (with β-blocker)
  • Shock-refractory VF/pVT
  • Neutral on mortality in HFrEF (SCD-HeFT) — not a
  • substitute for an ICD
  • stop drug ± steroids
  • Thyroid Hypothyroidism (more common in iodine-sufficient areas);
  • thyrotoxicosis (types 1 and 2)
  • TSH (± free T4) at baseline and every
  • 4–6 months

Key highlightsClass I agents

  • Quinidine survives mainly for Brugada/early-repolarisation VF storm; causes diarrhoea, cinchonism, TdP, ↑ digoxin.
  • Procainamide IV 10–17 mg/kg; stop if QRS ↑ > 50% or hypotension; NAPA accumulates in renal failure; lupuslike syndrome.
  • Disopyramide: anticholinergic, negative inotrope — useful in obstructive HCM.
  • Lidocaine works in ischaemic, depolarised tissue; CNS toxicity; prophylaxis in MI is harmful.
  • Mexiletine: LQT3 and adjunct for recurrent VT.
  • Flecainide/propafenone: contraindicated in CAD, LV dysfunction, severe LVH, Brugada; add an AV-nodal blocker to prevent 1:1 flutter.
  • Stop/reduce class Ic if QRS widens > 25%; PIP doses flecainide 200–300 mg, propafenone 450–600 mg.

KEY AMIODARONE INTERACTIONS

Warfarin: INR ↑ (CYP2C9) → reduce dose ~30–50%. Digoxin and flecainide: levels ↑ → halve dose. Simvastatin ≤ 20 mg (CYP3A4 myopathy); avoid other QT-prolonging drugs; sofosbuvir → severe bradycardia (avoid).

β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem → additive bradycardia/AV block.

Dronedarone

Non-iodinated, less lipophilic amiodarone analogue (half-life ~24 h); fewer thyroid/lung effects but less effective.

Dose: 400 mg twice daily with meals (large first-pass effect).

ANDROMEDA: in recently decompensated, severe HF with LV dysfunction, mortality roughly doubled (8.1% vs 3.8%). PALLAS: in permanent AF, doubled death, stroke and HF events. ATHENA: in paroxysmal/persistent AF with risk factors, reduced CV hospitalisation or death.

Contraindicated: HFrEF/unstable or recently decompensated HF (NYHA IV or recent hospitalisation), permanent AF, QTc ≥ 500 ms, significant bradycardia/AV block without pacing, severe hepatic impairment, prior amiodarone liver/lung toxicity, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and co-administration with dabigatran.

Raises serum creatinine by ~0.1 mg/dL (inhibits tubular secretion; GFR unchanged). Monitor LFTs (rare severe hepatic failure) and check that AF has not become permanent.

Increases digoxin levels (halve dose) and statin exposure.

Sotalol

Racemic mixture: l-isomer is a β-blocker; both isomers block IKr. β-blockade dominates at low doses, class III action at ≥ 160 mg/day.

16.8 β-Blockers, Calcium Blockers, Adenosine, Digoxin & Others

β-Blockers (class II)

The only antiarrhythmic class that consistently reduces sudden death (post-MI, HFrEF) — the backbone of VA therapy, LQTS (non-selective nadolol or propranolol preferred) and CPVT.

Acute IV: esmolol 0.5 mg/kg bolus then 0.05–0.3 mg/kg/min (half-life ~9 min — ideal when haemodynamics are uncertain); metoprolol 2.5–5 mg IV, repeatable.

Avoid in decompensated HF, severe bronchospasm, pre-excited AF, cocaine-associated tachycardia (relative).

Non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (class IV)

IV verapamil 5–10 mg (0.075–0.15 mg/kg) over 2 min; IV diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg over 2 min. Terminate ~90% of AV-node-dependent SVT.

Contraindicated: HFrEF, hypotension, WCT of unknown origin, pre-excited AF, concurrent IV β-blocker, sinus-node disease or AV block.

Specific use: verapamil-sensitive fascicular VT (Belhassen VT) — RBBB morphology with left (superior) axis from the left posterior fascicle in a young patient with a normal heart.

Adenosine

Key highlightsClass III agents

  • Amiodarone: half-life ~50 days; IV 150 mg/10 min → 1 mg/min × 6 h → 0.5 mg/min × 18 h; arrest dose 300 mg.
  • Monitor TSH every 4–6 months, LFTs every 6 months, CXR yearly, PFT/DLCO at baseline and for symptoms.
  • AIT type 1 (iodine, abnormal gland, thionamides) vs type 2 (thyroiditis, normal gland, steroids).
  • Amiodarone: halve digoxin and flecainide; reduce warfarin ~30–50%; simvastatin ≤ 20 mg; avoid sofosbuvir.
  • Dronedarone is contraindicated in decompensated/HFrEF (ANDROMEDA) and permanent AF (PALLAS); creatinine rises ~0.1 mg/dL harmlessly.
  • Sotalol: renal; interval by CrCl; avoid baseline QTc > 450 ms; stop at > 500 ms.
  • Dofetilide: in-hospital ≥ 3 days; CrCl-based dose (500/250/125 µg bid); contraindicated if CrCl < 20 or QTc > 440 ms; no verapamil, HCTZ, trimethoprim.
  • Ibutilide 1 mg over 10 min — best for flutter; TdP up to ~4%. Vernakalant 3 mg/kg — avoid if SBP < 100, recent ACS, severe AS, NYHA III–IV.

16.9 Proarrhythmia, QT Prolongation, TdP & Electrolytes

Proarrhythmia is a new or worsened arrhythmia caused by a drug at therapeutic or near-therapeutic concentrations. It is predictable from the drug's mechanism and the patient's substrate.

Key highlightsβ-blockers, CCBs, adenosine, digoxin

  • β-blockers are the only AADs that reduce sudden death; nadolol/propranolol preferred in LQTS.
  • Verapamil 5–10 mg / diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV — never in WCT of unknown origin, HFrEF or pre-excited AF.
  • Adenosine 6 → 12 mg (ESC up to 18 mg); reduce to ~3 mg with central line, dipyridamole, heart transplant; theophylline blocks it.
  • Adenosine can induce AF — hazardous with pre-excitation; safe in pregnancy.
  • Digoxin toxicity: PVCs/bigeminy, AT with block, accelerated junctional rhythm, regularised AF, bidirectional VT; xanthopsia.
  • Fab indications: life-threatening arrhythmia, K⁺ > 5.0 mmol/L in acute overdose, ingestion > 10 mg, level ≥ 10 ng/mL.
  • Amiodarone, dronedarone, verapamil, quinidine, propafenone raise digoxin levels (halve digoxin with amiodarone).
  • Verapamil-sensitive fascicular VT: RBBB + superior axis, structurally normal heart.

MECHANISM — WHY PACING AND ISOPRENALINE WORK

TdP arises from EADs in a heterogeneously prolonged ventricle; IKr blockers prolong the AP most at slow rates (reverse use-dependence). Raising the heart rate shortens the QT and removes the long–short sequence that initiates TdP. Isoprenaline is avoided in congenital LQTS (especially LQT1/LQT2), where adrenergic stimulation is itself the trigger.

Electrolytes and the ECG

  • severe (> ~8) Very wide QRS merging with T — sine-wave VF, asystole, PEA
  • Hypocalcaemia Long ST segment → long QT (T wave normal) TdP (uncommon)

Hypercalcaemia Short ST/QT; Osborn-like J wave when severe Bradyarrhythmia, AV block; potentiates digoxin

Hypomagnesaemia Similar to hypokalaemia TdP; refractory hypokalaemia

K⁺ thresholds are approximate — ECG correlation with serum K⁺ is poor; a normal ECG does not exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia. ARRHYTHMIA FUNDAMENTALS: MECHANISMS, ECG APPROACH & ANTIARRHYTHMIC

DRUGS

BOARD PEARL — HYPERKALAEMIA WITH ARRHYTHMIA

ECG changes of hyperkalaemia mandate immediate IV calcium (e.g. 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride or 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate) to stabilise the membrane — it acts within minutes but does not lower K⁺.

Then shift K⁺ (insulin–glucose, nebulised salbutamol) and remove it. Temporary pacing often fails to capture in severe hyperkalaemia.

16.10 The Electrophysiology Study at Board Level

An electrophysiology study (EPS) records intracardiac electrograms (high RA, His bundle, coronary sinus, RV apex) and uses programmed stimulation to measure conduction, refractoriness and inducibility. Complications are uncommon (< ~1% — vascular injury, tamponade, AV block, thromboembolism).

Key highlightsProarrhythmia, QT & TdP

  • TdP: class Ia/III and non-cardiac IKr blockers; pause-dependent onset (long–short sequence).
  • Class Ic proarrhythmia: incessant wide slow VT in structural disease; 1:1 atrial flutter.
  • QTc > 500 ms or rise > 60 ms = high risk → reduce/stop drug. Bazett over-corrects at fast rates.
  • TdP: defibrillate if sustained; MgSO₄ 2 g IV; K⁺ to 4.5–5.0; pacing/isoprenaline to raise HR (not in congenital LQTS).
  • Hypokalaemia → U waves; hyperkalaemia → peaked T → PR ↑/P loss → wide QRS → sine wave.
  • Hypocalcaemia lengthens the ST segment (long QT); hypercalcaemia shortens it.
  • Class Ic and amiodarone raise defibrillation thresholds; Ic raises pacing thresholds.

Key highlightsEP study

  • Normal AH 50–120 ms; normal HV 35–55 ms.
  • HV ≥ 70 ms + syncope + bifascicular block → permanent pacing (ESC 2021 I B).
  • AH jump ≥ 50 ms per 10 ms decrement = dual AV-nodal physiology.
  • Only inducible sustained monomorphic VT is a specific EPS finding.
  • His-refractory PVC resetting the atrium proves an accessory pathway.
  • V-A-A-V after ventricular overdrive = atrial tachycardia.
  • High-risk pathway at EPS: SPERRI ≤ 250 ms, AP ERP ≤ 250 ms, multiple APs, inducible AVRT.

16.11 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 66-year-old man with an anterior MI 4 years ago presents with palpitations. BP 112/70 mmHg, alert, no chest pain. ECG: regular WCT at 170 bpm, QRS 170 ms, LBBB-like morphology with a Q wave in V6. An anaesthetist is available and sedation risk is low. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

Answer D Tolerated SMVT in a post-MI patient: ESC 2022 recommends DC cardioversion as first-line (I B) when sedation risk is low. Procainamide is IIa and amiodarone IIb. Verapamil is contraindicated in WCT; adenosine will not help scar VT; lidocaine is less effective.

Q2 A regular WCT at 190 bpm is recorded in a 58-year-old woman. You apply the Vereckei algorithm. Which single finding in lead aVR establishes VT at the first step?

Answer B An initial R wave in aVR means activation starts inferiorly/apically and travels up toward aVR — only VT does this. A vi/vt > 1 (option C) favours SVT; a sharp initial negative deflection is the normal/aberrant pattern.

Q3 A 72-year-old man with persistent AF and HFrEF is started on dofetilide in hospital. Creatinine clearance is 45 mL/min; baseline QTc 420 ms. Three hours after the first dose, QTc is 490 ms. What is the correct action?

Answer B At CrCl 40–60 mL/min the starting dose is 250 µg twice daily. QTc rose by 17% (> 15%), so the dose is halved to 125 µg twice daily. If QTc exceeds 500 ms after later doses, stop. Increasing the dose or switching to sotalol is unsafe.

Q4 A 60-year-old woman on amiodarone for 2 years develops weight loss and palpitations. Free T4 is high, TSH suppressed. Thyroid ultrasound shows a normal-sized gland with absent Doppler flow; radio-iodine uptake is very low. The best treatment is:

Answer C Normal gland, absent vascularity and low uptake = type 2 AIT (destructive thyroiditis), treated with glucocorticoids. Thionamides ± perchlorate treat type 1 (iodine-induced, abnormal gland). Radio-iodine is useless with low uptake. ARRHYTHMIA FUNDAMENTALS: MECHANISMS, ECG APPROACH & ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUGS

Q5 A 45-year-old with paroxysmal AF and a structurally normal heart takes flecainide 100 mg twice daily alone. During a run he develops a regular WCT at 220 bpm. After cardioversion, which change would best have prevented this event?

Answer B Class Ic drugs slow atrial flutter enough for 1:1 AV conduction, with use-dependent QRS widening mimicking VT. An AV-nodal blocker must accompany flecainide. Increasing flecainide worsens the problem; digoxin is weak during exercise.

Q6 A 70-year-old woman receiving clarithromycin and furosemide has recurrent self-terminating polymorphic VT after pauses. QTc 560 ms, K⁺ 3.2 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ normal. BP is maintained between runs. The most appropriate immediate drug is:

Answer C Acquired LQTS with pause-dependent TdP: stop clarithromycin, give MgSO₄ 2 g IV (effective with normal Mg²⁺) and raise K⁺ to 4.5–5.0. Amiodarone, procainamide and sotalol prolong QT further; β-blockade would slow the rate and worsen pauses.

Q7 An 82-year-old woman on digoxin and recently started amiodarone presents with vomiting and yellow vision. ECG: bidirectional VT with runs of hypotension. K⁺ 5.8 mmol/L, creatinine raised. The best next treatment is: IV calcium chloride

Answer C Life-threatening digoxin toxicity (bidirectional VT, hyperkalaemia, renal impairment, amiodarone interaction) is an absolute indication for digoxin Fab. Cardioversion risks VF; digoxin is not dialysable; pacing may provoke arrhythmias.

Q8 In which patient is dronedarone contraindicated?

Answer C PALLAS showed dronedarone doubles death, stroke and HF events in permanent AF. Paroxysmal/persistent AF with CAD or stable HFpEF are acceptable indications; apixaban does not interact significantly (dabigatran does).

Q9 A 30-year-old with a structurally normal heart has repetitive monomorphic VT with LBBB morphology and inferior axis, provoked by exercise and terminated by IV adenosine. The most likely mechanism is:

Answer B RVOT VT is due to cAMP-mediated DADs; adenosine lowers cAMP and terminates it — a unique VT response. Scar and bundle-branch re-entry need structural disease; EADs cause TdP.

Q10 A 74-year-old man has two episodes of unexplained syncope. ECG: RBBB with left anterior fascicular block, PR 180 ms. Echo and monitoring are unremarkable. EPS shows HV 78 ms. The best management is:

Answer C Unexplained syncope with bifascicular block and HV ≥ 70 ms is a Class I indication for pacing (ESC 2021). An ICD is not indicated with preserved LV function; a loop recorder is the path only when EPS is negative.

17.1 Classification & Clinical Approach

DEFINITION

Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT): an atrial and/or ventricular rate > 100 bpm at rest whose mechanism involves tissue from the His bundle or above. Paroxysmal SVT (PSVT) is the subset with abrupt onset and offset — in practice AVNRT, AVRT and focal AT. AF is conventionally discussed separately.

Epidemiology

PSVT prevalence ~2.25 per 1000; incidence ~35 per 100 000 person-years; about twice as common in women.

AVNRT is the commonest PSVT in adults (peak in middle age, female predominance). AVRT dominates in children and adolescents and becomes uncommon after 60 (< 10% of SVT). Focal AT becomes proportionally more frequent with age.

History and examination

Abrupt onset and offset ("switch on–switch off"), regular palpitations, termination with breath-holding or Valsalva → re-entry involving the AV node.

Frog sign — rapid regular neck pulsations from atria contracting against closed AV valves: suggests AVNRT (simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation).

Polyuria after an episode (atrial natriuretic peptide), chest tightness, dyspnoea; true syncope is uncommon — if present, think of a fast pre-excited AF or VT.

Incessant forms (PJRT, focal AT, atypical AVNRT) can cause tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, which is reversible after rate control or ablation.

The key diagnostic document — ask patients to attend during an episode

Ambulatory monitoring Holter (daily symptoms), event/patch recorder, smartphone/wearable ECG (infrequent episodes); implantable loop recorder for rare, severe episodes

Echocardiography Structural disease (Ebstein anomaly, HCM, ACHD) and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy

  • Bloods Thyroid function, full blood count, electrolytes
  • Test Purpose
  • Exercise test Exercise-induced SVT; loss of pre-excitation (risk stratification)

EPS Diagnosis when ECG documentation is lacking but history is typical; usually combined with ablation

BOARD PEARL

A patient with a typical history of abrupt, regular palpitations terminated by vagal manoeuvres but no ECG documentation can be referred directly for EPS with a view to ablation — you do not need to "catch" the rhythm first. Do not start class I/III drugs empirically.

17.2 ECG Discriminators in Narrow-Complex Tachycardia

The P wave is the key. Find it, count it against the QRS, and measure where it falls in the cardiac cycle. Figure 17.1 · Position of the P wave (red) in the three short-/long-RP patterns. RP is measured from QRS onset to P onset.

Key highlightsClassification & approach

  • SVT = rate > 100 bpm with mechanism at or above the His bundle.
  • AVNRT is the most common adult PSVT; AVRT the most common in children; AT increases with age.
  • Frog sign (neck pounding) = simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction → AVNRT.
  • Syncope during "SVT" should prompt consideration of pre-excited AF or VT.
  • Always review the sinus-rhythm ECG for a delta wave and obtain a 12-lead during tachycardia.
  • Incessant SVT (PJRT, AT) → tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy — reversible.
  • Typical AVNRT
  • P inside/at end of QRS
  • pseudo r′ V1 · RP < 90 ms
  • Orthodromic AVRT
  • P in ST segment
  • RP > 90 ms but RP < PR
  • Long-RP tachycardia
  • P just before next QRS
  • AT · atypical AVNRT · PJRT
  • Finding Interpretation
  • Negative P in II, III, aVF with long
  • RP
  • PJRT, atypical AVNRT, or low (CS-os) focal AT
  • More P waves than QRS (AV
  • block)
  • AT or flutter; AVRT excluded; AVNRT rarely (block below the circuit)
  • QRS alternans Classically AVRT, but largely rate-related and non-specific
  • BBB that slows the tachycardia
  • (cycle length ↑)
  • AVRT using a pathway on the same side as the BBB (Coumel's law)
  • Onset with a PAC and long PR Typical AVNRT (antegrade conduction switches to slow pathway) Warm-up/cool-down, variable rate Automatic AT or sinus tachycardia
  • Rate ~150 bpm with sawtooth in
  • inferior leads
  • Atrial flutter 2:1
MECHANISM — WHY AVRT CANNOT HAVE A VERY SHORT RP

In AVNRT the atria and ventricles are activated in parallel from the node, so P and QRS coincide. In orthodromic AVRT they are activated in series: the impulse must travel through the His–Purkinje system, the ventricular muscle and then the pathway before reaching the atrium. That journey takes > 70 ms intracardiac (≈ > 90 ms on the surface ECG), so a P wave hidden in the QRS rules out AVRT.

DON'T CONFUSE — ST DEPRESSION DURING SVT

Widespread ST depression during a fast SVT (and T-wave inversion for hours afterwards) is common, raterelated and usually does not indicate coronary disease; ischaemic work-up is driven by symptoms and risk factors, not by the tachycardia ECG. ST elevation in aVR during SVT is similarly non-specific.

Key highlightsECG discriminators

  • Pseudo r′ in V1 or pseudo S in inferior leads (not present in sinus rhythm) = typical AVNRT.
  • RP < 90 ms surface (VA < 70 ms) excludes AVRT.
  • Short RP with P in ST segment → orthodromic AVRT.
  • Long RP → AT, sinus/SNRT, atypical AVNRT, PJRT.
  • AV block with ongoing tachycardia → AT/flutter; excludes AVRT.
  • Coumel's law: ipsilateral BBB slows AVRT (longer circuit).
  • Rate-related ST depression during SVT is not a marker of CAD.

17.3 Acute Management of Regular SVT

Vagal manoeuvres

Modified Valsalva (REVERT trial): standard strain (~40 mmHg for 15 s, e.g. blowing into a 10 mL syringe to move the plunger) performed semi-recumbent, then immediately lie flat with legs raised to ~45° for 15 s. Sinus rhythm at 1 min: 43% vs 17% with standard Valsalva. Leg raise after strain boosts venous return and the vagal overshoot.

Carotid sinus massage: unilateral, ~5 s, with monitoring; avoid with carotid bruit or prior TIA/stroke. Eyeball pressure is abandoned (retinal injury).

Diving reflex (face immersion in cold water) is useful in infants.

Conventional manoeuvres succeed in roughly 20–50%; they slow the node and may unmask flutter/AT.

Adenosine

6 mg rapid bolus via antecubital or larger vein with immediate 20 mL saline flush, record a rhythm strip; if no effect, 12 mg (ESC 2019: 6–18 mg). Terminates ~90–95% of AVNRT/orthodromic AVRT.

Reduce the initial dose (e.g. 3 mg) with a central line, dipyridamole, carbamazepine, or in hearttransplant recipients; theophylline/caffeine blunt the effect. Warn the patient of transient flushing, chest discomfort and dyspnoea. Keep a defibrillator available: adenosine can trigger AF, which is dangerous with a manifest pathway.

Avoid in severe asthma; safe in pregnancy.

Second-line and new options

IV verapamil 5–10 mg or diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg — terminate ~90%; avoid in hypotension, HFrEF, preexcitation, possible VT. IV esmolol or metoprolol — less effective at terminating, but good for rate control and for recurrence. Etripamil nasal spray (70 mg, repeat once after 10 min if needed) — a short-acting L-type Ca²⁺ blocker for patient self-treatment of PSVT. FDA-approved December 2025 after RAPID (conversion within 30 min 64% vs 31% placebo). Postdates the ESC 2019 guideline.

Pill-in-the-pocket (single oral dose of diltiazem + propranolol, or of a β-blocker/CCB) for infrequent, prolonged but well-tolerated episodes in patients without pre-excitation or LV dysfunction.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2019 (VS 2003 ESC/ACC/AHA)
  • IV verapamil/diltiazem and IV β-blockers downgraded from I to IIa — adenosine and vagal manoeuvres come first.
  • Procainamide for undiagnosed WCT IIa (was I); amiodarone IIb (was I); sotalol and lidocaine dropped for WCT.
  • Modified Valsalva formally endorsed (supine, leg elevation).
  • IV amiodarone in pre-excited AF became Class III.
EXAM TRAP

An irregular, very fast, broad and bizarre tachycardia in a young patient is pre-excited AF, not SVT with aberrancy. Adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, β-blockers, digoxin and IV amiodarone can all accelerate conduction over the pathway and precipitate VF.

Key highlightsAcute management

  • Unstable → synchronised cardioversion (I B).
  • Modified Valsalva (strain then supine leg raise): 43% vs 17% conversion.
  • Adenosine 6 → 12 mg (ESC up to 18 mg) with rapid flush — Class I.
  • Lower adenosine dose with central line, dipyridamole, carbamazepine, heart transplant; theophylline antagonises.
  • IV verapamil/diltiazem (IIa B) or β-blocker (IIa C) if adenosine fails.
  • Carotid massage: unilateral, 5 s; avoid with bruit or recent TIA/stroke.
  • Etripamil 70 mg nasal spray — self-administered PSVT termination (FDA 2025).

17.4 Sinus Tachycardias: IST, SNRT & POTS

Physiological sinus tachycardia (rate > 100 bpm, P positive in I, II, aVF and biphasic/negative in V1) is a response, not a disease: fever, hypovolaemia, anaemia, pain, anxiety, thyrotoxicosis, PE, HF, sepsis, drugs (βagonists, caffeine, cocaine, amphetamines) and β-blocker withdrawal. Treat the cause — never "rate-control" compensatory sinus tachycardia.

EXAM TRAP

In POTS the tachycardia is compensatory (low stroke volume, venous pooling). Full-dose β-blockade often worsens fatigue and orthostatic intolerance — only low-dose non-selective β-blockade is suggested. Sinusnode modification/ablation for IST has high recurrence and can leave the patient needing a pacemaker; it is not a routine option. For POTS assessment see the syncope chapter.

Key highlightsSinus tachycardias

  • Physiological sinus tachycardia: treat the cause, not the rate.
  • IST: resting rate > 100, mean 24-h rate > 90 bpm; young women; ivabradine ± β-blocker (IIa B).
  • SNRT: abrupt on/off with sinus-like P; ablation (IIa C) if drugs fail.
  • POTS: HR ↑ ≥ 30 bpm within 10 min of standing without hypotension.
  • POTS first-line = exercise reconditioning (IIa B); fluids/salt, midodrine, pyridostigmine, low-dose β-blocker, ivabradine (IIb).
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Chronic therapy
  • Catheter ablation for recurrent focal AT, especially incessant or causing tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy.
  • I B
  • β-blocker or verapamil/diltiazem (no HFrEF), or flecainide/propafenone (no structural/ischaemic disease), if ablation not desirable/feasible.
  • IIa C
  • Ivabradine with a β-blocker if the above fail. IIb C
  • Amiodarone if the above fail. IIb C

17.5 Focal & Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia

Focal atrial tachycardia

Regular atrial rhythm at 100–250 bpm arising from a single site with centrifugal spread. Mechanisms: automaticity, triggered activity or micro-re-entry. Common sites: crista terminalis (commonest right-sided), tricuspid and mitral annuli, coronary sinus ostium, atrial appendages, pulmonary vein ostia (commonest left-sided), perinodal region, non-coronary cusp.

Narrow P, shorter than sinus P Peri-septal/para-Hisian origin

Features: warm-up/cool-down (automatic), AV block with the tachycardia continuing, P waves with an isoelectric baseline between them (vs flutter).

Digoxin toxicity causes AT with block; hypokalaemia and acute illness (infection, COPD exacerbation, alcohol) promote automatic AT.

Incessant AT is a leading cause of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, especially in children.

BOARD PEARL

DC cardioversion terminates re-entrant and triggered AT but not automatic AT, which restarts within beats. Adenosine terminates triggered (cAMP-dependent) AT, transiently suppresses automatic AT, and in micro-re-entrant AT typically causes AV block without termination.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)

Irregular rhythm > 100 bpm with ≥ 3 distinct P-wave morphologies and variable PR intervals, isoelectric baseline between P waves (below 100 bpm = wandering atrial pacemaker/multifocal atrial rhythm). Associated with COPD/hypoxaemia, pulmonary hypertension, hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia,

theophylline and β-agonists; often precedes AF.

Treat the underlying condition first (I C); IV β-blocker or verapamil/diltiazem (IIa B); oral verapamil/ diltiazem or selective β-blocker for recurrences (IIa B); AV-node ablation with (biventricular/His) pacing for refractory cases with LV dysfunction (IIa C). Cardioversion and antiarrhythmics are ineffective.

17.6 AV Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia

AVNRT is re-entry within the AV junction using two functionally distinct inputs: a fast pathway (superior, near the apex of the triangle of Koch; fast conduction, long refractory period) and a slow pathway (inferior extension along the tricuspid annulus in front of the coronary-sinus ostium; slow conduction, short refractory period). Dual AV-nodal physiology is found in a substantial minority of normal people who never develop AVNRT. Neither atria nor ventricles are required for the circuit — so AV block (rarely) or VA block can occur without terminating the tachycardia.

Key highlightsAtrial tachycardias

  • Focal AT: 100–250 bpm, isoelectric baseline, AV block does not stop it.
  • Crista terminalis (RA) and pulmonary veins (LA) are the commonest foci; positive P in V1 → left atrium.
  • Ablation is Class I for recurrent/incessant focal AT or tachycardiomyopathy.
  • Automatic AT is not cardioverted by DC shock.
  • MAT: ≥ 3 P morphologies; COPD, theophylline, low Mg²⁺ — treat the lungs and electrolytes; verapamil/βblocker (IIa B).
  • AT with block + GI upset + xanthopsia = digoxin toxicity.
  • Type Frequency Circuit ECG
  • Typical (slow–fast) ~90% Antegrade slow, retrograde
  • fast
  • Short RP (< 90 ms): P buried in or at end of QRS;
  • pseudo r′ V1, pseudo S inferior

  • slow)
  • ~5–10%
  • combined

  • slow

  • Typical AVNRT terminates with adenosine, vagal manoeuvres and nodal blockers (it lives in the node).
MECHANISM — WHY SLOW-PATHWAY ABLATION IS SAFE

The slow pathway lies inferiorly, between the tricuspid annulus and the coronary-sinus ostium, well away from the compact node and His bundle (superior/anterior). Ablating there abolishes the circuit while leaving fast-pathway conduction intact. The risk of AV block rises as energy is delivered more superiorly (midseptum), hence the anatomical approach and careful monitoring for fast junctional rhythm with VA block during ablation.

EXAM TRAP

The ESC 2019 guideline removed class Ic, sotalol and amiodarone from chronic AVNRT therapy — the only drug options are β-blockers and non-DHP CCBs (IIa). ACC/AHA 2015 still lists flecainide/propafenone (no structural disease) and, weakly, sotalol, dofetilide, amiodarone and digoxin.

17.7 Accessory Pathways, AVRT & WPW

Accessory pathways (APs) are strands of working myocardium crossing the AV groove that bypass the AV node. Unlike the node they usually conduct non-decrementally (conduction time constant as rate rises) and are insensitive to adenosine and nodal blockers. WPW pattern = pre-excitation on the ECG; WPW syndrome = pre-excitation plus arrhythmia.

Epidemiology & associations
  • WPW pattern in 0.15–0.25% of the population; ~0.55% in
  • first-degree relatives
  • Ebstein anomaly (~25%; right-sided, often multiple)
  • PRKAG2 cardiomyopathy, Danon disease, HCM
  • Multiple pathways in ~5–10%
Pathway types
  • Manifest: antegrade conduction → delta wave (usually
  • bidirectional)
  • Concealed (~30%): retrograde-only → normal sinus ECG,
  • orthodromic AVRT only, no risk from pre-excited AF
  • Decremental variants: PJRT (retrograde), atriofascicular/
  • Mahaim (antegrade)

The pre-excited ECG

Short PR (< 120 ms), delta wave (slurred initial QRS), wide QRS (> 110–120 ms) with secondary ST–T changes opposite to the delta wave.

Degree of pre-excitation depends on pathway location and AV-nodal speed: left lateral pathways (far from the sinus node) may show minimal pre-excitation ; right-sided pathways are usually obvious. Pre-excitation increases with vagal manoeuvres, adenosine or atrial pacing (node slows, pathway does not).

Delta-wave polarity can mimic infarction (negative delta = "pseudo-Q") or hypertrophy.

Intermittent pre-excitation (beat-to-beat loss of the delta wave in sinus rhythm) implies a long pathway refractory period — a low-risk marker.

Localising the pathway

  • Posteroseptal / inferior
  • paraseptal (~20–30%)

Negative delta in III and aVF; transition V1–V2; negative delta in II suggests epicardial (CS diverticulum/middle cardiac vein)

Right free wall (~10–20%) Negative delta (QS/rS) in V1, late transition (≥ V3–V4), LBBB-like; positive delta in I Anteroseptal /

superoparaseptal (~2–5%)

Negative delta V1–V2, positive delta in II, III, aVF (inferior axis); close to His — ablation risk of AV block

Key highlightsAVNRT

  • Typical slow–fast AVNRT ≈ 90%: short RP (< 90 ms), pseudo r′ in V1, pseudo S in inferior leads.
  • Atypical fast–slow: long RP with negative inferior P — differential PJRT and low AT.
  • Atria and ventricles are not required — AV block during tachycardia does not exclude AVNRT, though it is rare.
  • Ablation of the slow pathway: Class I, success > 95%, AV block ~0.1–0.4%.
  • Drugs if ablation declined: β-blocker or verapamil/diltiazem (IIa B); no treatment is acceptable for rare, brief episodes.
  • Rule of thumb: the delta wave points away from the pathway; V1 separates right (negative) from left (positive).
  • AV re-entrant tachycardias

Catheter ablation of the AP(s) in symptomatic, recurrent AVRT. I B

β-blockers or verapamil/diltiazem (no HFrEF) if no pre-excitation on resting ECG and ablation not desirable.

IIa B

Propafenone or flecainide (no ischaemic/structural disease) if ablation not desirable. IIb B Digoxin, β-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil and amiodarone in pre-excited AF. III B

Key highlightsAccessory pathways & AVRT

  • WPW pattern: PR < 120 ms, delta wave, QRS > 110–120 ms; prevalence 0.15–0.25%.
  • Concealed pathways (~30%): normal sinus ECG, only orthodromic AVRT, no pre-excited AF risk.
  • Left free wall is the commonest location (~50–60%); positive delta in V1 → left-sided.
  • Orthodromic AVRT ≈ 90–95% of AVRT: narrow QRS, RP > 90 ms.
  • Antidromic AVRT/pre-excited tachycardias: ibutilide, procainamide, flecainide/propafenone or cardioversion (IIa B).
  • Ebstein anomaly: ~25% have (often multiple, right-sided) pathways.
  • PJRT: incessant long-RP, deep negative inferior P, decremental posteroseptal AP, tachycardiomyopathy.
  • Mahaim: LBBB-like antidromic tachycardia via right-sided atriofascicular pathway.
  • Low-risk (non-invasive) High-risk (EPS, with isoprenaline)
  • Intermittent pre-excitation on ECG or Holter
  • Abrupt, complete loss of the delta wave during exercise
  • testing
  • Loss of pre-excitation with drug challenge (e.g.
  • procainamide)
  • SPERRI ≤ 250 ms during induced AF
  • AP antegrade ERP ≤ 250 ms
  • Multiple accessory pathways
  • Inducible AP-mediated tachycardia

17.8 Pre-excited AF & Asymptomatic Pre-excitation

In pre-excited AF each atrial impulse can reach the ventricle through the pathway. A pathway with a short antegrade refractory period can conduct at rates > 250–300 bpm, degenerating into VF — the mechanism of sudden death in WPW. The danger depends on how short the pathway's refractory period is, not how fast it conducts.

MECHANISM — WHY AV-NODAL BLOCKERS KILL IN PRE-EXCITED AF

AF impulses compete for the ventricle via two routes. Blocking the node (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, β-blocker, digoxin) removes concealed retrograde penetration of the pathway from nodally conducted beats, so more impulses pass the pathway; verapamil and IV β-blockers also cause vasodilatation and reflex sympathetic activation; digoxin may shorten the pathway refractory period. IV amiodarone's early effect is mainly nodal and vasodilatory. Result: faster pre-excited rate → VF.

Asymptomatic pre-excitation

Most people with an incidental WPW pattern (~80%) never develop arrhythmias; the risk of sudden death is low but sometimes the first manifestation — highest in children/young adults. Risk stratification tests the pathway's antegrade refractoriness.

  • drugs
  • Ibutilide or procainamide (IIa) Ibutilide or procainamide (I)
EXAM TRAP

Gradual disappearance of the delta wave during exercise is not reassuring — it may just reflect faster AVnodal conduction masking the pathway. Only abrupt, complete loss of pre-excitation (sudden normalisation of PR and QRS) indicates a long pathway refractory period.

17.9 Junctional Tachycardias

Non-re-entrant junctional tachycardias arise from enhanced automaticity or triggered activity in the AV node/His bundle. They are uncommon in adults and are recognised by a narrow QRS identical to sinus, with AV dissociation or retrograde (1:1) P waves.

DON'T CONFUSE — JUNCTIONAL TACHYCARDIA VS AVNRT

Both give a narrow QRS with P waves near the QRS. JET shows AV dissociation and warm-up and is not terminated by adenosine or pacing; AVNRT starts and stops abruptly with PACs, has 1:1 VA relation, and terminates with adenosine. During slow-pathway ablation, a transient accelerated junctional rhythm is expected — junctional beats with VA block warn of impending AV block.

Key highlightsPre-excited AF & risk stratification

  • Pre-excited AF: irregular, very fast (> 200–250 bpm), varying QRS width — risk of VF.
  • Stable pre-excited AF: IV ibutilide or procainamide (IIa B); unstable: synchronised cardioversion (I B).
  • Digoxin, β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, adenosine and IV amiodarone are harmful (III).
  • High-risk EPS: SPERRI ≤ 250 ms, AP ERP ≤ 250 ms, multiple APs, inducible AVRT → ablate (I B).
  • Low-risk markers: intermittent pre-excitation; abrupt loss on exercise.
  • High-risk occupations and competitive athletes → EPS (I B) even if asymptomatic.
  • ESC is more interventional than ACC/AHA 2015 (ablation Class I vs IIa).

Key highlightsJunctional tachycardias

  • JET: automatic, AV dissociation, classically post-operative in infants; treat with cooling, less catecholamine, amiodarone.
  • Non-paroxysmal junctional tachycardia (70–130 bpm): digoxin toxicity, inferior MI, post-op, myocarditis.
  • Junctional rhythms are not cardioverted or terminated by adenosine.
  • Ablation of focal junctional tachycardia carries a real risk of AV block.

17.10 Chronic Therapy & Catheter Ablation

Catheter ablation is the first-line chronic therapy for symptomatic recurrent AVNRT, AVRT and focal AT (Class I B) — it is curative, improves quality of life and avoids lifelong drugs. Drugs are reserved for patients who decline or are unsuitable for ablation. Three-dimensional electroanatomical mapping allows minimalor zero-fluoroscopy procedures (important in pregnancy and children).

BOARD PEARL — ABLATION FIRST,EVEN IN THE YOUNG
  • For a young woman with recurrent AVNRT, the board answer is ablation rather than lifelong verapamil.
  • Women planning pregnancy are an especially strong indication (Class I in ESC 2019), and older patients and women are known to be under-referred.

17.11 SVT in Pregnancy, ACHD & Athletes

Pregnancy

Pregnancy increases the frequency of SVT episodes (higher heart rate, volume and catecholamine sensitivity). Maternal and fetal outcomes are good with prompt treatment. The ideal strategy is ablation before conception in women with symptomatic recurrent SVT.

Avoid all antiarrhythmic drugs in the first trimester if possible. I C

β₁-selective blockers (except atenolol) or verapamil, in that order, to prevent SVT without WPW. IIa C Flecainide or propafenone to prevent SVT with WPW and no ischaemic/structural disease. IIa C Fluoroless catheter ablation for drug-refractory or poorly tolerated SVT in experienced centres. IIa C Amiodarone. III C

The 2025 ESC Guidelines on CVD and pregnancy carry the same principles (ablation before pregnancy, adenosine and cardioversion safe, β₁-selective blockers preferred, avoid amiodarone); consult them for current class/level wording.

Key highlightsChronic therapy & ablation

  • Ablation is Class I first-line for recurrent symptomatic AVNRT, AVRT and focal AT.
  • AVNRT ablation > 95% success, AV block ~0.1–0.4%; AP ablation ~95%.
  • Septal pathways carry the highest risk of AV block; cryoablation lowers it at the cost of recurrence.
  • Drugs if ablation declined: β-blocker/CCB (only without pre-excitation); class Ic for AVRT/AT without structural disease.
  • ESC 2019 dropped sotalol, dofetilide and digoxin for SVT; ACC/AHA 2015 retains them as IIb.
Safe / preferred in pregnancy
  • Vagal manoeuvres, adenosine
  • DC cardioversion (all trimesters; fetal monitoring
  • afterwards)
  • Metoprolol, bisoprolol, propranolol; verapamil; digoxin
  • Flecainide / propafenone for WPW or β-blocker failure (no
  • structural disease)
Avoid
  • Atenolol — fetal growth restriction
  • Amiodarone — fetal hypothyroidism, growth restriction,
  • prematurity
  • Any drug in the first trimester if possible
  • Fluoroscopy — use zero-fluoroscopy mapping; ideally
  • ablate in the 2nd trimester if unavoidable

Adults with congenital heart disease

Macro-re-entrant AT (intra-atrial re-entry around surgical scars) dominates; APs are common in Ebstein anomaly; twin AV nodes in complex AV septal defects/heterotaxy.

Anticoagulate focal AT/flutter in ACHD as for AF (I C). Acute treatment follows the standard algorithm. Ablation in experienced centres (IIa C); consider pre-operative or intra-operative ablation when surgery is planned (IIa C).

Sotalol is not recommended as first-line (III C — proarrhythmia/mortality); flecainide/propafenone not first-line with ventricular dysfunction or severe fibrosis (III C).

Athletes and occupation

Exclude structural disease, thyroid disease, electrolyte disorders and stimulant/performance-enhancing drugs.

ESC 2020 sports: pre-excitation with AVRT/AF or high-risk asymptomatic pathway → ablation; return to all sports ~1 month after successful ablation. PSVT → ablation recommended; if declined, avoid sports with high intrinsic risk should consciousness be lost.

High-risk occupations (pilots, professional drivers) with pre-excitation → EPS (I B).

Key highlightsSpecial situations

  • Ablation before pregnancy for recurrent symptomatic SVT (I C).
  • Pregnancy: vagal → adenosine (I C); cardioversion safe in all trimesters; β₁-selective blocker (not atenolol) → verapamil for prevention.
  • Flecainide/propafenone for SVT with WPW in pregnancy (IIa C); amiodarone contraindicated (III C).
  • Drug-refractory SVT in pregnancy → zero-fluoroscopy ablation in expert centre (IIa C).
  • ACHD: anticoagulate AT/flutter as AF; sotalol not first-line (III).
  • Athletes: ablate, return ~1 month after successful ablation.

17.12 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 34-year-old woman has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. No P waves are visible, but V1 shows an r′ absent on her previous ECG. The first treatment should be:

Answer B Pseudo r′ in V1 = typical AVNRT. In a stable patient, vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva) come first (I B); adenosine follows if they fail (I B). Verapamil is second-line (IIa); cardioversion is for instability.

Q2 A 22-year-old man presents with palpitations and dizziness. ECG: irregular, broad-complex tachycardia at up to 280 bpm with beat-to-beat variation in QRS width. BP 105/65 mmHg. The best drug is:

Answer D Irregular, very fast WCT with variable width = pre-excited AF. Stable patients: IV procainamide or ibutilide (IIa B). Adenosine, diltiazem, digoxin and IV amiodarone (III B) can accelerate pathway conduction and provoke VF.

Q3 A 28-year-old airline pilot has an incidental delta wave on a medical ECG. He has never had palpitations. The most appropriate next step according to ESC 2019 is:

Answer C ESC 2019: EPS with isoprenaline is Class I for asymptomatic pre-excitation in high-risk occupations (pilots, professional drivers) and competitive athletes. Non-invasive tests alone are insufficient here; empirical drugs are not indicated.

Q4 During EPS in an asymptomatic 19-year-old athlete with pre-excitation, induced AF shows a shortest pre-excited R–R interval of 220 ms. The recommendation is:

Answer C SPERRI ≤ 250 ms is a high-risk property — catheter ablation is Class I B. Return to sport ~1 month after successful ablation. An ICD has no role; β-blockers do not protect against pathway conduction.

Q5 A narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 bpm develops LBBB during the episode; the cycle length lengthens from 350 to 390 ms while the QRS is wide. The most likely diagnosis is:

Answer B Coumel's law: BBB ipsilateral to the pathway lengthens the AVRT circuit (the impulse must cross the septum to reach the pathway), so the cycle length increases. LBBB slowing implicates a left-sided pathway. AVNRT and AT are unaffected by BBB.

Q6 A 10-year-old boy has an incessant long-RP tachycardia at 150 bpm with deep negative P waves in II, III and aVF, and LVEF 35%. The most likely diagnosis and treatment are:

Answer B Incessant long-RP tachycardia with deep negative inferior P waves in a child = PJRT (decremental posteroseptal pathway), a classic cause of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Ablation succeeds in > 90% and the LV usually recovers.

Q7 A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks of pregnancy has recurrent AVNRT despite vagal manoeuvres; episodes

Answer C β₁-selective blockers (except atenolol, which causes growth restriction) are first choice for SVT prevention in pregnancy (IIa C), then verapamil. Amiodarone is Class III; flecainide is reserved for WPW or β-blocker failure; sotalol is not preferred.

Q8 A 26-year-old woman has a resting sinus rate of 110 bpm, mean 24-h heart rate 98 bpm, normal thyroid function, haemoglobin and echo. β-blockers caused fatigue. The most appropriate therapy is:

Answer B IST after exclusion of secondary causes: ivabradine alone or with a β-blocker (IIa B) — it lowers sinus rate without negative inotropy or hypotension. Sinus-node ablation has high recurrence and pacing risk.

Q9 A 76-year-old man with COPD exacerbation on nebulised salbutamol and theophylline has an irregular

Answer C MAT: treating the underlying condition is Class I; magnesium and potassium repletion and review of theophylline/βagonists are key. Cardioversion and antiarrhythmics are ineffective; verapamil or a selective β-blocker can then control rate (IIa B).

Q10 Adenosine 12 mg given for a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm produces transient 4:1 AV block revealing sawtooth waves in the inferior leads; the tachycardia resumes. The diagnosis is:

Answer C Adenosine that produces AV block without terminating the tachycardia reveals an atrial mechanism; sawtooth inferior waves at ~300/min with 2:1 conduction at 150 bpm = typical flutter. AVNRT/AVRT would terminate.
