18.1 Definitions, Classification & Mechanisms

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia in adults, with a lifetime risk of roughly 1 in 3 after middle age. It is a marker and driver of atrial cardiomyopathy: it increases the risk of stroke about 5-fold, heart failure about 3-fold, and is associated with dementia and all-cause death. Prevalence rises steeply with age, obesity, hypertension and alcohol.

DEFINITION — ECG DIAGNOSIS OF CLINICAL AF

A standard 12-lead ECG, or a single-lead tracing of ≥ 30 seconds, showing irregularly irregular RR intervals with no distinct repeating P waves (when AV conduction is intact). ESC 2024 requires that the tracing be reviewed by a physician to make the diagnosis ( I ). Wearable/photoplethysmography alerts are screening signals, never a diagnosis.

Temporal patterns (ESC) and stages (ACC/AHA)

BOARD PEARL

The pattern of AF (paroxysmal, persistent, permanent) does not change the stroke risk decision. OAC is based on the risk score, not on how often or how long the AF lasts — although higher AF burden carries somewhat more risk, the label never removes the indication.

Mechanisms — trigger, substrate and modulators

Trigger
  • Ectopic firing from pulmonary vein sleeves (the basis of
  • PVI)
  • Non-PV foci: SVC, coronary sinus, LA posterior wall,
  • ligament of Marshall
  • Autonomic surges (vagal nocturnal AF; adrenergic
  • exercise AF)
Substrate
  • Atrial stretch and fibrosis → conduction heterogeneity
  • Shortened, dispersed refractoriness → multiple wavelets /
  • rotors

Inflammation, epicardial fat, ageing

MECHANISM — "AF BEGETS AF"

Rapid atrial rates overload myocytes with Ca²⁺; within days the cells protect themselves by down-regulating L-type Ca²⁺ current, which shortens the atrial effective refractory period (electrical remodelling).

Weeks to months later, fibrosis and dilatation follow (structural remodelling). Shorter refractoriness and slower conduction shrink the wavelength (refractory period × conduction velocity), so more re-entrant circuits fit in the atria — AF sustains itself. This is why early rhythm control works better and why persistent AF is harder to ablate.

Symptoms and consequences

EXAM TRAP
  • Up to one-third of patients are asymptomatic, and the first presentation may be an ischaemic stroke.
  • Symptom status does not change the anticoagulation decision — only the rate/rhythm strategy.

Key highlightsDefinitions & mechanisms

  • Diagnosis needs a 12-lead ECG or a single-lead strip of ≥ 30 s reviewed by a physician.
  • Paroxysmal ≤ 7 days; persistent > 7 days; long-standing persistent ≥ 12 months; permanent = decision to abandon rhythm control.
  • ACC/AHA 2023 uses stages: 1 at risk, 2 pre-AF, 3 AF (3A–3D), 4 permanent.
  • PV ectopy is the dominant trigger; fibrosis and short refractoriness are the substrate.
  • Electrical remodelling (shortened ERP) starts within days — "AF begets AF".
  • AF pattern does not decide OAC — the stroke-risk score does.
  • AF raises stroke risk ~5× and HF risk ~3×; ~one-third are asymptomatic.

18.2 AF-CARE, Screening & Initial Evaluation

The ESC 2024 guideline replaced the ABC pathway with AF-CARE. The deliberate change is that comorbidity and risk-factor management comes first and applies to every patient, regardless of stroke risk.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2024 (VS ESC 2020)
  • ABC pathway → AF-CARE, with comorbidity management first.
  • CHA₂DS₂-VASc → CHA₂DS₂-VA (female sex removed); one threshold for all.
  • Cardioversion without prior OAC/TOE: 48 h → 24 h; "wait-and-see" formally endorsed.
  • First-line ablation in paroxysmal AF upgraded to I A; ablation in HFrEF with suspected
  • tachycardiomyopathy I .
  • Early rhythm control (within 12 months) added (EAST-AFNET 4).
  • New recommendations: device-detected subclinical AF ( IIb ), SGLT2 inhibitors, alcohol ≤ 3 drinks/ week, posterior pericardiotomy.

Screening

Screening is attractive because silent AF causes strokes, but hard-outcome benefit is modest. LOOP (implantable loop recorders in high-risk elderly) found much more AF but no significant reduction in stroke; STROKESTOP (intermittent handheld ECG in 75–76-year-olds) showed a small net benefit on a composite outcome.

IIa B

In addition, ESC 2024 advises opportunistic rhythm assessment (pulse check or ECG) at healthcare contacts in everyone aged ≥ 65 years. ACC/AHA 2023 makes no recommendation for population screening, citing lack of hard-outcome data — a classic difference.

Initial evaluation of every new AF

CLINICAL APPROACH — THE FOUR QUESTIONS AT THE FIRST VISIT

Is the patient haemodynamically unstable? → emergency synchronised DC cardioversion.

Is there a reversible trigger (sepsis, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol binge, surgery, PE)? → treat it, but still assess stroke risk.

What is the thromboembolic risk? → OAC decision.

What does the patient need for symptoms? → rate control for all; rhythm control when it improves symptoms or outcomes.

18.3 [C] Comorbidity & Risk-Factor Management

Risk-factor modification reduces AF burden, recurrence after ablation and progression. The LEGACY and ARREST-AF cohorts showed a dose–response between weight loss and freedom from AF; the Alcohol-AF trial showed abstinence reduced recurrence in regular drinkers.

Key highlightsAF-CARE, screening & evaluation

  • AF-CARE = Comorbidities, Avoid stroke, Reduce symptoms (rate/rhythm), Evaluate dynamically. "C" comes first and applies to all patients, whatever their stroke risk.
  • Reassess at 6 months, then at least yearly.
  • Systematic ECG screening: ≥ 75 y, or ≥ 65 y with risk factors (ESC IIa ); ACC/AHA does not recommend population screening.
  • Always check TSH, renal function (DOAC dosing) and an echo in new AF.
  • AF triggered by an acute illness still carries long-term recurrence and stroke risk — reassess, do not dismiss.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Lifestyle
  • CHANGED Weight loss in overweight/obese patients, targeting a ≥ 10% reduction in body weight. I B Tailored exercise programme in paroxysmal or persistent AF. I B
  • NEW Reduce alcohol to ≤ 3 standard drinks (≤ 30 g) per week. I B
  • Bariatric surgery with a rhythm-control strategy in obese patients. IIb C
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea
  • Management of OSA to reduce AF incidence, progression and recurrence. IIb B
  • Using symptom-based questionnaires alone to screen for OSA in AF. III B
EXAM TRAP

Endurance athletes have more AF (often vagal, nocturnal): the relationship between exercise and AF is Ushaped. The advice is moderate exercise — not "more is better". And caffeine does not need to be stopped. 18.4 [A] Stroke Risk & Oral Anticoagulation

About 90% of AF-related thrombi form in the left atrial appendage (LAA), where stasis, endothelial dysfunction and hypercoagulability meet (Virchow's triad). Oral anticoagulation reduces stroke by about two-thirds and mortality by about one-quarter; aspirin gives little protection and similar bleeding.

Key highlightsComorbidity & risk factors

  • Weight loss ≥ 10% is Class I in both guidelines.
  • ESC alcohol limit: ≤ 3 drinks (≤ 30 g) per week.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors for AF + HF at any LVEF (ESC I A).
  • Treat hypertension — the commonest modifiable AF risk factor.
  • Do not screen for OSA with symptom questionnaires alone (ESC III ).
  • Caffeine abstinence does not prevent AF (ACC/AHA III ).
  • Thromboembolic risk scores
MECHANISM — WHY ESC DROPPED "SC"

Female sex is a risk modifier, not an independent risk factor: a woman with no other risk factor has very low risk, and the extra point only amplifies risk when other factors are present. Removing it gives one threshold for everyone and avoids the confusing "≥ 2 in men / ≥ 3 in women" rule.

CHANGED OAC should be considered for CHA₂DS₂-VA = 1. IIa C

OAC in AF with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or cardiac amyloidosis, regardless of the score. I B Which drug

DOACs in preference to VKAs, except in mechanical heart valves or moderate–severe mitral stenosis. I A Full standard DOAC dose unless the patient meets drug-specific dose-reduction criteria. I B Switch VKA → DOAC in eligible patients who fail to maintain INR control (TTR < 70%). I B NEW Keep a stable VKA rather than switching in patients aged ≥ 75 years with polypharmacy (FRAILAF). IIb B

  • What not to do
  • Antiplatelet therapy as an alternative to OAC for stroke prevention. III A
  • Adding antiplatelet therapy to OAC for the purpose of stroke prevention. III B
  • Using bleeding-risk scores to decide whether to start or withdraw OAC. III B

DOAC choice and dosing

EXAM TRAP — INAPPROPRIATE UNDER-DOSING
  • The commonest DOAC prescribing error is off-label dose reduction (e.g. apixaban 2.5 mg for age alone).
  • One apixaban criterion is not enough — it needs two of age ≥ 80, weight ≤ 60 kg, creatinine ≥ 1.5 mg/dL .
  • Under-dosing increases stroke without reducing bleeding.

When DOACs are contraindicated — VKA only

BOARD PEARL — DOAC TRIALS IN ONE LINE EACH

RE-LY (dabigatran 150): fewer ischaemic strokes than warfarin — the only DOAC superior for ischaemic stroke; more GI bleeding.

  • ARISTOTLE (apixaban): superior for stroke/SE, less major bleeding and lower mortality.
  • ROCKET-AF (rivaroxaban): non-inferior; similar major bleeding; more GI bleeding.
  • ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (edoxaban 60): non-inferior; less bleeding.
  • All DOACs roughly halve intracranial haemorrhage compared with warfarin.

OAC after ischaemic stroke and in special groups

Timing after AF-related ischaemic stroke: early DOAC start is safe (ELAN, TIMING, OPTIMAS) — broadly within 48 h for minor/moderate stroke and around day 6–7 for major stroke, individualised to infarct size and haemorrhagic transformation.

Elderly and frail: age alone is never a reason to withhold OAC; falls risk rarely outweighs stroke benefit. Cancer-associated AF: DOACs acceptable, watching interactions and GI/GU tumour bleeding. Pregnancy: DOACs contraindicated; LMWH (or VKA in 2nd trimester in selected cases).

18.5 Bleeding, Reversal & LAA Occlusion

Managing bleeding on OAC

DON'T CONFUSE

Idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor). Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors. Protamine is for heparin, and vitamin K works only for VKAs (and takes hours).

Key highlightsStroke risk & OAC

  • ESC 2024 uses CHA₂DS₂-VA: OAC I if ≥ 2; IIa if 1.
  • ACC/AHA 2023: OAC if annual risk ≥ 2% (score ≥ 2 men / ≥ 3 women); reasonable at 1–2%.
  • HCM or cardiac amyloidosis with AF → OAC regardless of score.
  • DOAC over VKA except mechanical valve or moderate–severe MS.
  • Apixaban 2.5 mg bid only with ≥ 2 of: ≥ 80 y, ≤ 60 kg, Cr ≥ 1.5 mg/dL.
  • Edoxaban 30 mg with any one of CrCl ≤ 50, ≤ 60 kg, P-gp inhibitor; dabigatran is ~80% renally cleared.
  • Aspirin is not an alternative to OAC ( III ); bleeding scores must not be used to withhold OAC.
  • HAS-BLED ≥ 3 = fix modifiable factors and review more often.
  • Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO)
  • Percutaneous LAAO (Watchman, Amulet) plugs the appendage; it still needs short-term antithrombotic therapy after implantation, and device-related thrombus and peri-device leak are the key complications.
  • Surgical LAA occlusion/exclusion is done during cardiac surgery.
  • PROTECT-AF / PREVAIL: Watchman non-inferior to warfarin for the composite; less haemorrhagic stroke, but more ischaemic stroke early.
  • PRAGUE-17: LAAO non-inferior to DOAC in high-risk patients.
  • OPTION (2024): after AF ablation, LAAO had less bleeding than continued OAC with non-inferior efficacy.
  • LAAOS III: surgical LAA occlusion during cardiac surgery added to OAC reduced stroke/systemic embolism by about one-third (HR 0.67).
EXAM TRAP

After surgical LAA occlusion (LAAOS III) the patient continues OAC — the benefit was additive. Do not stop anticoagulation because the appendage was closed.

Key highlightsBleeding, reversal & LAAO

  • Dabigatran → idarucizumab 5 g IV (also dialysable).
  • Apixaban/rivaroxaban → andexanet alfa, or 4F-PCC 50 IU/kg.
  • Warfarin → 4F-PCC + vitamin K 5–10 mg IV.
  • Activated charcoal if a DOAC was taken within 2–4 h.
  • After a bleed is controlled and its cause treated, most patients should restart OAC.
  • ~90% of AF thrombi are in the LAA.
  • Surgical LAA closure during cardiac surgery + OAC: ESC I (LAAOS III, ~33% fewer strokes).
  • Percutaneous LAAO for OAC contraindication: ESC IIb vs ACC/AHA IIa .
  • 18.6 [R] Rate Control
  • Rate control is part of the management of every patient with AF — as initial therapy, as an adjunct to rhythm control, or as the sole strategy. It improves symptoms and prevents tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy.
  • Target heart rate
  • RACE II randomised permanent AF to lenient (resting HR < 110 bpm) or strict (< 80 bpm at rest, < 110 bpm on moderate exercise) control: lenient was non-inferior for CV death, HF hospitalisation, stroke, bleeding and arrhythmic events, and easier to achieve. Hence lenient control (< 110 bpm) is the initial target; tighten it if symptoms persist or LV function falls.
EXAM TRAP — PRE-EXCITED AF (WPW)

Irregular, very fast (> 250 bpm), broad and bizarre QRS complexes of varying width = AF over an accessory pathway. Never give AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin — and IV amiodarone is also avoided): blocking the node pushes conduction down the pathway → VF. Unstable → DC cardioversion; stable → IV procainamide or ibutilide; then ablate the pathway.

Pace and ablate

AV-node ablation plus pacing gives definitive rate regularisation. Because RV pacing can depress LV function, CRT or conduction-system (His/left bundle branch area) pacing is preferred. APAF-CRT showed that ablate-and-CRT reduced mortality compared with drugs in severely symptomatic permanent AF with narrow QRS and at least one HF hospitalisation. The patient becomes pacemaker-dependent and still needs OAC. 18.7 [R] Rhythm Control: Cardioversion & Drugs

Rhythm control aims to restore and maintain sinus rhythm. Its first goal is symptom relief; since EASTAFNET 4 it also has an outcome goal in recently diagnosed AF.

LANDMARK — EAST-AFNET 4

2,789 patients with AF diagnosed within 12 months and cardiovascular risk factors were randomised to early rhythm control (AADs or ablation) vs usual care (mostly rate control). Early rhythm control reduced the composite of CV death, stroke, and hospitalisation for HF or ACS (HR 0.79) over ~5 years, without more time in hospital or safety signal. This overturned the AFFIRM-era teaching that rhythm control has no outcome benefit — AFFIRM enrolled older patients with long-standing AF and relied on toxic AADs.

IIa C

ACC/AHA 2023 is concordant: rhythm control in recently diagnosed AF (< 1 year) "can be useful" ( IIa B-R), and a trial of rhythm control is recommended in reduced LV function with persistent or high-burden AF to test whether AF is the cause ( I B-R).

Key highlightsRate control

  • Initial target: resting HR < 110 bpm (RACE II; ESC IIa B); ACC/AHA: < 100–110 bpm.
  • Beta-blockers and digoxin at any LVEF; diltiazem/verapamil only if LVEF > 40%.
  • Digoxin does not control exercise heart rate.
  • Pre-excited AF: no AV-nodal blockers — DC cardioversion or procainamide/ibutilide.
  • Amiodarone is a last-line rate agent and may convert AF — anticoagulation matters.
  • Refractory cases: AV-node ablation + pacing (prefer CRT/conduction-system pacing); OAC continues.
  • Cardioversion — anticoagulation rules
  • Cardioversion by any method carries a thromboembolic risk from existing LA thrombus and from postconversion atrial stunning (mechanical recovery lags electrical recovery by up to several weeks). Hence the classic "3 weeks before, 4 weeks after".

IIa B

Continue OAC for at least 4 weeks after cardioversion, and long term if thromboembolic risk factors are present, irrespective of the rhythm outcome.

I B

After cardioversion ≥ 4 weeks, then per CHA₂DS₂-VA ≥ 4 weeks, then per stroke risk

OAC ≥ 4 weeks after; long-term according to CHA₂DS₂-VA

MECHANISM — WHY STROKE RISK PERSISTS AFTER SUCCESSFUL CARDIOVERSION

Sinus rhythm on the ECG does not mean a contracting appendage. LAA emptying velocities stay low for days to weeks (stunning), so thrombus can form after the shock. Long-term, the atrial cardiomyopathy that caused AF persists, and AF often recurs silently — which is why OAC follows the risk score, not the rhythm .

Electrical cardioversion — practical points

Synchronised biphasic shock; anterior–posterior pad position is more effective than antero-lateral; higher initial energy (e.g. 150–200 J or maximum) improves first-shock success.

Pre-treatment with amiodarone, ibutilide, flecainide or sotalol increases success and reduces early recurrence.

Check potassium and digoxin toxicity; pacemakers/ICDs should be interrogated afterwards.

Pharmacological cardioversion

HFrEF, CAD, severe LVH Slow (hours); hypotension, phlebitis

Pill-in-the-pocket: selected patients with infrequent paroxysmal AF and no structural heart disease can selfadminister oral flecainide or propafenone after a first, monitored, safe in-hospital trial — combined with an AV-nodal blocker to prevent 1:1 flutter. Pharmacological cardioversion is not recommended in sinus node dysfunction, AV block or QTc > 500 ms without pacing backup.

Long-term antiarrhythmic drugs

AADs reduce recurrence by roughly half; the drug is chosen for safety first, efficacy second. The board logic is "what structural heart disease is present?".

18.8 Catheter & Surgical Ablation

The cornerstone of every AF ablation is pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) — electrical isolation of the PV antra so that PV triggers cannot reach the atrium. Energy sources: radiofrequency, cryoballoon and, since 2024, pulsed-field ablation (PFA), which is largely tissue-selective (myocardium over oesophagus and phrenic nerve). Freedom from AF at 1 year is ~70–80% in paroxysmal and lower in persistent AF; repeat procedures are common.

Evidence in brief

CABANA AF, age ≥ 65 or risk factors ITT: no significant reduction in death/stroke/bleeding/ arrest; better QoL and fewer recurrences → ablation is for

  • symptoms
  • CASTLE-AF AF + HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 35%) with ICD/
  • CRT-D
  • Ablation reduced death or HF hospitalisation
  • (~29% vs 45%)
  • CASTLE-HTx End-stage HF + AF referred for
  • transplant
  • Ablation reduced death, LVAD implantation or urgent
  • transplant (~8% vs 30%); stopped early for benefit
  • RAFT-AF, AMICA AF + HF Neutral / non-significant — benefit depends on patient
  • selection

Key highlightsRhythm control & cardioversion

  • EAST-AFNET 4: rhythm control within 12 months of diagnosis reduced CV death/stroke/HF-ACS hospitalisation (HR 0.79).
  • ESC 2024: cardioversion without prior OAC/TOE only if AF < 24 h; ACC/AHA keeps 48 h.
  • Otherwise ≥ 3 weeks therapeutic OAC or TOE; always ≥ 4 weeks OAC afterwards.
  • Wait-and-see for spontaneous conversion within 48 h is acceptable (RACE 7; ESC IIa ).
  • Long-term OAC depends on the score, not on whether sinus rhythm was restored.
  • Class IC drugs only without structural heart disease, always with an AV-nodal blocker.
  • HFrEF → amiodarone; dronedarone is contraindicated in advanced/recent decompensated HF and permanent AF.
  • Vernakalant contraindications: SBP < 100, ACS < 30 days, NYHA III–IV, severe AS, long QT.
  • Trial Population Finding → consequence
  • CAMERA-MRI Persistent AF + idiopathic LV
  • dysfunction
  • LVEF improved markedly, especially without LGE fibrosis
  • on CMR

Uninterrupted OAC in patients undergoing catheter ablation. I A

OAC for at least 2 months after ablation regardless of risk; thereafter according to CHA₂DS₂-VA, not according to perceived success.

I C

I A I A
  • First-line, paroxysmal I A I A — "generally younger, few
  • comorbidities"
  • First-line, others /
  • persistent
  • IIb C (persistent) IIa B-R (paroxysmal or persistent)
  • HFrEF I if tachycardiomyopathy likely; IIa
  • selected HFrEF
  • I in appropriate HFrEF patients on
  • GDMT

Symptomatic atrial flutter CTI ablation (see 18.10) I A

BOARD PEARL

Successful ablation is not a reason to stop OAC. Asymptomatic recurrences are frequent and the underlying atrial substrate persists: continue OAC according to the stroke-risk score . After any ablation, OAC is mandatory for at least 2 months.

Complications of catheter ablation

Surgical and hybrid ablation

Concomitant surgical ablation (e.g. Cox-Maze/PVI) is recommended in patients undergoing mitral valve surgery with AF, and is reasonable in other cardiac operations to improve rhythm outcomes. Endoscopic or hybrid (epicardial + endocardial) ablation should be considered in symptomatic persistent AF refractory to AADs, or after failed catheter ablation.

OAC continues after surgical ablation in patients at elevated thromboembolic risk.

Key highlightsAblation

  • PVI is the cornerstone; PFA is the newest energy source.
  • First-line ablation in paroxysmal AF: Class I A in both guidelines.
  • First-line in persistent AF: ESC IIb C vs ACC/AHA IIa .
  • HFrEF: ESC I if tachycardiomyopathy likely, IIa otherwise; ACC/AHA I .
  • CASTLE-AF (LVEF ≤ 35%) and CASTLE-HTx (end-stage HF) — ablation improved hard outcomes.
  • CABANA: no ITT reduction in hard endpoints — ablation is primarily for symptoms outside HF.
  • OAC ≥ 2 months after ablation, then by score, irrespective of success.
  • Fever + stroke/GI bleed weeks after ablation = atrio-oesophageal fistula → CT, not endoscopy.
  • ACC/AHA 2023 similarly supports anticoagulation for POAF when safe from a surgical-bleeding standpoint, and emphasises reassessment of rhythm and stroke risk at about 60–90 days. Pre-operative beta-blockers should be continued in patients already taking them.
  • Device-detected subclinical AF (AHRE / SCAF)

18.9 Special Situations

Post-operative AF (POAF)

POAF occurs in ~20–40% after cardiac surgery (peak day 2–4) and in a smaller proportion after non-cardiac surgery. It is not benign: it predicts long-term AF recurrence, stroke and death.

DEFINITION

Atrial high-rate episodes (AHRE) are device-recorded atrial tachyarrhythmias (typically ≥ 175 bpm, ≥ 5–6 min). Once confirmed as AF on stored electrograms and asymptomatic, it is called device-detected subclinical AF. Its stroke risk (~1%/year) is lower than that of ECG-documented clinical AF.

EXAM TRAP

If device-detected AF progresses to episodes lasting ≥ 24 h or is documented on a surface ECG, it becomes clinical AF — manage with the ordinary CHA₂DS₂-VA rules. ACC/AHA 2023 (written before ARTESIA) gave IIa for AHRE ≥ 24 h with score ≥ 2, IIb for 5 min–24 h with score ≥ 3, and no OAC ( III ) for AHRE < 5 min.

AF with ACS or PCI (pointer)

Full antithrombotic combinations are covered in the coronary chapters; the board rules are: Use a DOAC (not VKA) plus clopidogrel (the P2Y12 inhibitor of choice; avoid prasugrel/ticagrelor in triple therapy).

Default after uncomplicated PCI: triple therapy (OAC + aspirin + clopidogrel) for up to 1 week, then OAC + clopidogrel up to 12 months (ACS) or 6 months (CCS).

Extend triple therapy up to 1 month only when ischaemic risk is high and bleeding risk acceptable. Beyond 12 months: OAC monotherapy in stable CAD (AFIRE).

Use the stroke-prevention DOAC dose (e.g. rivaroxaban 15 mg in PIONEER AF-PCI; apixaban 5 mg bid in AUGUSTUS) — and PPI protection.

Other examinable settings

Setting Key management point

Thyrotoxicosis Beta-blocker for rate; restore euthyroidism before cardioversion; OAC per risk score Acute illness / sepsis Treat the trigger; high recurrence later — reassess and follow up Pregnancy Beta-blocker (not atenolol) for rate; DC cardioversion safe; LMWH/VKA — no DOACs Athletes Vagal AF; reduce training; ablation often preferred to drugs

Cancer Drug interactions (ibrutinib causes AF); DOACs usually acceptable

Key highlightsSpecial situations

  • POAF after cardiac surgery ~20–40%, peak day 2–4; amiodarone prophylaxis I A.
  • Posterior left pericardiotomy prevents POAF ( IIa ).
  • OAC for POAF: non-cardiac surgery IIa ; cardiac surgery IIb (ESC 2024).
  • Subclinical AF: DOAC may be considered ( IIb ) — ARTESIA fewer strokes but more bleeding; NOAH-AFNET 6 neutral.
  • Device AF ≥ 24 h or on surface ECG = clinical AF.
  • AF + PCI: DOAC + clopidogrel; aspirin ≤ 1 week by default; OAC alone after 12 months.
  • HCM + AF: anticoagulate regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VA.

18.10 Atrial Flutter

Atrial flutter is a macro-re-entrant atrial tachycardia. In typical flutter the circuit runs around the tricuspid annulus and depends on conduction through the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) — the narrow strip between the IVC and tricuspid valve, bounded anatomically so it is the ideal ablation target. Atypical flutters use scar (post-surgery, post-ablation) or LA circuits.

BOARD PEARL — "150=FLUTTER UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE"

A regular tachycardia at almost exactly 150 bpm should prompt a search for a second flutter wave hidden in the QRS or T wave. Adenosine or vagal manoeuvres transiently increase AV block and unmask the flutter waves — they do not terminate flutter.

EXAM TRAP — 1:1 FLUTTER WITH CLASSIC DRUGS

Flecainide or propafenone slow the flutter circuit (e.g. from 300 to 220/min), allowing the AV node to conduct 1:1 — a broad-complex tachycardia at ~220 bpm with collapse. Always co-prescribe an AV-nodal blocker with class IC drugs.

Management

and dangerous alone

Long-term CTI ablation: acute success > 95%, endpoint = bidirectional isthmus block; first-line for recurrent symptomatic typical flutter (ESC 2019 SVT I ; ACC/AHA 2023 I A)

MECHANISM — WHY AF APPEARS AFTER FLUTTER ABLATION

Flutter and AF share the same atrial substrate; flutter often starts as AF that organises around the tricuspid annulus. CTI ablation cures the flutter circuit but not the substrate — a large proportion (up to about half) develop AF during follow-up. OAC decisions therefore remain driven by the risk score, and continued rhythm surveillance is needed.

DON'T CONFUSE — FLUTTER VS FOCAL ATRIAL TACHYCARDIA VS AF
  • Flutter: continuous undulating sawtooth baseline, rate ~300, no isoelectric line in inferior leads. Focal AT: discrete P waves with isoelectric baseline, rate usually 150–250.
  • AF: chaotic f waves, variable in shape, amplitude and timing; irregularly irregular RR.

Key highlightsAtrial flutter

  • Typical flutter = CTI-dependent macro-re-entry around the tricuspid annulus.
  • Counter-clockwise: negative sawtooth in II, III, aVF and positive in V1.
  • Atrial rate ~300; 2:1 block → regular tachycardia at ~150 bpm.
  • Adenosine unmasks flutter waves but does not terminate flutter.
  • Class IC drugs can cause 1:1 conduction — always add an AV-nodal blocker.
  • Anticoagulate exactly as for AF.
  • DC cardioversion works at low energy (50–100 J); ibutilide is more effective in flutter than in AF.
  • CTI ablation: > 95% success; many later develop AF.

18.11 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 68-year-old woman with paroxysmal AF has no other medical history. BP 128/76 mmHg, normal echo. Using the ESC 2024 guideline, what is the most appropriate stroke-prevention recommendation?

Answer B Age 65–74 scores 1; female sex no longer counts in CHA₂DS₂-VA, so the score is 1 → OAC should be considered ( IIa ). Aspirin is never an alternative ( III ). Under CHA₂DS₂-VASc she would score 2, which in a woman equates to the same "reasonable" (IIa) zone in ACC/AHA.

Q2 An 82-year-old man (weight 74 kg, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL) with persistent AF is starting apixaban. What is the correct dose?

Answer B Apixaban is reduced to 2.5 mg bid only with two of: age ≥ 80, weight ≤ 60 kg, creatinine ≥ 1.5 mg/dL. He meets only one, so full dose. Off-label under-dosing raises stroke risk without reducing bleeding.

Q3 A 55-year-old man presents with palpitations that began 30 hours ago. He is haemodynamically stable, CHA₂DS₂- VA = 1, not anticoagulated. He wants sinus rhythm today. According to ESC 2024, the next best step is: Immediate DC cardioversion without anticoagulation

Answer B ESC 2024 lowered the no-anticoagulation threshold to 24 h. At 30 h without 3 weeks of OAC, early cardioversion needs TOE exclusion of thrombus ( I B) with OAC started and continued ≥ 4 weeks. Under ACC/AHA's 48-h rule, option A would have been debated — a classic difference.

Q4 A 60-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve develops AF. Which anticoagulant is appropriate?

Answer C Mechanical valves are an absolute contraindication to DOACs (RE-ALIGN: more thrombosis and bleeding with dabigatran). Use a VKA with the INR target set by the valve (mitral mechanical usually higher than 2–3). LAAO does not protect the prosthesis.

Q5 A 24-year-old man collapses with an irregular broad-complex tachycardia at 260 bpm with varying QRS width. BP 105/70 mmHg. Which drug is most appropriate?

Answer D Irregular, very fast, variable broad QRS = pre-excited AF. AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, digoxin, betablockers) can precipitate VF. Stable → procainamide or ibutilide; unstable → DC cardioversion; then ablate the pathway.

Q6 A 64-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%), CRT-D, and symptomatic persistent AF despite optimal GDMT asks about further treatment. Which trial best supports catheter ablation to reduce death or HF hospitalisation?

Answer C CASTLE-AF (LVEF ≤ 35%, ICD/CRT-D) showed fewer deaths or HF hospitalisations with ablation. CABANA was neutral on hard endpoints (ITT), EAST-AFNET 4 tested early rhythm control in recent AF, RACE II rate targets, AFFIRM rate vs drug rhythm control.

Q7 A 76-year-old woman with a dual-chamber pacemaker has 3-hour device-detected atrial high-rate episodes confirmed as AF, no ECG-documented AF, CHA₂DS₂-VA = 3, low bleeding risk. ESC 2024 position?

Answer B After ARTESIA (fewer strokes, more bleeding) and NOAH-AFNET 6 (neutral), ESC 2024 says a DOAC may be considered in device-detected subclinical AF with elevated risk and low bleeding risk ( IIb B). It is not Class I, and aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention.

Q8 A patient on flecainide for paroxysmal AF presents with a regular broad-complex tachycardia at 220 bpm. The most likely explanation is:

Answer B Class IC drugs slow the flutter circuit so the AV node can conduct 1:1, and use-dependent QRS widening makes it broad. Prevention: always combine IC drugs with a beta-blocker or non-DHP calcium-channel blocker.

Q9 A 58-year-old underwent successful PVI 4 months ago and is in sinus rhythm on repeated Holters. CHA₂DS₂-VA = 2. He asks to stop his DOAC. The best advice is:

Answer C OAC after ablation follows the stroke-risk score, not the apparent success (ESC I C). Silent recurrence is common and the atrial substrate persists. Minimum OAC after any ablation is 2 months.

Q10 A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm shows negative sawtooth waves in II, III, aVF and positive deflections in V1. The recurrence prevention of choice is:

Answer B Counter-clockwise typical flutter (2:1 at ~150 bpm). CTI ablation cures it in > 95% and is first-line for recurrent symptomatic flutter. Flecainide alone risks 1:1 conduction; PVI treats AF, not the CTI circuit.

Numbers that win marks

19.1 Classification, PVCs & PVC-Induced Cardiomyopathy

Ventricular arrhythmias (VA) range from isolated premature ventricular complexes (PVCs) in a normal heart to ventricular fibrillation (VF). Two questions organise every case: is there structural heart disease (SHD) or a primary electrical disease? and is the arrhythmia haemodynamically tolerated? The answer to the first question determines prognosis; the second determines what you do in the next five minutes.

Evaluating PVCs and NSVT

The first-line work-up of any newly documented VA (frequent PVCs, NSVT or SMVT) is a 12-lead ECG of the arrhythmia, a baseline 12-lead ECG and an echocardiogram (ESC Class I). CMR is added when SHD other than CAD is suspected, or when the presentation is atypical for an idiopathic origin (older age, RBBB-morphology PVCs, multiple morphologies). A ≥ 24 h Holter quantifies the burden.

BENIGN PROFILE (IDIOPATHIC)
  • Single morphology from a typical site (RVOT,
  • fascicle)
  • Suppressed by exercise
  • Normal ECG, echo, family history

Long coupling interval

MALIGNANT PROFILE
  • Multifocal PVCs, burden rising with exercise
  • Short-coupled PVC (on the T wave) initiating
  • PVT
  • NSVT cycle length < 300 ms
  • Q waves, fragmented QRS, LGE on CMR

PVC-induced (and PVC-aggravated) cardiomyopathy

Frequent PVCs can cause a reversible, dyssynchrony- and irregularity-mediated LV dysfunction. The PVC burden is the strongest predictor: a burden of at least 10% is the minimum threshold, and risk rises steeply above 20%. Because the daily burden fluctuates, repeated or longer (e.g. 14-day) monitoring is sometimes needed.

Response to suppression LVEF normalises Partial or none

Other markers of adverse remodelling: PVC QRS width > 150 ms, epicardial origin, superior axis, interpolated PVCs, associated NSVT, male sex, long duration of symptoms.

Treatment — normal LV function, symptomatic

NEW Catheter ablation first-line for symptomatic idiopathic VT/PVCs from the RVOT or left fascicles I B Beta-blocker or non-DHP CCB for symptomatic idiopathic VT/PVCs from other sites I C

  • Ablation or flecainide for symptomatic PVCs from other sites IIa C
  • Ablation in asymptomatic patients with repeatedly > 20% PVC burden at follow-up IIb B
  • Amiodarone as first-line for idiopathic PVCs/VT III C

Treatment — LV dysfunction

Catheter ablation in CM suspected to be caused by frequent, predominantly monomorphic PVCs I C AADs if ablation not desired, high-risk or unsuccessful IIa C

Ablation or AADs in CRT non-responders whose PVCs limit biventricular pacing IIa C

ESC VS ACC/AHA — PVC-INDUCED CARDIOMYOPATHY

ESC 2022 makes ablation the first-line therapy for PVC-induced CM (Class I). The 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS guideline recommends ablation when AADs are ineffective, not tolerated or not preferred. Only ESC gives a recommendation (IIb) for ablation in asymptomatic high-burden patients.

19.2 Idiopathic VT: Outflow Tract & Fascicular

Idiopathic VT occurs without SHD or a channelopathy, accounts for about 10% of VT referrals, usually presents under 50 years with palpitations, and carries a benign prognosis — an ICD is not indicated . Two mechanisms dominate: cAMP-mediated triggered activity (outflow tract VT — adenosine-sensitive) and reentry within the left Purkinje network (fascicular VT — verapamil-sensitive).

Sustained paroxysmal VT

QRS morphology LBBB + inferior axis (tall R in II, III, aVF) RBBB + left superior axis (left posterior fascicle, ~90%)

  • QRS width Broad Relatively narrow (~120–140 ms) — mistaken for
  • SVT
  • Acute drug IV beta-blocker; adenosine may terminate IV verapamil (Belhassen VT)

Long-term Ablation first-line (success > 90% RVOT) Ablation first-line; verapamil if declined Localising the outflow tract origin

  • RVOT: LBBB, inferior axis, precordial R-wave transition at
  • or after V3.
  • LVOT / aortic cusp: transition at or before V2, broad R in
  • V1–V2; V2 transition ratio ≥ 0.6 favours LVOT.
  • Transition in V3: equivocal — either side.
  • Negative lead I: leftward/posterior RVOT or LVOT; positive
  • lead I: free wall / septal right-sided.
  • Notching in inferior leads: RVOT free wall.
  • LV summit / epicardial: pseudo-delta wave, MDI ≥ 0.55 —
  • harder ablation.
DON'T CONFUSE — RVOT VT VS ARVC

ARVC can mimic RVOT VT (LBBB, inferior axis). Suspect ARVC with epsilon waves, T inversion beyond V1– V3 in sinus rhythm, multiple VT morphologies, LBBB with superior axis, RV dilatation or LGE, family history of SCD, and VT that is not adenosine-sensitive. When in doubt → CMR.

Key highlightsPVCs & PVC-induced CM

  • VT = ≥ 3 beats at > 100 bpm; sustained = ≥ 30 s or needing termination.
  • First-line evaluation of any new VA: 12-lead ECG of the arrhythmia + baseline ECG + echo (Class I).
  • PVC burden ≥ 10% = minimum threshold for PVC-induced CM; risk climbs above 20%.
  • Burden > 10% with normal LV → periodic LV function surveillance (I C).
  • No LGE + narrow QRS + normalisation after suppression = PVC-induced CM.
  • Ablation is first-line for symptomatic RVOT/fascicular PVCs and for PVC-induced CM (ESC Class I).
  • Amiodarone is not first-line for idiopathic PVCs (Class III).
DON'T CONFUSE — FASCICULAR VT VS BUNDLE BRANCH RE-ENTRY VT

Bundle branch re-entry (BBR) VT is a macro-re-entry using the bundle branches (usually down the RB, up the LB → LBBB morphology) in a diseased His–Purkinje system: dilated CM, post-valve surgery, myotonic dystrophy. Baseline ECG shows conduction delay with long HV. It is fast, poorly tolerated, and cured by ablation of the right bundle (an ICD is still usually needed for the substrate).

EXAM TRAP

Verapamil cures the young man's fascicular VT — but IV verapamil for a broad-complex tachycardia of unknown mechanism is contraindicated (Class III): in scar VT it causes haemodynamic collapse. Give it only when the ECG signature (RBBB + left axis, QRS ~130 ms, young, structurally normal heart) is unequivocal.

Key highlightsIdiopathic VT

  • Idiopathic VT: no SHD, benign, no ICD; ablation is first-line for RVOT and fascicular origin.
  • RVOT VT = LBBB + inferior axis + transition ≥ V3; adenosine-sensitive (triggered, cAMP).
  • Transition ≤ V2 → LVOT/aortic cusp origin.
  • Fascicular (Belhassen) VT = RBBB + left superior axis, QRS ~120–140 ms, verapamil-sensitive re-entry.
  • Acute therapy of tolerated idiopathic VT: IV beta-blocker (RVOT) or IV verapamil (fascicular) — ESC I C.
  • Always exclude ARVC before labelling "RVOT VT" idiopathic.
  • BBR-VT: LBBB morphology, diseased conduction system, long HV — ablate the right bundle.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • IV verapamil for broad-QRS tachycardia of unknown mechanism III B

19.3 Scar-Related VT & Acute Management of SMVT

In patients with SHD, sustained monomorphic VT (SMVT) is almost always scar-related re-entry: surviving myocyte bundles within fibrosis form slowly conducting channels (the protected isthmus) that the wavefront traverses before exiting into healthy myocardium. After MI the circuit is predominantly subendocardial; in non-ischaemic CM, ARVC and sarcoid it is more often intramural or epicardial — which is why ablation outcomes are worse there.

MECHANISM — WHY REVASCULARISATION DOES NOT CURE MONOMORPHIC VT

Acute ischaemia produces polymorphic VT/VF. A monomorphic VT requires a fixed anatomical circuit, i.e. an old scar. Revascularisation removes ischaemia but not scar, so SMVT in a patient with prior MI must never be attributed to "reversible ischaemia" — even if troponin is mildly raised (VT itself raises troponin).

Acute management of a regular broad-complex tachycardia

BOARD PEARL — PROCAINAMIDE BEATS AMIODARONE FOR ACUTE TERMINATION

In the PROCAMIO trial IV procainamide terminated tolerated SMVT more often and with fewer major cardiac adverse events than IV amiodarone. That is why ESC gives procainamide IIa and amiodarone only IIb for acute termination. Amiodarone remains the drug for preventing recurrence and for storm.

Long-term management of scar VT

TRIALS THAT MOVED THE GUIDELINES
  • VANISH: VT on amiodarone → ablation beat
  • escalation (↑ amiodarone / add mexiletine) →
  • ablation Class I.
  • VANISH2: ischaemic VT → first-line ablation
  • reduced the composite of death, storm and shocks
  • vs AADs.
  • PARTITA: ablation after the first appropriate shock
  • reduced death/HF hospitalisation.
ANTIARRHYTHMIC DRUGS — THE RULES
  • Only beta-blockers reduce mortality; other AADs
  • reduce symptoms/shocks.
  • Class IC (flecainide) contraindicated after MI
  • (CAST).
  • Amiodarone raises defibrillation threshold and may
  • slow VT below the detection zone.
  • Sotalol: QT-monitor, renal dose-adjust.

19.4 Electrical Storm

Electrical storm — ≥ 3 sustained VA episodes in 24 h needing termination — is a medical emergency with high short- and medium-term mortality. It feeds on a vicious circle: shocks → pain and fear → catecholamine surge → more VA. Management therefore attacks the substrate, the trigger and the sympathetic drive at the same time.

IV magnesium with potassium supplementation for TdP I C

Isoprenaline or transvenous pacing to raise heart rate in acquired LQTS with recurrent TdP despite correction and Mg²⁺

I C

Catheter ablation for storm due to SMVT refractory to AADs I B

Ablation for recurrent PVT/VF triggered by a similar PVC, unresponsive to drugs/revascularisation IIa C Deep sedation / intubation for intractable storm IIa C

Quinidine in CAD with storm from recurrent PVT when other AADs fail IIb C

Autonomic modulation (stellate ganglion block, thoracic epidural anaesthesia, LCSD) when drugs and ablation fail

  • IIb C
  • Mechanical circulatory support for drug-refractory storm with cardiogenic shock IIb C

Key highlightsScar VT & acute SMVT

  • SMVT in SHD = scar re-entry through a protected isthmus; subendocardial after MI, epicardial/intramural in NICM.
  • Unstable VT → synchronised DC cardioversion; stable VT with low sedation risk → DCCV is still first-line (I B).
  • Stable SMVT with SHD: IV procainamide (IIa) > IV amiodarone (IIb) for termination.
  • IV verapamil in WCT of unknown mechanism is Class III.
  • Monomorphic VT is never "explained" by ischaemia; revascularisation alone does not prevent recurrence.
  • VT recurring on amiodarone → ablation (I B), not drug escalation (VANISH).
  • Tolerated SMVT, LVEF ≥ 40% → ablation may replace ICD in expert centres (IIa C).
  • Only beta-blockers reduce mortality; prophylactic non-beta-blocker AADs in CAD are Class III.
EXAM TRAP — THE STORM THAT NEEDS A FASTER HEART RATE

If VF recurs despite sedation and beta-blockade and the resting sinus rate is slow, think of arrhythmias driven by low adrenergic tone or pauses: Brugada syndrome, early repolarization syndrome, pause-dependent TdP, SQTS. Here isoprenaline — not a beta-blocker — is the answer (± quinidine for Brugada/ERS).

Key highlightsElectrical storm

  • Storm = ≥ 3 sustained VA episodes in 24 h requiring ATP/shock.
  • First step: interrogate the ICD — confirm appropriate therapy and reprogram.
  • Correct K⁺, Mg²⁺, ischaemia, HF; stop QT-prolonging drugs.
  • SHD storm: sedation + non-selective β-blocker + IV amiodarone (I B); ablation if refractory SMVT (I B).
  • TdP: IV magnesium, potassium, and raise the heart rate (isoprenaline or pacing).
  • Brugada/ERS/idiopathic VF storm: isoprenaline (IIa), quinidine.
  • Rescue: deep sedation (IIa), stellate block/TEA/LCSD (IIb), MCS (IIb).

19.5 ICD for Prevention of SCD & the Wearable Defibrillator

The ICD is the only therapy proven to terminate VF reliably, but it does not prevent VA and carries lifelong risks (inappropriate shocks, lead failure, infection). Two general rules frame every indication: the patient must have a reasonable expectation of good-quality survival > 1 year (ESC I C), and an ICD is not implanted during incessant VA until the arrhythmia is controlled (ESC III C).

Secondary prevention

An ICD is recommended after documented VF or haemodynamically not-tolerated VT in the absence of a reversible cause (ESC I A; AHA/ACC/HRS 1 B-R). The AVID, CASH and CIDS meta-analysis showed a ~28% relative reduction in mortality versus amiodarone.

WHEN SUSTAINED VA DOES NOT MANDATE AN ICD
  • PVT/VF within the first 48 h of an acute MI (and no later recurrence).
  • PVT/VF during acute ischaemia that is fully treated by revascularisation, with preserved LVEF. Idiopathic monomorphic VT (outflow tract, fascicular) in a structurally normal heart.
  • Clearly reversible, non-recurring cause (e.g. drug toxicity) — but the ESC still asks for an individual risk evaluation (IIa C), and a monomorphic VT should never be attributed to electrolytes alone.

Primary prevention — the numbers that decide

IIa C

LMNA carrier with estimated 5-year VA risk ≥ 10% plus NSVT, LVEF < 50% or AV conduction delay IIa C Condition-specific rules for HCM, ARVC, sarcoid and ACHD are covered in the cardiomyopathy and congenital chapters.

MECHANISM — WHY THE 40-DAY RULE EXISTS

Early after MI, a large share of deaths are from re-infarction, rupture, pump failure or PEA — not VF — and LVEF often recovers once stunning resolves. In DINAMIT (6–40 days) and IRIS (5–31 days) early ICDs reduced arrhythmic death but non-arrhythmic death rose equally, so total mortality was unchanged . Hence: wait, optimise therapy, re-measure EF.

BOARD PEARL — DANISH AND THE NON-ISCHAEMIC ICD

DANISH (NICM, LVEF ≤ 35%, most with CRT) found no reduction in all-cause death with a primary-prevention ICD, although SCD halved and patients < 68–70 years appeared to benefit. ESC therefore rates NICM ICD IIa; ACC/AHA kept Class 1. Age, comorbidity and CMR scar should shape the decision.

Wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD)

A vest with dry electrodes that detects VT/VF and shocks after an alarm the conscious patient can abort. It is a bridge, not a substitute for an ICD. In VEST (post-MI, LVEF ≤ 35%) it did not significantly reduce the primary endpoint of arrhythmic death, partly because of poor wear-time adherence.

ESC 2022: secondary-prevention indication but temporarily unable to receive an ICD (e.g. after infected-device extraction) — IIa ; selected patients early after MI — IIb .

AHA/ACC/HRS 2017: ICD explanted for infection after prior SCA/sustained VA — 2a; high risk but not yet ICD-eligible (< 40 days post-MI with LVEF ≤ 35%, new NICM, < 90 days post-revascularisation, myocarditis, awaiting transplant) — 2b.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2022 (ESC VA/SCD VS 2015)

Primary-prevention ICD in non-ischaemic CM downgraded to IIa (DANISH); new IIa for NYHA I ischaemic CM with LVEF ≤ 30% and for LVEF ≤ 40% + NSVT + inducible SMVT.

Catheter ablation promoted: first-line for RVOT/fascicular VT and PVC-induced CM (I); preferred over AAD escalation for VT on amiodarone (I); alternative to ICD in tolerated SMVT with LVEF ≥ 40% (IIa). Channelopathies: LQTS diagnostic threshold QTc ≥ 480 ms or score > 3; β-blocker for genotype-positive/normalQT (IIa); induced Brugada type 1 no longer diagnostic on its own; ICD for Brugada with arrhythmic syncope IIa.

VA in the acute coronary syndrome

ICD in SCA survivors with coronary vasospasm IIa C

Early VA (< 48 h after STEMI, 4–12% of patients) raises in-hospital mortality but does not by itself indicate an ICD. Urgent reperfusion is the most effective antiarrhythmic.

19.6 Long QT Syndrome & Drug-Induced Torsades

Congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS; prevalence ~1 in 2000) is a disorder of ventricular repolarisation: reduced outward K⁺ current or persistent inward Na⁺ current prolongs the action potential, allowing early afterdepolarisations (EADs) to trigger TdP, usually in an adrenergic setting. Untreated, asymptomatic patients have an annual SCD risk well under 0.5%; prior syncope raises it roughly 10-fold.

Measuring the QT

Measure in lead II or V5 using the tangent method (end of T = intersection of the steepest down-slope tangent with the baseline); exclude U waves separated from T.

Bazett (QT/√RR) over-corrects at fast heart rates — use Fridericia or a rate < 90 bpm for reliable values. Normal QTc: < 450 ms (men), < 460 ms (women). QTc > 500 ms = high TdP risk, whatever the cause. Brisk standing unmasks LQTS (QT fails to shorten as HR rises); QTc ≥ 480 ms at the 4th minute of recovery after exercise is a diagnostic point (LQT1).

Key highlightsICD & WCD

  • ICD only with expected good-quality survival > 1 year; not during incessant VA.
  • Secondary prevention: VF or not-tolerated VT without reversible cause (ESC I A); ~28% mortality reduction vs amiodarone.
  • VF within 48 h of MI, or fully revascularised ischaemic PVT with good EF → no ICD.
  • Ischaemic, NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤ 35% after ≥ 3 months OMT → ICD I A (both).
  • NYHA I ischaemic: LVEF ≤ 30% (ESC IIa; ACC 1).
  • NICM LVEF ≤ 35%: ESC IIa A vs ACC 1 A (DANISH).
  • Wait ≥ 40 days after MI (ICD earlier = III A) and ≥ 90 days after revascularisation (ACC); re-image EF at 6–12 weeks if ≤ 40%.
  • WCD = bridge; ESC IIa for secondary-prevention patients temporarily without ICD; VEST was neutral for its primary endpoint.
SYNDROMIC FORMS
  • Romano–Ward: autosomal dominant, cardiac only
  • (LQT1–3).
  • Jervell and Lange-Nielsen: autosomal recessive,
  • congenital sensorineural deafness, very long QT,
  • high risk.
  • Andersen–Tawil (KCNJ2, IK1): prominent U waves,
  • bidirectional VT, periodic paralysis, dysmorphism.
  • Timothy (CACNA1C): syndactyly, CHD, autism,
  • extreme QT.
MECHANISM — WHY Β-BLOCKERS WORK BEST
IN LQT 1
  • IKs is the current that normally shortens the action potential when sympathetic tone rises. Without it (LQT1), exercise prolongs rather than shortens repolarisation,
  • so blocking the adrenergic surge removes the trigger.
  • LQT3 events occur at slow rates, so β-blockers help
  • less and late-Na⁺ blockade (mexiletine) is added.

Diagnosis — the modified Schwartz (LQTS) score

Genetics Pathogenic variant 3.5

*TdP and syncope are mutually exclusive (count the higher). Score > 3 = LQTS (ESC 2022). In the original Schwartz score ≥ 3.5 = high probability; congenital deafness scores 0.5.

LCSD or ICD) — 2b

Symptomatic on βblockerICD Class I; LCSD if ICD declined Intensify: genotype drugs, LCSD and/or ICD — Class 1

EXAM TRAP — WHICH BETA-BLOCKER?

Metoprolol and atenolol are the wrong answer for LQTS (and CPVT): breakthrough events are more frequent. The board answer is nadolol (long-acting, once daily) or propranolol . Also: an ICD is never a substitute for β-blockade — shocks are catecholaminergic and can provoke storm.

Acquired (drug-induced) long QT and torsades

Most TdP in adults is acquired: an IKr-blocking drug (sotalol, dofetilide, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, haloperidol, methadone, ondansetron, hydroxychloroquine) plus "reduced repolarisation reserve": female sex, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia/pauses, HF/LVH, renal or hepatic impairment, drug interactions, or a latent congenital variant. The typical onset is short–long–short: a pause followed by a PVC on the enlarged, notched T wave.

STOP THE DRUG WHEN
  • QTc > 500 ms, or
  • QTc rises > 60 ms from baseline, or
  • New T–U wave distortion / TdP.
TREAT TDP
  • Unstable/sustained → defibrillate (it is polymorphic
  • — unsynchronised).
  • IV magnesium sulphate 2 g even if Mg²⁺ normal.
  • K⁺ to 4.5–5.0 mmol/L.
  • Raise HR: isoprenaline or temporary pacing
  • (~90–110 bpm).
  • Amiodarone is not the answer (prolongs QT).

Key highlightsLong QT syndrome

  • ESC diagnosis: QTc ≥ 480 ms, or score > 3, or pathogenic variant (any QT); QTc 460–479 + arrhythmic syncope → consider.
  • LQT1 = KCNQ1/IKs, swimming/exercise; LQT2 = KCNH2/IKr, noise & post-partum, notched T; LQT3 = SCN5A gain, sleep, long ST.
  • Non-selective β-blocker (nadolol, propranolol) for all with QT prolongation (I B); genotype-positive, normal QTc → IIa.
  • Mexiletine for LQT3 (I C).
  • ICD: after cardiac arrest (I B) or symptomatic despite therapy (I C); asymptomatic high-risk by 1-2-3 calculator (IIb).
  • LCSD when ICD declined/contraindicated or shocks despite therapy (I C).
  • Epinephrine challenge and EP study are Class III in LQTS.
  • Drug-induced TdP: stop drug at QTc > 500 ms or Δ > 60 ms; Mg²⁺, K⁺, raise heart rate.

19.7 Brugada Syndrome

Brugada syndrome (BrS) is characterised by coved ST elevation in the right precordial leads and a risk of polymorphic VT/VF, typically at rest or during sleep, in a structurally normal heart. It is ~8–10× more common in men, prevalent in South-East Asia (the "sudden unexplained nocturnal death syndrome"), and usually manifests in the 3rd–4th decade. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance; a pathogenic SCN5A (loss-of-function) variant is found in only ~20% of probands.

MECHANISM — THE RVOT EPICARDIUM

Two complementary hypotheses: repolarisation — loss of INa unmasks a prominent Ito-mediated notch in RVOT epicardium (not endocardium), creating a transmural voltage gradient (coved ST) and phase-2 reentry; and depolarisation — slow conduction through fibrotic RVOT epicardium. The ablation target is exactly this epicardial RVOT substrate.

ECG diagnosis

Type 1 (diagnostic): coved ST elevation ≥ 2 mm (0.2 mV) followed by a negative T wave in ≥ 1 right precordial lead (V1 or V2), recorded in the standard or high (2nd–3rd) intercostal spaces. Type 2 (saddleback): ST elevation with a positive/biphasic T wave — suggestive only; not diagnostic. Type 1 may be spontaneous, fever-induced or drug-induced (sodium-channel blocker challenge). Only a spontaneous type 1 carries appreciable arrhythmic risk.

Procainamide 10 mg/kg over 10 min

Perform with resuscitation facilities; isoprenaline is the antidote. Not indicated if a spontaneous type 1 has already been recorded (ESC III C).

BRUGADA PHENOCOPIES — EXCLUDE BEFORE DIAGNOSING BRS

RV ischaemia / proximal RCA or LAD occlusion, acute PE, pericarditis/myocarditis, ARVC, hyperkalaemia, hypercalcaemia, mechanical RVOT compression (pectus excavatum, mediastinal tumour), tricyclic, lithium, cocaine or class IC toxicity, hypothermia, post-cardioversion. A phenocopy resolves when the cause is removed and the Na⁺-blocker test is negative.

PES in asymptomatic spontaneous type 1 IIb B

ICD in selected asymptomatic patients with VF inducible by PES using up to 2 extrastimuli IIb C Catheter ablation in asymptomatic BrS III C

BOARD PEARL — SHANGHAI SCORE

The 2016 J-wave consensus Shanghai score weights ECG (spontaneous type 1 = 3.5, fever-induced = 3, druginduced = 2), history, family history and genetics: ≥ 3.5 = probable/definite BrS; 2–3 = possible; < 2 = nondiagnostic. It explains why a drug-induced pattern alone does not make the diagnosis.

Key highlightsBrugada syndrome

  • Type 1 = coved ST ≥ 2 mm + negative T in ≥ 1 of V1–V2 (standard or high intercostal spaces). Only type 1 is diagnostic.
  • Men ≫ women; VF at rest/sleep; fever and Na⁺-channel blockers unmask it.
  • SCN5A loss-of-function found in only ~20%; genetic testing is Class I in probands but a negative test does not exclude BrS.
  • Challenge: ajmaline 1 mg/kg, flecainide 2 mg/kg (max 150 mg), procainamide 10 mg/kg; not if spontaneous type 1 already seen.
  • ICD: arrest or sustained VT (I C); arrhythmic syncope with type 1 (ESC IIa, ACC 1).
  • Treat fever aggressively; avoid ST-raising drugs, cocaine, alcohol excess.
  • Storm → isoprenaline; recurrent shocks → quinidine or epicardial RVOT ablation.
  • Ablation in asymptomatic BrS is Class III.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Diagnose CPVT with structurally normal heart, normal ECG and exercise/emotion-induced bidirectional or polymorphic VT; or a disease-causing variant
  • I C
  • Genetic testing and counselling I C
  • Epinephrine/isoprenaline challenge when exercise testing is not possible IIb C
  • Avoid competitive sport, strenuous exercise and stressful environments I C
  • β-blocker, ideally non-selective (nadolol, propranolol), in all clinically diagnosed CPVT I C β-blocker in genotype-positive, phenotype-negative patients IIa C
  • Add flecainide for recurrent syncope, PVT/bidirectional VT or persistent exertional PVCs on maximal βblocker IIa C
  • ICD + β-blocker + flecainide after aborted cardiac arrest I C
  • ICD for arrhythmic syncope and/or documented VT despite maximal β-blocker and flecainide IIa C LCSD when β-blocker + flecainide ineffective, not tolerated or contraindicated IIa C
  • PES for risk stratification III C

19.8 CPVT, Short QT, Early Repolarization & Idiopathic VF

Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (CPVT)

CPVT (~1 in 10 000) presents in childhood or adolescence with exercise- or emotion-induced syncope or arrest; the resting ECG and echo are normal. Most cases are autosomal dominant gain-of-function RYR2 variants (~60%); a recessive form involves CASQ2; TRDN and calmodulin genes cause atypical forms.

MECHANISM — DELAYED AFTERDEPOLARISATIONS

A leaky ryanodine receptor releases Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during diastole when adrenergic stimulation loads the store. The Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger extrudes it, generating an inward current → DADs → triggered beats. Alternating foci in the two ventricles produce the signature bidirectional VT. Flecainide works partly by directly inhibiting RyR2 release.

Exercise testing is the cornerstone of diagnosis: ectopy appears at a reproducible heart-rate threshold (often ~110–130 bpm) and escalates from PVCs → bigeminy → couplets → bidirectional/polymorphic VT as the rate rises.

EXAM TRAP — THE ICD CAN KILL IN CPVT

A painful shock releases catecholamines → more VT → more shocks (shock storm). Shocks for CPVT often terminate the "bidirectional" DAD-driven rhythm poorly. Hence the ICD is programmed with long detection times and high rate cut-offs, and is never a stand-alone therapy — optimise β-blocker + flecainide ± LCSD first.

Short QT syndrome (SQTS)

Very rare; gain-of-function K⁺ channel variants (KCNH2, KCNQ1, KCNJ2) or loss of SLC4A3. Presents with AF at a young age, syncope or VF — even in infancy. Tall, peaked T waves; QT fails to lengthen at slow rates.

ILR in young SQTS patients IIa C

Quinidine if ICD indicated but declined/contraindicated, or asymptomatic with family history of SCD IIb C PES for risk stratification III C

Early repolarization pattern (ERP) and syndrome (ERS)

ERP = J-point elevation ≥ 1 mm in ≥ 2 adjacent inferior and/or lateral leads (notch or slur on the terminal QRS). It is common (up to 5–13% of the population; young men, athletes) and usually benign. ERS is diagnosed only in a patient resuscitated from unexplained VF/PVT who has ERP. High-risk ERP features: J wave ≥ 2 mm, dynamic J-point changes, horizontal/descending ST after the J point, inferior + lateral distribution.

19.9 The Unexplained Sudden Death: Autopsy, Genetics & Family

Screening

Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is an unexpected natural death from a cardiac cause, within 1 h of symptom onset if witnessed, or within 24 h of last being seen well if unwitnessed. Coronary disease causes ~75–80% of SCD overall, but under the age of 35–40 inherited cardiomyopathies and channelopathies dominate . When autopsy and toxicology are negative the death is labelled sudden arrhythmic death syndrome (SADS); up to 20–40% of SADS families carry an inherited arrhythmia syndrome on clinical screening.

Key highlightsCPVT, SQTS, ERS, IVF

  • CPVT: normal resting ECG, exercise-induced bidirectional VT; RYR2 (AD) or CASQ2 (AR); diagnose with exercise testing.
  • CPVT therapy: nadolol/propranolol (I) → add flecainide (IIa) → LCSD (IIa); ICD after arrest (I) with β-blocker + flecainide.
  • SQTS: QTc ≤ 360 ms + variant/family history/VF survival (I); QTc ≤ 320 ms alone (IIa); quinidine is the drug.
  • ERP = J-point ≥ 1 mm in ≥ 2 inferior/lateral leads — common and benign; ERS needs resuscitated VF.
  • ICD for ERS after arrest (I B); never for isolated asymptomatic ERP (III).
  • IVF is a diagnosis of exclusion; ICD (I B); Purkinje-PVC ablation and quinidine for recurrences.
  • Isoprenaline treats storm in Brugada, ERS, IVF and SQTS; β-blockers treat LQTS and CPVT.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Post-mortem genetic testing targeted to primary electrical disease after SADS when decedent < 50 y and/or circumstances suggest it
  • I B
  • Hypothesis-free exome/genome sequencing after SADS III B
  • The relatives
  • Evaluate first-degree relatives, obligate carriers and symptomatic relatives of SADS decedents, especially decedent < 50 y
  • I B
  • Baseline family evaluation: history, examination, standard + high precordial ECG, echo, exercise test I B Cascade genetic testing when a pathogenic variant is found in the decedent/proband I B
  • Follow children of SADS decedents until adulthood if no diagnosis I C
  • Na⁺-blocker test in relatives ≥ 16 years when suspicion of BrS is raised IIa B
  • Ambulatory monitoring and CMR in relatives IIb C
  • Follow-up of asymptomatic adult relatives with normal evaluation III C
  • Genetic testing — the rules
  • Test when a condition with a likely genetic basis and SCD risk is diagnosed in a living or deceased person (I B); interpret variants with an accepted framework (ACMG classes 1–5) (I C).
  • Only class 4 (likely pathogenic) or class 5 (pathogenic) variants are used for diagnosis and cascade testing; a variant of uncertain significance (VUS, class 3) must never drive testing or treatment of relatives — re-evaluate it periodically and study segregation.
  • A negative genetic result does not exclude disease; testing an index patient with insufficient evidence of a genetic disease is Class III.
  • Yield: LQTS ~75%, CPVT ~60%, BrS ~20%, ERS/IVF low.
BOARD PEARL — START AGES FOR FAMILY SCREENING

Relatives of a BrS/SADS proband: ECG with high precordial leads from ~10 years; Na⁺-blocker challenge from > 16 years (younger children risk false negatives and complications). Clinical follow-up every 1–3 years if phenotype or class 4/5 variant present; discharge adults with a negative phenotype and no variant.

Key highlightsSCD, genetics & families

  • SCD: within 1 h of symptoms (witnessed) or 24 h of last seen well (unwitnessed).
  • CAD dominates overall; inherited disease dominates < 35–40 years.
  • Autopsy always in unexpected SD < 50 y; keep DNA; cardiac pathologist; toxicology.
  • SCA survivor without obvious cause: coronary imaging + CMR + Na⁺-blocker test + exercise test (all I B).
  • Only class 4/5 variants guide cascade testing; VUS never does; hypothesis-free exome after SADS is III.
  • SADS relatives: ECG (incl. high leads), echo, exercise test (I B); Na⁺-blocker test ≥ 16 y (IIa).
  • Asymptomatic adult relatives with normal work-up are discharged (follow-up III).

19.10 Cardiac Arrest & Post-Resuscitation Care

Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survival to discharge remains only ~10% overall, but reaches 30–50% for a witnessed VF arrest with immediate bystander CPR and early defibrillation. The initial rhythm is now more often non-shockable (PEA/asystole) than VF. The single most powerful modifiable determinant of survival is the time to high-quality CPR and defibrillation — each minute of untreated VF lowers survival by roughly 7–10%.

Advanced life support — the board essentials

Reversible causes 4 H: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia & metabolic, hypothermia · 4 T: thrombosis (coronary/PE), tamponade, tension pneumothorax, toxins

Post-cardiac arrest care

After ROSC the post-cardiac arrest syndrome combines hypoxic–ischaemic brain injury, myocardial dysfunction (stunning, often recovering in 48–72 h), systemic ischaemia–reperfusion response and the persisting precipitating disease. Care is bundled: airway and ventilation, haemodynamics, coronary strategy, temperature control, seizures and prognostication.

Treat clinically apparent seizures 1 C-LD

Multimodal prognostication consolidated no earlier than 72 h after return to normothermia and off sedation

2a B-NR

AHA uses Class 1 / 2a / 2b / 3 and LOE B-R, B-NR, C-LD, C-EO; badge colours map to the ESC equivalents.

MAP target > 60–65 mmHg ≥ 65 mmHg

No ST elevation Delayed/selective angiography; consider early wholebody CT to find the causeDelayed/selective angiography (emergent = 3: No Benefit)

Prognostication Multimodal algorithm ≥ 72 h after ROSC Multimodal, ≥ 72 h after normothermia

TRIALS THAT CHANGED PRACTICE
  • TTM2: 33 °C vs fever avoidance (≤ 37.8 °C) — no
  • difference in death or function → "hypothermia"
  • became "temperature control".
  • COACT and TOMAHAWK: in resuscitated patients
  • without ST elevation, immediate angiography did
  • not improve survival vs delayed/selective.
  • DOSE-VF: vector change or double sequential
  • defibrillation improved survival in refractory VF.
EXAM TRAPS
  • Comatose post-ROSC, no ST elevation, stable →
  • not emergency angiography.
  • ST elevation after ROSC → emergent angiography
  • even if comatose.
  • Never prognosticate a poor outcome before 72 h,
  • and never on a single test.
  • Pre-hospital cooling with cold IV fluids is not
  • recommended.

Key highlightsCardiac arrest & post-resuscitation care

  • CPR: 100–120/min, 5–6 cm, pauses < 10 s; shock then immediately resume CPR for 2 min.
  • Adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 min; amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg (or lidocaine) for refractory VF.
  • Emergent angiography if ST elevation after ROSC (1 B-NR); not routinely without it (3 B-R) — COACT, TOMAHAWK.
  • AHA 2025: temperature control 32–37.5 °C for ≥ 36 h; ERC/ESICM: prevent fever ≤ 37.5 °C for ≥ 72 h.
  • MAP ≥ 65 mmHg; PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg; avoid hyperoxia (SpO₂ 90–98% AHA; 94–98% ERC).
  • Prognosticate with multimodal tools ≥ 72 h, never on a single test.
  • Refractory VF: vector change or double sequential defibrillation (DOSE-VF).

19.11 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 42-year-old woman has palpitations. Holter shows monomorphic PVCs, burden 18%, with LBBB morphology, inferior axis and precordial transition in V4. Echo: LVEF 45%, LV mildly dilated; CMR shows no LGE. What is the best next step?

Answer C Burden > 10%, reduced EF and no LGE = PVC-induced CM; RVOT origin (LBBB, inferior axis, late transition). Ablation is Class I and first-line. Amiodarone is not first-line; ICD is irrelevant for a reversible cause; watching risks further decline.

Q2 A 22-year-old man presents with a regular broad-complex tachycardia at 170 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg. QRS 130 ms, RBBB morphology with left superior axis. Echo is normal. Which drug is most likely to terminate the arrhythmia?

Answer B RBBB + left superior axis, narrow-ish QRS in a young man with a normal heart = left posterior fascicular (verapamilsensitive) re-entry. Adenosine and β-blockers rarely work; lidocaine is for ischaemic VT.

Q3 A 64-year-old man with prior anterior MI (LVEF 30%) and a secondary-prevention ICD has had two shocks for monomorphic VT in a month despite amiodarone 200 mg daily and bisoprolol. What does the ESC recommend?

Answer C Recurrent SMVT despite chronic amiodarone → ablation in preference to escalating AADs (ESC I B), per VANISH. Options A, B are exactly the "escalation" arm that lost. Sotalol substitution is for patients on β-blocker alone (IIa).

Q4 A 58-year-old man had an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI 3 weeks ago. LVEF is 30%, NYHA II, on full GDMT. He asks about an ICD. What is correct?

Answer C ICD within 40 days of MI is Class III (DINAMIT, IRIS). Re-measure EF at 6–12 weeks (I C); ACC also asks ≥ 90 days after revascularisation. Revascularisation does not remove the indication if EF stays ≤ 35%.

Q5 A 55-year-old woman with non-ischaemic DCM (LVEF 32%, NYHA II, QRS 110 ms) has been on optimal therapy for 4 months. CMR shows mid-wall LGE. What is the ESC 2022 class for a primary-prevention ICD?

Answer B ESC rates the NICM primary-prevention ICD IIa A (downgraded after DANISH); ACC/AHA keep Class 1. LGE strengthens the case. QRS 110 ms means no CRT indication.

Q6 A 16-year-old swimmer collapses in the pool and is resuscitated. Resting QTc is 490 ms with broad-based T waves. Which therapy is the cornerstone of long-term management, in addition to an ICD?

Answer B Swimming trigger + broad T = LQT1. Non-selective β-blockers (nadolol, propranolol) are preferred; metoprolol has more breakthrough events. Mexiletine is for LQT3; quinidine prolongs QT.

Q7 A 38-year-old man has a coved ST elevation of 3 mm with T-wave inversion in V1–V2 recorded during a febrile illness. He had an episode of nocturnal syncope with agonal breathing last month. Echo is normal. What is the most appropriate management per ESC 2022?

Answer C A fever-induced type 1 pattern plus arrhythmic syncope/nocturnal agonal respiration makes BrS (IIa) and an ICD should be considered for arrhythmic syncope (ESC IIa; ACC 1). A challenge adds nothing once type 1 is recorded; ablation is for recurrent shocks; β-blockers have no role.

Q8 A 12-year-old girl faints while running. Resting ECG and echo are normal. Treadmill test shows PVCs at 120 bpm progressing to alternating-axis VT at 150 bpm. Despite nadolol at maximal dose she has further exertional couplets. The next step is to add:

Answer B CPVT with incomplete control on maximal non-selective β-blocker → add flecainide (IIa C). An ICD alone risks shock storm; LCSD is the next step if β-blocker + flecainide fail.

Q9 A 61-year-old man is resuscitated from VF out of hospital (ROSC at 15 min). He remains comatose. ECG shows sinus rhythm with RBBB, no ST elevation; BP 110/70 on low-dose noradrenaline, no recurrent arrhythmia. Which statement is correct?

Answer C COACT and TOMAHAWK: no benefit of immediate angiography without ST elevation, shock or instability (AHA 3: No Benefit). Temperature control is 32–37.5 °C (not mandatory 33 °C); prognosticate ≥ 72 h; avoid hyperoxia.

Q10 A 34-year-old man dies suddenly in his sleep. Autopsy and toxicology are negative. His 14-year-old son and 40- year-old sister ask for screening. Which is not appropriate?

Answer D Na⁺-channel blocker testing in relatives is reserved for those ≥ 16 years with raised suspicion (IIa). ECG with high leads, echo and exercise test are Class I; targeted post-mortem genetics is I; children of SADS decedents are followed to adulthood.

20.1 Sinus Node Dysfunction

Sinus node dysfunction (SND, sick sinus syndrome) is a disease of the elderly — most often idiopathic fibrosis of the sinus node and atrial myocardium — that presents as fatigue, dizziness or syncope. It is the commonest indication for pacing in many Western series. Crucially, pacing for SND improves symptoms but not survival ; therefore the indication rests on symptom–rhythm correlation.

Paroxysmal AF/flutter with long post-conversion pause on termination

Chronotropic incompetence Failure to reach ~80–85% of age-predicted maximum HR (or HR reserve) on exercise

EXTRINSIC (REVERSIBLE)CAUSES TO EXCLUDE
  • Drugs: β-blockers, non-DHP CCBs, digoxin,
  • amiodarone, ivabradine, lithium, donepezil,
  • clonidine
  • Hypothyroidism, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia,
  • raised ICP
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea (nocturnal pauses)
  • High vagal tone: athletes, vomiting, sleep
  • Inferior MI (usually transient)
DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
  • Holter / event recorder; ILR for infrequent
  • symptoms (< monthly) — ESC I A
  • Exercise test for chronotropic incompetence (IIa B)
  • EP study rarely: SNRT > 1500 ms, corrected SNRT >
  • 525 ms abnormal
  • Imaging for SHD (I C); CMR/PET for infiltrative
  • disease, especially age < 60
EXAM TRAP — THE FIT YOUNG ATHLETE

Resting HR 38 bpm, nocturnal pauses of 2.5 s and Mobitz I at night in an asymptomatic athlete are physiological (vagal). They resolve with exercise and do not need a pacemaker; detraining for 3 months confirms reversibility.

Key highlightsSinus node dysfunction

  • SND pacing is for symptoms — it does not improve survival.
  • Pacing Class I B when symptoms are clearly attributed; asymptomatic SND → Class III.
  • Tachy–brady: pace to allow rate-control drugs (I B) — or ablate AF to avoid pacing (IIa).
  • ILR for infrequent (< monthly) unexplained symptoms/syncope (ESC I A).
  • SA exit block: pause = exact multiple of P–P; sinus arrest: not a multiple.
  • In SND, choose DDD and minimise V-pacing (I A).
  • Exclude drugs, hypothyroidism, OSA and athletic vagotonia first.

  • The HV interval
  • On the His bundle electrogram, the AH interval (normal ~50–120 ms) reflects AV nodal conduction and the HV interval (normal 35–55 ms) reflects His–Purkinje conduction. An HV ≥ 70 ms in a patient with syncope and bundle branch block is an indication for pacing ; HV ≥ 100 ms marks a very high risk of complete heart block. Block below the His deflection during incremental atrial pacing (at rates where the AV node should conduct) is similarly diagnostic.

20.2 AV Block: Types & Level of Block

The prognosis of AV block depends less on its "degree" than on its level. Block in the AV node is usually benign, rate-responsive and backed up by a narrow junctional escape at 40–60 bpm. Block in the His–Purkinje system (infranodal) is unpredictable, progresses and has a slow, broad ventricular escape (20–40 bpm) — it causes syncope and sudden death.

Often infranodal

Third degree Complete AV dissociation, atrial rate > ventricular rate Narrow escape → nodal/His; broad escape → infranodal

MECHANISM — WHY EXERCISE UNMASKS INFRANODAL BLOCK

His–Purkinje refractoriness does not shorten much with sympathetic tone. As the sinus rate rises, P waves arrive while the diseased bundle is still refractory, so conduction ratios fall (2:1 → 3:1). The AV node, rich in autonomic innervation, does the opposite. Exercise-induced second- or third-degree AV block is infranodal until proven otherwise and needs pacing.

DON'T CONFUSE — BLOCKED PAC AND VAGAL AV BLOCK
  • Blocked (non-conducted) PAC: the most common cause of a pause — the non-conducted P is premature and often buried in the T wave.
  • Vagal paroxysmal AV block: sinus slowing precedes the block (PP lengthens) and PR prolongs — benign, nodal, often with nausea, cough, micturition.
  • Idiopathic paroxysmal AV block: block triggered by a pause or premature beat with no sinus slowing (phase-4 His– Purkinje block) — infranodal, needs pacing.

Key highlightsAV block

  • Level beats degree: nodal = benign; infranodal = progression, slow broad escape, syncope, SCD.
  • Mobitz I narrow QRS → nodal; Mobitz II → infranodal; 2:1 → judge by QRS width and PR.
  • High-grade = ≥ 2 consecutive non-conducted P waves.
  • Atropine/exercise improve nodal block and worsen infranodal block; carotid massage does the reverse.
  • Normal HV 35–55 ms; HV ≥ 70 ms + syncope + BBB → pace; HV ≥ 100 ms = very high risk.
  • Exercise-induced 2nd/3rd degree AVB is infranodal → pace.
  • Lyme and inferior MI cause nodal block that usually resolves; anterior MI block is infranodal.

20.3 Bundle Branch & Fascicular Blocks

EXAM TRAP — "TRIFASCICULAR BLOCK"

Bifascicular block + first-degree AV block is commonly called "trifascicular", but the long PR is usually nodal. Asymptomatic bifascicular block, with or without a long PR, is not an indication for pacing (Class III) . The issue is syncope: then do an EP study or empirical pacing.

Reflex syncope and unexplained falls

Pacing is a last resort in reflex syncope because the vasodepressor component persists. The ESC reserves dual-chamber pacing (Class I A) for patients aged > 40 years with severe, unpredictable, recurrent syncope and documented symptomatic asystole > 3 s or asymptomatic pause > 6 s (sinus arrest or AVB), cardi★ KEY HIGHLIGHTS Bundle branch & fascicular blocks LAFB: axis −45° to −90°, qR aVL; LPFB: right axis after excluding RVH/lateral MI.

Special settings

Conduction disturbances after TAVI

New LBBB occurs in up to a quarter to a half of patients after self-expanding valves and permanent pacing in ~3–25%. Pre-existing RBBB is the strongest predictor of pacemaker need; others are first-degree AVB, LAFB, deep implantation, self-expanding valves, oversizing, short membranous septum and LVOT calcium.

Ambulatory ECG monitoring (7–30 days) or EPS for new LBBB with QRS > 150 ms or PR > 240 ms without further prolongation over > 48 h

IIa C

Ambulatory monitoring or EPS for pre-existing conduction disease with QRS or PR prolongation > 20 ms

  • IIb C
  • Prophylactic pacing before TAVI in RBBB without another indication III C
  • EPS ≥ 3 days after TAVI; HV ≥ 70 ms is taken as positive for pacing.

Temporary pacing

Transvenous temporary pacing for haemodynamically compromising bradycardia refractory to IV chronotropes (atropine, isoprenaline, adrenaline) — ESC I C.

Transcutaneous pacing if transvenous is not possible/available (IIa C) — painful, capture often unreliable; confirm with a palpable pulse, not the ECG.

For prolonged temporary pacing (e.g. infected device awaiting re-implantation), use an active-fixation lead connected to an externalised pacemaker (IIa C).

Atropine is ineffective (and may worsen block) in infranodal block and heart transplant recipients (denervated heart).

Key highlightsPacing indications

  • 3rd-degree, Mobitz II, infranodal 2:1 and high-grade AVB → pace irrespective of symptoms (I C).
  • Symptomatic Mobitz I or 1st-degree AVB with PR > 300 ms → IIa; asymptomatic nodal block → III.
  • Reflex syncope: DDD only if > 40 y with documented asystole > 3 s (symptomatic) / > 6 s (asymptomatic), CICSS or asystolic tilt (I A).
  • Post-MI and post-surgery AVB: wait ≥ 5 days; SND post-surgery: up to 6 weeks.
  • TAVI: pace for CHB/high-grade AVB persisting 24–48 h or new alternating BBB (I); RBBB is the strongest predictor.
  • Myotonic dystrophy: any 2nd/3rd-degree AVB or HV ≥ 70 ms → pace (I C).
  • LMNA or sarcoid with a pacing indication → consider ICD/CRT-D instead of a simple pacemaker.
  • ACC/AHA: LVEF 36–50% + expected V-pacing > 40% → physiologic pacing (2a).

  • Chronotropic incompetence Add rate response (R)
  • Paroxysmal AF + SND DDD with mode switch; atrial ATP may be considered (IIb B)

20.5 Pacing Modes, NBG Code & Mode Selection

BOARD PEARL — DUAL-CHAMBER PACING DOES NOT S AV E LIVES

Across MOST, CTOPP, UKPACE and DANPACE, physiological (atrial-based) pacing reduced AF and pacemaker syndrome and improved quality of life, but did not reduce mortality or stroke significantly compared with ventricular pacing. The harm lies in RV pacing burden: cumulative V-pacing > 40% (MOST, DAVID) increased HF hospitalisation and AF.

Pacemaker syndrome and pacing-induced cardiomyopathy

PACEMAKER SYNDROME
  • Loss of AV synchrony, typically VVI with
  • retrograde VA conduction: atria contract against
  • closed AV valves.
  • Fatigue, dizziness, dyspnoea, pulsation in neck,
  • cannon a waves, BP fall (> 20 mmHg) when
  • pacing begins.
  • Fix: upgrade to DDD, or lower rate / add hysteresis
  • to favour intrinsic rhythm.
PACING-INDUCED CARDIOMYOPATHY
  • LVEF fall (usually ≥ 10% to < 50%) with RV-pacing
  • burden ≥ 20%; affects ~10–20%.
  • Risk: baseline LVEF 36–50%, broad paced QRS,
  • high burden.
  • Fix: upgrade to CRT (ESC IIa B if LVEF ≤ 35% and
  • symptomatic) or conduction system pacing.

20.6 Conduction System & Leadless Pacing

Conventional RV-apical pacing activates the ventricles cell-to-cell from the apex — an iatrogenic LBBB. Conduction system pacing (CSP) captures the native His–Purkinje system so that both ventricles are activated rapidly and synchronously.

Key highlightsModes & selection

  • NBG: paced – sensed – response – rate modulation – multisite.
  • Permanent AF → VVIR (I C). SND → DDD minimising V-pacing (I A). AVB in SR → DDD over VVI (IIa A).
  • Physiological pacing reduces AF and pacemaker syndrome, not mortality.
  • RV-pacing burden > 40% → more HF and AF (MOST, DAVID).
  • Pacemaker syndrome = VVI + retrograde VA conduction → cannon a waves, hypotension → upgrade to DDD.
  • Pacing-induced CM: RV pacing ≥ 20%, LVEF drop ≥ 10% → upgrade to CRT/CSP.
  • Mode switch (DDD → DDI/VDI) prevents tracking of atrial tachyarrhythmias.
  • Feature His bundle pacing (HBP) Left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP)
  • Paced QRS Identical to native (selective) or near-native RBBB-like pattern in V1 (qR/rSR′), short, constant V6 R-wave peak time
  • Thresholds / sensing Higher thresholds, rise over time; small R
  • waves; atrial/His oversensing
  • Low, stable thresholds; good R-wave sensing
  • Distal (infra-Hisian)
  • block
  • May fail to correct Bypasses more distal disease
  • Backup RV lead Often advised (IIa C in dependency, infranodal
  • block, AVJ ablation)
  • Usually not required
