  • uncertain extraction

IIa B

Backup RV lead in pacemaker dependency, high-grade/infranodal AVB, high thresholds, planned AVJ ablation, sensing issues

IIa C

IIb C

WHAT CHANGED AFTER 2021 — THE 2023 HRS PHYSIOLOGIC PACING GUIDELINE
  • Endorses both HBP and LBBAP (LBBAP was only "promising" in ESC 2021).
  • LVEF 36–50% with expected ventricular pacing > 40%: CSP or biventricular pacing is reasonable to reduce HF risk (Class 2a).
  • LVEF ≤ 35% with LBBB: biventricular CRT remains the standard; CSP is an alternative, particularly when CS lead placement fails or response is inadequate.
  • Large outcome RCTs of CSP vs BiV CRT are ongoing — expect the next ESC pacing guideline to upgrade CSP.

Leadless pacemakers

Self-contained capsules (~2 cm³) implanted via the femoral vein into the RV septum with tines or a helix. They eliminate the pocket and transvenous lead — the source of most infections, haematomas and lead fractures. Early systems were single-chamber VVIR; AV-synchronous (VDD, accelerometer-sensed atrial contraction) and dual-chamber (two communicating capsules) systems now exist.

  • Lower infection risk — ideal for dialysis, prior CIED

20.7 Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy

In LBBB the septum contracts early and the lateral wall late, wasting work, lengthening systole, shortening diastolic filling and producing functional MR. Biventricular pacing (RV lead + LV lead via a lateral/posterolateral coronary sinus tributary) re-synchronises contraction: it improves symptoms, LVEF and MR, reverses remodelling and reduces HF hospitalisation and death (CARE-HF for CRT-P mortality; COMPANION; MADIT-CRT and RAFT in mild HF).

MECHANISM — WHY QRS MORPHOLOGY MATTERS MORE THAN WIDTH

CRT corrects electrical dyssynchrony of the LBBB type (late lateral wall). RBBB or non-specific IVCD delays the RV or reflects diffuse myocardial disease, so pacing the lateral LV adds little. True LBBB ≥ 150 ms is the best predictor of response ; female sex, non-ischaemic aetiology and small scar burden also predict superresponse. Echo "mechanical dyssynchrony" does not select patients (PROSPECT) and CRT harms narrowQRS patients (EchoCRT).

Key highlightsCSP & leadless pacing

  • RV-apical pacing = iatrogenic LBBB; CSP restores synchronous activation.
  • HBP: native QRS but higher, rising thresholds and sensing issues; backup RV lead if dependent (IIa C).
  • LBBAP: RBBB-like paced QRS in V1, low stable thresholds, overcomes distal block.
  • ESC 2021: HBP IIa B when CS lead fails; IIb C instead of RV pacing if LVEF > 40% and > 20% pacing expected.
  • HRS 2023: LVEF 36–50% with > 40% expected pacing → CSP or BiV (2a).
  • Leadless: IIa B for no venous access or high infection risk (dialysis, prior infection); risk = perforation, no CRT/ ICD.

  • "Ablate and pace": CRT rather than RV pacing in HFmrEF IIa C

Maximising response

Aim for biventricular pacing as close to 100% as possible — outcomes fall when it is < 98%. Causes of loss: AF with fast conduction, frequent PVCs, long programmed AV delay, LV lead dislodgement or phrenic stimulation.

Non-response (~30%): non-LBBB or borderline QRS, extensive or posterolateral scar, apical/anterior LV lead, suboptimal AV/VV timing, untreated MR or AF. Define response as clinical improvement or LVESV reduction ≥ 15%.

Post-implant: re-evaluate diuretic dose and up-titrate GDMT (CRT often permits higher β-blocker doses).

EXAM TRAP — THE PACED QRS IN CRT

Effective biventricular pacing typically shows a dominant R in V1 and a Q/negative QRS in lead I (LV activated first, from the lateral wall). A paced LBBB pattern (QS in V1, positive lead I) in a CRT patient suggests loss of LV capture (RV-only pacing).

20.8 Device Troubleshooting, Magnet & MRI

Almost every paced-ECG question reduces to three failures — capture, sensing and output — plus a handful of normal behaviours that look abnormal. Start with: Are there spikes? Does each spike capture? Is the device seeing what it should (and nothing else)?

Key highlightsCRT

  • CRT: LVEF ≤ 35%, symptomatic on OMT, SR, LBBB ≥ 150 ms → I A.
  • LBBB 130–149 → IIa; non-LBBB ≥ 150 → IIa; non-LBBB 130–149 → IIb; QRS < 130 ms → III (EchoCRT).
  • ACC/AHA uses a lower limit of 120 ms vs ESC 130 ms.
  • HFrEF (LVEF < 40%) needing ventricular pacing for AVB → CRT rather than RV pacing (I A), any NYHA class.
  • AF: CRT needs ≥ 90–95% (ideally ≥ 98%) BiV capture — add AVJ ablation if not achieved.
  • CRT-D if ICD indicated (I A); otherwise CRT-D vs CRT-P by shared decision (IIa B).
  • Loss of LV capture: paced QRS turns to LBBB pattern (positive lead I, QS in V1).
LEAD INTEGRITY BY IMPEDANCE
  • Normal pacing impedance ~300–1200 Ω; the trend
  • matters most.
  • Abrupt rise → conductor fracture (or loose setscrew).
  • Abrupt fall → insulation breach (current leak,
  • muscle stimulation).
  • Intermittent noise with arm movement / pocket
  • manipulation → fracture (subclavian crush).
NORMAL BEHAVIOURS THAT LOOK ABNORMAL
  • Fusion / pseudofusion: spike coincides with
  • intrinsic QRS — timing, not malfunction.
  • Hysteresis: device waits for a slower rate before
  • pacing at the base rate.
  • Ventricular safety pacing: V spike ~100–120 ms
  • after an A spike when something is sensed in the
  • crosstalk window.
  • Sleep rate / rate response changes.

Tachycardias in the dual-chamber patient

Reduce sensor sensitivity

Runaway pacemaker Generator failure (historic) — very fast pacing Emergency: disconnect/cut lead

MECHANISM — UPPER-RATE BEHAVIOUR

When the sinus rate exceeds the maximum tracking rate, the device lengthens the AV interval beat by beat until a P falls in PVARP and is not tracked → pacemaker Wenckebach. At even faster rates, every second P falls into the total atrial refractory period (TARP = AV delay + PVARP) → abrupt 2:1 block. The 2:1 rate = 60 000 / TARP (ms); e.g. TARP 400 ms → 2:1 at 150 bpm. Short TARP in young active patients avoids sudden exertional rate halving.

Magnet response

EXAM TRAP — THE PACING-DEPENDENT PATIENT WITH AN ICD IN THEATRE

A magnet on an ICD disables shocks but leaves the pacemaker in its sensing mode — diathermy noise can still inhibit pacing and cause asystole. A pacing-dependent ICD patient needs reprogramming to asynchronous pacing (VOO/DOO) with tachytherapies off , continuous monitoring and external pads, then reinterrogation afterwards.

Surgery, cardioversion and MRI

Surgery: prefer bipolar diathermy; if monopolar, short bursts with return pad away from the generator; below-umbilicus diathermy rarely interferes. Interrogate before (if not in the last 12 months) and after surgery when reprogrammed or exposed to EMI.

Cardioversion: anteroposterior pads at least 8–10 cm from the generator; interrogate afterwards. Radiotherapy: risk rises with cumulative device dose (> 2–5 Gy) and neutron-producing beams (> 10 MV); relocation is rarely needed.

Key highlightsTroubleshooting

  • Loss of capture: spike without response — think dislodgement, hyperkalaemia, IC drugs, MI.
  • Undersensing = too many spikes; oversensing = too few (pauses) — magnet abolishes oversensing pauses.
  • Impedance rise → fracture; fall → insulation break.
  • PMT: retrograde P tracked at upper rate; terminate with magnet, prevent by lengthening PVARP. 2:1 upper-rate block at 60 000/TARP; TARP = AV delay + PVARP.
  • Magnet: pacemaker → asynchronous pacing; ICD → suspends tachytherapy only.
  • MRI-conditional system → MRI safe per protocol (I A); non-conditional without abandoned/epicardial leads → IIa B.

20.9 ICD Therapy, Programming & CIED Infection

(Indications for ICD therapy are covered in Chapter 19.) This section deals with which ICD, how to program it, and what to do after a shock.

BOARD PEARL — MADIT-R IT

High-rate (≥ 200 bpm) or delayed therapy (60 s delay at 170–199 bpm) cut inappropriate therapy by ~75–80% and reduced mortality versus conventional programming. Every shock — appropriate or not — is associated with worse outcomes, so let self-terminating VT stop on its own and try ATP first.

After a shock

Generator replacement / lead replacement 1 week / 1 month

Professional (Group 2) drivers with an ICD are generally permanently restricted; national regulations apply. CIED infection and lead extraction (pointer)

CIED infection affects ~1–2% of implants, more after generator replacement/upgrade, with CRT-D, haematoma, renal failure, diabetes, fever at implant and early re-intervention. Pathogens: coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus. Prevention: antibiotic prophylaxis within 1 h of incision (ESC I A), chlorhexidine– alcohol skin prep (IIa B), no heparin bridging (III A), defer implant in fever until afebrile ≥ 24 h, antibacterial envelope in high-risk re-interventions (IIb B; WRAP-IT).

CLINICAL APPROACH — SUSPECTED CIED INFECTION

≥ 2 blood cultures before antibiotics, TOE (lead/valve vegetations), consider PET-CT; never aspirate the pocket. Definite pocket infection, erosion or CIED endocarditis → complete system removal (generator and all leads) plus antibiotics; antibiotics alone fail.

S. aureus bacteraemia in a CIED carrier → high suspicion of device infection even without pocket signs. Re-implant on the contralateral side once cultures are negative (≥ 72 h; longer with valve vegetations); reassess whether a device is still needed; consider leadless PM or S-ICD; WCD as bridge.

Transvenous lead extraction in experienced centres with surgical backup; major complications ~1–2% (SVC tear, tamponade).

Key highlightsICD therapy & infection

  • Primary prevention without pacing need → single-chamber ICD (I A); S-ICD is an alternative when no pacing/ ATP/CRT needed (IIa B).
  • Program long detection (≥ 6–12 s or 30 intervals), therapy zone ≥ 188 bpm, ATP first, discriminators to 230 bpm.
  • Inappropriate shocks: SVT/AF (commonest) or oversensing (lead fracture, T wave, EMI).
  • Magnet on ICD suspends shocks only; interrogate every shock.
  • Driving (private): 3 months after secondary-prevention implant or appropriate shock; 2 weeks after primaryprevention implant.
  • CIED infection → remove the entire system; antibiotics alone are inadequate.
  • Prophylactic antibiotic within 1 h of incision (I A); no heparin bridging (III A).

20.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 74-year-old man has 2:1 AV block with QRS 100 ms and PR 280 ms in conducted beats. On walking, conduction improves to 1:1. He is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?

Answer B Narrow QRS, long PR and improvement with exercise = supra-Hisian (nodal) 2:1 block. Asymptomatic nodal block does not need pacing; review AV-nodal drugs. An EPS is only needed if the level is unclear.

Q2 A 68-year-old woman with RBBB + LAFB has two episodes of unexplained syncope. LVEF 55%. Holter is unremarkable. EP study shows HV 78 ms. Next step?

Answer C Syncope + bifascicular block + HV ≥ 70 ms = Class I B pacing indication. ILR is for a negative EPS. With preserved EF, an ICD is not indicated.

Q3 Two days after an uncomplicated TAVI with a self-expanding valve, a patient with pre-existing RBBB has intermittent complete heart block. What is correct?

Answer B Complete/high-degree AVB persisting 24–48 h after TAVI → permanent pacing (I B); pre-existing RBBB with any new conduction disturbance also justifies early pacing (IIa B). Waiting longer risks sudden asystole.

Q4 A 70-year-old with a VVI pacemaker for intermittent AV block complains of fatigue, dizziness and neck pulsations. BP falls from 140/80 to 112/70 mmHg when ventricular pacing starts. Irregular cannon a waves are seen. Best management?

Answer B Classic pacemaker syndrome (VVI with VA conduction): hypotension on pacing, cannon a waves. Restore AV synchrony with DDD. A higher rate increases VVI pacing and worsens it.

Q5 A 66-year-old with ischaemic cardiomyopathy, LVEF 30%, NYHA II on optimal therapy for 6 months, sinus rhythm, QRS 138 ms with RBBB morphology. Which device, per ESC?

Answer B ICD is Class I (ischaemic, NYHA II, LVEF ≤ 35%). Non-LBBB QRS 130–149 ms gives CRT only IIb B. CRT-D is Class I only when CRT itself is also indicated.

Q6 A 72-year-old with LVEF 35% (NYHA I) develops complete heart block. Which pacing strategy does the ESC recommend?

Answer C HFrEF (LVEF < 40%) with high-degree AVB needing ventricular pacing → CRT rather than RV pacing, regardless of NYHA class (ESC I A; BLOCK-HF).

Q7 A patient with a DDD pacemaker has a regular V-paced tachycardia at 130 bpm (upper tracking rate 130) starting after a PVC. Retrograde P waves follow each paced QRS. Immediate management?

Answer B Endless-loop PMT: retrograde P waves tracked at the upper rate. A magnet makes the device asynchronous and breaks the loop; long term, lengthen PVARP. Adenosine may work by blocking VA conduction but the magnet is simplest and definitive.

Q8 A pacemaker-dependent patient with a dual-chamber ICD requires abdominal surgery with monopolar diathermy. What is the correct peri-operative plan?

Answer C A magnet on an ICD suspends shocks but does not make pacing asynchronous — diathermy could inhibit pacing in a dependent patient. Reprogram to VOO/DOO, disable tachytherapy, apply pads, re-interrogate afterwards.

Q9 A 58-year-old with a primary-prevention ICD receives three shocks while doing arm exercises in the gym. Interrogation shows high-frequency, non-physiological signals on the ventricular channel and an RV lead impedance rising from 500 to 2400 Ω. Most likely cause?

Answer C Non-physiological noise provoked by arm movement plus a sharp rise in impedance = conductor fracture. Insulation breach lowers impedance; T-wave oversensing shows double counting of physiological signals.

Q10 A 45-year-old on haemodialysis via a left arm fistula, with occluded right subclavian vein and prior pocket infection, needs pacing for paroxysmal complete heart block with normal LVEF. Best option?

Answer B No usable upper-limb venous access and high infection risk (dialysis, prior infection) → leadless pacemaker (ESC IIa B). An S-ICD cannot pace; epicardial CRT is unnecessary with normal EF.

Syncope

Transient loss of consciousness — separating the benign faint from the warning sign of sudden death.

What the board expects you to know

  • The three families of syncope and the clinical clues that point to each.
  • The high-risk features that demand admission or urgent evaluation, and the ECG findings that are diagnostic of arrhythmic syncope.
  • Exact criteria for carotid sinus massage, orthostatic hypotension (classical, initial, delayed) and POTS.
  • Indications for tilt testing, ILR, EPS and pacing — and where ESC and ACC/AHA/HRS differ.
  • Stepwise treatment of reflex syncope and orthostatic hypotension, and the principles of driving advice.

Numbers that win marks

≥ 20 / ≥ 10OH (mmHg) — SBP/DBP fall within
3 min≥ 30 bpm POTS — HR rise within 10 min, no OH
> 3 s / > 50CSM positive — pause / SBP fall (mmHg)
> 40 yCSM & pacing — age threshold (ESC)

21.1 Definition, Classification & Mechanisms

DEFINITION

Syncope is transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) due to cerebral hypoperfusion , characterised by rapid onset, short duration and spontaneous complete recovery. TLOC is the umbrella term; syncope is one of its causes, alongside epileptic seizures, psychogenic pseudosyncope and rare causes.

Syncope is common: about 1 in 3 people faint at least once, with peaks in adolescence and after age 65. It accounts for ~1% of emergency department (ED) visits. Reflex syncope is the commonest cause at every age; orthostatic hypotension becomes important in the elderly; cardiac syncope is less common but carries the prognosis.

Classification

MECHANISM — TWO WAYS TO LOSE BLOOD PRESSURE

Arterial BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance. Low peripheral resistance dominates in reflex vasodepression and autonomic failure. Low cardiac output results from a cardioinhibitory reflex (bradycardia/asystole), arrhythmia, structural obstruction or reduced venous return (volume depletion, venous pooling). Cessation of cerebral flow for only 6–8 s, or a fall of systolic BP to ~50–60 mmHg at heart level, causes loss of consciousness.

MECHANISM — THE VASOVAGAL (BEZOLD–JARISCH)CASCADE

Upright posture pools 500–800 mL of blood in the legs and splanchnic bed. In susceptible people, reduced venous return with vigorous contraction of an under-filled ventricle (and central triggers such as emotion) produces a paradoxical withdrawal of sympathetic tone (vasodepression) and a surge of vagal tone (cardioinhibition — bradycardia or asystole). The VASIS classification of the tilt response follows this: type 1 mixed, type 2A cardioinhibitory without asystole, type 2B with asystole > 3 s, type 3 pure vasodepressor.

Mimics of syncope (TLOC that is not syncope)

Colour Pallor Cyanosis Normal

Other non-syncopal causes: falls without LOC, cataplexy, vertebrobasilar TIA (focal signs, rarely LOC), subclavian steal, hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, intoxication, subarachnoid haemorrhage.

EXAM TRAP

Urinary incontinence does not distinguish syncope from seizure — it occurs in both. Brief jerking during a faint ("convulsive syncope") is common and is not epilepsy. Lateral tongue biting, prolonged confusion and head turning favour a seizure.

Key highlightsDefinition & classification

  • Syncope = TLOC from cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid, spontaneous, complete recovery.
  • Three families: reflex, orthostatic hypotension, cardiac.
  • Reflex syncope is the commonest cause at all ages; cardiac syncope carries the worst prognosis.
  • Cerebral flow arrest for 6–8 s causes LOC.
  • VASIS type 2B = cardioinhibitory response with asystole > 3 s.
  • Drugs are the commonest cause of orthostatic hypotension.
  • Incontinence does not discriminate; lateral tongue bite and prolonged confusion favour epilepsy.

21.2 Initial Evaluation & Risk Stratification

The initial evaluation — careful history (from patient and witness), physical examination including supine and standing BP, and a 12-lead ECG — establishes a diagnosis in a large proportion of patients and is Class I in both guidelines. It must answer three questions: Is it syncope? Is the cause clear? Is the patient at high risk of death or serious events?

  • # Finding
  • 2 Mobitz II second-degree or third-degree AV block
  • 3 Alternating left and right bundle branch block
  • 4 VT or rapid paroxysmal SVT
  • 5 Non-sustained polymorphic VT with long or short QT interval
  • 6 Pacemaker or ICD malfunction with cardiac pauses

Where to manage — the ED pathway

Risk scores

Scores are sensitive but not better than good clinical judgement, and they predict outcomes that are often not caused by the syncope itself. ESC 2018 advises that ED risk scores should not be used alone; ACC/AHA/ HRS 2017 says their use "may be reasonable" ( IIb B-NR).

BOARD PEARL — THE ACC/AHA/HRS VIEW OF ROUTINE TESTS

Targeted blood tests (haematocrit, troponin, BNP, D-dimer, glucose) are used only when clinically indicated. Routine comprehensive laboratory testing, routine neuroimaging and routine EEG are not useful ( III ) in syncope without focal neurological findings. Carotid Doppler has no role in evaluating syncope.

Key highlightsInitial evaluation & risk

  • History + examination (supine/standing BP) + ECG is Class I and diagnoses many patients.
  • Major high-risk event features: exertional or supine syncope; palpitation immediately before; new chest pain/ dyspnoea/headache.
  • Diagnostic ECG: sinus bradycardia < 40 bpm or pauses > 3 s awake; Mobitz II/3rd-degree block; alternating BBB; VT/rapid SVT; NSVT with long/short QT; device malfunction.
  • Unexplained SBP < 90 mmHg in the ED = high risk.
  • Low risk → discharge ( I ); intermediate → ED observation/syncope unit ( IIa ); high risk → intensive evaluation ( I ).
  • Canadian Syncope Risk Score has 9 items (troponin, QTc > 480, QRS > 130…); scores never replace judgement.
  • No routine neuroimaging, EEG or carotid Doppler.

21.3 Diagnostic Tests

Tests are chosen by the suspected mechanism and the frequency of events: monitor for as long as it takes to catch a spontaneous event, provoke reflexes when reflex syncope is suspected, and image when structural disease is suspected. Carotid sinus massage (CSM)

CLINICAL APPROACH — PERFORMING CSM
  • Massage each carotid sinus firmly for up to 10 s, right side first, with continuous ECG and beat-to-beat BP.
  • Perform both supine and upright (on a tilt table) — up to one-third of positive responses appear only when upright.
  • Positive: ventricular pause > 3 s and/or fall in SBP > 50 mmHg.
  • Neurological complications are rare (well under 1%).
DON'T CONFUSE — HYPERSENSITIVITY VS SYNDROME

Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is the abnormal response alone — common and often asymptomatic in older men. Carotid sinus syndrome requires the response plus reproduction of the patient's spontaneous symptoms in a compatible clinical picture. Only the syndrome justifies treatment.

Active standing test

Measure BP (manual sphygmomanometer or beat-to-beat) supine and then during active standing for 3 minutes (ESC I C). Beat-to-beat devices capture initial OH (first 15–30 s) that an intermittent cuff will miss. Criteria are detailed in Section 21.4.

Tilt-table testing

DEFINITION — THE PROTOCOL

Supine rest, then passive head-up tilt at 60–70° for 20–45 min; if negative, provocation with sublingual glyceryl trinitrate (300–400 µg, "Italian protocol") or IV isoproterenol. A positive test reproduces the patient's symptoms with the characteristic hypotension and/or bradycardia.

Tilt testing to assess the efficacy of treatment. III B

ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 similarly rates tilt testing reasonable ( IIa ) when vasovagal syncope is suspected but not established, for suspected delayed OH, to distinguish convulsive syncope from epilepsy, and for suspected pseudosyncope; it is not recommended to predict response to drug therapy ( III ).

EXAM TRAP

A positive tilt test shows susceptibility to reflex hypotension, not the mechanism of the spontaneous event. An asystolic tilt response does not reliably predict asystole in real life — which is why pacing decisions rest mainly on spontaneous documented pauses (ILR), not on tilt alone. Tilt also has limited specificity in the elderly.

ECG monitoring — match the tool to the frequency

In high-risk patients in whom comprehensive evaluation has not found a cause or led to specific treatment, and who have no conventional indication for an ICD or pacemaker.

I A

In suspected or certain reflex syncope with frequent or severe episodes (to guide pacing). IIa B In suspected epilepsy when treatment has proven ineffective. IIb B

In unexplained falls. IIb B

BOARD PEARL — WHAT AN ILR RECORDING MEANS

Diagnostic: correlation between syncope and an arrhythmia (brady or tachy) — or syncope with sinus rhythm, which excludes arrhythmia.

Diagnostic even without symptoms: Mobitz II or complete AV block, ventricular pauses > 3 s (except in young trained people, during sleep, or rate-controlled AF), rapid prolonged SVT or VT.

  • Presyncope correlated with a rhythm is a less reliable surrogate than syncope itself.
  • Electrophysiological study (EPS)

Coronary angiography Only for suspected ischaemia as in non-syncope patients — not for syncope alone Video recording Home video of spontaneous events is very helpful to separate syncope, epilepsy and pseudosyncope; in-hospital video during tilt increases reliability

Autonomic tests Valsalva, deep-breathing, 24-h ambulatory BP (nocturnal hypertension, "non-dipping" in autonomic failure) when neurogenic OH is suspected

Key highlightsDiagnostic tests

  • CSM: age > 40, supine and upright, 10 s each side; positive = pause > 3 s and/or SBP fall > 50 mmHg reproducing symptoms.
  • Avoid CSM after TIA/stroke within 3 months or with bruits ( III ).
  • Tilt: 60–70°, then GTN 300–400 µg; IIa for suspected reflex syncope, OH, POTS, pseudosyncope; not to assess treatment ( III ).
  • Holter only if events ≥ weekly; external loop if ≤ 4 weeks apart; ILR for infrequent recurrent events ( I A).
  • ILR asymptomatic diagnostic findings: Mobitz II/CHB, pause > 3 s awake, rapid SVT/VT.
  • EPS: I in scar-related disease; IIa bifascicular block — HV ≥ 70 ms → pace.
  • Exercise testing for syncope during or shortly after exertion (ESC I ).

21.4 Orthostatic Hypotension & Intolerance Syndromes

On standing, gravity shifts blood to the legs and splanchnic bed; the baroreflex normally raises HR by ~10–15 bpm and increases vascular tone so that BP barely falls. When the reflex arc fails (autonomic failure), is overwhelmed (volume depletion, vasodilator drugs) or over-reacts (POTS), orthostatic intolerance results.

Young, prodrome, recurrent

Supine hypertension (SBP ≥ 140 mmHg supine) often coexists with neurogenic OH and complicates treatment.

MECHANISM — NEUROGENIC VS NON-NEUROGENIC OH

In non-neurogenic OH (hypovolaemia, drugs) the baroreflex is intact, so HR rises briskly as BP falls. In neurogenic OH the efferent sympathetic limb fails, so BP falls but HR hardly rises — a ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio < 0.5 bpm/mmHg suggests neurogenic OH. Look for Parkinsonism, cerebellar signs (MSA), neuropathy (diabetes, amyloid), bladder/bowel and erectile dysfunction.

EXAM TRAP

A 3-minute cuff measurement is normal in initial OH (BP has already recovered) and may be normal in delayed OH (it has not yet fallen). A young patient who "greys out" within seconds of standing up has initial OH; an elderly patient who faints after 5–10 minutes upright may have delayed OH — tilt testing shows it.

Management of orthostatic hypotension

POTS — management

Non-drug first: explanation; fluids 2–3 L/day and liberal salt; compression garments; graded, initially recumbent exercise (rowing, recumbent bike, swimming) to reverse deconditioning.

Drugs (off-label, limited evidence): low-dose propranolol, ivabradine (rate), midodrine (vasoconstriction), fludrocortisone (volume), pyridostigmine.

Look for associated conditions: joint hypermobility, mast-cell activation, post-viral syndromes; avoid labelling inappropriate sinus tachycardia (resting tachycardia) as POTS.

21.5 Management of Reflex Syncope

The prognosis of reflex syncope is excellent — it does not increase mortality. Treatment aims to prevent recurrence and injury , and intensity is matched to frequency, severity (injury, no prodrome) and risk activity (driving, high-risk work). Most patients need only explanation and reassurance.

Key highlightsOrthostatic syndromes

  • Classical OH: SBP ≥ 20 / DBP ≥ 10 mmHg fall (or SBP < 90) within 3 min.
  • Initial OH: SBP fall > 40 / DBP > 20 mmHg within 15 s — needs beat-to-beat BP.
  • Delayed OH: beyond 3 min — found on tilt.
  • POTS: HR rise ≥ 30 bpm (≥ 40 aged 12–19) or > 120 bpm within 10 min, no OH, symptoms > 3 months.
  • Neurogenic OH: BP falls with little HR rise (ΔHR/ΔSBP < 0.5).
  • OH treatment: stop culprit drugs, salt/water (2–3 L, 10 g NaCl), stockings/binders, head-up sleeping, midodrine or fludrocortisone ( IIa ).
  • Midodrine: last dose ≥ 4 h before lying down — supine hypertension.

Drugs

Fludrocortisone in young patients with orthostatic VVS, low–normal BP and no contraindication. IIb B Midodrine in patients with the orthostatic form of VVS. IIb B

Beta-blockers in reflex syncope. III A

Cardiac pacing

Pacing to reduce recurrences in patients aged > 40 years with spontaneous documented symptomatic asystolic pause(s) > 3 s or asymptomatic pause(s) > 6 s due to sinus arrest, AV block or both.

IIa B

Pacing in cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome with recurrent, unpredictable syncope, age > 40 years.

IIa B

Pacing in patients with a tilt-induced asystolic response and recurrent, frequent, unpredictable syncope, age > 40 years.

IIb B

Pacing in adenosine-sensitive syncope (sudden syncope without prodrome, normal heart). IIb B Pacing in the absence of a documented cardioinhibitory reflex. III B

MECHANISM — WHY PACING HELPS SOME FAINTERS BUT NOT OTHERS

Pacing prevents bradycardia/asystole but cannot prevent vasodepression. It works only when cardioinhibition dominates — hence the requirement for a documented spontaneous asystolic pause and age > 40 (older patients have less vasodepressor-dominant faints and fewer alternatives). ISSUE-3 (ILR-documented asystole, age ≥ 40) showed dual-chamber pacing substantially reduced recurrence; closed-loop stimulation pacing (SPAIN, BIOSync CLS) benefits patients with tilt-induced asystole.

Physical counter-pressure manoeuvres (PCM)

Leg crossing with muscle tensing, hand-gripping, arm tensing, or squatting at the first prodromal symptom raise BP by increasing venous return and peripheral resistance. They need a prodrome long enough to act, so they suit young patients with recognisable warning symptoms (PC-Trial).

EXAM TRAP

Beta-blockers for vasovagal syncope are a favourite distractor. ESC gives them III A (POST trial: no benefit overall); ACC/AHA allows only a weak IIb in patients ≥ 42 (POST sub-analysis). The pacing mode of choice in reflex syncope is dual-chamber (with rate-drop or closed-loop algorithms) — never single-chamber ventricular pacing.

E MERGING — CARDIO NEURO ABLATION

Catheter ablation of the atrial ganglionated plexi reduces vagal efferent tone and can abolish cardioinhibitory reflex syncope in young patients in whom pacing is unattractive. Randomised data are small; it is not yet included in the 2018 ESC or 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS recommendations — expect it in the ESC guideline on syncope and cardiovascular autonomic disorders scheduled for 2027.

Key highlightsReflex syncope treatment

  • Reflex syncope does not increase mortality — education and reassurance are Class I for everyone.
  • PCM: IIa with prodrome, age < 60 (ESC).
  • Fludrocortisone and midodrine: ESC IIb ; midodrine ACC/AHA IIa .
  • Beta-blockers: ESC III A.
  • Reduce antihypertensives in vasodepressor syncope, target SBP ~140 mmHg ( IIa ).
  • Pacing (dual-chamber): age > 40 with documented symptomatic pause > 3 s or asymptomatic pause > 6 s ( IIa B).
  • Cardioinhibitory CSS, age > 40: pacing IIa ; tilt-induced asystole only IIb .
  • No pacing without documented cardioinhibition ( III ).

21.6 Cardiac Syncope, Driving & the Syncope Unit

Cardiac syncope is treated by treating its cause. The key principle: treat the arrhythmia that causes syncope, but decide on an ICD by the risk of sudden death — which may persist even after the cause of syncope has been corrected.

Arrhythmic syncope — treatment map

CLINICAL APPROACH — THE ELDERLY FALL E R

In older adults, syncope and falls overlap: amnesia for loss of consciousness is common, so an "unexplained fall" may be syncope. Evaluate with orthostatic BP (including delayed), medication review (the most fixable cause), CSM, and consider an ILR ( IIb ). Multifactorial causes are the rule.

Driving

Driving advice balances the risk of recurrence while driving against the harm of restriction. The risk is low for most syncope patients; it is highest when syncope is unpredictable (no prodrome), occurs while seated or driving, or has an untreated cardiac cause. Commercial/professional (Group 2) drivers face stricter rules than private (Group 1) drivers. National law always takes precedence.

The syncope unit

A syncope unit is a facility with a standardised approach to TLOC, run by dedicated staff with access to tilt testing, beat-to-beat BP, autonomic tests, ambulatory ECG/ILR and rapid access to echo, EPS and pacing. It can be hospital- or community-based. ESC 2018 promotes syncope units because a structured pathway reduces admissions, unexplained cases and costs and improves diagnostic yield; they also receive intermediate-risk patients from the ED for rapid out-patient evaluation.

WHAT WAS NEW IN ESC 2018 (VS 2009)
  • A dedicated ED risk-stratification pathway with explicit low- and high-risk features.
  • ILR moved earlier in the work-up of recurrent unexplained syncope ( I A) and extended to suspected reflex syncope, epilepsy and falls.
  • Home video recording of events formally recommended; syncope units promoted.
  • Pacing criteria in reflex syncope tied to documented asystole (> 3 s symptomatic / > 6 s asymptomatic) and age > 40.
  • Beta-blockers for reflex syncope downgraded to III A.

Key highlightsCardiac syncope, driving & syncope unit

  • Treat the cause of syncope, but decide on an ICD by sudden-death risk.
  • Intrinsic Mobitz II/CHB with syncope → pace ( I ) even without rhythm–symptom correlation.
  • Bifascicular block + unexplained syncope → EPS; HV ≥ 70 ms → pace; negative EPS → ILR.
  • Unexplained syncope in HCM, LQTS on beta-blocker, Brugada or ARVC raises ICD consideration.
  • Driving: single mild reflex syncope — no restriction for private drivers; unpredictable or cardiac syncope needs treatment first.
  • Group 2 (professional) drivers face stricter limits.
  • Syncope units reduce admissions and unexplained cases; the next ESC guideline is scheduled for 2027.

21.7 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 19-year-old woman faints while having blood taken. She felt hot, nauseated and sweaty, then lost

Answer C Classic emotional vasovagal syncope with low-risk features: diagnosis is made clinically ( I C) and the patient can be discharged after explanation. Brief jerks are convulsive syncope, not epilepsy; no EEG, MRI or tilt is needed.

Q2 A 72-year-old man with a previous anterior MI (LVEF 40%) has abrupt syncope while seated, without prodrome. ECG shows Q waves. Echo and Holter are unremarkable. The most appropriate next investigation is:

Answer C Unexplained syncope with previous MI/scar is a Class I B indication for EPS to seek inducible monomorphic VT (→ ICD). Tilt and CSM target reflex mechanisms; a 2-week loop recorder is unlikely to capture a rare event.

Q3 A 68-year-old man has recurrent syncope when shaving. Carotid sinus massage in the upright position produces a 4.5-s ventricular pause with reproduction of his symptoms. Best management?

Answer B Cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome: pause > 3 s reproducing spontaneous symptoms, age > 40, recurrent unpredictable syncope → pacing ( IIa B), dual-chamber preferred. Beta-blockers could worsen it; carotid surgery is irrelevant.

Q4 Which finding contraindicates carotid sinus massage?

Answer B CSM should be avoided after TIA/stroke within 3 months, or with carotid bruits unless Doppler excludes significant stenosis ( III C). Age is not a contraindication — CSM is indicated in those > 40.

Q5 A 24-year-old woman reports palpitations and light-headedness when standing, for 8 months after a viral illness. Supine HR 72 bpm, BP 112/70; after 8 minutes standing HR 118 bpm, BP 110/72. The diagnosis is:

Answer C HR rise of 46 bpm within 10 min without BP fall and chronic (> 3 months) symptoms = POTS, commonly post-viral in young women. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a resting tachycardia.

Q6 A 70-year-old man with Parkinson's disease faints on standing. BP falls from 150/85 supine to 102/68 mmHg at 2 min with HR 70 → 74 bpm. This pattern indicates:

Answer B SBP fall of 48 mmHg within 3 min meets OH criteria; the almost absent HR response (ΔHR/ΔSBP < 0.5) indicates failed sympathetic efferents — neurogenic OH, typical of Parkinson's with autonomic failure. Supine hypertension often coexists.

Q7 A 45-year-old man has recurrent unexplained syncope (3 episodes in 2 years) with no high-risk features and a normal work-up. The next step per ESC 2018 is:

Answer B Recurrent infrequent syncope of uncertain origin, no high-risk criteria and a high chance of recurrence within battery life → early ILR ( I A). Holter is only useful if events are ≥ weekly; EPS has low yield with a normal ECG and heart.

Q8 A 52-year-old woman with recurrent vasovagal syncope has an ILR showing a 7-s sinus arrest during a typical faint. The best treatment is:

Answer C Age > 40 with a documented spontaneous symptomatic asystolic pause > 3 s → dual-chamber pacing (ESC IIa B; ISSUE-3). Ventricular-only pacing is inferior; beta-blockers are Class III.

Q9 Which ECG finding is diagnostic of arrhythmic syncope at initial evaluation (ESC 2018)?

Answer C Alternating LBBB and RBBB indicates trifascicular disease and is diagnostic ( I C). Sinus bradycardia counts only if < 40 bpm awake in an untrained person; Mobitz I in sleep and isolated RBBB are not diagnostic.

Q10 A 66-year-old with bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB), LVEF 55%, has unexplained syncope. EPS shows HV interval 78 ms. Management?

Answer B In syncope with bifascicular block, HV ≥ 70 ms (or infra-His block with pacing/drug challenge) is diagnostic and pacing is Class I . An ILR is the step when EPS is negative; an ICD is not indicated with normal LVEF.

22.1 The Pericardium & the IMPS Framework

The pericardium is a double-layered sac: a fibrous outer parietal layer and a serous visceral layer (epicardium). It normally contains 10–50 mL of plasma ultrafiltrate and is < 2 mm thick (CT/CMR upper normal ≈ 3–4 mm). Its three functions are examinable because each explains a disease: it limits acute cardiac dilatation (the steep pressure–volume curve behind tamponade), it couples the two ventricles (ventricular interdependence behind pulsus paradoxus and constriction), and it isolates the heart from intrathoracic pressure changes (lost in constriction → Kussmaul sign).

MECHANISM — THE PERICARDIAL PRESSURE–VOLUME CURVE

The curve is flat at first (reserve volume) and then almost vertical. Speed of accumulation matters more than volume : 150–200 mL of blood entering over minutes (free-wall rupture, perforation) can tamponade, whereas > 1–2 L accumulating over months (hypothyroidism, uraemia) may be well tolerated because the pericardium stretches.

The ESC 2025 concept: inflammatory myopericardial syndrome

The ESC 2025 guideline — the first to cover myocarditis and pericarditis together — introduced the umbrella term inflammatory myopericardial syndrome (IMPS). The pericardium and myocardium share aetiologies (viruses, autoimmunity, drugs, vaccines) and frequently overlap, so the clinical label reflects the predominant compartment: pericarditis, myopericarditis (pericarditis-predominant with myocardial involvement), perimyocarditis/myocarditis (myocarditis-predominant). A new companion term, inflammatory cardiomyopathy, designates chronic myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction and remodelling.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 (VS ESC 2015 PERICARDIAL DISEASES)
  • One guideline for myocarditis and pericarditis under the IMPS umbrella.
  • CMR evidence of pericardial inflammation (oedema/LGE) now counts toward the diagnosis of pericarditis.
  • IL-1 antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept) upgraded to a Class I option for recurrent pericarditis with raised CRP after failure of first-line therapy — ahead of prolonged corticosteroids.
  • Rigid exercise bans replaced by an initial restriction (about 1 month) followed by individualised return guided by symptoms, CRP and imaging.
  • Colchicine may be considered in pregnancy (IIb) — the old contraindication was removed.
  • Constriction: anti-inflammatory therapy for newly diagnosed constriction with active inflammation; pericardiectomy concentrated in expert centres.

Aetiology

In developed countries viral or idiopathic pericarditis accounts for 80–90% of cases in immunocompetent patients; "idiopathic" usually means viral with an unproven agent. In developing countries — Egypt's rural areas, sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia — tuberculosis is the leading cause of large effusion and constriction, especially with HIV.

22.2 Acute Pericarditis — Diagnosis & Triage

Acute pericarditis causes about 5% of emergency presentations with non-ischaemic chest pain and 0.1% of hospital admissions. Young and middle-aged men predominate. The pain is sharp, retrosternal or leftsided, pleuritic, relieved by sitting forward and worse lying supine; radiation to the trapezius ridge is highly specific because the phrenic nerve supplies the pericardium and traverses to the trapezius.

Key highlightsPericardium & IMPS

  • Normal pericardial fluid 10–50 mL; normal thickness < 2 mm (≤ 3–4 mm on CT/CMR).
  • Rate of accumulation, not volume, determines tamponade — 150–200 mL can kill if acute.
  • Viral/idiopathic = 80–90% in developed countries; TB dominates in endemic regions.
  • ESC 2025 unifies myocarditis and pericarditis as IMPS; the label follows the predominant compartment.
  • Incessant > 4–6 wk without remission; recurrent after a 4–6 wk symptom-free gap; chronic > 3 months.
  • Autoinflammatory disease (FMF, TRAPS) hides behind a proportion of "idiopathic" recurrent cases.
  • Classic criteria (ESC 2015: ≥ 2 of 4) Current framing (ESC 2025 / ACC 2025)
  • Pericarditic chest pain (~85–90%)
  • Pericardial friction rub (≤ 33%)
  • New widespread ST elevation or PR depression
  • (up to 60%)
  • New or worsening pericardial effusion (up to 60%)
  • Compatible clinical presentation (chest pain) plus ≥ 1
  • objective sign of pericardial inflammation:
  • rub · typical ECG · effusion · raised CRP · imaging
  • inflammation (CMR oedema/LGE, CT enhancement)
  • Supportive findings: raised CRP/ESR and WBC; pericardial inflammation on CT or CMR. Troponin rise indicates myocardial involvement (myopericarditis) rather than supporting pericarditis itself.
  • The ECG — four stages

First-line work-up

All patients: auscultation, ECG, transthoracic echo, chest X-ray, CRP (and/or ESR), full blood count, renal and liver function, and troponin (Class I). CT and/or CMR are second-level tests. Routine viral serology is not recommended. Targeted tests (ANA, TB testing, thyroid, cytology) follow clinical suspicion or high-risk features.

Major (independent) predictors Minor predictors

Any major or minor predictor → admit and investigate. No predictor → outpatient management with empiric antiinflammatories and review after 1 week.

EXAM TRAP

A patient with a pericardial rub, diffuse ST elevation and a troponin of several times normal has myopericarditis, not "pericarditis plus NSTEMI". In a young patient without risk factors, the next step is CMR (or coronary CT/angiography only if ACS remains plausible) — not thrombolysis.

Key highlightsAcute pericarditis — diagnosis

  • Diagnosis: compatible chest pain + ≥ 1 inflammatory sign (rub, ECG, effusion, CRP, imaging); classic ESC 2015 rule = ≥ 2 of 4.
  • Rub is heard in ≤ 33%; ECG changes and effusion in up to 60% each.
  • aVR shows ST depression and PR elevation — the mirror image of diffuse ST elevation/PR depression.
  • T inversion appears only after ST returns to baseline (unlike STEMI).
  • Major high-risk features: fever > 38 °C, subacute onset, effusion > 20 mm, tamponade, no response to NSAID in 1 week.
  • Minor: myopericarditis, immunosuppression, trauma, oral anticoagulation — any predictor → admission.
  • Troponin rise = myocardial involvement; CMR is the key second-level test.

22.3 Treatment of Acute Pericarditis

The goals are symptom relief and — above all — prevention of recurrence, which colchicine roughly halves . The backbone is a high-dose anti-inflammatory (aspirin or an NSAID) plus colchicine, with gastroprotection, activity restriction and CRP-guided tapering.

Drug therapy

Aspirin or NSAID plus colchicine as first-line therapy (colchicine for 3 months, weight-adjusted). I A CRP should be measured to guide treatment length and assess response. IIa C

Low-to-moderate dose corticosteroids when aspirin/NSAIDs + colchicine are contraindicated or have failed, after excluding infection (or when there is a specific indication, e.g. autoimmune disease). IIa C

Corticosteroids as first-line therapy. III C

Activity

CHANGED Restrict strenuous exercise initially (≈ 1 month), then individualised return once symptoms, CRP, ECG and imaging have normalised (ESC 2025; replaces the fixed 3-month ban for athletes of 2015).

— —

Classes shown are those of ESC 2015 carried into ESC 2025 unless marked changed; the ESC 2025 first-line combination is confirmed as Class I A.

MECHANISM — WHY COLCHICINE WORKS AND STEROIDS BACK FIRE

Colchicine binds tubulin, blocking neutrophil migration and assembly of the NLRP3 inflammasome that releases interleukin-1β — the central cytokine of recurrent pericarditis (autoinflammatory, innate-immune).

Corticosteroids suppress symptoms rapidly but favour viral replication and prolong the disease; relapse on tapering creates steroid dependence. Hence the board mantra: steroids are second-line, low dose, slow taper.

Corticosteroids — how to use them if you must

Prednisone 0.2–0.5 mg/kg/day — not 1 mg/kg (higher doses carry more relapses and side-effects). Keep the starting dose until symptoms resolve and CRP normalises, then taper slowly; the critical threshold is 10–15 mg/day, below which decrements of only 1.0–2.5 mg every 2–6 weeks are used. Always add colchicine; bone protection (calcium, vitamin D; bisphosphonate for prolonged use in atrisk patients). Exclude TB, bacterial and neoplastic causes first.

BOARD PEARL

Treatment is tapered only when symptoms have resolved and CRP has normalised, one drug class at a time — colchicine is the last to stop. Colchicine is contraindicated in severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30); watch strong CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein inhibitors (clarithromycin, ciclosporin, verapamil). The main side-effect is diarrhoea (~5–10%).

Key highlightsTreatment of acute pericarditis

  • First-line: aspirin 750–1000 mg tds or ibuprofen 600 mg tds for 1–2 wk + colchicine (Class I A).
  • Colchicine 0.5 mg bd (≥ 70 kg) or od (< 70 kg), no loading, for 3 months; 6 months for recurrence.
  • Aspirin is the anti-inflammatory of choice after MI (NSAIDs impair healing).
  • Steroids only second-line: prednisone 0.2–0.5 mg/kg/day, slow taper below 15 mg; never first-line (Class III).
  • Taper only after symptom resolution and normal CRP; colchicine stopped last.
  • ESC 2025: initial ≈ 1-month exercise restriction, then individualised return.

22.4 Incessant, Recurrent & Chronic Pericarditis

Recurrence follows 15–30% of first episodes treated without colchicine and up to 50% after a first recurrence. Most recurrences are autoinflammatory — innate immunity with IL-1β overproduction — rather than persistent infection. Risk factors: inadequate first treatment (short course, no colchicine), corticosteroid use, female sex, raised CRP, and failure of initial NSAID.

DEFINITION — THE RECURRENT-PERICARDITIS PHENOTYPES

Inflammatory phenotype: fever, raised CRP, pleuropericardial involvement, CMR LGE — high response to IL-1 blockade.

Non-inflammatory phenotype: pain with normal CRP and no imaging inflammation — reconsider the diagnosis (musculoskeletal, functional pain) before escalating.

The step-up ladder

IIb C

IL-1 row: new ESC 2025 recommendation (in ESC 2015, anakinra was a IIb C option). Remaining rows as ESC 2015, retained in 2025.

BOARD PEARL — I L-1 BLOCKERS

IL-1 blockers work spectacularly while given (symptoms and CRP settle within days) but recurrences return on abrupt withdrawal ; they are therefore continued for months (often ≥ 12–18 months) and tapered slowly. They are the preferred escape from steroid dependence. In recurrent "idiopathic" disease with periodic fevers or a family history, consider genetic testing for autoinflammatory syndromes (MEFV for FMF, TNFRSF1A for TRAPS).

DON'T CONFUSE

Recurrence requires a symptom-free interval of 4–6 weeks. Symptoms that never fully resolved, or flare during tapering, represent incessant pericarditis — usually under-treatment or premature tapering, managed by restarting the previously effective dose. Prognosis. Recurrent idiopathic pericarditis is disabling but rarely dangerous: tamponade is uncommon and constriction is rare (< 1%) after viral/idiopathic pericarditis, compared with 2–5% after immune-mediated, post-traumatic or neoplastic disease, and 20–30% after bacterial (especially purulent and TB) pericarditis.

22.5 Myopericarditis & Post-Cardiac Injury Syndromes

Myopericarditis

Myopericarditis is pericarditis with myocardial involvement — raised troponin, with normal or only mildly reduced LV function. When myocardial involvement dominates (new regional or global LV dysfunction) the label is perimyocarditis/myocarditis and management follows the myocarditis pathway. Myocardial involvement is found in up to 15% of pericarditis cases; the prognosis of pericarditis-predominant disease is good. Investigate: exclude ACS when clinically plausible (coronary angiography/CT); CMR confirms myocardial oedema/LGE (updated Lake Louise: one T2-based + one T1-based criterion).

Treat: hospitalise for monitoring; aspirin/NSAID at the lowest effective dose (animal data suggest high doses may worsen myocarditis) + colchicine; paracetamol as analgesic alternative.

Exercise: longer restriction than for isolated pericarditis; return individualised after normalisation of biomarkers, ECG, Holter, echo ± CMR (classically 6 months for competitive athletes with myocarditis). Post-cardiac injury syndromes (PCIS)

PCIS is an umbrella for autoimmune pericarditis ± effusion following injury to the pericardium or myocardium: post-MI pericarditis, post-pericardiotomy syndrome (PPS), and post-traumatic pericarditis (iatrogenic: PCI perforation, lead insertion, ablation, TAVI). The diagnosis follows the same criteria as acute pericarditis after an injury, with a latency of days to weeks.

Key highlightsRecurrent pericarditis

  • Recurrence rate 15–30% after a first episode without colchicine, up to 50% after a first recurrence.
  • Biggest modifiable risk factors: no colchicine and prior corticosteroid use.
  • Colchicine for ≥ 6 months in recurrence (Class I A).
  • ESC 2025: IL-1 antagonists are Class I for recurrent pericarditis with raised CRP after first-line failure (steroiddependent, colchicine-resistant).
  • Anakinra 1–2 mg/kg/day (max 100 mg) daily; rilonacept 320 mg load then 160 mg weekly.
  • Relapse on abrupt IL-1 withdrawal → slow taper over months.
  • Constriction risk: < 1% viral/idiopathic, 2–5% immune/neoplastic, 20–30% bacterial.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Anti-inflammatory therapy for PCIS to hasten remission and reduce recurrences. I B
  • Aspirin is the first choice for post-MI pericarditis and in patients already on antiplatelet therapy. I C Colchicine added to aspirin/NSAID for treatment of PCIS, as for acute pericarditis. IIa B Weight-adjusted colchicine for 1 month after cardiac surgery to prevent PPS (if no contraindication and tolerated).
  • IIa A
  • Careful follow-up for possible evolution to constriction, with echo every 6–12 months according to features.
  • IIa C
  • ESC 2015 classes, retained in ESC 2025. COPPS trial: peri-operative colchicine ↓ PPS; COPPS-2: less benefit, more GI side-effects.
EXAM TRAP

Post-operative pericardial effusion ≠ PPS. Effusions are seen in most patients after cardiac surgery and are usually benign; late post-operative tamponade (often loculated, posterior, compressing the atria) may lack classic signs — have a low threshold for TOE or CT in an unwell patient after surgery. NSAIDs do not help asymptomatic post-operative effusions without inflammation (POPE-2 with colchicine was also negative).

22.6 Pericardial Effusion & Cardiac Tamponade

Any condition that inflames the pericardium or impairs lymphatic/venous drainage can cause an effusion. Approximately 50–60% of effusions are related to a known disease (cancer, hypothyroidism, renal failure, surgery, connective tissue disease). Isolated large effusions without inflammation are commonly idiopathic but can be the first sign of cancer or TB.

Key highlightsMyopericarditis & PCIS

  • Myopericarditis = pericarditis + troponin rise with preserved/mildly reduced LV function; good prognosis.
  • Exclude ACS when plausible; CMR confirms myocardial inflammation.
  • Lower NSAID doses + colchicine; longer exercise restriction than pure pericarditis.
  • Early post-MI pericarditis at 1–3 days; Dressler at 1–6 weeks — both mean larger infarcts, now rare with reperfusion.
  • Aspirin is preferred post-MI; avoid NSAIDs and steroids early after MI.
  • Colchicine for 1 month to prevent PPS after cardiac surgery: IIa A (COPPS).
  • Post-MI effusion > 10 mm — think subacute free-wall rupture.
  • Basis Categories
  • Composition Transudate · Exudate · Blood · Pus · Chyle · Air (rare)
CLINICAL APPROACH — TRIAGE OF AN EFFUSION (ESC)

Tamponade, or suspected bacterial or neoplastic aetiology → pericardiocentesis/drainage (Class I). Raised inflammatory markers → treat as pericarditis (aspirin/NSAID + colchicine).

Known associated disease (hypothyroidism, renal failure, cancer, CTD) → treat the disease. None of the above: large (> 20 mm) chronic (> 3 months) idiopathic effusion → consider drainage (about a third progress to tamponade unpredictably); mild/moderate → follow-up.

Follow-up: mild idiopathic — no routine echo; moderate — echo every 6 months; large — every 3–6 months.

Tamponade — physiology

Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening, slow or rapid compression of the heart due to accumulation of fluid, pus, blood, clot or gas. When intrapericardial pressure exceeds chamber diastolic pressure, filling falls; all diastolic pressures rise and equalise at about the level of pericardial pressure (typically 15–20 mmHg). Because total cardiac volume is fixed, venous return occurs only when blood leaves the heart — during ventricular systole — hence the preserved x descent and absent y descent.

MECHANISM — PULSUS PARADOXUS

Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure → RV filling rises. In a fixed pericardial space the septum bows left, LV filling falls and LV stroke volume drops. Result: an inspiratory fall in systolic BP > 10 mmHg. Pulsus may be absent when the LV cannot be squeezed by the septum or RV filling cannot vary: severe AR, large ASD, LV dysfunction with high LVEDP, positive-pressure ventilation, RV hypertrophy/severe PH, and localised (loculated) effusion. It also occurs outside tamponade — severe asthma/COPD, massive PE, RV infarction, obesity, hypovolaemic shock.

Echocardiographic

RA systolic collapse Earliest, sensitive; specific if collapse lasts > 1/3 of the cardiac cycle RV diastolic collapse More specific (~85–90%); may be absent with RVH or PH

IVC plethora Diameter > 21 mm with < 50% inspiratory collapse — very sensitive, poorly specific Respiratory flow variation Mitral E inspiratory fall > 25–30%; tricuspid E rise > 40–60% Septal shift Inspiratory leftward septal motion; swinging heart

EXAM TRAP — LOW-PRESSURE TAMPONADE

In hypovolaemia (dialysis, haemorrhage, overdiuresis) tamponade can occur with RA pressure of only 6–12 mmHg, a normal JVP and no pulsus. Echo shows chamber collapse. A fluid bolus may transiently help; diuretics and vasodilators are harmful (Class III) in any tamponade.

Urgent pericardiocentesis or cardiac surgery to treat tamponade. I C

Pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage for symptomatic moderate-to-large effusions not responsive to medical therapy, and for suspected unknown bacterial or neoplastic aetiology.

I C

Management of effusion should be targeted at the aetiology. I C

Aspirin/NSAID/colchicine and treatment of pericarditis when effusion is associated with systemic inflammation.

I C

Use of vasodilators and diuretics in the presence of tamponade. III C

ESC 2015 recommendations, retained in the ESC 2025 guideline. An ESC triage score (aetiology, clinical presentation, imaging) with a score ≥ 6 favours immediate drainage.

22.7 Pericardiocentesis & Surgical Drainage

Pericardiocentesis is performed under echo or fluoroscopic guidance (blind procedures only in extremis). With echo guidance, major complication rates are about 1–1.5%. The subxiphoid approach is traditional; echo often shows an apical or parasternal window closer to the fluid. A pigtail catheter is left for extended drainage until output falls below about 25–30 mL/day, which reduces recurrence.

Key highlightsEffusion & tamponade

  • Effusion size: mild < 10 mm, moderate 10–20 mm, large > 20 mm.
  • Drain for tamponade or suspected bacterial/neoplastic effusion (Class I).
  • Tamponade: absent y descent, pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg, electrical alternans.
  • RA collapse = sensitive; RV diastolic collapse = specific; IVC plethora = most sensitive, least specific.
  • Mitral inflow variation > 25–30%, tricuspid > 40–60%.
  • Pulsus absent in AR, ASD, high LVEDP, IPPV, RVH, loculated effusion.
  • Diuretics/vasodilators in tamponade: Class III.
CONTRAINDICATIONS
  • Absolute: aortic dissection with
  • haemopericardium (go to surgery).
  • Relative: uncorrected coagulopathy,
  • anticoagulation, platelets < 50 × 10⁹/L, small,
  • posterior or loculated effusions.
  • Myocardial rupture and traumatic
  • haemopericardium → surgery.
WHEN TO CHOOSE SURGERY (WINDOW/
PERICARDIECTOMY)
  • Purulent effusion with adhesions/loculation
  • Recurrent effusion after drainage
  • (malignant)
  • Loculated or posterior effusion; clotted
  • haemopericardium
  • Need for pericardial biopsy

Pericardial fluid analysis

Key highlightsDrainage

  • Echo- or fluoroscopy-guided pericardiocentesis; complication rate ≈ 1–1.5%.
  • Leave a drain until output < 25–30 mL/day to reduce recurrence.
  • Aortic dissection with haemopericardium = surgery, not needle (controlled aspiration only to temporise if surgery unavailable).
  • Surgery for purulent/loculated/recurrent effusions, clot, trauma, myocardial rupture.
  • ADA > 40 U/L and unstimulated IFN-γ point to TB.
  • Haemodynamics — the three principles
  • Early rapid filling then abrupt halt: filling is unimpeded in early diastole (high atrial pressure, rapid y descent) and stops when the heart hits the rigid shell → dip-and-plateau ("square-root") ventricular pressure and a pericardial knock.
  • Dissociation of intrathoracic and intracardiac pressures: inspiration lowers pulmonary venous pressure but not LV diastolic pressure (shielded by the shell) → the pulmonary vein–LV gradient falls → less LV filling on inspiration.
  • Exaggerated ventricular interdependence: fixed total volume — whatever the LV loses, the RV gains → septal shift and discordant LV/RV systolic pressures.
  • Figure 22.1 · Simultaneous LV and RV pressures. In constriction the peaks move in opposite directions with respiration (systolic area index > 1.1); in restriction they move together.
  • Clinical features
  • Predominantly right-sided failure with clear lungs: raised JVP with prominent y descent (Friedreich sign), Kussmaul sign (JVP fails to fall or rises on inspiration), hepatomegaly, ascites out of proportion to oedema (may mimic cirrhosis — a classic diagnostic trap), pericardial knock (early diastolic, earlier and higher-pitched than S3), AF in about a third. Pulsus paradoxus is present in only about a third. CXR calcification (lateral view) in a minority.

22.8 Constrictive Pericarditis & Its Variants

Constrictive pericarditis is impaired diastolic filling caused by a thickened, fibrotic and often calcified — but sometimes normal-thickness (~18–20%) — pericardium. It can follow virtually any pericarditis. In developed countries the leading causes are idiopathic/viral, post-cardiac surgery and mediastinal radiation; in developing countries tuberculosis dominates.

Inspiratory diastolic reversal

Atria / wall thickness Mild atrial enlargement; normal walls Biatrial enlargement; thick walls (infiltration) Pulmonary artery pressure Usually PASP < 50 mmHg Often > 50–60 mmHg

  • Catheterisation
  • LVEDP vs RVEDP Equal (within ≤ 5 mmHg) LVEDP exceeds RVEDP by > 5 mmHg
  • RVEDP/RVSP ratio > 1/3 < 1/3
  • LV/RV systolic pressures
  • in inspiration
  • Discordant (systolic area index > 1.1) Concordant

  • oedema if active inflammation; real-time

BOARD PEARL — THE MAY O ECHO CRITERIA

Respiration-related ventricular septal shift + medial e′ ≥ 9 cm/s + hepatic-vein expiratory diastolic reversal ratio ≥ 0.79 . Septal shift plus either of the others gives the best balance of sensitivity (~87%) and specificity (~91%). The preserved e′ reflects normal myocardial relaxation — the defect is outside the muscle; the lateral annulus is tethered by the scarred pericardium, so medial exceeds lateral e′ (annulus reversus).

EXAM TRAP

Equalisation of diastolic pressures and dip-and-plateau are not specific — they occur in restriction too. The single most discriminating invasive finding is dynamic respiratory discordance of LV and RV systolic pressures (systolic area index > 1.1: sensitivity ~97%).

Variants

22.9 Specific Aetiologies

Tuberculous pericarditis

The commonest cause of pericardial disease in TB-endemic regions and in HIV. Presents subacutely with fever, night sweats, weight loss and a large effusion; untreated mortality is high and constriction develops in ~20–30%. Diagnosis: pericardial fluid ADA > 40 U/L, unstimulated IFN-γ, Xpert MTB/RIF, culture; pericardial biopsy (granulomas). In endemic areas, an exudative lymphocytic effusion with no other cause is treated empirically.

Key highlightsConstriction

  • Causes: idiopathic/viral, post-surgery, radiation (developed); TB (developing).
  • Pericardium is of normal thickness in up to ~20% of surgically proven constriction.
  • Signs: Kussmaul, steep y descent, pericardial knock, ascites > oedema.
  • Echo: septal bounce, mitral E variation > 25%, medial e′ ≥ 9 cm/s, annulus reversus, expiratory hepatic-vein reversal.
  • Cath: LVEDP ≈ RVEDP (≤ 5 mmHg), RVEDP/RVSP > 1/3, PASP < 50, discordant systolic pressures.
  • BNP low in constriction, high in restriction.
  • Transient constriction: treat inflammation for 2–3 months before surgery.
  • Effusive-constrictive: RA pressure stays high (fails to fall 50% or below 10 mmHg) after drainage.
  • Pericardiectomy (Class I) mortality 6–12%; worst after radiation.
  • Purulent (bacterial) pericarditis
  • Rare but lethal (mortality ≈ 40% even with treatment; near 100% untreated). Staphylococci, streptococci, pneumococci, Gram-negatives and anaerobes; spread from pneumonia/empyema, endocarditis, surgery or bacteraemia. Management: urgent pericardiocentesis for diagnosis (Class I), IV antibiotics, drainage with rinsing via subxiphoid pericardiostomy (IIa), intrapericardial thrombolysis for loculation (IIa), and pericardiectomy for dense adhesions, loculation, recurrent tamponade or progression to constriction (IIa).
  • Neoplastic pericardial disease
  • Secondary tumours are ≈ 40× more common than primary (mesothelioma, sarcoma). Lung and breast cancer, lymphoma and leukaemia, melanoma account for most. Up to two-thirds of effusions in cancer patients are, however, non-malignant (radiation, drugs, infection). Cytology confirms; biopsy if needed.

Systemic antineoplastic treatment in confirmed cases. I B

Extended pericardial drainage in suspected or definite neoplastic effusion to prevent recurrence. I B Intrapericardial cytostatic/sclerosing agents — cisplatin for lung cancer, thiotepa for breast cancer. IIa B Radiotherapy for radiosensitive tumours (lymphoma, leukaemia). IIa B

Surgical pericardiotomy (window) when pericardiocentesis cannot be performed; percutaneous balloon pericardiotomy to prevent recurrence.

IIb B

BOARD PEARL — IMMUNE CHECKPOINT INHIBITORS

ICI therapy (anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4) can cause pericarditis, effusion and tamponade — sometimes with myocarditis and myositis ("triple M" overlap). Treat with high-dose corticosteroids and withhold the ICI; this is one of the few settings where steroids are first-line.

Uraemic and dialysis-related pericarditis

Radiation-induced pericardial disease

After mediastinal radiotherapy (Hodgkin lymphoma, breast, lung, oesophagus). Acute pericarditis during or soon after treatment (now rare); delayed pericarditis/effusion months later; constriction up to 15–20 years later. Risk rises with dose (> 30 Gy) and field. Pericardiectomy outcomes are the worst of all aetiologies because of concurrent myocardial fibrosis, valve disease and coronary disease — assess all three before surgery.

Other situations

Key highlightsSpecific aetiologies

  • TB: ADA > 40 U/L; treat 6 months; pericardiectomy if no improvement at 4–8 weeks; steroids only if HIVnegative (IIb).
  • Purulent: mortality ≈ 40% despite treatment — urgent drainage, IV antibiotics, rinsing/fibrinolysis, early surgery.
  • Malignant: lung, breast, lymphoma; extended drainage (Class I B); cisplatin (lung) / thiotepa (breast) intrapericardially.
  • Uraemic vs dialysis pericarditis separated at 8 weeks of dialysis; ECG often without ST elevation; treat with dialysis.
  • Colchicine is contraindicated in severe CKD.
  • Radiation constriction can appear 15–20 years later; worst pericardiectomy outcome.
  • Dissection with haemopericardium: surgery, never routine pericardiocentesis.
  • Pregnancy: stop NSAIDs at 20 weeks; colchicine now IIb (ESC 2025).

22.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 32-year-old man (weight 82 kg) has 3 days of pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward. ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; CRP is 48 mg/L, troponin normal, and echo shows a 6-mm effusion. He is afebrile. What is the most appropriate management?

Answer C Low-risk acute pericarditis: outpatient NSAID + colchicine. At ≥ 70 kg colchicine is 0.5 mg twice daily for 3 months (Class I A). One month is too short; steroids are not first-line (Class III); colchicine alone is inadequate.

Q2 A 45-year-old woman has her third episode of pericarditis in 14 months. She relapsed each time prednisone was reduced below 10 mg/day despite ibuprofen and colchicine. CRP is 62 mg/L; CMR shows pericardial LGE. According to ESC 2025, the next best step is:

Answer A Recurrent pericarditis with raised CRP, steroid dependence and imaging inflammation — the ESC 2025 Class I indication for IL-1 blockade (steroid-sparing). Higher steroid doses worsen recurrence; pericardiectomy is a last resort; colchicine should be continued.

Q3 Which of the following is a major predictor of poor prognosis in acute pericarditis requiring hospital admission?

Answer D Large effusion (> 20 mm) is a major predictor, as are fever > 38 °C, subacute onset, tamponade and NSAID failure. Troponin rise, anticoagulation, immunosuppression and trauma are minor predictors.

Q4 A patient with metastatic lung cancer is hypotensive with a large circumferential effusion. Which echo finding is the most specific for tamponade?

Answer E RV diastolic collapse is the most specific sign. IVC plethora is the most sensitive but least specific; brief RA collapse is early and sensitive (specific only if > 1/3 of the cycle); effusion size alone does not define tamponade.

Q5 Pulsus paradoxus would be most likely to be absent in tamponade in a patient with:

Answer B In severe AR, the LV fills from the aorta regardless of respiration, abolishing pulsus. Other causes of absent pulsus: ASD, high LVEDP, positive-pressure ventilation, RVH, loculated effusion.

Q6 A 60-year-old with previous CABG has ascites, JVP rising on inspiration and a high-pitched early diastolic sound. NT-proBNP is 180 pg/mL. Echo: septal bounce, mitral E variation 32%, medial e′ 12 cm/s greater than lateral e′. Most likely diagnosis?

Answer D Post-CABG right-heart failure with Kussmaul sign, knock, low BNP, septal bounce, mitral variation > 25% and preserved medial e′ > lateral (annulus reversus) = constriction. Amyloid gives high BNP and low e′.

Q7 At catheterisation, which finding best distinguishes constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy?

Answer A Dynamic ventricular discordance (systolic area index > 1.1) reflects enhanced interdependence — specific to constriction. Dip-and-plateau, equalisation and steep y descent occur in both.

Q8 A patient with tamponade undergoes pericardiocentesis; intrapericardial pressure falls from 16 to 1 mmHg, but RA pressure remains 17 mmHg with Kussmaul sign. The diagnosis is:

Answer B Failure of RA pressure to fall by 50% or below 10 mmHg after the intrapericardial pressure is normalised defines effusive-constrictive pericarditis (visceral constriction).

Q9 A 28-year-old HIV-negative man from a TB-endemic area has a large lymphocytic exudative effusion; ADA 78 U/ L. After drainage and 6 weeks of anti-TB therapy he develops worsening constrictive physiology. Next step?

Answer E ESC: pericardiectomy if the patient fails to improve or deteriorates after 4–8 weeks of anti-TB therapy (Class I C). Steroids (IIb, HIV-negative) do not reverse established constriction.

Q10 A haemodialysis patient (on dialysis for 2 years) has pleuritic chest pain and a moderate effusion without tamponade. ECG shows no ST elevation. Most appropriate first step?

Answer C Dialysis-associated pericarditis (after ≥ 8 weeks of dialysis) is treated by intensifying dialysis. Colchicine is contraindicated in severe renal impairment; drainage is reserved for tamponade or failure of dialysis.

23.1 Epidemiology, Risk Factors & Pathophysiology

Venous thromboembolism (VTE) — deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) — is the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome after MI and stroke. Annual incidence of PE is about 39–115 per 100 000; incidence rises roughly 8-fold between the fifth decade and age ≥ 80. About half of patients with proximal DVT have (often silent) PE, and ~70% of PE patients have DVT when searched for.

Moderate (OR 2–9) Arthroscopic knee surgery · cancer (highest in metastatic disease) · chemotherapy · central venous lines · oral contraceptives, HRT, IVF · post-partum period · infection (pneumonia, UTI, HIV) · IBD, autoimmune disease · paralytic stroke · thrombophilia · superficial vein thrombosis · ESAs · transfusion

Weak (OR < 2) Bed rest > 3 days · prolonged travel · obesity · age · pregnancy · varicose veins · laparoscopic surgery · diabetes · hypertension

DEFINITION — PROVOKED VS UNPROVOKED (THE DURATION DECISION)

Major transient/reversible factor: surgery with general anaesthesia > 30 min, bed-bound in hospital ≥ 3 days, trauma with fracture — within 3 months. Recurrence risk after stopping: < 3%/year.

Minor transient: minor surgery, oestrogen therapy, pregnancy/puerperium, long-haul flight, hospitalisation < 3 days — recurrence 3–8%/year.

Persistent: active cancer, IBD, autoimmune disease; no identifiable risk factor ("unprovoked") — recurrence > 8%/year.

ESC 2019 replaced the term "unprovoked" with this graded description of the risk factor.

Pathophysiology — why patients die of RV failure

MECHANISM — THE RV DEATH SPIRAL

Obstruction plus vasoconstriction (thromboxane A2, serotonin) raise PVR → the thin-walled RV dilates → ↑ wall tension, ↑ O₂ demand, and leftward septal shift reduces LV filling (interdependence) → ↓ cardiac output and systemic BP → ↓ RV coronary perfusion → RV ischaemia, further failure and obstructive shock. A previously normal RV cannot generate mPAP > 40 mmHg (systolic ≈ 60 mmHg) acutely — a higher PASP suggests chronic disease (CTEPH).

Hypoxaemia results from V/Q mismatch, low mixed venous O₂ (low output) and, in ~a third, right-to-left shunting through a PFO — which also explains paradoxical embolism. Small distal emboli cause pulmonary infarction (pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, pleural effusion) despite little haemodynamic effect.

23.2 Clinical Probability & D-dimer

Symptoms are non-specific: dyspnoea (commonest), pleuritic pain, cough, haemoptysis, syncope (suggests a large clot burden), tachycardia, tachypnoea. The diagnostic strategy always starts with pre-test probability — it decides whether D-dimer is useful and how to interpret imaging.

D-dimer — a rule-out test

D-dimer has a high negative predictive value (sensitivity of ELISA assays > 95%) but poor specificity: it rises with age, cancer, pregnancy, infection, inflammation and hospitalisation. Use it only in non-highprobability patients; never in high probability (Class III A), where a negative result does not safely exclude PE.

30%; ESC IIa B

Key highlightsEpidemiology & pathophysiology

  • VTE = third commonest acute CV syndrome; incidence rises ≈ 8-fold with age.
  • Strong risk factors (OR > 10): fracture, arthroplasty, major trauma, spinal injury, previous VTE, recent HF/AF/MI admission.
  • Major transient factor → recurrence < 3%/yr; no identifiable factor → > 8%/yr.
  • Death in PE is from acute RV failure and obstructive shock.
  • A naïve RV cannot generate mPAP > 40 mmHg; higher values imply chronic disease (CTEPH).
  • Paradoxical embolism and severe hypoxaemia occur through a PFO.

A 68-year-old with a Wells score of 7 (PE likely) and a D-dimer of 450 µg/L does not have PE excluded — high/likely probability goes straight to CTPA. Conversely, a 75-year-old with PE-unlikely score and D-dimer 700 µg/L is excluded by the age-adjusted cut-off (750).

23.3 Imaging & Diagnostic Algorithms

Accept VTE if CUS shows proximal DVT in a patient with suspected PE. I A

NEW Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off (age × 10 µg/L above 50 years) as an alternative to the fixed cutoff.

IIa B

NEW D-dimer cut-offs adapted to clinical probability (YEARS) as an alternative to the fixed cut-off. IIa B D-dimer measurement in patients with high clinical probability. III A

MRA to rule out PE. III A

BOARD PEARL

In a shocked patient too unstable for CT, unequivocal RV dysfunction on bedside echo is enough to give thrombolysis ; a normal RV virtually excludes PE as the cause of shock. In a stable patient echo is not a diagnostic test for PE.

Key highlightsImaging

  • CTPA is the imaging test of choice; a normal CTPA excludes PE in non-high probability (I A).
  • Normal perfusion scan excludes PE (I A); V/Q preferred in pregnancy, CKD, contrast allergy.
  • Proximal DVT on CUS in suspected PE = treat without further imaging (I A).
  • Echo signs: RV/LV > 1.0, TAPSE < 16 mm, McConnell, 60/60.
  • Unstable + RV dysfunction + CT not feasible → reperfuse; unstable + normal RV → look elsewhere.
  • Commonest ECG finding: sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 specific but insensitive.

23.4 Severity Assessment & Risk Stratification

Stratification decides the setting (home vs ward vs ICU) and the need for reperfusion. It proceeds in two steps: haemodynamic status first, then — in stable patients — clinical scores, RV imaging and biomarkers.

EXAM TRAP

RV dilatation on CT (RV/LV ≥ 1.0) with a positive troponin but normal BP = intermediate-high, not high risk. Such patients get anticoagulation and monitoring; thrombolysis is reserved for haemodynamic deterioration (PEITHO: tenecteplase prevented decompensation but caused more major bleeding (11.5% vs 2.4%) and stroke (2.4% vs 0.2%), with no mortality benefit).

The AHA/ACC 2026 clinical categories

The first ACC/AHA practice guideline on acute PE (2026, ten societies) retired "massive/submassive" and introduced PE clinical categories A–E, designed to separate patients who are merely "sick-looking" from those in incipient or overt cardiopulmonary failure.

C3 Abnormal RV and ≥ 1 abnormal biomarker

D1 Incipient cardiopulmonary failure Transient hypotension (SBP < 90 or fall > 40 mmHg lasting < 15 min or fluid-responsive), e.g. syncope

  • E2 Refractory shock or cardiac arrest ("catastrophic PE")

23.5 Initial Anticoagulation & Supportive Care

Anticoagulation prevents clot propagation and early recurrence; it does not lyse the embolus (endogenous fibrinolysis does). For most stable patients a DOAC is the first choice. Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is reserved for situations where reperfusion may be needed, severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min) or severe obesity — because it is short-acting and reversible.

Haemodynamic and respiratory support in high-risk PE

Fluids cautiously — a small challenge (≤ 500 mL) only if CVP is low; volume loading of a dilated RV worsens septal shift.

Vasopressor: noradrenaline to restore systemic pressure and RV coronary perfusion; dobutamine for low output (IIa C).

Oxygen if SaO₂ < 90%; high-flow nasal O₂ preferred. Avoid intubation if possible — induction agents cause hypotension and positive pressure reduces venous return (AHA/ACC 2026: deep sedation/ ventilation harmful unless necessary).

VA-ECMO for refractory collapse or arrest, combined with surgical embolectomy or catheter therapy (ESC IIb C).

Key highlightsInitial anticoagulation

  • Start anticoagulation while awaiting imaging in high/intermediate probability (I C).
  • DOAC over VKA (I A); LMWH/fondaparinux over UFH (I A).
  • Apixaban 10 mg bd × 7 d; rivaroxaban 15 mg bd × 21 d — no heparin lead-in needed.
  • Edoxaban and dabigatran require ≥ 5 days of parenteral heparin first.
  • UFH for high-risk PE, planned reperfusion, CrCl < 30: 80 U/kg then 18 U/kg/h.
  • DOACs contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation, APS, severe CKD (III C).
  • In shock: noradrenaline, cautious fluids (≤ 500 mL), avoid intubation, ECMO if refractory.
