23.6 Reperfusion Therapy & PERT

Systemic thrombolysis

Thrombolysis restores pulmonary perfusion faster than heparin, with greatest benefit when given within 48 h of symptom onset (still useful up to 6–14 days). In high-risk PE it reduces death and recurrence; ≈ 92% of patients show clinical and echo improvement within 36 h. The cost is major bleeding (≈ 10%) and intracranial haemorrhage (≈ 1.5–2%).

WHAT'S NEW IN THE AHA/ACC 2026 PE GUIDELINE

Categories A–E replace massive/submassive; lactate measurement is Class 1 in categories C–E. PERT assessment Class 1 for C–E; clinical contact ≈ 1 week after discharge and review within 3 months (Class 1).

Systemic lysis loses primacy in shock — lysis, CDT, mechanical thrombectomy and surgery each 2a in category E.

LMWH preferred over UFH in hospitalised patients; DOAC over VKA.

After the initial phase, stop at 3–6 months only for a first PE with a resolved transient factor; otherwise continue with reduced-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban.

Key highlightsReperfusion

  • Systemic lysis for high-risk PE (ESC I B): alteplase 100 mg over 2 h; 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min in arrest.
  • Greatest benefit within 48 h; useful up to 6–14 days.
  • Absolute CI: haemorrhagic stroke ever, ischaemic stroke < 6 months, CNS tumour, major trauma/surgery < 3 weeks, bleeding diathesis, active bleeding.
  • Surgery (I C) or catheter therapy (IIa C) if lysis contraindicated or failed.
  • Rescue lysis for deterioration on anticoagulation (I B); routine lysis in intermediate risk — III B.
  • ECMO: IIb C with embolectomy/CDT.
  • AHA/ACC 2026: PERT Class 1 for C–E; all advanced therapies 2a in category E.

23.7 Duration of Anticoagulation

All patients receive at least 3 months of therapeutic anticoagulation (I A). The question at 3 months is whether the risk of recurrence off treatment exceeds the risk of bleeding on it — decided by the nature of the index risk factor.

IIa A

NEW First PE with a persistent risk factor other than APS, or with a minor transient/reversible factor: extended anticoagulation should be considered.

IIa C

NEW If extended anticoagulation is chosen (no cancer): reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg bd or rivaroxaban 10 mg od after 6 months of therapeutic anticoagulation.

IIa A

Aspirin or sulodexide for patients who refuse or cannot take any oral anticoagulant. IIb B Regular reassessment of tolerance, adherence, renal/hepatic function and bleeding risk on extended therapy.

I C

BOARD PEARL — THE EVIDENCE FOR REDUCED DOSE

AMPLIFY-EXT (apixaban 2.5 or 5 mg bd vs placebo) and EINSTEIN-CHOICE (rivaroxaban 10 or 20 mg vs aspirin) showed that the reduced dose prevents recurrence as well as the full dose, with bleeding similar to placebo/aspirin. Reduced doses are for extended prevention after ≥ 6 months — never for the initial treatment phase, and not validated in cancer.

DON'T CONFUSE — THROMBOPHILIA TESTING

Inherited thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S, antithrombin deficiency) rarely changes management and is not tested routinely. The exception that matters is APS — test antiphospholipid antibodies when it would change the drug (young patient, unprovoked VTE, arterial events, pregnancy morbidity), because it mandates warfarin.

Key highlightsDuration

  • Minimum 3 months for all (I A).
  • Major transient factor → stop at 3 months (I B).
  • Recurrent VTE (not major transient) → indefinite (I B); APS → indefinite VKA (I B).
  • No identifiable risk factor → extended should be considered (IIa A).
  • Extended: apixaban 2.5 mg bd or rivaroxaban 10 mg od after 6 months (ESC IIa A; AHA/ACC 2026 Class 1).
  • Aspirin only if all anticoagulants refused/not tolerated (IIb B).
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Incidental PE treated like symptomatic PE if segmental or more proximal, multiple subsegmental, or single subsegmental with DVT.
  • IIa B
  • Apixaban (Caravaggio, 2020) post-dates ESC 2019; ASH 2021 and ESC 2022 Cardio-Oncology guidance endorse apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban, preferring LMWH or apixaban with unresected luminal GI/GU cancer or high bleeding risk.
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • In APS — especially triple-positive (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I) — DOACs are contraindicated: TRAPS (rivaroxaban vs warfarin) was stopped early for excess arterial events (stroke, MI). Use warfarin (INR 2–3) indefinitely after a thrombotic event.
  • Pregnancy
  • PE is a leading cause of maternal death in high-income countries; risk is highest in the post-partum period (≈ 6 weeks). D-dimer rises through pregnancy but a negative result (pregnancy-adapted YEARS or Geneva) still helps.

23.8 Special Populations — Cancer, APS, Pregnancy

Cancer-associated VTE

Cancer increases VTE risk ≈ 4–7-fold (highest with pancreatic, gastric, brain, lung, haematological malignancy and metastatic disease); recurrence and bleeding are both higher. Trials: Hokusai-VTE Cancer (edoxaban non-inferior to dalteparin; more GI bleeding in GI cancer), SELECT-D (rivaroxaban; more bleeding in GI/GU cancer), Caravaggio (apixaban non-inferior without excess major bleeding).

NOACs during pregnancy or lactation. III C

Continue anticoagulation for at least 6 weeks post-partum and a minimum total of 3 months. Warfarin is avoided in pregnancy (embryopathy weeks 6–12, fetal bleeding) but is compatible with breastfeeding, as is LMWH.

Key highlightsSpecial populations

  • Cancer: LMWH for 6 months (IIa A) or edoxaban/rivaroxaban if no GI cancer (IIa B/C); apixaban (Caravaggio) also used.
  • Continue anticoagulation while cancer is active (IIa B).
  • APS (especially triple-positive): warfarin, not DOAC (TRAPS).
  • Pregnancy: fixed-dose LMWH on early-pregnancy weight (I B); no DOACs (III C); no neuraxial needle within 24 h of therapeutic LMWH.
  • Post-partum: continue ≥ 6 weeks, total ≥ 3 months.
  • Obesity: apixaban/rivaroxaban at any weight (ISTH 2021).
  • After PE — follow-up and CTEPH
  • Up to half of survivors report persistent dyspnoea or reduced exercise capacity ("post-PE syndrome").
  • CTEPH develops in ≈ 2–3% (range 0.1–9%) within 2 years; risk factors include recurrent/large PE, unprovoked PE, APS, splenectomy, ventriculo-atrial shunts, chronic inflammatory disease, and an echo PASP > 60 mmHg at presentation.

23.9 IVC Filters, DVT & Follow-up After PE

Inferior vena cava filters

Routine use of IVC filters (e.g., in addition to anticoagulation). III A

PREPIC showed filters reduce PE but increase DVT with no survival gain; PREPIC-2 found no benefit of adding a filter to anticoagulation. Use retrievable filters, start anticoagulation as soon as it is safe, and remove the filter. AHA/ACC 2026 also classifies routine filters in anticoagulated patients as Class 3: Harm.

Deep vein thrombosis — key management points

Iliofemoral DVT Catheter-directed lysis/thrombectomy only for selected patients — phlegmasia cerulea dolens (limb threat), severe symptoms; ATTRACT: no reduction in post-thrombotic

syndrome overall

Post-thrombotic syndrome Occurs in 20–50%; routine compression stockings not proven (SOX) — use for symptoms Superficial vein thrombosis Length ≥ 5 cm: fondaparinux 2.5 mg od for 45 days (CALISTO); within 3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction → treat as DVT

Upper-extremity DVT Often catheter- or device-related; anticoagulate ≥ 3 months; keep a functioning line; think thoracic outlet (Paget–Schroetter) in young athletes

EXAM TRAP

CT is less sensitive than V/Q for chronic thromboembolism. A normal V/Q scan effectively excludes CTEPH ; the screening test of choice in a breathless survivor is therefore V/Q scintigraphy, not CTPA. Echo PH probability comes first, but the diagnosis of CTEPH requires RHC after ≥ 3 months of effective anticoagulation (Chapter 24).

Key highlightsFilters, DVT & follow-up

  • IVC filter: absolute CI to anticoagulation or recurrence despite it (IIa C); routine use III A.
  • Prefer retrievable filters; remove once anticoagulation possible.
  • Distal DVT: anticoagulate 3 months or serial CUS.
  • Catheter therapy for DVT only for limb threat (phlegmasia) or severe iliofemoral disease (ATTRACT negative).
  • Superficial thrombosis ≥ 5 cm: fondaparinux 2.5 mg × 45 days.
  • Review all PE patients at 3–6 months (I B).
  • CTEPH ≈ 2–3%; V/Q scan is the screening test; refer mismatched defects to a CTEPH centre (I C).

23.10 Self-Assessment

Q1 A 78-year-old woman has pleuritic pain 5 days after a long-haul flight. HR 92, SaO₂ 96%, no leg signs, and an alternative diagnosis seems equally likely (Wells 0). D-dimer is 690 µg/L (assay cut-off 500). The next step is: CTPA

Answer E PE-unlikely probability; age-adjusted cut-off = 78 × 10 = 780 µg/L, so 690 is negative and PE is excluded (ESC IIa B). CTPA would be over-investigation.

Q2 A 55-year-old man is found hypotensive (BP 78/50) 2 days after hip surgery. CT is not immediately available. Bedside echo shows a dilated, hypokinetic RV with a D-shaped LV. What is the most appropriate step?

Answer A Suspected high-risk PE with unequivocal RV dysfunction and CT not feasible → treat as PE. Recent surgery is a relative issue weighed against imminent death; surgical or catheter reperfusion if lysis contraindicated/available. UFH alone is inadequate; filters do not treat shock.

Q3 A 62-year-old with confirmed PE: BP 124/78, HR 112, sPESI 1, RV/LV ratio 1.3 on CT, hs-troponin raised. The ESC risk class and management are:

Answer D No haemodynamic instability + sPESI ≥ 1 + both RV dysfunction and raised troponin = intermediate-high. Routine thrombolysis is III B (PEITHO); monitor and give rescue reperfusion if he deteriorates.

Q4 Under the AHA/ACC 2026 system, a normotensive PE patient with sPESI 2, RV dilatation and raised troponin, but lactate 3.4 mmol/L and falling urine output, is category:

Answer B Normotensive shock (lactate > 2, oliguria) defines D2 — incipient cardiopulmonary failure — regardless of the RV/ biomarker profile that would otherwise be C3.

Q5 Which is an absolute contraindication to systemic thrombolysis for PE?

Answer C Ischaemic stroke within 6 months is absolute. TIA within 6 months, oral anticoagulation, first post-partum week and SBP > 180 are relative.

Q6 A 40-year-old man has a first PE 3 weeks after a femoral fracture treated surgically. After 3 months of apixaban he is well. Best plan?

Answer A First PE with a major transient/reversible risk factor (surgery/fracture): stop after 3 months (I B) — recurrence < 3%/yr. Thrombophilia testing does not change this.

Q7 A 35-year-old woman with SLE has unprovoked PE; lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2GPI antibodies are all positive on repeat testing. Long-term therapy of choice?

Answer C Triple-positive APS: indefinite VKA (I B). DOACs are contraindicated (III C) — TRAPS showed excess arterial thrombosis with rivaroxaban.

Q8 A 29-year-old at 24 weeks' gestation has PE confirmed on low-dose CTPA; she is haemodynamically stable. Treatment?

Answer D Fixed-dose therapeutic LMWH (I B); continue ≥ 6 weeks post-partum and ≥ 3 months total. DOACs (III C) and warfarin are avoided in pregnancy.

Q9 A patient develops PE 5 days after craniotomy for glioma (active bleeding risk makes anticoagulation absolutely contraindicated). Best management?

Answer B Absolute contraindication to anticoagulation is an IIa C indication for an IVC filter; use a retrievable device, anticoagulate when safe and retrieve.

Q10 Four months after an unprovoked PE a patient on apixaban has persistent exertional dyspnoea. Echo: TR velocity 3.6 m/s. The best next investigation is:

Answer E Suspected CTEPH: V/Q scintigraphy is the screening test (a normal scan excludes it); mismatched defects → CTEPH centre for RHC and imaging (I C). CTPA can miss chronic disease.

What the board expects you to know

  • The five clinical groups and the diagnostic pathway: echo probability → V/Q → RHC → vasoreactivity testing.

24.1 Haemodynamic Definitions

Normal resting mPAP is 14 ± 3 mmHg (upper limit ≈ 20). The ESC/ERS 2022 guideline — adopting the 6th WSPH and confirmed by the 7th WSPH (2024) — lowered the PH threshold from ≥ 25 to > 20 mmHg and the PVR threshold from 3 to 2 WU . All definitions require right heart catheterisation (RHC).

1 (PAH),3,4,5
  • Isolated post-capillary
  • (IpcPH)
  • mPAP > 20; PAWP > 15; PVR ≤ 2 WU 2, 5
  • Combined pre- and postcapillary (CpcPH)mPAP > 20; PAWP > 15; PVR > 2 WU 2, 5
  • Unclassified PH mPAP > 20; PAWP ≤ 15; PVR ≤ 2 High-flow states (shunts, liver disease,
  • anaemia)
  • Exercise PH mPAP/CO slope > 3 mmHg/L/min
  • between rest and exercise

Early pulmonary vascular or left heart disease

Wood units (mmHg·min/L) are preferred; × 80 converts to dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. "Severe" pre-capillary PH in lung disease: PVR > 5 WU; "severe pre-capillary component" in CpcPH: PVR > 5 WU.

MECHANISM — OH M'S LAW OF THE LUNG

PVR = (mPAP − PAWP) / CO. The numerator is the transpulmonary gradient (TPG). mPAP can rise for three reasons: ↑ flow (shunt, anaemia — PVR normal), ↑ downstream pressure (left heart disease — high PAWP), or ↑ resistance (vascular remodelling). Only the third is "pulmonary vascular disease" and only it responds to pulmonary vasodilators. The diastolic pressure gradient (dPAP − PAWP) is no longer used to define CpcPH.

WHAT CHANGED IN 2022 (VS ESC/ERS 2015)
  • PH threshold: mPAP ≥ 25 → > 20 mmHg; PVR ≥ 3 → > 2 WU.
  • Exercise PH re-introduced (mPAP/CO slope > 3).
  • Risk assessment: 3 strata at diagnosis; 4 strata at follow-up (low, intermediate-low, intermediate-high, high).
  • Initial dual oral therapy (ERA + PDE5i) Class I for most PAH; monotherapy for PAH with
  • cardiopulmonary comorbidities.
  • Echo: TAPSE/sPAP ratio added as a marker of RV–PA coupling; group 1 now requires PVR > 2 WU.

Key highlightsDefinitions

  • PH = mPAP > 20 mmHg at rest (RHC).
  • Pre-capillary: PAWP ≤ 15 + PVR > 2 WU.
  • IpcPH: PAWP > 15, PVR ≤ 2; CpcPH: PAWP > 15, PVR > 2.
  • Exercise PH: mPAP/CO slope > 3 mmHg/L/min.
  • PVR = (mPAP − PAWP)/CO; 1 WU = 80 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵.
  • Severe PH in lung disease: PVR > 5 WU.
  • Definite association Possible association
  • Aminorex, fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine, benfluorex
  • (anorexigens)
  • Methamphetamines
  • Dasatinib (partly reversible on withdrawal)
  • Toxic rapeseed oil
  • Cocaine, amphetamines, phenylpropanolamine, Ltryptophan, St John's wort
  • Interferon α/β, alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide,
  • mitomycin C — PVOD)
  • Bosutinib, ponatinib, carfilzomib, leflunomide, directacting HCV antivirals, indirubin (Qing-Dai) Genetics of PAH
  • BMPR2 mutations (autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance ≈ 20%) are found in ≈ 75% of familial PAH and ~15–20% of sporadic IPAH; carriers present younger with more severe disease and are rarely vasoreactive. Other genes: ACVRL1/ENG (HHT), TBX4 (childhood PAH), SOX17 (CHD-associated), KCNK3, CAV1, SMAD9, GDF2; biallelic EIF2AK4 (autosomal recessive) causes heritable PVOD/PCH. Genetic counselling and testing are offered in IPAH, HPAH, DPAH and PVOD.

24.2 Clinical Classification

BOARD PEARL — FREQUENCY

Group 2 (left heart disease) is by far the commonest cause of PH , followed by group 3 (lung disease). PAH is rare (≈ 15–60 per million), with IPAH the commonest subtype, followed by CTD-PAH (systemic sclerosis foremost). In Egypt and endemic regions, schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, portal-hypertension–associated) is an important PAH cause.

Key highlightsClassification

  • Five groups: PAH, left heart, lung/hypoxia, PA obstruction (CTEPH), unclear/multifactorial.
  • Group 2 is the most common; PAH is rare (≈ 15–60/million).
  • Definite drug causes: anorexigens, methamphetamine, dasatinib, toxic rapeseed oil.
  • BMPR2 in ≈ 75% of HPAH, 15–20% of IPAH; EIF2AK4 → PVOD (recessive).
  • Sarcoidosis, haemolytic anaemia, myeloproliferative disease and CKD are group 5.
  • Schistosomiasis-PAH belongs to group 1.4.

  • > 1.0
  • Septal flattening (LV eccentricity
  • index > 1.1)
  • TAPSE/sPAP < 0.55 mm/mmHg
  • RVOT acceleration time < 105 ms and/
  • or mid-systolic notching
  • Early diastolic PR velocity > 2.2 m/s
  • PA diameter > aortic root or > 25 mm
  • IVC diameter > 21 mm with reduced

  • < 20% quiet)

24.3 Diagnosis — Echo Probability to RHC

Symptoms reflect RV dysfunction and are non-specific: exertional dyspnoea (commonest), fatigue, exertional chest pain (RV ischaemia) and exertional syncope (fixed output — a high-risk sign). Signs: loud P2, left parasternal heave, TR pansystolic murmur, Graham Steell murmur (PR), raised JVP with large v waves, hepatomegaly and oedema. Hoarseness (Ortner syndrome, left recurrent laryngeal compression by a dilated PA) and angina from left main compression by an aneurysmal PA are classic extras.

Echocardiographic probability of PH

EXAM TRAP

PH is never diagnosed by echo. The estimated sPAP (4 × TRV² + RAP) is unreliable (under- and over-estimates by > 10 mmHg in up to half of patients); the guideline therefore grades probability using the measured TR velocity, not the calculated pressure.

CMR RV volumes/EF, SVI (prognosis), shunts

Laboratory BNP/NT-proBNP, LFT, TFT, HIV, hepatitis, autoimmune screen (ANA, anti-centromere, Scl-70), antiphospholipid antibodies

Abdominal ultrasound Portal hypertension, cirrhosis

CPET Low peak VO₂, high VE/VCO₂ slope, low end-tidal CO₂

RHC Confirms PH and its type; vasoreactivity testing; mortality < 0.1% in expert centres Vasoreactivity testing

Performed at RHC in IPAH, HPAH and DPAH only — the patients who may respond to high-dose calciumchannel blockers (≈ 10% of IPAH are acute responders, and only about half of those remain long-term responders).

DEFINITION — POSITIVE ACUTE VASOREACTIVITY RESPONSE

Fall in mPAP by ≥ 10 mmHg to reach an absolute value ≤ 40 mmHg, with an increased or unchanged cardiac output. Agents: inhaled nitric oxide (20–40 ppm), inhaled iloprost, or IV epoprostenol. Never test with CCBs (risk of collapse).

High-dose CCB for responders: nifedipine (up to 120–240 mg/day) or amlodipine (up to 20 mg/day) if bradycardic tendency; diltiazem (240–720 mg/day) if relative tachycardia. Avoid verapamil (negative inotropy). Reassess after 3–4 months; continue only if WHO FC I–II with marked haemodynamic improvement (mPAP < 30 and PVR < 4 WU); otherwise add PAH therapy.

V/Q lung scan in unexplained PH to assess for CTEPH. I C

RHC to confirm the diagnosis of PH (especially PAH or CTEPH) and support treatment decisions. I B Vasoreactivity testing in IPAH, HPAH or DPAH to identify candidates for high-dose CCB. I B Vasoreactivity testing in other forms of PAH or PH. III C

Annual screening for PAH in asymptomatic patients with systemic sclerosis (DETECT algorithm in those with DLCO < 60%).

I B

Echo screening for PAH in liver-transplant candidates (portopulmonary hypertension). I C

Key highlightsDiagnosis

  • Echo probability rests on TRV: ≤ 2.8 low (if no other signs), 2.9–3.4 intermediate/high, > 3.4 high.
  • Other signs from ≥ 2 categories: ventricles, PA, IVC/RA (e.g., RVOT AT < 105 ms, RA area > 18 cm²).
  • TAPSE/sPAP < 0.55 = poor RV–PA coupling.
  • V/Q scan screens for CTEPH (I C); normal scan excludes it.
  • RHC is mandatory for diagnosis (I B).
  • Vasoreactivity only in IPAH/HPAH/DPAH: mPAP ↓ ≥ 10 to ≤ 40 mmHg, CO unchanged/↑.
  • Long-term CCB response: FC I–II, mPAP < 30, PVR < 4 WU at 3–4 months.
  • Very low DLCO suggests PVOD or SSc-PAH.

24.4 PAH — Risk Stratification

Treatment in PAH is goal-orientated: the aim is to reach and maintain a low-risk profile (estimated 1-year mortality < 5%). ESC/ERS 2022 uses a comprehensive 3-strata model at diagnosis and a simpler 4-strata model at follow-up, which better discriminates the large intermediate group.

Key highlightsRisk stratification

  • Treatment goal: low risk (1-year mortality < 5%).
  • 3 strata at diagnosis: low < 5%, intermediate 5–20%, high > 20%.
  • 4 strata at follow-up using WHO FC, 6MWD, BNP/NT-proBNP.
  • 6MWD cut-offs: 440 / 320 / 165 m.
  • NT-proBNP cut-offs: 300 / 650 / 1100 ng/L.
  • Haemodynamic low-risk: RAP < 8, CI ≥ 2.5, SvO₂ > 65%.

24.5 PAH — Treatment

MECHANISM — THREE CLASSIC PATHWAYS PLUS A FOURTH

Endothelin pathway (↑ ET-1 → vasoconstriction, proliferation) → endothelin receptor antagonists (ERA).

Nitric oxide pathway (↓ NO → ↓ cGMP) → PDE5 inhibitors (prevent cGMP breakdown) or the sGC stimulator riociguat (↑ cGMP production).

Prostacyclin pathway (↓ PGI₂ → ↓ cAMP) → prostacyclin analogues and the IP-receptor agonist selexipag.

Activin/BMP signalling imbalance (↓ BMPR2 anti-proliferative, ↑ activin pro-proliferative) → sotatercept, the first anti-remodelling therapy.

Recommendation Class Level

Anticoagulation is not generally recommended in PAH, but may be considered individually (e.g., IPAH/ HPAH with no bleeding risk).

IIb C

ACEi, ARB, ARNI, SGLT2i, β-blockers or ivabradine in PAH unless required by comorbidity. III C The treatment algorithm

NEW Intermediate-low risk on ERA + PDE5i: switch PDE5i to riociguat. IIb B

Intermediate-high or high risk on oral therapy: add IV epoprostenol or IV/SC treprostinil and refer for lung-transplant evaluation.

IIa C

NEW Initial monotherapy (PDE5i or ERA) in IPAH/HPAH/DPAH with cardiopulmonary comorbidities. IIa C Combining riociguat with a PDE5i. III B

Sotatercept — the fourth pathway

Sotatercept is a fusion protein of the activin receptor type IIA extracellular domain and IgG1 Fc — a ligand trap for activins and GDFs that rebalances pro- and anti-proliferative signalling and partially reverses vascular remodelling. It post-dates ESC/ERS 2022 (FDA approval 2024, EMA 2024) and was incorporated into the 7th WSPH algorithm as add-on therapy.

CLINICAL APPROACH — END-STAGE PAH
  • Lung transplantation (usually bilateral): refer early — intermediate-high/high risk despite optimal therapy, or REVEAL > 7; list if high risk despite maximal therapy.
  • Balloon atrial septostomy or Potts shunt: palliative right-to-left decompression in refractory RV failure (bridge/palliation).
  • ICU: treat triggers (infection, arrhythmia — restore sinus rhythm), noradrenaline/dobutamine, avoid intubation, VA-ECMO only as bridge to transplant or recovery.

Key highlightsPAH treatment

  • Vasoreactive IPAH/HPAH/DPAH → high-dose CCB (≈ 10% of IPAH).
  • Most PAH: initial ERA + PDE5i (I B); high risk: add IV/SC prostacyclin (IIa C).
  • Comorbid (left-heart) phenotype → initial monotherapy (IIa C).
  • Follow-up intermediate-low → add selexipag (IIa B) or switch to riociguat (IIb B).
  • Intermediate-high/high → parenteral prostacyclin + transplant referral (IIa C).
  • Riociguat + PDE5i = contraindicated (III B); PDE5i + nitrates contraindicated.
  • Epoprostenol: only therapy with an RCT mortality benefit; t½ minutes — never interrupt.
  • Sotatercept 0.3 → 0.7 mg/kg SC every 3 weeks; watch Hb, platelets, telangiectasia.
  • ERAs and riociguat are teratogenic; oxygen if PaO₂ < 8 kPa.

24.6 PH in Left Heart & Lung Disease

Group 2 — PH associated with left heart disease (PH-LHD)

The commonest form of PH: present in up to ~50% of HFrEF/HFpEF and in most patients with severe mitral disease and symptomatic AS. Raised left atrial pressure is transmitted backwards (IpcPH); chronic exposure can add pulmonary vascular remodelling (CpcPH) — which carries a much worse prognosis and, when PVR is > 5 WU, signals a severe pre-capillary component.

DON'T CONFUSE — HFPEF-PH VS PAH

Clear lungs, low DLCO

At RHC, a borderline PAWP (13–15 mmHg) in a high-probability HFpEF patient may be unmasked by fluid challenge (500 mL over 5 min; PAWP > 18 mmHg) or exercise (PAWP/CO slope > 2 mmHg/L/min).

EXAM TRAP

Pulmonary vasodilators in PH-LHD increase pulmonary blood flow into a stiff, high-pressure left heart → pulmonary oedema. Trials were neutral or harmful (e.g., bosentan and epoprostenol in HFrEF; SIOVAC — sildenafil after valve surgery — worse outcomes). Treat the left heart (GDMT, valve intervention); in HFrEF with CpcPH, PVR > 5 WU is a relative contraindication to heart transplantation (reversibility tested with vasodilators).

Group 3 — PH associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia

Mostly mild-to-moderate in COPD and ILD; severe PH (PVR > 5 WU) is uncommon but carries a poor prognosis — suspect a pulmonary vascular phenotype (disproportionate PH, very low DLCO, preserved spirometry). Management: treat the lung disease and hypoxaemia (long-term oxygen), consider referral to a PH centre and lung transplantation.

Recommendation Class Level

Referral to a PH centre for patients with suspected severe PH or uncertainty about the treatment strategy.

I C

NEW Inhaled treprostinil in PH associated with ILD (INCREASE trial: ↑ 6MWD, fewer exacerbations). IIb B PDE5i may be considered in severe PH with COPD/ILD, individualised in a PH centre. IIb C Ambrisentan in PH associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. III B

Riociguat in PH associated with idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (RISE-IIP stopped for harm). III B

24.7 Chronic Thromboembolic PH

CTEPH results from incomplete resolution of thromboemboli, organised into fibrotic obstructions, plus a secondary small-vessel arteriopathy in non-occluded territories. It is the only potentially curable form of PH. About 25% of patients have no history of acute PE. The broader term chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease (CTEPD) includes symptomatic patients with mismatched defects but without PH at rest.

DEFINITION — CTEPH

Pre-capillary PH (mPAP > 20, PAWP ≤ 15, PVR > 2 WU) with mismatched perfusion defects on V/Q and signs of chronic thromboembolic disease on CTPA/angiography (webs, bands, pouches, abrupt narrowing, mosaic perfusion, bronchial collaterals), after at least 3 months of effective anticoagulation.

Key highlightsGroups 2 and 3

  • Group 2 is the commonest PH; CpcPH (PVR > 2 WU) worsens prognosis.
  • PAH drugs in PH-LHD: Class III A — risk of pulmonary oedema.
  • Fluid challenge (500 mL) unmasks occult post-capillary PH (PAWP > 18).
  • PVR > 5 WU = severe pre-capillary component; relative CI to heart transplant.
  • PH-ILD: inhaled treprostinil (IIb B); ambrisentan (IPF) and riociguat (IIP) are Class III.
  • Treat hypoxaemia: O₂ is the mainstay in group 3.
BOARD PEARL

Every patient with CTEPH should be assessed for surgery first — "operability" is decided by an expert CTEPH team, not by the referring physician . PAH drugs should not delay referral for PEA. Pre-operative riociguat or BPA ("bridging") in operable patients is not routine.

24.8 Special Settings — Congenital, Pregnancy & Others

PAH associated with congenital heart disease and Eisenmenger syndrome

Eisenmenger syndrome is the extreme end of CHD-PAH: a large systemic-to-pulmonary shunt leads to severe, irreversible pulmonary vascular disease and shunt reversal (right-to-left) with cyanosis. Post-tricuspid shunts (VSD, PDA, AVSD) cause it early (infancy/childhood); pre-tricuspid shunts (ASD) rarely and late. Survival is better than IPAH with comparable haemodynamics because the RV was "trained" from birth and the shunt decompresses it.

Targeted therapy Bosentan in Eisenmenger FC III (BREATHE-5: ↑ 6MWD, ↓ PVR, no worsening of saturation) — ESC Class I

Key highlightsCTEPH

  • Diagnosis only after ≥ 3 months of effective anticoagulation; V/Q mismatch + chronic CT signs + RHC. ≈ 25% have no history of acute PE; incidence after PE ≈ 2–3%.
  • PEA = treatment of choice (I B); mortality < 5% in expert centres.
  • BPA for inoperable or residual distal disease (I B).
  • Riociguat for inoperable or persistent PH after PEA (I B).
  • Lifelong anticoagulation (I C); VKA if APS.
  • Issue Key point
  • Shunt closure ESC 2020/2022 (ASD example): PVR < 3 WU → close; 3–5 WU → consider if significant L→R shunt (Qp:Qs > 1.5); ≥ 5 WU → only if PVR falls below 5 on PAH therapy (treat-and-repair); Eisenmenger — closure contraindicated
  • Complications Haemoptysis, paradoxical embolism/brain abscess (air filters on IV lines), gout, gallstones, arrhythmia, sudden death
  • Avoid Dehydration, high altitude, strenuous exercise, systemic vasodilators, pregnancy (mortality ~30–50% historically)
  • Pregnancy and PH
  • All forms of PAH are mWHO class IV — pregnancy is contraindicated (ESC 2025 CVD & Pregnancy; ESC/ERS 2022 I C). Pregnancy-related haemodynamic load (↑ blood volume and CO, peripartum fluid shifts) overwhelms a fixed-PVR RV; maternal death or transplantation is still reported in ≈ 20% of pregnancies in PAH, most often in the late third trimester and the first weeks post-partum.
  • Contraception: highly effective methods (IUD, progestogen implant); bosentan reduces hormonal contraceptive efficacy; oestrogen-containing methods are avoided (thrombosis).
  • If pregnant: counsel on termination; if continuing — expert PH-obstetric centre, stop ERAs and riociguat (teratogenic), continue/start PDE5i and prostanoids (IV epoprostenol in severe disease), planned delivery (usually caesarean or assisted vaginal) with careful regional anaesthesia, close postpartum monitoring.

PAH therapy

PVOD / PCH Very low DLCO, severe hypoxaemia, CT: septal lines, centrilobular ground-glass, mediastinal nodes; pulmonary oedema with PAH vasodilators; EIF2AK4; early transplant referral

  • Sickle cell disease Group 5; haemolysis-related; high mortality even with mild PH
  • Hereditary haemorrhagic
  • telangiectasia
  • ACVRL1/ENG — PAH, or high-output PH from hepatic AVMs (group 5/unclassified)

Key highlightsSpecial settings

  • Eisenmenger: post-tricuspid shunts early; differential cyanosis with PDA.
  • No routine venesection; only for hyperviscosity with Hct > 65%; correct iron deficiency.
  • Bosentan in Eisenmenger FC III (BREATHE-5).
  • ASD closure: PVR < 3 WU close; 3–5 consider; ≥ 5 only if reversible; Eisenmenger never.
  • PAH = mWHO IV — pregnancy contraindicated; stop ERAs/riociguat, use PDE5i/prostanoids if pregnant.
  • Portopulmonary: stop β-blockers; severe PoPH → treat before liver transplant.
  • PVOD: very low DLCO, septal lines, oedema with vasodilators — early transplant.

24.9 Self-Assessment

Q1 RHC in a breathless 58-year-old: mPAP 32 mmHg, PAWP 19 mmHg, CO 4.5 L/min. The haemodynamic

Answer C PVR = (mPAP − PAWP)/CO = (32 − 19)/4.5 ≈ 2.9 WU. PAWP > 15 with PVR > 2 WU = combined pre- and postcapillary PH. IpcPH would need PVR ≤ 2 WU. Always calculate PVR before labelling post-capillary PH.

Q2 A 36-year-old woman with IPAH undergoes vasoreactivity testing with inhaled NO. Which result defines a positive response?

Answer B Positive response: mPAP ↓ ≥ 10 mmHg to an absolute ≤ 40 mmHg with CO unchanged or increased. A (46 mmHg) misses the absolute target; C falls only 6; D and E have a falling CO.

Q3 A 42-year-old with newly diagnosed IPAH (non-vasoreactive), WHO FC III, 6MWD 360 m, NT-proBNP 820 ng/L, no comorbidities. Initial therapy?

Answer E Intermediate risk, no comorbidity → initial dual oral ERA + PDE5i (I B; AMBITION). CCB only if vasoreactive; IV epoprostenol monotherapy is not the standard; riociguat + PDE5i is contraindicated.

Q4 After 4 months on macitentan + tadalafil, the patient in Q3 is FC III, 6MWD 290 m, NT-proBNP 900 ng/L. According to the 4-strata model and current algorithms, the best next step is:

Answer A FC III (3), 6MWD 290 (3), NT-proBNP 900 (3) → intermediate-high risk. Add parenteral prostacyclin (IIa C) — the 7th WSPH also supports sotatercept — and start transplant evaluation. Riociguat must not be combined with a PDE5i.

Q5 A 74-year-old obese woman with hypertension, AF and diabetes has echo TRV 3.3 m/s, LA enlargement and E/e′ 16. RHC: mPAP 34, PAWP 20, PVR 1.8 WU. Best management?

Answer D IpcPH due to HFpEF (PAWP > 15, PVR ≤ 2). PAH drugs in PH-LHD are Class III A; treat the left heart.

Q6 The preferred screening test for CTEPH in a patient with unexplained PH is:

Answer B V/Q scanning has higher sensitivity than CTPA for chronic thromboembolism; a normal scan excludes CTEPH (I C).

Q7 A patient with CTEPH has organised thrombus in both main and lobar pulmonary arteries; the CTEPH team deems it surgically accessible. Treatment of choice?

Answer A PEA is the treatment of choice for operable CTEPH (I B) and potentially curative. BPA and riociguat are for inoperable or residual disease.

Q8 A patient with PAH treated with sotatercept requires which monitoring before dosing?

Answer E Sotatercept raises haemoglobin and lowers platelets; both are checked before initial doses and periodically. Telangiectasia and bleeding are other class effects.

Q9 A 25-year-old with a large unrepaired VSD has cyanosis, SaO₂ 82%, Hct 62% and no hyperviscosity symptoms. PVR 12 WU. Which is correct?

Answer C Eisenmenger (PVR 12 WU, shunt reversal): closure is contraindicated; venesection only for symptomatic hyperviscosity; bosentan improves exercise capacity (BREATHE-5); pregnancy is contraindicated (mWHO IV).

Q10 A 50-year-old with suspected IPAH has DLCO 28%, CT showing septal lines, centrilobular ground-glass opacities and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. After starting epoprostenol he develops acute pulmonary oedema. Diagnosis?

Answer D Very low DLCO, septal lines, centrilobular ground-glass and nodes = PVOD; vasodilators increase flow into obstructed venules → pulmonary oedema. Refer early for lung transplantation.

25.1 The Normal Aorta, Measurement & Imaging

Anatomy and function

The aorta is divided into five segments: the root (annulus → sinotubular junction, containing the sinuses of Valsalva), the tubular ascending aorta (STJ → innominate artery), the arch (innominate → left subclavian), the descending thoracic aorta (left subclavian → diaphragm) and the abdominal aorta (diaphragm → bifurcation, usually at L4). The wall has three layers — intima, a thick elastic media (the load-bearing layer) and adventitia containing the vasa vasorum. Its elastic recoil (the Windkessel function) converts intermittent LV ejection into continuous flow and sustains diastolic coronary perfusion. With age the media stiffens, pulse-wave velocity rises, the reflected wave returns in systole, and isolated systolic hypertension results. The aorta also grows slowly with age — roughly 1 mm per decade in adults.

MECHANISM — LAPLACE IN THE AORTA

Wall stress ∝ pressure × radius / wall thickness. As the aorta dilates, stress rises, which drives further dilatation — a vicious circle that explains the exponential rise in dissection/rupture risk at large diameters and why lowering both pressure and the rate of pressure rise (dP/dt) is the cornerstone of medical therapy.

Normal dimensions and definitions

Normal infrarenal aorta ~15–24 mm Smaller in women

Dilatation Diameter above the upper normal limit (z-score ≥ 2) Z-score = SD above predicted for BSA/age

  • Aneurysm Permanent localised dilatation ≥ 50% above
  • expected (≥ 1.5 ×)
  • Involves all three layers (true
  • aneurysm)
  • AAA Infrarenal aortic diameter ≥ 30 mm 25–29 mm = "subaneurysmal" (ectatic)

Pseudoaneurysm Contained rupture — wall formed by adventitia/periaortic tissuePost-trauma, post-surgery, infection Aortic size index (ASI) Diameter (cm) ÷ BSA (m²) Used in Turner syndrome, small adults

Aortic height index (AHI) Diameter (cm) ÷ height (m) Height indexing avoids obesity bias of BSA

WHAT CHANGED IN 2024 (ESC)
  • Aortic and peripheral arterial diseases merged into one guideline (replacing ESC 2014 aortic and ESC/ ESVS 2017 PAD documents).
  • Greater emphasis on indexing diameters to height/BSA and on standardised measurement (same modality, same method, same phase of the cycle during follow-up).
  • TEM classification of aortic dissection introduced alongside Stanford.
  • Strong push towards multidisciplinary "aortic teams" and high-volume aortic centres.

How to measure

Measure perpendicular to the blood-flow axis (double-oblique reconstruction on CT/MRI — axial slices overestimate a tortuous aorta).

Echo (root/ascending): end-diastole, leading-edge-to-leading-edge convention in the parasternal longaxis view. CT/MRI: ECG-gated acquisition for the root and ascending aorta (removes motion artefact that mimics a flap).

AAA on ultrasound: maximal antero-posterior outer-to-outer diameter.

For serial follow-up use the same modality, the same measurement convention and compare images side-by-side ; changes < 3 mm are usually within measurement error.

BOARD PEARL

For surveillance of a young patient with Marfan or another genetic aortopathy, MRI is preferred over repeated CT to limit cumulative radiation; TTE is adequate when the dilated segment is the root and is well seen.

  • • •
  • • •
  • • •

Key highlightsNormal aorta & imaging

  • Normal adult thoracic aorta is usually < 40 mm; aneurysm = dilatation ≥ 50% above expected; AAA = infrarenal ≥ 30 mm.
  • Wall stress rises with radius (Laplace) — risk of dissection/rupture climbs steeply with size.
  • Measure perpendicular to flow; echo root at end-diastole, leading edge to leading edge.
  • CT angiography is first-line for suspected acute aortic syndrome; TOE if the patient is too unstable to move.
  • TOE blind spot = distal ascending aorta/proximal arch (tracheal air).
  • MRI is preferred for lifelong surveillance of young patients with heritable aortopathy.
  • Index diameters to BSA (ASI) or height (AHI) in small patients and in Turner syndrome.

25.2 Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm

Epidemiology and aetiology

Thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA) are usually silent and found incidentally. About 60% involve the root/ascending aorta, ~40% the descending aorta, and ~10% the arch (segments overlap). The biology differs by segment: ascending aneurysms reflect medial degeneration (often genetic or valve-related); descending aneurysms behave like atherosclerotic disease .

Root / ascending
  • Degenerative medial disease ("cystic medial necrosis") ±
  • hypertension, age
  • Bicuspid aortic valve aortopathy
  • Heritable TAD: Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vEDS, familial
  • nonsyndromic TAD
  • Turner syndrome
  • Aortitis (GCA, Takayasu, syphilis)
  • Post-stenotic dilatation (AS)
Descending / thoracoabdominal
  • Atherosclerosis — smoking, hypertension, age
  • Chronic dissection with false-lumen expansion (most
  • common cause of rapid growth)
  • Infection (mycotic), trauma (pseudoaneurysm)
  • Heritable TAD (can affect any segment)

Natural history

Average growth: ascending ~1 mm/year; descending ~3 mm/year. Faster in Marfan/Loeys-Dietz and in chronic dissection.

The "hinge points": risk of dissection/rupture rises sharply above 55–60 mm for the ascending aorta and 60–70 mm for the descending aorta.

Paradox: most type A dissections occur at diameters < 55 mm — because there are far more patients with moderately dilated aortas. Diameter is necessary but not sufficient for risk prediction; growth rate, genetics and family history matter.

Factors that lower the surgical threshold: rapid growth, family history of dissection at small diameter, genetic variant, uncontrolled hypertension, short stature, desire for pregnancy, need for other cardiac surgery.

Clinical features

Most are asymptomatic. Large aneurysms compress adjacent structures: hoarseness (left recurrent laryngeal nerve), stridor, dysphagia, SVC syndrome, or chest/back pain. New pain in a known aneurysm = impending rupture until proven otherwise and warrants urgent repair regardless of size. Root dilatation causes aortic regurgitation via annular and STJ dilatation.

Medical therapy

Strict BP control (target per hypertension guidelines, generally < 130/80 mmHg; lower if tolerated); smoking cessation.

β-blockers and/or ARBs are the usual first choices (reduce dP/dt and TGF-β signalling, respectively) — proven mainly in Marfan syndrome.

Statins for atherosclerotic (descending) disease.

Avoid fluoroquinolones where alternatives exist (association with aneurysm/dissection) — advice, not a trial-proven rule.

Exercise: moderate aerobic activity encouraged; avoid heavy isometric (straining) exercise and competitive contact sport in significant dilatation.

Thresholds for intervention — the core table

Descending thoracic aorta

Repair threshold: ≥ 55 mm when TEVAR is anatomically feasible (TEVAR preferred over open surgery — lower early mortality and paraplegia); ≥ 60 mm when open surgery is the only option.

TEVAR needs landing zones of healthy aorta (≈ ≥ 20 mm length) proximally and distally; left subclavian coverage may need revascularisation (carotid-subclavian bypass) to protect the spinal cord, left arm and a LIMA graft.

Spinal cord ischaemia (paraplegia) is the signature complication — risk reduced by cerebrospinal fluid drainage and maintaining MAP.

EXAM TRAP

Do not apply the AAA thresholds to the thoracic aorta, and do not apply the "55 mm" sporadic threshold to a patient with Marfan syndrome, a TGFBR variant, a family history of dissection or someone already going to theatre for an aortic valve — each lowers the threshold by about 5–10 mm .

Surveillance of the thoracic aorta

Key highlightsThoracic aortic aneurysm

  • Sporadic root/ascending aneurysm: surgery at ≥ 55 mm (ESC I B); ESC > 52 mm and ACC ≥ 50 mm if low risk in an expert centre.
  • Growth ≥ 0.5 cm in 1 year or ≥ 0.3 cm/year × 2 years lowers the threshold (ACC/AHA 2022).
  • Replace the ascending aorta at ≥ 45 mm if the patient is already having aortic valve surgery.
  • Marfan: ≥ 50 mm, or ≥ 45 mm with risk factors.
  • Descending TAA: TEVAR at ≥ 55 mm; open repair at ≥ 60 mm; thoracoabdominal endovascular repair at ≥ 60 mm.
  • Symptomatic aneurysm = repair regardless of size.
  • Spinal cord ischaemia is the key complication of descending/thoracoabdominal repair — CSF drainage protects.
  • First re-image at 6 months after detection, then yearly if ≥ 45 mm.

25.3 Heritable Aortopathy, Bicuspid Aortopathy & Pregnancy

Heritable thoracic aortic disease (HTAD) accounts for roughly 20% of thoracic aneurysms and dissections. Its defining feature is that dissection can occur at smaller diameters, at younger ages, and in family clusters — hence lower surgical thresholds, whole-aorta imaging and cascade family screening.

MECHANISM — TWO PATHWAYS TO A WEAK MEDIA

Extracellular matrix defect: fibrillin-1 (FBN1, Marfan) and type III collagen (COL3A1, vascular EDS) — structurally deficient wall.

TGF-β signalling: TGFBR1/2, SMAD2/3, TGFB2/3 (Loeys-Dietz) — paradoxically increased TGF-β signalling in the wall; the rationale for ARBs (losartan) in Marfan.

Smooth-muscle contractile unit: ACTA2, MYH11, MYLK, PRKG1 — nonsyndromic familial TAD; ACTA2 also causes premature CAD, stroke/moyamoya.

Marfan syndrome — the diagnosis (revised Ghent)

The two cardinal features are aortic root dilatation (z ≥ 2) and ectopia lentis. Without a family history, MFS is diagnosed by any of:

  • Aortic root z ≥ 2 + ectopia lentis.
  • Aortic root z ≥ 2 + causal FBN1 variant.
  • Aortic root z ≥ 2 + systemic score ≥ 7 points.
  • Ectopia lentis + FBN1 variant previously associated with aortic disease.

With a family history of MFS, one of ectopia lentis, systemic score ≥ 7, or aortic root z ≥ 2 (≥ 3 if under 20 years) is enough.

DON'T CONFUSE
  • Marfan: lens dislocates upward; homocystinuria: lens dislocates downward, intellectual disability, thrombosis — not an aortopathy.
  • Loeys-Dietz lacks ectopia lentis but has hypertelorism, bifid uvula and diffuse arterial tortuosity — more aggressive than Marfan.
  • vEDS is an arterial rupture disease more than an aneurysm disease; "classic" EDS rarely affects the aorta.
  • Bicuspid aortopathy
  • BAV affects ~1–2% of the population (male : female ≈ 3 : 1).
  • Two phenotypes: ascending (tubular) — commonest, often with AS, related to jet haemodynamics; root phenotype — younger men, often with AR, genetic behaviour and higher dissection risk.
  • Absolute dissection risk is low, but ~8× the general population.
  • Image the whole thoracic aorta (CT/MRI) at diagnosis if TTE views are incomplete, and when the aorta exceeds 45 mm.
  • First-degree relatives of patients with BAV and aortopathy (especially root phenotype) should have echo screening.
  • Coarctation coexists in a proportion; conversely ~50% of coarctation patients have BAV.

Genetic testing and family screening

BOARD PEARL

In Marfan syndrome the ESC recommends β-blocker or ARB (losartan/irbesartan) at maximally tolerated dose to slow root growth; head-to-head trials show similar efficacy. The combination can be used if growth continues . ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy — switch before conception.

Pregnancy in aortopathy

Pregnancy increases cardiac output and blood volume and hormonally weakens the aortic wall; dissection clusters in the third trimester and early postpartum. Counselling is based on diagnosis and indexed size.

CLINICAL APPROACH — THE PREGNANT PATIENT WITH AORTOPATHY
  • Before pregnancy: image whole aorta; prophylactic surgery if above the mWHO IV threshold; stop ARB.
  • During: continue β-blocker (labetalol/metoprolol) throughout; echo every 4–12 weeks depending on size; strict BP control.
  • Delivery: caesarean section should be considered when the ascending aorta is > 45 mm (or prior dissection); vaginal delivery with epidural and assisted second stage when smaller.
  • Postpartum: highest-risk period — continue surveillance for several weeks.

25.4 Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

Epidemiology and risk factors

An AAA is an infrarenal aortic diameter ≥ 30 mm; about 90% are infrarenal. Prevalence in screened men over 65 has fallen to around 1–3% as smoking has declined. The pathology is inflammatory degradation of the media (matrix metalloproteinases, elastin loss) rather than simple atherosclerosis.

Risk factors
  • Smoking — strongest modifiable factor; also accelerates
  • growth and rupture
  • Male sex, age > 65
  • Family history (first-degree relative)
  • Hypertension, atherosclerosis elsewhere, COPD
Negative associations
  • Diabetes — lower prevalence and slower growth (classic
  • exam fact)
  • Female sex — less common but rupture risk ~3–4×
  • higher at a given diameter

Key highlightsHeritable & bicuspid aortopathy, pregnancy

  • HTAD ≈ 20% of TAD; dissection occurs at smaller diameters and younger ages.
  • Marfan: surgery ≥ 50 mm (≥ 45 mm with risk factors); β-blocker or ARB at maximal dose.
  • Loeys-Dietz (TGFBR1/2): surgery ~≥ 45 mm, lower with high-risk features; image head to pelvis. vEDS: no size threshold — rupture at normal diameters; celiprolol; avoid invasive procedures.
  • Turner: index to body size — ASI > 2.5 cm/m² is the danger zone for surgery and pregnancy.
  • BAV aortopathy: ≥ 55 mm (≥ 50 mm root phenotype/risk factors; ≥ 45 mm at AVR).
  • Revised Ghent: aortic root z ≥ 2 + ectopia lentis (or FBN1, or systemic score ≥ 7).
  • Pregnancy not recommended: Marfan > 45 mm, BAV > 50 mm, Turner ASI > 2.5, any vEDS.
  • Caesarean section considered when ascending aorta > 45 mm; dissection risk peaks in 3rd trimester/ postpartum.
  • Natural history

Population screening of older men (MASS trial) reduces AAA-related mortality by roughly 40–50% over long-term follow-up. A single normal scan at 65 effectively excludes future clinically significant AAA.

aorto-enteric fistula (herald GI bleed, usually after graft).

EXAM TRAP

A patient with known AAA, back pain and a normal blood pressure is not safe — a contained retroperitoneal leak often precedes free rupture. In suspected rupture use permissive hypotension (SBP ~70–90 mmHg, conscious patient) and go straight to CT/theatre; EVAR is preferred when anatomy allows.

Indications for repair

Key highlightsAbdominal aortic aneurysm

  • AAA = infrarenal aorta ≥ 30 mm; smoking is the dominant risk factor; diabetes is protective.
  • Repair: men ≥ 55 mm, women ≥ 50 mm, growth ≥ 10 mm/year, or any symptoms.
  • Early repair of 40–55 mm AAA does not improve survival.
  • Screening: men ≥ 65 who have smoked (ESC and ACC Class I); ESC adds first-degree relatives from 50 y (Class I).
  • EVAR: lower early mortality, similar long-term survival, more re-interventions, lifelong imaging.
  • Endoleak type I and III — treat; type II (commonest) — observe unless sac grows.
  • No drug slows AAA growth; statin + antiplatelet + BP control + stop smoking.
  • Rupture triad: pain + hypotension + pulsatile mass — permissive hypotension, immediate repair.
  • Phase Time from onset Note
  • Subacute 15–90 days Preferred window for pre-emptive TEVAR in type B
  • Chronic > 90 days Aneurysmal false-lumen growth

25.5 Acute Aortic Syndromes — Classification & Diagnosis

DEFINITION

Acute aortic syndrome (AAS) is an emergency in which the aortic wall integrity is acutely disrupted: classic dissection (intimal tear → blood splits the media into true and false lumens; ~85–90%), intramural haematoma (IMH; blood in the media without an intimal tear), penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (PAU), and contained or free rupture. Incidence ≈ 3–16 per 100 000 per year, two-thirds men.

Classification

BOARD PEARL
  • Untreated acute type A dissection kills about 0.5–1% per hour early on — roughly half die within 48 h.
  • Causes of death: rupture into the pericardium (tamponade), acute severe AR, coronary malperfusion, and stroke. Type B kills mainly through malperfusion and rupture.
  • Predisposing conditions
  • Hypertension (~70%; especially type B)
  • Existing aneurysm / previous aortic or valve surgery
  • HTAD (Marfan, LDS, vEDS, Turner), BAV
  • Iatrogenic: catheterisation, cannulation, IABP
  • Cocaine/amphetamines; heavy weightlifting (Valsalva
  • surges)
  • Pregnancy (3rd trimester, postpartum)
  • Aortitis; fluoroquinolone exposure (association)
  • Atherosclerosis (PAU, IMH in the elderly)

Clinical features

EXAM TRAP — THE "STEMI" THAT IS A DISSECTION

Inferior ST elevation + tearing pain radiating to the back + pulse deficit or new AR murmur = type A dissection involving the RCA ostium. Thrombolysis or potent antithrombotic loading is catastrophic — obtain bedside echo/CT before the cath lab when the story fits. Conversely, a normal chest radiograph (normal in ~10–20%) does not exclude dissection.

The ADD risk score and D-dimer

Hypotension or shock

In the ADvISED study, ADD-RS ≤ 1 plus D-dimer < 500 ng/mL had a failure rate of only ~0.3%. D-dimer is sensitive (~97%) but non-specific, and may be falsely low with a thrombosed false lumen, IMH, PAU or late presentation. With ADD-RS ≥ 2 a negative D-dimer cannot exclude AAS.

Imaging findings

Dissection: intimal flap separating true lumen (usually smaller, systolic expansion) from false lumen (larger, slower flow, may thrombose, "cobweb" strands).

TTE: flap in root, AR, pericardial effusion/tamponade, regional wall-motion abnormality; sensitivity for type A ~70–80% only.

CT: also defines entry tear, extent, branch involvement (static vs dynamic obstruction) and landing zones.

IMH: crescentic or circular wall thickening > 5 mm, hyperdense on non-contrast CT, without flow or flap — always perform a non-contrast phase.

PAU: contrast-filled out-pouching through a calcified atheromatous plaque, typically descending aorta of elderly smokers.

DON'T CONFUSE — IMH VS PAU VS THROMBUS
  • IMH: smooth crescent, intima displaced inward with intimal calcium lying inside the haematoma, no ulcer.
  • PAU: focal crater through plaque with atheroma elsewhere; may be surrounded by IMH.
  • Mural thrombus: irregular luminal surface, intimal calcium outside the thrombus.
  • Ulcer-like projection in an IMH (focal intimal disruption) is a high-risk feature, not a PAU.

25.6 Acute Aortic Syndromes — Management & Follow-up

Immediate medical therapy ("anti-impulse" therapy)

The goal is to reduce the force of ejection (dP/dt) and wall stress while definitive treatment is arranged. The ESC 2024 targets are SBP < 120 mmHg and heart rate < 60 bpm , reached quickly but compatibly with end-organ perfusion.

contraindicated

Diltiazem or verapamil IV Non-dihydropyridine CCB for rate control

3. Then vasodilator Nitroprusside, nicardipine, clevidipine, GTN Only after β-blockade — alone they cause reflex tachycardia and ↑ dP/dt

  • Monitoring Arterial line (arm with higher pressure),
  • urine output, lactate
  • Branch involvement may cause pseudo-hypotension
  • in one arm
EXAM TRAP — THE HYPOTENSIVE DISSECTION

Hypotension in type A means tamponade, rupture, acute severe AR or coronary malperfusion until proven otherwise — the answer is the operating theatre, not more fluid or inotropes.

Avoid pericardiocentesis in tamponade due to type A dissection: restoring pressure may re-open bleeding. If the patient is peri-arrest and surgery cannot be immediate, a controlled drainage of small volumes to maintain perfusion is the exception.

β-blockers are poorly tolerated with acute severe AR (they remove the compensatory tachycardia) — another reason for immediate surgery.

Definitive management by type

Key highlightsAAS classification & diagnosis

  • Stanford A = ascending involved (any entry) → surgery; Stanford B = ascending spared.
  • DeBakey I (ascending → beyond), II (ascending only), III (descending; IIIa above, IIIb below diaphragm).
  • TEM = Type (A/B/non-A non-B), Entry (E0–E3), Malperfusion (M0–M3) — endorsed by ESC 2024.
  • Acute < 14 days, subacute 15–90 days, chronic > 90 days.
  • Untreated type A: mortality ~0.5–1%/h, ~50% at 48 h.
  • ADD-RS ≤ 1 + D-dimer < 500 ng/mL safely rules out AAS; ADD-RS ≥ 2 → direct CT.
  • CT angiography is first-line (include non-contrast phase for IMH); TOE if unstable.
  • Inferior STEMI + tearing pain = RCA dissection — no thrombolysis.
  • Recommendation Class Level
  • Emergency surgery for acute type A aortic dissection. I B
  • Urgent surgery for type A intramural haematoma. I C
  • NEW Surgery for type A penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer. I —
  • Type B
  • Medical therapy (pain and BP/HR control) for uncomplicated type B dissection. I C
  • TEVAR for complicated type B dissection (rupture, malperfusion, rapid expansion, refractory pain/ hypertension).
  • I —
  • Pre-emptive TEVAR (subacute phase) for uncomplicated type B with high-risk imaging/clinical features.
  • IIa B
  • CHANGED TEVAR for complicated type B intramural haematoma (upgraded). I —
  • "—" = level of evidence not independently verified for this edition; class verified.
Type A — surgery
  • Replace the ascending aorta (± hemiarch), resect the primary entry tear, resuspend or replace the aortic valve; root replacement if the root is dissected/dilated; frozen elephant trunk for arch/proximal descending entry tears.
  • Operative mortality ~15–20% versus > 50% at one month with medical therapy alone.
  • Advanced age alone is not a contraindication; reasons to reconsider include coma/established massive stroke, prolonged CPR, severe frailty — individual Heart Team decision.
  • With severe mesenteric malperfusion some centres reperfuse the gut first (endovascular), then repair the aorta.
Type B — medical therapy, TEVAR when complicated
    "Complicated" = intervene (TEVAR)
    • Rupture or impending rupture (haemothorax, growing
    • periaortic haematoma)
    • Malperfusion (visceral, renal, limb, spinal)
    • Rapid aortic expansion
    • Refractory pain or hypertension despite full therapy
    "Uncomplicated, high-risk" = consider TEVAR
    • Total aortic diameter ≥ 40 mm
    • False lumen diameter ≥ 20–22 mm
    • Primary entry tear ≥ 10 mm (esp. on inner curvature)
    • Partial false-lumen thrombosis
    • Bloody pleural effusion; radiographic-only malperfusion;
    • readmission

    TEVAR covers the entry tear, redirects flow into the true lumen and promotes false-lumen thrombosis ("aortic remodelling"). In INSTEAD-XL, pre-emptive TEVAR added to medical therapy in stable type B dissection reduced aorta-specific mortality and disease progression at 5 years, despite no early benefit. Ideal timing is the subacute phase (after ~2 weeks, before 90 days), when the flap is still mobile but the aorta is less fragile. Retrograde type A dissection complicates ~2% of TEVAR procedures.

    BOARD PEARL

    Treat IMH and PAU "like dissection" by location : ascending involvement → surgery; descending → medical therapy first, endovascular repair when complicated. The same anti-impulse targets apply.

    Long-term management and follow-up

    Lifelong BP control < 130/80 mmHg, β-blocker-based; avoid heavy isometric exercise; stop smoking; screen for HTAD (young age, family history).

    Imaging after acute dissection (medical or repaired): at about 1, 6 and 12 months, then yearly if stable (CT or MRI; MRI preferred in the young); after TEVAR, CT at 1 month then per device protocol. Chronic false-lumen aneurysm: repair at ~55–60 mm or with growth.

    Late death is usually from false-lumen aneurysm rupture, re-dissection or coronary disease. First-degree relatives of dissection patients without an obvious cause should be offered aortic imaging ± genetic testing.

    Traumatic aortic injury

    Blunt deceleration injury tears the aorta at the isthmus (just distal to the left subclavian, at the ligamentum arteriosum) in ~90%. Most victims die at the scene; survivors have a contained pseudoaneurysm. Diagnose with CT; TEVAR is preferred over open repair for significant injuries (grade III pseudoaneurysm, grade IV rupture), while minimal intimal tears (grade I) are managed medically with imaging follow-up.

    25.7 Aortitis, Coarctation & Other Aortic Conditions

    Aortitis

    Inflammation of the aortic wall may be non-infectious (large-vessel vasculitis — by far the commonest) or infectious. It presents with constitutional symptoms and raised inflammatory markers, and leads to aneurysm (from medial destruction) or stenosis (from wall thickening/fibrosis).

    Immunosuppression

    Syphilis (tertiary) Decades after infection Ascending aneurysm, "treebark" intima, AR, coronary ostial stenosis

    • Penicillin + surgery
    • Mycotic (infective) Salmonella, S. aureus,
    • streptococci; bacteraemia,
    • IE
    • Saccular, rapidly growing
    • aneurysm, often atypical site
    • Prolonged antibiotics + resection/
    • repair

    Imaging: CT/MR angiography shows concentric wall thickening; FDG-PET/CT demonstrates active wall inflammation and helps monitor activity. In GCA, the ESC recommends imaging of the aorta at diagnosis and during follow-up because thoracic aneurysm may develop years later.

    Key highlightsAAS management

    • Targets: SBP < 120 mmHg, HR < 60 bpm; IV β-blocker before any vasodilator.
    • β-blocker contraindicated → IV diltiazem/verapamil.
    • Type A dissection/IMH/PAU → emergency surgery (ESC I); age alone is no contraindication.
    • Tamponade in type A → theatre; avoid pericardiocentesis (only controlled small-volume drainage if peri-arrest).
    • Complicated type B (rupture, malperfusion, expansion, refractory pain/HTN) → TEVAR (I).
    • Uncomplicated type B → medical therapy (I); TEVAR in subacute phase if high-risk (ESC IIa, ACC 2b).
    • High-risk type B: aorta ≥ 40 mm, false lumen ≥ 20–22 mm, entry tear ≥ 10 mm.
    • Follow-up imaging at 1, 6, 12 months then yearly; BP < 130/80 lifelong.
    • Blunt trauma tears the isthmus; TEVAR is first choice for significant injury.
    DON'T CONFUSE — GCA VS TAKAYASU
    • Age is the discriminator: GCA > 50, Takayasu < 40 at onset.
    • Takayasu → renovascular hypertension, absent radial pulses, subclavian steal; GCA → cranial symptoms and late thoracic aneurysm.
    • Never revascularise a Takayasu lesion during active inflammation — restenosis and anastomotic failure are frequent.

    Coarctation of the aorta — pointer

    Covered in the Adult Congenital chapter; the aortic essentials: a discrete narrowing near the ligamentum arteriosum causing upper-limb hypertension, radio-femoral delay, rib notching (posterior ribs 3–8) and the "figure-3" sign. Associations: BAV (~50%), intracranial berry aneurysm (~10%), Turner syndrome. ESC 2020 ACHD: repair is indicated in hypertensive patients with an arm–leg gradient and a peak-to-peak (invasive) gradient ≥ 20 mmHg ; stenting is preferred in adults when anatomy allows. Lifelong follow-up targets hypertension, recoarctation and aneurysm at the repair site (especially after patch repair).

    Other aortic conditions

    Mobile aortic thrombus Often in non-atherosclerotic aorta; embolises. Anticoagulation; TEVAR/surgery if persistent or recurrent embolism.

    Coral reef aorta Rock-hard calcific lesions of the visceral/suprarenal aorta → hypertension, renal and mesenteric ischaemia, claudication.

    Pseudoaneurysm Contained rupture (trauma, anastomosis, infection) — high rupture risk; repair (usually endovascular).

    Porcelain aorta Circumferential calcification of the ascending aorta — precludes cross-clamping; favours TAVI over SAVR.

    Key highlightsAortitis, coarctation & other conditions

    • GCA (> 50 y) → late thoracic aneurysm: image the aorta at diagnosis and in follow-up.
    • Takayasu (< 40 y, women) → arch-branch and renal stenoses; revascularise only when quiescent.
    • Syphilitic aortitis: ascending aneurysm, AR and coronary ostial stenosis.
    • Mycotic aneurysm: saccular, rapidly growing, Salmonella/S. aureus — antibiotics + repair.
    • Coarctation: BAV in ~50%; repair if peak-to-peak gradient ≥ 20 mmHg with hypertension; stent in adults.
    • Complex aortic arch plaque ≥ 4 mm → antiplatelet + statin (not warfarin).
    • Cholesterol emboli: livedo, AKI, eosinophilia, low complement after catheterisation.

    25.8 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 58-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve is referred for surgical AVR for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis. CT shows a tubular ascending aorta of 47 mm; surgical risk is low. What is the best management of the ascending aorta?

    Answer B When the aortic valve is being operated on, replace the ascending aorta at ≥ 45 mm in low-risk patients (ESC 2024; ACC/AHA 2022 ≥ 4.5 cm) — the added risk is small and avoids a later redo. 55 mm is the stand-alone threshold; TAVI leaves the aorta untreated.

    Q2 A 46-year-old woman presents with sudden, severe interscapular pain. She has no connective-tissue disease, no known aortic disease and a normal examination with equal arm pressures. ECG and troponin are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

    Answer C ADD-RS = 1 (pain features only). With ADD-RS ≤ 1, a D-dimer < 500 ng/mL makes AAS very unlikely (failure ~0.3%, ADvISED). CT is first if ADD-RS ≥ 2 or D-dimer positive; a normal CXR never excludes dissection.

    Q3 A 62-year-old man with CT-confirmed acute type B dissection has BP 190/105 mmHg and HR 105 bpm. Which initial IV regimen is most appropriate?

    Answer C Rate control first (IV β-blocker, target HR < 60), then a vasodilator for SBP < 120. Vasodilators alone (A, B, E) provoke reflex tachycardia and increase dP/dt; sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled hypotension.

    Q4 A 71-year-old asymptomatic woman, ex-smoker, has an infrarenal AAA of 52 mm on surveillance (47 mm one year ago). She is fit with suitable EVAR anatomy. What is recommended?

    Answer C Women: repair at ≥ 50 mm (rupture risk higher at any size); growth of 5 mm in a year also meets rapid-growth criteria. 55 mm is the male threshold; no drug slows AAA growth.

    Q5 A 55-year-old man has acute type B dissection. Pain and BP settle on IV therapy; there is no malperfusion. CT shows total aortic diameter 44 mm and a primary entry tear of 14 mm. Which statement is most accurate?

    Answer C Uncomplicated type B with high-risk features (diameter ≥ 40 mm, entry tear ≥ 10 mm): pre-emptive TEVAR in the subacute phase should be considered (ESC IIa; ACC/AHA 2b). Emergency intervention is for complicated dissection; open surgery is not first line.

    Q6 A 27-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome (aortic root 47 mm, stable on losartan) wishes to become pregnant. What is the best advice?

    Answer C Marfan with aorta > 45 mm = mWHO IV — pregnancy not recommended; offer prophylactic root replacement first. ARBs are teratogenic (stop before conception); a β-blocker is continued throughout any pregnancy.

    Q7 A 19-year-old with hypertelorism, bifid uvula and tortuous neck arteries has an aortic root of 44 mm. Which statement is true?

    Answer C Loeys-Dietz (TGFBR1/2 etc.): aggressive disease, surgery ~≥ 45 mm (lower with high-risk features) and aneurysms anywhere, so head-to-pelvis imaging. No ectopia lentis (Marfan); celiprolol is for vEDS; avoid fluoroquinolones.

    Q8 Six months after EVAR, CT shows contrast in the aneurysm sac filling from a lumbar artery; sac diameter is unchanged. What is the best management?

    Answer C Type II endoleak (lumbar/IMA back-bleeding) is the commonest and often benign — observe unless the sac enlarges (≈ ≥ 10 mm). Types I and III need prompt correction (cuff, relining).

    Q9 A 66-year-old hypertensive man has tearing chest pain radiating to the back, inferior ST elevation, a diastolic murmur and a right radial pulse weaker than the left. The cath lab is being activated. What is the next best step?

    Answer C Pain character, AR murmur and pulse deficit point to type A dissection involving the RCA. Antithrombotic loading or thrombolysis may be fatal; confirm with bedside echo and CT, then emergency surgery.

    Q10 An 82-year-old woman has acute chest pain. CT shows a crescentic 12 mm hyperdense thickening of the ascending aortic wall without flap or intimal tear; ascending aorta 52 mm, small pericardial effusion. What is the diagnosis and management?

    Answer B Crescentic hyperdense wall thickening without a flap = IMH; ascending involvement = type A, with high-risk features (thickness ≥ 10 mm, diameter ≥ 50 mm, effusion) — urgent surgery (ESC I). Age alone does not preclude surgery.

    Key sources

    • Mazzolai L, et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases. Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538– 3700.
    • Isselbacher EM, et al. 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease. Circulation 2022;146:e334–e482 / J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;80:e223–e393.
    • Regitz-Zagrosek V, et al. 2018 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular diseases during pregnancy. Eur Heart J 2018;39:3165–3241 (and 2025 update).
    • Baumgartner H, et al. 2020 ESC Guidelines for adult congenital heart disease. Eur Heart J 2021;42:563–645.
    • Wanhainen A, et al. ESVS 2024 Clinical Practice Guidelines on abdominal aorto-iliac artery aneurysms. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2024.
    • Nazerian P, et al. ADvISED study. Circulation 2018;137:250–258.
    • Braunwald's Heart Disease, 13th ed., Ch. 39.

    Peripheral Arterial, Carotid & Cerebrovascular Disease

    One disease, many territories — the ankle index, the carotid bulb, the renal and mesenteric beds, and the brain that the heart embolises to.

    What the board expects you to know

    • The medical package for PAD — antiplatelet choice, low-dose rivaroxaban (COMPASS/VOYAGER), LDL and BP targets, exercise, cilostazol — and where ESC and ACC/AHA differ.

    • Carotid duplex grading, symptomatic vs asymptomatic thresholds, timing of CEA and CEA vs CAS.
