    Numbers that win marks

    ≤ 0.90ABI — diagnostic of PAD
    ≤ 0.70TBI — PAD when ABI > 1.40
    2.5 mg bidRivaroxaban + aspirin — COMPASS/VOYAGER
    ≥ 12 weeksSupervised exercise — 3×/week,
    30–60 min≤ 14 days CEA — symptomatic 50–99% stenosis
    ≤ 48 hDOAC start — minor/moderate AF stroke (ELAN)

    26.1 Lower Extremity PAD — Presentation & Diagnosis

    TERMINOLOGY

    ESC uses peripheral arterial diseases for all arterial beds other than the coronaries and aorta (carotid, vertebral, upper limb, renal, mesenteric, lower limb). In daily and ACC/AHA usage PAD means lower extremity atherosclerotic disease. Two or more affected beds (including coronary) = polyvascular disease — the highest-risk phenotype.

    Epidemiology and prognosis

    > 200 million people affected worldwide; prevalence rises steeply after 60–70 years.

    Risk factors: smoking (strongest — dose-dependent) and diabetes, then hypertension, dyslipidaemia, CKD, age; Lp(a) in premature disease.

    Only ~10–30% have classic claudication; the majority are asymptomatic or atypical — yet they carry the same systemic risk.

    The limb is rarely lost but the patient often dies of MI or stroke : in claudicants, 5-year major amputation ~1–3%, whereas cardiovascular events occur in ~20%. CLTI carries ~20–25% one-year mortality.

    Symptoms and examination

    The ankle-brachial index

    ABI (per leg) = higher ankle systolic pressure (dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial) ÷ higher of the two brachial pressures, measured with a Doppler probe after 5–10 min supine rest. It is the first-line diagnostic test (ACC/AHA 2024 Class 1 for patients with suggestive history/examination).

    Borderline Exercise ABI

    ABI ≤ 0.90 Diagnostic of PAD (sens ~75%, spec ~85–95%) Risk-factor treatment; DUS if revascularisation considered

    TBI ≤ 0.70 Diagnostic of PAD when ABI unreliable Toe pressure also informs wound-healing potential Severity is often graded as mild–moderate (ABI 0.40–0.90) and severe (ABI < 0.40). Both a low ABI (≤ 0.90) and a high ABI (> 1.40) independently predict cardiovascular death.

    BOARD PEARL — EXERCISE TESTING

    Symptoms of claudication with a normal resting ABI: do a treadmill test. PAD is confirmed by a post-exercise fall in ankle pressure > 30 mmHg or a fall in ABI > 20% . Exercise testing also objectifies walking distance before and after therapy.

    EXAM TRAP

    A diabetic with a non-healing foot ulcer and an ABI of 1.6 does not have normal perfusion — the arteries are incompressible. Measure toe pressure/TBI (TBI ≤ 0.70; toe pressure < 30 mmHg predicts poor healing) or TcPO₂.

    Imaging

    Duplex ultrasound — first-line anatomical test: localises and grades stenosis (peak systolic velocity ratio ≥ 2.0–2.5 ≈ ≥ 50% stenosis).

    CTA / MRA — when revascularisation is planned (CTA overcalls in heavy calcification; MRA avoids iodinated contrast).

    Catheter angiography (DSA) — reserved for use with endovascular treatment.

    Screen other beds when clinically relevant: AAA (DUS), carotid in symptomatic patients, coronary symptoms.

    Clinical classifications

    Key highlightsPAD presentation & diagnosis

    • ABI = higher ankle pressure ÷ higher brachial pressure; ≤ 0.90 diagnoses PAD.
    • ABI 0.91–0.99 borderline; 1.00–1.40 normal; > 1.40 incompressible → TBI (≤ 0.70 abnormal).
    • Normal resting ABI + claudication → exercise ABI: ankle pressure fall > 30 mmHg or ABI fall > 20%.
    • Most PAD patients are asymptomatic; cardiovascular death, not amputation, dominates prognosis.
    • Leriche: buttock claudication, impotence, absent femoral pulses (aorto-iliac).
    • Fontaine IIa/IIb split at 200 m; Fontaine III–IV = Rutherford 4–6 = CLTI.
    • Duplex first for anatomy; CTA/MRA when planning revascularisation.
    • Recommendation Class Level
    • Symptomatic PAD: long-term single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 75–100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg). I A NEW Symptomatic PAD with high ischaemic risk and no high bleeding risk: rivaroxaban
    • 2.5 mg twice daily + aspirin 100 mg daily.
    • IIa A
    • Asymptomatic PAD with diabetes: aspirin may be considered. IIb A
    • After revascularisation / acute limb ischaemia
    • NEW After lower-limb revascularisation, in patients without high bleeding risk: rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid + aspirin.
    • IIa B
    • After revascularisation for ALI: DAPT or rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid + aspirin. IIa C

    26.2 PAD — Medical & Antithrombotic Therapy

    Medical therapy has two goals: reduce MACE (MI, stroke, CV death) and reduce MALE (major adverse limb events: acute limb ischaemia, major amputation, urgent revascularisation) — plus improve walking. Every patient with PAD needs the full secondary-prevention package regardless of symptoms.

    Risk-factor targets

    WHAT CHANGED IN 2024 (ESC)
    • LDL-C target lowered from < 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) to < 1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) with ≥ 50% reduction. BP target tightened from < 140/90 to SBP 120–129 mmHg.
    • Low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin incorporated for symptomatic PAD with high ischaemic risk and after revascularisation.
    • "Multisite artery disease" renamed polyvascular disease.

    Antithrombotic therapy

    MECHANISM — WHY A "VASCULAR DOSE" OF RIVAROXABAN

    Limb events are driven by thrombin generation on unstable plaque and on stents/grafts. Adding a factor Xa inhibitor at a quarter of the AF dose (2.5 mg bid) targets thrombin with a bleeding cost that is acceptable — dual pathway inhibition (platelet + coagulation).

    Exercise and symptom-relieving drugs

    Supervised exercise therapy is first-line for claudication (ESC I; ACC/AHA 1 A): walking to moderate– severe claudication pain, rest, repeat — ≥ 3 sessions/week, 30–60 min, for at least 12 weeks. Structured home-based programmes are the alternative.

    In CLEVER (aorto-iliac disease), supervised exercise improved walking time at least as much as stenting at 6 months — exercise before revascularisation for claudication .

    Cilostazol 100 mg bid (PDE-3 inhibitor, vasodilator + antiplatelet) improves walking distance (ACC/AHA 1 A); contraindicated in heart failure of any severity. Benefit appears after 4–12 weeks.

    Naftidrofuryl may be considered (ESC); pentoxifylline and chelation are ineffective (ACC/AHA Class 3). Revascularisation for claudication is considered only after ~3 months of optimal medical and exercise therapy with persistent lifestyle-limiting symptoms.

    EXAM TRAP

    The claudicant with HFrEF asking for "the tablet that helps walking" — cilostazol is contraindicated (PDE-3 inhibitors increased mortality in HF). And a patient with PAD and AF needs full-dose OAC for the AF, not additional routine antiplatelet therapy in stable disease.

    Polyvascular disease and screening other beds

    Roughly one in two to three patients with lower-limb PAD has coronary disease, and ~15–25% have ≥ 50% carotid stenosis; each additional affected bed adds incremental risk of MACE.

    Screening for asymptomatic disease in other beds is justified only when it changes management — e.g. ABI before saphenous vein harvesting for CABG, carotid duplex in patients with recent TIA/stroke before CABG, and AAA ultrasound in PAD patients at risk.

    Polyvascular disease is where the intensive package pays most: LDL-C < 55 mg/dL, dual pathway inhibition (rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid + aspirin, ESC IIa A) if bleeding risk is not high.

    26.3 Revascularisation, CLTI & Acute Limb Ischaemia

    Principles of revascularisation

    Key highlightsPAD medical therapy

    • SAPT (aspirin or clopidogrel) for all symptomatic PAD (I A).
    • Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid + aspirin 100 mg: ESC IIa (high ischaemic, low bleeding risk; IIa B after revascularisation) vs ACC/AHA Class 1.
    • COMPASS: MALE ↓ ~45%; VOYAGER: composite ↓ 15% after revascularisation, mainly ALI.
    • Full-dose OAC for PAD alone is harmful (WAVE).
    • ESC LDL-C < 55 mg/dL + ≥ 50% reduction; SBP 120–129.
    • Supervised exercise ≥ 3×/week, 30–60 min, ≥ 12 weeks — first-line for claudication.
    • Cilostazol 100 mg bid improves walking; contraindicated in HF.
    • SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA for diabetics with PAD; β-blockers are safe.
    • Subset Revascularise? Rationale
    • CLTI Yes — as soon as feasible (ACC/AHA 1 B-R) Limb salvage, wound healing,
    • pain relief
    • ALI Yes — urgency by Rutherford category Viability of limb (and life)

    Angiosome-directed where possible

    Conduit: autologous great saphenous vein beats prosthetic grafts below the knee. ESC and ACC/AHA advise sparing the GSV in PAD patients who may need CABG in future, and vice versa checking leg perfusion before harvesting vein for CABG.

    After endovascular therapy: DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 1–6 months, or rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid + aspirin (VOYAGER); SAPT long term.

    After revascularisation, follow up with clinical assessment, ABI and — for vein grafts — duplex surveillance.

    Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI)

    DEFINITION

    CLTI: PAD with ischaemic rest pain, non-healing wound/ulcer or gangrene for > 2 weeks, with objective evidence of hypoperfusion — typically ankle pressure < 50 mmHg, toe pressure < 30 mmHg or TcPO₂ < 30 mmHg. Rest pain is worse at night and relieved by hanging the leg over the bed (gravity).

    CLINICAL APPROACH — CLTI
    • Refer urgently to a multidisciplinary vascular/diabetic foot team; stage with WIf I (limb threat) and anatomical complexity (GLASS).
    • Revascularise as soon as feasible; treat infection (debridement, antibiotics), offload the foot, control pain.

    BEST-CLI: surgical bypass with an adequate single-segment GSV beat endovascular-first for MALE/ death; no difference without adequate vein. BASIL-2: in mainly infrapopliteal disease, endovascularfirst had better amputation-free survival than vein bypass. Primary amputation when the limb is non-salvageable, non-ambulatory patients with contractures, or overwhelming sepsis.

    • Full secondary prevention — one-year mortality approaches that of many cancers.
    • Acute limb ischaemia (ALI)

    ALI is a sudden decrease in limb perfusion (< 2 weeks) threatening viability. Skeletal muscle tolerates roughly 4–6 hours of warm ischaemia — time is muscle. Classic features: the 6 Ps — pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paraesthesia, paralysis (the last two signal a threatened limb).

    BOARD PEARL

    The discriminating test at the bedside is sensation and movement : once the patient cannot move the toes or has sensory loss above them, the limb is immediately threatened (IIb) and needs emergency revascularisation. An audible venous Doppler signal separates a threatened (II) from an irreversible (III) limb. After embolic ALI from AF, lifelong OAC is indicated.

    Non-atherosclerotic causes of limb ischaemia

    Key highlightsRevascularisation, CLTI & ALI

    • Do not revascularise asymptomatic PAD; claudication only after ~3 months exercise + OMT; CLTI always if feasible.
    • Common femoral disease → endarterectomy; aorto-iliac → endovascular first; long femoro-popliteal occlusion → GSV bypass.
    • CLTI: rest pain/ulcer/gangrene > 2 weeks + ankle pressure < 50, toe pressure < 30, TcPO₂ < 30 mmHg.
    • WIfI ischaemia grade 3 = ABI ≤ 0.39, toe pressure < 30 mmHg.
    • BEST-CLI favours vein bypass when good GSV exists; BASIL-2 favours endovascular for infrapopliteal disease.
    • ALI: heparin immediately; Rutherford I viable, IIa marginally, IIb immediately threatened, III irreversible.
    • IIb = sensory loss beyond toes or weakness → emergency revascularisation; III → amputation.
    • Reperfusion: compartment syndrome (fasciotomy), hyperkalaemia, rhabdomyolysis.

    26.4 Carotid, Vertebral & Subclavian Disease

    Why carotid stenosis matters

    Atherosclerosis at the carotid bifurcation causes ~10–15% of ischaemic strokes, mostly by artery-to-artery embolism rather than low flow. Risk is highest in the first days after a TIA or minor stroke (up to ~20% recurrence within 2 weeks in severe symptomatic stenosis), which is why speed to endarterectomy is the single most important examinable concept.

    Symptomatic = ipsilateral carotid-territory TIA, amaurosis fugax (transient monocular blindness) or non-disabling stroke within the previous 6 months.

    A carotid bruit is a poor marker of stenosis; screening of the unselected population is not recommended.

    Grading stenosis

    ESVS and ESC recommend grading by the NASCET method (narrowest residual lumen vs the normal distal ICA). The older ECST method compares with the estimated original bulb diameter and gives higher numbers (NASCET 50% ≈ ECST 75%; NASCET 70% ≈ ECST 85%).

    EXAM TRAP

    Velocities can fall in near-occlusion (string sign) and rise in the contralateral ICA when one side is occluded — overestimating that side. In near-occlusion the benefit of CEA is marginal; revascularisation is generally reserved for recurrent symptoms. Complete occlusion is never an indication for CEA.

    Symptomatic carotid stenosis

    MECHANISM — WHY "THE SOONER THE BETTER"

    A recently symptomatic plaque is unstable (thin cap, ulceration, intraplaque haemorrhage) and keeps embolising. Pooled NASCET/ECST data show that the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke is about 5 when CEA is done within 2 weeks but rises steeply thereafter; for 50–69% stenosis

    the benefit is almost lost beyond 12 weeks . Women and patients > 75 years gain most from early surgery.

    CEA versus CAS

    DAPT for ≥ 1 month, then SAPT

    Transcarotid artery revascularisation (TCAR, with flow reversal) is an alternative in North America for high-surgical-risk patients.

    Asymptomatic carotid stenosis

    With modern best medical therapy the annual ipsilateral stroke risk is low (≈ 1% or less), so intervention must be selective: stenosis 60–99% + one or more high-risk features + life expectancy > 5 years + centre stroke/death rate ≤ 3%.

    High-risk features (ESVS 2023)
    • Silent ipsilateral infarction on CT/MRI
    • Stenosis progression (> 20%)
    • Spontaneous embolisation on transcranial Doppler
    • Impaired cerebrovascular reserve
    • Large, echolucent plaque or juxtaluminal black area
    • Intraplaque haemorrhage on MRI
    • Contralateral TIA/stroke
    Recommendations
    • BMT for all: antiplatelet (aspirin), statin, BP control (ESC/
    • ESVS).
    • Asymptomatic 60–99% + ≥ 1 high-risk feature, average
    • surgical risk: CEA should be considered (IIa B).
    • CAS may be considered as an alternative (IIb B).
    • No high-risk feature → BMT alone.
    • ACC/AHA: CEA reasonable for asymptomatic ≥ 70% in
    • low-risk patients.

    Carotid disease and cardiac surgery

    Before CABG, duplex screening is advised in patients with TIA/stroke in the previous 6 months (ESC 2024 downgraded to IIa B); not in urgent CABG without recent neurological events.

    Recently symptomatic 50–99% stenosis should be revascularised (CEA before or with CABG); routine prophylactic CEA for asymptomatic stenosis before CABG is not recommended — most perioperative strokes are aortic/embolic, not carotid.

    Vertebral and subclavian disease

    Key highlightsCarotid, vertebral & subclavian

    • Symptomatic = carotid-territory event within 6 months; grade by NASCET.
    • Duplex ≥ 70%: PSV > 230 cm/s, EDV > 100, ratio > 4; 50–69%: PSV 125–230.
    • Symptomatic 70–99% → CEA (I A); 50–69% → CEA (IIa A); < 50% → no (III); occlusion → never.
    • Operate within 14 days; peri-operative stroke/death must be < 6% (symptomatic) or ≤ 3% (asymptomatic).
    • Age ≥ 70 → CEA over CAS; CAS: more stroke, CEA: more MI and cranial nerve injury.
    • Asymptomatic 60–99% → CEA only with high-risk features and life expectancy > 5 years (IIa B).
    • DAPT ≥ 1 month after CAS.
    • Inter-arm SBP difference ≥ 15 mmHg → subclavian stenosis; coronary-subclavian steal after LIMA grafting.
    • Feature Atherosclerotic RAS (~90%) Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD)
    • Screen other beds Coronary, carotid, PAD, AAA Head-to-pelvis imaging once in life (cervical/ intracranial FMD, aneurysms)

    26.5 Renal & Mesenteric Artery Disease

    Renal artery disease

    Clinical clues to RAS
    • Hypertension onset < 30 y (FMD) or severe onset > 55 y
    • Resistant, malignant or accelerated hypertension
    • Creatinine rise > 30% after ACEi/ARB
    • Flash pulmonary oedema (Pickering syndrome) with
    • preserved LV
    • Kidney size asymmetry > 1.5 cm; abdominal bruit;
    • unexplained hypokalaemia
    Diagnosis
    • Duplex first: PSV > 200 cm/s ≈ ≥ 60% stenosis; renalaortic ratio > 3.5
    • Resistive index > 0.80 suggests parenchymal disease —
    • poor response to revascularisation
    • CTA (eGFR ≥ 60) or MRA (no gadolinium if eGFR very
    • low)
    • Captopril scintigraphy, renin measurements: not
    • recommended
    • ACEi/ARB are recommended for hypertension with unilateral RAS; use with caution (monitor creatinine) in bilateral severe RAS or a solitary kidney.

    Revascularisation may be considered for recurrent flash pulmonary oedema or unexplained recurrent HF with severe (usually bilateral) RAS , rapidly declining renal function, or resistant hypertension — in selected patients only.

    Mesenteric artery disease

    DON'T CONFUSE
    • Median arcuate ligament (Dunbar) syndrome: coeliac compression that worsens in expiration, young women — not atherosclerosis.
    • Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia: low-output states, cardiac surgery, digoxin/vasopressors — treat the haemodynamics (± intra-arterial vasodilator).
    • Mesenteric venous thrombosis: thrombophilia, cirrhosis, malignancy — anticoagulation.

    26.6 Stroke Prevention, PFO & Cardioembolic Stroke

    Mechanism first — TOAST classification

    Key highlightsRenal & mesenteric disease

    • Atherosclerotic RAS: ostial, older patients; routine stenting not recommended (ASTRAL, CORAL; ESC III A).
    • FMD: young women, mid-distal "string of beads" — balloon angioplasty without stent (IIa B).
    • RAS clues: creatinine rise > 30% on ACEi/ARB, flash pulmonary oedema, kidney asymmetry > 1.5 cm.
    • Duplex: renal PSV > 200 cm/s / RAR > 3.5; RI > 0.80 predicts poor response.
    • Consider renal revascularisation for recurrent flash pulmonary oedema with severe bilateral RAS.
    • AMI: pain out of proportion → immediate CTA; endovascular first for SMA occlusion (ESC 2024 I B).
    • CMI: post-prandial pain, food fear, weight loss; ≥ 2 vessels diseased; revascularise without nutritional delay.
    EXAM TRAP — ESUS

    Embolic stroke of undetermined source is not an indication for empirical anticoagulation: rivaroxaban (NAVIGATE-ESUS) and dabigatran (RE-SPECT ESUS) were no better than aspirin. The right next step is prolonged rhythm monitoring (e.g. implantable loop recorder) to find occult AF, and a search for PFO in the young.

    Patent foramen ovale and cryptogenic stroke

    A PFO is present in ~25% of adults, so most PFOs found after a stroke are bystanders. Closure trials (CLOSE, RESPECT, REDUCE, DEFENSE-PFO) showed a reduction in recurrent stroke in carefully selected patients aged ~18–60 with a non-lacunar cryptogenic stroke, especially with an atrial septal aneurysm or a large shunt. The cost is new-onset AF (~2–5%, mostly transient and within 45 days) and device complications.

    Cortical infarct on imaging 1 Age 60–69 / ≥ 70 1 / 0

    A higher score (young, no vascular risk factors, cortical infarct) means the PFO is more likely to be the culprit; a RoPE ≥ 7 is the usual cut-off.

    When to start anticoagulation after AF-related stroke

    The tension is between early recurrent embolism (highest in the first 2 weeks) and haemorrhagic transformation of the infarct (larger infarcts bleed more). The old empirical "1-3-6-12 day" rule (TIA → day 1; small → day 3; moderate → day 6; large → day 12) has been superseded by randomised evidence showing that early DOAC start is safe.

    Delay; individualise

    BOARD PEARL

    AF detected after a stroke ("AF detected after stroke") still earns OAC. A patient who has a stroke while on a DOAC should not simply be switched to another DOAC or have an antiplatelet added — look for a competing mechanism (carotid disease, adherence, dosing error, LAA thrombus).

    Key highlightsStroke prevention, PFO & cardioembolism

    • Minor stroke (NIHSS ≤ 3)/high-risk TIA (ABCD² ≥ 4): aspirin + clopidogrel for 21–90 days (I A).
    • Post-stroke targets: LDL-C < 70 mg/dL (AHA/ASA; ESC < 55), BP < 130/80.
    • Intracranial 70–99%: DAPT up to 90 days; no first-line stenting (SAMMPRIS).
    • ESUS → no empirical OAC; prolonged monitoring for AF.
    • PFO closure: age 18–60 (–65), non-lacunar cryptogenic stroke, RoPE ≥ 7 and/or ASA/large shunt (PASCAL possible/probable).
    • PASCAL "unlikely" (RoPE < 7, no high-risk feature) → no closure.
    • ELAN: DOAC within 48 h (minor/moderate) or day 6–7 (major) is safe; replaces the 1-3-6-12 rule.
    • Endocarditis-related stroke: no anticoagulation or thrombolysis.

    26.7 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD has calf pain on walking. Pulses are difficult to feel; ABI is 1.52 on the right and 1.48 on the left. What is the best next test?

    Answer B ABI > 1.40 = non-compressible calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD) — the ABI is uninterpretable, not normal. Toe arteries are usually spared from calcification: TBI ≤ 0.70 diagnoses PAD.

    Q2 A 64-year-old smoker has typical calf claudication at 150 m. Resting ABI is 0.98. Which finding after treadmill exercise confirms PAD?

    Answer B Borderline resting ABI with typical symptoms → exercise test. Diagnostic: fall in ankle pressure > 30 mmHg or ABI fall > 20%. A 10% fall is within normal variation.

    Q3 A 70-year-old man with prior femoro-popliteal stenting for claudication and stable CAD, eGFR 65, no bleeding history, is on aspirin 100 mg. Which addition is supported by trial evidence to reduce both MACE and major limb events?

    Answer C Dual pathway inhibition — rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bid + aspirin — reduced MACE and MALE in COMPASS and limb/CV events after revascularisation in VOYAGER PAD (ESC IIa; ACC/AHA Class 1). Full-dose OAC (D, E) increases bleeding without benefit; EUCLID showed ticagrelor ≈ clopidogrel.

    Q4 A 66-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 30%) has lifestyle-limiting claudication despite 3 months of supervised exercise. Which drug is contraindicated?

    Answer B Cilostazol (PDE-3 inhibitor) is contraindicated in heart failure of any severity. Statins, clopidogrel, β-blockers and ACEi are all appropriate in PAD with HFrEF.

    Q5 A 74-year-old woman with AF not on anticoagulation has a cold, pale right leg for 5 hours. She has numbness of the foot and forefoot and cannot dorsiflex the toes; venous Doppler signal is audible, arterial is absent. After IV heparin, what is the best management?

    Answer B Sensory loss beyond the toes and motor weakness with audible venous signal = Rutherford IIb (immediately threatened) — emergency revascularisation; for an embolus from AF, surgical embolectomy. Slow thrombolysis suits IIa; amputation is for III (paralysis, no venous signal).

    Q6 A 72-year-old man had a 20-minute episode of right-hand weakness and dysphasia 4 days ago. Duplex shows left ICA PSV 290 cm/s, EDV 120 cm/s, ICA/CCA ratio 5. He is fit for surgery. What is the best management?

    Answer C Duplex = ≥ 70% stenosis (PSV > 230, EDV > 100, ratio > 4) and symptomatic within 6 months → CEA (I A) within 14 days. At age ≥ 70, CEA is preferred over CAS (higher peri-procedural stroke with stenting, especially early after symptoms).

    Q7 A 69-year-old asymptomatic man awaiting elective CABG has a 75% right ICA stenosis on screening duplex; no previous TIA/stroke, no silent infarcts on imaging, stable plaque. What is recommended?

    Answer D Routine prophylactic carotid revascularisation for asymptomatic stenosis before CABG is not recommended; perioperative strokes are mostly aortic/embolic. Consider revascularisation before CABG only for recently symptomatic 50– 99% stenosis.

    Q8 A 62-year-old woman with bilateral atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (80% right, 70% left) has had two admissions with flash pulmonary oedema despite a normal LVEF and optimised therapy. What is the most appropriate step?

    Answer C Routine stenting of atherosclerotic RAS is not recommended (ASTRAL, CORAL), but recurrent flash pulmonary oedema with severe bilateral RAS is the accepted exception where revascularisation may be considered. Plain angioplasty is for FMD; captopril scintigraphy is obsolete; ACEi is hazardous in bilateral severe RAS.

    Q9 A 38-year-old non-smoking normotensive woman without diabetes has a cortical embolic stroke with no other cause after full work-up including 30-day monitoring. TOE shows a PFO with an atrial septal aneurysm and a large shunt. Her RoPE score is 9. What is the best advice?

    Answer C RoPE ≥ 7 plus atrial septal aneurysm/large shunt = PASCAL "probable" — the group with the greatest benefit from device closure (CLOSE, RESPECT, REDUCE), followed by antiplatelet therapy. OAC is not superior without another indication.

    Q10 A 76-year-old man with newly diagnosed AF has a minor ischaemic stroke (infarct 1.2 cm, NIHSS 2); no haemorrhage on MRI; BP controlled. When should apixaban be started?

    Answer A ELAN: for minor or moderate strokes, DOAC within 48 h was at least as safe as later start (sICH 0.2% both) with fewer recurrent events. Day 12–14 applies only to the "late" arm for major strokes; DAPT is inferior to OAC for AF.

    27.1 Principles & Risk Estimation

    Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) is driven by a small number of causal, modifiable exposures: apoB-containing lipoproteins, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and adiposity. The absolute benefit of any preventive drug equals relative risk reduction × baseline absolute risk — so the first step is always to estimate absolute risk.

    DEFINITIONS
    • Primordial prevention — preventing risk factors from developing (population diet, tobacco control).
    • Primary prevention — treating risk factors in people without clinical ASCVD.
    • Secondary prevention — preventing recurrence after an ASCVD event (ACS, stroke/TIA, PAD, revascularisation) or with unequivocal plaque on imaging.

    Who does NOT need a risk calculator

    Both ESC and ACC/AHA place certain patients directly into a high or very-high-risk category; calculators were not derived in them and under-estimate their risk.

    FH with ASCVD or with another major risk factor

    High risk Markedly elevated single risk factor: TC > 8 mmol/L (310 mg/dL), LDL-C > 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/ dL) or BP ≥ 180/110 mmHg

    • FH without other major risk factors
    • Diabetes without TOD, duration ≥ 10 y or with another risk factor

    Moderate CKD — eGFR 30–59

    Moderate risk Young diabetics (T1DM < 35 y; T2DM < 50 y) with duration < 10 y and no other risk factor ESC/EAS 2019 Dyslipidaemias and ESC 2021 Prevention. Diabetes-specific risk now uses SCORE2-Diabetes (Chapter 29). SCORE2 and SCORE2-OP (ESC)

    SCORE2 (age 40–69) and SCORE2-OP (age ≥ 70) estimate the 10-year risk of fatal AND non-fatal CVD (MI, stroke, CV death) — replacing the old SCORE, which predicted fatal events only. Inputs: age, sex, smoking, SBP and non-HDL-C. They are recalibrated to four risk regions (low, moderate, high, very high) by national CVD mortality; Egypt and most Arab countries fall into the high or very-high regions, so the correct chart matters.

    Very high ≥ 20% < 1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) and ≥ 50% ↓

    2025 Focused Update of the 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias (Eur Heart J 2025).

    BOARD PEARL — LIFETIME RISK IN THE YOUNG

    A 40-year-old smoker with SBP 160 mmHg may have a 10-year risk of only 3–4%, yet a very high lifetime risk. ESC 2021 therefore uses age-specific thresholds and encourages lifetime-benefit tools (LIFE-CVD).

    The corollary: in the elderly, a high 10-year risk is driven by age itself — use SCORE2-OP and weigh frailty, competing risk and patient preference.

    ESC 2021 stepwise approach

    ESC 2021 introduced a stepwise treatment-intensification concept: after risk classification, Step 1 goals are applied to everyone in the category (e.g. SBP < 140 → 130 mmHg, LDL-C < 2.6 mmol/L in high-risk apparently healthy people, smoking cessation), and Step 2 intensifies to the final goals (SBP < 130, LDL-C < 1.8 or < 1.4 mmol/L) after shared decision-making that weighs residual/lifetime risk, comorbidity, frailty and preference. PREVENT (ACC/AHA)

    The AHA PREVENT equations (2023) replace the Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) in the 2025 BP and 2026 dyslipidaemia guidelines. Key differences an examiner will test: Age range 30–79 years; includes a 30-year risk

    • estimate.
    • Predicts total CVD, ASCVD and heart failure.
    • Race removed as a variable.
    • Adds eGFR, statin and antihypertensive use;
    • optional UACR, HbA1c and a social-deprivation
    • index.
    • PCE over-estimated risk by roughly 2-fold;
    • PREVENT yields lower absolute numbers, so
    • treatment thresholds were lowered.
    EXAM TRAP

    Do not run SCORE2 in a patient who already has ASCVD, diabetes with target-organ damage, CKD or FH — they are categorised directly. And SCORE2 is not valid in secondary hypertension (e.g. primary aldosteronism) or in pregnancy.

    Key highlightsPrinciples & risk estimation

    • SCORE2 (40–69) and SCORE2-OP (≥ 70) predict fatal + non-fatal 10-year CVD using non-HDL-C, and are region-calibrated.
    • ESC 2021 thresholds are age-specific: very high risk = ≥ 7.5% (< 50 y), ≥ 10% (50–69 y), ≥ 15% (≥ 70 y).
    • ESC/EAS 2025 lipid categories: low < 2%, moderate 2–< 10%, high 10–< 20%, very high ≥ 20%.
    • Documented ASCVD (clinical or unequivocal imaging), eGFR < 30, and diabetes with TOD = very high risk without a calculator.
    • LDL-C > 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL), BP ≥ 180/110 or eGFR 30–59 = high risk.
    • PREVENT (ages 30–79) replaced the PCE in US guidelines: no race term, adds eGFR, predicts HF; categories < 3 / 3–5 / 5–10 / ≥ 10%.
    • Absolute benefit = relative risk reduction × baseline risk — treat the risk, not the number.
    • Domain Examples (thresholds)
    • Subclinical atherosclerosis CAC score, carotid or femoral plaque on ultrasound, ABI < 0.9 ESC 2021 Prevention, ESC/EAS 2025, ACC/AHA 2019 and 2026.
    • Coronary artery calcium (CAC) score
    • A non-contrast, ECG-gated CT quantifies calcified plaque in Agatston units (AU). It is the single most powerful re-classifier of risk in intermediate-risk primary prevention, and — uniquely — a score of zero can de-escalate therapy.

    27.2 Risk Modifiers & Coronary Calcium

    Risk scores capture the major factors only. Risk modifiers (ESC) or risk-enhancing factors (ACC/AHA) are used when an individual lies near a treatment threshold, to move them up — or, in the case of CAC = 0, down.

    WHAT CHANGED IN 2025–2026
    • ESC/EAS 2025: risk modifiers — including elevated CAC, hs-CRP, Lp(a) > 50 mg/dL and subclinical plaque — upgraded to Class IIa (LOE B) for reclassification.
    • ACC/AHA 2026: selective CAC recommended in borderline/intermediate risk men ≥ 40 y and women ≥ 45 y; absolute CAC and its age/sex percentile both carry prognostic value.
    DON'T CONFUSE

    CAC score (non-contrast, calcified plaque burden, prevention tool) vs CCTA (contrast, stenosis and noncalcified plaque, symptomatic patients). Statins increase plaque calcification (densification) — so CAC rises on therapy; do not repeat CAC to "monitor" a treated patient.

    Key highlightsRisk modifiers & CAC

    • Use modifiers only near a decision threshold — they reclassify, they do not replace the score.
    • Premature family history: first-degree male < 55 y, female < 65 y (ACC/AHA; ESC uses < 60 for women in FH scores).
    • hs-CRP ≥ 2 mg/L, Lp(a) > 50 mg/dL, apoB ≥ 130 mg/dL, TG ≥ 175 mg/dL = enhancers.
    • Pre-eclampsia and premature menopause (< 40 y) are sex-specific enhancers.
    • CAC 0 → defer statin (not in diabetes, smokers, FH); CAC ≥ 100 or ≥ 75th percentile → statin.
    • CAC rises on statins — never use it to monitor therapy.

    27.3 Lifestyle & Smoking Cessation

    Lifestyle is the foundation at every risk level and the only intervention for most low-risk people. Boards test the numeric targets.

    Tobacco — why it matters

    A lifelong smoker has about a 50% chance of dying from smoking and loses about 10 years of life; CV risk in smokers < 50 y is about 5-fold higher.

    Mechanisms: endothelial dysfunction, increased platelet activation and fibrinogen (prothrombotic), carbon monoxide (↓ O₂ delivery), sympathetic activation, oxidised LDL, ↓ HDL.

    Risk falls quickly after stopping — excess coronary risk roughly halves within 1–2 years; stopping after MI reduces mortality by about one third, more than most drugs.

    No safe threshold: even 1 cigarette/day carries about half the excess coronary risk of 20/day (non-linear dose–response).

    BOARD PEARL — E-CIGARETTES

    E-cigarettes deliver nicotine without combustion and help some smokers quit, but they are not risk-free (sympathetic activation, endothelial effects) and dual use is common. ESC 2021: they may be considered as a cessation aid only, with the aim of stopping them too. Heated-tobacco products are tobacco — not a cessation tool.

    Key highlightsLifestyle & smoking

    • Activity: 150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous per week + resistance training ≥ 2 days.
    • Salt < 5 g/day; alcohol < 100 g/week (ESC); waist < 94 / < 80 cm.
    • Smoking cessation after MI cuts mortality by about one third — the most powerful secondary-prevention "drug".
    • Varenicline is the most effective agent; start 1–2 weeks before quit date, continue 12 weeks.
    • NRT is safe in stable CAD and after ACS; combination NRT beats single-form NRT.
    • Even 1 cigarette/day carries roughly half the excess coronary risk of a pack a day.
    • Measuring lipids
    • Non-fasting samples are acceptable for screening and risk estimation; fasting is preferred when TG > 4.5 mmol/L (400 mg/dL).
    • LDL-C is usually calculated. Friedewald (LDL = TC − HDL − TG/2.2 in mmol/L) under-estimates LDL-C when TG is high or LDL-C is very low; it is invalid at TG > 4.5 mmol/L. The Martin–Hopkins or Sampson equations or direct LDL-C are preferred.
    • Non-HDL-C (TC − HDL-C) captures all apoB-containing particles; it is the secondary target, especially with high TG, diabetes, obesity or very low LDL-C.
    • ApoB counts atherogenic particles directly (one apoB per particle) — the most accurate measure of atherogenic burden when LDL-C and particle number are discordant.

    27.4 Lipoprotein Metabolism Essentials

    Every drug in this chapter acts on one step of lipoprotein traffic. Understand three pathways — exogenous (gut → chylomicrons), endogenous (liver → VLDL → IDL → LDL) and reverse cholesterol transport (HDL) — and the mechanism questions answer themselves.

    MECHANISM — THE LDL RECEPTOR IS THE HUB

    Hepatocyte cholesterol falls (statin blocks HMG-CoA reductase; bempedoic acid blocks ATP-citrate lyase upstream; ezetimibe blocks intestinal NPC1L1) → SREBP-2 activation → more LDL receptors → more LDL cleared .

    PCSK9 binds the LDL receptor and sends it to lysosomal degradation. PCSK9 antibodies (evolocumab, alirocumab) bind circulating PCSK9; inclisiran (siRNA) stops hepatic PCSK9 synthesis → receptors recycle.

    Statins also up-regulate PCSK9 — one reason why doubling a statin dose adds only about 6% more LDLC lowering ("rule of 6"). Therapies that rely on the receptor fail in receptor-negative homozygous FH; there, receptorindependent drugs (evinacumab, lomitapide, apheresis) are needed.

    SECONDARY DYSLIPIDAEMIA — EXCLUDE BEFORE LABELLING "PRIMARY"
    • Raise LDL-C
    • Hypothyroidism
    • Nephrotic syndrome
    • Cholestasis
    • Anorexia nervosa
    • Drugs: ciclosporin, progestins, anabolic
    • steroids, some antiretrovirals
    • Raise TG
    • Diabetes / insulin resistance, obesity
    • Alcohol
    • CKD, pregnancy
    • Drugs: oral oestrogen, glucocorticoids,
    • retinoids, thiazides, non-selective β-blockers,
    • atypical antipsychotics, protease inhibitors

    Key highlightsLipoprotein metabolism

    • LDL is the causal agent of ASCVD; each LDL, VLDL, IDL and Lp(a) particle carries one apoB-100.
    • Chylomicrons carry apoB-48 and cause pancreatitis, not atherosclerosis.
    • Statins, ezetimibe, bempedoic acid and PCSK9 blockade all work by increasing hepatic LDL-receptor activity.
    • Doubling a statin dose gives only about 6% extra LDL-C reduction.
    • Friedewald LDL-C is invalid if TG > 4.5 mmol/L (400 mg/dL) — use direct LDL-C, non-HDL-C or apoB.
    • Non-HDL-C goal = LDL-C goal + 0.8 mmol/L (30 mg/dL); apoB goals 65 / 80 / 100 mg/dL.
    • Always exclude hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome and cholestasis in new hypercholesterolaemia.

    27.5 LDL-C Targets: ESC vs ACC/AHA

    Three facts from the trials underpin every target: the relationship between LDL-C and risk is log-linear with no lower threshold; each 1 mmol/L (38.7 mg/dL) reduction lowers major vascular events by about 22% (CTT) irrespective of the drug used; and the absolute benefit is greatest in those at highest risk with the highest starting LDL-C. Hence the ESC motto: "the lower, the better — for longer".

    Acute coronary syndrome — 2025 focused update

    NEW Patients already on lipid-lowering therapy at the time of ACS: intensify therapy during the index hospitalisation.

    I C

    NEW Treatment-naïve ACS patients unlikely to reach goal with a statin alone: start high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe during the index hospitalisation.

    IIa B

    The 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline replaced the 2018 cholesterol guideline. Its headline change is that it re-introduced numeric LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals, converging with the ESC after nearly a decade of "statin-intensity and threshold" thinking.

    WHAT CHANGED — 2025 ESC/EAS AND 2026 ACC/AHA

    ESC/EAS 2025: goals unchanged; SCORE2/SCORE2-OP categories unified; combination therapy early in ACS; bempedoic acid, evinacumab and icosapent ethyl recommendations; statins for people with HIV aged ≥ 40 y ( I B, REPRIEVE); supplements not recommended ( III B).

    ACC/AHA 2026: goals restored; PREVENT replaces PCE; Lp(a) measured at least once in every adult; apoB to assess residual risk; LDL-lowering therapy for diabetes, CKD stage ≥ 3 and HIV at age 40–75 regardless of LDL-C.

    EXAM TRAP

    The ESC goal is both the absolute number and a ≥ 50% reduction. A very-high-risk patient whose baseline LDL-C is 1.6 mmol/L is not "at goal" at 1.3 mmol/L — the target is ≤ 0.8 mmol/L (50% of baseline). Conversely, never stop or reduce effective therapy because LDL-C is "too low": levels below 0.5 mmol/L in FOURIER and ODYSSEY were safe.

    Key highlightsLDL-C targets

    • Each 1 mmol/L LDL-C reduction → about 22% fewer major vascular events, independent of drug class.
    • ESC goals: very high < 1.4, high < 1.8, moderate < 2.6, low < 3.0 mmol/L; plus ≥ 50% reduction in high/very high risk.
    • Second event within 2 y on maximal statin: consider LDL-C < 1.0 mmol/L (IIb).
    • ESC 2025: in ACS, intensify during index admission (I); statin + ezetimibe upfront in naïve patients (IIa).
    • ACC/AHA 2026 restored goals: very high-risk ASCVD < 55, other ASCVD < 70, borderline/intermediate primary prevention < 100 mg/dL.
    • Very low LDL-C on therapy is safe — no lower threshold of harm has been identified.
    • Safety and interactions

    27.6 Statins & Statin Intolerance

    Statins are first-line in all risk categories requiring drug therapy. Beyond LDL-C lowering they have modest pleiotropic effects (↓ hs-CRP, plaque stabilisation), but the clinical benefit is explained by LDL-C reduction.

    Adverse effects
    • Muscle symptoms (see below); rhabdomyolysis
    • very rare (~1/10 000/year).
    • ALT rise — stop if persistently > 3× ULN; routine
    • monitoring not needed after baseline.
    • New-onset diabetes: ~1 extra case per 1000
    • patient-years, mostly in those with prediabetes —
    • benefit far outweighs risk.
    • No causal link to cancer, cognitive decline or
    • haemorrhagic stroke in trial meta-analyses
    • (SPARCL signal small).
    • Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding
    • (ACC/AHA 2026: defer most LLT during
    • conception, pregnancy and lactation).
    Interactions
    • CYP3A4 substrates: simvastatin, lovastatin,
    • atorvastatin. Inhibitors: clarithromycin, azoles,
    • HIV/HCV protease inhibitors, grapefruit,
    • ciclosporin.
    • Simvastatin caps: ≤ 20 mg with amiodarone or
    • amlodipine; ≤ 10 mg with diltiazem or
    • verapamil.
    • Rosuvastatin and pravastatin are not CYP3A4-
    • dependent (safer choice).
    • Gemfibrozil + any statin → avoid (inhibits
    • glucuronidation); fenofibrate is the fibrate of
    • choice with statins.
    • Statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS)

    Up to 10–20% of patients report muscle symptoms in observational practice, but in blinded trials the excess over placebo is small. N-of-1 trials (SAMSON, StatinWISE) showed that about 90% of symptoms also occur on placebo — the nocebo effect.

    CK>4×ULN?
    • ▼
    • NO
    • Stop statin 2–4 weeks → symptoms resolve?
    • ▼
    • Rechallenge: same statin lower dose, different statin
    • (rosuva/prava), or alternate-day dosing
    • YES
    • Stop statin; recheck CK in 2–6 weeks
    • ▼
    • If CK normalises: cautious low-dose rechallenge; if > 10×
    • ULN — do not rechallenge
    • ▼
    • Goal not met / intolerant of ≥ 2 statins → add ezetimibe → bempedoic acid → PCSK9 mAb / inclisiran
    DEFINITION — STATIN INTOLERANCE

    Inability to tolerate at least 2 different statins, one at the lowest approved daily dose, because of symptoms or laboratory abnormalities that resolve with dechallenge and are not explained by another cause (NLA/ ILEP). Partial intolerance (a tolerated low dose) is far more common than complete intolerance.

    BOARD PEARL — RISK FACTORS FOR SAMS

    Older age, female sex, low body mass, hypothyroidism, CKD, liver disease, heavy alcohol, strenuous exercise, East Asian ancestry (rosuvastatin exposure ↑ — start 5 mg), SLCO1B1 variants (simvastatin), and interacting drugs. Hypothyroidism both causes myopathy and raises LDL-C — always check TSH.

    27.7 Non-Statin LDL-Lowering Therapy

    Every major non-statin class has now shown outcome benefit proportional to its LDL-C reduction — the strongest confirmation that LDL-C, not the statin, is the target.

    Key highlightsStatins & intolerance

    • High intensity (≥ 50% ↓) = atorvastatin 40–80 or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg.
    • Simvastatin caps: 20 mg with amiodarone/amlodipine, 10 mg with diltiazem/verapamil; avoid simvastatin 80 mg.
    • Never combine gemfibrozil with a statin; fenofibrate is acceptable.
    • SAMSON/StatinWISE: about 90% of muscle symptoms are nocebo — rechallenge is the rule.
    • Rhabdomyolysis: CK usually > 10× ULN with renal injury — stop permanently.
    • Persistent CK elevation after stopping → anti-HMGCR necrotising myopathy.
    • Statin intolerance = failure of ≥ 2 statins, one at the lowest dose.
    • Stop statin if ALT persistently > 3× ULN; the diabetes signal (~1/1000 per year) never outweighs benefit.

    MECHANISM — WHY BEMPEDOIC ACID SPARES MUSCLE

    Bempedoic acid needs the enzyme very-long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase-1 (ACSVL1) for activation. ACSVL1 is present in the liver but not in skeletal muscle, so the drug inhibits cholesterol synthesis in hepatocytes only . The price is inhibition of renal uric-acid transport (OAT2) → hyperuricaemia and gout.

    CLINICAL APPROACH — HOW MUCH DO YOU NEED?
    • Calculate the % reduction required: (baseline − goal) / baseline.
    • High-intensity statin ≈ 50%; + ezetimibe ≈ 65%; + PCSK9 mAb ≈ 85%.
    • If the gap is > 50% (e.g. ACS with LDL-C 3.5 mmol/L and goal 1.4), start statin + ezetimibe upfront — the "strike early and strong" approach.
    EXAM TRAP

    Niacin (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE), CETP inhibitors (except the modest benefit of anacetrapib in REVEAL) and fibrates on top of statins (ACCORD-Lipid, PROMINENT) did not reduce events. Raising HDL-C is not a therapeutic goal.

    27.8 Hypertriglyceridaemia & Residual Risk

    Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (VLDL and remnants) are atherogenic because of the cholesterol and apoB they carry; lowering TG itself (fibrates, niacin, omega-3 mixtures) has not reduced events on top of statins. The one exception — icosapent ethyl — probably works through EPA-specific effects rather than TG lowering.

    Key highlightsNon-statin therapy

    • Sequence: max statin → ezetimibe (I B) → PCSK9 mAb in very high risk (I A); bempedoic acid in statin intolerance (I B, 2025).
    • Ezetimibe lowers LDL-C 20–25%; IMPROVE-IT proved "LDL-C lowering, not the statin" gives benefit.
    • PCSK9 mAbs lower LDL-C ~60% and Lp(a) ~25%; FOURIER and ODYSSEY both showed MACE ↓ 15%.
    • Inclisiran: siRNA dosed day 0, 3 months, then every 6 months; LDL-C ↓ ~50%.
    • CLEAR Outcomes: bempedoic acid in statin-intolerant patients → MACE ↓ 13%; watch gout and gallstones.
    • HoFH (receptor-negative): evinacumab (ANGPTL3), lomitapide, apheresis — PCSK9 blockade needs functioning receptors.
    • Supplements such as red yeast rice are Class III in ESC 2025.
    • Recommendation Class Level
    • High-risk or very-high-risk patients with TG 1.5–5.6 mmol/L (135–499 mg/dL) despite statin: icosapent ethyl 2 g twice daily in combination with the statin.
    • IIa B
    • Primary prevention patients at LDL-C goal with TG > 2.3 mmol/L: fenofibrate or bezafibrate may be considered with the statin.
    • IIb B
    • NEW Familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (TG usually > 750 mg/dL): volanesorsen (apoC-III
    • antisense) to lower TG and pancreatitis risk.
    • IIa B
    BOARD PEARL — AF WITH ICOSAPENT ETHYL

    High-dose omega-3 products increase atrial fibrillation in a dose-dependent manner (REDUCE-IT, STRENGTH and meta-analyses). A patient on icosapent ethyl presenting with new palpitations: think AF.

    They also modestly increase bleeding, especially with antithrombotics.

    DON'T CONFUSE — DYS BETA LIPOPROTEIN A EMI A

    Familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia (type III; apoE2/E2 plus a second hit such as obesity, diabetes or hypothyroidism) gives equally raised TC and TG (both ~7–10 mmol/L), palmar crease xanthomas (pathognomonic) and tuberoeruptive xanthomas. It responds very well to fibrates and statins.

    Key highlightsHypertriglyceridaemia

    • TG > 10 mmol/L (≈ 880–1000 mg/dL) → pancreatitis risk dominates: fat restriction, no alcohol, fibrate.
    • For moderate TG, statin to LDL-C/non-HDL-C goal comes first (I B).
    • Icosapent ethyl 2 g bd for TG 135–499 mg/dL on statin in high/very-high risk (IIa B) — REDUCE-IT MACE ↓ 25%.
    • EPA+DHA mixtures (STRENGTH) and low-dose fish oil are neutral — no class effect.
    • High-dose omega-3 → AF and bleeding.
    • Fibrates/niacin on top of statins have not reduced events; avoid gemfibrozil with statins.
    • Palmar crease xanthomas = dysbetalipoproteinaemia (apoE2/E2).

    27.9 Lipoprotein(a)

    Lp(a) is an LDL-like particle with apo(a) covalently attached to apoB-100. Its level is 70–90% genetically determined by the LPA gene (fewer kringle IV-2 repeats → smaller isoform → higher level), reaches adult values in early childhood and barely changes with diet or exercise. About 1 in 5 people have levels above 50 mg/dL; levels are higher in people of African ancestry.

    MECHANISM — THREE HARMFUL PROPERTIES

    Atherogenic — carries cholesterol into the arterial wall like LDL (per particle, more atherogenic than LDL).

    Pro-inflammatory — carries oxidised phospholipids that drive plaque inflammation and valve calcification (calcific aortic stenosis).

    Antifibrinolytic — apo(a) is homologous to plasminogen and may impair fibrinolysis.

    Management today

    No licensed Lp(a)-specific drug with proven outcome benefit yet — so treat the overall risk harder: lower LDL-C more aggressively and control BP, smoking and diabetes.

    PCSK9 mAbs lower Lp(a) by ~25%; post-hoc FOURIER/ODYSSEY data suggest greater absolute benefit when Lp(a) is high. Inclisiran lowers it by ~20%.

    Statins do not lower Lp(a) (may raise it modestly); niacin lowers it but gives no event benefit. Lipoprotein apheresis — for progressive ASCVD with very high Lp(a) in selected centres.

    In development: antisense pelacarsen (Lp(a)HORIZON), siRNAs olpasiran, lepodisiran, zerlasiran (Lp(a) ↓ > 80–90%), and oral muvalaplin. Outcome trials are the key open question.

    EXAM TRAP

    Lp(a) contributes to measured "LDL-C" (its cholesterol is included in the LDL-C assay/calculation). A patient with very high Lp(a) may appear statin-resistant because the Lp(a)-cholesterol fraction does not fall — check Lp(a) before labelling poor response or non-adherence.

    Key highlightsLipoprotein(a)

    • Lp(a) = LDL + apo(a); 70–90% genetically fixed; measure once in every adult.
    • ESC: > 50 mg/dL (> 105 nmol/L) is a risk modifier (IIa B); > 180 mg/dL ≈ HeFH-level lifetime risk.
    • ACC/AHA 2026: ≥ 125 nmol/L enhancer; ≥ 250 nmol/L high risk.
    • Linked to ASCVD and to calcific aortic stenosis.
    • Treatment: intensify LDL-C lowering and other risk factors; PCSK9 mAb lowers Lp(a) ~25%; apheresis in selected cases.
    • Statins do not lower Lp(a); high Lp(a) can mimic statin resistance.
    • Criterion Points
    • DNA analysis
    • Functional mutation in LDLR, APOB or PCSK9 8
    • Diagnosis (one score per group — the highest)
    • Definite FH > 8
    • Probable FH 6–8
    • Possible FH 3–5
    • Unlikely FH < 3

    27.10 Familial Hypercholesterolaemia

    Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) is an autosomal-dominant disorder of LDL clearance, the commonest monogenic disease in cardiology. Heterozygous FH affects about 1 in 200–300 people and, untreated, causes coronary disease decades early; homozygous FH affects about 1 in 300 000.

    EXAM TRAP — SCORING

    Only the single highest-scoring item within each group is counted. A patient with tendon xanthomas (6) and arcus < 45 y (4) scores 6 for the examination group, not 10.

    Management of heterozygous FH

    FH without ASCVD or another major risk factor = high risk → LDL-C < 1.8 mmol/L and ≥ 50% ↓. FH with ASCVD or another major risk factor = very high risk → < 1.4 mmol/L. Risk calculators do not apply. High-intensity statin + ezetimibe is usually needed; add a PCSK9 inhibitor if still above goal. Cascade screening of first-degree relatives (lipid profile ± genetic test) is the most cost-effective way to find new cases (I C).

    Children: diagnose from age 5 y (earlier if HoFH suspected); statin from about 6–10 y; LDL-C goal < 3.5 mmol/L (135 mg/dL) after age 10.

    Women: stop statins before conception and during pregnancy/lactation; bile-acid sequestrants or apheresis if needed.

    HOMOZYGOUS FH — RECOGNISE IT
    • Untreated LDL-C typically > 10 mmol/L (> 400 mg/dL); both parents with HeFH.
    • Cutaneous/tendon xanthomas before age 10 y; aortic root and supravalvular aortic stenosis; coronary disease in childhood or adolescence.
    • Treatment: statin + ezetimibe + PCSK9 mAb (if residual receptor activity), evinacumab, lomitapide, lipoprotein apheresis weekly or fortnightly; liver transplantation historically.

    Key highlightsFamilial hypercholesterolaemia

    • HeFH prevalence about 1 in 200–300; HoFH about 1 in 300 000.
    • LDLR mutations cause ~85–90%; PCSK9 gain-of-function; LDLRAP1 is recessive.
    • DLCN: definite > 8, probable 6–8, possible 3–5; tendon xanthoma = 6, LDL-C ≥ 8.5 mmol/L = 8, mutation = 8.
    • Count only the highest item per DLCN group.
    • FH = high risk; FH + ASCVD or another major risk factor = very high risk. Never use SCORE2.
    • Cascade screening of relatives; children treated from ~6–10 y, goal < 3.5 mmol/L.
    • HoFH: LDL-C > 10 mmol/L, childhood xanthomas, supravalvular AS → evinacumab, lomitapide, apheresis.

    27.11 Aspirin in Primary Prevention

    In secondary prevention low-dose aspirin is unequivocally beneficial. In primary prevention three contemporary trials in 2018 showed that the modest reduction in ischaemic events is offset by a similar absolute increase in major bleeding — in an era of statins, BP control and falling event rates.

    ACC/AHA 2019 Primary Prevention

    Aspirin 75–100 mg might be considered in selected adults aged 40–70 y at higher ASCVD risk and not at increased bleeding risk.

    • IIb A
    • Aspirin should not be given routinely for primary prevention in adults > 70 y. III B-R

    Aspirin should not be given for primary prevention at any age in people at increased bleeding risk. III C-LD USPSTF 2022: age 40–59 with 10-y risk ≥ 10% — individual decision (grade C); age ≥ 60 — do not initiate (grade D).

    BOARD PEARL — WHEN ASPIRIN IS "PRIMARY PREVENTION"

    A patient with a high CAC score (e.g. ≥ 100, particularly ≥ 400) and low bleeding risk is a reasonable aspirin candidate — the plaque makes this closer to secondary prevention. Likewise, unequivocal plaque on imaging places the patient in the ESC very-high-risk (ASCVD) category, where antiplatelet therapy follows chronic coronary syndrome guidance.

    Key highlightsAspirin in primary prevention

    • ARRIVE, ASCEND and ASPREE (2018): ischaemic benefit ≈ bleeding harm.
    • ESC 2021: consider aspirin only in diabetes at high/very-high risk (IIb A); not in low/moderate risk (III A).
    • ACC/AHA 2019: might be considered at age 40–70 with high risk and low bleeding risk (IIb A); not routinely at > 70 y (III).
    • USPSTF 2022: do not start aspirin for primary prevention at age ≥ 60 y.
    • ASPREE: aspirin in the elderly increased bleeding with no CV benefit.
    • High CAC or unequivocal plaque shifts the balance towards aspirin.

    27.12 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 58-year-old man had an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI 3 days ago. He was not on any lipid-lowering therapy. Admission LDL-C is 3.6 mmol/L (140 mg/dL). According to the 2025 ESC/EAS focused update, which is the most appropriate lipid strategy before discharge?

    Answer C The 2025 update endorses early combination therapy: treatment-naïve ACS patients unlikely to reach goal on a statin alone should start high-intensity statin + ezetimibe during the index admission (IIa B). A 60% reduction is needed (3.6 → < 1.4 mmol/L), beyond what a statin alone achieves. PCSK9 monotherapy and moderate-intensity statins are wrong first steps.

    Q2 A 45-year-old woman has LDL-C 6.8 mmol/L (263 mg/dL), tendon xanthomas on the Achilles tendons and arcus cornealis. Her father had an MI at 50. No genetic test is available. What is her Dutch Lipid Clinic Network score?

    Answer A Only the highest item in each group counts: family history (father with premature CAD) = 1; examination (tendon xanthoma 6 beats arcus 4) = 6; LDL-C 6.5–8.4 mmol/L = 5. Total 12 → definite FH (> 8). Adding arcus (answer B) or counting both is the classic error.

    Q3 A 62-year-old man with prior MI and LDL-C 1.3 mmol/L on atorvastatin 80 mg + ezetimibe has fasting TG 2.6 mmol/L (230 mg/dL). Which addition is supported by a positive outcome trial and a Class IIa ESC recommendation?

    Answer C REDUCE-IT (icosapent ethyl 4 g/day, TG 135–499 mg/dL on statin) reduced MACE by 25% → IIa B. Fibrates and niacin on statin have no outcome benefit; low-dose EPA+DHA and pemafibrate (PROMINENT) were neutral.

    Q4 A 66-year-old woman stopped atorvastatin and later rosuvastatin 5 mg because of diffuse myalgia (normal CK). She has type 2 diabetes and a SCORE2-Diabetes risk of 22%. LDL-C is 3.4 mmol/L. Which oral agent has shown reduction in MACE specifically in statin-intolerant patients?

    Answer B CLEAR Outcomes enrolled statin-intolerant patients: bempedoic acid reduced MACE by 13% → ESC 2025 Class I B. It is activated only in the liver, so muscle symptoms are rare. Ezetimibe's outcome data (IMPROVE-IT) are on top of a statin; red yeast rice is Class III.

    Q5 A 52-year-old asymptomatic man has an intermediate 10-year risk. He is a non-smoker without diabetes or family history of premature disease. A coronary artery calcium score is 0 AU. What is the most appropriate next step?

    Answer C CAC = 0 in an intermediate-risk patient without diabetes, smoking or strong family history carries a very low event rate — withholding statin and repeating CAC after several years is reasonable. CCTA is for symptoms; aspirin is not indicated.

    Q6 A 71-year-old man takes simvastatin 40 mg. He is started on a new drug for rate control of atrial fibrillation and 3 weeks later presents with severe proximal weakness, dark urine and CK 48× ULN. Which drug was most likely started?

    Answer C Diltiazem (and verapamil) inhibit CYP3A4 and raise simvastatin levels; the simvastatin cap is 10 mg with these drugs. Rhabdomyolysis follows. Beta-blockers, digoxin and apixaban have no such interaction.

    Q7 A 49-year-old man with an MI at 44 years has LDL-C 1.3 mmol/L on maximal therapy but a second MI now. His brother had a stroke at 46. Which single test is most likely to reveal an unrecognised inherited risk factor?

    Answer B Recurrent premature ASCVD despite controlled LDL-C with a family history is the textbook indication for Lp(a) — genetically determined and not reflected in routine lipids. hs-CRP is not inherited; homocysteine lowering has no benefit.

    Q8 A 74-year-old healthy woman with no vascular disease asks whether she should take aspirin 75 mg to "prevent a heart attack". Her 10-year risk is moderate, and she has no bleeding history. What is the best advice?

    Answer C ASPREE showed no benefit and more bleeding at ≥ 70 y; ACC/AHA 2019 gives Class III for routine primaryprevention aspirin in adults > 70 y, and ESC 2021 does not recommend it at moderate risk.

    Q9 A 36-year-old man has fasting TG 24 mmol/L (2120 mg/dL) after an episode of acute pancreatitis. He drinks heavily and has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. After treating the acute episode, which is the first priority in longterm management?

    Answer C With TG > 10 mmol/L, pancreatitis prevention dominates: remove secondary causes (alcohol, hyperglycaemia), restrict dietary fat and add a fibrate. Statins, PCSK9 inhibitors and ezetimibe target ASCVD risk, not chylomicronaemia.

    Q10 A 50-year-old woman with no CVD has a SCORE2 risk (high-risk region) of 12%. LDL-C is 3.8 mmol/L. Using the 2025 ESC/EAS categories, what is her LDL-C goal?

    Answer C SCORE2 10–< 20% = high risk in the 2025 categories → LDL-C < 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) with ≥ 50% reduction. < 1.4 applies at ≥ 20% or with ASCVD; < 1.0 is an optional goal after recurrent events.

    28.1 Definition & Classification

    Raised BP is the leading modifiable cause of death worldwide. Risk of coronary and stroke death rises continuously from about 115/75 mmHg; every 20/10 mmHg increase roughly doubles CV mortality, and every 10 mmHg SBP reduction lowers major CV events by about 20%, stroke by ~27% and HF by ~28%. Because the relationship is continuous, any definition is an operational threshold at which treatment does more good than harm.

    WHAT CHANGED IN ESC 2024
    • New category "elevated BP" (120–139/70–89) replaces "normal" and "high-normal"; grades 1–3 no longer drive treatment.
    • Decision to treat elevated BP depends on CV risk (SCORE2/SCORE2-OP ≥ 10% or a high-risk condition). Default SBP target lowered to 120–129 mmHg (from < 130–139 by age in 2018); DBP 70–79.
    • Broader primary-aldosteronism screening, renal denervation included, potassium-enriched salt substitutes, and a first dedicated section on women and sex-specific risk.

    Pathophysiology in one box

    MECHANISM — BP=CARDIAC OUTPUT×SVR

    Pressure natriuresis is reset: the kidney needs a higher pressure to excrete the daily sodium load (salt sensitivity — Guyton).

    RAAS and sympathetic overactivity → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, vascular remodelling. Arterial stiffness → early reflected wave → rising SBP, falling DBP → isolated systolic hypertension of the elderly (wide pulse pressure).

    Young hypertensives: high cardiac output / high DBP (think sympathetic, secondary causes); elderly: high SVR and stiffness.

    Key highlightsDefinition & classification

    • ESC 2024: non-elevated < 120/70, elevated 120–139/70–89, hypertension ≥ 140/90 mmHg.
    • AHA/ACC: stage 1 130–139/80–89, stage 2 ≥ 140/90 (unchanged in 2025).
    • ESH 2023 keeps grades 1–3; grade 3 = ≥ 180/110.
    • Each 10 mmHg SBP reduction ≈ 20% fewer major CV events.
    • Isolated systolic hypertension of the elderly reflects aortic stiffness.
    • Phenotype Office Out-of-office Significance

    • uncontrolled HTN
    • Uncontrolled on

    • Controlled Pseudo-resistance — do not escalate
    • Nocturnal HTN /
    • non-dipping

    28.2 BP Measurement & Out-of-Office Thresholds

    Most "treatment failures" are measurement failures. The board expects the standard technique and the outof-office equivalents.

    CLINICAL APPROACH — STANDARDISED OFFICE MEASUREMENT
    • Validated automated upper-arm device; cuff bladder covers 75–100% of arm circumference (too small a cuff over-reads).
    • Seated, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level, after 5 min rest; no caffeine, exercise or smoking for 30 min.
    • 3 readings 1–2 min apart; use the average of the last two.
    • Both arms at the first visit; use the higher arm thereafter. An inter-arm difference > 10 mmHg is associated with CV risk; > 15–20 mmHg suggests subclavian stenosis.
    • Standing BP at 1 and 3 min in the elderly, diabetics and anyone with dizziness.
    • Opportunistic screening (ESC 2024): at least every 3 years if age < 40 y, yearly at age ≥ 40 y.
    BOARD PEARL — ABPM VS HBPM
    • ABPM is the only method that measures night-time BP and dipping, the strongest predictor of outcome.
    • HBPM is better for long-term titration and adherence. Both are recommended to confirm the diagnosis (ESC 2024: out-of-office BP recommended for diagnosis, I B).

    Key highlightsMeasurement

    • Average of the last 2 of 3 seated readings, after 5 min rest, correct cuff.
    • ESC thresholds: office 140/90; home and daytime 135/85; 24-h 130/80; night 120/70.
    • White-coat HTN = high office, normal out-of-office; masked HTN = the reverse (and as dangerous as sustained HTN).
    • Non-dipping = nocturnal fall < 10% — think OSA, CKD, diabetes, secondary HTN.
    • Screen BP yearly from age 40 y; every 3 y before 40 (ESC 2024).
    • Inter-arm difference > 15–20 mmHg → subclavian stenosis; use the higher arm.
    • Organ Marker and threshold
    • Heart — echo LV mass index > 115 g/m² (men), > 95 g/m² (women); indexed to height2.7: > 50 / > 47 g/m2.7 Relative wall thickness > 0.42 = concentric geometry
    • LA dilatation, diastolic dysfunction (E/e′ > 14)
    • Kidney eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m²; UACR ≥ 30 mg/g (≥ 3 mg/mmol)
    • Arteries Carotid–femoral PWV > 10 m/s; carotid plaque; ABI < 0.9; CAC score
    • Retina Haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, exudates, papilloedema (advanced retinopathy)
    • Brain White-matter lesions, silent infarcts, microbleeds on MRI; cognitive impairment

    28.3 Evaluation & Hypertension-Mediated Organ Damage

    Evaluation has three goals: (1) quantify total CV risk, (2) detect hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD), and (3) screen for secondary causes. HMOD re-classifies a patient to high risk and lowers the threshold for drug treatment.

    DON'T CONFUSE — HYPERTENSIVE LVH VS HCM VS AMYLOID

    Hypertensive LVH is usually symmetrical and < 15 mm, regresses with treatment, and ECG voltage matches wall thickness. Wall ≥ 15 mm (≥ 13 mm with family history), asymmetric septal thickening or SAM → think HCM. Thick walls with low ECG voltage → think amyloidosis.

    28.4 Treatment Thresholds & Targets

    ESC 2024 makes the decision in two tiers: confirmed hypertension (≥ 140/90) is treated with drugs in (almost) everyone; elevated BP (130–139/80–89) is treated with drugs only when CV risk is high and BP persists after lifestyle measures.

    Key highlightsEvaluation & HMOD

    • Every patient: K⁺, creatinine/eGFR, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, UACR, ECG.
    • Sokolow–Lyon > 35 mm; Cornell > 28 mm men / > 20 mm women.
    • Echo LVH: LVMI > 115 (men) / > 95 g/m² (women); RWT > 0.42 = concentric.
    • Renal HMOD: eGFR < 60 or UACR ≥ 30 mg/g; vascular: PWV > 10 m/s, ABI < 0.9.
    • HMOD upgrades the patient to high risk → treat elevated BP with drugs.

    Thresholds

    Confirmed BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg: prompt lifestyle and pharmacological treatment irrespective of CV risk. I A NEW Elevated BP with sufficiently high CV risk: drug treatment if BP remains ≥ 130/80 after 3 months of lifestyle intervention.

    I A

    Targets

    CHANGED Target SBP 120–129 mmHg in most adults, provided treatment is well tolerated. I A Drug strategy

    CHANGED Initial low-dose two-drug combination (RAS blocker + CCB or thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic), preferably as a single-pill combination, for most patients with confirmed hypertension. I B

    Combining two RAS blockers (ACE inhibitor + ARB, or with aliskiren) is not recommended. III A Relaxations of the 120–129 target: if the target is not tolerated, aim for "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA). More lenient targets (SBP < 140) and monotherapy start are reasonable at age ≥ 85 y, with moderate-to-severe frailty, symptomatic orthostatic hypotension or limited life expectancy. Treatment that is tolerated should be continued lifelong, including beyond 85.

    EXAM TRAP — THE J-CURVE

    Low diastolic BP on treatment (< 60–70 mmHg) is often a marker of stiff arteries, not a cause of harm. Do not withhold SBP lowering in isolated systolic hypertension because DBP is 65; ESC 2024 aims at DBP 70–79 "ideally", but the SBP target takes priority. Caution in severe CAD with very low DBP.

    Key highlightsThresholds & targets

    • ESC 2024: drugs for all with confirmed BP ≥ 140/90 (I A).
    • Elevated BP + high risk (CVD, DM, CKD, HMOD, FH, SCORE2 ≥ 10%) → drugs if ≥ 130/80 after 3 months lifestyle (I A).
    • Target SBP 120–129 mmHg (I A); ALARA if not tolerated; lenient at ≥ 85 y, frailty, orthostatic hypotension.
    • AHA/ACC 2025: PREVENT ≥ 7.5% = high risk; target < 130/80, encourage SBP < 120.
    • SPRINT: SBP < 120 cut MACE 25% and death 27%.
    • HYVET: treating people ≥ 80 y reduces mortality — age is not a reason to withhold therapy.
    • Measure Target SBP ↓ (mmHg)
    • Weight loss ≈ 1 mmHg per kg lost; BMI 20–25; GLP-1 RA/tirzepatide in obesity (AHA/
    • ACC 2025)
    • ~5
    • DASH / Mediterranean diet Fruit, vegetables, low-fat dairy, whole grains, less saturated fat ~11 Exercise ≥ 150 min/week moderate aerobic (or 75 min vigorous) + dynamic
    • resistance; isometric training also lowers BP
    • ~4–8
    • Alcohol ESC: men < 100 g/week, ideally abstain; AHA/ACC 2025: abstinence
    • preferred, otherwise ≤ 2 (men) / ≤ 1 (women) drinks/day
    • ~4
    • SBP effects are approximate in hypertensive individuals (Braunwald Ch. 24; ESC 2024).
    • The drug algorithm

    28.5 Lifestyle & Drug Strategy

    BOARD PEARL — WHY COMBINATIONS FIRST

    Monotherapy controls BP in only about a third of patients; each drug at half dose achieves ~80% of its fulldose effect with fewer side effects, and adding a second class lowers BP about 5× more than doubling the first. A single pill improves adherence — the commonest cause of "resistance". Chlorthalidone and indapamide are preferred over hydrochlorothiazide for their longer duration of action (though the Diuretic Comparison Project showed no outcome difference vs HCTZ).

    EXAM TRAP — CREATININE RISE WITH RAS BLOCKADE

    A rise in creatinine of up to 30% after starting an ACEi/ARB is expected (reduced intraglomerular pressure) — continue. A rise > 30% should prompt a search for volume depletion, NSAIDs or bilateral renal artery stenosis.

    Key highlightsLifestyle & drug strategy

    • Salt < 5 g/day (sodium < 2 g); potassium-enriched salt substitutes reduce stroke and death.
    • DASH diet lowers SBP about 11 mmHg; ~1 mmHg per kg weight lost.
    • Step 1: ACEi/ARB + CCB or diuretic as SPC; Step 2: triple SPC; Step 3: spironolactone.
    • Never combine ACEi + ARB (III A).
    • β-blockers only for compelling indications (angina, post-MI, HFrEF, AF, pregnancy).
    • Creatinine rise ≤ 30% on RAS blockade is acceptable; > 30% → look for bilateral RAS.
    • ACEi, ARB, aliskiren and MRA are contraindicated in pregnancy.

    28.6 Resistant Hypertension

    DEFINITION

    ESC 2024: office BP ≥ 140/90 despite optimal/maximally tolerated doses of ≥ 3 drugs including a diuretic, confirmed by ABPM/HBPM with adherence verified.

    AHA/ACC: BP ≥ 130/80 on ≥ 3 drugs (including a diuretic), or controlled only with ≥ 4 drugs ("controlled resistant").

    • Refractory hypertension: uncontrolled on ≥ 5 drugs including chlorthalidone and an MRA.
    • Exclude pseudo-resistance first
    • Non-adherence — the commonest cause (up to
    • 50%); drug levels in urine/blood if available.
    • White-coat effect → ABPM.
    • Poor technique, small cuff.
    • Therapeutic inertia / sub-optimal doses or
    • combinations.
    • Interfering substances: NSAIDs, oral
    • contraceptives, decongestants, liquorice,
    • steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, VEGF inhibitors,
    • stimulants, alcohol.
    • High salt intake (24-h urinary sodium).
    • Secondary causes — especially primary
    • aldosteronism and OSA.

    Fourth-line options

    MECHANISM — WHY SPIRONOLACTONE WORKS IN "ESSENTIAL" RESISTANT HTN

    Resistant hypertension is predominantly a salt- and volume-retaining state with inappropriately high aldosterone (often unrecognised primary aldosteronism, obesity-related aldosterone excess, or OSA). Hence the hierarchy: diuretic optimisation → MRA → other agents . Low plasma renin predicts a good response.

    Key highlightsResistant hypertension

    • ESC: BP ≥ 140/90 on ≥ 3 drugs incl. a diuretic, confirmed out of office with adherence checked.
    • Non-adherence is the commonest cause of apparent resistance.
    • Screen every resistant patient for primary aldosteronism and OSA.
    • PATHWAY-2: spironolactone is the best 4th drug; amiloride is an alternative.
    • CLICK: chlorthalidone works in stage 4 CKD.
    • Renal denervation: IIb B (ESC 2024), eGFR > 40, experienced centre.
    • Aprocitentan: endothelin antagonist, oedema, teratogenic.

    28.7 Secondary Hypertension

    About 5–15% of hypertension has an identifiable cause; the proportion is higher in the young and in resistant disease. Primary aldosteronism is the commonest curable cause (~5–10% of all hypertensives, up to ~20% of resistant hypertension).

    Spironolactone / eplerenone

    EXAM TRAP — DRUGS AND THE ARR
    • False positive (renin suppressed): β-blockers, central α-agonists, NSAIDs.
    • False negative (renin raised): diuretics, ACEi/ARB, DHP-CCB, MRA, hypokalaemia.
    • A normal ARR on an ACEi/ARB with suppressed renin strongly suggests PA. Verapamil, hydralazine and doxazosin have minimal effect — the classic "switch" agents.

    Adrenal CT cannot distinguish a functioning adenoma from a non-functioning incidentaloma — hence adrenal vein sampling, especially after age ~35.

    Phaeochromocytoma / paraganglioma

    Screening test: plasma free metanephrines (or 24-h urinary fractionated metanephrines) — highest sensitivity.

    Localise with CT/MRI; functional imaging (⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET, MIBG) for multifocal or metastatic disease. Up to 30–40% are hereditary (MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDHx) — offer genetic testing.

    Pre-operative α-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 10–14 days, with liberal salt/fluid; β-blocker only after α-blockade (unopposed α-stimulation → crisis).

    Crisis: IV phentolamine (or nitroprusside, nicardipine).

    Renovascular hypertension

    Key highlightsSecondary hypertension

    • Primary aldosteronism is the commonest curable cause; ESC 2024 — consider screening all confirmed hypertensives; AHA/ACC 2025 — screen all resistant HTN regardless of K⁺.
    • ARR: β-blockers → false positive; diuretics/ACEi/ARB/MRA → false negative.
    • Unilateral PA (confirmed by adrenal vein sampling) → adrenalectomy; bilateral → MRA.
    • Phaeochromocytoma: plasma free metanephrines; α-blockade 10–14 days before β-blockade.
    • ASTRAL/CORAL: renal stenting no better than medical therapy for atherosclerotic RAS.
    • FMD: young woman, "string of beads" → angioplasty without stent.
    • OSA is present in most resistant hypertensives; CPAP helps modestly.

    28.8 Hypertensive Emergencies

    DEFINITIONS

    Hypertensive emergency: severe hypertension (usually grade 3, ≥ 180/110 ESC; > 180/120 AHA/ACC) with acute HMOD — often life-threatening; needs IV therapy in a monitored bed.

    Malignant hypertension: severe BP with bilateral retinal haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and/or papilloedema; may cause thrombotic microangiopathy and AKI.

    Hypertensive urgency (severe BP without acute HMOD): oral therapy, lower over 24–48 h, outpatient follow-up. Rapid lowering is harmful; sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated.

    MECHANISM — WHY NOT NORMALISE BP IMMEDIATELY?

    Chronic hypertension shifts the cerebral autoregulation curve to the right. A sudden fall to "normal" pressure drops cerebral (and renal, coronary) perfusion below the autoregulatory range → ischaemia. The exceptions — dissection, pulmonary oedema, ACS and pre-eclampsia — are those in which the immediate threat comes from the pressure itself.

    Key highlightsHypertensive emergencies

    • Emergency = severe BP + acute organ damage; urgency (no acute HMOD) → oral drugs over 24–48 h.
    • General rule: SBP/MAP ↓ ≤ 25% in 1 h → 160/100 over 2–6 h → normal over 24–48 h.
    • Dissection: β-blocker first, SBP < 120, HR < 60 within 20 min.
    • Pulmonary oedema and ACS: SBP < 140 immediately; nitrates.
    • Lysis: BP < 185/110 before, < 180/105 for 24 h after; no lysis — treat only if > 220/120.
    • Pre-eclampsia: SBP < 160, DBP < 105; labetalol/nifedipine + MgSO₄.
    • Sublingual nifedipine is never appropriate.
    • Group Target / threshold Preferred drugs & key points
    • HFrEF — Use HF drugs (ARNI/ACEi, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i); avoid nonDHP CCB, moxonidine, α-blockers Black patients As general population Start with CCB or thiazide (± RAS blocker); ACEi angioedema risk higher

    • ACC 2025; CHAP trial)
