    • childbearing age
    • — Avoid RAS blockers unless contraception is reliable; counsel
    • before conception
    • Orthostatic hypotension (OH)
    • Definition: sustained fall in SBP ≥ 20 mmHg and/or DBP ≥ 10 mmHg within 3 min of standing (or head-up tilt).
    • Common in the elderly, diabetes, Parkinson disease, autonomic failure; often coexists with supine hypertension.
    • Intensive BP treatment does not increase OH in trials (SPRINT) — treating hypertension may even reduce it. However, symptomatic OH justifies a lenient target (ESC 2024).
    • Management: withdraw α-blockers, nitrates, diuretics where possible; hydration, compression, head-up sleeping; midodrine or fludrocortisone for neurogenic OH; for supine hypertension use short-acting agents at bedtime.

    28.9 Special Populations

    BOARD PEARL — TIMING OF DOSING

    Bedtime dosing (Hygia) is not supported by the pragmatic TIME trial, which found no difference in outcomes between morning and evening dosing. Both ESC 2024 and AHA/ACC advise taking medication at the time most convenient for adherence.

    Key highlightsSpecial populations

    • Older fit adults: same SBP target (120–129); at ≥ 85 y or frail, individualise (SBP < 140 acceptable).
    • CKD with albuminuria: ACEi or ARB (never both); KDIGO SBP < 120 if tolerated.
    • Orthostatic hypotension: fall ≥ 20/10 mmHg within 3 min; symptomatic OH → lenient target.
    • Pregnancy: treat ≥ 140/90; labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa; ACEi/ARB/MRA contraindicated.
    • Cognitive impairment: SBP < 130 (AHA/ACC 2025, I A) — SPRINT-MIND.
    • TIME trial: morning vs evening dosing makes no difference to outcomes.

    28.10 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 54-year-old man has office BP averaging 134/84 mmHg on three visits, confirmed by home readings of 132/83. He has type 2 diabetes with albuminuria. According to ESC 2024, what is the correct classification and management?

    Answer C 134/84 lies in the ESC 2024 "elevated BP" band (120–139/70–89). Diabetes with albuminuria makes him high risk, so drugs are indicated if BP remains ≥ 130/80 after 3 months of lifestyle (I A). "Grade 1" starts at 140/90; "high-normal" no longer exists in ESC 2024.

    Q2 A 38-year-old woman has office BP 152/94 mmHg. 24-hour ABPM shows daytime mean 128/79, night-time 110/64, 24-h mean 122/75. What is the diagnosis?

    Answer C Office BP is raised but daytime (< 135/85), night-time (< 120/70) and 24-h (< 130/80) ABPM means are all normal → white-coat hypertension. Masked hypertension is the opposite pattern.

    Q3 A 61-year-old man has BP 158/96 despite amlodipine 10 mg, perindopril 10 mg and indapamide 2.5 mg, with verified adherence and confirmed by ABPM. K⁺ is 4.3 mmol/L, eGFR 70. Aldosterone-to-renin ratio is normal. What is the best next drug?

    Answer C True resistant hypertension after excluding pseudo-resistance and PA: spironolactone is the preferred fourth agent (PATHWAY-2 — better than bisoprolol and doxazosin). Adding an ARB to an ACEi is contraindicated.

    Q4 A 45-year-old woman with resistant hypertension has K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L, suppressed renin and a raised aldosterone. Confirmatory saline infusion is positive. CT shows a 1.2 cm left adrenal nodule. What is the next step?

    Answer B Adrenal CT cannot prove the nodule is the source; non-functioning incidentalomas are common and bilateral hyperplasia may coexist. Adrenal vein sampling lateralises aldosterone secretion before adrenalectomy in a surgical candidate.

    Q5 A 67-year-old man presents with tearing chest pain radiating to the back, BP 190/110, HR 104. CT confirms type B aortic dissection. Which is the first drug to give?

    Answer C In dissection, heart rate and dP/dt are lowered first with an IV β-blocker (esmolol/labetalol) to HR < 60, then SBP < 120 with a vasodilator. Starting nitroprusside or hydralazine first causes reflex tachycardia and increases shear stress.

    Q6 A 72-year-old woman presents 2 hours after onset of right hemiparesis. CT excludes haemorrhage; she is eligible for thrombolysis. BP is 196/112 mmHg. What must be achieved before alteplase/tenecteplase?

    Answer B Before thrombolysis, BP must be < 185/110 and then kept < 180/105 for 24 h. The 220/120 threshold applies to patients not receiving reperfusion therapy.

    Q7 A 29-year-old woman with hypertension has a renal duplex showing a mid-to-distal right renal artery stenosis with a beaded appearance on CT angiography. What is the most appropriate treatment?

    Answer C Young woman + mid/distal "string of beads" = fibromuscular dysplasia. Balloon angioplasty without stenting has a high success rate. ASTRAL/CORAL (no benefit of stenting) apply to atherosclerotic RAS.

    Q8 A 44-year-old man is being investigated for episodic headaches, sweating and palpitations with BP up to 220/120. Plasma free metanephrines are 6 times the upper limit; CT shows a 4 cm adrenal mass. Before surgery, which is correct?

    Answer B α-blockade first for 10–14 days with volume expansion; a β-blocker is added only afterwards for tachycardia. Starting a β-blocker first leaves α-receptors unopposed and can precipitate a crisis.

    Q9 A 58-year-old man starts ramipril for hypertension. Two weeks later creatinine has risen from 90 to 150 µmol/L (+67%). He had flash pulmonary oedema last year. What is the most likely explanation?

    Answer C A creatinine rise > 30% after an ACE inhibitor, especially with a history of flash pulmonary oedema, suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis to a solitary kidney). A rise up to 30% would be expected and acceptable.

    Q10 A fit 68-year-old man with newly diagnosed hypertension (office 162/98, confirmed on HBPM) and no comorbidity asks about treatment. According to ESC 2024, what is the preferred initial regimen?

    Answer B ESC 2024 recommends initial low-dose two-drug combination (RAS blocker + CCB or diuretic), preferably as a single pill, for most patients with confirmed hypertension (I B). Monotherapy is reserved for elevated BP, age ≥ 85 or frailty; ACEi + ARB is Class III; β-blockers need a compelling indication.

    29.1 Diabetes & CV Risk Assessment

    Type 2 diabetes (T2DM) roughly doubles the risk of ASCVD and increases the risk of heart failure 2–4-fold; CVD remains the leading cause of death in diabetes. The risk rises with duration, albuminuria, reduced eGFR, and early onset. Heart failure and CKD, not MI, are now the commonest first CV manifestations of T2DM in many cohorts.

    ESC 2023 recommends that all patients with CVD are screened for diabetes with fasting glucose and/or HbA1c ( I A). An OGTT detects additional cases (isolated post-load hyperglycaemia) when the result would change management.

    Risk categories in T2DM (ESC 2023)

    SCORE 2-DIABETES

    A diabetes-specific extension of SCORE2 for people with T2DM without ASCVD or severe TOD, aged 40–69 y. It adds age at diabetes diagnosis, HbA1c and eGFR to the SCORE2 inputs and estimates 10-year fatal + nonfatal CVD ( I B in ESC 2023). It replaced the older ESC rule that labelled almost every diabetic "high" or "very high" risk by duration alone.

    Screening for CVD in diabetes

    Annual UACR and eGFR; resting ECG; examine pulses and feet (ABI when PAD suspected).

    Natriuretic peptides: ADA 2026 recommends measuring BNP/NT-proBNP to detect stage B heart failure (asymptomatic structural disease) in adults with diabetes; echo if abnormal.

    Routine stress testing or CCTA in asymptomatic patients is not recommended — trials (DIAD, FACTOR-64) showed no outcome benefit.

    Opportunistic screening for AF (pulse or ECG) — AF is more common and more thrombogenic in diabetes (diabetes = 1 point in CHA₂DS₂-VA).

    Key highlightsDiabetes & CV risk

    • Diabetes: HbA1c ≥ 6.5%, FPG ≥ 7.0 mmol/L, 2-h OGTT ≥ 11.1 mmol/L.
    • Screen every patient with CVD for diabetes (I A).
    • Very high risk: ASCVD, severe TOD (eGFR < 45, UACR > 300 mg/g, ≥ 3 microvascular sites) or SCORE2- Diabetes ≥ 20%.
    • SCORE2-Diabetes (age 40–69) adds age at diagnosis, HbA1c and eGFR; high 10–< 20%, moderate 5–< 10%.
    • No routine ischaemia screening in asymptomatic diabetics; do check UACR, eGFR and natriuretic peptides.

    29.2 SGLT2 Inhibitors & GLP-1 Receptor Agonists

    The single most examined concept of modern cardio-diabetology: SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs with proven benefit are given for CV and kidney protection, independent of baseline HbA1c, HbA1c target and background metformin . The choice depends on the organ at risk — SGLT2i for HF and CKD, GLP-1 RA for atherosclerotic events, weight and (with semaglutide) kidney disease; many patients need both.

    • Pioglitazone may be considered in T2DM + ASCVD without HF. IIb B
    • T2DM without ASCVD or severe TOD
    • SCORE2-Diabetes ≥ 10%: SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA may be considered to reduce CV risk. IIb C

    Metformin should be considered in T2DM without ASCVD/severe TOD at low or moderate CV risk. IIa C T2DM with heart failure or CKD

    T2DM + HFrEF: SGLT2i (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin or sotagliflozin) to reduce HF hospitalisation and CV death.

    I A

    T2DM + HFmrEF/HFpEF: empagliflozin or dapagliflozin. I A

    T2DM + CKD with eGFR ≥ 20 mL/min/1.73 m²: SGLT2i with proven benefit to reduce CV and kidney failure risk.

    I A

    Saxagliptin is not recommended in T2DM with high HF risk. III B

    MECHANISM — WHY THE BENEFITS ARE GLUCOSE-INDEPENDENT
    • SGLT2 inhibitors
    • Natriuresis/osmotic diuresis → ↓ preload, ↓ BP
    • (~4 mmHg), ↓ interstitial congestion
    • Restored tubuloglomerular feedback →
    • afferent vasoconstriction → ↓ glomerular
    • hyperfiltration (explains early eGFR "dip")
    • Ketone use, ↓ uric acid, ↑ haematocrit (EPO)
    • GLP-1 RAs
    • Anti-atherosclerotic: ↓ weight, BP, postprandial
    • lipids, inflammation
    • Benefit mainly on MI and stroke, less on HF
    • hospitalisation (except in obesity-HFpEF)
    • Glucose-dependent insulin release → low
    • hypoglycaemia risk
    EXAM TRAP

    A patient with T2DM + ASCVD and HbA1c 6.4% on metformin should still receive an SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA with proven benefit — the indication is organ protection, not glucose. The typical wrong answer is "no change — HbA1c at target". If HbA1c falls too low, reduce the sulfonylurea or insulin instead.

    29.3 Glycaemic Targets & Older Agents

    Tight glucose control reduces microvascular complications early and macrovascular events only late (the UKPDS legacy effect). Aggressive lowering in established long-standing diabetes can be harmful, mostly through hypoglycaemia.

    Key highlightsSGLT2i & GLP-1 RA

    • T2DM + ASCVD: SGLT2i (I A) and/or GLP-1 RA (I A) with proven benefit, independent of HbA1c and metformin.
    • T2DM + HF (any EF) or CKD (eGFR ≥ 20): SGLT2i (I A).
    • No ASCVD, SCORE2-Diabetes ≥ 10%: SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA may be considered (IIb C).
    • EMPA-REG: CV death ↓ 38%; DECLARE: MACE neutral, HHF ↓; CREDENCE: kidney ↓ 30%.
    • LEADER ↓ 13%, SUSTAIN-6 ↓ 26%, REWIND ↓ 12%, SOUL ↓ 14% MACE; FLOW: kidney ↓ 24%.
    • SELECT: semaglutide 2.4 mg in non-diabetic obese patients with CVD → MACE ↓ 20%.
    • SGLT2i: stop 3 days pre-op — euglycaemic DKA; initial eGFR dip is expected.
    • GLP-1 RA contraindicated with medullary thyroid cancer/MEN2 history; saxagliptin ↑ HF (III).
    • Trial Design Lesson
    • VADT Veterans, long duration Neutral macrovascular; hypoglycaemia predicted CV death
    BOARD PEARL — HYPOGLYCAEMIA IS CARDIOTOXIC

    Hypoglycaemia triggers catecholamine release, QT prolongation, arrhythmias, platelet activation and myocardial ischaemia. Severe hypoglycaemia predicts CV death in ACCORD and VADT. Prefer agents with low hypoglycaemia risk (SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA, metformin, DPP-4i) in patients with CVD.

    Key highlightsGlycaemic targets

    • HbA1c < 7% (53 mmol/mol) for most (I A); relaxed < 8–8.5% in elderly/frail.
    • ACCORD: target < 6.0% ↑ mortality; UKPDS legacy effect shows early control pays later.
    • Inpatient/ACS: treat glucose > 10 mmol/L, target 7.8–10 mmol/L.
    • Pioglitazone and saxagliptin are harmful in HF.
    • Metformin: stop at eGFR < 30; safe in stable HF.
    • CGM time-in-range goal > 70%, time below range < 4%.

    29.4 BP, Lipid & Antithrombotic Targets in Diabetes

    IIb A

    When combination antithrombotic therapy is used, a proton-pump inhibitor is recommended to prevent GI bleeding.

    I A

    Note the discrepancy: the 2024 ESC hypertension guideline recommends SBP 120–129 for most adults, including diabetics; the 2023 diabetes guideline figures above predate it.

    factors

    By SCORE2-Diabetes Moderate-intensity statin at age 40–75

    CLINICAL APPROACH — ANTITHROMBOTIC THERAPY IN DIABETES WITH CAD

    Diabetes favours longer or more intense antithrombotic therapy when bleeding risk is low: DAPT beyond 12 months after MI (ticagrelor 60 mg bd, PEGASUS), or aspirin + rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd in CCS/ PAD (COMPASS — larger absolute benefit in diabetes).

    THEMIS: ticagrelor + aspirin in stable CAD with diabetes (no prior MI) — ischaemic benefit offset by bleeding; favourable in those with prior PCI.

    Diabetes does not change the choice of P2Y12 inhibitor in ACS; prasugrel/ticagrelor are preferred to clopidogrel.

    Key highlightsTargets in diabetes

    • ESC 2023 BP: SBP 130 (lower if tolerated, not < 120); 130–139 if > 65 y. ESC 2024 HTN: 120–129 for most.
    • ADA: BP < 130/80; LDL-C < 55 mg/dL with ASCVD, < 70 mg/dL if 40–75 with risk factors.
    • Very high risk: LDL-C < 1.4 mmol/L + ≥ 50% ↓; high risk: < 1.8 mmol/L.
    • Aspirin 75–100 mg with ASCVD (I A); primary prevention IIb A.
    • ASCEND: aspirin in diabetes ↓ MACE 12% but ↑ major bleeding 29%.
    • COMPASS dual pathway (rivaroxaban 2.5 mg bd + aspirin) — larger benefit in diabetes.

    29.5 Coronary Disease & Heart Failure in Diabetes

    Coronary artery disease

    Diffuse, multivessel, distal disease; silent ischaemia and atypical symptoms (autonomic neuropathy) — dyspnoea or fatigue may be the only anginal equivalent.

    Higher restenosis and stent thrombosis rates; worse outcomes after MI.

    Multivessel CAD in diabetes: CABG is preferred over PCI when surgical risk is acceptable — FREEDOM (death, MI ↓ with CABG; more stroke) ( I A, ESC 2023/2024 CCS). PCI is reasonable for single- or twovessel disease without proximal LAD, or low SYNTAX score. Use of the internal mammary artery is especially valuable; bilateral IMA does not clearly add benefit (ART).

    Heart failure

    MECHANISM — DIABETIC CARDIOMYOPATHY

    Hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance cause myocardial lipotoxicity, advanced glycation end-product cross-linking, microvascular dysfunction, fibrosis and mitochondrial inefficiency. The typical phenotype is concentric remodelling with diastolic dysfunction → HFpEF, frequently with obesity and CKD. SGLT2i address several of these mechanisms, which is why they work across the EF spectrum.

    DON'T CONFUSE — FINERENONE IN HF VS IN CKD

    FINEARTS-HF (HFmrEF/HFpEF, with or without diabetes): finerenone reduced total worsening-HF events and CV death by ~16%. FIDELIO/FIGARO-DKD: finerenone in T2DM with albuminuric CKD reduced kidney progression and CV events (mainly HHF). Steroidal MRAs (spironolactone) remain the HFrEF drug.

    29.6 Obesity: Drugs, Surgery & the Paradox

    Obesity raises BP, LDL/apoB and TG, causes insulin resistance, OSA, AF and HFpEF, and produces a direct cardiomyopathy through volume load and epicardial/visceral fat. Visceral (central) adiposity, not BMI itself, carries the metabolic risk .

    Key highlightsCAD & HF in diabetes

    • Multivessel CAD + diabetes → CABG over PCI (FREEDOM; I A).
    • Silent ischaemia and dyspnoea as an anginal equivalent are typical.
    • Diabetic cardiomyopathy → concentric remodelling → HFpEF.
    • SGLT2i recommended for HF at any EF in diabetes (I A).
    • SUMMIT: tirzepatide in obese HFpEF → CV death/worsening HF ↓ 38%.
    • Glitazones and saxagliptin must be avoided in HF.
    • Bariatric (metabolic) surgery
    • Indications (ASMBS/IFSO 2022): BMI ≥ 35 kg/m² regardless of comorbidity; BMI 30–34.9 with metabolic disease (lower thresholds in Asians). ESC 2023 (diabetes): consider in high/very-high-risk patients with BMI ≥ 35 when structured lifestyle and drug efforts fail.
    • Procedures: sleeve gastrectomy (commonest), Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (more diabetes remission).
    • Outcomes: ~25–30% weight loss; diabetes remission; SOS and cohort data show ↓ MI, stroke, HF and mortality; AF and LVH regress.
    • Cardiac caveats: post-bypass malabsorption of drugs (warfarin, levothyroxine, some DOACs — use caution with rivaroxaban/dabigatran absorption), hypoglycaemia, thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi — high-output HF).
    THE OBESITY PARADOX

    In established HF, CAD and after PCI, overweight and mildly obese patients often have lower mortality than normal-weight patients. Explanations: reverse causation (cardiac cachexia and frailty lower BMI in the sickest), collider/selection bias, BMI failing to distinguish fat from muscle, larger metabolic reserve, and earlier presentation. It does not mean obesity is protective: in SUMMIT, STEP-HFpEF and SELECT, intentional weight loss improved outcomes , and cardiorespiratory fitness abolishes most of the paradox. Unintentional weight loss in HF is a poor prognostic sign.

    Key highlightsObesity

    • Obesity BMI ≥ 30 (Asian ≥ 27.5); waist ≥ 102/88 cm (US) or ≥ 94/80 cm (Europe).
    • Tirzepatide ~20% and semaglutide 2.4 mg ~15% weight loss.
    • SELECT: semaglutide ↓ MACE 20% without diabetes; SUMMIT: tirzepatide ↓ HF events/CV death 38% in obese HFpEF.
    • Bariatric surgery: BMI ≥ 35, or 30–34.9 with metabolic disease; reduces CV events and mortality.
    • Obesity paradox reflects confounding and reverse causation — intentional weight loss is beneficial.

    29.7 Cardio-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome

    The 2023 AHA presidential advisory defined cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome as a systemic disorder arising from the interactions of obesity, diabetes, CKD and CVD. Its purpose is to stage patients so that prevention starts early and organ-protective drugs are used across specialties. The PREVENT equations were developed alongside it.

    BOARD PEARL — THE "FOUR PILLARS" OVERLAP

    The same drugs protect heart and kidney: RAS blocker + SGLT2i + finerenone (in diabetic CKD) + GLP-1 RA (in obesity/diabetes) — plus statin. Recognising a patient as CKM stage 2–3 (e.g. diabetes + albuminuria) should trigger all appropriate pillars, not only glucose control.

    29.8 CKD & the Heart

    CKD is a CV-risk multiplier: most patients with CKD die of CVD before reaching dialysis. Risk increases with both falling eGFR and rising albuminuria — the two axes of the KDIGO "heat map".

    Key highlightsCKM syndrome

    • CKM stages: 0 none · 1 adiposity/prediabetes · 2 metabolic risk factors or CKD · 3 subclinical CVD or risk equivalent · 4 clinical CVD (4b = kidney failure).
    • Stage 3 includes asymptomatic stage B HF (raised natriuretic peptides) and very-high-risk CKD.
    • TG ≥ 135 mg/dL is a stage 2 metabolic risk factor.
    • PREVENT (with eGFR) was developed with the CKM framework.
    • Shared therapy: RAS blocker, SGLT2i, finerenone, GLP-1 RA, statin.

    EXAM TRAP — CONTRAST AND CKD

    Do not withhold clinically indicated angiography in ACS because of CKD. Use iso-osmolar/low-osmolar contrast at the minimum volume and IV isotonic hydration (e.g. 1 mL/kg/h for 12 h before and up to 24 h after, halved if LVEF ≤ 35% or NYHA > II). N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate add no benefit (PRESERVE).

    Key highlightsCKD & the heart

    • KDIGO: G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 < 15; A2 UACR 30–300, A3 > 300 mg/g.
    • SGLT2i from eGFR ≥ 20 and continued to dialysis.
    • Finerenone: T2DM + CKD with eGFR ≥ 25, UACR ≥ 30 mg/g, K⁺ ≤ 5.0 (I A).
    • Statins in CKD not on dialysis (SHARP); do not start in dialysis (4D, AURORA).
    • Apixaban 2.5 mg bd with 2 of 3 criteria; rivaroxaban 15 mg if CrCl 15–49; dabigatran contraindicated < 30.
    • Enoxaparin once daily if CrCl < 30; fondaparinux avoided < 20.
    • In dialysis, SCD is the leading CV cause of death; diagnose MI by troponin dynamics.

    29.9 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 63-year-old man with T2DM had a PCI for NSTEMI a year ago. He takes metformin 1 g bd; HbA1c is 6.6%, eGFR 72, UACR normal, BMI 29. What is the most appropriate change to his diabetes therapy?

    Answer B T2DM + ASCVD → SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA with proven CV benefit is Class I A irrespective of HbA1c or metformin. "At target" is the classic trap; sulfonylureas and DPP-4i have no CV benefit; pioglitazone is only IIb and causes fluid retention.

    Q2 A 58-year-old woman with T2DM, eGFR 38 and UACR 620 mg/g takes maximal-dose losartan, empagliflozin and atorvastatin. K⁺ is 4.6 mmol/L. Which addition has been shown to reduce kidney and CV outcomes in this setting?

    Answer C Finerenone (FIDELIO/FIGARO-DKD) reduces kidney progression and CV events in T2DM with albuminuric CKD (eGFR ≥ 25, K⁺ ≤ 5.0) on maximal RAS blockade (I A). Dual RAS blockade (lisinopril, aliskiren) is harmful; spironolactone lacks outcome data here and causes more hyperkalaemia.

    Q3 A 60-year-old man with BMI 34, prior MI and no diabetes (HbA1c 5.8%) asks about weight-loss medication. Which agent has been shown to reduce MACE in this population?

    Answer C SELECT: semaglutide 2.4 mg in overweight/obese patients with established CVD and no diabetes reduced MACE by 20%. Liraglutide 3.0, orlistat and the sympathomimetic combinations have no MACE-reduction data (and the latter raise HR/ BP).

    Q4 A 70-year-old woman with T2DM and HFpEF (LVEF 55%, NYHA II–III, BMI 36) is on furosemide. Which drug class has Class I evidence for reducing HF hospitalisation and CV death in her?

    Answer C Empagliflozin (EMPEROR-Preserved) and dapagliflozin (DELIVER) reduce CV death/worsening HF in HFmrEF/HFpEF (I A in the 2023 HF update and diabetes guideline). Tirzepatide/semaglutide help obese HFpEF, but TZDs are contraindicated and DPP-4i/sulfonylureas/insulin have no HF benefit.

    Q5 A 54-year-old man with T2DM on dapagliflozin presents 2 days after laparoscopic cholecystectomy with vomiting, tachypnoea, glucose 9.8 mmol/L, pH 7.14, bicarbonate 9 and raised ketones. What is the diagnosis and the preventive rule?

    Answer B Ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose on an SGLT2i after surgery/fasting = euglycaemic DKA. SGLT2i should be withheld 3 days (4 for ertugliflozin) before elective surgery and restarted once eating and drinking normally.

    Q6 A 66-year-old man with T2DM has three-vessel CAD including proximal LAD, SYNTAX score 30, LVEF 50%, and low surgical risk. What is the preferred revascularisation strategy?

    Answer B In diabetes with multivessel CAD and acceptable surgical risk, CABG is preferred over PCI (FREEDOM: lower death and MI) — Class I A, particularly with intermediate–high SYNTAX scores.

    Q7 A 49-year-old woman has BMI 31, HbA1c 6.1%, BP 138/86 treated with amlodipine, TG 190 mg/dL, normal eGFR and UACR, and a normal echocardiogram and NT-proBNP. What is her AHA CKM stage?

    Answer C She has adiposity and prediabetes (stage 1 features) plus metabolic risk factors — treated hypertension and TG ≥ 135 mg/dL — without subclinical CVD, high-risk CKD or clinical CVD → CKM stage 2.

    Q8 An 82-year-old woman (weight 57 kg, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL) with AF needs anticoagulation. What is the correct apixaban dose?

    Answer B Apixaban 2.5 mg bd requires ≥ 2 of: age ≥ 80, weight ≤ 60 kg, creatinine ≥ 1.5 mg/dL. She meets age and weight → 2.5 mg bd. 10 mg bd is the VTE loading dose.

    Q9 A 67-year-old man starting haemodialysis has no history of ASCVD and LDL-C 3.2 mmol/L. He is not on a statin. What is the recommended lipid approach?

    Answer C Statin initiation in dialysis patients without ASCVD is not recommended (ESC/EAS III A; 4D and AURORA neutral). Patients already on a statin at dialysis start may continue it. SHARP benefit applied mainly to non-dialysis CKD.

    Q10 A 57-year-old man with T2DM, no ASCVD and no target-organ damage has a SCORE2-Diabetes 10-year risk of 14%. According to ESC 2023, what is his risk category and LDL-C goal?

    Answer B SCORE2-Diabetes 10–< 20% = high risk → LDL-C < 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) with ≥ 50% reduction. Very high risk requires ASCVD, severe TOD or SCORE2-Diabetes ≥ 20%.

    30.1 Principles: Classification, Shunt Physiology & Clues

    Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects about 8 per 1000 live births; more than 90% of affected children now reach adulthood, so adults outnumber children with CHD . The adult problems are rarely the original lesion — they are residua, sequelae and complications of repair: arrhythmia, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, endocarditis, re-intervention and pregnancy.

    Classifying complexity

    Lifelong care in an ACHD centre

    The ACC/AHA system adds a physiological stage A–D (NYHA class, arrhythmia, valve disease, shunt, PH, cyanosis, end-organ dysfunction, exercise capacity). In the 2025 ACC/AHA update, an episode of endocarditis within the past year places a patient in stage D.

    Shunt physiology — think in resistance and compliance

    MECHANISM

    The direction and size of a shunt depend on where it is. Pre-tricuspid shunts (ASD, PAPVR) are driven by the relative compliance of the two ventricles; post-tricuspid shunts (VSD, PDA) by the pressure difference and PVR. An ASD therefore volume-loads the right heart; a VSD or PDA volume-loads the left atrium and ventricle (the extra flow returns via the pulmonary veins). Pre-tricuspid shunts develop PAH late (adult life); large post-tricuspid shunts can cause irreversible pulmonary vascular disease within the first 1–2 years.

    Quantifying a shunt: Qp:Qs and PVR

    DEFINITION

    Qp:Qs = (SaO₂ − SmvO₂) ÷ (SpvO₂ − SpaO₂). Haemoglobin and O₂ consumption cancel out, so only saturations are needed.

    Mixed venous saturation for an atrial shunt: (3 × SVC + 1 × IVC) ÷ 4 — sampled proximal to the shunt. If pulmonary venous saturation is not sampled, assume 95–98% (or use SaO₂ if there is no right-to-left shunt).

    PVR (Wood units) = (mean PAP − PAWP) ÷ Qp. 1 WU = 80 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. Normal < 2 WU; the ESC/ERS 2022 PH definition uses mPAP > 20 mmHg and PVR > 2 WU.

    BOARD PEARL
    • Worked example: SaO₂ 95%, SVC 70%, IVC 78%, PA 85%, PV assumed 95%.
    • Mixed venous = (3 × 70 + 78) ÷ 4 = 72%
    • Qp:Qs = (95 − 72) ÷ (95 − 85) = 2.3 — a significant shunt.
    • Always use the saturation proximal to the shunt as "mixed venous".
    • PVR thresholds that govern closure (ESC 2020)
    WHAT CHANGED — ACC/AHA 2025 VS 2018

    Haemodynamic thresholds now expressed in Wood units aligned with the 2022 PH definition: secundum ASD closure framed around PVR ≤ 2 WU and a > 2 to < 5 WU zone with significant L→R shunt (2018 used PA pressure ≥ 50% systemic and PVR > 1/3 systemic).

    Transcatheter closure is the usual preference for isolated secundum ASD.

    Bedside and ECG clues

    30.2 Atrial Septal Defect & Patent Foramen Ovale

    ASD is the commonest CHD first diagnosed in adults and is more frequent in women (about 2 : 1). Patients are often asymptomatic until the 4th–5th decade, when falling LV compliance (hypertension, ageing) increases the left-to-right shunt, producing exercise intolerance, atrial arrhythmias and right heart failure.

    Key highlightsPrinciples of ACHD

    • Pre-tricuspid shunts load the RV; post-tricuspid shunts load the LA/LV — the dilated chamber is the marker of significance.
    • Qp:Qs = (SaO₂ − SmvO₂)/(SpvO₂ − SpaO₂); mixed venous for ASD = (3 SVC + IVC)/4.
    • Significant shunt: Qp:Qs > 1.5 or chamber dilatation.
    • Oximetry step-up: atrial ≥ 7%, ventricular ≥ 5%, PA ≥ 5%.
    • PVR < 3 WU close; 3–5 WU consider if Qp:Qs > 1.5; ≥ 5 WU or Eisenmenger — do not close (ESC 2020). rSR′ + right axis = secundum ASD; rSR′ + left axis = primum ASD.
    • ESC severe complexity always includes Fontan, Eisenmenger, cyanotic CHD and TGA other than arterial switch.
    • Type Share Anatomy Associations Closure
    • Unroofed coronary
    • sinus
    • < 1% Coronary sinus–LA wall Persistent left SVC Surgery
    • Investigation
    • TTE: RV volume overload is the key finding; subcostal views show the defect. Sinus venosus defects are easily missed on TTE → TOE, CMR or CT when the RV is unexplained dilated.
    • TOE before device closure: maximal diameter, rims (deficient aortic rim is acceptable; deficient posteroinferior/IVC rim is not), additional fenestrations, normal pulmonary venous drainage.
    • CMR/CT: Qp:Qs, RV volumes, pulmonary venous connections.
    • Catheterisation: only if non-invasive signs of raised PA pressure → PVR mandatory (Class I).

    Non-invasive signs of raised PAP: invasive PVR measurement mandatory. I C

    LV disease: balloon testing; weigh benefit vs rise in filling pressure (closure, fenestrated closure or no closure).

    I C

    Suspected paradoxical embolism (other causes excluded), no PAH or LV disease: closure regardless of size.

    IIa C

    PVR 3–5 WU: closure when significant L→R shunt (Qp:Qs > 1.5). IIa C

    PVR ≥ 5 WU: fenestrated closure if PVR falls < 5 WU after targeted PAH therapy and Qp:Qs > 1.5. IIb C Eisenmenger physiology, PVR ≥ 5 WU despite PAH therapy, or exercise desaturation: closure not recommended.

    III C

    EXAM TRAP

    A small secundum ASD with a normal-sized RV does not need closure — unless there has been a paradoxical embolism. Conversely, age alone is no barrier : closure after 40 still improves functional capacity and RV size, although it does not abolish the long-term risk of atrial arrhythmia.

    After closure
    • Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) for about 6 months after device closure; ESC 2023 IE guidance covers the first 6 months after prosthetic material.
    • Device erosion (rare, < 0.3%) — oversized device, deficient aortic rim; presents with pericardial effusion/ tamponade.
    • Atrial arrhythmias persist in older patients; repair after age 25–40 years warrants long-term follow-up; repair in childhood without residua needs none.

    Patent foramen ovale

    PFO is present in about 25% of adults: a flap-valve tunnel between septum primum and secundum that opens when RA pressure exceeds LA pressure (Valsalva, cough). It matters in cryptogenic stroke, decompression illness, platypnoea-orthodeoxia and possibly migraine with aura (no approved indication). Who benefits: age ≈ 18–60, non-lacunar embolic-pattern infarct, negative work-up (including prolonged rhythm monitoring), and a high-risk PFO — large shunt and/or atrial septal aneurysm (excursion ≥ 10 mm); a high RoPE score (≥ 7) makes the PFO more likely causal.

    Evidence: CLOSE, REDUCE and RESPECT — closure plus antiplatelet therapy reduces recurrent stroke versus antiplatelet therapy alone, at the cost of excess (mostly transient) AF.

    DON'T CONFUSE

    Platypnoea-orthodeoxia — dyspnoea and desaturation on sitting/standing, relieved lying flat — is a rightto-left shunt through a PFO/ASD with normal PA pressure , typically after pneumonectomy, with aortic root dilatation or a prominent Eustachian valve. It is an indication for closure.

    30.3 Ventricular & Atrioventricular Septal Defects

    VSD is the commonest CHD at birth, but most small muscular and perimembranous defects close spontaneously; in adults VSD accounts for about 10% of CHD. Adults present as small restrictive defects (loud murmur, IE risk, aortic cusp prolapse), repaired defects with residua, or Eisenmenger after a large defect was never closed.

    Key highlightsASD & PFO

    • Secundum ASD ≈ 70%; the only type suitable for device closure.
    • Superior sinus venosus ASD almost always has anomalous right upper pulmonary venous drainage — needs surgery; missed on TTE.
    • Primum ASD = partial AVSD: cleft mitral, left axis, first-degree AV block, Down syndrome.
    • Close any ASD with RV volume overload and PVR < 3 WU, regardless of symptoms (I B).
    • PVR 3–5 WU → consider (IIa); ≥ 5 WU → only fenestrated closure after PAH therapy (IIb).
    • LV disease/diastolic dysfunction → balloon occlusion test before closure.
    • Fixed wide split S2 is the classic sign; crochetage R wave in inferior leads.
    • PFO closure is for patients ≈ ≤ 60 years with embolic-pattern cryptogenic stroke and high-risk PFO (large shunt/ASA).
    • Type Share Key relations Adult issues
    • Inlet (AV canal type) ≈ 5% Beneath AV valves Part of AVSD; Down syndrome
    BOARD PEARL

    The murmur of a restrictive VSD is loudest when the defect is smallest (high gradient). A large VSD with rising PVR has a shortening, softer murmur and a loud P2; in Eisenmenger the shunt murmur disappears entirely.

    Partial AVSD (primum ASD)
    • Primum ASD +
    • cleft left AV valve; two separate AV valve orifices.
    • Physiology = ASD + MR.
    • Surgery (not device) if RV volume overload (I C).
    Complete AVSD
    • Primum ASD + large inlet VSD + single common
    • AV valve.
    • Repaired in infancy; unrepaired adults are
    • usually Eisenmenger.
    • No repair if Eisenmenger or PVR ≥ 5 WU with
    • exercise desaturation (III C).
    • ECG: left (superior) axis — the AV node and left bundle are displaced posteriorly-inferiorly; first-degree AV block; RBBB pattern.
    • Echo: both AV valves at the same level (loss of normal apical offset of the tricuspid); "goose-neck" deformity of the LVOT on angiography → risk of subaortic stenosis.
    • Late issues after repair: left AV valve regurgitation (commonest reason for reoperation), LVOTO, complete heart block, arrhythmias.
    • Asymptomatic severe left AV valve regurgitation: surgery (repair preferred) when LVESD ≥ 45 mm and/ or LVEF ≤ 60% (ESC 2020, I C).

    30.4 Patent Ductus Arteriosus

    The ductus connects the proximal descending aorta (just distal to the left subclavian artery) with the origin of the left pulmonary artery. Persistence beyond the neonatal period is associated with prematurity, maternal rubella and high altitude. Flow is aorta → PA in systole and diastole, producing the continuous "machinery" murmur that envelops S2, best heard below the left clavicle.

    Silent/tiny: incidental on echo — leave alone, no IE prophylaxis. Small audible: normal LV and PAP — closure mainly for recurrent endarteritis.

    Moderate: LA/LV dilatation, wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses; may present in adulthood with AF or HF — device closure.

    Large with PAH: murmur shortens to systolic only, loud P2. Eisenmenger: differential cyanosis — clubbed blue toes, pink right hand — closure contraindicated.

    Key highlightsVSD & AVSD

    • Perimembranous VSD ≈ 80%; conduction tissue runs along its posteroinferior rim.
    • Outlet (doubly committed) VSD → right coronary cusp prolapse and progressive AR; commoner in East Asians.
    • Close a VSD with LV volume overload and PVR < 3 WU regardless of symptoms (I C).
    • Recurrent IE through a small VSD → consider closure (IIa C).
    • AVSD: left axis, first-degree AV block, cleft left AV valve, Down syndrome.
    • Primum ASD is never device-closed — surgery.
    • Commonest reoperation after AVSD repair: left AV valve regurgitation; watch for LVOTO.

    Key highlightsPDA

    • PDA volume-loads the LA and LV (like VSD) — not the RV.
    • Continuous machinery murmur in the left infraclavicular area; wide pulse pressure.
    • Device closure is the method of choice (I C) when LV volume overload and PVR < 3 WU; check toe saturation for Eisenmenger physiology.
    • Silent PDA — leave alone; no IE prophylaxis.
    • Eisenmenger PDA → differential cyanosis: blue clubbed toes, pink fingers.

    30.5 Eisenmenger Syndrome & Cyanotic Heart Disease

    DEFINITION

    Eisenmenger syndrome is the extreme end of PAH associated with CHD: a large systemic-to-pulmonary shunt causes pulmonary vascular disease severe enough that PVR approaches or exceeds systemic resistance and the shunt reverses (right-to-left or bidirectional), producing cyanosis and secondary erythrocytosis. It is a multisystem disorder.

    Cardiac
    • Central cyanosis, clubbing, prominent a-wave,
    • RV heave, loud single P2.
    • Graham Steell murmur (PR); shunt murmur
    • absent.
    • ECG: RVH, right axis, RA enlargement.
    • Deaths: sudden death, HF, haemoptysis/
    • pulmonary haemorrhage.
    Systemic
    • Secondary erythrocytosis → hyperviscosity; iron
    • deficiency (microcytosis).
    • Bleeding and thrombosis (in situ PA thrombus);
    • thrombocytopenia.
    • Hyperuricaemia/gout; calcium-bilirubinate
    • gallstones; renal dysfunction.
    • Paradoxical emboli, brain abscess; hypertrophic
    • osteoarthropathy.

    Management — what to do and what to avoid

    Issue Board answer

    Situations to avoid Oestrogen contraception; IV air (use filters); dehydration, extreme heat, strenuous isometric exercise, high altitude, non-essential surgery (cardiac anaesthetist), transvenous pacing leads

    Pregnancy Maternal mortality historically > 30% — contraindicated (mWHO IV)

    EXAM TRAP — LABORATORY ARTEFACTS IN ERYTHROCYTOSIS

    Coagulation tests (INR, aPTT) are falsely prolonged when Hct > 55% unless the citrate volume is adjusted.

    Glucose may be falsely low (ongoing glycolysis by excess red cells).

    Haemoglobin that looks "normal" in a cyanotic patient means relative anaemia / iron deficiency .

    30.6 Left-Sided Obstruction & Coarctation

    Congenital valvular AS and bicuspid aortic valve

    Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the commonest congenital heart anomaly (about 1–2% of the population, male predominance). It causes AS (earlier than tricuspid calcific AS), AR, IE and an aortopathy independent of valve haemodynamics. Associations: coarctation, Turner syndrome, Shone complex. First-degree relatives should be screened with echocardiography. Intervention criteria for BAV stenosis follow the valvular heart disease guidelines (see the AS chapter).

    Key highlightsEisenmenger & cyanosis

    • Eisenmenger = shunt reversal due to PVR ≈ systemic; closing the defect is contraindicated.
    • Never phlebotomise routinely; only for symptomatic hyperviscosity with Hct > 65% after excluding dehydration/iron deficiency.
    • Treat iron deficiency — it mimics and worsens hyperviscosity.
    • Bosentan is the ERA with RCT evidence (BREATH-5) in Eisenmenger.
    • Avoid CCBs, dehydration, heat, pregnancy, oestrogen and transvenous leads; use IV air filters.
    • Brain abscess and paradoxical embolism are classic cyanotic complications.
    • Hct > 55% falsely prolongs INR/aPTT — adjust citrate.
    • Feature Subvalvular (subaortic) AS Valvular AS (BAV) Supravalvular AS
    • Hazard Recurrence after resection Aortic dilatation/
    • dissection
    • Coronary ostial stenosis, sudden death
    • under anaesthesia/sedation
    • Subaortic stenosis (ESC 2020): surgery if symptomatic with mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg or severe AR (I C); consider in asymptomatic patients with LVEF < 50%, severe AR with LVESD > 50 mm (25 mm/m²), or MG ≥ 40 mmHg with marked LVH or exercise BP fall (IIa C).
    • Supravalvular AS: surgery if symptomatic with MG ≥ 40 mmHg, or if MG < 40 mmHg but symptoms, LVEF < 50% or concomitant cardiac surgery is needed (I C).
    • Coarctation of the aorta
    • A discrete narrowing, typically at the ductal insertion just distal to the left subclavian artery, more common in men. It is a generalised arteriopathy, not a localised plumbing problem : hypertension, premature coronary disease, stroke and aortic complications persist after anatomically successful repair.
    Associations
    • BAV in ≈ 50–60%.
    • Intracranial (berry) aneurysm in ≈ 10%.
    • Turner syndrome (coarctation in ≈ 10–15%).
    • VSD, PDA, Shone complex, anomalous right
    • subclavian artery.
    Findings
    • Upper-limb hypertension; weak, delayed femoral
    • pulses.
    • Arm–leg systolic gradient > 20 mmHg suggests
    • significant coarctation.
    • Interscapular systolic or continuous (collateral)
    • murmur.
    • CXR: rib notching (inferior borders, ribs 3–9;
    • spares 1–2) and the "3" sign.

    Imaging: TTE (suprasternal CW Doppler with diastolic "tail" = significant); CMR/CT for the whole aorta, collaterals and after repair (aneurysm, re-coarctation). Brain MRA is reasonable to screen for aneurysm (ACC/AHA).

    Hypertension: diagnose with right-arm ambulatory BP monitoring; treat to guideline targets — betablockers, ACEi/ARB.

    CLINICAL APPROACH — CHOOSING THE REPAIR
    • Adults and older children: stenting (covered stent if tortuous/aneurysm risk) is first-line for native and recurrent coarctation.
    • Neonates/infants: surgery (resection with extended end-to-end anastomosis).
    • Late complications after surgery: aneurysm at repair site (especially Dacron patch aortoplasty), recoarctation, hypertension, ascending aortic dilatation (BAV).
    EXAM TRAP

    Echocardiographic peak Doppler gradient overestimates the invasive peak-to-peak gradient, and extensive collaterals can make a severe coarctation have a low gradient. That is why ESC gives an anatomical criterion (≥ 50% narrowing vs diaphragmatic aorta) in addition to the 20 mmHg invasive gradient.

    Key highlightsLeft-sided obstruction & coarctation

    • BAV ≈ 1–2% of people; screen first-degree relatives; aortopathy independent of stenosis.
    • Subaortic membrane: no ejection click, AR common, recurs after resection.
    • Supravalvular AS = Williams (ELN); right-arm BP > left; coronary ostial stenosis; anaesthesia risk.
    • Coarctation repair: invasive peak-to-peak ≥ 20 mmHg in a hypertensive patient (I C), stent preferred in adults. ≥ 50% narrowing vs diaphragmatic aorta justifies stenting even with gradient < 20 mmHg (IIa hypertensive / IIb normotensive).
    • Coarctation: BAV ≈ 50–60%, berry aneurysm ≈ 10%; rib notching spares ribs 1–2.
    • Ebstein anomaly
    • Apical displacement of the septal (and posterior) tricuspid leaflets with a large, sail-like anterior leaflet; part of the RV is "atrialised". Diagnostic echo criterion: apical displacement of the septal leaflet ≥ 8 mm/m² relative to the mitral hinge point. Maternal lithium exposure is a classic (weak) association.

    30.7 Pulmonary Stenosis & Ebstein Anomaly

    Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction

    Valvular PS (dome-shaped valve with fused commissures) accounts for about 80–90% of RVOTO. Other levels: infundibular (TOF, DCRV), supravalvular and branch PA stenosis (Williams, Alagille, congenital rubella). A dysplastic, thickened valve without commissural fusion is typical of Noonan syndrome and responds poorly to balloon dilatation.

    Examination Widely split S1 with loud "sail sound" (T1); multiple clicks; soft TR murmur despite severe TR (low RV pressure)

    ECG Giant P waves ("Himalayan"), RBBB with low-voltage/fragmented QRS in right leads, first-degree AV block, pre-excitation

    CXR "Box-shaped"/globular heart with oligaemic lungs

    Surgery Cone reconstruction (da Silva) of the tricuspid valve; ± bidirectional Glenn ("one-and-a-half ventricle") if RV small

    EXAM TRAP

    Closing the ASD in Ebstein can be harmful: the atrial communication may be the "pop-off" that preserves cardiac output when the small functional RV cannot handle full venous return. Test occlusion first. Also: pre-excited AF in Ebstein → never give AV-nodal blockers; DC cardioversion or procainamide/ibutilide, then ablate.

    30.8 Tetralogy of Fallot After Repair

    TOF is the commonest cyanotic CHD (about 10% of CHD). One developmental error — anterior–cephalad deviation of the outlet septum — produces all four components: subpulmonary (infundibular) stenosis, a large malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, and RVH. Associations: 22q11.2 deletion in about 15% (screen before pregnancy), right-sided aortic arch in about 25%, and coronary anomalies (e.g. LAD from RCA crossing the RVOT) in about 5%.

    Key highlightsPS & Ebstein

    • Severe PS: peak gradient > 64 mmHg (Vmax > 4 m/s) → intervene regardless of symptoms (I C).
    • Balloon valvuloplasty is first choice for valvar PS; dysplastic Noonan valves respond poorly.
    • Pulmonary ejection click softens with inspiration.
    • Ebstein: septal leaflet displacement ≥ 8 mm/m²; ASD/PFO ≈ 80–90%; accessory pathways ≈ 15–30%.
    • Ebstein ECG: giant P waves, RBBB, pre-excitation; CXR box-shaped heart.
    • Surgery (cone repair) for severe TR with symptoms/↓ exercise capacity (I C) or progressive RV dilatation (IIa C).
    • Ablate symptomatic arrhythmia/pre-excitation (I C) — ideally before or at surgery.
    • Recommendation Class Level
    • Asymptomatic severe PR and/or RVOTO with ≥ 1 of: ↓ objective exercise capacity; RVESVi ≥ 80 mL/m² and/or RVEDVi ≥ 160 mL/m² and/or TR ≥ moderate; progressive RV dysfunction; RVSP > 80 mmHg: consider PVR.
    • IIa C
    • Residual VSD with significant LV volume overload, or at the time of pulmonary valve surgery: consider closure.
    • IIa C
    • Arrhythmia and SCD
    • Sustained VT and undergoing PVR (surgical or transcatheter): pre-procedural mapping and transection of VT isthmuses.
    • IIa C
    • EP study with programmed stimulation for risk stratification when additional risk factors (LV/RV dysfunction, symptomatic NSVT, QRS ≥ 180 ms, extensive RV scar on CMR).
    • IIa C
    • Primary-prevention ICD in selected patients with multiple SCD risk factors (as above, or inducible VT). IIa C Catheter/surgical ablation for symptomatic sustained monomorphic VT with preserved biventricular function, as an alternative to ICD in expert centres.
    • IIb C

    30.9 Transposition of the Great Arteries

    In complete (d-)TGA there is ventriculo-arterial discordance: the aorta arises from the RV and the PA from the LV, creating two parallel circulations incompatible with life unless mixing occurs (PFO/ASD, PDA, VSD). Balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind) and prostaglandin buy time for surgery. It is male-predominant and is not usually associated with extracardiac syndromes.

    Key highlightsRepaired TOF

    • Transannular patch → free PR → RV dilatation: the commonest late problem.
    • Symptomatic severe PR (RF > 30–40%) or RVOT Vmax > 3 m/s → PVR (I C); TPVI preferred for conduits.
    • Asymptomatic: RVESVi ≥ 80 / RVEDVi ≥ 160 mL/m², RVSP > 80 mmHg, ↓ exercise or RV function → consider PVR (IIa C).
    • ACC/AHA 2025: RVESVi > 80 mL/m² is the preferred volumetric trigger.
    • SCD markers: QRS ≥ 180 ms (QRS width tracks RV dilatation), LV dysfunction, NSVT, extensive RV scar, inducible VT.
    • Map and ablate VT isthmuses at the time of PVR in patients with sustained VT (IIa C).
    • 22q11 deletion ≈ 15%; right aortic arch ≈ 25%; aortic root dilatation late.
    • Feature
    • Atrial switch (Mustard /
    • Senning) Arterial switch (Jatene) Rastelli
    • Era 1960s–late 1980s Standard since late 1980s TGA + VSD + PS
    • Principle Baffles redirect venous return at
    • atrial level; RV stays systemic
    • Great arteries transected and switched;
    • coronaries re-implanted; LeCompte
    • manoeuvre
    • LV → aorta tunnel through
    • VSD; RV–PA conduit
    • Main late
    • problems
    • Systemic RV failure
    • Systemic (tricuspid)
    • regurgitation
    • Sinus node dysfunction
    • IART/atrial flutter; SCD
    • Baffle stenosis (SVC limb
    • commonest) or leak
    • Pulmonary venous
    • obstruction; PH
    • Supravalvular PS/branch PA stenosis
    • (commonest reintervention)
    • Neo-aortic root dilatation, neo-aortic
    • AR
    • Coronary ostial stenosis → ischaemia/
    • SCD
    • Conduit stenosis/
    • regurgitation
    • LVOT (tunnel)
    • obstruction
    • Residual VSD;
    • arrhythmia
    • ESC
    • complexity
    • Severe Moderate Severe

    Symptomatic baffle stenosis: stenting when feasible. I C

    Baffle leak in a patient needing a transvenous PM/ICD: close the leak (covered stent) before inserting leads.

    IIa C

    Severe systemic TR without significant ventricular dysfunction (EF > 40%): consider valve repair/ replacement regardless of symptoms.

    • IIa C
    • PA banding to "retrain" the LV for a late arterial switch in adults. III C
    • After arterial switch
    • Coronary stenosis causing ischaemia: stenting or surgery. I C
    • Neo-aortic root > 55 mm (average adult stature): consider root surgery. IIa C

    Branch PA stenosis > 50% with RVSP > 50 mmHg and/or reduced lung perfusion: consider stenting regardless of symptoms.

    IIa C

    EXAM TRAP

    Facial and upper-limb swelling with dilated neck veins after a Mustard operation is SVC baffle obstruction — the commonest baffle stenosis — not "right heart failure". Treatment is stenting. In atrial-switch patients, sustained atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction can cause collapse or SCD: the systemic RV has poor preload reserve through the baffles.

    Congenitally corrected TGA (ccTGA, l-TGA)

    Double discordance: atrioventricular and ventriculo-arterial. Systemic venous blood → RA → morphological LV → PA; pulmonary venous blood → LA → morphological RV → aorta. The circulation is "physiologically corrected" but the RV and tricuspid valve are systemic.

    Associations
    • VSD (≈ 70%), PS/LVOTO, Ebstein-like tricuspid
    • valve.
    • Dextrocardia/mesocardia (≈ 20%).
    • Abnormal AV node position: complete heart
    • block ≈ 2% per year, may present in pregnancy
    • or after surgery.
    Clues
    • Loud single A2 (aorta anterior and leftward).
    • ECG: reversed septal activation — Q in V1–V2
    • (and III, aVF), no Q in V5–V6; AV block.
    • CXR: straight left upper cardiac border
    • (ascending aorta on the left).

    IIa C

    Complete AV block or > 40% ventricular pacing requirement: consider biventricular pacing. IIa C Symptomatic severe TR with more than mildly reduced systemic RV function (EF ≤ 40%): TV

    replacement may be considered.

    IIb C

    ACC/AHA 2025: rhythm control is generally preferred over rate control for atrial arrhythmias in a systemic RV or Fontan circulation; GDMT and CRT are extrapolated to the failing systemic ventricle with limited evidence. Replace the systemic tricuspid valve before RV EF falls below ≈ 40%.

    30.10 The Fontan Circulation

    The Fontan operation palliates a functionally univentricular heart (tricuspid atresia, hypoplastic left heart, double-inlet LV, unbalanced AVSD) by connecting the systemic veins directly to the pulmonary arteries, so that pulmonary blood flow is passive — there is no subpulmonary ventricle .

    The route is staged: a neonatal systemic–PA shunt, PA band or Norwood → bidirectional Glenn (SVC → RPA) at 4–6 months → total cavopulmonary connection (IVC → PA by lateral tunnel or extracardiac conduit, ± fenestration) at 2–4 years. The historical atriopulmonary Fontan (RA → PA) leaves a giant RA prone to IART and thrombus.

    Key highlightsTGA

    • Atrial switch leaves a systemic RV: RV failure, systemic TR, SND, IART, baffle problems, SCD.
    • Commonest baffle obstruction = SVC limb → upper-body venous congestion; stent it.
    • Close baffle leaks before transvenous leads (IIa C) — paradoxical embolism risk.
    • Arterial switch: supravalvular/branch PS (commonest reintervention), neo-aortic dilatation (surgery if > 55 mm, IIa), coronary ostial stenosis.
    • ccTGA: AV + VA discordance; complete heart block ≈ 2%/year; systemic TR.
    • ccTGA with severe TR: replace the TV while RV EF > 40% (I C if symptomatic).
    • Biventricular pacing if complete AV block or > 40% pacing expected (IIa C).
    MECHANISM — THE FONTAN PARADOX

    Cardiac output is limited not by the ventricle but by flow through the lungs: systemic venous pressure (typically 10–15 mmHg) is the only driving force. The ventricle is chronically preload-deprived, and the high venous pressure is transmitted to the liver, gut and lymphatics. Anything that raises PVR (hypoxia, PE, positive-pressure ventilation) or loses atrial transport (arrhythmia) causes abrupt low output.

    Plastic bronchitis Expectoration of lymphatic bronchial casts

    Cyanosis Fenestration, systemic-to-pulmonary venous collaterals, pulmonary AV malformations (loss of hepatic factor after Glenn)

    • Ventricular dysfunction /
    • AV valve regurgitation
    • "Failing Fontan"; transplant evaluation

    Other Renal dysfunction, reduced bone density, lymphatic abnormalities, obstruction in the Fontan pathway

    Women with a Fontan and any complication: counsel against pregnancy. I C

    Low threshold for catheterisation with unexplained oedema, exercise deterioration, new arrhythmia, cyanosis or haemoptysis.

    • I C
    • Proactive EP evaluation and ablation in patients with arrhythmias. IIa C

    Regular liver imaging (US, CT, MRI). IIa C

    ERA/PDE-5 inhibitors in selected patients with raised pulmonary pressure/resistance without raised ventricular EDP.

    IIb C

    Device closure of fenestration for significant cyanosis — only after excluding a rise in systemic venous pressure or fall in output.

    IIb C

    WHAT CHANGED — ACC/AHA 2025

    Liver surveillance hardened: at least annual liver imaging and laboratory tests (including αfetoprotein) and at least one hepatology consultation. Annual laboratory evaluation for all Fontan patients.

    Rhythm control preferred for atrial arrhythmias; specialised pacing strategies (epicardial leads are usually required after an extracardiac Fontan).

    EXAM TRAP

    A "stable" Fontan patient with 2:1 atrial flutter at 120 bpm is not stable: loss of atrial contraction and a short diastole in a preload-dependent circulation leads to rapid deterioration and atrial thrombus. The board answer is anticoagulate/TOE and cardiovert promptly — not rate control with digoxin.

    Key highlightsFontan

    • Fontan = passive pulmonary flow; CVP ≈ 10–15 mmHg is the driving pressure.
    • Atrial arrhythmia with rapid conduction = emergency → electrical cardioversion (I C).
    • Anticoagulate if atrial thrombus, arrhythmia or prior thromboembolism (I C).
    • FALD is near-universal; screen for cirrhosis and HCC — ACC/AHA 2025: annual imaging + AFP.
    • PLE: hypoalbuminaemia, ↑ faecal α1-antitrypsin; plastic bronchitis = bronchial casts.
    • Pregnancy contraindicated if any Fontan complication (I C).
    • Low threshold for catheterisation with oedema, ↓ exercise, new arrhythmia or cyanosis (I C).
    • Syndrome Genetics Cardiac lesions Extracardiac clues
    • Marfan (pointer) FBN1; AD Aortic root dilatation/dissection, MVP Ectopia lentis, tall stature — see aortic disease chapter
    • Offspring of a parent with non-syndromic CHD have a recurrence risk of about 3–5% (higher if the mother is affected) versus ≈ 1% in the population; autosomal dominant syndromes carry 50% — offer fetal echocardiography at 18–22 weeks . Maternal lithium → Ebstein; maternal diabetes → TGA, VSD.
    • Endocarditis prophylaxis in CHD (ESC 2023)

    30.11 Genetic Syndromes, Endocarditis & Lifelong Care

    Syndromes with a cardiac signature

    Ventricular assist devices. IIa C

    Only for dental procedures involving the gingiva, periapical region or perforation of the oral mucosa. Regimen: amoxicillin 2 g orally (or ampicillin IV) 30–60 min before. Penicillin allergy: cefalexin 2 g, azithromycin/clarithromycin 500 mg or doxycycline 100 mg. Clindamycin is no longer recommended (ESC 2023).

    ACC/AHA 2025 adds that endocarditis must be actively excluded in any patient with bioprosthetic pulmonary valve dysfunction (notably transcatheter valves).

    Lifelong care — cross-cutting issues

    Organisation: moderate/severe lesions in ACHD centres, with ACHD input for any cardiac or noncardiac procedure; IART is the commonest tachyarrhythmia; avoid transvenous leads with intracardiac shunts.

    Coronary anomalies: aortic origin with an interarterial course (especially left from the right sinus) causes SCD in young athletes. Pregnancy and contraception — see Chapter 31.

    Key highlightsSyndromes, IE & lifelong care

    • Down → AVSD; Turner → BAV/coarctation/aortic dilatation; Williams → supravalvular AS; Noonan → dysplastic PS + HCM.
    • 22q11 → conotruncal defects (TOF, truncus, interrupted arch B); Holt–Oram → ASD + thumb anomalies + AV block.
    • Parental non-syndromic CHD → ≈ 3–5% recurrence; offer fetal echo.
    • IE prophylaxis (dental only): prior IE (I B), prosthetic valves/material, cyanotic CHD, shunts/conduits; repaired CHD without residua — first 6 months only.
    • Amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 min before; clindamycin dropped in ESC 2023.
    • No prophylaxis for small VSD, secundum ASD or BAV alone.

    30.12 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 38-year-old woman with a secundum ASD undergoes catheterisation. Saturations: SVC 68%, IVC 76%, RA 84%, PA 86%, femoral artery 96%. Assuming pulmonary venous saturation 96%, what is the Qp:Qs?

    Answer C Mixed venous = (3×68 + 76)/4 = 70% (sampled proximal to the shunt). Qp:Qs = (96 − 70)/(96 − 86) = 2.6. Saturations alone suffice because O₂ consumption and Hb cancel; using RA saturation as mixed venous is the classic error.

    Q2 A 24-year-old man has a fixed split S2 and an apical pansystolic murmur. ECG: sinus rhythm, PR 230 ms, rSR′ in V1 and QRS axis −60°. Echo shows RV dilatation. Which is the most appropriate management?

    Answer B rSR′ with left (superior) axis and first-degree AV block plus MR = primum ASD (partial AVSD) with cleft mitral valve. Primum defects lack an inferior rim and lie next to the AV valves — never device-closed; surgery repairs the defect and the cleft (I C).

    Q3 A 52-year-old woman with a 24 mm secundum ASD has RV dilatation and TR velocity 3.6 m/s. Catheterisation: PVR 4 WU, Qp:Qs 1.9, no exercise desaturation, normal LV. According to ESC 2020, what is correct?

    Answer B PVR 3–5 WU with significant L→R shunt (Qp:Qs > 1.5) → closure should be considered (IIa C). Class I applies only with PVR < 3 WU; fenestrated closure after PAH therapy is the IIb option for PVR ≥ 5 WU.

    Q4 A 29-year-old man with hypertension (right-arm ambulatory BP 148/92) has weak femoral pulses. CMR: discrete native coarctation, 55% narrowing relative to the diaphragmatic aorta. Invasive peak-to-peak gradient 26 mmHg. Best next step?

    Answer C Hypertensive patient with invasive peak-to-peak ≥ 20 mmHg → repair (I C) with preference for stenting in adults. Balloon alone is less durable with more aneurysms; patch aortoplasty is linked to late aneurysm.

    Q5 A 34-year-old man had TOF repair with a transannular patch at age 4. He is asymptomatic. CMR: RF 48%, RVEDVi 165 mL/m², RVESVi 88 mL/m², RVEF 42%. QRS 172 ms. Best management?

    Answer C Asymptomatic severe PR with RVESVi ≥ 80 mL/m², RVEDVi ≥ 160 mL/m² and falling RVEF → PVR should be considered (IIa C) before irreversible RV dysfunction. ICD is for multiple SCD risk factors (QRS < 180 ms here, no VT).

    Q6 A 40-year-old woman with Eisenmenger VSD reports headache and fatigue. SaO₂ 82%, Hb 19.5 g/dL, Hct 61%, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 9 µg/L. What is the best next step?

    Answer B Microcytosis and low ferritin mean iron deficiency, which mimics and worsens hyperviscosity. Hct is < 65% and she is iron-deplete → phlebotomy is wrong (and never without isovolumic replacement). CCBs are harmful; routine warfarin is not indicated.

    Q7 A 45-year-old man who had a Mustard operation in infancy develops facial swelling, headaches when lying flat and dilated veins over the upper chest. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

    Answer C Upper-body venous congestion after atrial switch = SVC-limb baffle obstruction, the commonest baffle stenosis; treat by stenting (I C if symptomatic). IVC baffle obstruction causes hepatic congestion/ascites; pulmonary venous obstruction causes pulmonary oedema/PH.

    Q8 A 26-year-old woman with an extracardiac Fontan presents with palpitations for 20 hours. BP 96/60. ECG: atrial flutter with 2:1 block, rate 130 bpm. She is not anticoagulated. Best management?

    Answer C Sustained atrial arrhythmia with rapid conduction in a Fontan is an emergency → prompt electrical cardioversion (I C) after excluding thrombus, with anticoagulation. Waiting weeks or using negatively inotropic rate control risks collapse.

    Q9 A 30-year-old man with Ebstein anomaly presents with an irregular broad-complex tachycardia at 240 bpm, BP 110/70. Which drug should be avoided?

    Answer C Irregular broad-complex tachycardia in Ebstein = pre-excited AF via an accessory pathway. AV-nodal blockers (verapamil, adenosine, digoxin, beta-blockers) can accelerate conduction → VF. Cardiovert, or use procainamide/ibutilide, then ablate.

    Q10 According to ESC 2023, which patient requires antibiotic prophylaxis before a dental extraction?

    Answer C After repair with prosthetic material (device), prophylaxis is recommended for the first 6 months. Unrepaired small VSD, BAV, MVP and remote repair without residua are not high-risk groups.

    ≤ 5 mg/dayWarfarin — may continue in 1st trimester

    31.1 Physiological Changes of Pregnancy

    Cardiovascular disease complicates about 1–4% of pregnancies and is now the leading cause of indirect maternal death in high-income countries. Hypertensive disorders are the commonest cardiovascular problem (5–10% of pregnancies). Understanding the physiological timeline explains when each lesion decompensates.

    MECHANISM — THE THREE DANGER ZONES

    End of 2nd trimester (peak volume/CO): stenotic lesions (MS, AS) and ventricular dysfunction decompensate — gradients rise by ≈ 50% for the same valve area.

    Labour: each contraction autotransfuses 300–500 mL; CO rises a further 15–25% (more with pain); BP rises.

    Immediately post-partum: relief of caval compression and uterine autotransfusion raise preload abruptly — the commonest time for pulmonary oedema in MS and for decompensation in PAH . Haemodynamics normalise over ≈ 6 weeks (some changes persist for months).

    Imaging in pregnancy

    Echocardiography is first-line for any new signs or symptoms; CMR without gadolinium if echo is insufficient. Gadolinium is avoided.

    Ionising radiation: no measurable excess of malformation or fetal loss below ≈ 50 mGy fetal dose; a CXR, CTPA or coronary angiography delivers far less. Never withhold an indicated diagnostic or lifesaving procedure because of pregnancy — minimise dose (radial access, abdominal shielding is optional, low frame rate).

    Fetal echocardiography at 18–22 weeks when a parent has CHD or teratogen exposure.

    31.2 Risk Assessment & the Pregnancy Heart Team

    Every woman of child-bearing age with known or suspected cardiovascular or aortic disease needs prepregnancy counselling and risk assessment. The ESC uses the modified WHO (mWHO) classification; the 2025 guideline introduced mWHO 2.0, which keeps the five-tier lesion-based scale but refines it with the predictors of CARPREG II.

    Key highlightsPhysiology

    • Plasma volume ↑ 40–50%, CO ↑ 30–50%, HR ↑ 10–20 bpm; SVR and BP fall (nadir 2nd trimester).
    • Stenotic lesions decompensate in the late 2nd/3rd trimester — gradients rise ≈ 50%.
    • Each contraction autotransfuses 300–500 mL; the immediate post-partum period is the highest-risk moment for MS and PAH.
    • Supine hypotension from ≈ 20 weeks — left lateral tilt.
    • A diastolic murmur is never physiological in pregnancy.
    • Echo first; CMR without gadolinium; fetal dose < 50 mGy carries no measurable risk.
    WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 — MWHO 2.0 AND THE PREGNANCY HEART TEAM

    mWHO 2.0 integrates CARPREG II-derived risk modifiers into the lesion-based class, so the same lesion can be up-classified by, for example, prior cardiac events, poor functional class or ventricular dysfunction.

    Conditions previously unclassified are now placed on the scale — e.g. coronary artery disease, long QT syndrome, ARVC and TGA after arterial switch.

    Class IV is framed as extremely high risk requiring shared decision-making rather than an absolute prohibition.

    A new chapter defines the Pregnancy Heart Team (PHT): referral for mWHO 2.0 class ≥ II–III; PHT consultation before any cardiac surgery in pregnancy (Class I); hub-and-spoke care networks. A new chapter on adverse pregnancy outcomes (pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension/diabetes, preterm birth, SGA) as lifelong cardiovascular risk enhancers.

    Mechanical valve 3

    Ventricular dysfunction; high-risk left-sided valve disease/LVOTO; pulmonary hypertension; coronary artery disease; high-risk aortopathy

    • 2 each
    • No prior cardiac intervention; late first antenatal assessment (> 20 weeks) 1 each
    • Predicted maternal cardiac events: score 0–1 → 5%; 2 → 10%; 3 → 15%; 4 → 22%; > 4 → 41%
    BOARD PEARL

    CARPREG II is the only score that includes process-of-care variables (late booking, no prior intervention).

    The board message: the strongest single predictors of maternal events are a prior cardiac event/arrhythmia, poor functional class/cyanosis and a mechanical valve . Neonatal events track maternal NYHA class/cyanosis, left heart obstruction, anticoagulation, smoking and multiple gestation.

    • Pre-conception counselling — the checklist
    • Define the lesion and functional capacity: echo,
    • exercise test (a normal test predicts good
    • tolerance), NT-proBNP.
    • Intervene before pregnancy where indicated

    • Switch teratogenic drugs (ACEi/ARB/ARNI, MRA,
    • SGLT2i, amiodarone, ERA, statins, warfarin

    • Plan where to deliver and the mode of delivery;
    • involve the PHT for class ≥ II–III.
    • Contraception until pregnancy is safe; long-term
