    Key highlightsRisk assessment

    • mWHO event rates: I 2.5–5%, II ≈ 5–10%, II–III 10–19%, III 19–27%, IV 40–100%.
    • mWHO IV: PAH, EF < 30%/NYHA III–IV, PPCM with residual dysfunction, severe MS, symptomatic severe AS, severe aortic dilatation, vEDS, severe coarctation, complicated Fontan.
    • Mechanical valve = mWHO III.
    • mWHO 2.0 (2025) adds CARPREG II modifiers; class IV = extremely high risk with shared decision-making.
    • CARPREG II: 3 points each for prior event/arrhythmia, NYHA III–IV/cyanosis, mechanical valve.
    • Refer to the Pregnancy Heart Team at mWHO 2.0 ≥ II–III; PHT consultation before cardiac surgery (I).
    • Fix severe MS/AS and critical aortic disease before conception.
    • Recommendation Class Level
    • Symptoms or pulmonary hypertension: restricted activity and β1-selective blockers. I B
    • Therapeutic anticoagulation for AF, LA thrombus or prior embolism. I C
    • PMC in pregnancy for severe symptoms or sPAP > 50 mmHg despite medical therapy. IIa C
    • Aortic stenosis
    • Intervention before pregnancy in severe AS if symptomatic. I B
    • … or LVEF < 50%, or symptoms on exercise testing. I C
    • Balloon aortic valvuloplasty during pregnancy for severe AS with severe symptoms. IIa C
    • Classes from ESC 2018; principles unchanged in ESC 2025.
    • Choice of prosthesis in a young woman
    • Mechanical valves are durable but need anticoagulation — no anticoagulant regimen is safe for both mother and fetus. In ROPAC only about 58% of women with a mechanical valve had an uncomplicated pregnancy with a live birth, and valve thrombosis occurred in about 5%. Bioprostheses avoid anticoagulation but degenerate early and commit the woman to re-operation.

    31.3 Valvular Disease & Prosthetic Valves

    The rule is simple: stenotic lesions tolerate pregnancy badly; regurgitant lesions tolerate it well (the fall in SVR offloads regurgitation, whereas higher flow and heart rate raise gradients across a fixed orifice).

    Mitral stenosis

    Commonest serious valve lesion in pregnancy worldwide (rheumatic). HF develops in about half of women with MVA ≤ 1.5 cm², typically in the 2nd–3rd trimester, even if previously asymptomatic. Tachycardia shortens diastole → LA pressure rises steeply; new AF is poorly tolerated.

    Treatment: activity restriction, β1-selective blocker (metoprolol/bisoprolol), diuretics for congestion, anticoagulation if AF, LA thrombus or prior embolism.

    Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy during pregnancy (ideally after 20 weeks, experienced operator) for severe symptoms or sPAP > 50 mmHg despite medical therapy.

    Aortic stenosis

    Usually congenital (BAV) — check the ascending aorta. Asymptomatic severe AS with normal LV function and a normal exercise test usually tolerates pregnancy.

    Symptomatic severe AS, LVEF < 50% or symptoms/BP fall on exercise → intervene before pregnancy. During pregnancy: balloon valvuloplasty for severe symptoms refractory to medical therapy.

    WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 — PROSTHETIC VALVES
    • A bioprosthesis for a woman contemplating pregnancy who needs valve replacement is upgraded from IIa (2018) to Class I.
    • A structured anticoagulation plan must be in place before pregnancy or immediately when
    • pregnancy is recognised (I C).
    • First-trimester strategy now weighs not only the pre-pregnancy VKA dose but also additional thrombotic risk factors (valve position/type, prior thrombosis, AF).
    • The guideline acknowledges that the optimal anti-Xa range for LMWH has not been established.

    Anticoagulation of mechanical valves

    MECHANISM — THE TRADE-OFF

    Warfarin crosses the placenta: warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses) during weeks 6–12 is dose-dependent — rare at ≤ 5 mg/day ; fetopathy and fetal intracranial bleeding occur later. Heparins do not cross the placenta but give more valve thrombosis — especially LMWH with sub-therapeutic anti-Xa levels, and subcutaneous UFH (avoid). VKA throughout pregnancy carries the lowest maternal thrombotic risk.

    • planned delivery; stop UFH 4–6 h before, restart 4–6 h after delivery if no bleeding
    • Stage
    • Low-dose VKA (warfarin ≤ 5 mg/d;
    • phenprocoumon ≤ 3; acenocoumarol ≤ 2) High-dose VKA (warfarin > 5 mg/d)

    Labour on VKA Labour on VKA or < 2 weeks after stopping → caesarean delivery (fetus remains anticoagulated) (I C)

    EXAM TRAP

    A pregnant woman with a mechanical valve and new dyspnoea or an embolic event needs immediate echocardiography (TTE then TOE/fluoroscopy) for valve thrombosis (I C). Obstructive thrombosis in a critically ill woman: urgent surgery or fibrinolysis — fibrinolysis is preferred in many centres when surgery is unavailable or high-risk; DOACs are contraindicated for mechanical valves in and out of pregnancy.

    Key highlightsValves & prostheses

    • Stenotic lesions decompensate; regurgitant lesions are usually well tolerated.
    • MS with MVA < 1.5 cm² → intervene before pregnancy (I C); in pregnancy β1-blocker ± diuretic; PMC if refractory or sPAP > 50 mmHg.
    • Severe AS: intervene before pregnancy if symptomatic, LVEF < 50% or abnormal exercise test.
    • Mechanical valve = mWHO III; ≈ 58% uncomplicated live birth (ROPAC).
    • Warfarin ≤ 5 mg/d: may continue in first trimester; > 5 mg/d: LMWH/UFH weeks 6–12.
    • Peak anti-Xa 1.0–1.2 (mitral/right) or 0.8–1.2 IU/mL (aortic), weekly; trough ≥ 0.6.
    • VKA → heparin at 36 weeks; IV UFH ≥ 36 h before delivery; labour on VKA → caesarean.
    • ESC 2025: bioprosthesis upgraded to Class I for women contemplating pregnancy; structured anticoagulation plan (I C).

    31.4 Congenital Heart Disease & Pulmonary Hypertension

    Most women with repaired simple CHD tolerate pregnancy well. Risk rises with cyanosis, systemic RV, Fontan circulation, ventricular dysfunction and PAH. The ACC/AHA 2025 ACHD guideline emphasises that most pregnant women with ACHD can deliver vaginally with appropriate risk stratification.

    Pulmonary arterial hypertension and Eisenmenger

    Maternal mortality remains high; the highest-risk window is late gestation, delivery and the first weeks post-partum (RV failure, PH crisis, thrombosis).

    Pregnancy is not recommended in PAH (ESC 2018: III B); ESC 2025 adds a dedicated PAH section, acknowledges no validated haemodynamic cut-off predicts outcome, and frames class IV as shared decision-making. Termination should be discussed.

    If pregnant: expert centre; stop embryotoxic ERAs and riociguat; continue/start PDE-5 inhibitors and prostanoids; planned delivery with careful anaesthesia (slow epidural); avoid hypovolaemia and hypoxia.

    Right-heart catheterisation to confirm PAH may be performed in pregnancy under strict indications; CTEPH → therapeutic LMWH.

    EXAM TRAP
    • Carboprost (PGF2α, for post-partum haemorrhage) causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and bronchospasm — avoid in PAH and Eisenmenger. Ergometrine is avoided in aortic disease, hypertension and CAD.
    • Oxytocin is given as a slow infusion, never a rapid bolus (hypotension, tachycardia).

    31.5 Aortic Disease

    Pregnancy increases aortic wall stress (hyperdynamic circulation, hormonal effects on the media). Dissection clusters in the third trimester and early post-partum period. Risk depends on the underlying disorder and diameter.

    Aorta < 40 mm Vaginal delivery

    Aorta 40–45 mm Vaginal delivery with epidural and expedited second stage; caesarean may be considered Aorta > 45 mm or prior

    dissection

    Caesarean delivery ("high-risk aortopathy" is a listed caesarean indication in ESC 2025) Progressive dilatation Prophylactic surgery if aorta > 45 mm and growing rapidly; deliver first if fetus viable

    Key highlightsCHD & PAH

    • Most ACHD pregnancies can end in vaginal delivery (ACC/AHA 2025).
    • Fontan: advise against pregnancy if SaO₂ < 85%, ventricular dysfunction, ≥ moderate AV regurgitation, refractory arrhythmia or PLE; consider anticoagulation.
    • Systemic RV: advise against if NYHA III–IV, EF < 40% or severe TR.
    • Cyanosis with SaO₂ < 85%: live birth ≈ 12% — discourage pregnancy.
    • PAH/Eisenmenger = mWHO IV; peak risk around delivery and early puerperium.
    • Stop ERAs and riociguat (embryotoxic); PDE-5i and prostanoids may be used.
    • Avoid carboprost in PAH; avoid ergometrine in aortic disease; oxytocin as slow infusion.
    CLINICAL APPROACH — ACUTE AORTIC DISSECTION IN PREGNANCY
    • Type A before fetal viability: aortic surgery with the fetus in utero. After viability (≈ 28 weeks in most centres): caesarean delivery followed immediately by aortic repair in the same session.
    • Type B: medical therapy (IV β-blocker, BP control); TEVAR for complications.
    • Deliver all women with aortic dilatation or prior dissection in a centre with cardiothoracic surgery (I C).

    Key highlightsAortic disease

    • Not advised: Marfan/HTAD > 45 mm, BAV > 50 mm, Turner ASI > 25 mm/m², TOF > 50 mm, vEDS, prior dissection.
    • Dissection risk peaks in the 3rd trimester and early post-partum.
    • β-blocker throughout pregnancy in Marfan/HTAD (IIa C); celiprolol in vEDS (I C).
    • Echo every 4–12 weeks and up to 6 months post-partum.
    • Delivery: < 40 mm vaginal; 40–45 mm vaginal with epidural/expedited 2nd stage (or CS); > 45 mm caesarean.
    • Type A dissection after viability → caesarean then immediate aortic surgery.
    • Phase Management
    • Bromocriptine May be considered to stop lactation and enhance LV recovery; always with prophylactic/ therapeutic anticoagulation. Regimen: 2.5 mg daily for 1 week (uncomplicated) or 2.5 mg bd for 2 weeks then daily for 6 weeks (severe)
    • Anticoagulation If LV thrombus, systemic embolism, AF, or during bromocriptine
    • SCD protection Wearable cardioverter-defibrillator in the early months (LV often recovers); ICD decision after ≈ 6 months
    • Duration Continue HF therapy for ≥ 12 months after full LV recovery, then taper gradually (ESC 2025, IIa C)

    31.6 Cardiomyopathies & Peripartum Cardiomyopathy

    DEFINITION — PERIPARTUM CARDIOMYOPATHY (PPCM)

    An idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with HF secondary to LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF < 45%, LV not necessarily dilated) towards the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery — most often in the first post-partum month — when no other cause is found. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

    Risk factors
    • African ancestry; older maternal age;
    • multiparity.
    • Pre-eclampsia/hypertension (strongest
    • association); multiple gestation.
    • Smoking, diabetes, prolonged tocolysis.
    • Genetic: truncating TTN and other DCM variants
    • in ≈ 15%.
    Mechanism
    • Oxidative stress → cathepsin D cleaves prolactin
    • into a 16-kDa fragment that is anti-angiogenic
    • and cardiotoxic.
    • Placental anti-angiogenic factors (sFlt-1) — link
    • with pre-eclampsia.
    • Rationale for bromocriptine (blocks prolactin
    • release).

    SGLT2i/ivabradine

    Post-partum drugs Full GDMT (ACEi — enalapril/captopril if breastfeeding — or ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i if not breastfeeding)

    WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 — PPCM
    • Genetic counselling and testing is emphasised because of the high yield of pathogenic DCM variants (IIa C).
    • New: standard HF therapy for at least 12 months after full recovery of LVEF (IIa C).
    • Bromocriptine remains an option (ESC 2018: IIb B) — the evidence gap is acknowledged.
    BOARD PEARL — SUBSEQUENT PREGNANCY

    Recovery of LV function occurs in about half of patients (more in some series), usually within 6 months. If LVEF has not normalised, a subsequent pregnancy is not recommended (III C) — relapse carries high mortality. Even after full recovery, relapse risk is ≈ 20%, so counselling is mandatory (I C). Residual LV impairment after PPCM = mWHO IV; recovered = mWHO III.

    Other cardiomyopathies

    DCM: LVEF < 30% or NYHA III–IV = mWHO IV; EF 30–45% = III. Stop ACEi/ARB/ARNI/MRA/SGLT2i before conception; continue β-blocker.

    HCM: usually well tolerated (mWHO II–III); continue β-blockers; avoid hypovolaemia and vasodilators; mavacamten contraindicated (teratogenic, interacts with hormonal contraception). Caesarean for severe LVOTO; cautious epidural, avoid single-shot spinal.

    Vaginal delivery is recommended in most cardiomyopathies; caesarean for obstetric reasons, severe HF (EF < 30%/NYHA III–IV), severe outflow obstruction, or labour on oral anticoagulant.

    Key highlightsCardiomyopathies & PPCM

    • PPCM: LVEF < 45%, late pregnancy to months post-partum (mostly first month), diagnosis of exclusion.
    • Strongest association: pre-eclampsia/hypertension; genetic DCM variants ≈ 15% → offer genetic testing. 16-kDa prolactin fragment → rationale for bromocriptine, which must be given with anticoagulation.
    • Antepartum: β1-blocker, hydralazine/nitrate, diuretic; post-partum: full GDMT.
    • ESC 2025: continue HF therapy ≥ 12 months after LV recovery (IIa C).
    • No further pregnancy if LVEF not normalised (III C); recurrence ≈ 20% even after recovery.
    • HCM: continue β-blocker; mavacamten contraindicated; caesarean for severe LVOTO.

    31.7 Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

    Hypertension in pregnancy is defined on office (or in-hospital) readings as ≥ 140/90 mmHg, confirmed on repeat measurement; severe hypertension is ≥ 160/110 mmHg. The ESC/ESH grades used outside pregnancy do not apply.

    WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 — HYPERTENSION

    Pre-eclampsia defined beyond proteinuria (organ or uteroplacental dysfunction suffices). Drug treatment threshold unified at ≥ 140/90 mmHg for all pregnant women (2018 used ≥ 150/95 for uncomplicated pre-existing hypertension) — consistent with the CHAP trial.

    Target BP < 140/90 mmHg (I B).

    Severe hypertension threshold for emergency admission aligned to ≥ 160/110 mmHg (2018: SBP ≥ 170 or DBP ≥ 110).

    sFlt-1/PlGF ratio endorsed: ratio ≤ 38 rules out pre-eclampsia within the next week; ratio ≥ 85 (or PlGF very low) indicates high likelihood.

    Women with any adverse pregnancy outcome should receive lifelong cardiovascular risk assessment.

    Key highlightsHypertensive disorders

    • Hypertension ≥ 140/90; severe ≥ 160/110 = emergency admission (ESC 2025; 2018 used ≥ 170/110).
    • ESC 2025: treat at ≥ 140/90 in all; target < 140/90 (I B).
    • Pre-eclampsia no longer requires proteinuria — organ or uteroplacental dysfunction suffices. sFlt-1/PlGF ≤ 38 rules out pre-eclampsia for a week.
    • Aspirin from 12 to 36–37 weeks for moderate/high risk (I A).
    • Labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa first-line; ACEi/ARB/DRI contraindicated (III C); avoid atenolol.
    • MgSO₄ for eclampsia; IV GTN for pre-eclampsia with pulmonary oedema.
    • Deliver gestational HT/mild pre-eclampsia at 37 weeks; adverse pregnancy outcomes = lifelong CV risk.
    • Mechanism Share Features
    • Pregnancy-associated SCAD ≈ 40% Late pregnancy/early post-partum; left main/LAD, often multivessel; hormonal weakening of the media, high shear
    • Atherosclerosis ≈ 25–30% Older women with risk factors
    • Angiographically normal
    • coronaries
    • ≈ 15–20% Spasm (ergot derivatives), MINOCA
    • Coronary thrombosis without
    • atherosclerosis
    • ≈ 15% Hypercoagulability; paradoxical embolism

    31.8 Acute Coronary Syndromes & SCAD

    Pregnancy increases the risk of MI about 3–4-fold; risk factors are older maternal age, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, thrombophilia and pre-eclampsia. Most events occur in the third trimester and early postpartum period, and the mechanism is often non-atherosclerotic.

    Conservative management for stable NSTE-ACS with low-risk criteria. IIa C

    Breastfeeding while taking antiplatelet agents other than low-dose aspirin (lack of data). III C

    WHAT CHANGED IN 2025 — ACS

    Immediate invasive angiography is upgraded for high- and very-high-risk NSTE-ACS (2018: invasive strategy "should be considered", IIa).

    Diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, including mechanical circulatory support, should mirror nonpregnant practice — do not delay life-saving treatment. Clinically stable SCAD: conservative management preferred over revascularisation.

    CLINICAL APPROACH — PRACTICAL POINTS

    Radial access, minimal fluoroscopy; new-generation DES; DAPT duration may be shortened to allow delivery.

    Prasugrel, ticagrelor, GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors and bivalirudin: limited data — avoid unless essential. Fibrinolysis is a last resort (placental haemorrhage); it does not cross the placenta.

    SCAD: angiography with care (iatrogenic extension); PCI only for ongoing ischaemia/instability; βblocker; counsel about recurrence risk in a future pregnancy. If possible, delay delivery ≥ 2 weeks after MI; vaginal delivery preferred.

    Post-partum: statin, ACEi can resume (enalapril if breastfeeding).

    31.9 Arrhythmias & Cardiac Arrest

    Ectopic beats and sinus tachycardia are common and benign. SVT may appear or become more frequent; AF usually signals structural disease (MS, CHD). Sustained VT is rare but should prompt a search for PPCM, ischaemia, channelopathy or ARVC. Electrical cardioversion is safe at every stage of pregnancy .

    IIa C

    Classes from ESC 2018; ESC 2025 reaffirms cardioversion as initial therapy for unstable arrhythmias and β-blockers as preferred prophylaxis.

    Flecainide, propafenone, sotalol SVT/AF prevention when nodal agents fail (flecainide/propafenone for WPW; exclude structural disease)

    Amiodarone Avoid (fetal hypothyroidism/goitre, growth restriction) — only for life-threatening arrhythmia when others fail

    Key highlightsACS & SCAD

    • MI risk ↑ 3–4× in pregnancy; peaks in 3rd trimester and early post-partum.
    • SCAD is the leading cause (≈ 40%) — left main/LAD, often multivessel.
    • Primary PCI for STEMI (I C); radiation must not deter angiography.
    • DAPT = aspirin + clopidogrel (I C, 2025); avoid prasugrel, ticagrelor, GP IIb/IIIa, bivalirudin.
    • ESC 2025 upgrades immediate angiography for high/very-high-risk NSTE-ACS.
    • Stable SCAD → conservative management.
    • Breastfeeding only with low-dose aspirin, not other antiplatelets (III C).
    • Drug Use
    • Anticoagulation for AF LMWH or VKA according to trimester; DOACs contraindicated
    CLINICAL APPROACH — MATERNAL CARDIAC ARREST

    Standard ALS algorithm and standard defibrillation energies; remove fetal monitors if time allows. Continuous manual left uterine displacement from ≈ 20 weeks (uterus at/above the umbilicus) to relieve aortocaval compression.

    IV access above the diaphragm; early airway (higher aspiration risk, difficult intubation). Resuscitative hysterotomy (perimortem caesarean) if no ROSC within ≈ 4 minutes, aiming for delivery by 5 minutes — it improves maternal as well as fetal survival.

    Consider pregnancy-specific causes: haemorrhage, PE, amniotic fluid embolism, magnesium toxicity (give calcium), eclampsia, dissection, PPCM, local anaesthetic toxicity.

    Key highlightsArrhythmias

    • Electrical cardioversion is safe in all trimesters — first choice for instability and pre-excited AF.
    • SVT: vagal manoeuvres → adenosine; prevention with β1-selective blocker.
    • β-blockers throughout pregnancy and post-partum in LQTS (highest risk post-partum, esp. LQT2) and CPVT.
    • Avoid atenolol and amiodarone; DOACs contraindicated for AF.
    • ICD with echo guidance if needed beyond 8 weeks; zero-fluoroscopy ablation for refractory SVT.
    • Arrest: manual left uterine displacement; resuscitative hysterotomy within 4–5 min.
    • Recommendation Class Level
    • Thrombolysis for PE only with severe hypotension or shock. I C
    • Low-risk women on therapeutic LMWH: induction or caesarean 24 h after the last dose. I C High-risk women: convert LMWH to IV UFH ≥ 36 h before delivery; stop UFH 4–6 h before; normal aPTT before neuraxial anaesthesia.
    • I C
    • Planned delivery at about 39 weeks in women on therapeutic LMWH. IIa C
    • DOACs in pregnancy. III C
    • ESC 2018 classes; ESC 2025 adds the pregnancy-adapted YEARS algorithm, immediate LMWH on suspicion and more detailed prophylaxis guidance.
    • Therapeutic LMWH: e.g. enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily; routine anti-Xa monitoring is not needed for VTE (unlike mechanical valves), except at weight extremes or renal impairment.
    • Duration: throughout pregnancy and at least 6 weeks post-partum, with a minimum total of 3 months.
    • Warfarin or LMWH are both compatible with breastfeeding.
    • Neuraxial anaesthesia: ≥ 24 h after a therapeutic and ≥ 12 h after a prophylactic LMWH dose.
    • CTPA gives a lower fetal but higher maternal breast dose than perfusion scanning; both are acceptable — never omit imaging because of pregnancy .

    31.10 Venous Thromboembolism

    Pregnancy raises VTE risk about 4–5-fold, and the risk is highest in the first 6 weeks post-partum (especially after caesarean). PE is a leading direct cause of maternal death. Left-leg DVT predominates (compression of the left iliac vein by the right iliac artery).

    Not excluded → CTPA or V/Q (perfusion) scan

    Cardiovascular drugs in pregnancy and lactation

    • Safe; lower typical-use efficacy
    • Depot medroxyprogesterone Fluid retention, bone loss — less suitable in HF

    Emergency contraception Levonorgestrel or copper IUD

    EXAM TRAP

    Bosentan (enzyme inducer) reduces the efficacy of hormonal contraception — use a highly effective method plus a barrier method.

    IUD insertion can cause a vasovagal reaction — insert in hospital in Fontan, Eisenmenger or PAH patients.

    The 2025 ESC guideline asks for PHT-guided contraception counselling in mWHO 2.0 classes II–IV.

    Key highlightsDrugs, delivery & contraception

    • Contraindicated: ACEi/ARB/ARNI/DRI, MRA, SGLT2i, ivabradine, DOACs, ERAs, riociguat, mavacamten; avoid atenolol and amiodarone.
    • Breastfeeding-compatible: enalapril/captopril, metoprolol, labetalol, nifedipine, warfarin, LMWH, digoxin.
    • Statin continuation may be considered in very-high-risk women (ESC 2025, IIb C).
    • Vaginal delivery preferred (I B, 2025); no routine induction before 39 weeks (III C, new).
    • Caesarean: labour on VKA, high-risk aortopathy, severe HF, severe LVOTO.
    • No IE prophylaxis for delivery (III C).
    • Implant or LNG-IUS for high-risk women; avoid oestrogen when thrombotic risk is high; bosentan defeats hormonal methods.

    31.12 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 29-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin 4 mg daily (INR 3.0). She is 5 weeks pregnant and has no other thrombotic risk factors. After counselling, which strategy for the first trimester is supported by ESC guidance?

    Answer B Warfarin ≤ 5 mg/day carries a low embryopathy risk; continuing VKA in the first trimester after informed consent should be considered (IIa C) — 2025 also weighs extra thrombotic risk. DOACs are contraindicated; SC UFH and prophylactic LMWH give unacceptable valve thrombosis.

    Q2 A pregnant woman with a mechanical mitral prosthesis is managed with twice-daily enoxaparin. Which monitoring target is recommended?

    Answer C Peak anti-Xa 4–6 h post-dose of 1.0–1.2 IU/mL for mitral/right-sided valves (0.8–1.2 aortic), checked weekly; trough ≥ 0.6 may be added. LMWH without weekly monitoring is Class III.

    Q3 A 34-year-old woman presents 3 weeks after delivery of twins with orthopnoea. She had pre-eclampsia. LVEF 28%, LVEDD 56 mm, no prior cardiac history. She wishes to stop breastfeeding. Besides standard HF therapy, which addition is appropriate?

    Answer A PPCM (EF < 45%, post-partum, pre-eclampsia and twins as risk factors). Bromocriptine may be added to stop lactation and aid recovery but must be accompanied by anticoagulation because of thrombotic risk. Catecholamines may be harmful in PPCM.

    Q4 A 27-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome planning pregnancy has an aortic root of 47 mm. What is the best advice?

    Answer C Marfan with root > 45 mm = mWHO IV; pregnancy not advised — prophylactic root replacement first. β-blocker alone does not make pregnancy safe at this diameter.

    Q5 At 32 weeks, a primigravida has BP 166/112 mmHg on repeated readings, headache and proteinuria. Which initial drug is most appropriate?

    Answer B Severe hypertension (≥ 160/110) with pre-eclampsia is an emergency: IV labetalol (or oral nifedipine) plus MgSO₄. ACEi are contraindicated, atenolol is avoided, diuretics worsen plasma volume depletion, nitroprusside is a last resort.

    Q6 A 36-year-old woman, 10 days post-partum, has anterior ST elevation. She has no risk factors. What is the most likely mechanism?

    Answer C SCAD is the commonest cause of pregnancy-associated MI (≈ 40%), peaking late pregnancy/early post-partum, often left main/LAD. Atherosclerosis is less likely without risk factors.

    Q7 At 26 weeks, a woman with rheumatic MS (MVA 1.1 cm², sinus rhythm, HR 112 bpm) develops exertional dyspnoea; sPAP 45 mmHg. Best initial step?

    Answer B First line is a β1-selective blocker (prolongs diastolic filling) with activity restriction ± diuretic. PMC is reserved for severe symptoms or sPAP > 50 mmHg despite medical therapy.

    Q8 A woman with a mechanical aortic valve on warfarin (3 mg) goes into spontaneous labour at 35 weeks. What is the appropriate mode of delivery?

    Answer C Labour on a VKA (or within 2 weeks of stopping) mandates caesarean delivery because the fetus is anticoagulated and at risk of intracranial haemorrhage during vaginal birth (I C).

    Q9 Which woman falls into mWHO class IV?

    Answer D Previous PPCM with any residual LV impairment is mWHO IV. Mechanical valve and uncomplicated Fontan are III; repaired TOF is II; BAV with aorta < 45 mm is II–III.

    Q10 A 23-year-old woman with a Fontan circulation (SaO₂ 92%) requests reliable contraception. Which is the best choice?

    Answer C Fontan patients have high thrombotic risk — oestrogen-containing methods are avoided. The etonogestrel implant (or LNG-IUS, inserted in hospital) is highly effective and safe; barrier methods alone are unreliable.

    Key sources

    • 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular disease and pregnancy. Eur Heart J 2025 (doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ ehaf193).
    • 2018 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiovascular diseases during pregnancy. Eur Heart J 2018;39:3165–3241.
    • 2020 ACC/ AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease. Circulation 2021.
    • 2025 ACC/AHA/HRS/ISACHD/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Adults With Congenital Heart Disease. 2025.
    • ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 212: Pregnancy and Heart Disease (2019); ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia (2020); ACOG Practice Advisory on the CHAP trial (2022).
    • Silversides CK, et al. CARPREG II. J Am Coll Cardiol 2018.
    • Braunwald's Heart Disease, 13th ed., Ch. 86.

    Chapter 32

    The Cardiac Patient Undergoing Non-cardiac Surgery

    Estimate risk, test only when it changes management, protect the stent, time the knife — and look for the silent troponin afterwards.

    ESC 2022 Non-cardiac Surgery (with ESAIC) ACC/AHA 2024 Perioperative CV Management for Non-cardiac Surgery ESC 2024 Atrial Fibrillation ESC/EACTS 2025 Valvular Heart Disease

    What the board expects you to know

    • How surgical risk (< 1%, 1–5%, > 5%), patient risk, functional capacity and biomarkers combine into a testing decision.
    • Delay of elective surgery after PCI or ACS, and the P2Y12/aspirin/DOAC interruption intervals.
    • Which drugs to continue (β-blockers, statins), withhold (RAASi on the day, SGLT2i ≥ 3 days) or never start (highdose β-blocker on the day).
    • Which valve lesions must be fixed before surgery, and how to handle CIEDs.
    • Recognition and work-up of peri-operative myocardial injury and post-operative AF.

    Numbers that win marks

    ≥ 65 yAge — ESC trigger for ECG + biomarkers
    4 METsTwo flights of stairs — adequate capacity
    6 / 12 moDelay elective NCS — after elective PCI / ACS
    3–5 / 5 / 7 dStop ticagrelor / clopidogrel / prasugrel
    ≥ 3 daysSGLT2i — interrupt before NCS
    24 & 48 hPost-op hs-cTn — detect PMI

    32.1 Surgical & Patient Risk Stratification

    Peri-operative cardiovascular risk is the product of surgery-related risk (type, urgency, duration, blood loss, fluid shifts) and patient-related risk (age, CV disease, risk factors, functional capacity, frailty). Surgery triggers a stress response — catecholamine surge, hypercoagulability, inflammation, anaemia, hypotension and hypoxaemia — which unmasks supply–demand mismatch (type 2 MI) more often than plaque rupture (type 1 MI).

    Urgency of surgery

    EXAM TRAP — CAROTID PROCEDURES

    Asymptomatic carotid disease (CEA or CAS) and symptomatic CEA are intermediate risk, but symptomatic CAS is high risk in ESC 2022. EVAR is intermediate; open aortic surgery is high.

    Patient risk — indices and functional capacity

    Functional capacity: inability to climb 2 flights of stairs (≈ 4 METs) predicts complications. The Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) is more objective: DASI > 34 ≈ ≥ 4 METs (low risk). ESC 2022 IIa B; ACC/AHA 2024 prefers DASI over clinician estimate.

    Frailty screening with a validated tool in patients ≥ 70 years before intermediate/high-risk NCS (ESC IIa B).

    Smoking cessation > 4 weeks before surgery (I B) — best-documented lifestyle intervention.

    MECHANISM — WHY MOST PERI-OPERATIVE M IS ARE SILENT TYPE 2 EVENTS

    Tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia and hypoxaemia occur while the patient is sedated and on analgesics — the classic supply–demand mismatch without chest pain . That is why more than 80–90% of peri-operative myocardial injury is asymptomatic and can only be found by routine troponin surveillance.

    Key highlightsRisk stratification

    • Surgical risk: low < 1%, intermediate 1–5%, high > 5% 30-day CV death/MI/stroke.
    • Symptomatic carotid stenting and open aortic surgery are high risk; EVAR and CEA are intermediate.
    • ACC/AHA 2024 urgency: emergency < 2 h, urgent 2–24 h.
    • RCRI = 6 points: high-risk surgery, IHD, HF, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated DM, creatinine > 2 mg/dL.
    • Poor functional capacity = cannot climb 2 flights (< 4 METs) or DASI ≤ 34.
    • Frailty screening ≥ 70 y; smoking cessation > 4 weeks pre-op.

    32.2 Pre-operative Testing & Revascularisation

    The single most important principle in both guidelines: order a test only if the result will change peri-operative management. Testing is never a substitute for delaying surgery when it can safely be delayed, or for proceeding when surgery is urgent.

    Echocardiography and stress testing

    TTE before high-risk NCS with poor functional capacity and/or high NT-proBNP/BNP, or a murmur. I B Newly detected murmur with symptoms/signs of CVD: TTE before any NCS. I C

    New dyspnoea/oedema: ECG and NP before NCS; TTE if NP elevated. I C

    Stress imaging before high-risk elective NCS in patients with poor functional capacity and high likelihood of CAD or high clinical risk.

    I B

    Stress imaging before high-risk NCS in asymptomatic patients with poor functional capacity and previous PCI/CABG.

    IIa C

    Same indications for invasive angiography and revascularisation as in the non-surgical setting. I C Routine pre-operative evaluation of LV function. III C

    Routine stress imaging before NCS. III C

    Coronary revascularisation before surgery

    Prophylactic revascularisation of stable CAD does not improve outcomes (CARP trial: no benefit before vascular surgery).

    Revascularise before NCS only when it is indicated on its own merits: ACS, and in selected high-risk patients (e.g. left main, large ischaemic burden, refractory angina) before high-risk elective NCS. If NCS can be postponed ≥ 3 months, manage ACS exactly as in any ACS patient (I A).

    If PCI is needed, use new-generation DES (I A) — not BMS or balloon-only to "shorten DAPT".

    Key highlightsPre-operative testing

    • Test only if the result changes management; never delay emergency surgery for testing.
    • ESC: ECG + hs-cTn (pre-op, 24 h, 48 h) in CVD, risk factors or age ≥ 65 before intermediate/high-risk NCS (I B).
    • ACC/AHA 2024: BNP < 92 / NT-proBNP < 300 pg/mL = low risk.
    • TTE: poor capacity, raised NP, murmur, or new dyspnoea before high-risk NCS.
    • No routine prophylactic revascularisation of stable CAD (III B; CARP).
    • ACS before NCS that can wait ≥ 3 months → treat ACS first (I A); use DES (I A).

    32.3 Timing after PCI/ACS & Antiplatelet Therapy

    The danger after recent PCI is stent thrombosis when DAPT is interrupted in the prothrombotic post-operative state — mortality from peri-operative stent thrombosis is high. The competing danger is surgical bleeding. The solution is to time elective surgery after the mandatory DAPT period and keep aspirin whenever bleeding risk allows .

    WHAT CHANGED IN 2022 (ESC VS 2014)

    No longer distinguishes BMS from DES — new-generation DES for everyone who needs PCI.

    Explicit 6/12-month delays (I A) and a minimum 1-month DAPT window for time-sensitive surgery. Age ≥ 65 years introduced as a trigger for ECG and biomarkers; post-op hs-cTn surveillance at 24 and 48 h (I B).

    SGLT2i interruption ≥ 3 days, post-operative AF anticoagulation and MINS entered the guideline.

    BOARD PEARL — ASPIRIN FOR PRIMARY VS SECONDARY PREVENTION

    POISE-2 showed that starting or continuing aspirin for primary prevention around surgery increases major bleeding without reducing MI. So the rule is: keep aspirin after PCI / established CAD ; stop primaryprevention aspirin if the surgery bleeds. Bridging with IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors or cangrelor is reserved for very high stent-thrombosis risk when P2Y12 inhibition must stop.

    32.4 Oral Anticoagulants — Interruption & Bridging

    Three questions decide the plan: How much will the procedure bleed? How high is the thrombotic risk? Which anticoagulant, and what is the renal function?

    DOACs

    Minor bleeding-risk procedures (dental extraction, cataract, skin, many endoscopies, device implantation in some settings): operate without interruption (I B), ideally at trough — 12–24 h after last dose (I C).

    Low/high bleeding-risk procedures: stop according to drug and creatinine clearance (I B); no heparin bridging for DOACs .

    Very high bleeding risk (spinal/epidural anaesthesia): up to 5 half-lives off, restart after 24 h (IIa C). Reduced-dose DOAC post-operatively to lower bleeding is not recommended (III C); if bleeding risk is high, use prophylactic-dose heparin and postpone full dose 48–72 h (IIb C).

    ≥80≥24≥48≥24≥48
    50–79≥36≥72≥24≥48
    30–49≥48≥96≥24≥48

    15–29 Not indicated Not indicated ≥ 36 ≥ 48

    Resumption: 24 h after low-bleeding-risk and 48–72 h after high-bleeding-risk procedures, once haemostasis is secure. Based on ESC 2022 NCS and EHRA practical guide. Dabigatran is the most renally dependent (~80% renal clearance).

    Urgent surgery on a DOAC

    Stop the DOAC immediately (I C); check drug-specific levels (dilute thrombin time/ecarin for dabigatran; calibrated anti-Xa) if available (IIa C).

    Dabigatran + urgent intermediate/high-bleeding surgery → idarucizumab 5 g IV (IIa B).

    Key highlightsPCI timing & antiplatelets

    • Elective NCS: 6 months after elective PCI, 12 months after ACS (ESC I A).
    • Time-sensitive NCS: ≥ 1 month DAPT after elective PCI (I B); ≥ 3 months after high-risk ACS (IIa C).
    • ACC/AHA 2024: balloon angioplasty ≥ 14 days; DES for ACS 12 months; CCS 6 months.
    • Stop P2Y12: ticagrelor 3–5 d, clopidogrel 5 d, prasugrel 7 d.
    • Continue aspirin after PCI (I B); stop ≥ 7 days only for intracranial/spinal/vitreoretinal surgery.
    • Restart antiplatelets within 48 h.
    • Factor Xa inhibitors → andexanet alfa (licensed for bleeding, not tested for urgent surgery) or PCC/aPCC when specific agents are unavailable (IIa C).
    • Vitamin K antagonists and bridging
    • Stop warfarin ~5 days (acenocoumarol ~3 days) pre-op; aim INR < 1.5; restart the evening of or day after surgery.
    • Urgent reversal: 4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K (FFP only if PCC unavailable).
    • BRIDGE trial (AF on warfarin): bridging with LMWH did not reduce thromboembolism and doubled major bleeding — so bridging is for very high thrombotic risk only.

    Bridging in patients with low/moderate thrombotic risk. III B

    Post-operative indication for OAC: DOAC generally preferred over VKA (where DOAC indicated). I A

    DON'T CONFUSE — WHO IS "VERY HIGH THROMBOTIC RISK" ?
    • Mechanical mitral valve; older caged-ball/tilting-disc valves; mechanical AVR with AF, prior embolism, LV dysfunction or hypercoagulable state.
    • Stroke/TIA or VTE within 3 months; severe thrombophilia (antithrombin, protein C/S deficiency, APS). LV apical thrombus; AF with very high stroke risk (e.g. rheumatic MS).
    • Otherwise — e.g. bileaflet mechanical AVR in sinus rhythm, AF with moderate CHA₂DS₂-VA — no bridging.

    Key highlightsAnticoagulant management

    • Minor-bleeding procedures: do not stop OAC (I B); DOAC at trough 12–24 h.
    • DOAC: stop 24 h (low) / 48 h (high bleeding risk) with normal renal function; dabigatran longer as CrCl falls (up to 96 h).
    • No bridging for DOACs; no bridging for low/moderate thrombotic risk (III B; BRIDGE).
    • Bridge mechanical mitral/tricuspid valves, old-generation AVR, or AVR + risk factor (IIa C).
    • Warfarin: stop 5 days pre-op, INR < 1.5.
    • Urgent: idarucizumab for dabigatran (IIa B); PCC/andexanet for Xa inhibitors.

    32.5 Peri-operative Cardiovascular Drugs

    MECHANISM — THE POISE LESSON ON Β-BLOCKERS

    POISE (2008) gave metoprolol succinate 100 mg starting 2–4 h before surgery to β-blocker-naïve patients: MI fell, but stroke and total mortality rose — driven by hypotension and bradycardia. The lesson: β-blockers help by lowering heart rate slowly, not by being loaded on the day of surgery. Continue them if already prescribed; start them only well in advance, at low dose, titrated.

    Start statin peri-operatively in patients with an indication. IIa C

    Start β-blocker in advance of high-risk NCS in patients with ≥ 2 clinical risk factors (ideally ≥ 1 week before, low dose, target HR 60–70, SBP > 100 mmHg).

    • IIb A
    • Start β-blocker in advance in known CAD or myocardial ischaemia. IIb B
    • Routine peri-operative initiation of β-blockers. III A

    Interrupt

    Patients without HF: withhold RAAS inhibitors on the day of surgery to prevent hypotension. IIa B Hypertension treated with diuretics: withhold on the day of surgery. IIa B

    • NEW Interrupt SGLT2 inhibitors ≥ 3 days before intermediate/high-risk NCS (euglycaemic
    • ketoacidosis).

    IIa C

    EXAM TRAP — NEVER STOP THESE ABRUPTLY

    β-blockers: withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia and ischaemia — continue even on the morning of surgery.

    Clonidine: rebound hypertensive crisis.

    PAH therapies (prostanoids, ERAs, PDE5i): continue throughout (I C); IV prostanoid must never be interrupted.

    Antiarrhythmics that control SVT: continue (I C).

    Other peri-operative measures

    Anaemia: screen before intermediate/high-risk NCS; treat iron deficiency (IV iron) pre-op; cell salvage when blood loss > 500 mL is expected (I A); tranexamic acid for major bleeding (IIa A — POISE-3 reduced bleeding).

    Hypertension: do not defer surgery for stage 1–2 hypertension (III C); defer elective surgery if BP ≥ 180/110 mmHg; avoid intra-operative hypotension (MAP < 60–65 mmHg).

    Thromboprophylaxis: by patient and procedure risk (I A); extended 14–35 days after hip/knee arthroplasty and major cancer surgery.

    32.6 Specific Cardiac Conditions

    Valvular heart disease

    Obstructive lesions (AS, MS) tolerate the vasodilatation, tachycardia and volume shifts of anaesthesia worst; regurgitant lesions are usually tolerated if LV function is preserved. Clinical and echo assessment (if not recent) is recommended in all known or suspected VHD before intermediate/high-risk NCS (I C).

    Key highlightsPeri-operative drugs

    • Continue β-blockers and statins (I B); never start high-dose β-blocker on the day of surgery (POISE).
    • Start β-blocker only in selected patients, ≥ 1 week ahead, target HR 60–70 (IIb).
    • Withhold ACEi/ARB on the day of surgery if no HF (IIa B); diuretics likewise.
    • SGLT2i off ≥ 3 days (ESC); 3–4 days (ACC/AHA; ertugliflozin 4).
    • Primary-prevention aspirin and clonidine do not protect (POISE-2).
    • Don't defer surgery for stage 1–2 hypertension; defer elective surgery if ≥ 180/110.
    • Recommendation Class Level
    • Moderate–severe rheumatic MS with symptoms or SPAP > 50 mmHg: PMC or surgery before elective intermediate/high-risk NCS.
    • I C
    • Severe primary MR with LVESD ≥ 40 mm or LVEF < 60%, or symptomatic severe secondary MR despite GDMT/CRT: valve intervention should be considered before intermediate/high-risk NCS (Heart Team; transcatheter edge-to-edge repair often chosen).
    • Asymptomatic severe AS before low/intermediate-risk surgery: proceed with invasive BP monitoring, avoid hypotension and tachycardia, maintain sinus rhythm and preload.
    CLINICAL APPROACH — ANAESTHESIA IN SEVERE AS

    The stenotic valve fixes stroke volume; the hypertrophied LV needs preload and diastolic time. So: avoid hypotension, avoid tachycardia, maintain sinus rhythm, maintain preload . Use an arterial line; treat hypotension with an α-agonist (phenylephrine/noradrenaline) rather than inotropes; cardiovert new AF promptly. Neuraxial block (sudden sympathectomy) is used with great caution.

    Heart failure and cardiomyopathy

    Recommendation Class Level

    ICD or pacing-dependent patient with unipolar electrosurgery above the umbilicus: CIED check and reprogramming immediately before surgery.

    IIa C

    BOARD PEARL — WHAT A MAGNET DOES
    • Pacemaker + magnet → asynchronous pacing (VOO/DOO) at the magnet rate — protects a pacingdependent patient from electrocautery inhibition.
    • ICD + magnet → suspends tachy-therapies (shocks/ATP) but does not change bradycardia pacing — so a pacing-dependent ICD patient needs formal reprogramming to asynchronous mode.

    Electromagnetic interference is minimal below the umbilicus and with bipolar diathermy; keep the return pad away from the generator.

    Other conditions

    Diabetes / obesity / CKD Glucose control, obstructive sleep apnoea screening, avoid nephrotoxins and contrast where possible

    Key highlightsSpecific conditions

    • Symptomatic severe AS → AVR before elective intermediate/high-risk NCS (I C); asymptomatic severe AS before high-risk NCS (IIa C); BAV as bridge (IIb C).
    • Severe AR with LVESD > 50 mm or LVEF ≤ 50%, and rheumatic MS with SPAP > 50 mmHg → intervene first (I C).
    • AS anaesthesia: avoid hypotension and tachycardia; α-agonist for hypotension.
    • Pacing indication → implant PPM before NCS (IIa C); unstable AF → cardiovert (I B).
    • Magnet: pacemaker → asynchronous pacing; ICD → suspends shocks only.
    • PAH: continue therapy, ≥ 24 h post-op haemodynamic monitoring.

    32.7 Post-operative Complications — PMI/MINS & AF

    DEFINITIONS

    Peri-operative myocardial injury (PMI) — ESC 2022: an absolute rise in hs-cTn above the upper reference limit from the pre-operative value within the first 2–3 days after surgery, with or without symptoms.

    MINS (myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery; VISION): post-operative troponin elevation above the 99th centile judged ischaemic, within 30 days, with or without symptoms/ECG change.

    Peri-operative MI: PMI plus ischaemic symptoms, ECG changes, new imaging abnormality or thrombus (4th Universal Definition).

    • PMI occurs in about 15–20% of at-risk patients after major NCS; > 80% are asymptomatic.
    • MINS independently predicts 30-day and 1-year mortality — even when silent.

    Systematic work-up (I B) to find the mechanism: type 1 MI, type 2 MI (hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxaemia), cardiac non-ischaemic (AF, HF, myocarditis, Takotsubo) or extra-cardiac (PE, sepsis, stroke).

    Treat PE, AF, HF, sepsis, Takotsubo

    DON'T CONFUSE — TRIALS THAT SHAPED PERI-OPERATIVE CARE

    POISE Metoprolol started 2–4 h pre-op → ↓MI, ↑stroke and death

    POISE-2 Aspirin and clonidine → no benefit; more bleeding (aspirin) and hypotension (clonidine) POISE-3 Tranexamic acid → less bleeding; CV safety non-inferiority not established

    • VISION Post-op troponin (MINS) common, silent and linked to 30-day death
    • MANAGE Dabigatran 110 mg b.i.d. in MINS → fewer major vascular complications
    • CARP Prophylactic revascularisation before vascular surgery → no survival benefit
    • BRIDGE LMWH bridging in AF on warfarin → no less stroke, more bleeding

    Key highlightsPost-operative complications

    • PMI = hs-cTn rise > ULN from baseline in the first 2–3 days; > 80% silent — hence routine 24/48 h troponin.
    • MINS predicts mortality; work-up the mechanism (I B).
    • MINS with low bleeding risk: dabigatran 110 mg b.i.d. (IIb B, MANAGE).
    • POAF: correct triggers; unstable → DC cardioversion; consider long-term OAC if stroke risk (IIa B).
    • No routine β-blocker to prevent POAF (III B).
    • Post-op PE: anticoagulate without waiting for imaging if bleeding risk low; ≥ 3 months.

    32.8 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 58-year-old man had a DES implanted for NSTEMI 4 months ago and takes aspirin and ticagrelor. He is scheduled for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for biliary colic. What is the best plan?

    Answer C ESC 2022 (I A): delay elective NCS until 12 months after ACS (6 months after elective PCI). Symptomatic gallstones can usually wait; if it cannot, it becomes time-sensitive (≥ 3 months DAPT after high-risk ACS, IIa C). Stopping DAPT at 4 months for elective surgery risks stent thrombosis.

    Q2 A 66-year-old woman with a colon cancer needing resection within 6 weeks had elective PCI for stable angina 6 weeks ago. She takes aspirin and clopidogrel. What is recommended?

    Answer B Time-sensitive surgery (cancer) ≥ 1 month after elective PCI is acceptable (I B). Continue aspirin (I B), stop clopidogrel 5 days before (I B), restart within 48 h (I C). Six-month delay harms the cancer outcome.

    Q3 A 70-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes (no known CVD) is scheduled for elective hip replacement. According to ESC 2022, which pre-operative work-up is recommended?

    Answer B Age ≥ 65 years with risk factors before intermediate-risk NCS: ECG (I C) and hs-cTn before and at 24/48 h (I B); BNP IIa B. Routine stress testing or angiography is not indicated.

    Q4 A β-blocker-naïve 72-year-old with two RCRI risk factors is admitted the evening before an elective open aortic repair. The junior doctor proposes metoprolol succinate 100 mg 2 hours before surgery. The best response is: Agree — it reduces peri-operative MI and mortality

    Answer B POISE: metoprolol started 2–4 h pre-op reduced MI but increased stroke and death. ESC: routine initiation is III A; initiation in selected patients should be ≥ 1 week ahead, low dose, titrated (IIb). Clonidine and aspirin (POISE-2) do not help.

    Q5 A 64-year-old on dapagliflozin and ramipril for HFrEF (LVEF 35%, euvolaemic, NYHA II) is scheduled for major bowel surgery. Which is the most appropriate plan?

    Answer B Stop SGLT2i ≥ 3 days before intermediate/high-risk NCS (IIa C) to avoid euglycaemic ketoacidosis. In stable HF, RAASi continuation may be considered (IIb C); withholding on the day is advised in patients without HF.

    Q6 A 76-year-old man with exertional syncope has severe AS (Vmax 4.6 m/s). He is listed for elective total knee replacement. What should happen first?

    Answer B Symptomatic severe AS before elective intermediate/high-risk NCS → AVR first (I C). BAV is only a bridge when surgery is time-sensitive or AVR unfeasible (IIb C).

    Q7 A 69-year-old on apixaban 5 mg b.i.d. for AF (CHA₂DS₂-VA 3, CrCl 70 mL/min) needs a transurethral resection of a bladder tumour (high bleeding risk). What is the plan?

    Answer B Factor Xa inhibitors with CrCl ≥ 30: last dose ≥ 48 h before high-bleeding-risk surgery; no heparin bridging for DOACs; resume at 48–72 h. Bridging increases bleeding (BRIDGE principle).

    Q8 A pacing-dependent patient with a dual-chamber ICD is undergoing upper abdominal surgery with monopolar diathermy. Why is placing a magnet over the device alone inadequate?

    Answer B A magnet on an ICD suspends shocks/ATP but leaves bradycardia pacing unchanged, so electrocautery may inhibit pacing in a dependent patient. Formal reprogramming to asynchronous mode is required; pacemaker magnets (not ICD magnets) give asynchronous pacing.

    Q9 A 74-year-old has a routine hs-TnT of 68 ng/L on day 2 after hip fracture fixation (pre-op 14 ng/L). He is asymptomatic; ECG unchanged; Hb 82 g/L. What is the best interpretation and step?

    Answer B Absolute rise > ULN from pre-op = PMI; usually silent type 2 injury (here anaemia). Systematic work-up and trigger correction are Class I B; primary PCI is for STEMI. PMI carries prognostic weight, so it should not be ignored.

    Q10 A 65-year-old develops new AF on day 3 after lobectomy; it reverts after correction of K⁺ and Mg²⁺. CHA₂DS₂- VA is 3, bleeding risk low. What does ESC recommend?

    Answer B ESC 2022 NCS and ESC 2024 AF: long-term OAC should be considered after POAF following NCS in patients at stroke risk (IIa B). POAF predicts recurrence and stroke. Routine β-blocker prophylaxis for POAF is III B.

    Sports Cardiology & the Heart in Systemic Disease

    Separating the athlete's adaptation from the killer that mimics it — then recognising the heart as a target organ of endocrine, immune, neuromuscular, infectious and renal disease.

    33.1 Athlete's Heart versus Cardiomyopathy

    Athlete's heart is the physiological remodelling produced by regular, intense training: larger chambers, modest wall thickening, high vagal tone and a supranormal cardiac reserve. It is benign — but it overlaps with the phenotypes of the conditions that cause sudden death in young athletes. The board tests the grey zone.

    MECHANISM — TWO K IN DS OF TRAINING,TWO K IN DS OF REMODELLING

    Endurance (dynamic, isotonic) — rowing, cycling, running, swimming: volume load → eccentric hypertrophy, balanced dilatation of all four chambers, high stroke volume, bradycardia.

    Strength (static, isometric) — weightlifting, throwing: pressure load → mild concentric thickening; cavity usually normal.

    Most sports are mixed; the classic "Morganroth hypothesis" is a simplification, but remains examinable.

    LV LVEDD up to ~60 mm (occasionally more) in men; wall thickness usually ≤ 12 mm; LVEF lownormal (occasionally 45–50%) at rest with normal rise on exercise RV / atria Proportional RV dilatation; biatrial enlargement

    Diastolic function Normal or supranormal (high e′)

    Performance Peak VO₂ high (> 50 mL/kg/min in male endurance athletes, or > 120% predicted) Other Increased trabeculation (up to ~20%), higher coronary calcium scores in master endurance athletes, U-shaped relation with AF

    BOARD PEARL — ETHNICITY AND SEX MATTER

    Black (African/Afro-Caribbean) male athletes show more LVH (wall up to ~15–16 mm in a minority) and the "repolarisation variant": J-point/convex ST elevation followed by TWI in V1–V4 — normal.

    Female athletes rarely exceed a wall thickness of 11–12 mm; greater thickness points to HCM. The best discriminator in the grey zone is often cavity size plus CMR (LGE) plus detraining .

    Sudden cardiac death in athletes

    Key highlightsAthlete's heart

    • Endurance → eccentric, balanced 4-chamber dilatation; strength → mild concentric thickening.
    • HCM grey zone = wall 13–16 mm (men): athlete if LVEDD > 54 mm, normal diastole, regression with detraining, no LGE.
    • Female athlete wall > 12 mm → suspect HCM.
    • Physiological LV dilatation: LVEF may be 45–50% at rest but rises on exercise.
    • Isolated RV dilatation, regional RV wall-motion abnormality or TWI beyond V3 → investigate ARVC.
    • SCD < 35 y: cardiomyopathies, coronary anomalies, channelopathies, autopsy-negative; ≥ 35 y: CAD.
    • Category Findings
    • Normal (trainingrelated)
    • No further evaluation
    • Increased QRS voltage (LVH/RVH criteria)
    • Incomplete RBBB
    • Early repolarisation / ST elevation
    • Black athlete repolarisation variant (ST ↑ then TWI V1–V4)
    • TWI V1–V3 in age < 16
    • Sinus bradycardia ≥ 30 bpm, sinus arrhythmia
    • Ectopic atrial or junctional rhythm
    • 1st-degree AV block (PR 200–399 ms)
    • Mobitz I (Wenckebach) AV block
    • Borderline
    • Investigate only if ≥ 2
    • present
    • Left axis deviation (−30° to −90°)
    • Left atrial enlargement
    • Right axis deviation (> 120°)

    • Abnormal

    • TWI ≥ 1 mm in ≥ 2 contiguous leads (anterior beyond normal variants, lateral, inferior)
    • ST depression ≥ 0.5 mm in ≥ 2 leads

    33.2 Athlete ECG & Pre-participation Screening

    The International Criteria (2017) classify athlete ECG findings into three groups. They apply to athletes aged 12–35 years.

    EXAM TRAP — LATERAL T-WAVE INVERSION
    • Anterior TWI (V1–V4) may be normal in Black athletes (after J-point elevation) or adolescents < 16 years.
    • Lateral TWI (I, aVL, V5–V6) is never a normal training effect — it warrants echo and CMR (HCM may declare itself only years later), with follow-up even if initial imaging is normal.

    Pre-participation screening

    Recommendation Class Level

    Maximal exercise testing for prognostic purposes in sedentary adults at high risk who wish to begin high-intensity exercise.

    IIa C

    Uncontrolled hypertension (SBP > 160 mmHg): high-intensity exercise not recommended until controlled.

    III C

    33.3 Eligibility for Sport in Cardiovascular Disease

    The field has moved from disqualification to shared decision-making. ESC 2020 still gives disease-specific recommendations; the AHA/ACC 2025 scientific statement explicitly frames itself as "clinical considerations" rather than disqualification criteria, and is generally more permissive once risk has been assessed by an expert.

    Key highlightsAthlete ECG & screening

    • Normal: bradycardia ≥ 30 bpm, 1st-degree AVB, Mobitz I, voltage LVH, incomplete RBBB, early repolarisation.
    • Borderline (one alone = normal): axis deviation, atrial enlargement, complete RBBB.
    • Abnormal: TWI ≥ 1 mm in ≥ 2 leads, ST depression ≥ 0.5 mm, Q waves, LBBB, QRS ≥ 140 ms, pre-excitation, QTc ≥ 470/480 ms, Brugada type 1, ≥ 2 PVCs/10 s.
    • Lateral TWI → echo + CMR, even if echo normal.
    • Anterior TWI V1–V4 normal only in Black athletes (after J-point ↑) or age < 16 (V1–V3).
    • ESC: ECG-based screening (IIa C); AHA/ACC: history + examination.
    • Condition ESC 2020 AHA/ACC 2025 statement
    • Brugada Avoid core temperature > 39 °C (III C); asymptomatic:
    • sport may be considered (IIb C)
    • Reasonable to participate with
    • precautions (treat fever, avoid provoking
    • drugs)
    • WPW Asymptomatic competitive athlete: EP study for risk (I B);
    • ablation if documented arrhythmia (I C)
    • Similar — risk-stratify, ablate high-risk
    • pathways
    • CCS Low risk: competitive/leisure sport should be considered
    • (IIa C); high risk or residual ischaemia: no competitive
    • sport (III C)
    • Masters-athlete section: risk-stratify,
    • optimise therapy, SDM
    • ICD Follow the underlying disease; SDM for intensive/
    • competitive sport (IIa C); ICD is not a substitute for
    • disease-based restriction (III C)
    • Participation reasonable, including some
    • collision sports; restrict ~4–8 weeks after
    • implant
    • Aorta (nonsyndromic, BAV)Risk stratify with CT/CMR and exercise BP (I C); avoid
    • power sports; no competitive sport if high risk (III C)
    • Unexplained dilatation ≤ 42 mm:
    • participate; ≥ 45 mm: risk likely
    • outweighs benefit
    • HCM risk markers (ESC 2020): cardiac symptoms, prior arrest/unexplained syncope, moderate ESC risk score, LVOT gradient ≥ 30 mmHg at rest, abnormal exercise BP response, exercise-induced arrhythmias.
    WHAT CHANGED — AHA/ACC 2025 STATEMENT
    • Replaces the 2015 "eligibility and disqualification" task-force documents with shared decision-making as the organising principle.
    • Sports now described along a continuum of endurance and strength rather than the fixed static/ dynamic grid.
    • More permissive for HCM, LQTS, ICD carriers and myocarditis (earlier return), with a new mastersathlete (CAD) section.
    CLINICAL APPROACH — THE CHANNELOPATHY ATHLETE
    • LQT1 (KCNQ1): events with exercise, especially swimming — β-blocker (nadolol/propranolol), no QT drugs, electrolyte care.
    • LQT2: auditory triggers/emotion; LQT3: events at rest/sleep.
    • CPVT: exercise/emotion-induced bidirectional VT — β-blocker ± flecainide ± left cardiac sympathetic denervation; exercise test to confirm suppression before any participation.
    • Brugada: fever, not exercise, is the trigger — aggressive antipyresis.

    Key highlightsEligibility for sport

    • Modern principle: shared decision-making after expert risk assessment.
    • ARVC: high-intensity/competitive sport not recommended even in gene +/phenotype − (ESC III B) — exercise accelerates the disease.
    • HCM without risk markers: competitive sport may be considered (ESC IIb C).
    • LQTS: no high-intensity sport if QTc > 500 ms or confirmed LQTS with QTc ≥ 470/480 ms (ESC III B).
    • Asymptomatic pre-excitation in a competitive athlete → EP study (I B).
    • An ICD never replaces disease-based restriction (III C).
    • Brugada: avoid core temperature > 39 °C.

    33.4 Endocrine Disease & the Heart

    Thyroid disease

    DON'T CONFUSE — AMIODARONE AND THE THYROID
    • Amiodarone-induced
    • hypothyroidism
    • Wolff–Chaikoff effect (iodine load); commoner in iodine-replete areas →
    • levothyroxine, continue amiodarone
    • AIT type 1 Iodine-induced hormone synthesis in underlying nodular goitre/latent Graves;
    • ↑vascularity on Doppler → thionamides (± perchlorate)
    • AIT type 2 Destructive thyroiditis in a normal gland; low vascularity, low uptake →
    • glucocorticoids

    Pituitary and adrenal disorders

    EXAM TRAP — Β-BLOCKER IN PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA

    Giving a β-blocker before adequate α-blockade removes β₂-mediated vasodilatation and leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed → hypertensive crisis and acute pulmonary oedema . Labetalol alone (predominantly β) is also inadequate as the first agent.

    Carcinoid heart disease

    Occurs in about 20–50% of patients with carcinoid syndrome — i.e. neuroendocrine tumours (usually small-bowel) with hepatic metastases, which let vasoactive amines bypass hepatic inactivation. Serotonin (via 5-HT2B receptors) drives fibrous plaque on the right-sided valves: thickened, retracted, immobile leaflets → severe TR (commonest) and pulmonary stenosis/regurgitation. Left-sided involvement suggests a PFO/right-to-left shunt, bronchial carcinoid or very high hormone levels (lungs inactivate serotonin).

    Markers: high urinary 5-HIAA and NT-proBNP (screening); echo for all with carcinoid syndrome. Treatment: somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide), telotristat; valve replacement for symptomatic severe disease (bioprosthesis common), with octreotide cover to prevent carcinoid crisis. Same valvulopathy: ergot derivatives (methysergide, pergolide, cabergoline at high dose), fenfluramine/ benfluorex, MDMA — all 5-HT2B agonists (these affect left-sided valves too).

    Parathyroid and calcium

    Hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism)
    • Short QT (short ST segment)
    • Hypertension, valvular/annular calcification,
    • LVH
    Hypocalcaemia (hypoparathyroidism)
    • Long QT (long ST segment)
    • Rarely reversible HF (hypocalcaemic
    • cardiomyopathy)

    Key highlightsEndocrine disease

    • Hyperthyroidism: AF in ~10–15%; check TSH in all new AF; β-blocker and anticoagulate by stroke risk.
    • Hypothyroidism: bradycardia, pericardial effusion, diastolic hypertension, ↑LDL — start levothyroxine low in CAD.
    • AIT type 1 → thionamides; type 2 (destructive) → steroids; amiodarone hypothyroidism → levothyroxine, continue drug.
    • Phaeochromocytoma: metanephrines; α before β for 7–14 days pre-op.
    • Primary aldosteronism: commonest endocrine hypertension; more AF and LVH.
    • Carcinoid: needs liver metastases; right-sided valves (TR, PS); left-sided → PFO or bronchial primary.
    • Hypercalcaemia → short QT; hypocalcaemia → long QT.

    33.5 Connective Tissue & Inflammatory Arthritis

    Systemic inflammation accelerates atherosclerosis: in RA and SLE, cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death and occurs a decade or more early. Each disease also has a signature cardiac lesion that the board loves.

    BOARD PEARL — NEONATAL LUPUS

    A fetus with bradycardia at 18–24 weeks in a mother with anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (often asymptomatic, or with Sjögren/SLE) has congenital complete heart block — it is irreversible, with substantial mortality and most survivors needing a pacemaker. Hydroxychloroquine in anti-Ro-positive pregnancies reduces recurrence (~18% risk after an affected child).

    33.6 Vasculitides — Takayasu, GCA, Kawasaki & Others

    Late thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection

    Diagnosis MRA/CTA/PET: wall thickening, stenoses, aneurysms High ESR/CRP; temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) or biopsy; PET/CT for aorta

    • Treatment Steroids + steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate,
    • tocilizumab, anti-TNF); revascularise in the
    • quiescent phase — surgical bypass more durable
    • than stenting
    • High-dose steroids immediately (don't wait
    • for biopsy); tocilizumab reduces relapse and
    • steroid exposure; periodic aortic imaging
    EXAM TRAP — BP IN TAKAYASU

    Bilateral subclavian stenosis makes arm cuff pressures falsely low — hypertension from renal artery stenosis or coarctation-like aortic narrowing is missed. Measure leg pressures, and remember that "normal" arm BP with an aortic bruit and renal impairment is a Takayasu clue.

    Kawasaki disease

    Acute medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood (usually < 5 years) and the commonest cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries.

    Key highlightsConnective tissue disease

    • SLE: pericarditis commonest; Libman–Sacks (mitral) linked with APS; premature CAD.
    • APS: warfarin, not DOACs (especially triple-positive).
    • RA: CV risk ~1.5–2×; EULAR multiplier 1.5; pericardial effusion common.
    • Systemic sclerosis: myocardial fibrosis, conduction disease, PAH (~8–12%) — screen annually.
    • Ankylosing spondylitis: AR + AV block (HLA-B27).
    • Anti-Ro → congenital complete heart block, irreversible.
    • Element Details
    • Classic diagnosis Fever ≥ 5 days plus ≥ 4 of 5:
    • Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection
    • Oral changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue)
    • Polymorphous rash
    • Extremity changes (erythema/oedema → periungual desquamation in week 2–3)
    • Cervical lymphadenopathy ≥ 1.5 cm, usually unilateral
    • Incomplete KD Fever ≥ 5 days with 2–3 criteria + supportive labs (CRP, albumin, anaemia, ALT, platelets after day 7, WBC, urine WBC) or echo findings — common in infants
    • Coronary aneurysm risk ~25% untreated; ~4% with timely IVIG
    • Treatment IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion, ideally within 10 days of fever onset; aspirin (moderate/high dose acutely, then low dose 3–5 mg/kg/day until coronaries normal at 4–6 weeks); IVIG resistance → second IVIG, steroids, infliximab
    • Aneurysm size (Zscore)Small 2.5–< 5; medium 5–< 10; giant ≥ 10 or ≥ 8 mm
    • Giant aneurysm Low-dose aspirin plus anticoagulation (warfarin or LMWH); lifelong surveillance for stenosis/ thrombosis; adult presentation as MI
    DON'T CONFUSE — OTHER VASCULITIDES WITH CARDIAC CLUES
    • Polyarteritis
    • nodosa
    • Medium vessels, HBV association, ANCA-negative, coronary arteritis/aneurysms, renovascular hypertension; lungs spared
    • EGPA (Churg–
    • Strauss)
    • Asthma + eosinophilia; MPO-ANCA in ~40%; cardiac involvement is the main cause of death

    (eosinophilic myocarditis, endomyocardial fibrosis, pericarditis) — more common in ANCAnegative disease GPA (Wegener) PR3-ANCA; cardiac involvement uncommon (pericarditis, coronary arteritis, valve lesions) Behçet disease Venous thrombosis, pulmonary artery aneurysms, RV thrombus, aortic aneurysm; immunosuppression is the mainstay

    MIS-C Post-SARS-CoV-2 in children: shock, LV dysfunction, coronary dilatation — IVIG + steroids

    Key highlightsVasculitides

    • Takayasu: woman < 40, arm BP difference > 10 mmHg, renovascular hypertension, AR; revascularise when quiescent.
    • GCA: > 50, visual loss risk → steroids at once; late thoracic aneurysm; tocilizumab steroid-sparing.
    • Kawasaki: fever ≥ 5 days + ≥ 4/5 criteria; IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days + aspirin.
    • Kawasaki aneurysms: ~25% untreated → ~4% treated; giant (Z ≥ 10 or ≥ 8 mm) → add anticoagulation.
    • EGPA: cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death.
    • Behçet: pulmonary artery aneurysms and intracardiac thrombus.

    33.7 Neuromuscular Disorders

    Skeletal-muscle weakness masks cardiac symptoms, so cardiac disease is detected by scheduled surveillance (ECG, Holter, echo/CMR) rather than by complaint. Two patterns dominate: cardiomyopathy (dystrophinopathies, Friedreich) and conduction disease/sudden death (myotonic dystrophy, laminopathies).

    BOARD PEARL — MYOTONIC DYSTROPHY CLINICAL PICTURE

    Frontal balding, ptosis, hatchet face, grip myotonia (cannot release a handshake), early cataracts, diabetes, hypersomnolence — with a PR interval of 250 ms and QRS 130 ms. The next step is an EP study (HV interval), not reassurance: sudden death from AV block or VT is the major cardiac risk. These patients are also highly sensitive to anaesthetic agents and sedatives.

    Key highlightsNeuromuscular disorders

    • Duchenne: posterobasal/lateral LV fibrosis → tall R V1 + lateral Q waves; ACEi by ~age 10.
    • DMD surveillance: at diagnosis, every 2 y to 10, then yearly; CMR detects early LGE.
    • Becker: cardiomyopathy can outpace skeletal disease; carriers need screening.
    • Myotonic dystrophy: conduction disease + SCD; PR ≥ 240 / QRS ≥ 120 ms → EPS; HV ≥ 70 ms → pace.
    • Friedreich ataxia: concentric LVH (HCM-like) → DCM; TWI on ECG; cardiac death commonest.
    • LMNA / Emery–Dreifuss: prefer ICD over PPM.
    • Domain Findings
    • Diagnosis Serology with two different methods (IgG ELISA, IFA); PCR in acute/congenital/reactivation Prognosis Rassi score (NYHA, cardiomegaly, WMA, NSVT, low QRS voltage, male sex); LGE extent Treatment Antiparasitic benznidazole/nifurtimox: acute, congenital, children, reactivation, and chronic disease without advanced cardiomyopathy (BENEFIT: no benefit in established
    • cardiomyopathy)
    • GDMT for HF; amiodarone for VA (IIa C); ablation for recurrent SMVT (IIa C); anticoagulation for aneurysm with thrombus or embolism
    • Chronic kidney disease
    • CV disease is the leading cause of death in CKD; risk rises as eGFR falls and albuminuria increases.
    • Patients with advanced CKD are more likely to die of CVD than to reach dialysis.
    • Distinctive pathology: medial arterial calcification, LVH (volume/pressure load, anaemia, AV fistula), valve/annular calcification (accelerated AS), sudden death (in dialysis patients, arrhythmic/SCD is a major share of cardiac deaths).
    • Troponin is chronically elevated in CKD — diagnose MI from a rise and/or fall, not a single value.
    • Lipids: statin ± ezetimibe benefits non-dialysis CKD (SHARP); starting a statin in established haemodialysis did not reduce events (4D, AURORA) — but continue if already on one.
    • SGLT2 inhibitors reduce kidney and CV events in CKD with or without diabetes (DAPA-CKD, EMPAKIDNEY).

    33.8 HIV, Chagas Disease & Chronic Kidney Disease

    HIV infection

    With effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), the cardiac picture has shifted from opportunistic myocarditis and effusions to atherosclerotic disease in an ageing population.

    Myocardial disease HIV cardiomyopathy (low CD4, uncontrolled viraemia), myocardial fibrosis, HFpEF Pericardium Effusion (marker of advanced disease); tuberculous pericarditis in endemic areas Pulmonary hypertension HIV-associated PAH (~0.5%) — group 1

    Other Endocarditis (injection drug use), cardiac lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, QT prolongation (some ART)

    Chagas disease

    Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by the triatomine ("kissing") bug; also transfusion, transplant, congenital and oral routes. Commonest cause of non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy in Latin America; seen worldwide through migration.

    Acute phase: usually mild; acute myocarditis in < 1–5%; Romaña sign (unilateral eyelid oedema). Indeterminate phase: seropositive, normal ECG and heart — lifelong for most.

    Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy develops in ~20–30% after 10–30 years.

    Uraemic pericarditis
    • Before or within 8 weeks of starting dialysis;
    • often no ECG ST elevation (no epicardial
    • inflammation)
    • Treatment: intensify dialysis (heparin-free if
    • haemorrhagic effusion)
    Dialysis-associated pericarditis
    • After ≥ 8 weeks on dialysis — inadequate
    • dialysis/volume overload
    • Intensify dialysis; NSAIDs/colchicine less
    • effective and colchicine needs dose caution;
    • drainage for tamponade
    EXAM TRAP — HYPERKALAEMIA ON THE ECG

    Sequence with rising K⁺: peaked T waves → PR prolongation, P flattening → QRS widening → sine-wave → VF/asystole. The first step with ECG changes is IV calcium (membrane stabilisation; no effect on K⁺), then insulin–glucose, β₂-agonist, then removal (binders, dialysis).

    Key highlightsHIV, Chagas & CKD

    • HIV: ASCVD risk ~1.5–2×; pitavastatin 4 mg (REPRIEVE) ↓MACE ~35%; avoid simvastatin/lovastatin with ritonavir/cobicistat.
    • Chagas: RBBB + LAFB, apical aneurysm, thromboembolism; SCD commonest death.
    • Chagas chronic cardiomyopathy in ~20–30% after 10–30 y; benznidazole not effective in established cardiomyopathy (BENEFIT).
    • CKD: troponin chronically high — look for dynamic change.
    • Statin not started de novo in haemodialysis (4D, AURORA); statin/ezetimibe helps non-dialysis CKD (SHARP).
    • Uraemic pericarditis: often no ST elevation; treat with intensive dialysis.
    • Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes → IV calcium first.

    33.9 Self-Assessment

    Q1 A 21-year-old white male rower has a septal thickness of 14 mm, posterior wall 13 mm, LVEDD 58 mm, normal e′ and no SAM. ECG shows voltage LVH only. Peak VO₂ is 62 mL/kg/min. Which feature most strongly supports athlete's heart?

    Answer B In the grey zone (13–16 mm), an enlarged cavity (LVEDD > 54 mm) with normal or supranormal diastolic function favours physiological remodelling; high peak VO₂ supports it. Wall thickness alone cannot decide; voltage LVH is a normal athlete finding and does not discriminate.

    Q2 A 19-year-old white footballer has a screening ECG with T-wave inversion of 2 mm in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Echo is normal. What is the next step?

    Answer C Lateral TWI is abnormal by the International Criteria and may precede overt HCM; CMR is required even if echo is normal, with serial follow-up. It is not a training effect; angiography is not the first test; disqualification requires a diagnosis.

    Q3 Which ECG finding in a 24-year-old asymptomatic athlete requires no further evaluation when present in isolation?

    Answer C Left axis deviation is a borderline finding — investigate only if ≥ 2 borderline findings coexist. LBBB, Mobitz II, QTc ≥ 470 ms (men) and epsilon waves are abnormal and always need work-up.

    Q4 A 23-year-old woman with a PKP2 variant, no phenotype on ECG, echo or CMR, asks about competitive running. According to ESC 2020, what is recommended?

    Answer B ESC 2020: high-intensity recreational or any competitive sport is not recommended in ACM, including genotypepositive/phenotype-negative (III B) — endurance exercise accelerates penetrance, especially in PKP2. An ICD is never a substitute for restriction.

    Q5 A 45-year-old man with episodic headache, sweating and BP 210/120 mmHg has markedly raised plasma metanephrines and a 4-cm adrenal mass. What is the correct pre-operative preparation?

    Answer C α-blockade for 7–14 days first; β-blocker only after adequate α-blockade (unopposed α-constriction causes crisis). Labetalol alone is insufficient; operating without preparation risks intraoperative crisis.

    Q6 A 60-year-old man with flushing, diarrhoea and hepatic metastases from an ileal neuroendocrine tumour has a raised JVP with large v waves and a pulsatile liver. Which echo finding is most likely?

    Answer B Carcinoid heart disease (serotonin reaches the right heart because liver metastases bypass hepatic inactivation) causes fixed, retracted tricuspid (and pulmonary) leaflets — severe TR. Left-sided lesions imply a shunt or bronchial primary.

    Q7 A 28-year-old woman has left arm claudication, a BP of 100/60 left vs 135/80 mmHg right, a subclavian bruit, and raised CRP. What is the most likely diagnosis?

    Answer B Young woman, inter-arm BP difference > 10 mmHg, subclavian bruit and inflammation = Takayasu. GCA occurs after 50. Coarctation gives arm–leg, not arm–arm, differences (unless the left subclavian arises beyond it).

    Q8 A 3-year-old has 6 days of fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a polymorphous rash and swollen hands. What is the most appropriate treatment?

    Answer B Complete Kawasaki disease (fever ≥ 5 days + 4 criteria). IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days with aspirin cuts aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~4%. Antibiotics and aspirin alone do not prevent aneurysms.

    Q9 A 34-year-old man with myotonic dystrophy type 1 is asymptomatic. ECG shows PR 260 ms and QRS 128 ms. What is the best next step?

    Answer B In DM1, PR ≥ 240 ms or QRS ≥ 120 ms marks high risk of AV block/SCD; an EP study guides pacing (HV ≥ 70 ms → pacemaker). Reassurance ignores the leading cardiac cause of death; amiodarone is not indicated.

    Q10 A 52-year-old Bolivian-born man living in Europe has palpitations. ECG shows RBBB with left anterior fascicular block; echo reveals an apical aneurysm with a small thrombus; coronaries are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

    Answer B RBBB + LAFB and an apical aneurysm with thrombus and normal coronaries in a Latin American migrant is classic chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy — confirm with two serological tests. Sarcoid favours basal septum; Takotsubo is transient; old MI requires coronary disease.
